A sample of "low-fat dairy whitener" manufactured by Nestle India, drawn from the premises of Hotel Lalit in Connaught Place in the national capital, has been found "unsafe and substandard," the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said on Saturday (October 3, 2026).
In a post on social media, the food regulator said the sample was collected from the premises of Bharat Hotels Ltd (The Lalit), Connaught Place, New Delhi.
According to the FSSAI, the report of the food analyst’s laboratory declared the product “substandard” and “unsafe,” indicating non-compliance under the Food Safety and Standards (FSS) Act, 2006.
A copy of the laboratory analysis report was provided to the food business operator (FBO) for reference and necessary action, the regulator said. A notice has also been issued to Bharat Hotels Ltd over the non-compliant product.
The FBO was given an opportunity to appeal against the food analyst's report under the relevant section of the FSS Act, 2006, within the prescribed period. The FBO has also been directed to immediately stop the sale of the identified unsafe food product, the FSSAI added.

Delhi cash collector stages Rs 30 lakh fake robbery, arrested with associate
A Delhi cash collection employee allegedly faked a Rs 30 lakh robbery after finishing his rounds. CCTV checks and route verification exposed the plot, leading to both arrests and full recovery.
A 24-year-old cash collection employee in Delhi allegedly staged a fake robbery of Rs 30 lakh collected for his employer, but the plan unravelled after CCTV footage and other evidence did not match his version, police said on Saturday.
Police said the employee, Parveen Malhotra, and his alleged associate, Parveen alias Prem, have been arrested. The entire Rs 30 lakh has been recovered, along with the cash bag and the motorcycle used in the incident.
According to police, Malhotra worked as a cash collection employee at Madan Lal Plastic in Tikri Kalan. On October 1, he had collected Rs 30 lakh from three locations on his employer’s instructions.
While returning on his motorcycle, he allegedly told police that three men on a black motorcycle stopped him near Zakhira Flyover, snatched his cash bag and injured him in the chest with a blade.
A PCR call about the alleged robbery was received at Moti Nagar police station on October 2, after which a police team reached the spot and recorded Malhotra’s statement. A case was registered. During the investigation, police found discrepancies in his account.
They said his shirt did not have a matching cut despite the alleged chest injury, and CCTV footage from the location and time mentioned by him did not support his claim.
Police said further checks on his route and inconsistencies in his statements raised suspicion, after which he was questioned in detail. During interrogation, Malhotra allegedly told police that he had planned the robbery to keep the Rs 30 lakh.
He handed over the cash bag to his friend Prem at Keshav Puram Metro Station before injuring himself with a razor blade. He also allegedly damaged and threw away his mobile phone near Peeragarhi Metro Station to destroy evidence, police said.
Acting on the information provided by him, police raided Prem’s house in Bahadurgarh, Haryana, and recovered the entire Rs 30 lakh.
The motorcycle allegedly used by Malhotra was also recovered, police said. Malhotra, a resident of Paschim Vihar and originally from Alwar in Rajasthan, is 24, while Prem, 23, lives in Bahadurgarh and is alleged to be his associate. Further investigation is underway.
Police said the case began as a robbery complaint but the investigation later found that the alleged victim himself had planned it with the help of an associate, leading to the recovery of the full amount and the arrest of both men.

My family has spent four summers participating in demand response programs whereby utility companies pay customers to reduce energy use on the hottest summer days. Most summers have involved carefully precooling our New York City apartment before switching off the air conditioners and sweating it out during the designated demand response periods.
But this year, we kept our window air conditioners running throughout a heat dome event that drove daytime temperatures into the triple digits and made the nights oppressively hot. The difference was that we powered the air conditioners through two household batteries tucked away unobtrusively in the corners of our living room and bedroom.
We were among about 1,000 New York City households that took part in a free and growing program offered by the local startup Every Electric. The company’s proposition is simple: Get one or more batteries delivered to your home, plug the batteries into a standard wall electrical outlet, and then plug your window air conditioners into the batteries. Households can keep running air conditioners as usual during peak demand periods while also earning money through the local demand response program with the utility company Con Edison.
“Being able to make air conditioners drop off the grid without actually impacting the comfort of residents was really awesome to see,” said Andrew Wang, co-founder and CEO of Every Electric, in an interview with Ars.
Wang and cofounder Richard May first met while working together as postdoctoral researchers at the Columbia Electrochemical Energy Center at Columbia University in New York City. In 2023, they launched the startup under the name Standard Potential Co., with a focus on developing sodium-ion battery chemistry for commercialization.
But they soon pivoted to a very different business plan—deploying residential batteries across New York City households to create a network of energy storage resources acting as a virtual power plant. The company officially rebranded as Every Electric in 2026.

For years, Subway felt like the only relevant sandwich chain. Its 2008 "five, five dollar, five dollar footlong" jingle still lives in my head.
The Connecticut-founded fast-food giant operates over 35,000 restaurants worldwide, with the most recent 2025 industry data estimating an annual $9.2 billion in United States system-wide sales.
Subway remains the largest sandwich chain in the US, both in location count and estimated sales — but size isn't the whole picture.
Its US footprint has fallen from more than 27,000 locations in 2015 to fewer than 19,000 today, with more than 700 closures in 2025 alone. Subway's domestic location count has declined every year since its 2015 peak (though it has seen international growth).
In April 2024, Subway was sold to Roark Capital — a private equity firm that also has a large stake in sandwich-chain competitor Jimmy John's — for a reported $9.6 billion.
Meanwhile, Jersey Mike's made headlines in July 2026 after announcing plans to go public. It hit the New York Stock Exchange with a $1 billion IPO, one of the largest restaurant-sector debuts in recent years.
The New Jersey-founded sandwich chain now operates more than 3,300 locations across the US and Canada. Earlier this year, the chain also announced plans to expand into Europe by opening hundreds of locations across the UK and Ireland. By comparison, in 2015, it had just over 1,000 total locations.
Jersey Mike's financials track with its physical growth. In 2025, it posted more than $4 billion in US system-wide sales, a major feat for a chain that has far fewer locations than Subway yet has become one of its top competitors.
With all the buzz, I wanted to see which chain actually had better-tasting sandwiches and offered more value to customers.
To do so, I ordered a similar cold club sandwich, hot Philly cheesesteak, and chocolate-chip cookie at each, sticking to the chain's regular size and default preparations.
Here's how they stacked up.
I started at Jersey Mike's, a chain I'd never tried.
Walking in, the first thing I noticed was a wall decal that read, "It's not a real Jersey Mike's Sub without 'the juice,'" which I learned is a blend of oil and red-wine vinegar. It's one of the chain's specialties.
The "Mike's Way" preparation is another signature touch: finishing sandwiches with lettuce, onion, tomato, and "the juice."
Fans of the chain also tout its hearty portions and freshly sliced meats and cheeses. Customers can watch staff slice cold cuts with the large metal tools right behind the counter.
Then I went to Subway, where I'd eaten a handful of times.
I hadn't been to Subway since college, so I forgot the chain is basically a design-your-own sandwich bar.
The customization aspect is a major highlight, with rows of metal containers filled with veggies, meats, dressings, and cheeses.
Subway is also known for its freshly baked bread and offers multiple varieties to choose from — hence why the stores always smell divine.
Jersey Mike's menu seemed to cater to sandwich lovers.
Don't get me wrong, Jersey Mike's menu had plenty of subs and cheesesteaks — especially the latter, with unique flavors like bacon ranch and Buffalo chicken.
But for anything beyond a sandwich, or a sandwich-turned-bowl-or-wrap, you may want to look elsewhere.
My total at Jersey Mike's came to $22.70
I ordered a 7-inch Club Sub prepared Mike's Way (the default for cold sandwiches), a 7-inch Mike's Famous Philly, and a chocolate-chip cookie for $10.80, $10.40, and $1.50, respectively.
My total came to $22.70 before tax.
Subway's menu seemed more extensive.
In addition to subs and cheesesteaks, Subway offered pizza, nachos, and breakfast sandwiches, plus lighter and more health-forward options like salads, bowls, and protein pockets.
Salads usually call my name, but this time, I was on a mission.
My total at Subway came to $17.97.
To match my Jersey Mike's meal, I picked a 6-inch American Club Sub, a 6-inch Steak Philly, and a chocolate-chip cookie.
Each sandwich cost $8.49 and the cookie $0.99, so I paid $17.97 total before tax.
Mike's Club Sub looked incredible off the bat — and the taste followed suit.
Unrolling the oil-and-vinegar-stained paper, I held a bulky sandwich loaded with provolone cheese, ham, turkey, onion, lettuce, tomato, and bacon. The bread, slathered in mayonnaise, oil, vinegar, and oregano, felt pillowy with a crusty edge.
Beautiful, yes, but I was skeptical about a wet sandwich. After taking a bite, however, I officially understood the hype. "The juice" gave the bread some tang, and miraculously, it didn't make it soggy.
Better yet, the cheese was creamy and the deli meat relatively moist. Slices seemed individually stacked, not stuck together, so I could tell they were freshly cut.
Perhaps the best part was the equal proportions of ingredients, or the oregano that rounded out the flavors.
Unfortunately, the lettuce hung limp from "the juice," but given all the pros, I could forgive it.
Subway's All-American Club also impressed me, though it had a few drawbacks.
Following Jersey Mike's heaping sandwich almost felt unfair, but Subway's All-American Club held its own — for the most part. It contained the same ingredients, minus the oil, vinegar, and spices; instead of provolone cheese, it had American.
Subway's club sandwich had a smoky flavor, thanks to the ham and bacon. I appreciated the crunch from the bacon, onions, and lettuce, as well as the generous amount of American cheese.
However, the bread wasn't as soft as I'd expected, given Subway's reputation. In fact, it almost felt stale.
The turkey also missed the mark for me. I uncovered two thin slices, and they had little flavor and a dry texture. The ham had more taste, but it wasn't juicy, either.
My other qualm: The chain went way overboard on the mayonnaise.
Personally, I didn't understand the "famous" element of Mike's Famous Cheesesteak.
I wrongly assumed the cheesesteak would be as hefty as the club. It wasn't nearly as substantial.
To its credit, the hot sub contained sliced steak, grilled onions, grilled red peppers, and white American cheese, all with outstanding flavor. The steak had a nice tender bite.
It also had a solid meat-to-bread ratio, but the sandwich lost points in my book for the bread itself, which was too crusty. Additionally, I felt it needed another slice of cheese.
In my opinion, Mike's cheesesteak was just OK.
I wouldn't get Subway's cheesesteak again.
Subway's Steak Philly came with steak, American cheese, green peppers, red onions, and mayonnaise.
Now, not everyone will agree, but I didn't enjoy mayo on my cheesesteak — especially since the chain put so much of it. In the future, I'd probably order most of my Subway sandwiches sans mayo.
The raw peppers and onions also didn't work for me.
In this cheesesteak from Subway, the green peppers and red onions were left raw, so they were all I tasted.
With the crunchy veggies and heaping globs of mayo, it felt less like a cheesesteak and more like a steak sandwich. And with almost no cheese, it didn't have the melty element I craved.
A few bites were enough for me.
Jersey Mike's chocolate-chip cookie was soft and satisfying.
A prepackaged cookie didn't pique my interest, but I wanted to end the meal with something sweet. I'm glad I did.
Jersey Mike's chewy cookie had the fudgy, almost underbaked texture I love. Thick and dense with large chocolate pieces, it reminded me of Costco's Kirkland Signature cookies. (If you know, you know.)
However, at 3 ¼ inches and $1.50, it was smaller and pricier than Subway's.
Subway's chocolate-chip cookie was delicious in a different way.
At only $0.99, Subway's 4-inch chocolate-chip cookie proved hard to beat, and I liked that it came from the bakery case rather than a plastic bag.
It had a sweet, buttery flavor and tons of chocolate chips.
The texture was light, delicate, and melt-in-your-mouth soft. It hit the spot for a thinner cookie, especially with its ever-so-crisp edges.
In the end, Jersey Mike's Club Sub won me over.
Even though my club sandwich was pricier at Jersey Mike's versus Subway, it still felt like a better value. And to be fair, I got an extra inch in length at Jersey Mike's, too.
Compared to Subway's club, Jersey Mike's had juicier meat, softer bread, and more balanced proportions. Plus, the Mike's Way preparation gave it a subtle Italian flair that paired nicely with the salted meats.
My winners for Philly cheesesteaks and cookies weren't as clear.
Even though I wasn't the biggest fan of Jersey Mike's Philly cheesesteak, I still enjoyed it more than Subway's. That said, I wouldn't order either again.
The chocolate-chip cookies were a draw for me. Subway's cookie was incredibly tasty, plus it was bigger and less expensive, but I also enjoyed Jersey Mike's. I'd get both again in a heartbeat.
Ultimately, both chains had merits — but Jersey Mike's edged out the competition for sandwiches.
In the end, the so-called "best" depends on your personal taste, your real-time appetite, and what you're willing to pay.
For non-sandwich items, healthier-sounding options, and lower prices, Subway delivered. For sandwiches overall, Jersey Mike's edged out the competition.
In my opinion, Jersey Mike's biggest drawback was its somewhat limited menu — and the messiness of the sandwiches. Since the Club Sub ended up being my favorite, however, I let it slide. It was worth it for "the juice."
When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Subway said, "For over 60 years, Subway has been built on customization. While we offer standard builds, every freshly made sandwich can be tailored to a guest's preferences, from adding extra cheese and protein to swapping veggies and adjusting condiments. We celebrate our guests' individual tastes and encourage them to make each meal their own."
Business Insider reached out to Jersey Mike's for comment.

Unverified social media claims alleging that a female student was raped at Lovely Professional University (LPU) in Phagwara triggered protests on 27 September 2026, which escalated into vandalism, arson, clashes with police, and a nearly 12-hour blockade of NH-44. Police registered a case against an unidentified person but said they found no evidence so far to substantiate the rape allegation, while LPU denied the claim. The university suspended classes for 10 days and postponed examinations. Three FIRs have been registered over the violence, and an eight-member SIT is investigating the arson and other offences, with police saying they have identified suspects and gathered leads. Internet services have since resumed (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here and here) with the claim that it shows a Punjab Police officer allegedly stating that the incident at Lovely Professional University (LPU) was committed by a BJP worker and the nephew of Union Home Minister Amit Shah. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a Punjab Police officer saying the accused in the LPU case is a BJP worker and Amit Shah’s nephew.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. The original footage shows Phagwara SP Major Singh discussing the LPU rape allegations and stating that the police had not received any complaint. He does not say that the accused is a BJP worker or Amit Shah’s nephew. AI detection tools indicated that the audio was likely manipulated, and PIB Fact Check also confirmed that the video was digitally altered using AI technology. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A Google search using relevant keywords found no credible reports confirming that a Punjab Police officer said the accused in the LPU case is a BJP worker and Amit Shah’s nephew.
A close review of the viral video showed a Crime Tak watermark. A keyword search led us to the original video published on Crime Tak’s YouTube channel on 27 September 2026, featuring Phagwara SP Major Singh. The viral clip, from 09 to 27 seconds, contains statements about a student’s death and the rape allegations at LPU. However, these statements differ from the original footage, which shows Singh saying that the police had not received any complaint regarding rape and were ready to investigate if details were provided. We also noticed distortion around his face, as well as differences in his voice and manner of speech. The original video contains no statement linking the accused to the BJP or the Union Home Minister.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. This suggests that the original footage was paired with fabricated audio to make it appear that a Punjab Police officer said the accused in the LPU case is a BJP worker and Amit Shah’s nephew. This suggests that the original footage was paired with fabricated audio to make it appear that a Punjab Police officer said the accused in the LPU case is a BJP worker and Amit Shah’s nephew.
PIB Fact Check, in an X post on 28 September 2026, also debunked the claim, stating that the video is digitally manipulated and fake, with AI technology used to alter the content and create a misleading impression.
To sum up, this viral video allegedly shows a Punjab Police officer stating that the LPU accused is a BJP worker and Amit Shah’s nephew is AI-manipulated.

London – Never has so much cash flowed into a new technology as is pouring into AI, eclipsing the sums splurged on railways or the internet when those technological revolutions sucked in capital.
Cumulative spending globally on data centers alone could top $30 trillion by 2050, according to a projection by PwC, almost matching the value of outstanding U.S. Treasuries. It “dwarfs” what was spent in the railroad or dotcom booms, even after adjusting for inflation, PwC said.
Meanwhile, Anthropic, just one of the major firms in the AI race, plans to spend $518 billion in coming years, according to the IPO prospectus, which is more than 100 times its 2025 revenue. Its backers say AI technology will be more transformational than the advent of steam engines and the industrialization they powered.

Salem District Collector K. Elambahavath stated on Saturday, (October 3, 2026) that, ahead of the Deepavali festival, ₹4.42 crore has been set as the sales target for the Co-optex outlets.
The Collector inaugurated the Deepavali special discount sale at Salem Co-optex Thangam Pattu Maligai at First Agraharam.
Speaking to the reporters, the Collector said the State government has been providing special discounts of up to 30%, for the past 91 years, during festive seasons to uplift handloom weavers and provide continuous employment opportunities.
This year, for Deepavali, new designs of Kanchipuram silk saris with original lace, Arani silk saris, Salem silk saris, Thirubhuvanam silk saris, and new designs of soft silk saris are up for sale. Likewise, all types of cotton saris made in the Coimbatore, Madurai, Dindigul, Paramakudi, Tiruchi, and Salem areas, as well as Kalamkari cotton saris in elegant colours, have been kept for sale, the Collector added.
Stating that Co-optex also has a wide range of bedspreads, dhotis, lungis, towels, and cotton shirts, the Collector said that Co-optex’s export products such as aprons, kurtas, mattresses, gloves, screen fabrics, bedspreads with pillow cases, and printed bedspreads have been very popular among customers.
A sales target of ₹4.42 crore has been set for Co-optex outlets in the Salem district for Deepavali, of which ₹4.08 crore is allotted to the Salem co-optex Thangam Pattu Maligai outlet, and ₹34 lakh for the Attur Co-optex outlet. this year as well, the Tamil Nadu government is offering a special 30% discount on handloom varieties until November 30. During this period, the sales centres will be open on all holidays for the benefit of the customers, the Collector added.

India’s winter crops face risks as El Nino strengthens, soil moisture stays low
A deficient monsoon, depleted soil moisture and strengthening El Nino are raising risks for India’s winter crops, water availability and food supply.
Farmers are preparing for the winter cropping season, but India is entering a period of uncertainty as depleted soil moisture and a strengthening El Nino raise the risk of delayed sowing, lower acreage and weaker yields, while also putting pressure on water availability and food supplies.
The concern comes after the southwest monsoon ended with rainfall 12.6% below normal, making it the fourth-lowest monsoon rainfall since 2001. East and northeast India recorded a 25% deficit, while south peninsular India was 24% below normal, leaving several farming regions with limited moisture as the winter crop season approaches.
“The deficient southwest monsoon of 2026, closed with a 13% below the long-period average and 21% below last year, has left large tracts of the country with inadequate soil moisture,” founder of HnyB Tech-Incubations Pvt. Ltd Deepak Pareek said. “Combined with the prospect of a dry October under a strengthening El Nino, [this] spells serious trouble for rabi sowing and overall crop prospects.”
El Nino is the periodic warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean that can disrupt global weather patterns. Several global weather models, as well as the India Meteorological Department (IMD) in its latest forecast, have indicated that the phenomenon is strengthening and is expected to become very strong towards the end of this year, in November, when most of India sows its crops.
Soil moisture runs low as rabi sowing season nears
Rabi crops are sown after the southwest monsoon recedes, making the moisture accumulated during the monsoon crucial for planting. A Crisil Economics assessment said soil moisture levels as of August 20 were below the decadal average in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, northern Jharkhand, Bihar, Punjab, western Gujarat and parts of the northeast.
The IMD’s district-level data showed that 32% of districts were in the deficient rainfall category in September and another 16% in the large-deficient category.
High temperatures are also worsening the moisture stress. India’s average maximum temperature in September was 32.05°C, the highest for the month since 1901. The mean temperature of 27.72°C was the fifth-highest. According to the Indian weather bureau, October is also expected to see above-normal maximum and minimum temperatures across most of the country.
“Residual moisture is under strain in key rainfed belts of central, southern peninsula and east and northeast India,” Pareek said. This is particularly important for rainfed farmers, who have limited ability to compensate for a dry spell through irrigation.
Wheat has water cover, but gram and jowar face bigger risks
The rabi season accounts for roughly half of India’s foodgrain production. Wheat accounts for about 70% of rabi output, while rice, coarse cereals and pulses contribute roughly 10% each, according to a Crisil assessment.
More than 60% of India’s pulses production, largely gram, comes from the rabi season, while nearly 70% of jowar is grown during the season. Wheat has a relatively large irrigation buffer. More than 95% of wheat acreage is irrigated, compared with about 52% for gram and 25% for jowar.
That makes gram in Rajasthan and jowar in Karnataka and Maharashtra particularly vulnerable to inadequate soil moisture.
The impact will therefore not be uniform. Irrigated farmers may be able to maintain sowing by using groundwater and canals, while rainfed farmers could delay planting, reduce acreage or shift crops depending on water availability, Crisil noted.
Reservoirs offer a buffer, but water reserves are thinning
Meanwhile, the backup for rabi sowing—reservoirs—is already under pressure. As of October 1, storage in 178 major reservoirs was 1% below the long-period average and more than 20% lower than the same period last year.
Former agriculture secretary Devesh Choudhary said reservoir levels have so far held up to some extent because last year’s surplus rainfall helped maintain storage. “But this is not the same for several states, especially in the southern region where rabi crops will suffer,” he said.
The southern region faces the sharpest gap, with reservoirs holding 27.46 billion cubic metres, or 49.2% of live capacity, against 87.8% a year ago. Northern storage is at 60.5% of capacity, compared with 91% last year, while western reservoirs are at 84% against 97.1%. Central storage stands at 88%, down from 92.7%, and eastern storage at 82.7%, compared with 79% last year.
Reservoir levels are especially low in key rabi-producing states including Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan and Karnataka.
Maharashtra is the country’s largest producer of gram and jowar. Rajasthan is also a major producer of both gram and mustard. Karnataka is the second-largest producer of jowar, and Andhra Pradesh and Telangana grow maize and pulses in rabi.
With less water available for irrigation, farmers in these states may be forced to delay or reduce rabi sowing, while crops that do get planted are likely to face higher irrigation costs and lower productivity, said Choudhary**.**
He added that India would depend on western disturbances bringing winter rain and lower temperatures in the north for a good crop.
Drought footprint adds to the pressure
Even the latest drought assessment points to widespread moisture stress. Drought conditions, ranging from abnormally dry to more severe categories (D0+), covered 47.4% of the country’s area. States with the largest share of their area under any drought category included Goa at 100%, Arunachal Pradesh at 87.8%, Assam at 84.9%, Mizoram at 83.8%, Maharashtra at 82.4% and Sikkim at 81.8%.
Regionally, drought covered about 78% of the West, 74% of the Northeast, 52% of the South, 42% of the Northwest, 40% of the North, 32% of the East and 29% of Central India, according to the assessment.
El Nino clouds the rabi outlook
The immediate weather outlook is already pointing to a difficult start.
The IMD expects October rainfall to be below 85% of the long-period average for India as a whole. It expects below-normal rainfall over most parts of the country during October-December.
If the weather pattern produces a prolonged dry spell, farmers in rainfed areas could struggle to establish crops. Higher temperatures would further reduce available soil moisture, while inadequate winter rainfall could subsequently affect crop growth and productivity.
The government is also wary of what is to come. In a two-day rabi conference in Delhi held this week, agriculture secretary Atish Chandra said the coming rabi season is likely to be challenging for rainfed areas because of the El Nino weather pattern and that foodgrain production could be affected.
Agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh need crop plans based on water availability and soil moisture, with separate strategies for rainfed and irrigated areas. He also said delayed sowing could affect germination and productivity, making advance preparation essential.
The government has asked states and districts to first assess water availability and soil moisture, and then choose crops accordingly. In water-stressed areas, the government has called for less water-intensive crops such as pulses and oilseeds rather than wheat**, which** could run short of irrigation later.
According to Chouhan, the government is also preparing state-specific rabi plans, including drought-resistant crop strategies for Maharashtra and Karnataka, while states with better water availability—such as Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and West Bengal—may be asked to pursue more intensive production.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

As an Indian woman, I often feel myself oscillating between states of anxiety or anger. The anxiety is about doing the mental maths of how to stay safe – thinking about what I’m wearing, where I am going and how I’ll get there, and so on. The anger is at the sheer absurdity of this, and the stories of of sexual violence and harassment I read about every day. I am not the only one.
Last week, two particularly enraging incidents captured national attention. First, a video showing a group of men accused of harassing and molesting two teenagers at night in Bihar’s Jamui went viral. Then, a 17-year-old, out with a friend in Delhi, was allegedly gang-raped in a park by men posing as police. After, women in Bihar told Outlook how the incident in Jamui triggers greater controls and pressure on them. In Delhi, authorities curbed access to public parks and a premier women’s college, Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), briefly moved classes online.
I have noticed this pattern repeatedly: after incidents of sexual violence go viral on social media, the fallout further ensnares women. We are the ones who get told to avoid certain places, regulate our behaviour, dress modestly or be home earlier, thereby placing the burden of escaping this menace on us. Feminist activist Kavita Krishnan has described this phenomenon as “perhaps the most widespread form of gender-based violence in India”.
Instead of figuring out why sexual violence remains entrenched in our society, how patriarchal agency perpetuates such violence or what kind of social conditioning is needed for men, women are instead expected to take up less public space. (It is another matter that women might not be safe even inside their own homes.)
Regulating women is easy because “it does not require any institutional cost and, most of all, it sends the signal to concerned parents that the problem is being handled”, says Meena Kandasamy, a feminist author, whose latest novel, Fieldwork As a Sex Object, is about a woman’s life being upturned when a deepfake video using her face goes viral. “Their target audience is not the young women who feel unsafe but the rest of society.”
In my experience, this repression happens at three levels: first in the realm of family, then in broader society, and ultimately by the state. It begins at home, under the guise of protection, with arbitrary curfews or dress codes. It gets reinforced at a community level with institutions and social groups through moral policing, victim-blaming and the expectation that women should not put themselves in “unsafe” situations.
Then there is the response of the state. Restricting access to parks after sunset can surely reduce the number of people in those places, but it doesn’t address why women are unsafe there. Harassment and sexual violence are, unfortunately, not tied to timings or daylight. And further restricting women’s lives is not the solution to injustices foisted on them. All three, Kandasamy says, consider women as a “problem to be handled”.
“She’s not a citizen (for the state), a member (for the community), or an adult (for the family). She is treated like an inanimate but precious object – like a diamond that has to be locked up to prevent theft,” she said.
‘Moral policing’ of the wrong target
Women, however, are pushing back against this approach. In recent days, students from Delhi University have come out on the streets demanding safer public spaces including more street lighting, usable public toilets, more housing and scholarships for female students. Vedayana, 20, a student at Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), says locking up parks is not the solution: “If you are not putting up safety measures to make it accessible to women, then it is as good as saying that the park is only for men.”
The scale of the issue is devastatingly clear. A recently published survey of more than 4,000 women in New Delhi and Bengaluru, found that 65% of women in New Delhi and 29% in Bengaluru experienced harassment in public spaces in the past year.
Another 2024 study from India and Pakistan found that women’s overall mobility remains abysmally low, and what freedom they do have is almost entirely tied to education, employment or unpaid care work. Substantive mobility for leisure or pleasure is practically nonexistent.
Despite how widespread and urgent the problem is, the political response can further shake public confidence. A female minister from Bihar, commenting on the molestation video said: “Moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion.” Another minister from the state drew fire for describing it as an “isolated” incident”.
Minimising crimes against women reflects a political culture in which accountability becomes optional. Students such as Vedayana want this to change. Political parties, she tells me, should pledge to not give tickets or positions to anyone accused of sexual harassment. “We don’t want the leaders sitting at the top to perpetrate and preach rape culture,” she adds.
Parliament is not immune to accusations, either: the BJP politician Brij Bhushan Singh, who formerly headed the Wrestling Federation of India, was recently accused of sexual harassment by six female wrestlers – he denies the allegations, and was acquitted by a magistrate, in a case that is undergoing appeal. According to an analysis of 2024 parliamentarians by the Association for Democratic Reforms, 15 winning candidates declared cases related to crimes against women.
For Vedayana, changing the mentality has to begin early with families and the way boys are raised. “If you are in a position of authority, use it to influence people by speaking out against patriarchy and groom your sons first.”
What else we’re reading about
Golden girls | Indian women’s cricket team beat Sri Lanka by 147 runs to win gold at the Asian Games last week. Smriti Mandhana’s smashing 79 off 45 deliveries helped India reach a formidable 216 in 20 overs. Deepti Sharma’s three-wicket haul helped India end Sri Lanka’s hopes with just 69 runs on board. Sri Lanka settled for silver, while Pakistan claimed the bronze after beating Bangladesh.
Moma | A solo exhibition by one of south Asia’s most distinguished artists, Nilima Sheikh, opened at New York’s Museum of Modern Art at the weekend. Fractured Skies, presented in collaboration with the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in Delhi, will run until next June.
EC under fire | An explosive Indian Express investigation has revealed how two of the top three election officials objected at least 14 times over a period of 10 months to changes made by the Election Commission over its controversial exercise that has struck 130 million people from the voter rolls.
Count it
A number worth knowing
105
An inquiry committee probing the theft of donations from Ayodhya’s Ram Temple has uncovered 105 instances of cash being removed or concealed. The thefts were caught on CCTV cameras.
According to a preliminary report, some of the accused allegedly hid the money on themselves during the process of counting donations and then walked out.
Vibe check
Tony Klor’s city vlogs from Indian towns are “hella dope,” to use his own words. The 32-year-old American has visited about 200 cities around the country, taking his Instagram followers to places that rarely feature on a travel itinerary.
It’s a treat to watch him having the time of his life. He marched with Anganwadi workers in Nashik chanting “pay my didis”, ribbed with middle-aged uncles sweating it out in a park, whom he christened “Nizamaddies”. Wandering through the mining town of Ballari, which he describes as “highkey vibey”, he films its temple, church and mosque.
“A lot of people who watch my videos are Indians and they have no idea about these magnificent places in India,” the tech professional-turned-content creator says. “India is like the easiest place to make a friend in the world. People invite me to their weddings on the street that I met five minutes before that. Hospitality is so, so next-level.”

China funding UK research and sending it to Beijing's spies, MI5 warns
- Published
More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China's espionage operations against the UK via a front company working for its intelligence and security services, MI5 has warned.
In the highly unusual public alert, the UK's internal security service warned universities and academics that continuing ties with China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) could ultimately lead to criminal charges for aiding a foreign state.
Security minister Dan Jarvis said MI5's warning exposed attempts by Chinese intelligence agencies to use British academic research to undermine UK national security.
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said the accusation was "imaginary and purely fabricated".
Universities UK, which represents more than 140 institutions, meanwhile said it was reviewing the alert and focusing on "supporting our universities as they assess any implications for existing or future partnerships".
In June, MI5 and its closest partners in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, issued a joint warning that China's military intelligence services were targeting professional networking sites and online job platforms.
This new UK-specific alert goes further, revealing what the service says is a threat that has been growing within British academic institutions.
MI5 says that the CGTRI, sometimes translated as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), has "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS).
"MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage," it says.
"More than 100 UK-linked academics have contributed to projects funded by MSS via CGTRI," adding that in some cases the researches would not be aware of the front company's role in their project.

UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object.
"This activity supports Ministry of State Security espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security," MI5 said.
The security alert said that many academic institutions and individuals will have engaged with the CGTRI "in good faith" because the link back to Chinese state security had been "obfuscated".
It continued: "UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions."
The public alert raises the prospect that British academics who do not act on it immediately could ultimately fall foul of the law.
It stressed that the National Security Act, a key piece of legislation passed in 2023 to counter state espionage, created a new offence of assisting a foreign intelligence service where the individual ought to reasonably have known what they were doing so.
Jarvis said: "This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies."
He said he had now written to all university vice-chancellors to end relationships with the organisation.

Conservative MP Sir Iain Duncan-Smith, co-chair of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, told the BBC that several reports had suggested "British universities' dependence on Chinese students has opened them up to all sorts of problems" and that security checks should be stepped up.
Responding to the alert, Universities UK said universities "take their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously".
"The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes," said chief executive Vivienne Stern, "while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation".
"Close engagement between Government and the higher education sector is vital to ensuring that universities and the country continue to benefit from international collaboration while effectively managing national security risks."
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London hit back - saying it had already made "solemn representations" to the UK.
"The accusations made by the UK intelligence agency against the relevant Chinese entity are imaginary and purely fabricated," they said.
"Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial.
"We urge the UK intelligence authorities to stop spreading falsehoods and stop undermining educational exchanges and research cooperation between China and the UK."

Vijay calls Stalin’s remarks on Sathyabama ‘indecent, perverse’, says TVK will respond
Vijay strongly condemned Stalin's alleged remarks in a post on X, describing the DMK as a “force of evil”.
Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Saturday accused DMK president MK Stalin of making “indecent” and derogatory remarks about TVK's Dharapuram bypoll candidate P Sathyabama, alleging that the DMK leader mocked her physical appearance during an election campaign meeting.
Vijay strongly condemned Stalin's alleged remarks in a post on X, describing the DMK as a “force of evil” and accusing Stalin of speaking about Sathyabama in an indecent manner.
“Under the guise of a by-election campaign public meeting for the Dharapuram constituency, the DMK, a force of evil, through its leader Mr MK Stalin, has conducted a meeting full of slander and indecency,” Vijay said.
“Mr MK Stalin has derived sadistic pleasure by mocking the physical appearance and speaking with utmost indecency about our Dharapuram constituency candidate, sister Mrs Sathyabama,” he added.

What did Stalin say about Sathyabama?
Stalin made the remarks during a campaign meeting in Dharapuram on Friday while seeking votes for DMK candidate S Suganya. According to reports, Stalin referred to Sathyabama as “Petti Bama” and “Palti Bama” while questioning her decision to switch from the AIADMK to the TVK.
TVK leaders have alleged that the remarks amounted to body-shaming and criticised Stalin for targeting a woman candidate during the election campaign.
Vijay alleged that the comments reflected what he described as a broader pattern within the DMK and accused its leaders of making derogatory remarks about women.
“The people of Tamil Nadu have long realised that the DMK members are enemies of democracy, and that obscenity, malice, and perversion are deeply ingrained in their very DNA and mindset,” Vijay said.
He also said voters in Dharapuram would respond to the controversy through the electoral process.
“The people of Tamil Nadu and the voters of Dharapuram constituency are going to teach a fitting lesson to this evil faction, which is expert in speaking obscenely about women,” he said.
Vijay further criticised what he described as repeated comments about women by DMK leaders, saying he was expressing his condemnation as a representative of the women of Tamil Nadu.
“As a son, brother, and younger brother to the women of Tamil Nadu, I express my strong condemnation of the DMK, an evil force that continuously speaks obscenely about women,” he said.

TVK to approach Election Commission
The controversy comes ahead of the October 6 Dharapuram bypoll.
TVK Minister CTR Nirmal Kumar also condemned Stalin's alleged remarks while speaking to reporters at Coimbatore Airport. He alleged that Stalin had made derogatory and body-shaming comments about Sathyabama and said the party would approach the Election Commission over the issue.
“It is condemnable to make such remarks about a Scheduled Caste woman who is actively participating in electoral politics,” Nirmal Kumar said, while demanding that Stalin publicly apologise.
Nirmal Kumar also denied allegations that the TVK was distributing money to voters, saying such a practice was against the party's policy. He criticised the DMK's campaign and claimed that the party was making such statements out of frustration.
Why is Sathyabama contesting Dharapuram bypoll?
The Dharapuram by-election was necessitated after former AIADMK MLA P Sathyabama resigned and joined the TVK. She is now contesting the bypoll on a TVK ticket.

Taiwan receives 2 long-delayed US F-16Vs and awaits additional fighter jets
Taiwan has received the first two F-16V fighter jets from a long-delayed U.S. package, according to the island's air force
BANGKOK -- Taiwan on Friday received the first two of 65 F-16V fighter jets ordered from the U.S., the island's air force said, following years of delays.
The two F-16V Block 70 jets landed at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung. There are 63 more to be delivered. The self-ruled island, which is also claimed by Beijing as part of its territory, placed an order for the F-16Vs in 2019.
Taiwan largely purchases arms from the U.S., its largest unofficial ally, to boost its defenses in the face of a military threat from China. China sends fighter jets and ships toward the island almost daily. Taiwan’s defense minister said on Tuesday that the island remains in continuous discussions with the U.S. about their weapons sales.
The shipment is the first in a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion. The F-16Vs represent $8 billion, or roughly 25% of the entire backlog, according to Taiwan Security Monitor at George Mason University.
The order had been delayed partly owing to production and supply chain issues.
The delivery of the jets comes as the island waits for the U.S. administration to approve an additional $14 billion arms package.
That package has stalled after U.S. President Donald Trump in May met with China’s President Xi Jinping in May. U.S. defense sales to Taiwan are a major source of tension between the U.S. and China. Beijing has repeatedly called for Washington to halt sales to Taiwan, with Xi personally raising the issue with Trump.

NEW DELHI: India’s financial system is “very resilient”, but prolonged stability can encourage risk-taking and leave the system vulnerable to a new generation of shocks, Reserve Bank of India governor Sanjay Malhotra said Saturday, flagging risks from high global debt, stretched artificial-intelligence valuations, leverage outside banks and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven cyber threats. “It's not that I see any imminent signs of stress, but it is because we need to remind ourselves that we need to remain alert to these risks,” Malhotra said at the 5th Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi. The world has weathered repeated shocks since the 2020 pandemic, while India has enjoyed a long period of stability, backed by strong bank, corporate and household balance sheets. "But I may like to point out that it is these very prolonged periods of stability that can encourage risk taking and leverage. Fading memories of crises can weaken prudence," he said. Banking and financial stresses can build overnight but take years to resolve, and "they can be very painful", he said. India took more than a decade to clean up the legacy of excessive lending from the early 2000s. “So we cannot afford to become complacent,” he said. The RBI cannot prevent every shock, whether from the real economy, geopolitics, commodity prices or technological disruption. But it can ensure that the financial system acts as a "shock absorber", through prudent regulation, risk-based supervision, macro-prudential measures, liquidity support including emergency liquidity assistance, and resolution, Malhotra said. The international order built over decades is also under strain from geopolitical and geo-economic fragmentation. “For central banks, this, therefore, has important implications. We cannot look at price and financial stability in isolation from these developments,” he said. Malhotra identified several risks to global financial stability. Global debt has risen, maturities have shortened and bond yields have surged. The US 10-year Treasury touched a 24-year high of 5.34% on Thursday. Higher borrowing costs can narrow governments’ fiscal space and worsen debt dynamics, while tighter financial conditions could strain companies’ debt-servicing capacity. “For banks, sovereign bond losses may weaken their balance-sheets, precisely when the governments face fiscal pressures in supporting troubled banks. Moreover, emerging markets, especially those having high sovereign debt with non-residents, may face capital outflows as the carry trade unwinds,” he said. The AI investment cycle has supported global financial markets, but a slowdown in these investment or earnings as the cycle matures could trigger a sharp repricing of financial assets, particularly across the AI value chain. Hedge funds, option sellers, exchange-traded funds and other non-bank financial intermediaries have expanded leverage in equity and bond markets in pursuit of higher returns. “This is of concern especially when equity valuations are stretched,” Malhotra said. Private credit is another source of vulnerability, signalled by some high-profile defaults, according to the RBI governor. At the same time, the development of sophisticated AI with greater autonomy and problem-solving capabilities has made cyber risk the most immediate concern. “While each one of these risks individually may not be a matter of concern as of now, the simultaneous occurrence of these shocks can put significant pressure on the global financial architecture,” he said. India is also exposed to the West Asia conflict through higher commodity prices and external-sector pressures, but the "economy is navigating this phase from a position of strength", Malhotra said, citing relatively low inflation, the strongest growth among major economies and prudent fiscal consolidation. The country is also taking steps to strengthen its resilience, including diversifying import sources, increasing self-sufficiency in energy and other critical resources, and building strategic petroleum reserves. Government bond yields have risen in recent months, but more slowly than those of global peers, reflecting credible monetary policy and fiscal prudence, he said. A correction in AI-related valuations in advanced markets could also have a positive effect by encouraging capital inflows to India, Malhotra said. Malhotra outlined four priorities for policymakers: accept that shocks are inevitable and build further resilience; improve scenario analysis to assess new globally interconnected risks and their channels of contagion; strengthen the collection and sharing of data because “[quality] of data will determine quality of risk assessment”; and ensure system-wide resilience that extends beyond banks to markets, payment systems, technology infrastructure providers and critical third parties. Finally, innovations in AI, tokenization and new forms of financial intermediation must strengthen, rather than fragment, the foundations of trust, he said.
