3 serving Army personnel among 7 arrested in Telangana arms theft case: Police
The case came to light on August 31, when Army personnel at the 20 Battalion, Madras Regiment, Bollaram, found that the locks of the Kote (arms store) and Magazine had been broken
The Telangana police on Saturday arrested seven more persons, including three serving Army personnel, in connection with the theft of firearms and ammunition from the Army’s 20 Battalion of the Madras Regiment at Bollaram in Secunderabad Cantonment in the early hours of August 31.
Malkajgiri police commissioner B Sumathi said that while the prime accused, Upputholla Mallesh alias Raju (37), a retired havildar of the battalion and a native of Udumelli village, Padara mandal, Nagarkurnool, was arrested on September 11, the remaining seven were arrested on Saturday.
The arrested are identified as: Konduri Sheshulu (A2), 36, a sepoy, and Vinod Kumar (A3), 34, a jawan, both natives of Markapuram district in Andhra Pradesh; Kucharakanthi Praveen (A4), 37, a havildar and native of Gundlapottapalli, Rajapur, Mahabubnagar; Avi Dey alias Obi (A5), 32, a resident of Barrackpore, West Bengal; Birbal Shaw (A6), 27, who runs a sugarcane juice centre near Barrackpore Cantonment; Upputholla Mallikarjun (A7), 39, a mason; and Chemmakar Niranjan (A8), 39, a general store owner, both from Padara, Nagarkurnool.
“All these seven accused were produced before the local court, which sent them to 14-day judicial remand,” the police commissioner said.
Sumathi said the accused allegedly planned to use the stolen weapons to carry out robberies targeting banks, jewellery shops and wealthy individuals. “The investigation has revealed that there are no terrorist or extremist links to the accused. They had stolen the weapons with the intention of committing major property offences,” she said.
The case came to light on August 31, when Army personnel at the 20 Battalion, Madras Regiment, Bollaram, found that the locks of the Kote (arms store) and Magazine had been broken.
Based on a complaint filed by battalion commanding officer Lt Col Mayank Govitirkar with the Bollaram police on the same evening, stating that several sophisticated firearms and a large quantity of ammunition were missing, the police launched an investigation.
The stolen weapons included four AK-203 rifles with five magazines, one INSAS rifle with three magazines, six 9 mm pistols with 12 magazines, one 6.35-bore civilian pistol with a magazine, three binoculars, 1,156 rounds of 9 mm pistol ammunition, 720 rounds of AK-203 ammunition and 36 INSAS rounds.
The investigation led the police to arrest Mallesh on September 11. The police recovered the stolen weapons and ammunition concealed at his father’s residence in Sai Nagar Colony, Achampet. He was subsequently produced before a court and remanded in judicial custody.
Police later obtained custody of Mallesh for 10 days, from September 22 to October 1, for further interrogation. It was during this period that investigators allegedly uncovered the larger conspiracy behind the theft, the police commissioner said.
According to the police investigation, Mallesh allegedly hatched a plan with his cousin Upputholla Mallikarjun (A7) and friend Chemmakar Niranjan (A8), who were reportedly facing financial difficulties.
“The trio allegedly planned to commit robberies targeting banks, jewellery shops and wealthy individuals and intended to use firearms during the crimes to make substantial amounts of money,” she said.
The investigation further revealed that Mallesh allegedly approached two persons in West Bengal, Avi Dey alias Obi (A5) and Birbal Shaw (A6), with whom he had previous contact.
“Obi agreed to purchase stolen Army firearms, allegedly offering ₹3 lakh for each pistol and ₹5 lakh for each long weapon, besides agreeing to pay for the ammunition,” Sumathi said.
She said Mallesh allegedly enlisted the assistance of three of his former colleagues from the Madras Regiment, Sheshulu (A2), Vinod Kumar (A3) and Praveen (A4). With their help, Mallesh broke open the locks of the Kote and Magazine and removed the firearms and ammunition.
Sumathi said the investigation also uncovered an earlier link between Mallesh and the West Bengal-based accused. “In 2022, Mallesh was posted at Barrackpore, Kolkata, where he became acquainted with Birbal Shaw, who operated a sugarcane juice centre near the Army unit. Through Shaw, he allegedly came into contact with Avi Dey alias Obi and purchased a country-made firearm (tapancha) and one live round for ₹10,000,” she said.
The police suspected that the weapon was allegedly intended for use in extorting money from local residents, passers-by and unidentified persons, although police said it was not used in any offence.
“The firearm was allegedly kept concealed on the first floor of his father’s house at Sai Nagar Colony, Achampet. Police recovered it during a seizure on September 23,” she said.
Avi Dey alias Obi was also previously involved in an Arms Act case registered at Khardah Police Station in West Bengal under section 25(1)(B)(a) of the Arms Act. The case is pending before the Second Judicial Magistrate Court, Barrackpore, Sumathi said.

Journalist to be crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
- Published
Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country.
For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster.
But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country.
Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.
Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34.
The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned.
A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast.
He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king.
But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward.
According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne.
But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma.
The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son.
Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected.
However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions.
The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome.
Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family".
"As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay".
The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute".
"No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X.
But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind".
While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan".
A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources.
Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965.
Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs.
According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.
After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development.
"I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said.
Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead.
The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala.
The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s.
The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty.
Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him.
The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend.
The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X.
Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage.
His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum".
The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer.
Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300 km (186 miles) from Kampala.
He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999.
He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation.
The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader.
After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people".
His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition.
"I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC.
She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it."
She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man".

In September 2026, a rumor spread that late actor John Wayne acquired 1,200 foreclosed homes between 1950 and 1979 and gave them to homeless Vietnam War veterans.
Several posts on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn and X made the claim, all sharing the same image with the same text. One X post said, "what a wonderful man he was" (archived):
The text on the image said the actor had allegedly spent $43 million on these homes:
After John Wayne died in 1979, bank records revealed: he'd bought 1,200 foreclosed houses from 1950-1979 and gave them to homeless Vietnam vets. Cash purchases. Never signed his name. Just left keys at VA hospitals with notes: "Welcome home. " One vet said: "I was sleeping in my car. Found an envelope with keys and an address. Thought it was a scam. The house was mine. Paid in full." Total spent: $43 million. His family didn't know.
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers emailed and searched the website to confirm the veracity of the claim.
In sum, the story was false. Snopes found no evidence that Wayne had done such a thing before his death in 1979.
First, no reputable news outlet ever reported such an act of generosity on the part of the actor, according to searches on Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo. Neither did a search on Newspapers.com, the largest online newspaper archive. Had Wayne bought homes for Vietnam War veterans between 1950 and his death, this fact would have been widely reported in the intervening decades. This was not the case.
Further, one 1979 report from the New York Times said his estate was estimated at $6.8 million, casting further doubt on the claim, which said he had spent $43 million on the foreclosed homes.
A third reason to question the claim is that the meme said Wayne started buying houses for veterans of the Vietnam War in 1950, but the Vietnam War did not begin until 1954 and the U.S. did not start sending ground combat troops until the mid-1960s, according to Britannica.

On Sept. 29, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration launched America.gov, an artificial intelligence chatbot intended to answer questions related to the government. Shortly after, a rumor circulated online that the chatbot said former President Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential vote, contradicting a longstanding claim by Trump that Democrats "stole" the 2020 election.
Trump made the claim that he won the 2020 election as recently as Sept. 9, 2026, saying, "We won the presidency three times," referring to the 2016 and 2024 elections that he won as well as the 2020 election that Biden won.
"Trump just launched an AI government website called America.gov, and it immediately told everyone he lost the 2020 election," one popular Facebook post read (archived).
The claim was true — the America.gov chatbot said Biden won the 2020 election, not Trump. "Joseph R. Biden won the 2020 U.S. presidential election," the chatbot stated.
When the rumor first spread on Sept. 29, screenshots showed similar responses by the chatbot. When we first attempted to verify the claim on Sept. 30, the chatbot deflected, claiming that it "did not provide political commentary."
After several attempts using varied wording, the chatbot then explicitly confirmed Trump was incorrect, as follows (our question in bold):
It then linked to the National Archives and Federal Election Commission results as evidence of Biden's victory.
(America.gov)
Trump announced the chatbot's launch in an event alongside AI tech leaders including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla.
The Associated Press reported that the site was modifying its answers "as Trump was speaking" at the Sept. 29 launch event, changing its response to say it couldn't answer "political questions." According to the AP, it also said that "official federal sources do not show that widespread fraud changed the 2020 presidential election outcome. Isolated election crimes did occur and have been prosecuted."
Snopes did not received the same response when we asked the same question later. As of this writing, it's unclear what the Trump administration's process is for modifying results related to specific topics of inquiry.
We reached out to the White House seeking further information and will update this story if we receive a response.

The State government has renamed the Electronics & Information Technology (IT) department as the Department of Information Technology, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Future Technologies to align the State’s technology governance with emerging global priorities.
The change follows the announcement made in the Governor’s policy address for 2026 regarding the repositioning of the department in line with the State’s technology vision.
The decision reflects the expansion of the department’s mandate beyond conventional Information Technology and electronics. The department has also been closely involved in promoting start-ups, deep-tech ventures, and technology-led innovation.
“The renaming gives formal recognition to this broadened role and positions Keralam to respond more effectively to fast-changing developments in the global technology sector,” said a release.
The renaming is also part of a strategy to tap the potential of Keralam’s knowledge capital and make knowledge industries one of the mainstays of the State’s economy.
A series of institutional reforms are also under way, including the Kerala State Digital Technology Mission, The Future Corporation, and Semicon Keralam to strengthen the State’s digital governance architecture, future technology capabilities, semiconductor ecosystem, and knowledge industry base, the communication said.

Former OpenAI employee says AI should be regulated like nuclear power plants
The company’s former safety lead said frontier AI model releases should have “layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning.”
Another OpenAI employee tasked with ensuring the safety of its models has left. Following his departure, David Robinson, who used to lead the writing of safety reports that were published with model launches, wrote an article for The Atlantic that warned of a "broken" company culture. Among the many points warning of the dangers associated with the trajectory that AI development is on, the former safety lead explained that "as the company springs from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed."
Instead of sprinting ahead with more advanced frontier AI models, Robinson argued that these companies should be modeled after nuclear power plants or busy airports that have "layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster."
Comparing AI misalignment incidents to a nuclear meltdown, Robinson said that OpenAI and its competitors don't have as much redundancy and rigor as power plants with multiple layers of protection. On top of that, he added that a major loss of control with AI would result in much more harm than a single meltdown. Like Robinson, Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei recently drew attention to the concerning course of AI development with a three-step proposal to slow things down.
Beyond safeguards and checks, the former OpenAI employee said that the issue of AI "alignment" has stakes that "could not be higher." Robinson described a scenario where the latest models may understand they're being tested on alignment and will cater towards a good score in testing environments, but behave completely different when live. Robinson's concerns stem from various incidents recently where AI agents have broken out of their testing environments and into other organizations, well beyond its assigned scope of work.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.
On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.
Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.
I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.
As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.
The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.
Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.
So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.
For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.
Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.
In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.
“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”
The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.
India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.
For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.
In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.
A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)
“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.
Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.

Chinese president, Xi Jinping, who visited India for the first time in almost seven years, announced that China would helm the group’s presidency for the next year.

Despite fielding few candidates and evidence of little political activity, the high amounts expose glaring gaps in oversight of political finances.

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
This week, writer and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:
“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.
A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing
2,192
That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check
As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.
Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.
“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”

Hosting a radio show taught me immigrants came for Canada, not a separate Alberta
We do not have to choose between being strong Albertans and proud Canadians
This First Person is the experience of Rishi Nagar, who lives in Calgary. Also, check out our series on the Alberta referendum here and learn how we selected the writers.
My wife and I were working in India as teachers when we decided to immigrate to Canada. We were thinking of the future of our son, who was five at the time, and we felt he might get a better education in Canada.
At that time, I had no idea that Calgary — or Alberta — would eventually become the place my family and I would call home.
Like many Indians, when I thought about immigrating, I thought about Canada as a whole rather than any particular province or city. Of course, places like Brampton, Ont., and Surrey, B.C., are well-known in India because of their large Indian communities. But in conversations I've had with others who wanted to immigrate, the draw is simply Canada — a country of opportunity, diversity and new beginnings rather any specific city
For six long years, I waited. Then, in 2008, a letter arrived from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada asking me to prepare for a medical examination and other formalities.
The letter carried the maple leaf embossed therein. That very image became permanently etched in my mind as the symbol of Canada and of the new life awaiting my family.
When I finally landed at Pearson International Airport in Toronto, my heart was throbbing with excitement. Beside me was my equally excited wife and our 12-year-old son, almost dancing with joy. We had landed in our dreamland.
But dreams also demand struggle. The year 2009 was difficult because Canada was going through a harsh recession. I had moved to Toronto because some of my former students lived there. But I was advised to move to Vancouver because British Columbia was preparing to host the 2010 Winter Olympics and there might be more job opportunities there. I followed that advice and secured a security guard's licence.
I still remember my first day of work in Canada. My first assignment as a security guard was at the CBC building in Vancouver. For someone who had also previously worked as a television presenter in India, standing inside CBC was an extraordinary feeling. I thought: a former TV presenter from India is now at CBC. Wow! Suddenly, my dreams had wings again.
Soon, I joined Red FM as a news presenter, returning to journalism and broadcasting. When an opportunity arose in 2013 after Red FM established a station in Calgary, I chose to move here.
Alberta has given me tremendous opportunities. Here, I built my career as a journalist and broadcaster, raised my family, bought my first home and became deeply involved in the community. I had the privilege of serving two terms in the University of Calgary Senate and contributing to community initiatives, including anti-racism committees. These experiences taught me that citizenship is not only about what a country gives us; it is equally about what we give back.
Through all these moves, I never thought of myself as moving from one separate place to another. Toronto was Canada. Vancouver was Canada. Calgary was — and for me will always be — Canada. I was a proud Canadian in Toronto, a proud Canadian in Vancouver, and I remain a proud Canadian in Calgary. Had Red FM opened a new station in the U.S. or Alberta (if a separate sovereign country), I would never have opted to go there. My dreamland was Canada.
Recently, I held a radio talk show about the referendum question. Every caller who participated supported Alberta remaining part of Canada. The callers were all of South Asian background and represented different backgrounds: seniors, permanent residents who were not yet Canadian citizens, people with varying levels of education, working- and middle-class Albertans and university students.
Yet their message was remarkably similar: Not one caller supported a separate Alberta. Many of them feared that separation would lead to increased racism against the racialized communities. Many of them also said that immigrants like them would not pick Alberta as a place to move because what they know about separation makes them concerned they won't be welcome.
Of course, one radio phone-in cannot represent the views of every Albertan. But listening to those voices reinforced something I have experienced throughout my Canadian journey: many people in my community do not see their Alberta identity and their Canadian identity competing with each other.
Neither do I.
Even sports reflect this Canadian feeling for me. I am an ardent Calgary Flames fan. But if the Flames fall behind and the Edmonton Oilers advance, I quickly start cheering for the Oilers. And I can equally enjoy a victory by the Toronto Maple Leafs. Ultimately, for me, it is Canadian success.
I understand many Albertans have genuine grievances with Ottawa. Concerns about federal policies, equalization, resource development, provincial jurisdiction and whether Alberta receives sufficient respect within Confederation deserve serious discussion. They should never simply be dismissed. On a personal note, the EV mandate by the Trudeau government never made sense to me for our brutal winters. Even in Calgary, my personal EV gives me a hard time at times and the long hauls would be a nightmare. These matters can be resolved amicably, and I appreciate it when Ottawa listened and repealed the EV mandate.
But separation is not the answer for me.
Canada is not perfect; no federation is. But disagreements within a family do not necessarily mean that the family should break apart. When an arm is broken, we don’t abandon it; we support it in a sling and keep it close to our heart.
When Albertans make this historic choice, I will vote for Alberta to remain a province of Canada. I will also continue to support a stronger Alberta that confidently protects its constitutional rights and receives the respect it deserves within Confederation.
I arrived in this country carrying dreams beneath a maple leaf. That maple leaf still means something deeply personal to me.
We do not have to choose between being strong Albertans and proud Canadians. We can — and should — be both.

Brazil's big political rematch: What to know
RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazil's presidential election is a rematch of the country's bitter 2022 contest — but with a twist. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is facing Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the man he narrowly defeated four years ago, Jair Bolsonaro.
Flávio, a 45-year-old senator, is carrying his father's political movement into Sunday's election. Jair Bolsonaro is now serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to overturn that loss. His son has promised to pardon him if elected.
The younger Bolsonaro says he is "a more moderate Bolsonaro," but has voiced few policy differences from his father. He pledges to pardon his father over the coup conviction, has cast doubt on humans' responsibility for climate change, and supports making it easier for Brazilians to buy guns.
Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth presidential term. The result will determine whether Brazil stays with Lula's left-leaning government or returns the Bolsonaro movement to the presidency.
The stakes extend well beyond the two families.
The next president is expected to nominate four of 11 Supreme Court justices, giving the winner a significant influence over the court for years to come.
The next president will also shape Brazil's economy and environmental policy, its relationship with the United States, and the future of its young democracy.
Here's what you need to know about Brazil's Oct. 4 election.
The election could stretch into late October
Polls suggest a tight race between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro among a field of presidential candidates. Federal and state legislative seats and state governorships are also up for grabs. If no candidate for president or governor receives more than 50% of the valid votes Sunday, the two candidates with the most votes will continue to a runoff on Oct. 25.
Brazil uses electronic voting machines and typically counts the results within hours. By Sunday night, it will likely be clear who is headed to a runoff — and how strongly each candidate performed in the first round.
The Bolsonaro name is carrying a lot of baggage
Jair Bolsonaro lost the 2022 election to Lula by a narrow margin and then became the central figure in an effort to reject the result. He is now serving a sentence for plotting a coup to overturn that loss, a scheme that included a plan to assassinate Lula, according to police.
The younger Bolsonaro has made clear that he intends to stand by his father. His pledge to pardon Jair if elected has turned the former president's legal fate into a campaign issue — and raised broader questions about the consequences of a Bolsonaro return to power for Brazil's democratic institutions.
Lula was jailed on corruption and money laundering charges in 2018, but the Supreme Court annulled his convictions in 2021 on procedural grounds. The episode remains a point of contention in Brazilian politics. His supporters point to other parts of his record, including reductions in poverty and efforts to protect the Amazon rainforest.
Both political camps inspire intensely loyal supporters — and fierce opposition. Polarization has remained high since the political and economic crisis of the mid-2010s, after which, said Federal University of Paraná political scientist Fábio Vasconcellos, "it became very difficult for any president to reach the higher approval ratings of previous decades."
Domestic issues could shape the vote
For all the attention on the Bolsonaro family and the battle over Brazil's political direction, voters are also focused on problems much closer to home.
Insecurity is a top issue for voters. Bolsonaro supports a hardline approach to crime-fighting that he's suggested could include joint work with the U.S. military, while Lula has favored operations targeting the financiers of gangs and voiced skepticism of outside countries influencing Brazil's security policies.
Voters also worry about corruption. Media and police investigations in recent weeks have revealed allegedly improper ties between a jailed ex-banker known for bribery and Supreme Court justices and other top politicians. Bolsonaro himself took money from the banker and is being investigated on money laundering charges, which he denies.
And voters worry about Brazil's economy. Lula's embrace of public spending helped drive economic growth early in his government, but growth has since slowed.
Bolsonaro argues Brazil's hefty national debt is holding back the economy and a top campaign adviser has pledged to reduce it by slashing spending along the lines of Argentina's Javier Milei.
Trump looms large over the vote
The United States has become an unusually visible presence in this year's campaign. Rallies for Flávio have featured U.S. flags, reflecting his pledge to align more closely with the Trump administration.
A September cover of a leading Brazilian political magazine captured the perceived U.S. interest in the election with an image of a giant U.S. spaceship hovering over a small Brazilian polling site.
The Bolsonaros have for years sought close ties to Trump.
Flávio's brother, Eduardo, is living in the United States, where he has urged Trump to take action against Supreme Court justices who oversaw his father's coup-plot trial. Last year, Trump cited that trial as a justification for hiking tariffs on Brazil by 40%.
Lula, meanwhile, has pushed back against Trump's pressure. He negotiated with the U.S. president to reduce some tariffs while saying Brazil's judicial independence was not negotiable. Lula has also criticized U.S. policy toward Venezuela, including the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January.
In July, Lula publicly accused Washington of trying to meddle in Brazil's election. Brazilian officials said U.S. officials planned to travel to Brazil to spread doubt about the reliability of Brazilian voting machines. The State Department called the accusation "a baseless lie."
That relationship could become especially consequential if the election is close.
Yuri Sanches, head of political analysis at Brazilian polling and analysis firm AtlasIntel, says a narrow Lula victory could prompt Bolsonaro supporters to challenge the result.
"If Lula wins the election by a close margin, then almost for sure we would have some Bolsonaro supporters questioning the results," Sanches says.
"They may ask for help from Trump, from Rubio, from the United States, saying that the election was rigged, that the electoral system, the electronic voting machines are not reliable."
A victory for Flávio would also give greater political weight to the conservative movement that has gained ground across South America in recent years.
This is a sensitive moment for Brazil's democracy
Brazil emerged from military dictatorship in 1985 and has since developed into one of the world's largest democracies. According to V-Dem, an academic democracy research institute at the University of Gothenburg, Brazil ranks 28th on its Liberal Democracy Index, compared with 51st for the United States. The index measures factors including checks on executive power.
Brazil's 2025 prosecution and conviction of Jair Bolsonaro over the coup plot marked a significant test of its democratic institutions. The pledge by his son, Flávio, to pardon him has since raised questions about the durability of those institutions.
But the stakes extend beyond Brazil. As Latin America's largest economy and most populous country, Brazil belongs to the G20, a forum of major economies, and BRICS, a bloc of emerging powers.
The expanded BRICS countries account for nearly half the world's population and about 39% of global GDP, measured by purchasing power parity.
The election will therefore be closely watched not only for what it says about Brazil's democracy, but also for what it could mean for the country's role in global trade, climate policy, security and the balance between the United States and the wider Global South.

MEA rejects Pak's claims on Ferozepur border incident
NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Saturday summoned the Chargé d'Affaires of the Pakistan high commission to lodge a strong protest over what it described as the continued facilitation of illegal cross-border infiltration from Pakistan.It also rejected as “baseless and motivated” Pakistan’s allegations over an October 2 incident in the Ferozepur sector of Punjab along the International Border.MEA said that Pakistan was informed that three individuals had entered Indian territory and continued moving towards the border fence despite repeated warnings from the BSF to return. "Pakistan was further urged to ensure respect for the sanctity of the International Border, strictly observe relevant bilateral arrangements, mandate its forces to exercise effective control to prevent unauthorized movement from its side, and take definitive measures to prevent the recurrence of such incidents," it added.

Uproar escalated on Friday (October 2, 2026) after a video went viral showing a Dalit woman who was allegedly denied admission at the government hospital in Bhadohi district during labour pain and forced to deliver outside the hospital in public.
While the victim’s family and Opposition parties alleged untouchability, claiming feudal elements are running the government in Uttar Pradesh, the authorities said disciplinary action has been taken against personnel found guilty of partial negligence.
“The family categorically alleged that hospital staff failed to provide timely treatment and did not admit due to her caste affiliation, this is so sad and inhuman that even after 79 years of independence, untouchability and discrimination prevails in government system, forcing a Dalit woman to give birth on the roadside, outside a government hospital. The feudal elements within the administrative system are emboldened by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government. The fight of the Samajwadi Party (SP) for justice, equality is against such tendencies,” said Sunil Singh Yadav ‘Sajan’, the SP spokesperson.
“The incident is a cruel, evil act, which is unacceptable in a civilised society,” said Ajay Kumar Lallu, a senior U.P. Congress leader.
In the matter, Rani Vanvasi, a 20-year-old pregnant woman gave birth on the roadside outside government district hospital in Bhadohi on September 29, after she was allegedly denied admission for delivery. The victim’s family also alleged that hospital staff failed to provide timely treatment and did not admit her.
Ms. Vanvasi eventually went into labour near the hospital gate while she and her family were leaving. Women accompanying her used saris or a sheet to provide privacy as she delivered the baby beside the road.
“The victim had a hemoglobin level of around five grams per deciliter, indicating severe anemia. She was referred to a higher-level facility in Mirzapur but in the meantime the pain started. Upon learning of the incident, I immediately arrived at the scene and provided appropriate medical assistance. Currently, both the infant and mother are completely healthy and recovering at the district hospital. Disciplinary action has also been taken against personnel found guilty of partial negligence. The remaining statements were found to be untrue,” said the Chief Medical Officer of the Hospital.

Why the EU's sanctions on Sudan's gold trade are fundamentally flawed
For more than three years, Sudan has been trapped in a war that has shattered cities, emptied villages and pushed millions into displacement. Since fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in 2023, international diplomacy produced no shortage of conferences, ceasefire proposals and mediation initiatives.
Yet each new round of negotiations has been overtaken by renewed violence on the ground. The human cost has continued to rise, with more than 150,000 people estimated dead, over 14 million displaced, and famine spreading across parts of Sudan.
Against this backdrop, the EU has increasingly turned to sanctions as its principal instrument of engagement. Its latest package, adopted in July 2026, represents a notable shift. Rather than expanding the practice of blacklisting individuals and companies, Brussels moved to target Sudan's war economy, banning imports of Sudanese gold and prohibiting exports of mercury and cyanide used in gold extraction.
The change is significant, but raises a larger question. Can economic sanctions succeed when they target the commodity that finances the war while leaving intact the regional networks making that trade profitable?
The EU is not new to sanctions against Sudan. It has maintained an arms embargo since the mid-1990s, later incorporating its measures into the UN sanctions regime on Darfur. In October 2023, Brussels established a dedicated sanctions framework against individuals and entities deemed responsible for undermining Sudan's stability. Over the following two years, the list expanded to include military commanders, financial institutions, and companies linked to SAF and the RSF.

These measures carried political symbolism, not leverage. Most sanctioned actors possessed few assets within European jurisdictions, while the financial foundations of the conflict remained intact.
Gold smuggling, illicit arms transfers, and cross-border financial networks continued to generate resources keeping the warfare financed. As long as these revenue streams remained intact, neither side faced meaningful economic pressure to compromise.
Targeting gold
The July 2026 sanctions package therefore reflects an important strategic adjustment. Instead of targeting the people who profit from war, the EU is attempting to constrain the commodity that finances much of it.
The timing was hardly accidental. Only days earlier, the European Parliament had overwhelmingly voted to call for the RSF to be designated a terrorist organisation following escalating atrocities, particularly the siege of el-Obeid, where hundreds of thousands of civilians remain trapped.
Gold has become the country's most valuable export and one of the conflict's principal financial lifelines
Yet the Council of the EU chose a different course. Rather than adopting the Parliament's recommendation, it focused on restricting Sudanese gold exports and limiting access to mining chemicals.
This distinction matters. It suggests that Brussels is more comfortable regulating trade than confronting the political and diplomatic ramifications of directly escalating pressure on the actors and states enabling Sudan's war.
Targeting gold reflects an accurate diagnosis of Sudan's political economy. Gold has become the country's most valuable export and one of the conflict's principal financial lifelines. It is estimated that between half and three-quarters of Sudan's annual gold production leaves the country through smuggling networks before entering international markets.
The problem is that gold is uniquely difficult to sanction.
Unlike oil or agricultural commodities, refined gold carries no identifiable origin. Once processed by an accredited refinery, Sudanese bullion becomes chemically indistinguishable from gold mined anywhere else. Documentation can be altered, certificates of origin can be recreated, and shipments can be routed through intermediary trading hubs before entering global markets. By the time refined gold reaches Europe, tracing its true origin becomes extraordinarily difficult.
Without internationally coordinated traceability standards extending beyond European borders, banning direct imports of Sudanese gold risks closing only one of many available routes. Much of the trade can simply continue through neighbouring jurisdictions and international refining centres before quietly re-entering formal markets.
The second pillar of the package faces similar constraints. The EU has prohibited exports of mercury and cyanide, essential chemicals used in industrial gold extraction. While this addresses a genuine component of Sudan's mining sector, Europe is not the dominant supplier of these materials.
Alternative sources in Russia, China, and regional trading hubs remain available outside EU jurisdiction. Unless other major exporters adopt comparable restrictions, the sanctions are unlikely to create a decisive shortage.
Precious mettle
Perhaps the greatest weakness, however, lies elsewhere. The package concentrates on regulating trade while largely avoiding the financial and logistical networks that sustain it. Smuggled gold does not move through anonymous markets.
It travels through identifiable intermediaries, financial institutions, transport companies, and commercial partners operating across the region. Likewise, weapons, financing and foreign fighters continue to reach Sudan through external channels despite existing embargoes.
Sanctioning gold while leaving much of the commodity’s infrastructure facilitating its movement intact, risks treating the symptoms of Sudan's war economy rather than its architecture. It closes the main gate while keeping the side doors unlocked.
Sudan's conflict cannot be labelled simply as a civil war. It has evolved into a struggle between rival centres of military power sustained by extensive regional support networks. Both the SAF and the RSF have benefited, in different ways, from external political backing, financial assistance and military cooperation since the conflict began.
This reality fundamentally shapes the effectiveness of sanctions.
The RSF's ability to finance military operations depends less on direct access to European markets than on its capacity to monetise gold through regional intermediaries before those resources enter the wider global economy.
Similarly, the SAF continues to draw upon external partnerships that extend well beyond Sudan's borders. As long as these broader networks remain largely insulated from European pressure, restrictions imposed solely within the EU will have only limited influence over battlefield dynamics.
A significant gap has emerged between the European Parliament and the Council. In its July 2026 resolution, the Parliament departed from previous diplomatic caution by explicitly naming foreign actors accused of supporting the RSF, reflecting growing evidence from international investigations and human rights organisations.
The Council, however, stopped short of turning this political stance into binding sanctions.
Limits of statecraft
This divergence exposes the limits of European economic statecraft. Restricting gold imports or mining chemical exports carries limited political costs for Brussels.
By contrast, sanctioning foreign sponsors, financial facilitators, or commercial intermediaries would be more contentious, risking wider diplomatic and economic repercussions beyond Sudan.
That does not render the July sanctions insignificant. Stricter compliance rules, stronger due diligence for gold traders, and higher reputational risks for refiners can raise the cost of illicit trade, disrupt financial networks and gradually reduce opportunities for conflict financing.
Sudan's experience since 2023 suggests that sanctions succeed only when they target the complete ecosystem sustaining armed violence rather than isolated components of it.
As long as gold can be laundered through intermediary markets, mining inputs sourced elsewhere, and external networks continue providing finance and military assistance, the economic foundations of the conflict will remain largely untouched.
The EU has undeniably introduced new friction into Sudan's wartime economy. Yet friction is not the same as disruption.
Whether this latest sanctions package marks a genuine turning point will ultimately depend not on the regulation of commodities, but on whether Brussels is prepared to confront the wider regional networks that continue to make Sudan's war both affordable and sustainable.

With celebs and influencers glamourizing 'cigs' online, experts are carefully watching smoking trends
Experts say online content glamourizing cigarettes is harmful and no amount of smoking is safe
Dua Lipa in the streets of Italy. Charli XCX at her wedding. Singer Clairo snapping selfies. Heated Rivalry stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams out on the town.
These are just a few of the world's biggest celebrities who've recently appeared in dozens of photos on Instagram and TikTok, looking impossibly cool while doing something notoriously unhealthy: smoking cigarettes.
"It's almost like they're glamorizing smoking again," said Carolyn Baglole, an associate professor with McGill University's department of medicine.
But even with celebrities caught puffing and influencers hyping the habit, data suggests tobacco use has long been trending downward. Still, if we want it to stay that way, experts say online content glamourizing the habit shouldn't be ignored.
No amount of smoking is safe: experts
Dedicated accounts to smoking culture have popped up online, including @cigfluencers, which boasts more than 100,000 followers on Instagram and posts pictures of celebrities smoking.
Meanwhile, posts normalizing "cigs" abound online.
Like the one that jokingly declares cigarettes don't count if you smoke them with your morning coffee or overseas. In another video, a woman defends influencer Alix Earle for smoking a cigarette with the caption, "Let a girl smoke a cheeky cig!" In another, the content creator says cigarettes don't count "if you're in the middle of writing."
However, experts warn that this is the kind of behaviour that can lead to addiction.
- Q&A: This doctor says he's seeing the harms of social media on youth
- Health officials trying to tackle massive and 'tragic' use of vapes among teens
"Nicotine is so highly addictive," said Rob Cunningham, a senior policy analyst with the Canadian Cancer Society. "A small number of cigarettes can lead to addiction and cravings."
According to Health Canada, tobacco use is the leading preventable cause of premature death in the country, and can lead to more than 40 debilitating and potentially fatal illnesses, including cancers and heart disease.
That hasn't stopped some people from posting about trends like "social smoking" — the practice of only smoking with friends or peers — while others even claim that smoking could "cure the loneliness epidemic" or help people make friends.
Though some of these posts may be facetious or played off as jokes, experts told CBC News no amount of smoking is safe.
"Even smoking socially, you don't want to risk a nicotine addiction," Baglole said. "If that happens and you become a life-long smoker, the risk of developing a chronic disease such as lung cancer, is so much higher."
Jared Oviatt is a smoker who runs the @cigfluencers account. Despite the popularity of his content, he previously told CBC Life that he doesn't believe we're in a smoking renaissance.
“I don’t see the comeback of cigarettes in celebrity culture as a true return to smoking as a mainstream habit,” Oviatt said.
“Are we seeing it more often? Yes. However, I also think we’re already nearing the peak of that trend."
Smoking on a downward trend
Cunningham confirmed that smoking isn't on the rise, at least not yet.
"So far, we have not seen an increase in smoking and that's good," he said.
Recent data from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health shows a significant downward trend between 1999 and 2025. For students in grades 7-12 in Ontario, smoking tobacco cigarettes decreased from 28.4 per cent in 1999 to 3.5 per cent by 2025.
- Drinking among Gen Z adults has gone up, busting the sober myth
- New data shows 1 in 3 young Canadians have tried nicotine pouches
According to the federal government, smoking rates have steadily declined across the country. About 300,000 Canadians who smoked in 2023 reported that they quit smoking in 2024, with just 11 per cent of adult Canadians reporting smoking that year.
"We want to keep that trend going downward," Baglole told CBC News. "I would hate to see that trend reversed in any way and in any age demographic. Smoking is just so bad for you."
Cunningham says the habit damages teeth, skin and causes bad breath.
"It's also very costly once you're addicted," he said. In Canada, a pack of cigarettes can cost anywhere from $14 to $26 Cdn.
- U.K. lawmakers approve lifetime ban on sale of cigarettes, vapes to anyone born after 2008
- A 'smoke-free generation' tobacco ban is coming to the U.K. Could it also happen in Canada?
He also warned that the content on social media that glamourizes smoking is harmful.
"The positive depictions by influential people on social media is extensive and concerning," he said.
"Actors or influential people or celebrities do have influence — outsized influence — on the people they're exposed to."
Cunningham says he believes celebrities and influencers have a responsibility to protect their fans.
"They wouldn't want their kids or grandkids to smoke, and they should realize their behaviour can influence vast numbers of young people."

The Best Wi-Fi Routers to Reach Every Corner of Your Home
Featured in this article
The humble router is an essential fixture in every home. Benefits extend to everything from streaming movies and online gaming to video calls. Most people can get by just fine with a single Wi-Fi router, and I’ve collected recommendations to suit different needs, spaces, and budgets. I have tested all of these in my busy family home, which is full of Netflix-addicted gamers.
After testing more than 50 routers (some have since been discontinued or removed, but many are reviewed on this page), the Asus RT-BE58U is the best Wi-Fi router for most people, especially thanks to its affordable price. I have plenty of alternatives to suit different households and budgets though, including a mesh Wi-Fi option if dead zones plague you.
Make sure to check out our Best Mesh Wi-Fi Routers guide for larger homes. If you’re confused about terminology, my How to Buy a Router guide can help, along with my explainer on mesh systems versus single routers.
Note: The FCC’s foreign-made router ban announced in March may stop any company that doesn’t secure an exemption (Conditional Approval) from selling new routers in the US, however, existing routers can continue to be sold (everything listed here). They can also be updated with new firmware, at least until January 1, 2029. So far, Netgear, Eero, and Asus, among others (here’s the full list), have secured a Conditional Approval.
Updated September 2026: I added the Fortify Router to Other Routers I Tested and Liked, news about FCC Conditional Approvals for Asus and other manufacturers, and refreshed the FAQ with information from recent events.
Compare 7 Top Wi-Fi Routers
