Hidden cameras show some stores unlocking speed limits on e-bikes, selling e-scooters that go up to 120 km/h
Marketplace visited stores in GTA to see recommended ages and maximum speeds available
Whether it's children cruising down a suburban street, drivers delivering food downtown or a daredevil taking their need for speed to the highway, electric bikes and electric scooters are becoming more common across Canada.
A new hidden camera investigation by Marketplace shows how some stores are selling e-scooters and e-bikes with top speeds much higher than provincial speed limits and with recommended rider ages younger than provincial regulations allow.
Most provincial traffic laws limit e-bikes and e-scooters to 32 kilometres per hour or less. Age restrictions, meanwhile, vary across the country, ranging from 12 to 18. The territories and some provinces have no minimum age to ride.
That means it is mostly up to local police services to enforce these rules at a time when the number of injuries caused by these vehicles is climbing yearly, and public calls are growing for stronger, consistent rules nationwide and better enforcement.
Marketplace visited some of Canada's most well-known big box and specialty shops in the Greater Toronto Area — Amego, Emmo, EZbike, Best Buy, Canadian Tire and Costco — that sell popular brands. The undercover journalists tested how easy it is to find an e-bike or e-scooter that either had a maximum speed or age recommendation contravening Ontario limits.
In Ontario, e-scooter and e-bike riders must be at least 16. E-scooters cannot travel faster than 24 km/h on a flat surface, and e-bikes cannot travel faster than 32 km/h, according to provincial laws.
10 of 12 stores exceeded Ontario limits
Of the 12 stores journalists visited undercover, salespeople at six stores told us or showed us how to bypass built-in speed limits.
While most stores reminded us of Ontario rules, 10 stores sold e-bikes or e-scooters with maximum speeds beyond Ontario limits.
Stores are allowed to sell the e-bikes no matter how fast they go, but Michael Pasquali, founder of the Canadian Electric Bicycle Association (CEBA), says it's "heartbreaking."
"Shops that are selling products that are way beyond the legal limit, they're putting a lot of people in danger."
Seven stores also had e-scooters for sale with manufacturer-recommended rider ages under 16, though some medical experts say e-bikes and e-scooters are too unsafe for anyone under 16.
- Watch the full Marketplace investigation on Friday, Oct. 2, on CBC-TV and YouTube.
"It's not just a toy; it's a motorized vehicle," said April Kam, an emergency physician at McMaster Children's Hospital in Hamilton.
"We're seeing kids who are presenting with brain bleeds, with abdominal injuries, solid organ injuries."
Recently released data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information shows 150 people ages 15 and under were hospitalized for falls involving an e-scooter in the 2025-2026 fiscal year across Canada, compared to 54 the year prior. That's an increase of roughly 178 per cent — and reflects a steady year-over-year increase for the last three years.
The number of head injuries related to e-scooters has also increased, from 50 in the 2022-2023 fiscal year to 157 in the 2025-2026 fiscal year. Fractures, dislocations and or muscle and tendon injuries have more than doubled in that same period, with 544 last fiscal year.
The Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program released its own survey in August and found 10 children have died from using devices like e-scooters and e-bikes in 2025.
Meanwhile, sales for the electric rides have more than quadrupled in Canada since 2019, with roughly 372,000 e-bikes and 76,000 e-scooters sold so far this year, according to Statista.
Marketing to kids 'deceiving' parents, doctor says
The youngest age recommendation the Marketplace journalists found was at Canadian Tire — a Razor e-scooter that hits a maximum speed of 16 km/h and is recommended for children who are eight or older.
"That just boggles my mind. Kids at this age don't necessarily have the developmental ability to maneuver these motorized vehicles," said Kam, who is also president of the Canadian Paediatric Society's emergency medicine section.
"It's very concerning that there's this huge market for selling children these motorized vehicles, essentially, and deceiving the parents and family, marketing them as toys."
Razor, the manufacturer of that particular e-scooter at Canadian Tire, said in a statement its device meets U.S. safety guidelines that say eight-year-olds can operate slow-moving motorized vehicles.
The company said its e-scooter is safe when properly used, isn't meant to be on public roads and that riders should follow local laws.
In statements to Marketplace, Best Buy, Canadian Tire and Emmo said customers should follow local laws. Best Buy said rules for e-bikes and e-scooters are evolving and that it tries to keep product information updated.
Costco didn't comment on Marketplace's findings.
E-bike stores can modify speed controls
At an EZbike location in Richmond Hill, a salesperson told undercover journalists it sells e-scooters that can reach 120 km/h — a speed that could get you a ticket on most highways.
At other stores, some e-bikes have their speed limited to 32 kilometres, adhering to Ontario's rules. But when asked if they modify vehicles, a salesperson at an Emmo location in Toronto said yes, they could modify a bike to go up to 150 km/h for off-road use.
"That's horrible," said Pasquali, of CEBA, who owns his own e-bike store in Hamilton.
Emmo and the company that operates the Emmo stores Marketplace visited said in a statement that a product's technical capabilities should not be confused with what's allowed on the roads.
But as an employee at an Emmo in Vaughan, Ont., described it: bypassing the speed limiter is "just like a toggle switch."
Passing on that kind of advice is "extremely unethical," Pasquali said.
"If you're showing consumers how to push a button and make it faster or offering to modify it to go faster with the caveat that you keep it off road, well, that's technically right. But most consumers aren't doing that, right?"
A salesperson at an Amego store in North York, Ont., went a step further, unlocking the 32 km/h speed limit in front of undercover journalists and revving the motor, showing the e-bike exceeding the speed limit and saying it could hit a top speed of roughly 50 km/h.
Amego said in a statement it does not offer or perform modifications, and its salesperson likely exaggerated the top speed.
EZbike didn't comment on Marketplace's findings.
Mom wants change after son's devastating injury
Amy Richards, of St. John's, became one of those parents pleading for change after watching her son spend 102 days in the hospital after losing control of his e-scooter.
Jayden King, 14, was riding his e-scooter on a quiet street in May when he hit a speed bump and lost control.
King's mom says he was wearing a helmet at the time of the accident but suffered a traumatic brain injury. He spent 21 days in a coma and had to have part of his skull surgically removed due to brain swelling. Once he's healthier, King will have to undergo another surgery to get the rest of his skull put back in place, Richards said.
He learned to walk, talk and eat again but still lives with a long list of issues, including memory loss.
"I can't remember nothing in my whole life," King said. He says there's not a chance he'll ride an e-scooter again.
Newfoundland and Labrador has no rules governing e-bikes or e-scooters, but a spokesperson for Government Services said in a statement that it has consulted the public and is looking at changes to the Highway Traffic Act to include micro-mobility devices.
Richards said it should have happened a long time ago, and no one under 16 should be able to ride one.
"We need to protect our children. That should come first and foremost," she said.
Pasquali says the federal government needs to step in and stop the sale and importation of e-bikes and e-scooters that can be modified with the flick of a switch.
Safety is top priority, federal minister says
Canada's Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon told Marketplace in an interview in late September that he has heard stories of people being injured riding e-bikes and e-scooters, and he wants to talk to his provincial counterparts about how to respond.
Most of the legislation governing e-bikes and e-scooters is provincial, he said, and there is "impetus" for provinces and municipalities to act.
But, MacKinon also said the federal government needs "to absolutely consider what we will do in terms of regulating the safety of those devices."
"We'll always work with safety in mind. Safety is our principal priority."

Mito – Ibaraki Gov. Kazuhiko Oigawa has said that he has no intention of consenting to proceed to a preliminary survey, the second stage of the three-tier selection process for choosing a final disposal site for high-level radioactive waste from nuclear power plants.
“I don’t plan to give my approval” for such a survey, the governor told a news conference Friday. “My position will not change,” he added, also ruling out the possibility of hosting such a facility.
The remarks came after Sadayuki Suzuki, mayor of Hitachiomiya in Ibaraki, announced Wednesday that his city will accept a literature survey, the first stage of the selection process.
Conducting a preliminary survey requires the consent of the prefectural governor.
Ibaraki “has already contributed to the central government’s energy policy significantly by shouldering burdens,” mainly from hosting Japan Atomic Power Co.’s Tokai No. 2 nuclear plant in the village of Tokai, Oigawa said.
“I think there is an imbalance between the benefits and the burden,” he added.
The governor also said that areas without nuclear power plants should be considered candidates for a final disposal site first.
Meanwhile, Suzuki said Friday, “I see the situation differently from the governor.”
On whether the city will seek help from the central government, the mayor said, “I might consider that possibility if we reach a conclusion that we need to advance cooperation for the future (of our city) during upcoming briefing sessions for our residents.”
The same day, Suzuki sent a document to industry minister Ryosei Akazawa indicating his intention to accept the literature survey.

- Published
Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.
The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.
Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.
The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.
Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation.
"I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.
When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin.
The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window.
"One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.
Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.
The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.
Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.
The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.
As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.
He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe.
"People were calling for help, some were already very weak."
But no-one came to help, he and others allege.
"While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency.
"We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door.
"We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."
Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.
The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye.
"The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.
As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja.
A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened.
It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable.
No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said.
As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event.

Pakistan-made cosmetics that continued to find their way to Hyderabad more than a year after India shut the door on imports from the neighbouring country have now led investigators to Mumbai’s Crawford Market, pointing to a wider supply chain behind the banned products.
The development comes amid a separate public-health concern over some of the skin-whitening products. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) last month specifically warned consumers against two Pakistan-made creams after tests found excessive levels of heavy metals.
Both ‘Goree Beauty Cream’ and ‘Chandni Whitening Cream’, named in the September 8 CDSCO alert, were among the products found during raids on three shops in Hyderabad this week.
An officer involved in the investigation said the cosmetics seized in Hyderabad were allegedly being sourced from Crawford Market in Mumbai. “Investigators are now looking further up the chain to establish how the products entered India and reached wholesale and retail markets despite restrictions on their import.
Imports from Pakistan prohibited since May 2025
India prohibited the direct or indirect import or transit of all goods originating in or exported from Pakistan on May 2, 2025. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade imposed the restriction through a notification, citing national security and public policy.
The prohibition extends to goods entering India indirectly, meaning routing Pakistan-origin products through another country does not by itself make their import permissible.
Cosmetics imported into India are additionally governed by the Cosmetics Rules, 2020. Products must be registered with the Central Licensing Authority before import and are required to comply with prescribed quality and safety standards.
The CDSCO had stepped up scrutiny even before the latest Hyderabad seizure. In July, it directed its zonal offices, State licensing authorities and officers at ports to maintain enhanced surveillance following instances of imported cosmetics being sold in domestic markets without valid import registration certificates.
Heavy metals found in two creams
The health regulator followed this with a more pointed warning on September 8. After testing Goree Beauty Cream and Chandni Whitening Cream, it said neither had been issued a registration certificate for import and that the products contained heavy metals beyond specified limits, which could pose health risks, including toxic effects. Consumers were advised not to purchase or use them.
The Hyderabad investigation has meanwhile opened another line of inquiry. According to the officer, investigators found that an ointment originating from the United Kingdom was allegedly being mixed with cosmetic products and the resulting preparation sold for skin-lightening purposes.
Samples of the products have been sent for forensic examination, and investigators are awaiting the laboratory findings to establish their composition and determine the substances present in them.
Officials have raised concerns about potentially carcinogenic substances, but the forensic results are awaited. The precise health implications of the seized preparations are therefore yet to be established.
The latest investigation follows raids by the Hyderabad police and CDSCO at Beauty Ladies Emporium, Beauty Queen Shop and S.J. Medical Shop in the Habeeb Nagar and Nampally areas, where cosmetics valued at about ₹7 lakh were seized.
The stock included several Pakistan-made whitening creams, soaps and other cosmetic products. Five persons were identified in connection with their alleged sale and distribution.
The Crawford Market link also comes against the backdrop of enforcement action in Mumbai itself, where Pakistan-made cosmetics valued at about ₹12 lakh were seized during a raid in July.

JSW Group’s B2B ecommerce marketplace JSW One Platforms narrowed its consolidated net loss by 50.9% to ₹106.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹217 Cr in the previous financial year, helped by revenue growth outpacing the rise in expenses. Its operating revenue jumped 44.9% to ₹5,743.4 Cr from ₹3,962.8 Cr in FY25, according to its DRHP. The company runs a technology-led platform that combines procurement of manufacturing and construction materials with logistics, processing, and access to credit. Including other income of ₹44.2 Cr, total income stood at ₹5,787.6 Cr in FY26, compared with ₹3,979.5 Cr a year earlier. The financial disclosures come as JSW One prepares for a proposed ₹3,054 Cr IPO. For the June quarter of FY27, JSW One reported a consolidated profit of ₹14.2 Cr on an operating revenue of ₹1,642.5 Cr. The DRHP did not disclose the comparable Q1 FY26 numbers. What Drove JSW One’s Revenue Growth In FY26? Sales of goods remained JSW One’s largest revenue source, rising 45.5% to ₹5,619.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹3,862.1 Cr in FY25. This business includes steel and related products, cement, and other construction materials. The company attributed the growth primarily to the expansion of its private brands and service centre business. Steel volumes increased 51.2% to 27.1 Lakh tonnes, while cement volumes rose 23.9% to 2.6 Lakh tonnes. Services revenue grew 11.4% to ₹109.6 Cr from ₹98.4 Cr. Within this, commission income from the MSME business increased to ₹100.3 Cr from ₹83 Cr, while homes business commissions rose to ₹9.3 Cr from ₹7.5 Cr. Financial services revenue increased more than sixfold to ₹14.2 Cr from ₹2.3 Cr, although it contributed just 0.2% of consolidated operating revenue. Where Did JSW One Spend? JSW One’s total expenses increased 40.5% to ₹5,894.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹4,196.5 Cr in FY25. Material Purchases: Purchases of stock-in-trade, its largest expense, rose 42.7% to ₹5,444.1 Cr from ₹3,815.4 Cr as the company procured more materials to support its distribution and private brands businesses. Employee Costs: Employee benefit expenses declined 1.2% to ₹264.3 Cr from ₹267.6 Cr. The decline was driven by lower share-based payment expenses, which fell to ₹16 Cr from ₹59.5 Cr. However, salaries and wages increased to ₹217 Cr from ₹185.7 Cr. Transportation Costs: Transportation expenses climbed 58% to ₹152.1 Cr from ₹96.2 Cr, reflecting the expansion of its delivery network and higher freight costs. Technology Expenses: Platform and technology expenses increased 32.9% to ₹29.6 Cr from ₹22.3 Cr, driven by higher transaction volumes and associated cloud hosting, software licensing, and maintenance costs. Inside JSW One’s B2B Ecommerce Business Promoted by JSW Steel and JSW Cement, JSW One operates a B2B ecommerce marketplace for manufacturing and construction MSMEs. Its technology platform allows customers to discover and compare materials, place orders, arrange financing, and track fulfilment. The business combines a commission-based marketplace with a distribution model. In marketplace transactions, JSW One earns a commission for connecting buyers and sellers. Through subsidiary JSW One Distribution, it also purchases materials, arranges processing and customisation, and sells them to customers, recognising the full sale value as revenue. Its offerings overlap with those of startups such as OfBusiness, Infra.Market, and Zetwerk across materials procurement, construction supplies, and manufacturing services. Incorporated as JSW Retail in 2018, the company was renamed JSW One Platforms in December 2020. It launched the JSW One MSME and JSW One Homes portals in 2021, subsequently expanding into private brands and lending. Its subsidiary JSW One Finance received its NBFC registration in 2024. JSW One raised ₹205 Cr in a Series A round led by Mitsui & Co. in April 2023 at a valuation of ₹2,750 Cr. It later closed a ₹575 Cr funding round in October last year, with participation from SBI, Principal Asset Management, One-Up, International Conveyors, Scarlett Ventures, and JSW Steel. JSW One’s ₹3,054 Cr IPO Plan JSW One’s proposed IPO comprises a fresh issue of ₹1,300 Cr and an OFS of ₹1,754 Cr. JSW Steel plans to sell shares worth up to ₹811 Cr, JSW Cement up to ₹123 Cr, and Mitsui & Co. up to ₹820 Cr through the OFS. From the fresh issue proceeds, the company plans to invest ₹500 Cr in JSW One Finance to strengthen its capital base, ₹350 Cr in technology and platform development, and ₹125 Cr in marketing and brand-building through JSW One Distribution. The remaining net proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes. JSW One may also undertake a pre-IPO placement of up to ₹260 Cr, which would reduce the fresh issue size by the amount raised. A row of Biblical proportions has erupted in the run-up to Brazil’s presidential election, with the country’s patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, emerging as an unlikely kingmaker in the deadlocked race.
Ahead of Sunday’s vote, the two frontrunners – the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro – are level in the polls.
But in recent days, speculation that Bolsonaro – son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro – might strip the widely cherished patroness of her position have caused a nationwide outcry, leaving some to question if it could tip the knife-edge election in favour of Lula, who is Catholic.
“It could sway things one way or the other,” said Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has been tracking the unusual election row.
It remains unclear precisely how the commotion began, but debate over the issue exploded last week when a remark by Bolsonaro, whose movement includes many evangelical Christians, went viral online. In a recent broadcast, the former senator said one of his first acts as president would be to “decree that Brazil belongs to the Lord Jesus Christ”.
Some Catholics took that as a sign that the Protestant politician planned to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida, although only the Vatican – which declared her Brazil’s patroness in 1930 – has the authority to do so.
Those suspicions were reinforced by Bolsonaro’s reported links to JB Carvalho, an evangelical leader who has previously called for the patroness’s removal. In 2007, another Bolsonaro ally tried to introduce legislation to the same effect, although the bill was dropped.
Bolsonaro has called claims he plans to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida “fake news”. He alleged the rumours were being spread by Lula supporters, as well as members of the Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation. The conference rejected the charge.
Lula’s leftwing movement has taken advantage of the furore, keenly aware it could hurt the far-right candidate’s chances in a country where nearly 57% of the population is Catholic. With the result expected to be even tighter than the last one – when Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% – even a small number of votes could mean the difference between victory and defeat.
Lula has appeared on the campaign trail holding statuettes of the Virgin Mary while his wife, Janja da Silva, has worn a pendant honouring Our Lady of Aparecida. “As long as I’m president, no one will disrespect Our Lady of Aparecida. No one. People need to learn to respect all religions,” Lula told a rally in the Amazon. Lula’s vice-president and running mate, a devout Catholic called Geraldo Alckmin, published a video describing how he had received messages from Catholics “worried about the direction of the country and the terrible news that has been circulating”. Alckmin assured voters he and Lula would preserve and protect “religious traditions, so sacred to Brazilian families”.
The row speaks to the rivalry and tensions between Brazil’s once dominant Catholic church and the evangelical movement, which has grown rapidly since the 80s.
Traumann said: “It touched a raw nerve, which is the growing power of the evangelicals. Evangelicals make up about 30% of the population, but their political power is much greater than 30% – and within Bolsonarismo it is even more significant”.
Traumann believed that, irrespective of whether Bolsonaro really did intend to remove the patroness, the furore had tapped into “a genuine fear among Catholics of being pushed outside the system”. “I have no doubt that this is going to be important [in the election]. [Flávio Bolsonaro] knows it has landed badly,” he added.
Luiz Antônio Simas, a historian and author of the book So Many Marys: Our Lady in Popular Culture, said the outcry “was a symptom of the popularity that Aparecida and the Virgin Mary in general have in the formation of our culture”.
“For Brazilian popular culture, Our Lady of Aparecida transcends altars … She is extremely powerful as a defining element of what we envision Brazilian popular culture to be,” Simas said, noting how Brazil’s “Black Madonna” was present in samba parades, football culture and Afro-Brazilian faiths.
While the debate flared up on the eve of the election, Simas said Our Lady of Aparecida was a long-running point of tension between Catholics and evangelicals, who oppose the Catholic veneration of saints and images. He recalled a major outcry in 1995 when a neo-Pentecostal pastor kicked a statue of Our Lady of Aparecida on TV.
Simas believed religious racism was at the heart of the outcry, given that Our Lady of Aparecida was a black representation of the Virgin Mary. “When all of this comes into contact with a turbulent political context, in a country experiencing the tensions of a highly contested pre-election scenario, all these controversies come to the surface,” Simas added.

The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination”.
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates, where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

In 1995, gender studies researcher Judy Chu found herself chauffeuring around her 13-year-old brother and his friend. The boys’ curiosity got the better of them, and they asked what she was learning: adolescent girls’ development, she told them.
A guide for raising boys to be resilient men
Addressing male loneliness starts in childhood.
One of the boys looked at her and said, “‘You should study boys. You can start with me,’” Chu recalled. So she did. That fall, she spoke to 13-year-old boys from home for her clinical interviewing class.
In the years since, Chu has researched boys between the ages 12 and 18 — their wishes, their desires, what they wanted from their friendships and romantic relationships — and discovered some felt largely unknown. There was a gap between what the world expected of them — the stoic, strong, independent stereotypes that have persisted for centuries — and how they saw themselves, but had internalized so many messages for so long that they felt like they had no choice but to accept this version of masculinity. Chu theorized that these beliefs must have taken root during their childhood, and she later published a book on the subject.
Key takeaways
- By many measures, including academic achievement and labor force participation, men are behind their female peers.
- Rather than address these issues in adulthood, many therapists and gender studies researchers agree that pushing back against rigid gender stereotypes in childhood could help foster more resilient men.
- Parents, teachers, coaches, and other adults in boys’ lives should empower boys to be in touch with their emotions, to encourage open conversation, and develop deep friendships, according to experts.
When toddlers enter school, she discovered, they begin learning the rules of boyhood. “Regardless of what their parents had encouraged or enabled at home, they were learning that at school, if you wanted to be seen as and treated as one of the boys and you wanted to be with the boys, you wanted to play with the boys, be friends with the boys, there were rules you had to follow,” Chu said. “It was kind of like a microcosm of our society, which is if you want people to see you as and treat you as a quote unquote real boy or real man, you need to prove yourself.”
Since Chu’s work on the subject, American culture has changed to address gender inequities — the ones that negatively affect girls. As a part of this movement, girls were empowered to be more autonomous and pursue careers and financial independence to build a life beyond marriage and childrearing. (Though it should be said, women still trail men in earnings, outpace them in household responsibilities, and have higher rates of anxiety, depression, and PTSD.)
But boys are still stuck in place.
Across the country, lawmakers have promoted policies and legislation aimed at helping men reach their potential. In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a 2025 executive order outlining education, career, and mental health initiatives targeting men. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore created the state’s Young Men and Boys Initiative, focusing on men’s health, employment, and community connections. But these programs are reactive, attempting to disrupt decades of socialization. At the same time, the rise of the manosphere and misogynist online spaces and increasingly right-leaning voting trends among men signal a cohort of young men at a turning point.
Recent studies have found that boys are less likely to graduate high school on time compared to girls — that gap is even bigger for Black and Hispanic boys — and fewer young men obtain bachelor’s degrees compared to their female peers. And as fewer men graduate from college, fewer participate in the labor force, too. The suicide rate among men is nearly four times higher than that of women. While men and women report similar rates of loneliness and number of friends, men are less likely to turn to their social networks for support. Out of the over 750,000 jobs created since Donald Trump took office in 2025, men have gained none of them.
So what will it take to help men get unstuck? If we are truly committed to ending the male loneliness crisis, to tackling suicide and gun violence — society has the power to change things for the next generation, experts said. Rather than aiming to reach men after the constraining masculine worldviews have already taken root, we can prevent them from warping boys’ sense of self in the first place: To help men, we must change how boys are raised.
Reject the myth of the “real boy”
In 2023, psychologist Michael Reichert conducted a nationally representative survey of more than 2,000 American men, asking them questions about their lives, relationships, internet habits, and sources of social support. One finding was particularly staggering: two-thirds of young men between the ages of 18 and 23 felt like no one really knew them well. (In a follow-up report two years later, in which women were also surveyed, equal percentages of men and women — about 50 percent — said they were not truly known.) The conclusion Reichert came to, he told Vox, was “boyhood is failing at the most important task.” American society is producing young adults who feel like they’re on their own, “a tragic outcome of a boyhood that’s not preparing our males for a resilient life in a world where things are harder, more complicated,” said Reichert, the executive director of the Center for the Study of Boys’ and Girls’ Lives at the University of Pennsylvania.
Because the idea of what a man looks like and how a man behaves is so ingrained, boys are taught to conform from an early age, experts said. From their earliest years, as evidenced in Chu’s work, boys are taught to adhere to stereotypical gender norms reinforced through comments like “boys don’t cry,” “toughen up,” and “don’t be a girl.”
“It starts with mothers having a fear of turning their son into a mama’s boy, so they push them away at young ages — three and four years old. Go play with your dad, go play with your older male siblings,” Joseph Derrick Nelson, an associate professor in the department of educational studies at Swarthmore College, told Vox. Fathers, for their part, tend to emphasize self-defense, goal pursuit, and overcoming adversity with their sons, Reichert said. Black boys in particular are perceived as older and less innocent than their white counterparts, only pushing them further toward rigid gender roles, Nelson said. If they don’t conform, they may be teased by other boys.
A large part of proving yourself as a “real boy” means rejecting anything deemed feminine, including emotional vulnerability and relationships. As babies and young children, boys and girls are equally emotionally expressive, but by the time they start school, boys show fewer emotions and use less emotional language. When boys are taught that showing their feelings or forging deep friendships is girly, they stop prioritizing those relationships. That shift happens during the teen years, when boys go from reporting having best friends with whom they can share their deepest secrets, to feeling like they’ve drifted apart from these very connections by the end of high school. And it’s not for lack of desire, Chu said, or some inherent biological difference: Boys have simply learned not to show their need for affection, to hide their sadness, to not be tender.
A new paradigm for raising boys, experts said, begins with how masculinity is first presented at home and in school.
To encourage boys to be better in touch with their emotions means adults should not pit masculinity against femininity, Christopher Reigeluth, an associate professor at Oregon Health and Science University, told Vox. This goes beyond simply telling boys not to conceal their feelings, but making clear that confiding these feelings in a friend and fostering platonic connections isn’t girly: it’s a universal human need.
In schools, specialized emotional education in curricula can help boys express their emotions and embrace vulnerability.
Simply, talk to them
One of the easiest ways to do this is to allow and encourage boys to engage in an activity traditionally seen as more feminine: talking.
Reichert, the psychologist, has led an emotional literacy program in a boys’ school for over 30 years. In that time, he’s seen the sentiment among students shift from skepticism to genuine interest. “It has become, by 2026, the most popular program in the school,” Reichert said, due to an increased cultural awareness of emotional health. In the group, students discuss their daily stressors and hardships, and they learn that letting their peers see them for who they are — connecting with them — benefits their well-being.
Before joining Reichert’s peer counseling group, high school senior Chris Burnetta expressed his emotions on the field. “You’re almost allowed to be emotional when you’re playing sports, and you’re not allowed to be emotional when you’re not,” Burnetta, 18, told Vox. In middle school, he attended a co-ed school and found himself performing aspects of masculinity to impress his female classmates. But once he met older classmates who he respected and wanted to emulate, he discovered many of them attended the counseling group and encouraged him to go, too. “I don’t want to speak for everyone, but I think for guys in general, looking up at people above you gives you a big impression and a big influence on how you want to live your life and what you want to be like,” he said.
Seeing his peers so enthusiastically discuss their struggles and triumphs helps foster maturity and gives him permission to show his emotions, Burnetta said, an outlet he never had before.
Adolescence, a time when many behavioral health patterns are forged or discarded, is the time to engrain healthy social habits in boys — and for parents to be explicit, Matt Englar-Carlson, a professor of counseling and the director of the Center for Boys and Men at California State University, Fullerton, told Vox. Now is the time to have dedicated phone-free time as a family, to give them opportunities to share how they’re feeling without fixing their problems, to listen to them even when they’re frustrating you. When his own son was younger, Englar-Carlson thought he knew all the tricks: showing empathy, trying to help. “Me doing that with him actually was making him feel worse, I think,” he said. Instead, Englar-Carlson took a lighter touch. He would acknowledge when his son was upset, but wouldn’t press a conversation. Whenever his son was ready to talk, he was available.
One easy way to do this? Talk to them when you’re driving. As my colleague Rachel Miller previously reported, not having to make direct eye contact can make it a little easier for kids to be vulnerable.
And if you’re a man, make sure you’re leading by example: Be willing to share your own moments of embarrassment, disappointment, and sadness, so they know it’s okay for them to do the same.
Help them foster non-romantic intimacy
While in school, boys have ample avenues for connection through classes and sports, even if they aren’t interacting with others on a deeper level. It’s when they lose access to these organized outlets for socialization in adulthood that they slide into isolation or start looking to their romantic partners to fulfill all of their social needs.
The idea that emotional intimacy is reserved for your significant other is how society gets to a point where 15 percent of men say they don’t have any close friends. Those without a partner are even more adrift: Men are less satisfied being single than their female counterparts. “We teach boys to not ask for help… figure it out on their own,” Nelson said. “I don’t know why we’re surprised when they become adult men and struggle with building relationships and close and connected communities, because all they’ve been taught, even since they were young children, was about figuring it out on their own and denying emotions, suppressing emotions, that then leaves you not in relationship and quite lonely.”
In the absence of in-person friendships, digital spaces provide an attractive alternative. While not altogether negative, some online forums — interactive video games, sports gambling, the manosphere — enable young men to further retreat from society. While pursuing community, boys may find their way to adult-centric spaces, which can be rife with misogynistic and patriarchal messages, feeding the belief that the only way to advance is through hyperconsumption, materialism, looksmaxxing, and dominating women, Nelson said. “They’re quarantining themselves to their rooms and their tech devices and these online communities where they play video games, they gamble on sports, and they have conversations with other boys and young men online about somehow feeling disadvantaged as men in our society,” he said.
Burnetta, the high school senior, said he and many of his classmates’ feeds are populated with “super masculine” content that sometimes pokes fun at men who open up about their feelings, which can further add to the stereotype that men should not be emotional.
Even if boys don’t necessarily agree with these sentiments, they often don’t have other alternatives online. “I don’t think a lot of boys go on to YouTube…and say, ‘I really want to find the most misogynistic content I can find. That’s what I’m looking for,’” said Englar-Carlson, the director of the Center for Boys and Men. They may have simply wanted to watch a video about sports but were fed an ad for betting and then fell down the rabbit hole. Because traditional masculinity content is often fed to boys via their social media feeds, a brief introduction to these themes only leads to more.
By young adulthood, they will have a fairly concrete idea of what’s expected of them as a man. In a 2017 study, young men largely agreed that the cornerstones of masculinity are self-sufficiency, toughness, physical attractiveness, being a financial provider, heterosexuality, hypersexuality, aggression, and control. Notably, they said they feel external pressure from family, friends, and society to meet these ideals.
If adults start with the understanding that boys are emotional and they have the same social needs as girls, they can encourage them to make friends before they learn otherwise.
Teachers can recognize the signs of loneliness in young boys (resisting authority, talking back, and challenging boundaries) and use it as an opportunity to connect with their students instead of reprimanding them — because when they feel heard, their behavior softens. “What are these behaviors communicating to me from this boy about a met or unmet need, and how can I be responsive to it in my classroom? How can I help them facilitate close and connected friendships with not only their peers, but also with me as their teacher, like a primary adult in their lives?” Nelson said. When young boys simply get kicked out of class, they might fall behind and internalize a “bad boy” persona, he said, a cycle that enforces stereotypes and comes at the cost of their education.
The story of masculinity online and from political leaders is that men must be protectors, high earners, and muscular and strong, and when boys fail to meet that standard (which they inevitably do because they are children), they are made to feel inadequate. “They’re struggling in school, they’re having a difficult time finding work, but everything about what they’re learning about to live in America is about the dream, the aspirations, acquiring, hitting these life milestones,” Nelson said.
Demonstrate an alternative masculinity
But for some young men, the most impactful interventions take place while they’re young. Growing up, Michael Dean looked to his father and his friends’ fathers for how to be a man. These men often spoke of the importance of providing for a family, being decisive, and being a stable force. Dean thought everyone was raised with these values and had similar upbringings until he reached high school and joined Reichert’s peer counseling program.
His junior year, one of Dean’s teammates on the football team suggested that some of the young men check out the group to discuss any problems at school, issues with parents, friends, or partners. Dean was frustrated with his performance on the field and decided to attend. Hearing from his classmates — their grief, their struggles — helped give him perspective. He also learned how to be an emotional outlet for the people he loves, including his younger brother.
“I never felt that I had to be some kind of way or be some kind of man based on traditional values of being that strong, tough guy and to keep persevering through. I could definitely see that through my dad, and I did have that belief for a little while as I was in middle school and in the beginning of high school,” Dean, now 21, told Vox. “I learned that that’s not necessarily what it means to be a man, and I can make my own judgment through my own experiences and listening to other people to help me figure out what it means in my own belief to be a man.”
For Dean, learning how to be a man began when he was a child, but his path to adulthood was punctuated by formative adults — his mother, Reichert, and yes, even his dad — who fostered a safe environment to be vulnerable and emotional. Now, when he’s lonely, he knows he can call his family, friends, or his girlfriend for support. These are the outlets experts hope men feel empowered to call upon.
“If we’re really going to make a bigger difference with having healthier men who have connected friendships, who are emotionally expressive and connected in their friendships,” Reigeluth said, “it’s got to start with boys.”

Pargat Singh appointed Punjab Congress chief after Warring's exit, takes charge ahead of 2027 Assembly polls
Amarinder Singh Raja Warring, who had headed the state unit since April 2022, met Rahul Gandhi in Delhi and submitted his resignation.
The Indian National Congress on Friday appointed former Olympian and Jalandhar Cantonment MLA Pargat Singh as the new president of the Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee (PPCC).
Singh will replace Amarinder Singh Raja Warring, and take charge ahead of the 2027 Assembly polls in Punjab. Warring, who had headed the state unit since April 2022, met Congress MP Rahul Gandhi in Delhi and submitted his resignation.
The Jalandhar Cantonment MLA's elevation comes after months of differences within the Punjab Congress. Congress’s Punjab affairs in-charge Sachin Pilot had held consultations with state leaders before the leadership change.
Three-time Jalandar Cantonment MLA, experienced legislator
Pargat, 61, is a three-time MLA from Jalandhar Cantonment, having first won the seat in 2012 and retaining it in 2017 and 2022.
Pargat’s appointment brings an experienced legislator to the helm of Punjab Congress at a time when the party is seeking to bridge differences among its senior leaders and strengthen its organisation ahead of the polls.
Also Read | Why Warring's position in Punjab Congress became untenable once Pilot replaced Baghel
International hockey career
Before entering electoral politics, Singh had a long international hockey career and captained the Indian team at the 1992 Barcelona and 1996 Atlanta Olympics. He was also part of the Indian teams at the 1988 Seoul Olympics and several World Cups.
Born in Mithapur, Jalandhar, Pargat played for Punjab Police and was associated with Indian Railways. He served as Punjab’s director of sports and was credited with pushing sports infrastructure, including hockey turfs, in villages during his tenure. He was appointed India’s national hockey coach in 1998. He was conferred the Arjuna Award in 1989 and the Padma Shri in 1998.
Entry into politics
Pargat entered electoral politics with the Shiromani Akali Dal and won the Jalandhar Cantonment seat in 2012. He subsequently joined the Congress and retained the constituency in 2017 and 2022. He served as a cabinet minister in the Charanjit Singh Channi government from September 2021 to March 2022.
Within the Congress, Pargat has also held organisational responsibilities. In 2021, then PPCC president Navjot Singh Sidhu appointed him general secretary (organisation) of the state unit.
Pargat will now have the task of leading the party organisation into the 2027 assembly election while coordinating leaders from different factions and preparing the Congress for a contest in which organisational consolidation will be a key focus.

When my husband and I were planning our honeymoon along the Amalfi Coast, we had three criteria for every hotel we booked: superb dining, a dreamy wellness program, and a wow factor. We wanted something like a breathtaking view or spa-inspired bathroom, something that would keep us on our just-married high.
Years later, having traded newlywed life for the life of new parents, we were adamant that we would continue traveling. At 2 months old, our daughter Mabel had a passport. Before her first birthday, she'd clocked two international trips — one to Paris and one to the Dominican Republic — along with a domestic jaunt to Asheville. 
With each new hotel check-in during this new phase of life, I found that what I needed from my hotel stays started to shift.
The parent effect
I've had a long career in the travel space, with a decade spent on staff at "Fodor's Travel" and "Condé Nast Traveler," and now as a freelance travel writer. 
Hotels have always been front and center in my career and personal life. In my early years, I built digital products and guided editorial strategy centered on hotel evaluation, and later in my career, I was boots-on-the-ground reporting on the guest experience at luxury hotels around the world. My reporting always focused on the details the industry celebrates: the architecture, the spa, the lobby bar, the Michelin-starred restaurant.
But traveling with my daughter forced me to notice a different set of details, ones that most travelers, and many hotels, overlook.
Suddenly, I cared less about the premium wine list and more about if the in-room blackout curtains actually worked. I found myself checking how flexible the dinner hours were, whether there were affordable laundry services with same-day turnaround, whether the mini fridge could fit several bottles of milk, and whether there was a park within walking distance. The things I rarely, if ever, considered had suddenly become the things that could make or break my stay.
My new definition of five-star hospitality
Parenthood isn't for the weak. It shifts priorities and redirects attention in a way that can feel merciless. But it also brings a unique perspective and reveals the world to you in completely new ways: the joy of wide sidewalks, chasing park butterflies, and picking ice cream solely based on what color moves you that day. 
When it came to enjoying my lifelong passion for travel, parenthood didn't lower my standards for hotels, it just gave me an entirely new set of them. And for hotels looking to build and maintain guest loyalty, widening the focus on which amenities matter most is crucial. Because if there's one thing humans have proven they won't stop doing, it's making more humans.
More on traveling with kids
The hospitality industry has certainly gotten better at welcoming those new arrivals. "Family-friendly" no longer only implies overly stimulating Disney vacations or an unsettlingly warm kiddie pool. The growing trend of on-site kids clubs and child-friendly programming has also made traveling with children easier and more enjoyable. But if hotels truly wish to earn the loyalty of traveling parents, the focus needs to shift slightly.
I expect more now
Those traditional family amenities are low-hanging fruit, and the properties paying the most attention to families know it.
The details that have come to matter most to me are much smaller: a hotel that asks what my daughter's favorite snack is before we arrive, a staff member who remembers her name, or a housekeeper who tucks her favorite stuffy neatly into the made bed. These things aren't particularly glamorous. Nor do they require big budgets. Instead, they remind me that true hospitality is about personalization and customization, across ages, and that the smallest details often say more about a hotel's hospitality than its most expensive upgrades ever could.
For this traveling mom, attention is my new favorite amenity. Because at the end of the day, I didn't stop caring about the palatial marble bathroom anchored by a vanity with his-and-hers sinks, I just also want there to be a step stool so my daughter can reach the faucet.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

The US Coast Guard is searching for an air ambulance jet with six people onboard that lost contact with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) during a flight from Bermuda to Boston early on Saturday morning.
In a statement to the Guardian, an FAA spokesperson said that the agency issued a search-and-rescue alert notice for a Gulfstream G-100 at about 1.20am local time on Saturday.
The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers onboard when it departed Bermuda’s LF Wade international airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport, obtained by the Associated Press.
NBC News reported that the plane was carrying out a medical evacuation in Bermuda, citing a statement from Clarence Togeretz, the director of flight operations at Latitude Air Ambulance, the aircraft’s operator.
“We always get rather concerned when our crew doesn’t report to us in a timely manner,” he told NBC News. “But I will say that again, optimistically and positively, that doesn’t mean that the worst has happened.”
NBC also reported that the Massachusetts port authority, which operates Boston Logan international airport, said the aircraft did not arrive as scheduled. A port authority spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with those onboard and their loved ones as the search continues.”
The FAA is coordinating with the Rescue Coordination Center and the US Coast Guard to locate the aircraft.
The search area as of Saturday morning was off the coast of the island of Nantucket, Massachusetts, the coast guard said in a statement posted to X.
Air and surface crews have launched in search of the aircraft, the statement added.
Citing a source with knowledge of the investigation, ABC News reported there were no Americans onboard the plane, though the identities of those onboard were not immediately released.
Officials believe the plane rapidly descended 7,500ft before hitting the water, according to the outlet’s source.

School officials can’t figure out how their building became a bat haven with eight found in just over two weeks
Washington’s protected-wildlife rules limit how the school can handle the creatures

At least some of the Halloween decorations are alive at one Washington elementary school – but officials still can't figure out how the bats keep getting inside.
Eight bats have been found at Edgerton Elementary School in Puyallup, about 10 miles southeast of Tacoma, over 17 days. The latest was a dead one found Thursday in a mechanical room by district maintenance staff, according to the Puyallup School District's Bat Activity Tracker.
“Based on its condition, it appeared to have been there for some time,” a Puyallup School District spokesperson told The Independent Thursday. “This is the third bat that has been found in the mechanical room, and that pattern is helping inform where our investigation and mitigation efforts are currently focused.”
No human contact was reported in Thursday’s encounter, and the bat was disposed of under established protocols, the spokesperson said. Health Services is consulting with the Tacoma-Pierce County Health Department as a precaution.
Pest-control professionals will begin exclusion work at the school over the weekend, focusing first on the building’s exterior near the mechanical room to identify and seal potential entry points. The work may take multiple visits, the spokesperson said. So far, repeated inspections have found no evidence that the bats are roosting inside the school, its website states.
The first incident was reported September 14, when teachers found two live bats in a downstairs hallway near the cafeteria and gym. One staff member had potential contact with a bat, prompting Health Services to consult with the local health department and recommend medical attention, officials said.
Three days later, on September 17, a teacher spotted another live bat in the downstairs main hallway before classes began. Then, on September 23, a night-shift custodian found two more live creatures in the downstairs kindergarten hallway. Both were safely contained and removed, according to the district.
The two other latest incidents occurred in the upstairs mechanical area. On September 28, a live bat was found underneath the door to a mechanical room. The following day, officials discovered a dead animal inside the upstairs mechanical room.
An added obstacle to this problem is that Washington classifies all bat species as protected wildlife, meaning there are rules governing how they can be handled, according to the Washington Department of Fish & Wildlife. The school district can, however, safely remove bats found inside the school and is working to address the activity without violating state wildlife protections.
Students and staff are being told not to touch or attempt to capture a bat if they see one. Instead, they should leave the area and immediately notify a teacher, administrator or other school employee so the animal can be handled appropriately.
If a child physically comes into contact with a bat, parents are advised to contact the child's healthcare provider and notify the school and district Health Services immediately. Health officials can assess the circumstances and determine whether additional medical follow-up is needed.
Human rabies cases are extremely rare in Washington, with just two identified in the past 75 years, according to the Washington State Department of Health. Both were linked to the bat rabies virus. In 1995, a 4-year-old child died of rabies four weeks after a bat was found in her bedroom. Two years later, in 1997, a 64-year-old man also died of rabies, though the source of his exposure was unknown.
The Independent has contacted the Puyallup School District for comment.

By the time Mr. Saravanan turned 87, he had a severely narrowed aortic valve that was impacting his daily activities to an extent where he required oxygen support for about a month. Post the successful completion of a Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (TAVI) procedure, however, he recovered at an impressive pace. In just four days, he regained the strength to venture outdoors and cast his vote for the municipal elections. He lived an independent lifestyle till he crossed the milestone of 93 years old and finally breathed his last due to a fall while playing with his grandchildren.
Mr. Saravanan’s journey tells us the story of how far medical advancement in treating aortic valve disease has progressed. For those who qualify, TAVI offers a unique technique to replace the faulty aortic valve without undergoing the traditional open-heart surgery.
Understanding the aortic valve
The aortic valve forms one of the four valves within the human heart structure. It lies between the largest artery called the aorta and the main ventricle of the heart that pumps oxygen-rich blood across the entire body system. Each beat allows the leaflets of the valve, also known as cusps, to open for the outflow of blood and shut to stop any back flow.
With increasing years, calcium deposits on these valves make them thickened and rigid. The term for this is ‘aortic stenosis’. This condition is most prevalent as age advances over 70 years, when the calcification of the valve becomes prominent due to wear and tear. In many cases, patients present with aortic stenosis at an earlier stage of life due to a birth defect in the aortic valve. Being born with only two cusps of the valve instead of three, makes such valves prone to wear out sooner.
Why the narrowed valve is a problem
With a narrowing of the aortic valve, the heart needs to exert additional pressure to ensure flow of the blood through the restricted space. Early signs could be subtle: a task which had been manageable might now need an extra halt in between; routine tasks could suddenly drain energy like never before.
As symptoms intensify with time, the patient might encounter shortness of breath, discomfort in the chest area, dizziness or even fainting spells. These indicate worsening of the condition and must be addressed without further delay. A test known as an echocardiography is a painless diagnostic procedure using ultrasonic waves to assess the extent of narrowing of the valve, besides assessing cardiac function.
Commencement of symptomatic severe aortic stenosis marks an ominous milestone. It heralds rapid progression towards end-stage illness. Untreated, aortic stenosis inevitably results in heart failure and can lead to sudden cardiac death.
When the valve needs replacing
For several decades, severe aortic valve diseases were treated only with open heart surgery. TAVI has revolutionised the entire process for eligible patients. . In TAVI, a biological valve, usually bovine or porcine tissue stitched within a metallic frame, is placed at the tip of a catheter. The catheter is then typically inserted through the leg artery and moved all the way into the heart. At the site of the damaged valve, the new valve is deployed and it starts operating instantly.
Unlike traditional surgical procedures for valve replacement, TAVI doesn’t involve cutting through the chest bone. It is often performed under local anaesthesia with mild sedation depending on individual patient circumstances.
Its main benefit lies in quick mobilisation and most patients can be discharged within a few days after the procedure.
There can be no denying the fact that TAVI is evolving rapidly as an interventional cardiovascular technique. Its origins lay in its development for patients who were deemed too risky for any kind of surgical intervention. Over time, it has become the procedure of choice in most patients with aortic stenosis over 65 years.
Matching patients to treatments
It is important to understand that TAVI is not an option for everyone with aortic stenosis. It should be considered carefully in younger patients and in people with certain types of bicuspid aortic valve, an enlarged aorta or a need for additional bypass surgery.
Many factors come into play when determining what would work best for a given patient. Among the factors to consider are: age, general health status, longevity prospects, valve robustness, anatomical considerations, and potential need for further procedures down the line.
Advanced imaging technologies enable the medical team to analyse the anatomy of the patient, select the most appropriate path of intervention and decide on the correct valve and its size. There cannot be any one-size-fits-all strategy here. The treatment must focus on the unique circumstances of each person.
It is important to keep future treatment options open as each tissue valve can only last upto 10-12 years. This is why the heart team plays a significant role. Cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, and imaging experts work together to plan the most suitable treatment option for that individual.
What patients should know
For patients diagnosed with aortic stenosis and found suitable for TAVI, the procedure can improve quality of life and help them live longer. By easing symptoms such as breathlessness, tiredness and chest discomfort, it may make everyday activities easier again. The decision should also be part of a lifelong heart valve plan that considers how long the replacement valve may last and what treatment options might be needed in the future.
(Dr. G. Sengottuvelu is senior consultant – interventional cardiology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. drgseng@gmail.com)
