Congress attacks Manipur govt over Rs 8,927 crore unspent funds cited in CAG report
The Manipur Congress has cited the latest CAG report to question the state government's utilisation of budgeted funds. It says the figures raise concerns over spending, debt, incomplete projects and financial accountability.
The Manipur Congress has questioned the state government's financial management, citing the latest Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) report to flag the non-utilisation of Rs 8,927.55 crore from the total budgeted amount of Rs 37,392.66 crore in 2024-25.
Addressing a press conference at Congress Bhavan in Imphal on Saturday, Congress Legislature Party (CLP) leader K Meghachandra raised concerns over low capital expenditure, incomplete projects, gaps in Central assistance and the state's rising debt burden.
The CAG's State Finances Audit Report for 2024-25 was tabled in the Manipur Assembly on September 11. Meghachandra said the findings pointed to weaknesses in financial planning and budget execution, particularly at a time when the state is dealing with an ongoing crisis and requires greater spending on rehabilitation, development and essential public services.
23.88% OF BUDGETED AMOUNT REMAINED UNSPENT
Of the Rs 37,392.66 crore budget provision for 2024-25, Rs 8,927.55 crore remained unspent, amounting to an overall saving of 23.88 per cent, Meghachandra said, citing the CAG report.
He also highlighted the gap in capital expenditure. Against a capital budget of Rs 8,989.60 crore, the state spent Rs 2,704.23 crore, leaving around Rs 6,285 crore unspent.
“This is not merely about figures in government accounts. It is about whether public money allocated for development, infrastructure, health and welfare is being effectively utilised for the people,” he said.
CONGRESS FLAGS GAP IN CENTRAL ASSISTANCE
Meghachandra also questioned the difference between the budgeted and actual Central assistance received by Manipur.
According to figures cited by him from the CAG report, Rs 16,015.85 crore was budgeted as grants-in-aid from the Centre, while actual receipts stood at Rs 5,473.21 crore. This represented a difference of about Rs 10,542.64 crore.
“Why could this government not utilise the funds which were our share?” he asked, demanding an explanation for the shortfall.
He said the figures needed to be considered alongside the state government's repeated assertions that lack of funds and dependence on Central assistance were constraining expenditure.
BORROWINGS RISE, MOST USED TO REPAY OLD DEBT
The Congress leader also raised concerns over Manipur's borrowing pattern.
He said the state raised gross borrowings of Rs 11,599.08 crore in 2024-25. Of this, Rs 9,420.41 crore, or 81.22 per cent, went towards repayment of earlier principal.
According to figures cited by Meghachandra, Manipur's gross debt and other obligations increased from Rs 18,871.79 crore in 2023-24 to Rs 20,846.88 crore at the end of 2024-25. Interest payments during the year stood at Rs 1,022.23 crore.
He further cited a figure of Rs 32,590.57 crore for the state's total outstanding debt and liabilities as of March 31, 2026, based on the 2025-26 revised estimates.
“How long will the government continue to increase the state's debt and liabilities, and what is the plan to ensure sustainable public finances?” he asked.
138 PROJECTS REMAIN INCOMPLETE
Meghachandra also flagged the number of incomplete projects in the state.
He said 138 projects remained incomplete despite Rs 473.53 crore already having been spent on them. He warned that delays could deprive people of the intended benefits of these projects.
“It is a serious matter. In a small state like Manipur, 138 projects remain incomplete. How is this happening?” he said.
CONGRESS QUESTIONS SAVINGS UNDER DISASTER MANAGEMENT
Another issue raised by Meghachandra was the amount saved under Relief and Disaster Management.
He referred to savings of Rs 229.94 crore under the grant in 2024-25 and said substantial savings had also been recorded under the same grant in previous years.
“The CAG is not an opposition party. It is the constitutional auditor of public money,” he said.
Meghachandra said the report raised questions about budget utilisation, financial planning and execution. He asked the government to explain why large amounts remained unspent, how it planned to manage the state's growing debt and how funds earmarked for development and public welfare would be utilised effectively.
“These are not merely questions of accounting. They are questions of financial accountability and accountability to the people of Manipur,” he said.

Seoul warns 'further action' if Ukraine does not apologise over prisoner-of-war row
- Published
South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung has threatened to take unspecified "further action" if Ukraine does not issue a public apology for revealing that two North Korean prisoners of war had been sent to the South.
Ukraine's leader Volodymyr Zelensky made the disclosure to the UN general assembly last week, angering Seoul, who said the move was meant to stay secret.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Thursday described the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding", adding that Kyiv was "working" to resolve it.
Lee rejected this characterisation on X, saying it concerned "the dignity of the Korean people and the nation".
Lee's office said last week that it was Ukraine that requested for the move to be kept secret, partly to protect the North Koreans' families, and also because Kyiv wanted to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Zelensky's office responded, saying the two countries had no such agreement to keep the move confidential, further escalating the situation.
Lee himself faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure, with the South Korean opposition accusing him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
The two soldiers, who were among thousands of North Koreans supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
Speaking to Ukrainian media on Thursday, Sybiha, the foreign minister, said he "hopes that this situation will be resolved in the very near future".
"We are working on it. For us, South Korea is an important country. And I really hope for momentum, continuation, and concrete results that we are truly achieving with them," he said.
Lee, in response, accused Kyiv of attempting to "bring war on the Korean Peninsula".
"We express serious regret that, instead of acknowledging the facts of the agreement and apologising, they are talking about an imminent military clash between the North and South," he said in an X post.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has adhered to its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.

When it comes to income and taxation, documents and money trail form an important part of the process. This is particularly important when income from any of your sources is in cash. In one such case, a landlord faced income tax scrutiny due to cash deposits made on account of rental income that he received.
The Bangalore bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) recently held that rental income already disclosed to the income tax authorities can be considered as an identifiable source of cash deposited into a bank account at a later date.
Even where a landlord claims to have collected rent in cash, the subsequent deposit of that money cannot be disregarded merely because the rental earnings have already been taxed.
In this case, the tribunal clarified that disclosed rental receipts must be considered while examining the taxpayer's cash flow.
What the case is about
A man in Bengaluru owned properties that he rented out and collected the rent in cash. He also received substantial amounts as rental advances, but again in cash. During 
demonetisation
, when Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes ceased to be legal tender, the landlord in this case deposited Rs 14.96 lakh in cash into his bank account.
The man had income from three sources: salary, house property and other sources. Between November 9 and December 30, 2016, he deposited as much as Rs 14.96 lakh into his bank account. This prompted the 
Income Tax Department
 to select his return for scrutiny to establish the source of the cash.
The Assessing Officer (AO) at Koramangala subsequently issued a tax notice requiring him to explain where the deposited cash had come from.
The man on his part submitted that the deposits were on account of the money that he had accumulated over a period from income sources already disclosed to the department.
His cash position included an opening balance of Rs 10,05,793 on April 1, 2016, in addition to rental income, advances received from tenants, bank withdrawals and other receipts during the financial year.
He supported his explanation with cash books, bank statements, cash-flow statements, financial statements and records showing how the cash moved over time. The AO remained unconvinced and classified the entire deposit of Rs 14,96,500 as 'unexplained money' under Section 69A.
The tax officer rejected the man’s explanation, following which he challenged the decision before the Bangalore ITAT.
The Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), or CIT(A) also sustained the addition.
The concerns underlying the decision included the substantial cash balance claimed by the man, his comparatively modest household withdrawals and certain receipts recorded shortly before demonetisation.
The landlord ultimately succeeded before the tribunal in August 2026.
How did the landlord win the case?
The ITAT Bangalore ordered the deletion of the entire addition of Rs 14,96,500 made under Section 69A. With that addition removed, the issue of applying Section 115BBE to the amount also became irrelevant. The man’s appeal was accordingly allowed.
Chartered Accountant Suresh Surana told ET that the man faced an 'unexplained cash' notice under Section 69A after the AO refused to accept his explanation for the cash deposited during demonetisation.
The Bangalore ITAT took a different view after examining the records. It found that the man had established a continuous trail demonstrating the availability of cash.
His cash-flow statement reflected an opening balance of Rs 4.72 lakh as of April 1, 2015, followed by cash received through rent, bank withdrawals and other disclosed sources. These transactions resulted in a cash balance of Rs 10.05 lakh on April 1, 2016. Additional cash inflows were also documented for the period from April to October 2016, according to the ET report.
Surana says: “Thus, the explanation was not based on a sudden cash entry immediately before demonetisation but on a running cash-flow extending from the preceding financial year.”
Surana said one of the key considerations in the man’s favour was that the Assessing Officer had based the assessment on a mistaken assumption that the cash deposits arose from business transactions or “cash sales”.
The man had never stated that he was engaged in such a business. His explanation throughout was that the money had accumulated from rental collections, advances received from tenants, bank withdrawals and other sources already disclosed to the tax authorities.
The ITAT Bangalore, therefore, found that rejecting his explanation because he could not establish cash sales or produce business books did not deal with the actual source of funds he had put forward.

Surana said the tribunal also disagreed with the argument that rental earnings could not be treated as a source for the bank deposits simply because they had already been taxed under the head “Income from House Property”.
Significance of what ITAT said
The ITAT clarified that whether a receipt is taxable and whether it can explain the availability of cash are two distinct issues. Where rent declared to the tax authorities was genuinely collected in cash, those receipts could subsequently be deposited into a bank account.
Surana says: “Similarly, there was no statutory requirement requiring an individual to immediately deposit cash receipts into a bank merely because the Income Tax Department considered the amount retained in cash to be high.”
In other words, suspicion over the amount of cash accumulated by a taxpayer cannot, by itself, justify an addition.
Surana said that when a taxpayer identifies the source of funds and submits a cash-flow statement along with supporting documents, the department must assess the material objectively. It must also produce affirmative evidence to establish why the taxpayer's explanation is incorrect.
In this matter, there was no evidence to establish that the cash-flow statement was fabricated, that the declared rental receipts had not actually been collected, that the rental advances were fictitious or that the cash available with him had already been utilised for other purposes.
Surana said the ITAT Bangalore consequently held that the man’s explanation could not be discarded simply because the tax authorities regarded his accumulated cash balance as unusually large.
The taxpayer succeeded because he demonstrated a credible and consistent trail explaining both the origin of the money and its continued availability. In contrast, the department's decision to reject his explanation rested largely on doubts and assumptions, without evidence contradicting the records he had submitted.

A chronic autoimmune skin condition in which the body’s immune system mistakes melanocytes (cells which produce melanin, giving colour to your skin, hair and eyes) as enemies and attacks them. This leads to patches of depigmentation anywhere in your body. This condition is known as vitiligo.
Types of vitiligo
The main types of vitiligo are non-segmental and segmental vitiligo.
Non-segmental vitiligo is the most common form, where colour loss appears symmetrically on both sides of the body, such as both hands or both knees. Segmental vitiligo, on the other hand, often starts at a younger age and affects only one side or a single specific area of the body.
What causes vitiligo?
While the primary reason for vitiligo is not fully understood, it is seen to be caused by various factors, from genetics to immune dysfunction.
Research has shown that vitiligo is primarily a T-cell–mediated autoimmune disease where CD8+ cytotoxic T cells attack and destroy skin pigment cells called melanocytes, leading to white patches on the skin.
Having a family member with vitiligo or other autoimmune diseases is shown to have an increased risk, suggesting shared genetic susceptibility. Environmental factors like oxidative stress, skin trauma, and certain chemicals can sometimes trigger or worsen vitiligo in genetically susceptible people.
Vitiligo is also often associated with other autoimmune conditions, especially autoimmune thyroid disease, so clinicians may screen for these in some patients.
Symptoms of vitiligo
The main symptom of vitiligo is depigmentation and the appearance of patches on your body. This can be anywhere from your face and hands to your knees or feet. Hair in the affected area may also turn white.
There are various ways through which doctors can help you diagnose vitiligo and determine what type of vitiligo you may have. One major examination done is the Wood’s lamp examination, where ultraviolet light is used to distinguish vitiligo from other hypopigmented conditions.
Treatment options
Treatment for vitiligo is mostly connected to re-pigmentation, or slowing progression, depending on the type of vitiligo and patient preference rather than a guaranteed cure.
There are various types of topical treatments (like creams for external use) which can often help with inflammation, as well as medical light treatments like narrowband UVB phototherapy and excimer laser or lamp. Availability of certain treatments also changes from country to country and by the patient’s age group. There are situations where oral medication is also used for the short term. People with stable vitiligo can also consider surgical options if other treatments are not working, and depigmentation therapy if a major part of the person’s natural pigmentation is lost.

Vaccine schedules, catch-up vaccination, and common misconceptions about immunisation were among the issues discussed by doctors at The Hindu’s Health Webinar Series on ‘Vaccines: Armour Against Infectious Diseases’ held on Sunday.
Janani Sankar, medical director, Kanchi Kamakoti CHILDS Trust Hospital, Chennai, explained the recommended vaccination schedule for children, the importance of completing the required doses and what parents can do when a child misses a scheduled vaccine. She also addressed questions about vaccination during minor illnesses, such as a cold, cough or fever, and concerns about children receiving multiple vaccines.
Dr. Sankar discussed common reactions following vaccination and symptoms that may require medical attention, as well as vaccines recommended for children in specific situations.
Dilip Mathai, senior consultant in Infectious Diseases, Naruvi Hospitals, and Professor of Medicine and Adult Infectious Diseases, discussed vaccination in adults, including how vaccination needs may change with age and individual circumstances. He explained options for adults who do not have records of earlier vaccinations, and the role of catch-up vaccination. He also discussed travel vaccination, including the need to consider recommended vaccines based on the destination and travel plans.
Vaccination during pregnancy and considerations for people taking long-term medicines or living with chronic conditions were also discussed.
The doctors also addressed questions on vaccine safety, side-effects, information circulating on social media, vaccination after an infectious disease, and immunisation during outbreaks.
The webinar was moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, senior reporter, The Hindu.
The webinar can be viewed at https://newsth.live/vaccination.

Croatia vs England; UEFA Nations League Group A3
Croatia vs England. UEFA Nations League Group A3.
Stadion HNK Rijeka.
Croatia 0-7 England: Amazing Nations League win as Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka each score twice in huge victory
Match report as England put SEVEN past Croatia in Rijeka in an emphatic victory in their Nations League Group A3 fixture; Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka scored twice while Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers were also on target for the Three Lions
Saturday 3 October 2026 19:11, UK
England produced a dominant performance that will live long in the memory to defeat Croatia 7-0 in their Nations League tie in Rijeka.
In what must surely rank as one of England's best away results, Thomas Tuchel's side utterly overwhelmed their opponents. Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka scored two each but it was a stunning team performance that inflicted Croatia's biggest defeat.
The skipper opened the scoring by firing high into the roof of the net early on after being well fed by Jude Bellingham before Anthony Gordon's ingenuity engineered the second for Bellingham to score himself soon after. England were rampant from the outset.
- As it happened | Teams | Stats | Nations League tables
- England latest news blog | Nations League scores & news
The excellent Gordon had chances of his own before making it three. There had been some disquiet that Jarell Quansah had been preferred to Trent Alexander-Arnold but the Bayer Leverkusen man whipped in a quality cross for the Barcelona winger to nod in a third.
When Bellingham set up Bukayo Saka for the fourth before the break, Slaven Bilic looked shocked. Although Mateo Kovacic did miss a sitter, the score did not flatter England. It was an 'I-was-there moment' for the 100 away fans allowed in the stadium.
Croatia tried to be more aggressive after the break but a sensational team goal underlined England's superiority as Kane latched onto Elliot Anderson's cross to make it five. Saka soon latched onto an error for the sixth and Morgan Rogers capped it off late on.
Tuchel needed a strong showing during this quartet of Nations League games that concludes with a home game against the Czech Republic on Tuesday. The opening defeat to Spain followed by a win over a Czech side reduced to 10 men was insufficient.
This was as convincing as it gets against a Croatia team, led by Luka Modric, that looked unable to compete with the speed, strength and skill of an England side that included Alex Scott from the start for the first time. This was a significant win in Group A3 too.
With World Cup winners Spain currently boasting the perfect record, there is likely to be only more space available to qualify for the last eight of the Nations League in the spring. This win goes some way to securing that spot for England. A big boost for Tuchel.

8 - GOAL! Kane fired home after being fed by Bellingham
21 - GOAL! Bellingham made it two from Gordon's assist
39 - GOAL! Gordon headed in Quansah's right-wing cross

Keane: Bellingham can become a great
Roy Keane speaking on ITV:
"Everything you would want. A complete performance in possession. Goal threat. Scored the seven goals. Kept a clean sheet. Hunting in packs when they lost the ball.
"England were clinical as well. Excellent. All the plaudits have to go to England. They were fantastic.
"Bellingham can go on to become one of the greatest players of all time. There's still a lot more to come from him. He's a huge leader for England."
More history for Kane
On the day that the England captain moved within one cap of Peter Shilton's record, Kane scored for the third consecutive game in this Nations League break. With six goals in his last five games for Bayern Munich too, his relentlessness really is remarkable.
Fresh from scoring 73 goals all competitions for club and country last season, Kane has now netted in each of his last six away appearances for his country, with only three men previously having scored in that many consecutive away matches for the Three Lions.
The most recent of those was Stan Mortensen in 1948 and the only man to score in seven matches in a row is Tom Finney. Kane will need to score away from home against Spain next month to match that particular feat. On this form, do not rule that out.

Criminal syndicates targeting international students to smuggle Aussie reptiles, authorities warn
Australian reptiles are a lucrative trade on the black market for exotic animals, and authorities warn international students are increasingly being targeted to smuggle them out of the country.
Dani Yannopoulos from the National EPA said serious organised criminal networks are using global networks to move drugs, firearms and exotic animals.
"There's a demand for our unique wildlife," Ms Yannopoulos said.
She said the agency has seen a trend of international students being targeted to move the animals.
It follows a record number of specimens intercepted by authorities last year, including the second-highest number of reptiles seized in the past six years.
Ms Yannopoulos says young people were being targeted on social media and offered money to move wildlife, often without knowing the full extent of the operation.
"Sometimes they might know what's in the package, sometimes they don't; it might just be transporting from one state to another to get to an exit point."
An international student was sentenced to 18 months in prison last year for attempting to send native Australian reptiles to China. She had attempted to export 15 lizards from Queensland to China, with an estimated "street value" of $74, 207.
Under Australian law, it's illegal to export live native Australian mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians for commercial purposes, and disrupting the illegal trade is part of the remit of the newly established National EPA.
Loading...
Young people charged with attempted wildlife smuggling
Several young people have been allegedly involved in wildlife smuggling attempts recently.
In September, a 21-year-old man was charged with allegedly attempting to smuggle 163 native reptiles from Sydney to Hong Kong as air cargo.
In a separate case in July, a man in his 20s was fined more than $30,000 for attempting to post 65 reptiles from Western Australia to New South Wales.
The parcels were intercepted, with four lizards found dead, while another 51 had to be euthanised.
And last year, a 27-year-old man was sentenced to almost three years in prison for attempting to mail 27 reptiles to Hong Kong, including nine blue-tongue lizards.
Ms Yannopoulos said criminal networks recruited people at the lower levels of their operations to distance themselves.
"So anyone that they can use, any vulnerable person in particular, that they pay a little bit of money because they're going to be the first points of contact."
Where are they going?
Sebastian Chekunov, a researcher with Adelaide University's Wildlife Crime Research Hub, said individual Australian reptiles could fetch "anywhere from a few hundred [dollars] to over $10,000".
"When they're being smuggled out, they're mostly going to Hong Kong as a first step," Dr Chekunov said.
He said once native species made it overseas, they could often reach exotic pet markets in China, Europe, the US and Canada.
"Overseas, the consumers in the end markets, oftentimes they don't know that these animals have been smuggled out.
"You can just go into a pet shop and buy one.
"But then for the rarer species, we see people who own them are more like collectors.
"They want to get one of everything. They'll spend whatever money they can to get it."
Dr Chekunov said the transport could be harmful to the animals' wellbeing.
"They're often wrapped up tightly inside packages, not able to move, not given food and water for however long they're wrapped up."
What do the numbers say?
Figures provided to triple j hack by the National EPA show 1,048 wildlife specimens were intercepted in 2025, including 343 reptiles.
The animals intercepted included snakes, lizards, dragons, skinks, monitors and turtles.
Shingleback and blue-tongue lizards were in the highest numbers, accounting for 208 combined.
Authorities also intercepted 37 pythons and 15 lace monitors.
The number of specimens fluctuates significantly from year to year, with 211 intercepted in 2024 and 595 in 2023.
An increase in seizures containing invertebrates, such as ants or beetles, can significantly impact the count.
Reptile hobbyists respond
Australia also has a large community of legal reptile breeders and hobbyists, who say the illegal trade risks damaging the reputation of the industry.
Jayden, a reptile hobbyist who did not want his surname published, said most people in the reptile community strongly opposed smuggling.
"It's pretty frowned upon by the majority of the industry and hobbyists for reptiles. They're adamantly against smuggling," he said.
Jayden, who keeps two snakes, said illegal operators tended to work in secretive networks, making them difficult for the wider reptile community to identify.
"Those small circles of smugglers and such, they really keep to themselves and they essentially operate in the shadows," he said.
Authorities say licensed reptile breeders and hobbyists can play an important role in identifying suspicious activity and helping disrupt the illegal trade.

Mankind Pharma has announced ₹1 crore contribution to Captain Smit Machchhar and his family, describing the gesture as an expression of gratitude for his courage and leadership during what the company called an "unimaginable crisis".
The pharmaceutical company announced it through a statement on LinkedIn. Along with the post, it also shared a letter from its Vice Chairman and Managing Director Rajeev Juneja, in which he praised Machchhar for putting his crew and passengers before himself.
"Some acts of courage stay with an entire nation," Mankind Pharma said. "In a moment of unimaginable crisis, #CaptSmitMachchhar showed composure and responsibility, and put his crew and every passenger before himself."
Quick answers to key questions
Mankind Pharma contributed ₹1 crore as a gesture of gratitude for Machchhar's courage and leadership during a crisis when he prioritized the safety of his crew and passengers.
Captain Machchhar was injured but successfully opened the cockpit door, allowing crew members and passengers to overpower the co-pilot who attacked him, thus preventing a potential disaster.
Rajeev Juneja praised Machchhar as 'a hero of our times,' highlighting his composure and responsibility in a moment of extreme crisis, which served as an inspiration to many.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised Captain Machchhar for his bravery and presence of mind during the FlyDubai incident, calling it a moment of national pride.
On a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, Captain Machchhar was stabbed by his co-pilot in an apparent hijack attempt, which he thwarted through a courageous response.
The company said the contribution was its "humble expression of gratitude" and added, "Capt. Smit, you have made India proud. We salute you."
Juneja, while reposting Mankind Pharma's statement, wrote that the company believed that pride and appreciation should translate into meaningful action.
"When we witness an act of extraordinary courage and our hearts are filled with pride, we have a choice: let that emotion pass with time, or turn it into meaningful action," Juneja said.
He said the company decided to support Machchhar after seeing news about his actions, adding that Mankind wanted to go beyond praising his courage and "stand behind our words with meaningful action".
"Because emotions fade, but actions leave a lasting impact," Juneja said.
According to Juneja, the ₹1 crore contribution is Mankind Pharma's way of conveying that it recognises Machchhar's courage and stands with him and his family.
In the letter addressed to Machchhar, Juneja described him as "a hero of our times" and said his courage, composure and sense of responsibility had touched people in India and around the world.
Juneja said Machchhar demonstrated leadership at a time when fear and pressure were high and the lives of passengers and crew depended on his decisions.
"A leader is not tested when everything is going well. The real test comes in a moment of extreme crisis, when fear is natural, pressure is immense, and the lives of so many people depend on your decisions," he wrote.
He said Machchhar had thought about his crew and passengers and taken responsibility for the lives entrusted to him.
"No amount of money can ever equal the value of the lives you protected or the inspiration you have given to millions," Juneja wrote, describing the ₹1 crore contribution as a "small expression" of the company's respect, gratitude and admiration.
He concluded the letter by thanking Machchhar for putting others before himself and for "reminding all of us that, even in the most difficult moments, humanity must always come first".
Machchhar was reportedly stabbed with a knife by his co-pilot on the FlyDubai flight from UAE to Israel on Wednesday in an apparent act of hijack. Despite being seriously injured, Machchhar was able to open the cockpit door by activating the door release. This allowed the crew members and passengers to enter the cockpit and overpower the attacker.
The flight carrying 174 passengers was later diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi also had a telephonic conversation with Machchhar on Friday. PM Modi praised his courage and presence of mind during the incident.

Wu thrashes Trump to set up Yuan final in Shenzhen
- Published
Reigning world champion Wu Yize won six consecutive frames to beat Judd Trump 6-1 in the Shenzhen Open semi-finals.
Wu, who will leapfrog Trump in the rankings and move second in the world after the final, bounced back in dramatic fashion after losing the opening frame to set up an all-Chinese final against Yuan Sijun at the Bao'an Sports Centre on Sunday.
Yuan, 26, endured a much more difficult route to his maiden ranking final, battling through 6-5 against Englishman Jimmy Robertson.
World number two Trump, who won the Shanghai Masters in August, had gone into the Shenzhen semi-final in fine form after beating Mark Selby 5-0 in the last eight.
But after clinching the opening frame with a break of 77, the 2019 world champion handed the initiative to his opponent with a string of errors.
Wu, 22, capitalised to avenge a defeat by Trump at the last-four stage in Shanghai earlier this year, making three breaks of 50 or more in a scrappy encounter before clinching victory with a break of 110.
"When I was preparing for the evening match, I saw that Yuan had shed some tears," Wu told World Snooker Tour.
"I believe it is his first ranking final. Hopefully, we can put on a great match for everyone. Of course, I hope I can take the trophy home, but we will both give it everything we have."
An emotional Yuan found it much more difficult to get over the winning line, with the lead continually changing hands throughout the best-of-11 encounter before his opponent forced a deciding frame that took 50 minutes to complete and saw a total of 177 points scored.
Robertson put Yuan in a difficult snooker on the final red and clawed back 41 penalty points before himself being put in a snooker, with Yuan finally clearing to the pink to earn his place in the final of the inaugural event.
"I feel that my first ranking final has come a little bit late," said Yuan, who started the tournament as the world number 33 but would move to the cusp of the top 16 with victory on Sunday.
"Since the pandemic in 2020, the years in between have been quite difficult, and I feel it hasn't been easy. So after all these years, I just hope I can give myself something to show for it."

West Indies coach Daren Sammy, on the eve of the third and final ODI against India, said a win against the world’s top-ranked side would give his team the much-needed confidence at a time when the players brace for pay cuts back home.

Chasing 352, Hope, opening the batting, scored his second century on the bounce as the Caribbean outfit hunted down the target with 10 balls to spare.

Rohit Sharma (92, 85b, 10x4, 3x6) and Ruturaj Gaikwad (57, 69b, 1x4, 4x6) steadied the innings with a 137-run stand. The former started cautiously against a disciplined opening burst from Seales and Matthew Forde before shifting gears.
After Rohit’s departure, Rahul took charge. The latter hit boundaries through conventional strokes, the best being the straight drive off Seales. During his knock, Rahul surpassed 10,000 international runs. At the back end of the innings, he showcased his repertoire and brought up his ninth ODI ton in style, pulling Seales over fine-leg for a maximum.
However, on this day, Hope did spring eternal for West Indies.

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito says he is considering retirement and could hand Trump another nomination
Alito, 76, is one of six conservative justices on the nine-person Supreme Court

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito has revealed that he is considering retirement, potentially handing President Donald Trump another nomination.
“It’s something that I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term,” the 76-year-old justice told CBS News in a clip from an interview set to air Monday.
“But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place.”
There are already three Trump-nominated justices on the bench — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.
The Supreme Court’s 6-3 conservative lean wouldn’t change if Alito retired and Trump nominated a new justice. But Alito’s retirement would allow Trump to appoint a fourth justice to the court. Alito was nominated by then-President George W. Bush in the fall of 2005 and took his seat on the bench in January 2006.
Trump has lashed out at the Supreme Court for several rulings against him on controversial issues like his sweeping tariff policy and his challenge to birthright citizenship. Alito sided with Trump on those two issues.
The timing of a Supreme Court justice’s retirement is crucial because the party in power can change the court’s political leaning for decades.
Republicans blocked then-President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland in 2016 after conservative Justice Antonin Scalia died more than 11 months before Trump would be sworn into office. Trump then replaced Scalia with Gorsuch, who took his seat in April 2017.
While Trump has another two years in office, if Democrats take control of the Senate in November’s midterms, they could make it harder for a potential Alito replacement to be confirmed.
“You decided not to retire this year despite, I think, some pretty intense pressure from Republicans who thought, ‘Well, Republicans are in control of the Senate, so it would be easier to confirm your replacement,’” CBS News Chief Legal Correspondent Jan Crawford said in her interview with Alito.
When then-Fox Business host Maria Bartiromo asked Trump in April about rumors of Alito stepping down, the president said, “it’d be nice to say now I have somebody for 40 years,” but then praised the justice’s work.
“Justice Alito is an unbelievable justice and a brilliant justice — and he gets the country. He does what’s right for the country,” Trump said.
Alito said in his interview with CBS News that “it’s too hard to predict how, for anybody and particularly when you reach a certain age, what your situation will be a year from now, two years from now and so forth. And it’s too hard to predict what the political situation will be and what any president might do with respect to a replacement.”

Who are the mystery men who stepped in to keep the FlyDubai plane from crashing?
Three days have passed since FlyDubai attack but the two uniformed crew members who stepped in to stabilize and land the lane are still not publicly identified
JERUSALEM -- Who are the mystery pilots who stepped in to stabilize the FlyDubai flight as it hurtled toward disaster?
As of Saturday, three days after the uniformed crew members rushed to the cockpit to steady the Israel-bound plane carrying 182 people after a sickening plummet, they still haven't been publicly identified. FlyDubai has called them only on-duty crew members traveling on the plane. It’s not clear why the airline hasn't said more.
One passenger at the front of the plane, though, described the men’s actions in an interview with The Associated Press, giving one of the most detailed accounts of the yet-unsung heroes.
“This is one of the miracles,” said Daniel Schlichter, who was seated in the second row.
“That not in every flight they bring two extra pilots. In this case, they brought them because they should have brought the plane back from Tel Aviv to Dubai, and this is the only reason they were there.” The practice is called deadheading.
The two men responded after screaming passengers discovered what was unfolding in the cockpit. They said the copilot was attacking the captain over and over, and blood was everywhere. The captain, while badly wounded, managed to unlock the cockpit door.
After a passenger grabbed the copilot and pulled him out, and others grappled with the man to subdue him, Schlichter said that one of the traveling pilots practically hurtled the scrum to enter the cockpit and seize the controls.
“He was actually kind of jumping above the guys that were handling the terrorist, and he reached out to the pilot area and started to take over,” Schlichter said. “And then the other guy, the other pilot, joined in and they closed the door because they didn’t want anybody else to be there.”
Schlichter, like others, wasn’t sure where the two men had come from. But whoever the first one was, he moved very quickly.
“He acted really like a hero, taking over the plane and reacted like he understood exactly what is going on, and I think we owe him our lives not less than the other heroes that went on the flight,” Schlichter said.
Once the two entered the cockpit and closed the door, Schlichter wasn’t sure who did what inside. It took “quite a lot of minutes,” maybe 10 or more, to stabilize the plane after a descent so extreme that part of its rudder was torn away.
A mayday call was made as the men frantically sought a place to land.
Meanwhile, some of the frightened and wary passengers wondered about them and whether they could be trusted.
“After they managed to stabilize the airplane, actually they did not have any communication with us, and I have to tell you, I was worried about this,” Schlichter said.
He worried about an even worse situation — that the men might be “hijacking the plane into maybe Iran, or I don’t know where, because we’re actually not too far.”
But after about 45 minutes, he said, the pilots announced that they would be landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and everything was going to be OK.
With that, Schlichter said, he decided to trust them. And it turned out to be true.

Delhi’s new draft electoral roll has 97,53,577 names. In February 2025, 94,94,607 people voted in the Delhi assembly elections. Eighteen months later, the roll of eligible voters has just 2,58,970, or 2.7%, more names than the number of people who turned out to vote last year.
Now, in 24 of Delhi’s 70 assembly constituencies, the gap has disappeared altogether: The draft roll contains fewer names than the number of people who actually voted in those seats in 2025.
The numbers raise a fundamental question about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR): Has the exercise removed large numbers of people who were genuine, eligible voters and actually cast their ballots in 2025? Or did the electoral rolls used for that election contain a large number of names that should never have been there — including people who had died, shifted or were duplicated? The Election Commission of India (ECI) needs to account for the discrepancy.
An Alt News analysis of constituency-wise data procured and compiled by Mandate Analytics from ECI’s own records shows that the draft roll published on August 31, 2026, under the SIR has fewer names than the number of people who voted in the 2025 election in 24 constituencies.
Delhi SIR in Numbers
The SIR, which began in Bihar in June 2025, has resulted in more than 13 crore names being excluded from draft electoral rolls across 30 states and union territories, according to The Indian Express. In Delhi, the draft roll has shrunk by 58,73,159 names, or 37.6%, compared with the 2025 electoral roll.
The SIR began with a base list of 1.45 crore names — 11.16 lakh fewer than the electoral roll used for the 2025 election. Every elector on the base list was to receive an enumeration form from a booth level officer (BLO) and return the completed form. Forms that were not returned were marked “uncollectable” and assigned one of the ASDDO categories: absent, shifted, dead, duplicate or other. These electors were then excluded from the draft roll. Across Delhi, 47,56,722 forms, which is nearly a third of the base list, were marked uncollectable.
The exclusions were unevenly distributed. In South East Delhi, an average of 43.5% of the base-list names in each constituency were marked uncollectable, compared with 24.3% in Outer North Delhi.
The 24 Constituencies Which Throw up a Puzzle
In February 2025, Sangam Vihar had 2,05,647 names on its electoral roll, and 1,25,723 people voted. BJP’s Chandan Kumar Choudhary won the seat by 344 votes — the narrowest margin in the city. The SIR draft roll now lists 1,14,412 electors in Sangam Vihar: 91,235 fewer than the 2025 roll and 11,311 fewer than the number of people who actually voted.
The disparity extends across 24 constituencies. A total of 28,89,268 people voted in these seats in 2025, while the SIR draft roll now has just 27,66,145 names. This means that, even under the impossible assumption that every person on the current draft roll voted in 2025, at least 1,23,123 people who actually voted last year are no longer on the draft rolls of these constituencies.
That is a floor, not an estimate of the actual number. The real number of 2025 voters missing from the draft rolls can only be higher.
These 24 constituencies had 49,14,127 electors in 2025, of whom 58.8% voted. The SIR draft roll now contains 27,66,145 names — just 56.3% of the 2025 electorate, below the 58.8% turnout. In Tughlakabad, 56.1% of electors voted in 2025, while the draft roll contains just 49% of the 2025 electorate. In New Delhi, 56.7% voted; the draft roll contains 48.1%.
Across these constituencies, the electoral roll has fallen by 21,47,982 names, or 43.7%, since 2025. Of these, 4,10,759 names were already absent from the SIR base list, while 17,37,223 forms were marked uncollectable during the revision. Tughlakabad has the highest uncollectable rate in Delhi, at 47.8% of its base list.
All seven constituencies in South East Delhi — Jangpura, Kasturba Nagar, Sangam Vihar, Kalkaji, Tughlakabad, Badarpur and Okhla — are among the 24 constituencies where the draft roll is smaller than the number of people who voted in 2025.
In four seats the gap between the draft roll and 2025 turnout is larger than the margin that decided the seat. These are: Sangam Vihar, New Delhi, Delhi Cantt and Rajinder Nagar. In New Delhi, Arvind Kejriwal lost by 4,089 votes. The seat had 1,08,788 electors in 2025; the draft roll has 52,368, which is 9,318 short of the number of people who voted.
The Cuts are not Over
It is also worth remembering that the draft roll is not the final roll; it is likely to shrink further.
After the uncollectable forms were set aside, a second round of exclusions began. Electors whose names appeared on the draft roll are now being served notices requiring them to produce documents. Those unable to establish their eligibility risk being excluded from the final roll. In these 24 constituencies, 9,78,541 electors — about 35% of those on the draft roll — have been served notices. Across Delhi, the figure is 33.13 lakh.
The impact could extend well beyond these 24 constituencies. If just one in 10 of the electors served notices is ultimately excluded, 39 of Delhi’s 70 constituencies would have fewer names on the final roll than the number of people who voted there in 2025.
The Question the EC has to Answer
In other words, in February 2025, the ECI’s roll for these 24 constituencies had 49.14 lakh names, and 28.89 lakh people voted. Its own revision now leaves just 27.66 lakh names on the draft roll — fewer than the number of people who actually voted in those constituencies 18 months ago. And the roll is still shrinking.
The numbers demand an explanation. Either the SIR has excluded large numbers of genuine, living residents who voted in the 2025 election, or the rolls on which the ECI conducted that election contained lakhs of names that should not have been there. Either way, the discrepancy is one the Commission needs to account for.
It is also, in substance, the same Election Commission. The Delhi election was conducted under chief election commissioner (CEC) Rajiv Kumar, with Gyanesh Kumar and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu as election commissioners. Gyanesh Kumar took over as CEC on February 19, 2025, just days after the results. He has since overseen the SIR exercise.
Questions from Inside the Commission
These numbers come at a time when the SIR is itself facing scrutiny within the Election Commission.
An investigation by The Indian Express, published on September 23, reported that two of the three members of the Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, objected on record at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders issued during the nationwide rollout of the SIR. In several instances, they recorded that decisions had been taken without their knowledge. The report does not examine Delhi, but one of the concerns it raises is directly relevant to the revision here.
Who decided? The ECI has repeatedly responded to allegations of electoral-roll manipulation by pointing out that rolls in each constituency are prepared and maintained under the authority of the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO), a statutory official. But according to The Indian Express, both Commissioners raised concerns that this safeguard was being weakened. Joshi flagged the increasing centralisation of the electoral-roll database, while Sandhu recorded that state election officials had said they did not have full access to ERONet, the software used to maintain the rolls.
That raises a question for Delhi: when 17.37 lakh names were marked uncollectable across 24 constituencies, and all seven constituencies in South East Delhi were among those with the highest rates, who made those determinations? Were they made by the constituency-level EROs, as the statutory framework envisages, or were decisions being taken or directed elsewhere? The ECI has not publicly explained this.
Alt News has sent questions to the Election Commission of India seeking an explanation. This report will be updated if and when a response is received.
The constituency-level data used in this report was procured and compiled by Mandate Analytics from records published by the Election Commission of India and the chief electoral officer (CEO), Delhi. Alt News independently verified the figures against the original ECI and CEO Delhi documents. The constituency-wise figures for electors issued notices are as compiled by Mandate Analytics.

US President Donald Trump has announced a one-time Medicare payment for millions of seniors, with the administration saying the money is intended to help cover Part B premiums as the US heads towards November's midterm elections. The payment will be $90 per eligible beneficiary and is being drawn from the Medicare Improvement Fund, according to the Centres for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). The agency said the rebate will go to 20.8 million people enrolled in Original Medicare Part B who meet its eligibility conditions. Most eligible beneficiaries are expected to receive the money automatically. CMS said payments will generally arrive by direct deposit around 8 October, while people without direct deposit will receive a paper cheque later in October. The rebate is not available to everyone enrolled in Medicare. CMS said eligible beneficiaries must be enrolled in Original Medicare Part B and living in United States. They must also not be receiving premium assistance through Medicaid and must not be paying an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount, or IRMAA, on their Part B premiums. People enrolled in Medicare Advantage are also excluded from the rebate. the payment is designed to offset the October B premium. CMS lists the standard Part B premium for 2026 at $202.90 a month. Trump announced the initiative on Friday through Truth Social, describing it as a way to help seniors manage healthcare costs. The White House has framed the move as part of its broader effort to reduce expenses for Medicare beneficiaries. The announcement has also drawn attention because it comes weeks before the November midterm elections. The Wall Street Journal described it as another financial promise from Trump ahead of the vote, alongside his separate proposal for $5,000 payments to adult Americans in Republicans retain control of Congress. That proposal is distinct from the Medicare rebate and would require congressional action. The Journal reported that the broader payment plan could face significant legislative and economic hurdles. The Medicare payments, by contrast, are being issued through the existing Medicare Improvement Fund. The White House and the CMS say the fund contains money intended for improvements for Medicare's fee-for-service programme. The administration has also begun separate $500 refunds to people it says were overcharged for Affordable Care Act coverage. That programme is not connected to the Medicare rebate. The latest payment therefore has a narrower scope than some of Trump's other proposals. It is targeted at a defined group of Medicare beneficiaries, does not apply to Medicare Advantage enrollees and is intended specifically to offset Part B premium costs. For eligible seniors, the payment is expected to arrive automatically, either through direct deposit or by post. For those outside the eligibility criteria, however, no Medicare rebate is due under the programme. US, Australia suspend consular services in Brazil ahead of election
U.S. consular services and the Australian embassy have closed in Brazil due to security concerns
RIO DE JANEIRO -- U.S. consular services and the Australian embassy in Brazil closed Friday citing security concerns, two days before the country's presidential election, authorities from both countries said.
Also on Friday, Brazil’s federal police said they executed search and seizure warrants in Sao Paulo and the Federal District as part of an investigation into suspected plans that could threaten U.S. diplomatic facilities in Brazil.
Police described the operation as preventive and said it resulted from ongoing cooperation with foreign intelligence agencies. Investigators found no evidence to corroborate the initial reported risks, nor had they identified any suspects as being involved in criminal organizations.
An investigation is ongoing following the seizure of communication equipment, police said.
In a statement dated Thursday, the U.S. Embassy issued a security alert saying it would be suspending consular services at the embassy and consulates starting Friday.
The alert advised U.S. citizens seeking assistance not to visit the embassy, consulates or other diplomatic facilities, and instead contact the appropriate duty officer.
The Australian Embassy in Brasilia also said it was closing on Friday, citing the U.S. alert and advising Australians to avoid U.S. diplomatic facilities.
Asked Friday by The Associated Press about the suspension of consular services in Brazil, the U.S. State Department said it was working closely with its Brazilian counterparts to address security concerns.
U.S. embassies and consulates routinely issue alerts notifying U.S. citizens of threats, events, and changes happening locally, the department said.

Why Windows 11 is always using so much RAM
High RAM usage isn't always a problem that needs a fix.
Open Task Manager on a Windows 11 PC, and it's easy to panic no matter how much RAM you have. Even without many apps open, your computer will likely be using more than 50 percent of its memory. And while this seems like a problem, most of the time it isn't. While 16GB of RAM is the standard for modern computers, that doesn't mean it's no longer enough just because your PC is using almost all of it. This has more to do with how modern versions of Windows manage memory.
First, it's worth taking a look at what RAM is used for. Your computer's memory temporarily stores data that your processor needs to run apps and open files. It offers much faster speeds than your hard drive or SSD, so it's much quicker to access data from. The more RAM you have, the more items your computer can keep open and ready for you to switch between. Multitasking gets a lot better with more RAM.
What's actually using your RAM
The latest versions of Windows treat RAM as something to be used, not something to conserve. In the past, your computer would use only the RAM needed to run the programs you currently have open. However, unused RAM doesn't do anything for you — it ends up being a waste of resources. What Windows does now is figure out what you might need to run soon and keep that in RAM. That could be an app you open often, or a file you're regularly working on. This makes your computer feel a lot faster, because Windows has already preloaded what you need.
All of this happens under a process called SysMain (or SuperFetch in older versions of Windows). It learns your computer usage habits to keep important parts cached in standby memory. If you open Chrome every morning, there's a good chance Windows will keep it in RAM for you. The time it takes to open an app that's preloaded in RAM is significantly shorter than loading it from your storage drive. As a result, you may notice that your PC is using more than half of its available RAM, or sometimes almost 100 percent.
To see what's going on, press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager. Then go to the Performance tab on the left and select Memory — ignore In use and look at Available instead. Cached data counts as available because Windows can reclaim it instantly. The more RAM you have, the more Windows can use to keep your apps and files cached. That's why you shouldn't worry about how much RAM is being used in standby.
When high RAM usage becomes a problem
Despite this smart management, excessive RAM usage can still sometimes be a problem. If you've noticed your computer running slowly or apps crashing, or you're getting alerts that your computer is "low on memory," there might be something else going on.
In that case, check the Processes tab in Task Manager to see which apps are using the most RAM, and close any you don't need. Restart your PC if it's been a while, too. This will fix memory leaks (an issue where a program doesn't return memory it's done using to the available pool). Be sure to disable startup apps you don't use so they aren't hogging memory in the background.
Some third-party "memory cleaner" apps claim to help reduce RAM usage, but there are generally not worth using. While they might reduce the percentage of memory in use, having apps switch to the page file (part of your storage drive Windows uses as backup, pretend RAM) makes them slower. These apps also aren't a long-term solution, since the system will eventually reload everything again.
Some people choose to disable SysMain entirely and revert to the old RAM management system. While we wouldn't recommend this in most cases, on an older PC with a mechanical hard drive, the constant preloading can keep the disk busy and make the system sluggish. If that's the case for you, press Win + R, type services.msc and look for SysMain. Open its Properties, click Stop and set the startup type to Disabled. This will prevent Windows from preloading files and apps into your RAM.
But again, we don't recommend this unless you're on an old system with an HDD that's starved for RAM. If you're still stuck with 8GB of RAM (or less), the proper solution is upgrading to 16GB or more — even though RAM is more expensive than ever. In the meantime, you can also try changing a few settings to improve your experience on Windows 11 PCs.

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

Okuma, Fukushima Pref. – A supermarket opened in Okuma, Fukushima Prefecture, on Friday, becoming the first new store in the town since the 2011 accident at Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings’ Fukushima No. 1 nuclear power plant.
More than 500 people lined up ahead of the opening of the store, operated by Maruto, headquartered in the Fukushima Prefecture city of Iwaki.
The company expects demand from local residents who have returned from nuclear evacuations, as well as those engaged in reconstruction projects.
The supermarket has a sales floor area of about 2,000 square meters and houses a drugstore and a ¥100 shop. It also offers product delivery and reservation services.

Talking to the news agency ANI, Kakkar said that she was joining the party for the need to “defeat the regressive politics of the BJP.”

Gym owner Deepak Kumar, who identifies himself as Mohammad Deepak, was released on bail on Friday after being produced before a sub-divisional magistrate’s (SDM) court in Kotdwar following his preventive arrest over an alleged altercation with a local trader, officials said.
SDM Sandeep Kumar granted bail to Deepak, who was detained on Thursday by the Pauri Garhwal police under Section 170 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) as a preventive measure after an alleged altercation with local trader Sanjeev Tank over a Facebook post.
“The Kotdwar police have also registered an FIR in the matter under relevant sections of the BNS concerning criminal intimidation and the use of abusive language,” he said.

At about 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter, Nina, to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door.
Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he did not react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV.
Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737.
Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!”
Many of the details of what happened on flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos.
As the plane went into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in about a minute, most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children. But a small group rushed to the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot. One, a plumber, copied an action seen on TV documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive.
Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In the meantime, Manes had helped truss the co-pilot with a telephone cord while a dentist treated the injured Indian pilot, Smit Machchhar. It was a “great miracle”, Manes said on eventually reaching Tel Aviv on an emergency flight 10 hours later.
In a video call with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, broadcast live by TV networks, Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, said he had been “fighting for my life”.
The pilot successfully sent an alarm to air traffic control signalling the attack and then, as his strength ebbed, managed to unlock the cockpit security door.
“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machhchar said. “At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
For the moment, the identity of the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar is unknown, though regional sources said he was an Omani national who had joined flydubai – which is owned by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) government – between five and nine months ago.
The co-pilot was barred from flying in Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, the Associated Press quoted a source as saying on Saturday, and was subsequently hired by flydubai.
In Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. The worst scenario is he was trying to get into Israel,” said Arik Arad, the chair of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy Cyviation and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion airport
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, has claimed the co-pilot was exposed to “Islamist radical indoctrination”, saying Israeli investigators had found evidence on social media accounts that he wanted to “kill Jews”.
“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew: ‘Kill me, kill me,’” Netanyahu told Fox News, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.
Experts said there have been only a handful of instances of suicide by plane – cases where the pilot’s motivation is primarily to kill him or herself by crashing the plane, rather than using the plane as a weapon, as in the 9/11 attacks.
In 2015, the co-pilot of a low-cost German airline flight who had hidden evidence of psychiatric illness from his employers deliberately crashed, killing himself and 150 others. Suggestions that the crash of an AirIndia 787 in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have been fiercely disputed.
Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York.
“Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?”
Security services have been warning of a wave of radicalisation across the Middle East prompted by the war in Gaza, which came to an inconclusive halt with a fragile ceasefire a year ago. But there has been limited evidence as yet that any violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the conflict.
Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally.
“Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. You get a body count, media coverage, you get your message across, and this makes a plane the ultimate spectacular terrorist attack.”
There are now many questions for aviation security. Changes made to plane design after 9/11, which allowed pilots to lock cockpit doors from the inside, have long been controversial among experts. If Machchhar’s desperate efforts to allow access to the flight deck had been unsuccessful, there is little doubt all onboard FZ 1073 would have died.
There are also questions about screening of pilots. This can be expensive for airlines and could deprive them of valuable crew if too many fail more rigorous efforts to expose psychiatric illness or extremist views. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening, and some may hide physical or psychological problems for fear of being grounded.
Arad said: “The important issue … is that obviously pilots are not being screened enough. Lots needs to be done.”
Dubai international airport, the world’s busiest airport for international passenger traffic, has built some of its appeal on a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.
“They are very conscious of the fact – a little bit like Israel in many respects – that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.
The UAE has ordered investigators to “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it,” its attorney general, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, said on Thursday.
Arad foresees growing threats to civilian aviation from cyber-attacks and the malevolent use of AI, which could allow the targeting multiple planes simultaneously. But other experts pointed out there was no need for such sophistication to pose a threat.
Clarke said: “Whether or not it involves an attacker who was self-radicalised or part of a group, keeping things simple is always the best way to carry out an attack, and this came pretty damn close.”

The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalry
- Published
Snipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead.
Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two. This is a show of military might.
" We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan.
"Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important."
War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation.
With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific, there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower.
But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner.
It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight.
"We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is.
Binding tighter to the US
The war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific.
"We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says.
And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500.
A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing.
"Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said.
"China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects."
The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers.
But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties.
The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer.
But that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US.
"Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll.
"Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States."
The 'frenemy'
While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China.
Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner.
Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer.
Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015.
The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs.
And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up.
A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years.
Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges.
In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement.
Even with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary.
"There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments," says Lyons-Jones.
This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US.
Rise and fall of superpowers
Earlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be".
Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing.
"The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says.
But old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump, the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one.
"This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang.
And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act.
"There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says.
"It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."
