Quick Answer
Wanderlog, Stippl, Polarsteps, and TripWaffle can turn flight, hotel, train, and other confirmation emails into organized travel plans. They differ in AI planning, maps, collaboration, trip tracking, alerts, and pricing, so the best choice depends on how you travel.
While traveling is something we all look forward to, the preparation behind it is sometimes quite grueling. Especially when you are doing everything by yourself. You book a flight on one site, a hotel on another, and a rental car through a different source, maybe through a referral link sent to you on WhatsApp. Traveling isn’t just about downloading the right apps before you board the flight. It is also about having all your important info at your disposal.
Just to know whether your hotel booking said 2 PM or 12 PM, you have to dig through your inbox. This is such a universal travel headache that an entire category of apps has been developed just to fix this. This list contains 4 AI travel planner apps that can convert your forwarded emails into a clean, day-by-day plan — flights, hotels, activities all lined up in order.
Table of Contents
Best AI Travel Planners
I went over the internet and actually dug through four of the more talked-about names in this space — Wanderlog, Stippl, Polarsteps, and the newer, scrappier TripWaffle. These apps were put to the test to see what they are genuinely good at, where they fall short, and which one deserves a spot on your phone before your next trip. Let us go through them one by one.
Wanderlog: The one that does almost everything, and does most of it well
For me, Wanderlog has become the default travel planner app, and for good reason. The email trick works two ways here. You can either forward your flight and hotel confirmations email to a special address Wanderlog gives you, or you can just link your Gmail account and let it quietly scan your inbox for bookings automatically on its own. The details show up straight in your itinerary, and it eliminates typing in flight numbers and copying and pasting confirmation codes.
However, there is one thing that makes Wanderlog stand out from a plain inbox-scanner. After your bookings are in, Wanderlog does not just leave them sitting there as a list. It pins everything onto an actual map. You can drag your stops, reorder your day, and there is a route optimizer that can rearrange your stops to save you driving time. Wanderlog also works like a shared Google Doc. Add your travel companions by email, and everyone will have access to edit the same trip at the same time, see live changes, and more. For a group trip, this is a great thing to have.
Community members also contribute travel guides right inside the app, so you have all the interesting information about a new city you have landed. Speaking of the cons, some users have reported that once a trip is created, there is sometimes no way to edit locations cleanly, forcing them to delete and redo it. Then there is the paywall issue, where features such as offline access and automatic Gmail scanning are locked behind the Pro subscription.
Download Wanderlog: Android | iOS
Stippl: The AI-first planner that tries to be your whole travel toolkit
Stippl leans hard into AI to get there. You just need to tell it what kind of trip you want (relaxed, adventurous, culture-heavy, offbeat) and it generates out a full day-by-day itinerary for your destination in under two minutes. If you already have a rough plan and just need a day filled in, you can use Stippl for that too. Simply tap a single day, and it will generate activities, restaurants, and transport suggestions just for that slot.
For emails, it works the same familiar way. You just need to forward your booking emails, and Stippl will pick up flights, hotels, trains, and restaurant reservations and feed them to your trip automatically. Everything also gets synced to the calendar, so your itinerary shows up right alongside your regular meetings and reminders. Stippl sets itself apart from the other three by the fact that it leans into being a memory-keeper as well as a travel planner.
There is a scratch map feature that adds every country you have already visited. It gives the feel of a passport stamp collection you can show off. It can also stitch your trip photos into an automatic travel reel or photobook once you are back home, no editing required from your end. You can also purchase an eSIM from the app. Coming to the con, the AI-powered itinerary generation and offline mode sit behind a paywall. Some users have reported having run into crashes, slow email imports, and the odd date or flight not saving correctly, especially with overnight flights or long layovers. Do keep that in mind.
Download: iOS
Polarsteps: Built for tracking your journey, now sneaking in planning too
Polarsteps is a bit different than the other three apps on this list. It did not start as a booking organizer at all but as a way to automatically track where you have already been and turn it into a beautiful, shareable map, eliminating manual check-in anywhere. You just have to carry your phone, and the app quietly traces your route in the background using WiFi and mobile data with constant GPS pings. That said, Polarsteps is also slowly gaining proper trip-planning tools, and the confirmation-email feature is now part of it. You can forward your hotel or flight booking to the app, and it pulls out the address and other details automatically.
Polarsteps has also introduced an AI-powered itinerary builder. There is also the ability to manually add flights by looking them up by airline and flight number, though you cannot book through the app. Since tracking is Polarsteps’ specialty, once your trip ends, it can turn the whole route into a digital travel book that you can order and keep.
Speaking of the shortcomings, compared to Wanderlog or Stippl, Polarsteps’ booking-import feature is newer and less complete. Polarsteps traditionally allows just one person to add content per trip. This means that if you are planning a group trip, Polarsteps, as a travel planner, won’t be a good option. It is meant for solo travelers and backpackers, who care as much about documenting the journey as planning it.
TripWaffle: The newcomer that’s focused on one job
TripWaffle may be the least-known name here, but that is one of the reasons why it makes it to this list. It’s built by a small, independent team (led by a single developer, Guy King, based in Australia). Instead of trying to be a do-everything travel app, it does one thing and focuses on, which is turning forwarded confirmation emails into a clean itinerary.
The setup is about as simple as it gets. You sign up and send your booking confirmations to it from providers. Using AI, TripWaffle reads the email, pulls out the dates, times, confirmation numbers, and addresses, and puts everything into a day-by-day timeline with time zones and connecting flights already planned out.
TripWaffle earns its keep in the details that it can keep. You get live flight tracking with real position updates, alerts about delays, gate changes, and a “flight reliability score,” which tells you how a specific flight number has historically performed. You receive a pre-trip checklist email covering visa requirements, weather, and packing suggestions just a day before your departure. TripWaffle is completely free with no ads, no Pro tier, and no upsell, which is something none of the apps in this list provide. You do not get crowd-sourced attraction guides or any AI-generated itineraries from scratch.
So which one should you actually download?
Honestly, it depends on what kind of traveler you are. I travel a lot, and most of my stay is outside my home country. I would suggest you try multiple apps and then decide on the one that you want to keep. For me, the above apps do the job, and you should definitely check them out and see if they fit your bill or not. Before you purchase a subscription to any of the paid apps, do go through the free version thoroughly and see if that is what you are looking for or not.

Ishita Dutta recently opened up about filming a physically demanding sequence for Drishyam The Conclusion. In an interaction on Zahrajani daily’s podcast, the actress recalled shooting a rain sequence in which she and Shreya had to drag a body across a muddy field before dumping it into a pit. She explained that the scene involved real physical effort, as the team added weight to the bag to make it difficult to pull and create a realistic visual on screen.
Ishita Dutta recalls shooting a difficult rain sequence for Drishyam The Conclusion: “It was tough!”
Speaking about the sequence from Drishyam The Conclusion, Ishita Dutta said, “So the scene where we are dragging the body outside, so it's a rain sequence where it's raining and both of us are dragging. So initially when we were pulling na, it was too easy for us to pull, it was empty. So they actually filled it up with, with similar weight ka some samaan in that bori so that, you know, it looks like we are pulling. And it was tough! Because it was raining and there was mud and keechad and me and Shreya are pulling it and it is real! What you see, it is us really pulling something and trying to take it all across the field and dump it in the gaddha that we had created. So that scene was also very difficult. And we did it over four-five days. So, because they knew it was so tough and so draining plus raining, so they didn't want us to fall sick. So every day from 6:00 to 8:00, like two hours we'll finish part of the sequence so that it was easy and yeah.”
Ishita further explained that the challenging sequence in Drishyam The Conclusion was not completed in a single day. Since the shoot involved rain, mud and physically pulling the weighted bag across the field, the team divided the sequence over four to five days. The actress noted that they would work on the sequence for around two hours each day, from 6 pm to 8 pm, allowing them to complete the shoot without overexertion. Her recollection offers a glimpse into the physical demands involved in filming the sequence for Drishyam The Conclusion.

The Australian government faces significant “tech debt” that could bring a big bill for taxpayers after the OpenAI Medicare breach, as government agencies will need to fortify their defences against future attacks by AI agents.
This week, the home affairs department ordered all federal government agencies to conduct a “legacy technology stocktake” that requires a plan for each agency to “reduce legacy technology systems” to a level within the agency’s risk tolerance and appetite, the direction stated.
OpenAI this week revealed an internal agent had gained non-public access to the Services Australia Medicare statistics portal during a training task seeking information on government spending on skin conditions in Victoria. The agent was able to run commands, retrieve internal files, credentials, and write files.
While OpenAI has apologised to Australia for the incident, it has served as a wake up call for the federal government, with the government-wide review now under way.
The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, asked her department whether some of the A$160m funding allocated to the agency in the last budget for cyber upgrades can be accelerated.
The statistics portal, Gallagher told reporters last month, is a “legacy system.”
“It dates back decades.”
Services Australia will be far from alone in managing legacy systems. They can – but not all do – present a security risk for businesses and government as they age and vendors cease providing new security updates.
Prof Salil Kanhere, a University of New South Wales cybersecurity and AI expert said the age of the system alone does not tell an agency whether it needs replacing.
“A 15-year-old system that is properly supported, patched and properly isolated would perhaps present less risk than even a newer system that might not be properly maintained,” he said.
Those older systems with vulnerabilities are often known to human attackers, but AI agents persistent in looking for holes in a system may be able to discover them quicker.
Gartner, a technology analysis firm stated in a note to clients released after the Medicare hack that “technical debt, not a rogue AI agent attack” represented the greatest threat to legacy systems.
“Agentic AI’s interactions with [government] resources will greatly increase,” the firm stated. “Underinvestment is no longer sustainable and agencies should urgently prioritise funding in light of AI-driven risks.”
In the Australian government’s commonwealth cybersecurity posture in 2025 report released in February this year, 59% of federal agencies and departments reported their ability to implement the “essential eight” measures to reduce cyber risk was being affected by use of legacy technologies.
The essential eight includes requirements to patch applications and operating systems, using multi-factor authentication, and other security measures. Of those agencies being hindered by legacy tech, 34% blamed insufficient dedicated funding, while 18% said it was due to a lack of a viable replacement.
Prof Yang Xiang, from Monash University’s department of software systems and cybersecurity, said the government stocktake was “very necessary” and there was urgency to needing to audit all government systems.
“The agents bring significant changes in terms of the speed of getting into – hacking into – the system,” he said. “The cost to launch an attack is much reduced to launch an attack and with the help of agents, it is fairly easy for the hacker to launch a very large scale atack against any systems.”
Clearing the tech debt could prove costly for the federal government, but Xiang said agencies should identify priority systems for replacement. Kanhere said high-risk systems should take priority.
“You do the high risk stuff first, I think it is absolutely needed, and then put the perimeter around [other systems],” he said. “It is possible to do it quite systematically once they have a good understanding of what needs to be done.”
Some states have audited their legacy technology and have invested hundreds of millions to rectify the issues.
A Victoria government cybersecurity audit of its IT servers found 25% of the operating systems used by servers were no longer supported by the vendor, with 48% in extended support.
In a South Australian audit report of legacy ICT systems published in June, of the ten agencies reviewed, nearly half of the 11,602 hardware devices or appliances were determined to be legacy devices. Almost one quarter of the operating systems and applications were also determined to be legacy.
In one example, the Department for Child Protection’s case management system is now over 15 years old, and has limited vendor support.
The SA government has allocated $325.6m over the past three budgets in part to address legacy technology.
“Frontline workers spend significant time managing system limitations and maintaining records, reducing the time available to support vulnerable children and families.”
A 2025 Queensland government audit of IT systems found more than half of the 57 systems audited are at the end of life. Many of the systems identified by the government in 2012 as needing to be replaced were still in operation in 2025, including a patient administration system at Queensland Health, a forensic register at the Queensland Police Service, and a trust accounts system for young people in detention.
The Queensland government in the 2025 budget allocated $1bn over four years for IT investment, including replacing or updating legacy systems.
The Australian Cyber Security Centre said in recent guidance that the most effective way to mitigate risks associated with legacy IT is to replace it, and where it cannot be replaced, then legacy technology should potentially be segregated or isolated from the broader department network to restrict access to the rest of the department.

New York, Sep 23: On a day of high-stakes diplomacy on the global stage, President Donald Trump began his United Nations visit by telling a prominent US journalist, “You should not be here.”
“It's an honour to be here,” Trump said as he entered UN doors Tuesday ahead of his speech to the General Assembly and faced Kaitlan Collins of CNN, a frequent target of his ire.
“I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me.”
As Collins noted later on air, CNN said nothing of the kind. The administration had banned CNN from White House grounds days earlier — along with MS NOW and Politico — and removed the network from pool duty. But CNN had been admitted into the UN as regularly credentialed media.
In any case, the tense moment was a stark reminder of how dramatically the bitter conflict between Trump and news outlets whose coverage he objects to as “fake news" has escalated in just a few days.
The current ban was the subject of a joint lawsuit filed Monday by the three outlets, asking a judge to find the administration's move unconstitutional.
The White House had until Tuesday to respond, and a hearing is scheduled for Wednesday afternoon.
Later Tuesday, Trump doubled down on his remarks and said negative coverage was dangerous for the country.
Asked whether he would allow the outlets back in if the court rules against the White House, he said, “Well, it probably will, because this is a judge who's not a particularly fair judge.”
He was referring to US District Judge Timothy Kelly, whom he appointed in 2017 and who ordered a CNN journalist's access restored in a similar case in 2018.
“So you never know,” Trump added. "I think we have a right to clean out fake news."
Trump's comments echoed others he's made since announcing the ban Friday. He has referred to “purposely negative stories,” but cited no specific stories — only generally “fake news” — as justification for the ban.
The ban and lawsuit are part of a long-running conflict between the president — especially in his second term — and media outlets he finds unfavourable.
Trump has responded in the courtroom, or with regulatory action. He's also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms — as he has with CNN's Collins, most recently in a speech at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner.
On air, after her exchange with Trump on Tuesday, Collins said: “We never said we were not going to cover the president. We will do our best to cover him each and every day.”
Tuesday began with an item missing from the daily press schedule issued by the White House: It did not list the US network pool, a departure from the norm.
CNN had been the designated pool network for the president's trip to New York, according to a schedule that divides coverage of certain events between the five major networks. But Trump's ban removed it from pool duties.
The other pool members agreed, in solidarity, not to replace CNN with another network on the coverage, and further to suspend all pool coverage until further notice.
Other news outlets also took steps in solidarity. The Associated Press joined a number of news organisations, including The Washington Post and The New York Times, in a decision not to publish photographs of presidential events Monday.
It remains to be seen how long both the ban and the collective media action will continue.
In speeches and meetings Tuesday, Trump was seen plenty by global audiences, thanks to UNTV — the official United Nations broadcast arm — and pool journalists covering other international leaders.
Meanwhile, a sign was spotted in the White House workspace: “I stand with AP, CNN, MS NOW, Politico.”
One longtime TV analyst says the lack of constant coverage will prove damaging to a spotlight-loving president — which may be one reason the standoff ultimately ends.
“This ban is not going to go on forever because he doesn't want that to happen, anymore than anybody else,” said Robert Thompson, director of Syracuse University's Bleier Centre for Television and Popular Culture.
In the short term, Thompson said, audiences won't feel the impact in a lasting way — after all, he noted, there are many ways people get news outside of network coverage.
“We are not going to be deprived of important civic information,” Thompson said, as might have happened years ago when outlets and options were fewer.
On the other hand, if viewers were interested in what Trump said as he inaugurated a helipad at the White House on Monday, they were out of luck: The sound of Trump's whirring, waiting helicopter drowned out his remarks. TV network crews usually work to capture clearer audio.
On a deeper level, Thompson said, news consumers will be impacted in a more serious way. He called out Trump's remarks labelling negative media coverage "dangerous" as troubling.
“These casual remarks, not even disguised, about what we always considered basic freedoms of the press ... that, I think, is a lot more serious,” he said.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.
See more information on the partnership between Netherlands and WHO.

ParisLongchamp: Caballo De Mar upsets Scandinavia in Prix du Cadran
After surviving a lengthy stewards' enquiry, Caballo De Mar retained his Prix du Cadran crown, defeating red-hot favourite Scandinavia in a thrilling renewal of the Group 1 staying contest at ParisLongchamp.
Saturday 3 October 2026 17:07, UK
Caballo De Mar brought an end to Scandinavia’s eight-race winning run when repeating his win in the Qatar Prix du Cadran from 12 months ago in a thrilling finish at ParisLongchamp.
George Scott's stayer was delivered by Oisin Murphy at the furlong marker to grab the lead from Scandinavia and the fading pacesetter Queenstown.
As the pair locked horns through the final furlong, Scandinavia regained the lead only for Caballo De Mar to fight back in the shadow of the post to get up by a neck.
Connections had to sweat through a stewards' inquiry after an objection by Ryan Moore, whose mount Scandinavia, the 1-6 favourite, appeared to receive a bump from the 9-2 winner close to the finish.
Scandinavia's sequence had included five Group Ones, but Scott's charge is a formidable opponent at his best, particularly in Paris where he is now three from three in Group Ones.
Scott said: "What an amazing performance from the horse and the team at home.
"I was very emotional afterwards - he's just such a special horse to us and to come and win the Cadran again is great.
"He's an amazing horse and just a real character. He takes a lot of managing at home, he's very lazy and it's hard to get a grip on him."
The Newmarket handler felt beforehand he had a chance of beating the red-hot favourite, adding: "We wanted to track Scandinavia and it all went to plan. We managed to get well up on him and then he fought back.
"I thought if there was an opportunity to beat him it was today because my horse loves it here, he was showing all the right signs and Scandinavia had a very hard race in Ireland last time. We felt we could beat him today, but you're not going to say something like that.
"We'll see how he comes out of it, but he could go to Ascot on Champions Day."
Aidan O'Brien said of Scandinavia: "He ran a great race and it's been a long season for him.
"The ground was a little bit on the slower side for him. Ryan said he was coming back at him.
"That will be him finished for the season. I was never going to go to Ascot as the ground would definitely be gone for him by then."

Flames, smoke seen at Aramco facility south of Saudi capital
Aramco has been under attack from the Houthi group targeting the kingdom as part of the war in Yemen
Flames and smoke were seen rising from a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of the kingdom’s capital Riyadh on Saturday, an AFP journalist said.
The circumstances remained unclear but in recent weeks Aramco, majority-owned by the Saudi state, has come under attack from the Houthi group targeting the kingdom as part of the war in Yemen where Riyadh is backing the internationally recognised government.
Aramco remains the flagship company of the Saudi economy and one of the largest firms in the world by market capitalisation.
Last month, the Houthis said that they launched strikes targeting “sensitive sites” in Riyadh and Aramco facilities in the kingdom’s port city of Yanbu.

Odisha govt announces ₹11 lakh each for Indian women's hockey team players for Asian Games win
India ended a 44-year wait for the Asian Games women's hockey gold and qualified for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Odisha Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi on Saturday announced cash rewards of ₹11 lakh each for the players of the Indian women's hockey team for winning the gold medal at the Asian Games.
Each support staffer of the team will also be awarded ₹5.5 lakh.
India ended a 44-year wait for the Asian Games women's hockey gold and qualified for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics by upstaging defending champions and Olympic silver-medallists China 1-0 in the final on Friday.
Deep Dive
CMO Odisha, in a social media post, said, "Hon'ble Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi has announced a cash reward of ₹11 lakh each for the players and ₹5.5 lakh each for the support staff of the Indian women's hockey team in recognition of their historic gold medal at the Asian Games 2026."
The chief minister congratulated the team for their outstanding performance, determination and commitment, which have brought immense pride to the nation, it said.
The Odisha government stands firmly with Indian hockey and remains committed to supporting and nurturing sporting excellence, the CMO added.
"The cash prize for the players announced by the chief minister is over and above the one that has been announced by Hockey India yesterday," Odisha's Sports Department Secretary Bhupendra Singh Poonia told PTI.
The Indian women's hockey team had last won the gold medal at the Asian Games in 1982.
The Odisha government will remain the official sponsor of the Indian men's and women's hockey teams (both senior and junior) till 2036. In 2018, it became the first Indian state to sponsor national hockey teams.

Tasmanian victim-survivor had to wait 23 months for her own school and foster records to be released
In short:
Sam Morgan plans to sue the State of Tasmania over sexual and physical abuse she allegedly experienced while in foster care, and over physical abuse she allegedly experienced at a government high school.
Her civil court abuse claim has been delayed by almost two years while she waited for the education department to release her records.
What's next?
The department says it's "committed to reducing the wait time fulfil RTI requests", and is making changes.
For years, Sam Morgan kept the memories of the abuse she allegedly experienced while in foster care and at a Tasmanian government school buried.
When she was ready to seek justice, Ms Morgan made a Right to Information (RTI) request to have her foster care and school records, held by the state's education department, sent to her lawyer so she could start a civil court claim against the state.
It took 23 months for the documents to arrive.
"When it drags on for two years … the anxiety just becomes horrific,"
she said.
Ms Morgan alleges she was physically abused by a foster carer when she was aged 12 or 13, and sexually abused by a foster carer when she was a teenager. She also alleges she was physically abused at a Tasmanian government high school.
The abuse allegedly happened in the 1980s.
Ms Morgan said she was out having a coffee with her daughter when she found out the files had finally been received by her lawyer.
"It was a big surprise but a huge relief. I cried when I got home because it was just a relief," she said.
Her lawyer, Azita Arian, an associate in the abuse law team at Maurice Blackburn, said Ms Morgan was not the only person whose civil court abuse case had been held up because of delays in obtaining records.
"These are people who were abused in state care and they shouldn't have to wait almost two years to access their records," Ms Arian said.
She said the records were important because they helped establish when and where people were placed and could help identify foster carers and workers who are relevant to the claim.
She said, in some cases, the files may also document any disclosures of abuse.
Delays reducing choice
Ms Arian said the delays were reducing the choices victim-survivors had when seeking justice.
One of the options they have is the National Redress Scheme (NRS), which does not require the same level of documentation and evidence as a civil court claim, but compensation payments under the scheme are capped at $150,000.
Ms Arian said Ms Morgan had applied to the NRS and was offered a payment of $100,000.
After receiving advice that accepting the payment would essentially bar her from pursuing a civil claim, Ms Morgan has not accepted the offer.
Ms Arian said she had many clients also facing long waits for their records who could not afford to wait.
"Survivors are effectively tunnelled towards redress by default,"
she said.
Ms Morgan said the delays seemed "to just be really unfair".
"It's almost like the government does it to get people to pull out."
Ombudsman 'aware of the backlog'
Tasmania's ombudsman has also noted concerns about the delays with RTI applications to the education department.
In an email sent to Ms Morgan's lawyers in May, an officer from Ombudsman Tasmania said their office was "aware of the backlog of requests with the Department for Education, Children and Young People (the department) and concerned by the situation".
"Ombudsman Tasmania staff have been regularly meeting with the department to discuss concerns about the backlog," the officer wrote.
They said the department's "backlog reduction strategies" had "not yet achieved significant progress and the situation is being actively monitored".
The officer also said they were "aware of some applications such as those of your client that have been waiting 18 plus months".
Department 'committed to reducing the wait time'
A spokesperson for the Department for Education, Children and Young People said the department was "committed to reducing the wait time to fulfil RTI requests".
"Changes implemented this year, including additional and more senior resources, are expected to further address processing timeframes," they said.
"We will continue to actively engage with applicants or their advocates to identify and prioritise the critical information they need."
Justice Minister Guy Barnett, who has overall responsibility for Tasmania's RTI laws, was also contacted for comment.
An independent review of Tasmania's Right to Information framework last year found there had been a "rapid growth in volume of applications for access to personal information".
The authors, RTI expert Rick Snell and human rights lawyer Tim McCormack, wrote in their report that they considered the formal RTI application process was "ill-suited for handling requests to access personal information".
They recommended a new system that would protect privacy while letting individuals access their own information.
The Commission of Inquiry into the Tasmanian Government's Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in Institutional Settings also made recommendations aimed at streamlining the process for victim-survivors.
These recommendations were listed as being "in progress" in the government's most recent progress report.
Ms Morgan said she was fortunate to be able to wait the 23 months it took for her records to come through, but it was only the start of the process.
"I know I'm in for a long haul still, yet,"
she said.

Sukhveer Singh Maiserkhana raises teacher shortage in Punjab schools in emotional video
NEW DELHI: The Aam Aadmi Party on Saturday suspended Sukhveer Singh Maiserkhana, MLA from Punjab's Maur assembly constituency, citing his “involvement in anti-party activities and indiscipline”. This came after he posted an emotional video highlighting shortage of teachers in schools in his constituency."Dear Mr Sukhveer Singh, It has come to the notice of the Party that you have been found involved in anti-party activities and indiscipline. In view of the above, your primary membership from the Party is suspended with immediate effect," AAP said in a statement.
In the video, Maiserkhana appealed for adequate teaching staff in government schools and spoke about the difficulties faced by students due to the shortage. His remarks drew attention after he appeared emotional while raising the issue on social media.BJP leader Ravneet Singh Bittu shared the video and attacked the Punjab government over its education claims."Camera Claims vs Punjab’s Ground Reality! The tears of Aam Aadmi Party’s own MLA, Sukhveer Maisarkhana, expose the ground reality behind Punjab’s much-publicised ‘education model’" he said.
“When a ruling-party MLA has to come on social media and appeal for adequate teachers in schools in his own constituency, it raises serious questions about the situation faced by ordinary families and lakhs of students across Punjab,” he said.
"When a ruling-party MLA has to come on social media and appeal for adequate teachers in schools in his own constituency, it raises serious questions about the situation faced by ordinary families and lakhs of students across Punjab," he added.AAP has not, however, publicly linked the suspension to the specific remarks in the video beyond citing anti-party activities and indiscipline.

The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 used an axe to attempt to carry out a “terrorist attack” during the Israel-bound flight, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.
Disaster was narrowly averted on Wednesday when passengers and crew intervened to stop the co-pilot from his attempt to take control of the plane, which had 182 people on board and plunged 16,625ft in just over 30 seconds. The descent was so extreme that part of the rudder was ripped off.
Investigators have been trying to establish how the alleged attacker, who was seen by witnesses repeatedly stabbing the pilot in the cockpit, managed to smuggle a weapon on board.
But on Saturday, Gen Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, a UAE prosecutor, said the co-pilot had used a crash axe to mount the attack, an implement typically kept inside the cockpit to use in emergencies, such as crashes or fires, and which would not have needed to be brought onboard covertly.
“Investigations into the incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack,” Al Shamsi was quoted as saying by the state news agency WAM.
Multiple media outlets have named the co-pilot as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national. Speaking to the Associated Press, a Gulf diplomat said investigations were under way to establish whether he acted as a “lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups”.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline flydubai.
It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired.
A British university, Buckinghamshire New University, said a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management” at the institution. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the University.”
Flydubai said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation and it was not in a position to comment further, a spokesperson said on Saturday.
The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv have been suspended until further notice following the attack.
A former flydubai crew member told the Wall Street Journal that all its pilots are subject to security screening before flights, as well as medical checks at least once a year.
How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators. It also raises serious concerns about background checks in aviation recruitment. Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots out of its airspace who come from nations with which it does not maintain diplomatic relations. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.
Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the US and other western governments, an official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigation.
On Friday, Anwar Gargash, a senior adviser to the UAE president, called the attack a “dangerous terrorist act”. The incident is a test for the UAE government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.

One of the suits blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence", a lawyer for the family, Antonio Romanucci, said during a news conference on Thursday.

It cites the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows citizens to sue the government for personal injury, death, or property damage caused by the negligence of federal employees.
The second lawsuit targets ICE officer Jonathan Ross, who shot Good, as well as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House border chief Tom Homan and others, alleging a "conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents, and private actors".
Good was a 37-year-old mother of three who had just moved to the city. She was shot on 7 January in a traffic stop, which immigration authorities said occurred after she made "an attempt to kill or cause bodily harm to agents" in "an act of domestic terrorism".

Australia says platforms like Steam and Roblox have 'significant' child safety gaps
- Published
Australia's online safety regulator has found "significant gaps" in how popular gaming platforms protect children online.
In a new report it found inconsistent approaches in how Steam, Roblox, Fortnite and Minecraft implement child safety measures as research shows nine out of 10 children aged 8 to 17 in Australia have played online games.
"Australian children have a right to play online without being exposed to predators, sexual extortionists, violent extremist content or other harmful material," eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant said.
Roblox said it "prioritises the safety of our Australian community, especially the youngest users". The other platforms have been contacted for comment.
Weak safety on platforms allow "predatory adults" to make contact with children before grooming them, Inman Grant said, for sexual exploitation or radicalisation.
The report found that Valve - the US gaming giant that owns Steam and Steam Chat - was the only provider that did not use a type of technology widely used by the industry to detect and remove known harmful content.
Valve also did not "proactively" use tools to detect child sexual exploitation or violent material in chats, with current systems mainly flagging scams, the report found.
Roblox, along with Valve, were noted in the report as using only internal datasets to train language detection systems and for not regularly retraining these models.
"We expect these services to lift their game to identify and combat serious harms such as child sexual exploitation, sexual extortion and material and activity which promotes, incites or instructs violence," Inman-Grant said.
Minecraft and Fortnite, which does offer child accounts, generally let users self-declare their age, the report highlighted, meaning anyone who said they were adults could access "higher-risk communication features".
Steam also relied on users self-declaring their age but the report acknowledged the platform had recently introduced age checks using credit cards, and that Roblox had put in stronger age checks since last December.
Another issue raised by the report was the inconsistent manner in which the four gaming platforms shared information and participated in industry initiatives.
Mojang Studios, developer of Minecraft, and Roblox shared industry expertise in combating child sexual exploitation as well as violent extremism online, but Valve did not.
Elsewhere, Fortnite maker Epic Games failed to share instances of breaches with other platforms under a global programme that was designed to combat online child sexual exploitation and abuse.
The report was based on information collected by Australia's eSafety Commission on how the platforms were protecting users from serious online harm between October 2025 and March 2026.
Australia has made global headlines in recent years for its stance on online safety, after it introduced its world-leading social media ban for under-16s last December - which did not include gaming platforms - and a more recent push to force tech giants to offer users a chance to opt-out of social media algorithms.
A spokesperson for Roblox said it had "invested heavily" in its safeguards for children which include mandatory age checks.
Valve, Fortnite, and Microsoft - which owns Minecraft - have been contacted for comment.

School protests send shivers down French government's spine
- Published
It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble.
Since the student protests of May 1968 – memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) – every government has run scared of angry French youth.
Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in.
Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away.
For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colère (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed.
Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats".
A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country.
On Thursday – the high point so far – hundreds of lycées (where 15-18 year-olds finish their schooling) were being blockaded. On Friday, the situation had improved but around 400 lycées were closed in order to protect staff and students. Universities are beginning to join in.
Violence has erupted. On Thursday the main hall of a lycée in Nantes was destroyed by fire. Smaller fires too numerable to mention were lit at school entrance gates around the country. The cost of the damage is millions of euros.
According to Education Minister Édouard Geffray, 65 teaching staff including 40 school heads have been injured. "Most of the staff who were hurt said that the people they were facing… were not their own pupils," he said.
In addition, the government says that around 300 police and firefighters have been treated for injuries, and some 2,000 people – mainly minors – taken into custody. For their part, student groups say they have a long list of people injured by police. Two teenagers have serious eye injuries and one has lost many of his teeth.
The problem would be hard enough if it was just a question of meeting the protesters' demands. But there is another dimension – a political and social one – which makes this student crisis far more dangerous than in the past.
The demands do exist, even if they remain vague. They are about money – the lack of it – and the need for more teachers, smaller classes and better buildings.
On such matters, many in France would agree with the teenagers. Certainly using protest to demand money from government is such a national habit that even governments agree it's legitimate. And of course, things are indeed getting worse in the education system – because money is so tight.
This week Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu published his draft for next year's budget. The motif is "More cuts – and this time we're serious!"
Whether or not he manages to remove €54bn (£46bn) from state spending, as he promises, remains open to question.
But it is surely obvious that the era of public largesse to defuse social unrest in France is now in its twilight. Students demanding an extra school nurse or insulation in the dining-block are likely to be disappointed.
But that is the lesser of the worries.
The far greater fear is that these student protests are being manipulated by the hard left – and that the violence of recent days is a foretaste of what awaits a dangerously polarised society in the year of elections that is coming.
For the right and centre, there is no doubt that behind the student trouble lies the cunning hand of the France Unbowed party (LFI) and its popular presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
LFI leaders have regularly appeared next to the students – notably in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis whose mayor Bally Bagayoko was criticised for saying that "violence can sometimes be legitimate."
An internal report prepared for the Paris police department which was leaked to the media analysed the opening of the movement in Seine-Saint-Denis. It concluded that students were being "egged on by far-left elements from students unions… and political groups such as… LFI."
It said the tensions "could be part of a flame-kindling strategy… aimed at imposing their ideas ahead of the national elections".
In support of its conclusion, the report's writers cited the presence of protesters who are not themselves lycéens, the vagueness of the demands, the flying of Palestinian and Algerian flags, and the use of tactics – like calling for supplementary protests at police-stations - that come from the radical-left playbook.
The LFI strongly denies doing anything more than lending its natural support to a movement it regards as legitimate. On Thursday Mélenchon called on students to avoid violence "which only serves our enemies' interests".
But his opponents believe that the 75-year-old veteran – who stands a good chance of making it to the second round of the presidential elections in May, probably against the hard-right's Marine Le Pen – knows exactly what he is doing.
Polls show he has massive support – some 40% -- among 18-24 year-olds in France, and that this is concentrated in the populous, high-immigration city suburbs where his talk of a "new France" and "creolisation", to reflect France's changing language and population, are highly appreciated.
But young people are also the biggest abstainers in French elections, so the strategy – as the elections approach – will be to give constant reminders to this part of the population that the LFI is at their side, and that their vote can count.
Whether this will be enough to ensure victory for Mélenchon is another matter. He must surely take seriously the polls which all show him losing massively in a run-off against Le Pen.
If that happens, France will be in very unstable territory - for which the young people's protests of recent days will indeed have been a harbinger.

Sixty-three per cent of the 3,253 Water Supply Schemes (WSS) taken up under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in Jammu and Kashmir are non-operational despite expenditure of around Rs 7,000 crore, a House Committee of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly has found, raising serious questions over planning, execution, procurement, quality control and monitoring of the flagship rural drinking-water programme.
The findings are contained in the voluminous 1253-page report of the House Committee constituted to examine alleged irregularities in the implementation of JJM in the Union Territory. The report was laid before the Legislative Assembly on September 21 by committee chairman Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. The committee was constituted on April 9, 2025, to examine alleged irregularities in implementation of the Mission.
“The result is that 63 per cent of 3253 WSS involving an expenditure of Rs. 7000.00 crore are non-operational,” the report states. It adds that even the 37 percent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were “not fully operational”.
The committee said the institutional mechanism established to oversee JJM had failed to discharge its responsibilities effectively, resulting in inadequate planning, supervision and monitoring.
“The House Committee is of the considered view that there has been complete abdication of authority,” the report said, referring to the Apex Level Committee, Executive Committee and District Level Committees.
The panel attributed the failure to achieve the Mission’s objectives within the stipulated timeframe to what it described as “gross negligence” on the part of these committees and the officers who manned them.
According to the report, 37 per cent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were also “not fully operational” in several cases.
The committee also questioned official figures relating to Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs), saying discrepancies emerged between departmental records and ground conditions during field inspections.
The panel said records supplied to it contained what it described as “false claims” regarding the number of FHTCs provided in habitations and the number of habitations covered.
“On spot visits, the House Committee came to know that far less than the number of FHTC indicated in the record, have actually been provided benefit of the Safe and Adequate Drinking Water of the prescribed quality,” the report said.
The committee also questioned the department’s claim that 81 per cent of rural households in J&K had tap-water connections as of March 2025, saying the figures required physical verification.
The House Committee was headed by Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. Its 13 members were Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami, Ali Mohammad Dar, Altaf Ahmad Wani, Aijaz Ahmad Jan, Rajiv Jasrotia, Ranbir Singh Pathania, Tanvir Sadiq, Javaid Riyaz Bedar, Muzaffar Iqbal Khan, Rafiq Ahmad Naik, Arjun Singh Raju and Iftikar Ahmad.
The committee subsequently undertook field inspections to assess the implementation of JJM works. It inspected schemes in Rajouri and Poonch, among other areas, before finalising its findings.
One of the major concerns highlighted by the committee was the failure to establish the sustainability and adequacy of water sources before executing schemes.
The panel found instances where expenditure had been incurred on pumping systems, storage facilities, transmission networks and distribution infrastructure without adequately establishing the viability of the underlying water source.
In WSS Shirpora Bangil, the committee found high sulphur and iron content in the source and said this had rendered the scheme useless. It termed the expenditure “unfruitful” and directed fresh testing of the source.
“Providing of FHTC is immaterial in absence of safe and viable source,” the committee observed.
The report also cited schemes affected by land and source disputes. These included WSS Dachnipora in Pahalgam, WSS Lelhara, WSS Syed Mantaqi Khrew and WSS Greenland Wuyan. In WSS Bugam Dooniwari, the committee said Rs 10 crore had been spent without benefiting the targeted population because of a source dispute.
The committee has also scrutinised the decision to shift from GI pipes to HDPE pipes during JJM implementation.
It noted that the Jal Shakti Department, Jammu, authorised Executive Engineers in April 2023 to use HDPE pipes instead of GI pipes depending on site feasibility. However, an earlier technical committee had recommended modification of DPRs before the change.
The panel said the national-level communications cited in support of the shift did not mandate compulsory replacement of GI pipes with HDPE pipes and questioned why the decision was taken several years after the Mission’s launch.
It said the decision had significant financial and operational implications and “ought to have been taken by the Apex Level Committee”.
The report also records allegations made by retired IAS officer Ashok Parmar concerning procurement orders and changes in pipe specifications. Parmar alleged that procurement orders worth Rs 4,000 crore were placed without approval and that HDPE pipes were ordered in violation of approved DPRs. The committee recorded these as allegations and evidence presented before it, rather than independently establishing every allegation.
The committee separately examined tube-well projects and raised concerns over tendering, technical qualifications, quality assurance and functionality.
It said some tube wells had failed to meet desired standards and noted submissions that water from certain sources was unsuitable for human consumption. The committee observed that quality-assurance mechanisms appeared to have been inadequately enforced.
The panel also questioned the effectiveness of third-party monitoring agencies hired for audit and inspection of JJM works. It said field observations regarding faulty execution indicated that such agencies had failed to discharge their obligations adequately despite being paid for monitoring and audit work.
The committee has recommended constitution of a High-Level Committee to conduct a comprehensive audit of JJM and retrofitting schemes, including procurement of DI, GI and HDPE pipes and execution of civil works.
It has recommended identifying officers and engineers responsible for irregularities and initiating action against those found responsible under applicable rules.
The panel has also called for scrutiny of officers who served on the Apex Level, Executive and District Level Committees from their constitution until March 31, 2025, with their actions and omissions examined against the respective terms of reference.
A comprehensive technical, financial and administrative review of tube-well projects has also been recommended, covering functionality, water quality, payments released, pending liabilities and possible additional expenditure.
The committee said the problems identified were not confined to isolated technical failures but indicated “possible systemic deficiencies in planning, procurement, quality control, contract administration and project oversight”.
Its central finding is that the success of JJM cannot be measured merely through construction figures or tap connections recorded in official databases. The ultimate test, the committee said, is whether households are actually receiving safe and adequate drinking water.

'I am Jane Doe': Online rally to protect Cornell rape accuser's identity becomes a reckoning
It's being compared to the 2017 #MeToo movement
WARNING: This article references sexual assault and may affect those who have experienced sexual violence or know someone affected by it.
They're saying it in videos posted on TikTok in solidarity, in Instagram posts where they hope to protect her identity, and in comments on Threads where they share their own harrowing experiences:
"I am Jane Doe."
The repeated refrain, part of a wave of online support this week for the complainant in the Cornell University gang-rape allegations, is being compared to the cultural and structural reckoning of the 2017 #MeToo movement that changed the culture of silence around sexual assault.
The Cornell case recently came under the spotlight after the complainant, known in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16 alleging the Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed "the Cornell 7."
The #iamjanedoe movement seems to have been born out of an attempt to protect Jane Doe's identity after an independent journalist put out a public call Monday to name her "so we can all evaluate her veracity … since her lawsuit didn't hesitate to name and shame seven of her peers as gang-rapists."
He later claimed to have identified her, posting and then deleting her information, adding "the principle has been served."
The global response across the internet was swift.
"He is trying to expose her identity. We won't let him. I am Jane Doe," a content creator posted in a video on TikTok viewed more than 5.2 million times by Friday.
"You are Jane Doe, I am Jane Doe, we are ALL Jane Doe until no one is Jane Doe," someone else commented.
"We all are Jane Doe, good luck finding her, men," another person commented on one user's Instagram video.
Jane Doe alleges the men named in her lawsuit plied her with ketamine and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024. None of the fraternity members have been criminally charged. On Monday, after intense backlash, the Tompkins County district attorney announced he was reopening the investigation.
By Thursday evening, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she'd lost faith in the DA's ability to handle the case and was appointing New York attorney general Letitia James to oversee the investigation.
On Friday, Hochul says she intends to "close the loophole" in her state's law that currently makes it difficult for sexual assault survivors to claim they were mentally incapacitated during an assault if they were voluntarily intoxicated.
'It's happening all the time'
Takara Small, a technology journalist in Toronto, told CBC News Network Friday that the global movement is meant to confuse the algorithm and search engines, but that it's impossible to fully scrub a digital footprint.
"I understand this action, but I think it's important people don't share any information that could be linked to her," Small said.
There are currently thousands of online "I am Jane Doe" posts across multiple platforms, reaching millions of people. And while one of the goals is to bury any identifying information of the actual Jane Doe, it is also a moment of reckoning.
Many of the posters have been describing their own sexual assault experiences, the difficulties in coming forward and, in some cases, naming the people they say harmed them.

"Four men at once. I was 22," someone posted on TikTok.
"I was 18," someone posted on Instagram.
"People need to realize this is happening to so many women, not just one brave woman at Cornell University. It’s happening all the time. Everywhere to SOOO MANY women," she added.
In Canada, about 44 per cent of the population over age 15 say they have been sexually assaulted in their lifetime, with women three times as likely to say so as men, according to a 2025 survey by Statistics Canada. Fewer than one in 10 reported it to the police.
According to the U.S. Rape, Abuse and Incest National Network (RAINN), about one in four undergraduate women experience rape or sexual assault after enrolling in college.
'We are so damn tired'
U.S. journalist Katie Couric gathered some of the responses she'd seen online and posted them on Threads on Wednesday.
"The Cornell case has unleashed a torrent of first-person accounts from women revisiting traumatic experiences they had long kept buried," Couric wrote.
They included posts by one user who said they'd been assaulted by their professor, who was allowed to retire early and is now a dean at another school. Another said they'd been raped while asleep, still another said they had been drugged and raped for hours on a college campus while people watched and nobody was prosecuted.
"It feels like shouting into a void," someone commented. "It's infuriating."
The feeling was echoed on Substack, where an author asked what's really changed since #MeToo.
"The viral #MeToo movement in 2017 felt so significant because it was the largest collective reckoning of rape culture maybe ever, and happened mostly in an online space. It was the first time I said things out loud that I had kept to myself for most of my life," she wrote in a post Tuesday.
"The same is happening now with the Cornell 7, but we are almost 10 years on from #MeToo and we are so damn tired."
If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database.

For better or for worse, romance lovers have never been hornier for hockey. Now, the National Hockey League wants to cash in.
As part of its new “Hot for Hockey,” campaign, the NHL is rolling out romance novel-inspired short stories starring the league’s players on audiobook platforms. According to the Sports Business Journal, the league contacted popular hockey romance writers to write and narrate the 60 to 90 second stories, and will tap creators on BookTok, the romance-heavy literary subculture on TikTok, to promote the content.
The first batch of short stories, which dropped this week, feature players including the Philadelphia Flyers’ Trevor Zegras, the Carolina Hurricanes’ Sebastian Aho, and the Las Vegas Golden Knights’ Jack Eichel. They’re written by Pucking Wrong author C.R. Jane and more closely resemble back-cover summaries than actual romance novels. And, despite the nods to genre tropes, the players aren’t paired with romantic partners. Much more boringly, the stories appear to be a bid to get people to watch the actual games. The entirety of The Summer I Turned Gritty with Trevor Zegras is as follows:
“Trevor Zegras came to Philly looking for a fresh start. But after battling with Pittsburgh in the playoffs last year, he found out how gritty things could get. One heated summer later, Philly’s pretty boy is looking a whole lot grittier.”
Not all romance readers are thrilled about the campaign. Some argue that it makes players targets for sexual harassment. Others see the stories as cheap pandering that fails to engage with female and LGBTQ hockey fans’ concerns about homophobia and toxic masculinity in the sport.
“I cannot begin to describe the depths of my rage that this is actually happening,” Emily Rath, a best-selling hockey romance novelist, posted on Threads. “Yes, the NHL contacted me to participate. And I have never turned down an offer so fast.”
“They See Dollar Signs”
Romance novels focused on hockey players have been on the rise for years—the New York Public Library first highlighted the trend in 2019. Hockey romance burst into the mainstream with the massive success of romance novel-turned-streaming series Heated Rivalry, followed by Off Campus.
Jon Weinstein, a spokesperson for the NHL, tells WIRED in a statement that the campaign is a “playful nod to something that’s clearly going on in the cultural zeitgeist.”
“We were very proud to partner with real hockey authors, illustrators and voice actors in the space, and we’re grateful the players were willing to have a little fun with it too,” he says.
Yet many hockey romance fans applauded Rath and Chelsea Curto, the author of the steamy D.C. Stars series, for their refusal to participate in the campaign.
Rath, whose Jacksonville Rays series recounts a myriad of sexual relationships involving a fictional NHL team, said on Threads that the league’s slide deck for the campaign was filled with jokes she considered to be mockery of the genre, as well as what she alleged were AI cover renders. Curto also clocked the AI graphics, writing on Threads that it was probably for the best that she declined to be involved, as her books “can be very critical of the league.”
“They’re just encouraging the idea that women only care about hockey if it’s packaged like a romance novel,” Rath posted. “And they’re using popular authors and our credibility to launder their tarnished brand and lure in our readers.”
In Rath’s opinion, the NHL has failed to take accountability for or take action to address “racism, homophobia, and misogyny” in the league—a view shared by several hockey fans who spoke with WIRED. Lacey Conine, the founder of Double Hockey Stix—a clothing brand aimed at underrepresented hockey fans—says she initially thought news of the romance-centric campaign was satire.
“I had so many comments,” she says, “of people just being like, ‘This is disgusting. We hate this. What is this? How is the NHL this tone deaf?’”
In its current iteration, Conine says, the campaign feels like the NHL is “mocking you, and pandering to you, and making fun of you,” while failing to address fans’ concerns about aspects of hockey culture that can be hostile for fans that break the straight, white, male mold.
“I think that they see dollar signs,” Conine says. “They're trying to bring in Heated Rivalry fans—and then canceling Pride Nights. That tells you where they're at.”
While NHL commissioner Gary Bettman told reporters earlier this year that “every team does a Pride Night,” a handful of teams have moved away from themed nights that celebrate the LGBTQ community. That includes the Dallas Stars, which will not host a Pride Night this season, the team’s first time in five years without one. The Stars—which will host a night focused on romantic fantasy novel Iron Flame—did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. A portion of the Iron Flame event’s proceeds will go to the Trevor Project, a nonprofit focused on suicide prevention among LGBTQ youth.
The NHL banned players from wearing specialty-themed uniforms, such as Pride sweaters and tape, in June 2023. The decision on tape was later reversed, with the league emphasizing that it does not single out Pride specifically in its ban. The NHL also highlighted other partnerships with the LBGTQ groups, such as the annual Pride Cup.
Several female hockey fans say the NHL’s attempt to cater to romance readers falls flat because of how the sport’s governing bodies approach sexual assault allegations. Echo, a 35-year-old fan of the Montreal Canadiens who asked to be referred to by her first name to protect her privacy, says she believes the league aims to use “romanticized narratives to whitewash the insidious aspects of hockey culture and its players.”
The Globe and Mail reported in 2022 that Hockey Canada, the sport’s national governing body, had used players’ registration fees to build funds that covered certain expenses—among them, sexual assault claims, as well as other lawsuits. (A spokesperson for Hockey Canada, Jeremy Knight, said in an email that the organization has taken “considerable action to help drive systemic change” in the sport over the last four years.) Last year, five former Canadian Junior Hockey players were deemed eligible to play in the NHL after being acquitted in a high-profile sexual assault case. Three currently play in the league.
Players Can Face Sexual Harassment
NHL teams’ past hockey romance-centric campaigns have also raised concerns about the sexual harassment of players. In 2023, a player on the Seattle Kraken, Alexander Wennberg, and his wife, Felicia, posted about an influx in “predatory and exploiting” comments after the team’s social-media account published content aimed at BookTok.
The NHL said that players approved all content for the new campaign, which will be exclusively focused on hockey. (The NHL Players’ Association did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Still, Conine and other fans question if romance-inspired marketing focusing on specific players fuels an uncomfortable brand of sexualization and parasocial relationships.
“Fans are going to do what fans are going to do in their spaces and their time,” Conine says. But, when the league is “literally creating these narratives—I think there's a line there. And, I think they crossed it.”
Jess Rauchberg, a lecturer in the school of media and communication at the University of Leeds, notes that the campaign is essentially league-approved real-person fiction. Hockey RPF has existed since at least the late ’90s and often involves romantically or sexually coupling hockey players with other players.
“Breaking the fourth wall”—discussing RPF outside of fandom spaces or with players—has historically been seen as poor form. But as the NHL’s marketing efforts increasingly encourage fans to feel a personal connection with players, Rauchberg says, the division between RPF and marketing material has blurred.
A hockey fan herself, Rauchberg believes that hockey RPF and romance are popular because they allow fans to imagine a reality where their desires are represented. Sometimes that desire is for players to make out. Other times, it’s a league where players push back against rape culture and toxic masculinity.
“I describe them as fantasy novels,” Rauchberg says. “In real life, the players probably aren't like Ilya Rozanov, consent king.”
