When I found out I was pregnant with twins, I couldn't imagine how completely my life was about to turn upside down. Not just because those two little hearts beating on the ultrasound would soon become two babies crying at exactly the same time, but because of the whirlwind my life was about to become. Two more babies would follow, all in four years.
Very quickly, our home in Barcelona became a noisy, messy children's playground. Luckily, before the twins arrived, I had still had enough time to read tons of parenting books that promised to teach me how to do everything right.
Most of that parenting literature quickly went out the window. What remained was survival.
I took parenting very seriously
At the beginning, I was determined to help my twins discover the world in the best possible way. I followed the latest baby-led feeding trends, bought almost everything you could imagine to encourage their development, and watched them constantly. I took parenting very seriously.
Then two little girls arrived, one after the other, and family life became even harder to control. At times, I felt — and still do — like a juggler who had already dropped all the balls but was somehow still trying to keep the show going.
I tried hard to watch everything that all four of them did and step in before anyone became frustrated. Spoiler: It was physically and mentally impossible.
No plan ever worked perfectly. Whenever we decided to take a lovely family walk, one of the kids would suddenly have a meltdown or have a massive diaper blowout. If I solved one disagreement, another would start somewhere else.
Once, we even managed to go out for a coffee while one of the boys was in the middle of a tantrum. In all the chaos, we left the keys inside the house and had to break a window to get back in. At that point, tired of fighting against the elements, I gave up on perfectionism and control and decided — or perhaps was forced — to let life flow a little more. A little more Mediterranean.
Surprisingly, that was what worked for me.
Children in Spain are part of public life
I've loosened my grip, helped by the fact that I'm raising my children in Spain, where parenting can feel less closely supervised than what I often see described in the US. Children here are also very much part of public life. They don't disappear from restaurants when the sun goes down, and family life doesn't necessarily end when adult social life begins.
Even when I'm alone with my four kids, other adults talk to them naturally. People ask their names, their ages, what year they're in at school, and sometimes even about their friends. Waiters joke with them. Neighbors stop to talk to them. Other parents intervene casually if someone needs a hand. When my children feel comfortable, they answer for themselves.
That social life has changed the way I parent more than I expected.
We spend a lot of time outside, especially in summer, when evenings in Spain seem designed to stretch on forever. We eat at restaurants, walk along seafront promenades, and go to the fiestas mayores that fill towns and villages with music, food, rides, and people of every generation. It is completely normal to see children still outside late at night, running through a plaza while their parents or grandparents sit nearby talking.
My children play freely in busy squares while I stay close enough to see them. They build sandcastles on the beach while I watch from our chairs. They splash around in the shallow children's pool while I'm beside it. At puppet shows, they choose where they want to sit while I stay a few meters away on the promenade.
Restaurants have become another small training ground for independence. In bars and restaurants we know well, I sometimes let the older ones go to the counter, order something and pay themselves with my card. They know I'm there, and so do I. I supervise, but I try not to intervene unless they need me.
The first few times, I wanted to follow them and make sure they said everything correctly. Now I watch them work it out. Those tiny responsibilities seem to make them feel more confident and give them a small taste of freedom. And we all seem happier than when I was trying to keep them permanently within arm's reach.
My kids have more freedom in Spain
Spanish social life allows me to give them some of that freedom, and, unexpectedly, it has also made the logistics of having four very young children easier. When we're out, life doesn't have to stop because one child needs something. Someone can be eating while another is playing. A tired child can sleep while the rest of us finish dinner.
At home, something similar has happened. Because I can't immediately respond to four children at once — especially when I'm breastfeeding the baby or have her in my arms — they've had to learn to cooperate with one another.
And children, unsurprisingly, don't particularly enjoy waiting. So they've started finding their own solutions. The older ones help their younger sisters climb onto a ride at the park. If someone can't reach something, another child will sometimes get it. If one of them doesn't know how to do something, a sibling may step in before I do. Not always, of course. Sometimes the proposed solution is considerably worse than the original problem. But increasingly, I see them turning to one another instead of automatically turning to me.
I've also started letting them face their own everyday challenges, and I've found it's better for the entire family. Struggling with their shoes? I wait and give them time to work out how to put them on. Sometimes a sibling appears and helps. Fighting over a pencil? I watch from a little distance and see whether they can reach an agreement. Can't manage something at the playground? I wait to see whether a brother or sister will offer a hand.
If one of the baby's pacifiers falls on the floor, one of the older children will pick it up and wash it for her. If she crawls off her play mat, they know how to gently guide her back. If someone is too tired to finish dinner at a restaurant, we've pushed two chairs together and let a child fall asleep there while everyone else finishes eating.
Their little world is full of problems, but I'm learning that it's also full of solutions they can find without me.
After those years of raising children this way, I feel they're becoming increasingly independent and confident. I can see how much they enjoy those ordinary moments when they're allowed to decide something for themselves: ordering a drink, helping a sibling, choosing where to sit, or figuring out how to solve a small problem without an adult immediately taking over.
And I've realized something I never expected when I was pregnant with those twins and reading all those parenting books: sometimes being a good parent isn't about doing more for your children.
Sometimes it's knowing when to stand a few meters away and let them try.

The winter season in Delhi usually results in poor air quality, outbreaks of seasonal influenza, a heavy burden on hospitals and increasing medical expenses. Hidden within the yearly air quality reports is a health problem that is preventable, and yet costs the city’s citizens lakhs. Among the elderly, especially those who have diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart disease or a suppressed immune system, a viral infection can develop into bacterial pneumonia and require hospitalization. Industry estimates suggest that the average cost of a hospital stay is about ₹50,000, while intensive care can amount to ₹1 lakh. A single such incident can erase months’ worth of income and cause households relying on pensions and daily wages to slip down the income scale.
The battle against pneumonia
India has achieved real advances in the fight against pneumonia, mainly as a result of introducing the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) as part of the Universal Immunisation Programme in 2017 and through Mission Indradhanush. Free three-dose vaccinations are provided to infants, and by 2023, vaccination rates among infants in India had reached 83%, according to the WHO/UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC).
The grandparents of these infants, however, are almost completely unprotected: National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) 80th Round Data on Health reveals that vaccination coverage among people aged 60 and over is only 0.40 per cent. While one generation is covered by the national programme, the other is left to avail of vaccines from a private market they may struggle to afford.
This gap is most significant in Delhi, since in the winter, the conditions can turn common respiratory infections into serious health issues.
Toxic winters
In December 2025, the city experienced its most toxic month in six years, with an average Air Quality Index of 351. Colder months naturally place a greater strain on the respiratory system. Winter air, which tends to remain stagnant, traps particulate matter near the ground: prolonged exposure compromises the lungs’ defensive abilities.
Government records show that there were more than 2,00,000 cases of acute respiratory illness and 30,000 hospital admissions in just six Delhi government hospitals between 2022 and 2024. When the pollution lasted throughout December 2025, doctors reportedly noted a 20% to 30% increase in the number of patients with respiratory problems, including some who had never before had such a condition.
These figures do not reflect the full extent of the problem, as they exclude people treated in private clinics, those who take medication on their own, infections that have never been confirmed by a laboratory test, and cases recorded as pneumonia rather than influenza.
Vaccine present, policy absent
What makes the number of hospitalisations and their resultant expenditure tragic, is that a a significant portion of this could perhaps be avoided with a vaccine that is already available. The 2026 Indian consensus guidelines concerning immunisation in adults recommend pneumococcal vaccination based on age and level of risk. It recommends the PCV20 vaccine for all adults between the ages of 18-49 years with chronic medical conditions or those considered at risk based on their health and lifestyle, or a single dose of the vaccine for all adults aged 50 and above. The guidelines also include adults who have immunosuppression and chronic diseases. For residents of Delhi, in winter when pollution makes the air toxic, this could mean the difference between a minor ailment an episode of hospitalisation.
India has no National Adult Immunisation Policy, and as a result, vaccination rates rely on individual awareness, access to a doctor, and the ability to pay out of pocket, a situation that systematically excludes older people in lower-income families. While this a critical problem ahead of winter in Delhi, it is not merely a Delhi problem: in 2022, India was estimated to whom were 149 million people aged 60 and over, a large number of whom are still economically active and support households.The Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (2017-18) showed that of Indians aged 45 and over, only around 0.6% had received a pneumococcal vaccine, a figure that has not changed much since then.
The burden in lives
The figure for deaths due to pneumonia recorded by India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death in 2024 was 35,987, making it the leading cause of respiratory deaths, although it remains relatively out of the spotlight compared to other causes. Even this figure is an under estimate since the system covers only about one fifth to one quarter of all registered deaths nationally, and older people who die at home rather than in a hospital where certification takes place almost never get included at all.
Data on a year-by-year basis from Delhi shows that this is not an isolated occurrence but a consistent pattern, affecting precisely the group for whom a vaccine is already available but for whom no public system provides it.
Pollution raises the stakes
It is impossible for Delhi to solve its problem of air pollution by vaccination, and there is no suggestion here that it should. Reducing emissions at the source must continue to be the main course of action. However, the two measures operate at different stages of the same risk pathway. In the winter of 2025, the AQI reached 450 at a number of monitoring stations and people suffering from respiratory and cardiac conditions were told to remain indoors, a recommendation that is not a policy. When pollution increases baseline vulnerability, the removal of an additional infectious trigger becomes all the more important.
Before winter sets in this year, there is a concrete option available. Delhi could provide free pneumococcal vaccination to adults aged 60 and over who have recorded comorbidities via its present dispensary and mohalla clinic network and then assess both the uptake and the hospitalisation outcomes. The cost of each dose, at a few thousand rupees, is significantly lower compared to ₹65,000 for a hospitalisation episode.
Delhi already vaccinates the grandchildren; the medical case for vaccinating the grandparents is no different, it is merely administratively missing.

BCCI President Mithun Manhas on Saturday lauded the Indian men’s cricket team for retaining its Asian Games gold with a win over arch-rival Pakistan, and said the Shreyas Iyer-led outfit handled a high-pressure final well.
India defeated Pakistan by 19 runs in the final at Nisshin, Japan, emulating the women’s team which had also defended its gold medal last week.
“By far the best team of the tournament. We are the defending champions, and the performance they have shown this time is commendable,” Manhas told reporters here.
He was delighted to see the way the team handled pressure.
“They defeated arch-rivals Pakistan, who I feel don’t offer much competition anymore, and the way our team handled pressure situations…no other team in the world can do that,” he said.
He praised Tilak Varma and Abhishek Sharma for coming up with important knocks in the medal clash. “This is a team sport. Tilak Varma batted brilliantly, and Abhishek Sharma set the tone for the game. The job of openers is to build the game, and the middle order finishes the game. So, openers basically set the tone.

“Team India’s batting has been tremendous, and bowling…I would say that everyone defended a good total together,” he said.
The former Delhi cricketer also thanked ICC chief Jay Shah for doing commendable work to strengthen men’s and women’s teams during his tenure as BCCI secretary.
“I would like to thank Jay Shah once again here. He was the then (BCCI) secretary and his contribution has been significant in building this team.
“Not just for the men’s team, our women’s team has also won the World Cup. His contribution has been very big. So, a special thanks to him too,” he added.
Manhas dedicated the Asian Games victory to cricket fans and the Armed Forces.
“This victory, I believe, we should dedicate to the thousands of crores of fans who pray for the Indian team, and especially to those soldiers who sacrificed their lives for the country,” he said.
On cricket becoming an attraction in the Asian Games, Manhas said the sport is gaining some global traction.
“Different teams from around the world are participating, every country is getting involved in cricket, and it’s a very good thing that cricket is becoming global,” he said.
Manhas, who has close ties with cricket in the Valley, hoped to see more players from the region represent the country in future.
“Aquib Nabi, who comes from Baramulla, has reached here through a lot of hard work. When he played (in local cricket), BCCI was running it (J&K cricket) then. The BCCI has given its full support to this association now.
“We have promised to continue providing it in the future as well. There are a lot of talents here, and they just need to be nurtured and backed,” he said.

I'm almost 38 years old, and I just took my first solo trip for a work conference in Dover, Delaware, this September.
For a few months leading up to the trip, every time I thought about the logistics and emotions of leaving my kids, I felt a tight knot of anxiety. I was also nervous about traveling by myself to a large conference where the only person I knew was a work connection I'd only ever met via email.
When I visualized taking this trip, it was odd how much less anxious I felt when I inserted one or more of my kids, my husband, or a friend into the narrative. The idea of taking care of another person, or simply having company, seemed easier and less intimidating than spending that time alone, thinking only about myself.
I also thought about all the times I'd forgotten a phone charger or toothbrush and how often I'd relied on others when traveling.
I feared I was just too codependent to take a trip by myself and enjoy it.
Navigating without anyone else was better than I expected
I flew a red-eye from Phoenix to Philadelphia, then summoned an Uber for the 1.5-hour drive to Dover.
Before I left, I messaged two girlfriends and asked whether they always chose female Uber drivers to feel safer when traveling alone. They told me no, but they used some of Uber's other safety precautions, like sharing their location with someone. Before I left, I turned these features on. Thankfully, I felt comfortable in all of my rideshare scenarios and navigated to each place with relative ease.
I will admit I'm often forgetful, prone to losing my room key, and I struggle with running late. I was especially concerned about keeping my electronics charged, as my husband or teen son often handles that. But I found I was surprisingly more responsible when it was all on me.
Over the course of six days, I was never late to meetings, never lost anything important, and never let my phone die.
I wasn't lonely like I expected to be
Since I was going to a conference, I knew I'd be surrounded by people every day, but I might still feel alone since they were strangers to me.
While there were definitely awkward moments when I stood on the outskirts of conversations, I'm relatively chatty and friendly and was able to connect with others. My prior work connection turned out to be lovely in person as well, which definitely helped.
I also basked in the alone time in my hotel each evening. As a busy working mom, I hardly ever watch movies or have time to myself to do whatever I want, so I selected a long movie I'd wanted to see for a long time, caught up on work, and listened to an audiobook.
I got to enjoy doing things I love without having to check in with anyone else
Perhaps the best part of solo traveling came at the end, when I spent two additional days after the conference exploring nearby Wilmington and the surrounding area, nicknamed America's "Chateau Country."
I felt like I'd woken up in Europe.
In total, I toured three elaborate du Pont family mansions and sprawling gardens, visited an art museum, breakfasted at the iconic Hotel Du Pont, and returned to Longwood Gardens, which I remembered vividly from my childhood.
No one whined at me that they were tired, bored, or hungry. I didn't have to chase a toddler through the gardens or change plans because someone decided they were fed up with all this American history.
Getting to indulge in the things that interest me most made me realize I was pretty good company. I took my time ogling over presidential fine china and Tiffany glass and lingering over historians' stories of hand-painted murals and family trees.
I discovered that I liked hanging out with myself and that it's much easier than family travel. Besides, I made friends as I went, so I was never really lonely.
Would I solo travel again?
Absolutely.

I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's
- Published
Reporter Michael Graczyk has covered nearly 500 executions carried out in Texas, continuing even after his 2018 retirement from The Associated Press.
He remembers two instances where needles popped out before reinsertion for successful execution - but never one in which an inmate survived.
That's what happened this week in Tennessee, when 50-year-old inmate Christa Pike remained breathing and audibly snoring after two separate doses of pentobarbital, the barbiturate used in the state's lethal injection protocol.
Graczyk, 76, says he wasn't entirely surprised to hear of the anomaly - and had actually thought about the possibility during his decades-long career as a Texas journalist.
"It seems to me it was just a matter of time," he told BBC News.
Tennessee's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of pentobarbital-filled syringes in case the person being put to death does not die after the first set, according to AP, but does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Governor Bill Lee halted executions in the state after Wednesday night's failure, ordering an independent review into procedures. Botched executions have come under scrutiny over the past decade, since a shortage of the drugs used led some states to change the formula, or procure drugs from more questionable sources. Some states even brought back death by firing squad as an alternative.
Pike is now in hospital where she is receiving "life-saving care", according to her lawyer.
It's not uncommon for lethal injections - the most frequently used form of capital punishment in the 27 US states where the penalty is legal - to be "botched". The Death Penalty Information Center, a think-tank that does not take a stance on the death penalty, lists 64 botched executions since 1982, 51 of them lethal injections. In at least seven of those cases, the executions were halted because the IV line could not be set.
But Graczyk has never seen an execution fail after the injection was delivered.
"That has never happened here," Graczyk said of the Lone Star State.
Graczyk, who covered a wide range of topics for the AP during his 46 years with the news service, considers his prolific attendance at executions to be an important part of the job.
"There is no [greater] authority, power, or whatever you want to call it, that state or federal government has over us than the power to take our life," he said.
There have been 1,683 executions in the US since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre, which is when the US Supreme Court re-instated the death penalty. Texas has carried out by far the most of any state, with 602 executions. In 1982, it became the first state to use lethal injections to execute people.
"I always thought it was important for someone who has no stake in the outcome of a case to be there and to see the law being carried out and to make certain that it is done properly," Graczyk said.
"That someone is there to see it and tell others: Here's what I saw. Here's what happened."
He feels a particular responsibility to remember victims in his coverage and it's especially disheartening when he writes a story about an execution that doesn't make big news.
"I feel bad for the victims in the case," he said. "They are the forgotten folks. They always have been."
"Today, all the emphasis is on the inmate in Tennessee," he said. "No tears are being shed, other than the victim's immediate family, for the victim … and I understand that's the business we're in, but it doesn't mean it's right."
Pike's victim was Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old originally from Florida who loved to roller skate, smile and help others, according to descriptions given by her friends and family. Slemmer was tortured and killed by Pike, then 18, and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, after they met her at a job training camp.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was present in Tennessee on Wednesday for the execution attempt, telling NBC News afterwards that it "was a mess".
Texas, where Graczyk lives and works, does not allow observers in the execution chamber when the IV is being inserted, he said.
"So when we get into the chamber, the inmate's already hooked up."
In a lethal injection execution, the IV would typically be inserted in the crook of the person's arm, Graczyk said. But if that didn't work, sometimes it would go into the top of their hand, their leg, neck or other sites.
During successful executions, Graczyk said inmates become "visibly unconscious after just a few seconds". They are usually pronounced dead 20 to 40 minutes after the fatal dose is given, he said.
He still remembers the death of Jonathan Nobles, who was executed by lethal injection in Texas in 1998. He'd been handed the sentence after his conviction for the brutal 1986 stabbing murders of two Austin women, Kelley Fraquhar and Mitzi Johnson-Nalley.
Nobles sang "Silent Night" as his last words.
"He gets to 'Round yon virgin' and he stops talking," Graczyk told BBC News. "That's how long it took for the drug to kick in so he wasn't conscious anymore."
That scene has stuck with Graczyk for nearly 30 years.
"To this day, when I'm in church on Christmas, and the choir is singing Silent Night, and all the congregation is joining in Silent Night and they're all, you know, in the spirit of the season and the joy of the season, and I'm thinking of this execution, I'm sure I'm the only one in that congregation that is having that kind of recollection."
When people hear about his career covering executions, he said, they are usually curious.
"Most people don't get to watch someone die," he said.
But when people ask him about what he has witnessed, he tells them "it's not the only thing I did or do or have done".

Prashant Bhushan, Neha Bora among 160 detained on Day 2 of anti-CEC stir; Yogendra Yadav calls march on October 4
A day after over 1,000 protesters were detained, several lawyers, activists and students gathered at the protest site for a second consecutive day.
The Delhi Police on Saturday detained 160 protesters, including senior advocate Prashant Bhushan, political activist Yogendra Yadav, AISA president Neha Bora and activist Anjali Bhardwaj, during a protest march demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
A day after over 1,000 protesters were detained, several lawyers, activists and students gathered at the protest site as the agitation continued for a second day. AISA had issued a call for people to join the protest at 1 pm on Saturday. Meanwhile, Yogendra Yadav has called for a citizen's march again on Sunday, October 4.
Police said no permission had been granted for any protest on October 3, and that “no prior intimation” of any such stir was received by the cops. Prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 also remained in force in the New Delhi district for a second consecutive day, with cops saying this was to ensure public safety, maintain public order and facilitate smooth traffic movement.
Protest began with two-hour delay, protesters detained within 15 minutes
Deep Dive
Student activists from AISA and other organisations returned to Jantar Mantar on Saturday, and protesters initially gathered on the Ashoka Road at 1 pm. The route to the backside of the protest site was sealed, with multiple layers of barricades and hundreds of security personnel deployed across the area.
Nearly two hours after the scheduled time of the protest, AISA national president Neha Bora, Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal, Swaraj India leader Yogendra Yadav, Supreme Court lawyer Prashant Bhushan and RTI activist Anjali Bhardwaj began leading the march amid heavy security presence in and around Jantar Mantar.
The Delhi Police made announcements and attempted to disperse the crowd, eventually detaining several protesters. “Nearly 160 people were detained and were taken to different police stations,” a police official said, requesting anonymity.
Within 15 minutes of the starting of the march, which began at Vithal Bhai Patel House around 3 pm, the police began detaining people, AISA member and former JNUSU president N Sai Balaji told HT. Prashant Bhushan, Yogendra Yadav and Anjali Bhardwaj were taken to the Badarpur Police Station along with several others.
Yogendra Yadav calls for citizen's march; advocates Sibal, Bhushan back anti-CEC protest
Swaraj India leader Yogendra Yadav called for a citizen's march on October 4, saying it was to protest against alleged “police brutality”. He urged people to “rise against anti-women SIR” and “rise against Delhi Police”. He also said the protest was against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
Yadav said the protest would begin at 3 pm from India Gate, and protesters would march to Jantar Mantar.
Earlier today, senior advocates Kapil Sibal and Prashant Bhushan backed the anti-CEC stir as they joined AISA president Neha Bora and marched towards the Jantar Mantar. After being detained, Bhushan, in a video, said “police cannot silence the voice of the people.”
“On 3 October, lawyers and activists peacefully marching towards Jantar Mantar were taken into custody by the police. The more the repression, the more voices will take to the streets,” Bhushan said in the video, posted by Yadav on X.

Capcom plans to use AI to speed up the game development process
The company previously said it won’t use AI-generated content in its games.
Video game companies are increasingly leaning on AI to help develop new titles and Capcom will be the latest to embrace this approach. During a company conference, Capcom detailed the next steps for the RE Engine, its proprietary video game engine, that includes using AI to improve efficiency during the game development process. As first reported by GameBiz and IGN, Capcom's game engine would undergo a major improvement project called REX, to eventually become a "game engine of the AI generation."
Capcom's programmer Satoshi Ishida explained during the conference that the AI usage would mostly help with streamlining development workflows. Ishida explained that games and their assets have become much larger these days, leading to longer development times. From Capcom's latest remarks, it doesn't seem like the company will be using AI-generated assets in its video games, but instead employing AI to speed up the game development process.
Previously, Capcom said during a Q&A portion of a shareholders' meeting that it would explore ways to use AI to assist with things like graphics, sound and programming but clearly stated that it would not use AI-generated content in its games. This approach would line up with Capcom's desire to breathe new life into some of its older franchises, especially since the company saw success with the release of Onimusha: Way of the Sword. Other major game companies have also welcomed the use of AI for game development, like Epic Games who detailed that it would incorporate Claude and Gemini into Unreal Engine earlier this year.

Before the rains, caused by the deep depression over the Bay of Bengal, prices of these two vegetables remained below ₹30, and now the prices have gone up to ₹44 a kg. It may take two weeks for the prices to stabilise, Mr. Karunakar said.
But since the weather experts are talking about another system in the Bay of Bengal around October 15, prices are expected to rise again.

Ethiopian federal forces retake Mekelle airport from Tigrayan fighters, residents say
Ethiopian federal forces have retaken Mekelle’s airport from Tigrayan fighters
KAMPALA, Uganda -- Ethiopian federal forces have taken the airport in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, according to people in the city who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday, reversing a takeover by Tigrayan fighters that prompted the suspension of commercial flights last month.
It wasn't immediately clear when federal forces recaptured Alula Aba Nega Airport. Those who provided the information declined to be identified for fear of retribution amid uncertainty over who controlled the city.
Severe disruptions to internet and cellphone networks have made gathering and verifying information from Tigray difficult. Details of how the airport changed hands, including whether fighting took place there, remained unclear.
“The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm,” an Ethiopian general said on condition of anonymity.
Neither the Ethiopian government nor the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, had issued an official statement on the airport’s reported capture. It wasn’t clear who controlled Mekelle itself. An AP contributor in the city said residents feared looting amid the uncertainty.
“Many reports indicate that the government and allied forces have begun to control Tigray’s capital,” said Jalale Getachew Birru, an Ethiopia analyst for ACLED, an independent global monitor that collects, analyzes and maps data on conflict.
The AP could not independently verify those reports.
TPLF fighters seized the airport on Sept. 23, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to Mekelle and the Tigrayan cities of Axum and Shire. The African Union urged restraint, warning that renewed tensions threatened the peace agreement signed in 2022.
Federal troops are fighting alongside allied Tigrayan forces against the TPLF. The AP previously reported that the Tigray Peace Force, a breakaway faction of the Tigrayan rebels, was operating alongside federal forces in the neighboring Afar region.
The reported change in control follows a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea. Ethiopia on Thursday ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave and announced the closure of its embassy in Eritrea. Eritrea said that it would sever diplomatic ties.
Ethiopian authorities have accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, an allegation Eritrea has denied.
The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, if it takes control of Mekelle, is very likely to leave regional security in the hands of the Tigray Peace Force, which comprises former members of the Tigray Defense Forces, Birru said.
Abiy has tried and failed to subdue Tigray’s rebellious leaders in recent months, with TPLF Chairman Debretsion Gebremichael openly challenging him. Renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 peace deal that ended a devastating two-year war between federal troops, backed by Eritrea and allied militias, and the TPLF.
“This is an extraordinary and largely unexpected turn in a war whose direction looked very different only days ago,” Getachew Temare, an independent attorney and human rights defender who is from Ethiopia, said of the possible fall of Mekelle in an analysis posted on X. “But the most consequential question is not whether Mekelle falls. It is what this fall means politically.”
He said the emergence of the Tigray Peace Force makes the current conflict different from the previous one. When Mekelle fell to federal forces in November 2020, the TPLF “retained something far more important. A substantial political and social constituency for armed resistance remained intact. Within months, Tigrayan forces returned to Mekelle and the military balance was dramatically reversed.”
The fighting has brought renewed hardship to civilians still recovering from the previous 2020-2022 war. Residents of Mekelle told the AP earlier this week that communications, banking and other essential services had been disrupted.
In September, residents described fears of renewed isolation following the suspension of flights. They also reported that roads connecting Tigray and Afar had been closed to civilian traffic, although the AP couldn't independently verify the closures.
___
Kiyaro reported from Hamburg, Germany. Associated Press journalist Khaled Kazziha contributed from Nairobi, Kenya.

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.
The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.
On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.
Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.
His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.
The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”
Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.
The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.
“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.
Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

ICE is reportedly using a Palantir database to compile dossiers on protestors
An attorney representing protestors said this infringes on First Amendment rights.
As revealed by unsealed court documents, Department of Homeland Security agents are allegedly creating dossiers on those that are accused of observing or protesting Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. As first reported by Wired, these DHS files on protestors reportedly include sensitive info like photos and license plate numbers and are stored in a database built by Palantir called Investigative Case Management.
The new information comes from a partially unsealed court filing about a January ICE operation that took place in Maine, according to Wired. The filing is part of a class action lawsuit, which led to a redacted version becoming available to the public on Friday and revealing the purported database of ICE protestors.
According to the lawsuit, DHS agents would track and intimidate observers or protestors, sometimes by driving by their homes or labeling them as "Threat to Law Enforcement, Professional Protestor." In one example, an agent reportedly called one of the plaintiffs on her cell and suggested that she tell her spouse "not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist."
The lawyers representing the plaintiffs said that this sort of database creates a chilling effect on the First Amendment rights of protestors. On the other side, a DHS spokesperson told Wired that the case was "meritless" and denied the existence of such a database that labels and tracks "domestic terrorists."

Prem* is a young mathematics graduate from a village in Jharkhand. He was known as an energetic and supportive young person. Children from the village often approached him when they had difficulties with mathematics. When he was selected for a job with the Indian Railways, it was expected to be a moment of happiness. But the thought of leaving his parents, friends, village and the life he shared with them was difficult for him.
In the weeks following the job offer, Prem began having sleepless nights, worrying about how he would cope with a new life and new responsibilities. Gradually, he stopped talking to his family. He began to feel helpless and worthless, lost interest in everyday life and reached a point where he attempted to end his life.
What helped was having people around him who could understand not only what he was going through, but also the world he was coming from. A neighbourhood facilitator working in a community-based organisation was able to sit with him, listen to his worries and share his dukh-sukh. They understood why leaving his parents, friends and village felt so difficult and gave him space to talk about the fears he was carrying.
The support was not about asking him simply to adjust or move on. It helped him think about what mattered to him, what he wanted for his future and how he could remain connected to the people and place that were important to him while taking up the new opportunity. He eventually wrote to the department asking for another opportunity to join. He was invited again and went to work, while continuing to receive support.
Prem’s experience highlights that what looks like a positive life event from the outside can sometimes become overwhelming. A suicidal act can often happen suddenly, during a moment of intense crisis. But the distress behind that moment may have been building for much longer.
For Adivasi communities, distress can be shaped by circumstances that may never appear in a psychiatric consultation.
When distress is accumulates
A recent study in Jharkhand examined psychosocial distress and help-seeking among Adivasi Ho adolescents. It found that distress was often linked to family conflict, pressure around education and work, financial hardship, violence, separation and loss, and difficulties in relationships. Some adolescents withdrew and stopped sharing what they were going through; for some, this included thoughts of self-harm or suicide
These accounts do not offer a single explanation for suicide among Adivasi communities. They show how distress can accumulate across everyday life — in family conflict, having to leave school temporarily or reduce schooling to help with agricultural or household work, substance use, untreated illness, violence, displacement, loss of livelihood, lack of mentorship, identity-related stigma and self-doubt, or the erosion of community and belonging.
When communities are disrupted
Belonging is an important part of suicide prevention. Stereotypes, exclusion, humiliation, discrimination and pressure to hide one’s identity can affect how people see themselves and how connected they feel to society. Historically, Adivasi communities stayed together. But modern development, alongside education and employment opportunities, have in some cases, uprooted Adivasi people from their culture. Mainstream schools do not teach Adivasi children in their own mother tongue; their history is woefully under-represented in the school curricula.
Sandip Sing, a radiologist from the Munda community practising in rural West Bengal and a first-generation learner, says, “There is a rapid transition in accessing and navigating educational and professional spaces, often amid gaps in resources, networks, and institutional familiarity. Bridging these gaps can be challenging, particularly with unfamiliar systems.”
Many educated Adivasis may also have had fewer opportunities to engage with their community’s history, culture, language and traditions, and may have complex or evolving relationships with their Adivasi identities. This matters for mental health because belonging itself is a source of strength. When people are uprooted without finding a new sense of belonging, distress can deepen.
This does not mean that development itself causes mental illness or suicide. The concern is what happens when rapid social change is accompanied by displacement, loss of livelihood, cultural disconnection and weakening social support.
Collective strength, mentoring
The strength of Adivasi life also lies in ways of expressing emotions and sharing knowledge. Songs and dances are not simply cultural performances; they are ways of expressing emotions, maintaining connection and making sense of life. The Adivasi dance itself is a powerful metaphor. People dance in a chain, holding one another. The village headman, Majhi Baba, dances alongside everyone else. An 80-year-old and an eight-year-old can dance together. There is no hierarchy; the strength is in the circle. For suicide prevention, this collective strength matters.
Young people also need places where they can be themselves without constantly having to explain or defend who they are. Lilibiti Saren, a medical officer from the Santhal community working in tribal areas of Bankura, West Bengal, notes that she often finds young people in these communities lacking direction. “There is a need for proper mentorship,” she says.
Locally organised Adivasi youth spaces can help. Such spaces can offer young people opportunities to speak in their own language, share experiences, learn from peers and elders and explore what Adivasiyat — identity, history, relationships and belonging — means to them.
Access and pathways in care
Clinical care remains essential. A person experiencing suicidal thoughts may need assessment for depression, substance use, trauma, psychosis, previous attempts, suicidal intent, access to means and immediate safety. Treatment and follow-up can save lives.
But access to mental health care is itself a major challenge in many Adivasi areas. Services are often limited, distant and unevenly available.
And even when services are available, the pathways into care may not be optimal. An Adivasi person with lived experience of mental healthcare says: “I felt like the psychiatrists and the psychologists were not speaking to me. They were judging me for what I had done and they were trying to find symptoms instead of trying to understand me, my pain and my situation.”
This raises an important question: are our mental health systems listening as carefully as they are diagnosing?
When formal services are scarce, difficult to reach, or experienced as unfamiliar or judgmental, people may seek support elsewhere—including from family, community networks, faith healers or indigenous systems. These spaces may offer something that the formal system does not: familiar language, relationships, cultural understanding and a sense of belonging.
Adivasi mental health therefore cannot be treated simply as another category within rural health. Representation matters — from schools to healthcare institutions and policy making.
Models that could work
In Adivasi communities of Jharkhand, particularly among the Ho, Munda and Santhal communities, Madait refers to a tradition of voluntary help and collective support for someone who needs it or is in distress. It reflects an understanding that some difficulties are too large for one household to manage alone.
This may be a useful way to think about mental healthcare too. The question is not simply how services can be delivered to Adivasi communities, but how communities themselves can shape, participate in and lead the care they need.
The same principle can be seen in Dukhu-Sukhu Baithaki — community support group meetings where people experiencing mental health difficulties and their families can meet, share experiences and support one another. This model works in West Singhbhum, Jharkhand, where people living with mental health conditions come together each month. These spaces do not replace professional care. They bring community knowledge, relationships and mutual support into the process of recovery.
Education without a knowledge of one’s roots; development that comes with displacement and mental healthcare that does not see or hear the people who need help is no longer enough. For suicide prevention, we must ask not only, “What is wrong with the individual?”, but also, “ Where is the community support? Where is the system that understands them?”
Perhaps suicide prevention in Adivasi communities must begin there — not by doing things for Adivasis, but by doing them with Adivasis.

Filmmaker and producer Siddharth P Malhotra has had a good 2026. His Netflix film Ikka, starring Sunny Deol and Akshaye Khanna, grabbed a lot of eyeballs earlier this year. Now, his web show Shaque: Trust No One on the same platform has been doing well too.
EXCLUSIVE: Siddharth P Malhotra reveals Ikka sequel and Shaque Season 2 are in the works; also shares happiness at the response to Parineeti Chopra starrer show: “Haven’t got so many calls for a series before”
In an exclusive chat with Bollywood Hungama, Malhotra revealed that both the projects will have a second part. “Ikka has broken records. There is Ikka 2 being worked on. Shaque has now broken records and Shaque Season 2 is being done. It has been a great year. Shaque Season 2 won’t continue the same story. It will be a new story. But a season 2 is in the works. We are writing it,” he said.
Malhotra also shared that director Rensil D’Silva had earlier envisioned Shaque as a movie when he came up with the idea years ago. “It was a story Rensil had cracked about 8-9 years ago,” he said. “Initially, it was a feature film. Then we worked on it and we said that let’s see if we can make it into series. After writing it as a series, we realized that it has legs and potential. Then I sold it to Netflix. They liked the idea.”
Malhotra is happy with the response the show has generated in little over a week. “We have been getting a lot of feedback. It’s done really well. Even after one week, it’s at number one. In my whole career, I haven’t got so many calls for a series. Even people from South Bombay are calling and saying that they binged and enjoyed it. It’s a good feeling. Netflix is very happy. It’s done very well for them. It’s in the top 10 in 20-30 countries. When you go into a party or function, people are willingly saying that they found it very good. They will say it saamne se only when they actually liked it. If they didn’t, they would say that they haven’t watched it yet,” he said.
Shaque is a whodunit where the identity of the culprit is revealed at the end. In today’s times of social media, there is every chance of someone or the other revealing the climax. Malhotra said that one can’t control that. “Social media is good and bad. If somebody wants to reveal the climax, you can’t stop that person. As far as people are talking and commenting about the show, we are very happy. Now, even after revealing the climax, if people are still watching the show, it’s the writing team’s victory,” he said.
During the trailer launch of Shaque, lead actor Parineeti Chopra shared that she came to know after starting the shoot that she is pregnant. Hence, the makers ensured that she stayed at the same place where they were shooting, so that she doesn’t have to travel. Malhotra said that this wasn’t challenging for them. “It is the responsibility between Sapna (Malhotra) and me to take care of her. She could have said that she is pregnant and she won’t be able to shoot. But she is continued the shoot. So, we should take care of her, respect her and do the best we can,” he said.
As a director, Siddharth P Malhotra has made films on varied subjects like We Are Family (2010), Hichki (2018), Tribhanga (2021), Maharaj (2024) and Ikka (2026). When asked whether it has always been a conscious decision for him not to repeat genres, he said, “It’s not a conscious effort to not repeat a genre. It’s actually an effort to try and find a story I can resonate to. Actually, for me the genre is the same as they are all (stories of) human relationships. The worlds might be different but the stories are of human relations and complex situations.”
Malhotra has had a successful and long collaboration with Netflix with a series of projects like Tribhanga, Maharaj, Ikka and now Shaque. “I have known Monika (Shergill, Vice President, Content) from the time I did Sanjivani (TV show) and before that. Their team is very co-operative and collaborative. All the success of any show or film of Netflix is a collaborative effort. Their names don’t appear but they put in a lot of hard work. No single person can take credit of a success. It’s always a team work. Netflix has been a great collaborator and we are collaborating a lot now,” he said.

In October 2024, Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, through her Yield Giving fund, donated $30 million to Housing Trust Silicon Valley, providing the largest individual gift in the nonprofit’s history. The unrestricted donation was aimed at helping the organisation expand affordable housing opportunities across the 14-county Bay Area, one of the most expensive housing markets in the United States. As per Housing Trust TV, announcing the gift, Noni Ramos, chief executive of Housing Trust Silicon Valley, said the funding would enable the organisation to accelerate efforts to create more equitable and affordable communities. The nonprofit indicated that the money could be used to strengthen its loan fund, expand existing housing programmes and launch new initiatives focused on affordability and housing equity.
The gift came through MacKenzie Scott's Yield Giving philanthropic fund
The gift, announced in October 2024, came through Scott's Yield Giving philanthropic fund and stood as the largest single donation from an individual in Housing Trust's history. Housing Trust CEO Noni Ramos described the unrestricted contribution as an incredible surprise the organization felt deeply honored and grateful to receive, noting that the trust placed in the organization also carries a responsibility to translate that generosity into meaningful, lasting impact for the communities it serves.
Housing Trust's Board Chair, Joe Anzalone, framed the timing as especially significant, coming just as the organization was preparing to mark 25 years of funding affordable housing solutions. He pointed to the scale of Housing Trust's track record up to that point — having invested $615 million in the community, created more than 27,200 housing opportunities, and helped over 51,000 neighbors find affordable housing across the region, while helping leverage an additional $8.1 billion through its partners.
Founded in 2000, Housing Trust was created through a partnership between affordable housing advocates, businesses, and public and private sector leaders and foundations, aimed at meeting the Bay Area's growing need for affordable housing solutions.
A year later: the 10-year plan takes shape
Nearly a year after the initial gift, Housing Trust unveiled a detailed 10-year plan in September 2025 for how it intends to convert the $30 million into durable, long-term housing solutions across the region — a plan the organization says was shaped through input from staff, board members, and community stakeholders.
The roadmap centers on five major initiatives designed to direct the gift toward both expanded housing opportunity and stronger organizational capacity over the coming decade. According to the plan, the funding will help accelerate Housing Trust's core lending work, expand homeownership assistance programs, fuel new policy and innovation efforts, and strengthen the organization's overall long-term impact.
Concretely, that includes growing Housing Trust's core revolving loan fund and piloting new financing tools tailored specifically for developers. Michael Quinn, who leads much of this development-facing work at Housing Trust, described the approach as centered on problem-solving rather than simply designing new products, emphasizing that the organization is listening closely to what developers actually need most and shaping financing accordingly — whether that means adjusting timing, pricing, or loan terms to help projects overcome common barriers. The plan also calls for extending Housing Trust's first-time homebuyer programs into a wider geographic footprint across the region in the year ahead.
Real projects already benefiting
Even before the 10-year plan was formalized, Housing Trust's broader work continued delivering tangible results across the Bay Area. In Sunnyvale, the organization provided a $2 million predevelopment loan in partnership with Related California to support Meridian Apartments, which created 90 affordable homes for families in one of the region's most expensive cities. In San Rafael, Housing Trust backed Eden Housing with a $4 million loan for Vivalon, a 66-unit affordable housing development for older adults that pairs affordable housing with supportive services.
By the time of its 2025 Annual Report, marking its 25th anniversary, Housing Trust reported having invested more than $690 million total since its founding, helping create over 28,700 homes and open doors for roughly 53,800 neighbors across the greater Bay Area — figures that continue climbing as the MacKenzie Scott-funded plan moves into its early implementation phase.
Part of a broader pattern of giving
Housing Trust's gift wasn't an isolated act of generosity. MacKenzie Scott gave away roughly $2 billion in 2024 alone, spread across nearly 200 organizations focused largely on economic security, housing affordability, job stability, child development, and healthcare, bringing her five-year philanthropic total to more than $19 billion. Housing organizations across the country have been among her recurring areas of focus, with Housing Trust Silicon Valley standing as one of the more prominent recipients in that space.

A murder investigation has been launched after a 40-year-old man was shot dead in a “senseless act of violence” during a memorial service in west London, police have said.
Police were called on Friday at 7.47pm after multiple shots were heard in East Acton.
Officers attended alongside the London ambulance service. The victim was treated at the scene on the junction of Braybrook Street and Erconwald Street, however, he was pronounced dead.
The Metropolitan police said about 40 to 50 people were at the scene, including children. The man’s family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.
A postmortem examination is scheduled to establish the cause of death, but the victim is believed to have sustained a gunshot wound, the force added.
No arrests have been made.
DCI Brian Howie, who is leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts are with the family and friends of a man whose life was taken in a senseless act of violence.
“We understand a large number of people had gathered for a memorial service and what should have been a time to come together in remembrance has instead left a family devastated.
“We believe between 40 and 50 people, including children, were present when this incident occurred. Someone knows what happened and we need them to come forward.
“If you were around Erconwald Street, Braybrook Street, the surrounding roads or Wormwood Scrubs playground between 6pm and 8pm, please think carefully about what you saw. Did you see anyone carrying or concealing weapons, people on bicycles acting suspiciously or vehicles being driven at speed?
“We also want to hear from anyone with photographs, video, dashcam, doorbell or mobile phone footage or who has seen anything relevant on social media.”

Police have urged people adventuring in Tasmania to carry an appropriate communications device after two separate helicopter rescues on Saturday.
A New South Wales man fell while walking on Bruny Island North and called for help on his mobile phone, while in a separate incident, a walker fell ill on the west coast.
Both cases show the need for people to carry with them either a fully charged mobile phone or, in more remote areas, a personal locator beacon.
Two separate rescues involving Tasmania's rescue helicopter has prompted police to urge bushwalkers to carry communications devices when out and about.
A 62-year-old man from New South Wales has had what police described as a "lucky" escape from a cliff fall in southern Tasmania.
The man was walking alone on a track at Dennes Point on North Bruny Island on Saturday morning when he fell over and slipped about 10 metres down a steep hill towards the water.
Police said the man, who was not injured in the incident, contacted emergency services by mobile phone about 10:30am, with police attending the scene shortly afterwards.
A specialist police roping team was sent to the scene in the Westpac Rescue Helicopter, with the man rescued about 1pm.
Senior Constable Callum Herbert, from Search and Rescue, said the man had slipped about 10 metres down an unstable slope at the edge of a coastal track.
"He luckily stopped himself at the top of a further 40-metre cliff,"
Senior Constable Herbert said.
"A sensible decision was made to contact emergency services as in this case an attempt to self-rescue may have resulted in him falling further and could have had a catastrophic outcome.
"I remind all walkers to carry a charged mobile phone with them, no matter if the walk is only a short distance and also to remain vigilant around coastal areas, as the ground can be unstable due to loose vegetation and gravel."
Walkers activate beacon for rescue
In a separate incident on Saturday, a 44-year-old man was rescued from the Tyndall Range on Tasmania's west coast after becoming ill while bushwalking.
Police said the man was part of a group of three on a day walk from an overnight campsite when he became unable to continue.
The group activated a personal locator beacon (PLB) and contacted emergency services via satellite communications about 3pm.
Police said the Westpac Rescue Helicopter located the group and transported the man to the Royal Hobart Hospital for assessment last night.
The group was equipped for their overnight camping trip, with "appropriate supplies and communication equipment including their PLB which ensured a quick response from emergency services," police said.
Inspector Steve Jones said it was a "timely reminder for bushwalkers in remote areas to carry sufficient food, water, communication equipment and emergency shelter for unexpected delays".

Police say they arrested 18-year-old man driving vehicle and were investigating what happened

A vehicle drove into a crowd standing on a road to cheer on the Newcastle Knights rugby team north of Sydney on Saturday, injuring 10 people, including several children, Australian officials said.
Two of the injured – a 5-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man – were in critical condition, and the other eight were in stable condition at a hospital, according to New South Wales police.
Those in stable condition included another 5-year-old girl and a 2-year-old girl.
Police said they arrested the 18-year-old man driving the vehicle and were investigating what happened.
They said the crash was not believed to be related to terrorism.
Thousands had been cheering the team on this week as they trained, Australian Associated Press reported. Another large crowd was on the street Saturday morning to see the team bus off ahead of the rugby league finals match on Sunday.
Newcastle mayor Gavin Morris said in televised remarks it appeared the driver lost control of the car that hit the crowd.
“I’ve spoken to the authorities, a number of which, and look, first of all, it is under investigation, and the young driver is now with police, so it appears that he was revving the car in some form. He was excited. He was a supporter. He was, you know, a fan,” Mr Morris told ABC News.
“It appears that he’s lost control of the car, and he’s gone … sideways into the crowd.”
Thousands had lined the city's streets to farewell the Newcastle Knights rugby league team due to compete in the country's National Rugby League grand final in Sydney on Sunday, the Australian Broadcasting Corp reported.
Newcastle Knights CEO Peter Parr said: "Our thoughts and prayers are first and foremost with everyone who has been injured, their families and loved ones, and everyone who witnessed what occurred this morning."
NSW Police said the 18-year-old driver had allegedly been driving "erratically".
