Probe launched into luxury One Stanley project over alleged steel bar shortage
Buildings Department pulls in developer and contractors after report claims house has up to 75 per cent fewer steel bars than approved
Authorities have launched a probe into the building quality of a luxury residential development in one of Hong Kong’s most expensive neighbourhoods in the Southern district after receiving a complaint from an owner that insufficient steel bars were used during construction.
The Buildings Department said on Saturday it was “very concerned about the matter” relating to One Stanley in Stanley, but stressed that its previous inspections did not find any imminent danger.
The department said it would summon meetings with the developer, contractors and other relevant parties responsible for the development.
Public concerns have been brewing since Friday after a report by the online property news platform WuChatProp alleged that an on-site inspection of a house found insufficient steel bars had been used in some parts of the property. The number fell short by as much as 75 per cent of the approved building plans, according to the report.

United Nations, Sep 23: In his inaugural speech at the UN General Assembly, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said world leaders must set up global standards to oversee artificial intelligence because “fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance”.
Burnham said the UK will try to persuade other countries to adopt rules on transparency and access to AI models - and, even tougher, to get tech companies to sign on, too.
He said AI has immense potential but will also be “a source of disruption to the way we live and work - and a multiplier of risk”.
Burnham also said Russia and other states are using AI-augmented misinformation and disinformation to corrode democracy, something he said Britain has faced in the decade since it voted to leave the European Union.
He said he has asked British security chiefs to set up a National Centre for Information Defence to counter the threat.
Burnham also chaired a meeting at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday on the Israel-Palestine issue, alongside French President Emmanuel Macron, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan.
He said the two-state solution to Israel-Palestinian conflict must be kept alive.
Burnham said failure to deliver a two-state solution will “corrode trust” in politicians who have talked about the issue but not taken action.
He told delegates from dozens of countries that the UK has banned trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank because the “E1” settlement expansion plan is “a deliberate attempt to block a two-state solution.”
“We all live in an era of low trust in politics. Many people in this room, many politicians around the world, have spoken for decades about a two-state solution. But if we fail to back those words with deeds, we will further corrode trust in the political, diplomatic and international process,” the UK prime minister said. (AP)

The Embassy of the State of Palestine to India has questioned the description of the 1918 Battle of Haifa as the “liberation of Haifa”, saying that Indian soldiers who participated in the battle were serving under British command as part of an imperial military campaign that resulted in the occupation of Palestine.
In a five-page position paper titled “Rewriting of India–Palestine history: The battle of Haifa: liberation or occupation?”, the Palestinian Embassy said the terminology surrounding the battle required “careful and scholarly reflection” and argued that the event should be understood within the historical context of British military occupation of Palestine.
The Embassy said Palestine, including Haifa, was under Ottoman rule before 1918 and that British forces defeated the Ottoman Empire during the First World War, bringing Palestine under British occupation. Indian soldiers participated in the campaign as part of the British Indian Army, under British command.
It argued that describing them retrospectively as having “liberated Haifa” risked attributing to India a sovereign military decision that the country did not possess in 1918, when it was still under British rule.
The paper pointed to contemporary British terminology, saying military and parliamentary records referred to the operations in Palestine using terms such as “capture”, “take”, “fall” and “conquer”. It also noted that following the British military campaign, Palestine was administered under the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (OETA) until its replacement by a civil administration in July 1920.
The Embassy also cited India’s own historical records, including the 2014 publication Indian War Memorials Around the World, saying it does not describe the event as the “liberation of Haifa”.
According to the paper, the publication records that the “fortified town of Haifa fell to a cavalry charge by the Jodhpur Lancers” and that the 15th Imperial Service Cavalry Brigade “broke through and took the town”.
It also referred to the Teen Murti Memorial in New Delhi, stating that the memorial was established during British colonial rule to commemorate Indian soldiers who served and died during the First World War, and was not originally intended to commemorate relations between India and Israel.
The Embassy said the memorial refers to “Palestine and some of its cities” among the places associated with the military campaigns in which Indian soldiers served.
The paper further cited official Indian records to state that 491 Indian soldiers are recorded at Ramleh War Cemetery, 109 at the Gaza and Deir el Balah War Cemeteries and 47 at the Haifa Indian Cemetery, besides soldiers commemorated at other cemeteries and memorials across historical Palestine.
The Embassy questioned why Haifa had become the centre of a commemorative narrative when Indian soldiers had fought across a much wider region, including the Suez Canal, Gaza, Jerusalem, the Jordan Valley, Damascus and Aleppo.
It also said the first formal Israeli public ceremony commemorating the Indian soldiers was held in 2010, nearly a century after the battle.
The paper argued that Britain, rather than India, was the principal military power behind the campaign, as it financed, armed and commanded the operation. It questioned why the “liberation of Haifa” narrative centred on Indian soldiers while Britain’s role was not similarly emphasised.
The Embassy also stressed that the soldiers described as “Indian soldiers” served in the British Indian Army and came from different regions, communities and religions across British India, whose geographical and political boundaries differed from those of the present-day Republic of India.
The position paper placed the soldiers’ participation within the wider history of British colonial rule, noting that Indian troops were deployed in military campaigns far from their homeland.
It also referred to the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, arguing that the broader record of British rule should be considered when interpreting the role of Indian soldiers in the First World War.
The Embassy cited Mahatma Gandhi’s opposition to the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine at the expense of its indigenous population, including his statement that “Palestine belongs to the Arabs in the same sense that England belongs to the English.”
It further pointed out that India voted against UN Resolution 181 in 1947, which proposed partition and allocated Haifa to the proposed Jewish state, and questioned how the 1918 battle could subsequently be presented as a foundation for India-Israel historical ties.
The Embassy said describing the 1918 occupation of Haifa as a liberation “raises serious questions and concerns in Palestine”. It maintained that Haifa should be recognised as a Palestinian city at the time and that the battle took place in the context of the British military occupation of Palestine.
At the same time, the Embassy said its position was expressed with “full respect” for the sacrifice and memory of Indian soldiers and for India’s sovereign right to commemorate its history and fallen soldiers.
It called for historical remembrance of the Battle of Haifa to remain grounded in accuracy, balance and respect for the historical experiences of all concerned, while emphasising that the document represented the Palestinian Embassy’s perspective and was intended to contribute to discussion on the historical and legal questions surrounding the battle.

Concerns over the safety of drinking water have resurfaced in parts of Uri area of north Kashmir’s Baramulla district after residents of Gawalta village found a dead snake inside a pipeline supplying water to the locality, raising questions over the maintenance and monitoring of the public water supply network.
The incident comes weeks after a similar complaint from Karkroo Mohalla in Nambla, where residents had reported finding dead rats inside a water storage tank and supply pipelines.
Both incidents have generated severe resentment among the local population, who accused the Jal Shakti Department of not taking care of the water tanks, pipelines and other components of the supply network.
In the fresh incident, the residents said the Sokad-Gowlta Water Supply Scheme had remained non-functional for several days, leaving the village without regular drinking water.
They said that despite repeated requests to employees of the Jal Shakti Department, the problem was not addressed promptly.
“With the supply remaining disrupted, the local residents inspected the pipeline themselves on Monday and found a dead snake lodged inside it,” said Arif Hussain, a local resident.
The presence of the snake triggered concern among residents over the possibility of contamination and the overall hygiene of the water distribution system.
The residents of Gowlta have now urged the department to conduct an immediate inspection of the entire supply network, clean and disinfect the pipeline and ensure that only safe water is supplied to households.
They have also sought an inquiry into how the reptile entered the pipeline and demanded preventive measures, including regular inspection and sanitation of water infrastructure.
Residents said repeated complaints involving contamination or poor maintenance were a major issue in the area and the concerned authority should ensure monitoring of drinking-water schemes in the Uri area.

The OpenAI leader who just quit and issued a stark warning about safety says that, like other recent Big Tech defectors, he plans to help solve the problem from the outside.
David Robinson worked at OpenAI for three and a half years and ran transparency for the safety team. In an essay published Saturday in The Atlantic, he said he oversaw the company's "preparedness framework" and the writing of a slew of safety reports.
"Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them," he wrote.
"That's why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right."
Robinson said he hired a PR firm, Spitfire Strategies, to help him with the public attention he'll receive following his departure. "But the decision to speak out is mine alone," he added.
That might be aimed at claims from some that public resignations by workers from companies, including Anthropic and Google, are part of a coordinated effort to spread mistrust of AI and foment government regulation. Elon Musk, for instance, said that former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon's resignation and subsequent public appearances seem "like a setup," which Coxon denied.
In response to Robinson's essay, an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement that the company is working to ensure AI models don't outpace the safety measures they've implemented.
"As our models become more capable, we continue to strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today while building safety cases to anticipate the risks of future advances," the spokesperson said. "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down."
The spokesperson said OpenAI is taking steps to improve security for its AI models.
"We're making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process," the spokesperson said.
Robinson's departure comes two months after OpenAI agents escaped their system and hacked another AI company, Hugging Face, in July. OpenAI is not the only company struggling to balance the AI race with calls for guardrails. Last month, a small AI startup said it used Anthropic's Claude to hack into OpenAI's codebase, and The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies this spring.
More recently, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent hacked a government website in June.
Robinson's PR reps did not respond to an inquiry from Business Insider about his next steps. In The Atlantic, he suggested his game plan is in flux.
"Now I plan to work on the outside, in the hope that I can help more people understand the risks I saw, and strengthen the incentives OpenAI and other firms have to be safer," he wrote. "Like other colleagues, I'm figuring out exactly what that means."

Russia strikes second major bridge in Kyiv, mayor says
- Published
A Russian strike has hit a second major bridge in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko has said, as Russia ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital.
The attack on Saturday morning damaged the road surface and trolleybus overhead wires on the Northern Bridge, Klitschko said.
The strike comes after another key bridge in the city, Southern Bridge, has been targeted multiple times by Russian drones since Thursday, with Klitschko earlier warning that such attacks were "tearing Kyiv apart".
The two bridges link the eastern and western parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday, signalling a new stage in Moscow's attacks.
Writing on Telegram on Saturday, Klitschko said: "Hitting the North Bridge. Emergency services are on their way."

One missing Google Docs feature has a pretty easy workaround
If you go a little out of your way, you can make Google Docs much easier on the eyes.
Google Docs is an incredibly convenient application, and it's one that receives constant support and updates. Recently, Google has been releasing more and more new features to the word processor, bringing Gemini-powered content creation tools to Docs — alongside a myriad of other AI updates. However, there's one long-requested feature that has historically escaped (and continues to escape) Google Docs' repertoire.
Google's own word processor has a lot going for it, what with the way it seamlessly bridges between its different host platforms (as opposed to Microsoft Word, which is much clunkier on mobile). Interestingly, though, one of the features missing from Docs exposes a divide between versions of the product. That missing feature is dark mode — which is present on mobile but missing on the web version. Dark mode is a glaring omission on the website version of Google Docs, so it's lucky that there are ways to get around this shortcoming both within and without Google's direct remit.
Official routes to dark mode on Google Docs
Google began to make dark mode available to Docs on mobile in 2020, first with Android and later with the Apple version of the application. In either version, you can find dark mode via Menu > Settings > Theme (or Choose Theme if you're using Android). From there, you can choose Dark, Light or System Default.
Unfortunately, you won't find this range of brightness options on Google Docs' own website. Google hasn't listed an official reason for this favoritism toward the mobile end of its offerings, but it has at least offered a single in-house workaround via Chrome's experimental features. By searching chrome://flags in Chrome, you can access these features and search for "Auto Dark Mode for Web Contents" — but be warned: these features are experimental and could compromise browser data and device security, so you're taking a risk by toggling this feature.
Dark mode on Google Docs via browser extensions
Luckily, there are ways of accessing dark mode without risky experimental toggles. You don't have to wait for the future of Google Docs to access browser extensions today — and that includes Google Docs Dark Mode in the Chrome Web Store (or an alternative for your browser of choice, such as DocsAfterDark on Firefox). It's not the only extension that covers this area, but it's a great choice, and it's easy to get working.
A free download of this browser extension will automatically activate dark mode in Google Docs. However, if you want to change up your dark mode settings (or disable the extension entirely), you'll want to hit the Extensions icon next to the search bar (which looks like a puzzle piece and is in the top-right of the screen). Here, you can not only disable the mod, but you can also select a color theme and tweak individual sepia, contrast, grayscale and brightness settings. In addition, this extension will automatically disable dark mode for prints — so don't worry about toggling it on and off all the time.

Congo’s Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday (October 1, 2026). They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases, making up for nearly half of the confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.

Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation’s 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons ranging from how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

Algeria introduces death penalty for arsonists after deadly wildfires
- Published
Algeria has adopted a law imposing the death penalty on people convicted of arson of forests or fields after a series of deadly wildfires swept parts of the country.
Members of the national assembly voted through the bill, which also made child abduction a capital offence, on Thursday.
Capital punishment has been in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993.
The official death toll from the blazes stands at 12, but independent news outlets believe the figure to be much higher.
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice ministry to introduce the changes to the criminal law after more than 100 fires in the north-east of the country during an intense heatwave in northern Africa.
Under the law, anyone convicted of deliberately setting fire to forests, woods or fields could face execution.
The death penalty has also been extended to child kidnappings that involve torture, sexual assault or mutilation.
According to news agency AFP, Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa told parliament: "The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes."
The tougher penalties were justified because arson had reached "the level of organised crime", with investigations suggesting links to "foreign parties", Boudjemaa said.
The upper house, the Council of the Nation, will review the law before it is officially ratified by the president.
Investigative journalist Nozha Khelalef has been gathering the names of those believed to have died in the fires from death notices posted by families and information shared by some local authorities.
Her tally, listed on the independent news website Twala, external, puts the death toll at 200.
While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires in the summer, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country.

SBI Mutual Fund, under its various schemes, acquired an additional 1.18 Cr equity shares of Swiggy via open market transactions on Tuesday, the foodtech major informed the bourses earlier today. Following the purchase, its total shareholding in Swiggy rose to 14.16 Cr equity shares or around 5.1% of Swiggy’s total equity. The move allows Swiggy to pivot the business model of its quick commerce arm Instamart to an inventory-led model. While it currently serves as a marketplace that hosts seller entities, the new model will allow it to sell products after directly procuring them from brands. Hudson Williams wore this cardigan. Then the Indigenous designer's business went viral
Designer saw online sales spike and the $350 cardigan quickly sold out
When Canadian actor Hudson Williams stepped out wearing a piece by Canadian Indigenous designer Justin Jacob Louis on Wednesday, Louis didn't expect to go viral.
In fact, he nearly forgot it was happening.
The Samson Cree Nation-born designer was spending National Day for Truth and Reconciliation away from work. He was with his family, unplugged and out paddling on the lake.
And then he checked his phone.
"There was, like, a whole bunch of sales and the social media was lighting up and I was just like, 'What is going on? Did something happen?'" he said in an interview with CBC News.
"I realized that, like, every cardigan had sold out. At that time, there was like $12,000 in sales in a matter of an hour. And I was like, 'What the hell?'"
The Heated Rivalry star wore Louis's blue-and-black journey knit cardigan to the Kate Spade New York Global Summit on Women's Mental Health, along with an orange ribbon on his chest marking National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.
For Louis, seeing his work worn that day by a prominent Canadian actor made the moment "pretty special."
"There was intention and genuine interest in supporting us behind it, so that made it more meaningful for me," Louis said.
The cardigan, which costs $350, was designed by Louis, founder and creative director of Section 35 and the Justin Jacob Louis label. And it made its way to Williams as part of a last minute request.
How they connected
Louis said someone from Williams's team initially contacted him by email and over Instagram about the actor's interest in buying the piece — just last weekend.
Shipping it from his warehouse wasn't feasible within the timeframe, but he happened to have the right size at his studio in the Fraser Valley in Chilliwack, B.C.
Someone from Williams's team drove from Vancouver to Louis's studio that Sunday to pick it up.
Months of sales in two days
That choice had an immediate impact on Louis's small business.
The brand gained hundreds of new followers throughout the day. The cardigan sold out and other pieces began selling, too.
Louis estimates the shop did two to three months worth of sales in just two days.
While the brand hadn't planned on restocking the cardigan, the huge surge in demand persuaded Louis to open up pre-orders.
"For an independent small business, it helps out so much," he said. "It's just been kind of a whirlwind."
Design based on a dream
Louis says the design came to him in a dream he had while feeling disconnected and homesick and living about 12 hours from the community where he grew up.
In the dream, he was back at his father's place, walking across the pasture in winter under the night sky, wondering where his ancestors were.
"The stars in the sky lit up and then they turned into eyeballs and looked right at me," Louis said.
"It was just kind of like this reminder that they're always with you wherever you are, no matter how far from home you are."
Louis says Williams messaged him directly to thank him for the cardigan. They've stayed in touch, and the designer says he'd love to work with Williams again.
But for now, he's focused on continuing to design and build his labels.
Here's his advice to other designers and small businesses: stay intentional and true to your values and culture.
"That makes us who we are," he said. "Showcasing the beauty that exists within our communities. I think there's so much talent and the storytelling that comes from our people and our stories. It's what sets us apart. And I think staying true to that is so important."

The remains of medieval ruler Tsar Samuel will arrive in Bulgaria on Saturday amid great pomp and ceremony, after decades of negotiations with neighbouring Greece.
The remains – discovered in a Greek border area 60 years ago – are to be flown to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, onboard a military aircraft to be received with full state honours, including a fighter jet escort, a 21-gun salute and a procession to the Church of St Sophia, where the public will be able to pay respects.
The Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, said he hoped the handover would bolster Athens’s campaign to persuade Britain to return the Parthenon marbles, a collection of 2,500-year-old sculptures taken from the Acropolis and held by the British Museum.
“The global community is essentially re-evaluating its longstanding stance on protecting cultural heritage,” he said. “This shift is embodied by today’s initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation.”
Samuel was a warrior ruler who battled the Byzantine empire to expand his kingdom, but was ultimately defeated and died shortly afterwards in 1014. He is considered a symbol of Bulgaria’s national identity.
The handover of his remains follows an agreement earlier this week between the two countries’ culture ministers, under which Bulgaria will return religious relics taken from Greek monasteries during the first world war.
Several prominent Greek academics and religious leaders have raised concerns about the adequacy of Bulgaria’s contributions.
Mitsotakis and his Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, attended a ceremony at Thessaloniki’s Museum of Byzantine Civilization, where the remains were kept, before the handover.
“These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve and must have the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestors,” Radev said, speaking at the ceremony held at the museum.
“If in the past Tsar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us. He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger,” Radev said.

Amid the ongoing protests over the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the Campaign for Release of Workers and Activists of Noida (CaRWAN) on Saturday staged a separate protest near Jantar Mantar seeking the release of workers and activists jailed in connection with the April 13 Noida workers’ protest.
More than 100 protesters marched from Patel Chowk towards Jantar Mantar, and Delhi Police detained at least 70 of them before releasing them later in the day. The protesters alleged that the police forcefully detained and manhandled them, with female protesters allegedly being held by male officers.
‘Unlawful detention’
CaRWAN demanded that workers and activists who had been “unlawfully held by Uttar Pradesh Police and incarcerated for over five months” be released immediately.
“While there are protests going on against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, his daughter Medha Roopam, who is the District Magistrate of Gautam Buddha Nagar, issued NSA detention orders against Satyam Verma and Akriti Chaudhary,” CaRWAN member Anjali said during the protest.
Ms. Anjali said that while Mr. Verma, a translator and former journalist, continues to be detained under the National Security Act (NSA), 1980, Ms. Chaudhary remains in jail despite the Allahabad High Court quashing her detention under the NSA on September 2.
Six others, including activist Aditya Anand, workers Manisha and Rupesh, student leaders Yogesh Meena and Himanshu Thakur and artist Srishti Gupta are also in jail. The police have registered 11 FIRs against them.
“The Allahabad High Court called the police investigation on the basis of which the order was issued a ‘concocted story’ while quashing Ms. Chaudhary’s detention. The Uttar Pradesh government and police have been acting unlawfully since day one and people who have been working for social causes on the ground have been facing the brunt of it,” Ms. Anjali said.
For a cause
The protesters sat down near Jantar Mantar after the police asked them to clear the site. The police then allegedly forcefully took them into three buses, where female protesters were held by male officers and others were pushed and pulled by police personnel. Two buses were taken to Sector 23 Dwarka police station and one to Kapashera, where the detainees were later released, Ms. Anjali said.
“Female protesters were detained after 6 p.m.,” said Chitranshu, a protester.
Naureen, another member of CaRWAN, said the Uttar Pradesh police had tried to fabricate evidence and plant a mobile phone at Ms. Gupta’s house. “The police, working in alignment with the government, do not have any real evidence against them. We demand that they be released immediately,” she said.
Delhi University Professors Nandita Narain and N. Sachin were also part of the protest.
“Journalists like Satyam Verma and activists who are role models for all citizens have been held illegally and put behind bars. Regressive laws like the NSA have been imposed on them. These show the brutalities of both the police and those in power,” Ms. Narain said.

Neurable unveiled its very own pair of brain-scanning headphones on Thursday, the Neurable One. The company claims that wearing them helps you concentrate on whatever you’re doing—working, studying, or playing a video game.
When I spoke to Neurable earlier this year, the company said it planned to license its brain-scanning technology to power a flood of gadgets that were ready to enter the market. But it decided to launch its own hardware first.
“We wanted to take the product in-house,” Ramses Alcaide, Neurable’s cofounder and CEO, tells WIRED. “There were a lot of areas where we wanted to improve the product, and we wanted to move at a much faster rate. It also puts a little more capability for us to be able to show off what’s possible with the technology.”
The Boston company has until now relied on other brands to showcase its brain-scanning technology in their products, all of which promise to help people improve focus and provide data about your brain activity in a companion app. It began a few years ago by building its tech into some Master & Dynamic headphones. At the start of this year, Neurable showed off a gaming headset with HP's HyperX featuring two electroencephalography (EEG) sensors built in.
Like the original M&D MW75 Neuro headphones, the Neurable One features 12 EEG sensors in the nylon earpads that are used to monitor brain waves. The headphones cost $499 and will be available in October from Neurable’s website.
Alongside the new headphones is a new app (the old app will continue to exist for now for older hardware), which Alcaide says tracks eight brain metrics:
- Brain Age: Tracks your brain’s perceived age against your real age.
- Brain Battery: What you have left in reserve.
- Speed: How quickly you process information.
- Focus: How well your attention is holding.
- Load: How much effort you spend doing the task.
- Stress: How much tension you have doing the task.
- Sleepiness: How far you are drifting toward sleep.
- Alpha Peak Frequency: Your strongest resting rhythm, which Neurable claims is like the brain's heart rate variability.
The biggest hardware and software change with the Neurable One is that you no longer have to start a session in the app to capture brain activity. Instead, the Neurable One passively monitors your brain as soon as you put the headphones on—Alcaide likens it to wearing a Fitbit.
At that point, the sensors begin monitoring your brain activity to measure your focus. When it detects that you’re getting distracted, the headphones play a ping to get you back on track. If it thinks you're burning out instead, it’ll recommend a break so you can come back later fully recharged.
The headphone-app combo works similarly to help you fall asleep and to meditate. For example, with meditation, you can follow a guided session, and when the headphones detect you’re in the flow, the guide will stop talking so you stay in that zone. If it detects you’re drifting away, it’ll start guiding you back again. For sleep—designed for naps rather than proper bedtime—it can, over time, lower the headset volume of guided naps or soundscapes as it detects you falling asleep. (You can also turn off the EEG sensors and just use them as regular headphones if you want.)
Alcaide says when the app tells him his brain battery is low for the day, he’ll go to the sauna and go to bed early to help him recover. It can tell him when his peak brain speed hours are, allowing him to rejigger his schedule so he does his hardest work during those times. There’s also a check-in system called Cognitive Snapshot; when you trigger it, the app shows your current brain state and offers recommendations to improve it. That could be a guided meditation or small games to exercise those parts of your brain. The app also provides weekly or monthly reports to track your brain activity over time.
Neurable doesn’t have any new research or data to share that can speak to the effectiveness of its latest headphones. That research is in the works, but it will take time. So Neurable still points to previous research with the Mayo Clinic, which showed a 30 percent increase in focus in individuals using Neurable's headset versus people using Pomodoro techniques or other types of focus-sustaining systems. The study also saw a drop of about 10 percent in end-of-day burnout and an increase in end-of-day happiness.
The product isn’t categorized as a medical device, and Neurable says it isn’t designed to diagnose, treat, or monitor any conditions. The company also promises not to sell any of the data it collects about your brain—which could become very valuable in the future—and says it doesn't use that data for advertising. Alcaide says enterprise customers buy its headsets in bulk to help employees focus, but they’re not buying the headsets to monitor the workforce.
“It's because we know we're going to get higher productivity per employee; they're going to be happier, they're going to feel less burned out, it's a win-win for everybody,” he says. “It's like how sometimes companies get gym memberships for their employees.” He stresses that each user’s data stays with them.
Alcaide says the company partnered with an audio brand to help with the non-brain-scanning bits of the hardware, though he wouldn’t share the name. These cans have the “same premium sound” as the earlier M&D collaboration, with 40-mm beryllium drivers, six microphones, active noise cancellation, a transparency mode, and 22 hours of run time—12 if you have those EEG sensors running. It supports Bluetooth 5.2, and both AAC and aptX codecs. Neurable’s app is available on both Android and iOS.

Gloucester thrashed a limp Harlequins at Kingsholm to go to the top of the early Prem standings.
The Cherry and Whites ran in eight tries to make it two wins from two in the league and three on the bounce in all competitions.
Gloucester, who named three new signings in their starting line-up including Wales internationals Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake, completely outplayed their opponents in all facets of the match.
Visitors Quins, who handed a debut to England full-back George Furbank, struggled to get a handle on the game from the outset and remain bottom of the table without any points after failing to get on the scoreboard.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar on Saturday (October 3, 2026) briefed a parliamentary consultative committee on India's "multifaceted" engagement with Russia, highlighting shared ambitions to expand bilateral trade, investment, and energy cooperation.
Chairing the meeting on India-Russia relations, Mr. Jaishankar also apprised members of New Delhi's stance on the Ukraine conflict and its recent diplomatic efforts to contribute toward a peaceful settlement.
The External Affairs Minister further informed the panel that Russia has agreed to take around 70,000 Indian skilled workers this year, especially in the fields of construction and logistics, people familiar with the meeting said.
While discussing the trade and investment ties between the two countries, Mr. Jaishankar mentioned that there is a shared ambition to expand bilateral trade in a balanced manner, including through greater Indian exports to Russia in seven areas -- auto, pharma, food, marine products, engineering goods, chemicals and textiles, they said.
The External Affairs Minister, while highlighting India-Russia energy ties, said New Delhi's priority is to safeguard the interests of Indian consumers, they said.
Our approach is to maintain multiple sources of supply, he said, according to the people cited above.
In a social media post, Mr. Jaishankar said he highlighted various aspects of our multifaceted engagement including in trade, investments, energy, connectivity, culture and people-to-people domains.
The Minister said he also made a mention of India's "active support to dialogue and diplomacy to end the Ukraine conflict." The people cited above said India's recent efforts to contribute towards ending the Ukraine conflict and return of peace figured in the discussions.
Mr. Jaishankar also referred to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's meeting on August 31 with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek where he noted that "endless war must now give way to end of war".
Mr. Jaishankar travelled to Ukraine last month and also met with Foreign Ministers of Ukraine and Russia in New York few days ago on the margins of the UN General Assembly.
In his conversations, he noted that if India can be of any help in any manner to bring the war to an end, it was ready to do so, the people cited above said.
In this context, Mr. Putin's comments at Valdai Club in Moscow that PM Modi "has very good ideas for finding mutually acceptable solutions" to bring peace came up, they said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha's recent remarks appreciating India's efforts were also noted at the parliamentary consultative committee meeting, they added.
Mr. Jaishankar also apprised the panel members about the government's efforts to secure release of the Indians serving in the Russian military.
He said that the government has engaged with Russian authorities, including at the highest levels, for early discharge of all such individuals, the people said.
Mr. Jaishankar told the members that so far around 140 Indian nationals have been discharged and the Indian side is in touch with Russian authorities for the whereabouts of 55 Indian nationals who are reportedly working for the the Russian Army, they said.

South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders.
Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.
In a televised speech on Tuesday night, the president said local governments would have five months to address issues that compromised women’s safety, from broken streetlights to overgrown public spaces and abandoned buildings. He added that he had tasked five ministers to come up with a plan within 60 days to reduce alcohol-fuelled violence.
“Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” Ramaphosa said. “But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort.
“Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence or enforce a law.”
South Africa has been gripped by grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Eight of the women were found in the last three weeks, including Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who was discovered on 12 September after she went missing when she went for a run after work.
Ramaphosa said suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings and that the other cases would not be left to go cold. He added that police had not found evidence that a serial killer was responsible for all 11 killings, but that all possibilities were still being investigated.
He directly addressed South African men, urging them to challenge relatives, friends and colleagues who harassed, humiliated or abused women. “It is time for good men to stop being silent men,” he said.
“For too long, gender-based violence has been treated as a woman’s problem to solve. Women march, the women of our country organise, they speak out, they protest, they confront and they comfort survivors,” Ramaphosa said.
“Women change their routes home. Avoid going out at night and warn one another about dangerous places and dangerous men. We have placed the burden of male violence on women. That must change.”
Activists expressed their frustration that solid policy actions had not been taken years ago and scepticism that the measures Ramaphosa had announced would work.
Shenilla Mohamed, the executive director of Amnesty International South Africa, said: “These are not new issues and as a country we have been talking about ways to tackle the high numbers of [gender-based violence and femicide], especially since 2019 when women took to the streets to protest, and yet here we are again in the face of continued attacks against women.
“Amnesty International South Africa also notes the timelines put in place by the president, but this will only mean something if it results in action, and if there are consequences for inaction.”
Mpiwa Mangwiro-Tsanga and Bafana Khumalo, of Sonke Gender Justice, an NGO, said: “Our concern … is that the response remains heavily weighted towards what happens after violence has already occurred.”
They added: “Investigating unresolved cases, processing forensic evidence and repairing unsafe public spaces are necessary, but they do not constitute a comprehensive prevention strategy. It is concerning that the president is asking municipalities to do what is actually their mandate and yet they do not deliver on these.”

Fernandes rejects talk of Portugal rift after Ronaldo's abrupt departure
Oct 3 : Bruno Fernandes said on Saturday he had spoken to Cristiano Ronaldo and dismissed suggestions of a rift within Portugal's squad after the captain's abrupt departure from the national team's training camp cast doubt over his international future.
Portugal's record goalscorer Ronaldo, 41, left the camp in Copenhagen on Wednesday shortly after coach Jorge Jesus acknowledged tensions between the pair.
The Al-Nassr forward departed a day before Portugal's Nations League group-stage clash with Denmark, a match Jesus' side went on to win 4-2.
Ronaldo said on Instagram that he made the decision after Jesus' news conference and a conversation with Portuguese Football Federation President Pedro Proenca, adding that he would reveal his reasons "in due course".
"I had a chat with him and what I said to him is what I'll repeat here: the most important thing is that, whatever happens, Cristiano Ronaldo will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team, of our football and of the country," Fernandes told a news conference ahead of Sunday's Nations League match against Norway in Porto.
"For what he has achieved not only in Portugal, but all over the world. He has a place reserved not only amongst the all-time greats, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people.
"The most important thing is that we stop stirring up trouble; there are no divisions within the national team. It is one team and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside."
Spanish newspaper Marca reported that Portugal manager Jorge Jesus and Portuguese Football Federation President Pedro Proenca made an unsuccessful dash to Copenhagen airport in an attempt to persuade Ronaldo not to leave the squad.
"The most important thing is that this ends well, for both sides," the 32-year-old Manchester United captain added.
"We're completely out of the picture; we're aware of what you're saying and what we're seeing. We've spent a lot of time in the players' room playing cards; we're on the sidelines of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country doesn't become divided, doesn't take sides, and respects all parties..."
Jesus, meanwhile, sought to shift the focus back to Norway.
Portugal top Group A4 on nine points from three matches, with Norway third on three.
"The focus has to be on the national team, the match against Norway, and what we need to do well, in tune with our people," he said.
"But that doesn't mean I'm ignoring Cris. He's a symbol of the Portuguese national team; he's a symbol of Portugal - let that be quite clear.
"After the match, there'll be time to talk about that."

On Sept. 28, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump held an event at the White House to announce the planning of a new steel plant in Iowa. Joining him in the Oval Office for the event were several Iowa state leaders and officials.
Afterward, some social media users claimed Trump insulted Iowans during the event. For example, an X post (archived) displayed a video clip apparently recorded at the event and asserted, "Trump claims the federal government can 'supersede' Iowa and calls Iowans 'troubled people.'"
In the clip, Trump can be heard saying this: "And we can supersede the state, right? If we can supersede the state, it's good. Otherwise, it will never be good. They're very — they're really troubled people."
Users shared other posts claiming Trump called Iowans troubled people on Instagram (archived) and Threads (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and emailed us asking whether the claim was true.
It was not true. While the video clip is real and unedited, it omits important context that proves Trump didn't call Iowans "really troubled people." Trump was actually referring to Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and other Democratic leaders in that state.
The remark came immediately after an exchange in which Trump asked how Walz was treating the opening of a new iron mine in Minnesota. Given that this context was omitted, we have rated the clip miscaptioned.
Videos and transcripts of Trump's remarks at the event were uploaded online by C-SPAN and Roll Call. The conversation that led to Trump making the "troubled people" comment begin at about the 6:20 mark in the C-SPAN video and 6:07 in Roll Call's Vimeo video.
At that time, John Jovanovic, the Trump-nominated chairman and president of the Export-Import Bank of the United States, begins describing the opening of an iron mine in Minnesota that is meant to supply the Iowa steel plant (emphasis ours):
JOVANOVIC: Thank you, Mr. President. So, what we're really talking about today is America's economic security. And Mr. President, it's your plan in action, but it all starts mining more in America. The mine you mentioned is the first mine opened in America in 50-plus years focused on iron ore. EXIM financed it, but most importantly, it's found on the Iron Range in America, which for 145 years has been the most prolific iron ore deposit in the world. It helped build America. It helped win two world wars. You're helping resurrect it, Mr. President, with this first iron ore mine. That is why this plant is possible, because we are creating one American supply chain. And what you see again here today, Mr. President, is private capital flowing in to rebuild America and to build America's future, so we can assure that the warfighter of tomorrow in America is always well-equipped and that everyday Americans have what they need when they need it most. And this is what it's going to take to continue to deliver the American dream, Mr. President, for another 250 years.
TRUMP: And how is the governor treating you? Because I freed up the iron ore in that place, and I absolutely won the election, but they wouldn't — they cheat like hell. But how is the governor treating you? Because I freed it up and then they closed it, and the people were devastated because it is the finest iron ore in the world, they say. So how is the governor and these other people that don't — I mean, it's one of the worst-run places I've ever seen. How are they doing?
JOVANOVIC: You know, Mr. President, we were there only 10 days ago, actually, to initiate the mine. We set off 1.3 million pounds of explosives that put it into operation and that will be the iron ore that feeds this plant and to make steel in America the —
TRUMP: And we can supersede the state, right?
COMMERCE SECRETARY HOWARD LUTNICK: Yes.
JOVANOVIC: [unintelligible, cut off by Trump]
TRUMP: If we can supersede the state, it's good. Otherwise, the state will never be good. They're very — they're really troubled people. Thank you very much; great job you're doing, too, by the way. Secretary Lutnick, please.
The mine Jovanovic referred to is owned by Mesabi Metallics in northern Minnesota, where part of the American Iron Range is located. Mesabi Metallics is the same company investing in the steel plant in Iowa.
Local news reports on the fraught history of the mine suggest its struggles have largely been tied to the parent company of Mesabi Metallics, Essar. The India-based company first started work on the mine and an accompanying steel mill in 2007 before shuttering its plans for the mine in 2015 and filing for bankruptcy in 2016. Essar still owes Minnesota more than $22 million in infrastructure debt, according to Iowa news channel KWQC.
As Jovanovic said, Trump administration officials were at the opening of the iron mine in Minnesota about 10 days earlier. If Trump's concern was about opening the mine, he'd have no reason to call for the federal government to "supersede" Minnesota. According to Essar itself, Minnesota State Auditor Julie Blaha said in 2024, "After years of uncertainty, it's encouraging to see Mesabi Metallics breathing new life into this major mining operation."
While the context makes it clear that Trump was referencing Walz and his administration in Minnesota, not Iowans, Snopes reached out to the White House to seek confirmation on whom exactly Trump believed to be "really troubled people." We'll update this story if and when we receive a response to our question.
For further reading, Snopes recently investigated a claim asserting Trump's renaming of "artificial intelligence" to "super intelligence" is a play to profit off of .SI domain names.

Inside the study for a remedy to fight Congo's deadliest Ebola outbreak
More than 250 participants have been enrolled in a trial for a drug that could stop them from contracting Ebola in Congo
RWAMPARA, Congo -- More than 250 participants have been enrolled in a trial for a drug that could stop them from contracting Ebola in Congo, in what experts have described as a critical step to try to fight the deadliest outbreak of the disease in the Central African country.
The drug is targeted at Bundibugyo virus, which is responsible for the fast-moving outbreak and is without an approved vaccine or treatment. The trial began in July and is one of several studies launched to find some protection and another way of at least slowing the outbreak.
The Associated Press spoke this week to participants and doctors at the health center where the trial is taking place in the eastern province of Ituri, the epicenter of the outbreak. The participants include people who have been exposed to the disease in this outbreak, among them health workers and patients’ relatives.
At least 8,300 confirmed cases, including 4,000 deaths, have been recorded since this Ebola outbreak was declared in mid-May in eastern Congo. It has spread to seven provinces and continues to outpace efforts to track and slow it, authorities say.
The trial is testing Gilead's experimental antiviral pill, called obeldesivir, which is given soon after suspected contact with the virus to prevent the disease from developing. That approach is called post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP.
One participant in the trial known as EBO-PEP told AP that she enrolled in the study in August after her husband tested positive for Ebola. She says so far no one from her family developed symptoms.
She and other trial participants requested anonymity to protect their privacy due to the sensitive nature of the Ebola outbreak and the medical protocol involved.
Ebola disease only spreads once symptoms begin. People exposed to infected patients have to wait to see if they get sick. Finding people at high risk of incubating the Bundibugyo virus — also known as contact tracing — has proved difficult in Congo.
Another participant said two of their family members had caught Ebola, and one of them had died. “This disease is killing. It’s better to take precautions,” he said.
The trial, coordinated by ALIMA, a medical nonprofit, aims to recruit nearly 1,000 adults or children over the age of 12 who have come into contact with a confirmed case within the last five days but have no symptoms. Half will get a placebo.
Participants are monitored in person every day for 21 days, with a final phone call after 42 days, according to Dr. Godefroid Basara, who is working on the trial.
ALIMA said that if trial participants begin to develop symptoms, they will immediately receive supportive treatment, which has been shown to be helpful when symptoms are caught early.
If the pill proves effective, it could help break the infection chain.
“It differs from a vaccine, which may take days or weeks to provide protection. It is also different from curative treatment because it is intended for people who are not yet showing symptoms,” ALIMA research coordinator Dr. Guilavogui Jean Paul Yassa said.
Dr. Jacques Zawadi, an investigating physician working with ALIMA at the trial center, said most participants are happy to take part in the study, but it had been challenging encouraging some people who live far from the center to sign up.
He said the study is sometimes disrupted when participants find out their family members have died from the disease.
“This is the biggest challenge we face. When a person is emotionally affected, it is not easy to reason with them and ensure they return to the study,” he said.
The trial partners also include Congo’s National Institute of Biomedical Research and the French institute ANRS Emerging Infectious Diseases.
As new vaccines are under development elsewhere, Congo started vaccinating health workers with the Ervebo vaccine which was effective during previous Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common virus. Authorities have said Ervebo could offer some protection against Bundibugyo, but whether the vaccine can actually prevent illness is still being studied.
On Thursday, humanitarian organization Doctors Without Borders said a staff member had tested positive for Ebola and was being evacuated to the Netherlands. In June, a humanitarian physician with ALIMA also tested positive after returning to France from one of the virus hot spots.
The World Health Organization has said the outbreak continues to outpace efforts to track and slow the spread, and is set to exceed West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016 — the deadliest on record — which killed 11,000 people.

The face-off between Mumbai airport operator Mumbai International Airport Ltd (MIAL) and airlines has intensified, with carriers rejecting the proposed temporary reduction of international departure slots at Terminal 2 (T2) from October 25, according to a CNBC-TV18 report.
MIAL, controlled of Adani Group, has proposed temporarily discontinuing 265 of 770 weekly international departure slots at T2, representing a 33% reduction. The move is linked to the planned redevelopment of Terminal 1 (T1), which is currently used for domestic operations.
According to PTI, MIAL has communicated the proposed reduction to 46 airlines operating international services from T2. The vacated capacity will be used to accommodate domestic traffic as T1 is closed for redevelopment.
Airlines have formally rejected the proposed reduction, CNBC-TV18 reported, citing sources familiar with their response to MIAL's communication.
The carriers have said they support the refurbishment and redevelopment of T1 but argued that this should not be treated as consent to flight cancellations or a reduction in T2 operations.
Airlines have also raised concerns over the lack of what they consider meaningful consultation on the proposed 33% reduction, its operational implications and the specific flights that could be affected.
The timing of the proposed reduction is a major concern for airlines.
According to CNBC-TV18, airlines have pointed out that the winter schedule was approved in June 2026, and carriers have already planned their networks, aircraft deployment and passenger commitments accordingly.
They have argued that any reduction in approved capacity should follow a transparent consultation and coordination process because of its potential impact on flight schedules, aircraft deployment and passengers.
The airlines have also said they have not consented to the proposed slot cancellations and that the reduction should not be imposed unilaterally.
MIAL's proposed schedule would require IndiGo to temporarily discontinue 74 weekly international departure slots from Mumbai, while Air India would face a reduction of 33 weekly slots.
PTI reported that IndiGo currently operates 224 weekly international flights from Mumbai, while Air India operates 100.
Other airlines facing reductions include: Akasa Air - 11 weekly international flights; Air India Express - 7; SpiceJet - 5; Etihad Airways - 10; Emirates - 10.
Etihad and Emirates currently operate 28 weekly services each from Mumbai.
MIAL has said the reduction is part of the transition linked to the redevelopment of T1.
According to CNBC-TV18, the airport operator has given airlines until October 6 to identify the specific slots they want to temporarily discontinue. If airlines do not respond, MIAL has said it will determine the slots itself.
MIAL plans to begin reallocating the vacated T2 infrastructure from October 26, including check-in counters, baggage belts, boarding gates and operational office space, to scheduled domestic operators.
The objective is to facilitate the movement of around 5 million passengers a year from T1 to T2.
With MIAL proceeding with the T1 redevelopment plan and the proposed T2 flight reductions, airlines are seeking intervention from the Civil Aviation Ministry.
The airlines want a detailed stakeholder meeting on the T1 redevelopment plan and have asked the government to ensure that operational measures are not implemented unilaterally without airline agreement.
They have also raised concerns about the impact on passengers, particularly where bookings may already have been made for flights included in the approved winter schedule.

Medical plane with 6 on board missing off Massachusetts coast
- Published
US authorities are searching for six people after a medical plane bound for Boston, Massachusetts went missing early Saturday morning.
The Federal Aviation Administration told the BBC that it lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane and put out a search and rescue notice just after 1:00 local time (6:00 GMT).
An air and water search is underway off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island, according to the US Coast Guard's Northeast District.
The plane departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was slated to land at Boston's Logan International at 1:30 EDT (6:30 GMT).
According to the tail number released by the Coast Guard, the plane belonged to Latitude Air Ambulances, a company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
FlightAware's tracker shows the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had some things to say about pro-regulation tech leaders that might go down better with fava beans and a nice Chianti.
During a Saturday appearance on "The Axios Show," Bessent compared CEOs who want the government to slap guardrails on AI to a reviled cinematic figure.
"I mean, it's kind of like Hannibal Lecter: Stop me before I kill again," Bessent said. "This alarmism without solutions by some of the AI community — that's not leadership."
Bessent invoked "The Silence of the Lambs" serial killer while saying that AI bosses who want Washington to erect guardrails for the tech they are building should slow down development themselves without government intervention.
Bessent's comments are in line with the White House's response to the chorus of AI leaders who last month called for an organized slowdown among AI companies, citing fears that their technology is getting out of control.
Some, like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, asked the US government to step in and regulate the companies.
President Donald Trump brought together AI CEOs for a meeting at the White House that resulted in a voluntary self-policing pledge.
Bessent said that AI companies appear to be taking the White House's advice. He cited OpenAI's recent decision to shelve a new model after internal tests raised questions about whether the AI would follow users' instructions.
"The labs have been very cooperative," he said.
Others in the AI community have warned that the race to dominate the space is sparking a dangerous disregard for safety guardrails.
"You can't do safety from second place," Sarah Heck, Anthropic's head of public policy, said on X last week.
An OpenAI safety leader, David Robinson, publicly announced his resignation on Saturday, saying he believes the company is moving too fast to ensure its models can't wreak havoc on society.

Democrat James Talarico has opened a narrow lead over Republican Ken Paxton in the race for a US Senate seat in Texas, an unusual development in a state where Republicans have dominated statewide elections for decades. Lloyd Bentsen, a Democrat, was re-elected to the Senate from Texas in 1988 and after that no candidate from the party could win from the state. A Fox News poll of Texas likely voters conducted from September 24 to 28 showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 49%. The two-point advantage is within the poll's margin of error of three percentage points. Among registered voters, however, Talarico's lead widened to seven points, compared with a three-point advantage in July. A separate New York Times/Siena University poll conducted from September 21 to 30 put Talarico six points ahead of Paxton. The result has renewed questions over whether Democrats could break their long drought in statewide Texas politics in the 2026 midterms. The polling does not necessarily indicate that Texas has turned Democratic. Instead, the numbers point to a combination of Paxton's weaknesses, divisions within the Republican electorate, Talarico's support among key voter groups and a difficult political environment for Republicans. One of the clearest differences between the two candidates is their personal ratings. Talarico has a net positive rating of eight points, with 52% of likely voters viewing him favourably and 44% unfavourably. Paxton, meanwhile, has a net negative rating of 18 points, with 40% favourable and 58% unfavourable ratings. The Fox News poll also found that Republicans were six times more likely to view Paxton unfavourably than Democrats were to view Talarico unfavourably. The Republican nominee's support is also affected by divisions within the party. Non-MAGA Republicans were more than five times as likely as MAGA Republicans to support Talarico, at 22% versus 4%. The poll found that 20% of likely voters who supported Republican Senator John Cornyn in the March primary now back Talarico. Talarico's advantage extends beyond the Democratic base. The Fox poll found strong support for the Democrat among moderates, with 65% backing him. He also led among Hispanic voters at 64%, voters under 35 at 62% and Black voters at 79%. Paxton's strongest groups included White evangelical Christians, White men without a college degree, rural voters and people aged 65 and above. The polling suggests that Paxton's challenge is not simply holding the Republican base together but also winning over voters who are less firmly aligned with the GOP. Trump won Texas by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024, but his current approval rating in the state is underwater, according to the Fox poll. The survey found 44% of Texans approving of Trump's performance and 55% disapproving. While 15% of voters who disapprove of Trump still support Paxton, only 9% of those who approve of Trump support Talarico. The New York Times also reported that a September Texas Southern University survey put Trump's approval rating seven points underwater in the state. The Fox survey found that seven in 10 Texans consider the cost of living extremely important to their Senate vote. Twice as many voters said they were falling behind financially as said they were getting ahead -- 35% versus 16%. Those who said they were falling behind financially backed Talarico by 32 points, while voters who said they were getting ahead favoured Paxton by 48 points. Talarico also held leads among voters who considered the cost of living, artificial intelligence and Trump extremely important to their Senate vote. Voters focused on immigration, meanwhile, favoured Paxton by 20 points. COVID-19 made the weaknesses in our pandemic preparedness at national and global levels painfully clear. But a new study highlights that even at the first, local steps of an outbreak with pandemic-potential, we are worryingly underprepared.
Health officials in New York set up a regional test of healthcare facilities to identify and respond to a patient with a mystery infection that could pose a pandemic-level threat. But things didn’t go well. Overall, responses were slow, appropriate use of personal protective equipment was spotty, and only 60 percent of facilities passed the basics of the test—an overall failing grade.
“These drills identified needs for health care workers and health care facility staff member training to achieve earlier identification, masking, and isolation of potentially infectious febrile patients,” the officials wrote in the study, which was published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.
The drill centered on “professional patient actors,” who staggered into healthcare facilities feigning expected symptoms of an H5 bird flu infection—a virus type thought to have pandemic potential. The actors wore makeup to look unwell, used eye drops and petroleum jelly to mimic having conjunctivitis (aka pink eye), and had a fake cough. They complained about feeling weak and feverish and reported taking a Motrin (fever reducer) before coming in. When questioned, they said they hadn’t traveled out of the country and, if asked about any sick contacts, would respond, “Does a sick bird count?” They would tell a sad tale of trying to save a sick duck they found in a park. In the story, the duck doesn’t make it, and the now-ill patient didn’t wear any gloves while handling it. The chatty actor would tell this story without prompting.
To pass the test, a healthcare facility needed to mask the patient and put them in an isolation room. Ideally, the masking would occur within a minute or less of the patient walking in, and isolation would occur in 10 minutes or less. For this drill, both masking and isolation were enough to pass, regardless of timing.

Women given cycling shorts to wear on popular Oktoberfest ride after upskirting incidents
At least 32,000 videos of women on the Teufelsrad ride at the world’s largest beer festival are in circulation, say reports

Women have been provided with cycling shorts at a popular Oktoberfest ride in Germany to prevent them being upskirted after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged online.
The Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, is a rotating ride, which riders sit or lay down on while it spins. The motion means that skirts and dresses sometimes fly up but these instances have been filmed and shared widely online.
Elisabeth Polaczy, 80, who operates the popular attraction, told the BBC that she has been forced to hand out free shorts to women and girls to protect them from people who may be filming in the crowd at the beer festival.
She said that at the festival this year, which began on 19 September and ends on Sunday, she has handed out more than 100 pairs of the shorts.
“I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure,” she said.
The ride is surrounded by signs and police posters warning against filming but she she said that it is impossible to control everyone.
According to Süddeutsche Zeitung, a Munich-based daily publication, there are at least 32,000 videos of women on the Teufelsrad in circulation and some have apparently been viewed millions of times.
Some waitresses say they have also started wearing shorts under their dirndls (a traditional German folk dress worn by some staff at Oktoberfest).
Local broadcaster BR reported that sometimes images have been digitally altered to show the staff naked. According to an investigation by the outlet, a group of professional YouTubers from Ukraine and some from Bavaria were behind the footage. One woman earned made €9,000 (£7,650) from a single clip.
A Bavarian police spokesperson told the BBC that it has been running a poster campaign warning against upskirting at the beer festival since 2025.
Upskirting is a term to describe the act of taking a sexually intrusive photograph up someone’s skirt or dress without permission.
In Germany, the offence carries a two-year prison sentence, having been criminalised in 2020. In the UK, the practice became illegal in 2019 with the passing of the Voyeurism (Offences) Act following a high-profile campaign by activist Gina Martin.
Munich’s Oktoberfest is the world’s largest beer festival and is frequented by over six million people over a 16-day period.
While a majority of people attending the event are from Munich, millions also fly in from across the world to attend.
About 600 police officers were expected to be on duty around the festival in addition to Bavarian riot police, specialised pickpocket investigators, and international task forces from eight countries, dpa reported.
AI-powered cameras were also put in place this year to detect large crowds.

Srinagar, Sep 22: Minister for Food, Civil Supplies & Consumer Affairs (FS&CA), Information Technology (IT), Youth Services & Sports, and Science & Technology, Satish Sharma, on Tuesday said that 221 out of 355 Gram Panchayats (GPs) in Jammu and Kashmir have either existing or constructed playfields under the One Panchayat-One Playfield initiative.

Quoting information received from the Rural Development Department, Satish Sharma said that 221 out of 355 Gram Panchayats covered under the initiative have playfields, either already existing or newly constructed.
Giving details of Dooru Constituency, the Minister informed the House that 37 out of 66 Gram Panchayats have playfields. He said the Youth Services & Sports Department has taken up two playfield projects in Dooru Constituency during the past three years. The Playfield at Larkipora near ADV Road Bathuno, taken up during 2024-25 at a cost of Rs 48.55 lakh, has achieved 90 per cent completion, added. He apprised that another Playfield at Shangren has been taken up as a new work during 2026-27 at an estimated cost of Rs 80 lakh.
Satish Sharma further informed that 26 playfield sites have been approved under AAP 2026-27 as part of VB-G RAM-G by the Rural Development Department, Anantnag, where suitable government land has been made available by the Revenue Department. He said that development of playfields by the Youth Services & Sports Department is undertaken after following all requisite formalities, including availability of encumbrance-free land, transfer of land and availability of funds.
He said that sports infrastructure in Dooru Constituency is being progressively improved and upgraded through the J&K Sports Council and Directorate of Youth Services & Sports.

The Minister informed that a DPR amounting Rs 1,035.98 lakh has been prepared for upgradation of Sports Stadium Dooru and is presently under consideration by the Department. The proposed works included pavilion building with change rooms, seating tiers with canopy, cricket competition pitches, net practice pitches, dugouts, synthetic volleyball court, mechanical roller and floodlights, he added.
Regarding proposals for development of playfields at Sayen/Sagam, Sadiwara, Chowgund, Qammar, Dudwangan, Akingam, Hiller Kokernag and other identified locations, Satish Sharma said the sites are under consideration for land transfer and development. He informed that the process for transfer of land to the Youth Services & Sports Department is underway with the Revenue Department while in the case of Sadiwara and Hiller Kokernag, the land-transfer process is yet to be initiated.
The Minister said that once the land preparation and transfer processes are finalised, the department would consider the required development works, subject to availability of funds, land and feasibility. He also informed that a DPR amounting Rs 150 lakh has been prepared for development of the SayenSagam playfield, envisaging ground expansion through cutting and filling, protection works, seating tiers, cricket competition pitches, net practice pitches and a synthetic volleyball court.
