The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

A video showing a man with a disability being assaulted by a group of men is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows a Muslim being harassed in India. Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing an old handicapped muslim being harassed by a few men in India.
Fact: The viral video is scripted content from a YouTube channel called Muklesur Bhaijaan 2.0, which regularly posts similar videos on social media. The channel’s bio states that it shares scripted content. We also found several other videos on the channel featuring the same elderly man. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of the key frames from the viral video led us to a YouTube channel named Muklesur Bhaijaan 2.0, where the same video was uploaded and published on 15 December 2025, with the description ‘ak muslim chacha ko mara chapri na | #shortsvideo bike rider | bike rider vs chapri.’
We noticed that he regularly uploads similar fight videos. His YouTube bio also states that he uploads riding vlogs and scripted videos.
The old man shown being harassed in the video has appeared in several other similar videos published by the same channel (here, here, here). Factly had previously debunked a similar claim featuring the same old man seen in the viral video.
To sum up, the video showing an old disabled man being assaulted by a few men is scripted, not a real incident.

Punjabi social media influencer and makeup artist Mad Sandhu was shot dead by two unidentified motorcycle-borne assailants in Amritsar on Saturday evening (October 4), police said. Sandhu, whose real name was Madhusudan, was attacked on Loharka Road at around 6 pm.
According to police, the attackers opened fire at Sandhu and fled the scene on a motorcycle. He was rushed to a hospital but succumbed to his injuries.
Who was Mad Sandhu?
Mad Sandhu was a familiar face on Punjabi social media and digital platforms, where he spoke openly about makeup artistry, the film industry, fashion and gender issues.
He had built a substantial following on Instagram, with around 2.26 lakh followers. Sandhu was also known for appearing on podcasts, where he discussed his experiences in the makeup and entertainment industries and spoke candidly about issues related to gender and identity.
Sandhu had also acted in the Punjabi film Oye Bhole Oye.
His outspoken online presence and distinctive fashion and makeup choices had attracted both support and criticism on social media.
Mad Sandhu shot at close range
The shooting took place when Sandhu went to a shop to collect his car, which he had given for washing, police said.
Two unidentified men on a motorcycle allegedly opened fire at him. Around two to three rounds were fired, according to police. An eyewitness said Sandhu was shot at close range.
A purported video circulating on social media showed Sandhu lying on the road in a pool of blood while some people attempted to lift him.
Police reached the spot after receiving information about the shooting. Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police Sirivennela said investigators had some leads and would apprehend the accused soon.
The motive behind the killing has not yet been established. Police said they were investigating the case from multiple angles.
Sandhu had faced backlash over social media content
Sandhu had previously faced criticism and backlash over his social media content, clothing and fashion choices.
A few months ago, a Nihang Sikh had publicly objected to Sandhu's content and clothing, telling him that his videos could have a negative influence on young people.

Want to stay on top of the science and politics driving biotech today? Sign up to get our biotech newsletter in your inbox.
I am newly enamored with Hans Zinsser, a Harvard bacteriologist who in 1935 wrote “Rats, Lice and History,” a rather charming “biography” of typhus. Got it for a buck at an estate sale.
Favorite line: “there is no arsphenamin for the psychic treponema” — which, in context, basically means, “pretension has no cure.”
He’s the Oscar Wilde of infectious disease, I’m telling you. Or, like, Damian.
The need-to-know this morning
- Sanofi and Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, the duo behind the hugely successful drug Dupixent, are re-upping their partnership, with the companies announcing an expanded collaboration on a new series of antibodies for immunological diseases.
A journey to witness China’s biotech boom up close
It’s no secret that China’s biotech industry is increasingly setting the pace for science. But STAT’s Jason Mast traveled to Shanghai to get an up-close look at the competition that’s making Americans nervous.
There, at Jefferies’ first life sciences conference in China, executives boasted about developing drugs faster and cheaper than their American counterparts. They walked through their pipelines in English, as local Mandarin-speaking representatives from hulking multinationals like GSK, Merck, and Sanofi roamed the halls, scouting potential prospects between bites of duck sandwiches and dragonfruit.
Chinese-designed drugs now account for roughly half the global pipeline and more than half the potential value of licensing and collaboration deals — and Morgan Stanley projects they could represent 35% of FDA approvals by 2030.
“The best minds will all go there,” one China-focused investment banker told STAT. “Because the big pharma senior R&D guys are there, the general perception is, OK, ‘I might have the infrastructure, CRO work, whatever here but I still want my CSO to be in Kendall Square.’”
HHS wants AI to reinvent clinical trials
HHS announced yesterday that it is launching a new five-year effort to speed up clinical trials by using artificial intelligence, computational modeling, and more flexible study designs that blur the traditional boundaries between trial phases.
The ARPA-H program, dubbed SURPASS, will solicit ideas from teams from the realms of statistics, AI, clinical trial operations, and regulation. Neurodegenerative diseases of particular interest, STAT’s Margaret Manto writes.
The idea is to perhaps gradually replace some human control group data with in silico information — and develop AI systems that could streamline trial operations. HHS also announced initiatives to expand the number of clinical trial sites, build a national research data resource, and let patients contribute their own data. The details — including how much money is behind the effort — remain fuzzy.
Can Eric Cantor fix PhRMA’s woes in Washington?
Eric Cantor, the former House majority leader, is taking over PhRMA at a challenging moment for the drug industry, STAT’s Daniel Payne writes. Among other things, populist anger over medicine prices has scrambled the old political alliances that once made Republicans reliable allies of pharma.
Cantor built a reputation as a savvy GOP strategist before a stunning primary defeat in 2014. Now, he’ll have to navigate President Trump’s push to strongarm drugmakers into lowering prices. Democrats, meanwhile, plan to approach the industry with scrutiny of their own.
Cantor’s bipartisan relationships and dealmaking experience make him well suited to the job, many industry folk say. But there’s a certain irony here. Cantor will be defending drugmakers against a populist backlash — the same force that ended his congressional run.
A Huntington’s patient isn’t fazed by new UniQure data
When UniQure released data this week showing its gene therapy for Huntington’s disease slowed progression of the condition after four years by 44%, down sharply from 75% at three years, its stock tank. At least one patient took another view.
“This isn’t a cure,” advocate Lauren Holder, who is living with early-stage disease, told STAT’s Adam Feuerstein, explaining why she was not discouraged by the latest data on AMT-130. To her, even a few years of substantially slower decline would mean precious additional time with quality of life.
But Holder is far less sanguine about UniQure’s proposed confirmatory study, which would randomize roughly 200 Huntington’s patients to AMT-130 or standard treatment for three years if the gene therapy wins accelerated approval. Holder called that design “not ethical,” arguing that patients assigned to the control group would lose years without an effective treatment while also being unable to join other research.

Hospitals across the State are up against a shortage of drugs for treating non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Several commonly prescribed drugs for blood sugar management (metformin), hypertension (telmasartan), and cholesterol (atorvastatin) are in short supply in hospitals, even as authorities have assured that these will be back in stock within a week.
“It is not as though we are running short on all drugs. But NCD drugs are medicines that people should be taking without fail as a matter of routine and disruptions in its supply can be worrying. We anticipated this shortage last month and moved fast to make local purchases so our patients do not miss the medication,” the medical officer at a family health centre in Thiruvananthapuram said.
“NCD drugs are in short supply but we have not had any issues because our hospital management committee has adequate funds, apart from the substantial resources that our block panchayat sets aside every year for purchasing drugs, for making local purchases. If a substantial amount of drugs has to be purchased, then we float a tender. However, there are also health institutions in smaller panchayats which might be struggling to make local purchase because of insufficient funds,” the superintendent at a taluk hospital in the suburbs said.
Ideally, when a patient registered at the NCD clinic of a particular healthcare institution comes for review, the hospital should have at least 30 days’ stock of the NCD drugs for the patient to take home. In the present situation, many hospitals are not able to ensure that.
Medical officers said this year, the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) released only the drug supplies of the first quarter and that the second quarter release of June did not happen at all which led to the shortage of some drugs, including NCD drugs.
The KMSCL purchases around ₹700-800 crore worth of medicines every year for supplying to around 8,000 government healthcare institutions. In its last procurement exercise, 180 items reportedly received no bids, while suppliers quoted higher prices for another 171 items. This resulted in re-tendering and delays in placing fresh orders.
According to sources, the supply orders given in January-March, for some 18 non-bidder drugs, were cancelled by the new government because the prices quoted were considered far too high, which triggered the present shortage. However, fresh procurement orders have been placed and the supplies are expected to arrive within a week, it was pointed out.
The fact that the KMSCL owes over ₹2,200 crore to various pharma firms, for drugs purchased for hospitals as well as the drugs purchased by hospitals for patients under the Karunya Arogya Suraksha Padhati, has not helped the situation. The massive delays in payment is one of the reasons why many pharma forms do not respond to tenders floated by the KMSCL.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan had directed that the procurement procedures for the next financial year begin in October itself and that the entire process be completed by the end of December.
He also directed that middlemen be removed from the tender processes and that agencies dealing directly in imported medicines also be allowed to take part in tenders. He said a comprehensive overhaul was under way at the KMSCL
According to sources, there are also efforts to form a consortium with medical service corporations of other States so that common purchase tenders can be floated, which might likely bring prices further down.

Uttarakhand man missing in Mauritius for 6 days, family seeks govt help
A Dehradun man working at a restaurant in Mauritius has been missing for six days, with his family raising questions over four men he allegedly left with and seeking government intervention.
A man from Uttarakhand's Dehradun has been missing in Mauritius for six days, leaving his family desperately seeking answers and prompting his relatives to appeal to the Centre and state government to intervene and coordinate with the Mauritius authorities to speed up the search.
Dharmendra Bisht, a resident of Patel Nagar in Dehradun, was working as a manager at a Thai restaurant in Mauritius, according to his family. His relatives say they have been unable to contact him since the evening of September 27 and have not received any concrete information about his whereabouts.
The family has raised questions over four young men who they claim came into contact with Dharmendra before he went missing. However, the allegations have not been independently verified and the circumstances surrounding his disappearance remain under investigation.
FAMILY SAYS DHARMENDRA DISAPPEARED AFTER CRICKET
According to the family, Dharmendra had gone to play cricket on the morning of September 27.
The family claims that four young men came into contact with him during this time and allegedly took him along with them. Relatives say Dharmendra has not been traced since.
The family has named the four men as Ayush Bisht, Gaurav Mehta, Bhupendra Rana and Rahul Rana.
Relatives claim Dharmendra's mobile phone and clothes were later found with Ayush Bisht.
The family was informed about Dharmendra's disappearance on September 28. They also say they were told that he had gone somewhere on leave.
However, relatives claim Dharmendra had not told them about taking leave and that they had no information about any such plan.
FAMILY RAISES QUESTIONS OVER FOUR MEN
Dharmendra's relatives have raised questions over the role of the four men he allegedly went with before disappearing.
The family says it is particularly concerned because there has been no contact from Dharmendra and they have not received clear information about what happened after he left with the men.
The allegations against the four men have not been independently confirmed.
The family wants the circumstances surrounding Dharmendra's disappearance and the role, if any, of the four men to be investigated.
COMPANY ACCUSED OF NOT SHARING INFORMATION
Dharmendra was reportedly working at Thai Food Gang restaurant, operated by Sitar Pure Veg Company Limited in Mauritius.
His family has alleged that the company management has not provided them with sufficient information since his disappearance.
Relatives also say they have not received clear information about the action being taken by the Mauritius police. The family claims it does not even know whether a formal complaint has been registered in the case.
The family has further alleged that the restaurant management appears to be supporting the four men named by them.
These allegations have not been independently verified.
SISTER SEEKS HELP FROM GOVERNMENTS
Dharmendra's sister, Hema Rautela, has appealed to the Uttarakhand government and the Centre for help in tracing her brother.
She has sought the intervention of Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami and Union Minister of State Ajay Tamta.
According to the family, Tamta's office has taken the matter seriously and sought intervention through the Indian Embassy, with a request for the Mauritius government to look into the case.
FAMILY SEEKS MEA INTERVENTION
The family wants the Ministry of External Affairs to coordinate directly with the Mauritius administration and local police to speed up the search for Dharmendra.
Relatives have also sought an investigation into a video that they claim has gone viral and could be connected to the case.
Hema said several days had passed since her brother went missing but the family had still not received any reliable information about his whereabouts.
She has sought an impartial investigation and urged authorities to trace Dharmendra as soon as possible.
The family has also informed local police about the matter.
For now, the circumstances surrounding Dharmendra's disappearance, as well as the alleged involvement of the four men named by his relatives, await official investigation and confirmation.

Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest'
- Published
Just a year ago, Jude Bellingham's place in the England squad was up in the air. Now he is being talked about as having the potential to be one of football's "greatest of all time".
The Real Madrid man was left out of Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions squad in October 2025 and his place at the World Cup was called into question, with the German head coach saying Bellingham wouldn't get star treatment.
But Bellingham did of course make the squad for the World Cup and was arguably his team's standout performer, finishing as England's top scorer with seven goals as they reached the semi-finals and finished third.
He has already shown that he is world class with starring performances for club and country, but the way he helped England to dismantle Croatia 7-0 in the Nations League on Saturday looked like someone perhaps reaching a new level.
The 23-year-old was instrumental in Rijeka, scoring as well as registering a hat-trick of assists. He even ended the match wearing the captain's armband as England inflicted the heaviest defeat in Croatia's history.
"Bellingham can go on to be one of the greatest players of all time," former Manchester United and Republic of Ireland midfielder Roy Keane said on ITV after the game.
"At this moment in time, he is an amazing footballer. The package – his running power, his delivery, his goal threat. The way he is progressing as a player, I still think there is a lot more to come from him."
Bellingham, recently voted England's player of the year for the second year in a row, is now "nailed on as the 10" for the future, former England defender Matt Upson told BBC Radio 5 Live.
Keane added: "He has been fantastic in possession, but what he does out of possession lifts all these other players.
"If you have a player that good in your team, who is amazing in possession and he's playing for Real Madrid and doing brilliant things, but his work rate off the ball... that will just inspire other players. He is a huge leader for them."
'Push for next level or other teams will catch up'
England's front four will share praise for the way in which they demolished the Croatian backline.
Record goalscorer Harry Kane scored twice, as did Bukayo Saka, with Anthony Gordon scoring and assisting too.
And Kane will be back in the spotlight on Tuesday when he can equal Peter Shilton's all-time England men's appearance record against the Czech Republic at Wembley.
In moving to 89 goals for his country, the 33-year-old again showed how irreplaceable he is for England, but, when he was rested with 20 minutes to go, it was Bellingham who took the captain's armband.
And that highlighted the younger man's importance as a leader within the squad.
Bellingham was also directly involved in more than two goals in an England game for the first time, and he became the first player to record three assists in a game for the Three Lions since Trent Alexander-Arnold against San Marino in November 2021.
It was Bellingham's performance in front of goal that impressed former England striker Ian Wright.
"When Bellingham is on the pitch, he is always driving forward and going again and again," Wright said.
"He was involved in everything. His athleticism, his technical ability, his intensity. He never lets up, the way he gets in the box, he is always in there unmarked. He is always in there."
Bellingham showed every aspect of his game against Croatia and Tuchel was asked by BBC Sport if he had gone to another level.
"Yes, at the moment it seems like it, and you always need to," Tuchel said.
"It's like you can never stand still. You have to develop and you have to push for the next level, otherwise other teams will catch up."
Tuchel, who said the performance was a way to "move on" after the disappointment of England's World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina, said that he "adjusted some things" following the tournament, giving players, including Bellingham, "a lot of responsibility".
Saka was part of the front four and Bellingham assisted his first goal with a high quality cross.
"He was amazing tonight," Saka said of Bellingham.
"He deserved player of the year and he deserved man of the match tonight too. He was special.
"[I'm] happy to play with him and happy to have him in the England team."

Super League Grand Final: Wakefield Trinity make history with 23-10 victory over Warrington Wolves
Wakefield Trinity become the sixth team to win Super League; they have done it on the first time of asking; it finishes off a remarkable story after they were relegated in 2023
Last Updated: 03/10/26 8:10pm
Wakefield Trinity were crowned Super League champions for the first time in the club's history with a 23-10 victory over Warrington Wolves in the Grand Final at Old Trafford.
It is the first time Wakefield have made the Grand Final and they achieved their greatest glory on their first attempt.
They also become the sixth winner of Super League, joining Wigan Warriors, St Helens, Leeds Rhinos, Bradford Bulls and Hull KR.

It rounds out a fairy-tale story for Wakefield who were relegated in 2023, returned to Super League in the 2025 season, and have now written themselves into the history books as champions.
Wakefield held a dominant 19-0 half-time lead thanks to converted tries from Cameron Scott, Isaiah Vagana and Jazz Tevaga, Max Jowitt staying calm under pressure with the boot.
The extra point was then added by Jack Sinfield with just minutes left in the first half.
Early in the second half there was drama as Corey Hall was sent to the sin bin for a high shot on Arron Lindop. Lindop scored with Wakefield a player down, and added a second later on, Ewan Irwin converting the first.
However, a try from Trinity winger Tom Johnstone was enough for them to stay far enough ahead and seal immortality.
Johnstone picked up the Rob Burrow Award for his phenomenal display in both attack and defence.
Wakefield complete the fairy tale with stunning Grand Final win
In front of an electric and sold-out Old Trafford, it was a flawless first 40 from Wakefield Trinity.
They thought they had opened the scoring on the sixth minute when Johnstone went over in the corner. However, on review, it was clear he had been held up then forced into touch.
It took only six minutes longer though for the Yorkshire side to get on the board thanks to a sublime no-look, one-handed flick pass from Lachlan Walmsley which sent Scott walking in and with the Jowitt conversion, they had a 6-0 lead.
While it was end-to-end stuff, metres were coming much more easily to Wakefield with their pack proving too strong. That meant every set ended in pressure.
In the 25th minute, a brilliant Jake Trueman pressure kick saw Johnstone jump highest and find Vagana on his shoulder to walk in. Jowitt added the extras once again.
Just over 10 minutes later, Tyson Smoothy went close and then was followed by Tevaga who threw a dummy and then used his power to barrel over. Jowitt stayed perfect with the boot to extend Wakefield's lead further.
With less than two minutes remaining of the opening half, Jack Sinfield used some big-game nous to send over a drop goal to give Wakefield a more than three-score lead, and left Warrington with a mountain to climb at 19-0 down.
There was drama immediately in the second half when Wakefield's Corey Hall was sent to the sin bin for a high shot on Arron Lindop to give Warrington their opportunity to hit back, and they did.
Irwin threw a lovely dummy and then passed to open up the space and with a player advantage, Lindop had all the room to walk over in front of the Warrington faithful. Irwin converted to bring the scoreline to 19-6.
Warrington thought they had gone in again through Matty Ashton just minutes later, but a forward pass ruled out what would have been a score that brought the game right back in the balance
However, with numerical parity restored, it did not take long for Wakefield to get back on top once again and off the back of huge metres from Caleb Hamlin-Uele, they sent it out to Johnstone who used his step to pull off a sensational finish and with a 23-6 lead and 20 minutes to play, the Wakefield end was bouncing.
Warrington would not give up and with eight minutes left on the clock they kept the last tackle alive; Irwin sent over a looping pass and Lindop was in for his second. However, this time Irwin could not convert and the score was 23-10.
However the clock quickly ran away, Wakefield stayed strong, and immortality was theirs as the full-time hooter went and their name was etched onto the Super League trophy.
Jowitt: A rollercoaster of a year for me - highs are worth the lows
Wakefield's Max Jowitt to Sky Sports:
"A million per cent the highs are worth the lows.
"It didn't feel real that we were playing a Grand Final until we got here today.
"A rollercoaster of a year for me personally after dropping down to the reserves, not finding form, but I got my opportunity at the back end of the year.
"For this to be my last game for Wakefield, I will never forget it."

Chinese lithium mine registers wider vein, bolstering Beijing’s battery supply
A deposit in Sichuan has registered over 1 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, adding to China’s stores of the valuable metal
China has announced the expansion of the resource base for a major lithium deposit in the southwestern province of Sichuan by about 70 per cent, strengthening the country’s potential long-term supply for the metal – an essential component in the production of batteries for electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage.
After recent detection efforts, the Jiada Lithium Mine has registered about 1.05 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent in the deposit, bringing its total resources to 2.53 million tonnes, state news agency Xinhua reported on Thursday. The increase reinforces the mine’s status as a major hard-rock lithium deposit.
Dazhong Mining, the project’s developer, said in a filing that the additional resources had passed review and registration by the Ministry of Natural Resources. They comprise 33.52 million tonnes of ore containing about 423,800 tonnes of lithium oxide, with an average grade of 1.26 per cent.
The addition represents a 70.5 per cent increase from the previously registered 1.48 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, according to the filing.

On July 15, Raj Rani, 52, an ASHA worker in Yamunagar, Haryana had just completed her tasks for the day when she felt a throbbing pain in her left arm and in the middle of her chin. Since this pain had persisted for a few days, she went to the Community Health Centre (CHC) in Vyaspur to get an electrocardiogram (ECG) done.
The Additional Senior Medical Officer at the centre, Gunjeet Singh, saw the results of the ECG, gave her a dose of drugs including blood thinners and clotbusters, called a ‘loading dose’, and asked her to rush to the district hospital at Ambala Cantonment, two hours away, for further treatment.
Raj Rani had single-vessel disease, with a major coronary artery blocked. “At the district hospital, they scheduled my angioplasty the next day and I got one stent in my heart,” said Raj Rani. “I told my doctors to give me good treatment so I could resume my work as an ASHA. They reassured me that I would be able to do my duties, because I was lucky: I came in time,” she said.
Had this happened even two months ago, Raj Rani would not have received the diagnosis that would have led to quick treatment. Even though the Vyaspur CHC had an ECG machine, there was no technician to conduct it and while the medical officers could interpret the results, they were not very confident.
What changed
On May 29 this year, the Haryana government tied up with Sunfox Technologies, a health-tech startup, as part of Public-Private Partnership (PPP), to set up a tele-ECG network called Spandan One. Each medical centre in Haryana received a tele-ECG device that connects to smartphone and tablets, can be operated by frontline workers and gives a clinician-reviewed result in less than three minutes.
To date, nearly 600 government health facilities including primary health centres (PHCs), CHCs, sub-divisional hospitals and district hospitals have been equipped by a tele-ECG device along with training in using it. As of September 17, 33,854 ECG tests were conducted; 9,287 ECGs were abnormal and 1,342 critical cases were detected according to the Spandan dashboard.
In the remote Ranjitpur PHC in Yamunagar district, there is a steady increase in the footfall of patients due to the tele-ECG service available. “This is a new building we started using just six months ago; there is no fixed nurse or staff or even furniture,” said Varun Singh, medical officer who has been running the centre with staff on deputation and through borrowed furniture from other centres. “Ever since we got the tele-ECG, people have been coming to the centre asking for it,” he said.
One recent morning, Ram Saran, 75, come to the PHC with his son Mangaram to get his reports examined by Dr. Singh. Mr. Saran had been experiencing a feeling of his heart racing and breathlessness for many months. He had gotten an ECG and blood tests for ₹1200 at a private hospital at Vyaspur but wanted confirmation from the government doctor. The nursing officer at the PHC put the electrodes on Mr. Saran and an ECG graph formed in the tablet in her hands, with a message that the report was being analysed. Two and half minutes later, the report was ready to be downloaded. Mr. Saran had an ‘abnormal ECG’ and he was asked to consult a cardiologist and a copy of the report was sent to his mobile phone.
Dr. Singh then consulted with Mr. Saran and his son and told them to visit the hospital at Ambala Cant. at the earliest. “Before this initiative, I would not be able to interpret ECGs with this level of sophistication. The patient would need to visit a cardiologist available two hours away and wait a long time in the OPD for the diagnosis,” said Dr. Singh. For patients who are diagnosed with critical ECGs, an alarm goes off in the tablet to draw the attention of the healthcare worker and a prescription is generated so that patients receive life-saving medicines while the referral to a higher centre is being made.
“We never thought that we would get results within a few minutes of doing the ECG. This tele-ECG service is available in all centres in Yamunagar and is available in even other remote locations in the districts. This is a very welcome step,” said Shama Parveen, senior medical officer, Yamunagar CHC.
Primary care matters
Even though PHCs are the first point of contact of medical care for rural patients, they often do not have the necessary equipment or manpower to diagnose and treat heart ailments. A 2024 pre-print that assessed the availability of cardiac care in Vadodara district in Gujarat found only 44.11% of the surveyed PHCs had functional ECGs and employed them where indicated. In most cases patients were simply referred to higher centres for treatment. The time lost due to travel between centres can prove to be fatal for patients.
The impact of Haryana’s initiative has been incredible, said Kuldeep Singh, former Director General, Health Services (DGHS), Haryana who spearheaded the partnership. ECGs and early treatment for heart attacks is now available in rural centres that had earlier not registered a single heart attack due to lack of diagnosis. “We are already witnessing a 20% reduction in deaths in the emergency departments of district hospitals because patients are being stabilised before rushing here,” he said, adding that these are early assessments and more data is still being collected.
After primary care
Once the patient is stabilised with a loading dose, they are sent to higher centres such as district hospitals with Catherisation Labs where angiographies and angioplasties are performed. “Given the geography of Haryana, most patients reach the higher centre within one hour of the diagnosis, saving lives and heart muscles,” said Dr. Singh.
The Haryana government is also in a PPP with private providers to equip and run cath labs in four locations in the State–Panchkula, Gurugram, Faridabad and Ambala Cant. and is planning to soon expand to more locations.
As part of the agreement with the Haryana government, Sunfox Technologies provides equipment, training and on-going support for its tele-ECG system apart from maintaining a live dashboard monitoring cases. “Through the dashboard, we have real-time patient information which has given us rich insights–for example we now know that patients between 30-49 years have a higher incidence of cardiac issues than those over 50 years,” said Rajat Jain, CEO of the startup. Data has also shown that the incidence of critical ECGs among women in the age group of 30-49 is as much as men and greater than men in the age group of 70+, dispelling the belief that men have a greater risk for heart disease than women. “These kinds of insights are very important for policymakers but were never accessible before,” he said.
Challenges in the process
While the project is picking up steam in Haryana, there are some teething issues – many of the centres have to conduct repeat ECGs to get accurate ECG readings if they were not conducted properly the first time. A bump in the road was that the State’s nursing union had issued a diktat stating that nurses should not be conducting the ECGs as the post of ECG technicians has remained vacant in most health centres. The DGHS, however, later issued a letter stating that healthcare workers cannot deny conducting life-saving diagnosis and would face disciplinary action if they failed to do so. There is also the question of what happens when the partnership between the government and Sunfox Technologies ends: would the pathway to diagnosis and treatment change or would it have improved by then?
Looking ahead
Making ECGs available at PHCs is a great start but we need to do much more to improve the public health system as a whole to respond well to non-communicable diseases and their complications, said Chetanya Malik, a doctor who practices in Surguja, a remote district in Chattisgarh for the non-profit Sangwari. In Chhattisgarh, an ECG facility is only available at the district hospital, revealing the vastness of the need and the unevenness of primary care provided within the country. Dr. Malik also noted the need for patients to be given support in finding transport and for referrals to higher centres to be seamless to help solve the problem of cardiac emergencies.
India’s public health systems have, for decades now, remained focused on infectious diseases and maternal and child health — both still important, but the time has come to also realign the systems to care for non-communicable diseases. Heart disease alone is estimated to account for nearly 27% of all deaths in India. The need is enormous, and the technology is available. It is time all States implement such programmes, pointed out Dr. Kuldeep Singh.

Russian aerial strikes snarl traffic on 3 Kyiv bridges in a new disruption tactic
Russian aerial attacks have forced the partial closure of three bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, causing traffic chaos
KYIV, Ukraine -- Russian aerial attacks forced the partial closure Friday of three bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital’s mayor said, in Moscow’s latest effort to disrupt life in the city.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s top diplomat said officials have received separate proposals for a partial truce with Russia from the United States, India, Turkey and Egypt. The proposals envision halting attacks on energy infrastructure, which have caused fuel shortages in Russia and power outages in Ukraine, and on Black Sea shipping needed to get vital grain exports to world markets.
The Russian strikes forcing the full or partial closure of three of Kyiv’s six road bridges caused traffic logjams and appeared to be a new tactic in its campaign to torment the city’s residents. Previously, Russia has hit apartment blocks, supermarket warehouses, gas stations and data centers, among other targets, in an escalation of attacks.
The aerial war has intensified in recent months as fighting along the roughly 1,250-kilometer front line snaking through northern, eastern and southern Ukraine became virtually deadlocked. Russia invaded its neighbor more than 4 ½ years ago, and there are no concrete signs that a peace settlement might be possible.
However, Ukraine has this year made some progress against Russia’s bigger army, according to the Institute for the Study of War.
Russian forces lost control over almost 300 square kilometers (116 square miles) between March and September, the Washington-based think tank said in a report late Thursday. Also, it said that the Russian military suffered over 46,000 casualties in September, the highest monthly number this year. It did not say how many Ukrainian troops were killed or wounded.
Russia fired more than 100 drones at Ukraine overnight, striking Kyiv and eight other regions, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Almost half of the drones were the jet-powered type that are especially hard to stop, he said.
A drone hit a high-rise apartment block in Kyiv, killing one person, he said. At least four people were reported wounded elsewhere.
Zelenskyy repeated his appeal for foreign countries to close loopholes in international sanctions on Russia and to add more restrictions on its trade. He said Russia's drones and missiles are “critically dependent” on foreign components.
“Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
Ukraine has also bombarded Russia with the long-range drones and missiles it now produces, aiming at military manufacturing plants and oil refineries.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Friday that its air defenses overnight downed 646 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.
One person was wounded in Russia’s southwestern Volgograd region, Gov. Andrei Bocharov said. The attack targeted “industrial infrastructure,” he said, without providing details.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the partial truce proposals presented to Kyiv by four countries were the first time India has offered to play a role.
India is trying to balance its ties with Russia against its growing partnerships with the United States and other Western powers. A new U.S. sanctions package on Russia could impose up to 100% tariffs on New Delhi as a major importer of Russian oil.
Sybiha said Kyiv is ready to accept a ceasefire if it stops Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power grid — as well as Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries — and on cargo vessels exporting grain and other farm products through the Black Sea.
“We are ready for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire, but only in that combination. Energy and a ceasefire in the Black Sea,” Sybiha told reporters Thursday, in comments embargoed until Friday.
He repeated Ukraine’s offer of an unconditional ceasefire on the front line. But Moscow has rejected a ceasefire, saying a comprehensive peace deal must be agreed rather than a temporary truce.
Sybiha said Ukraine is requesting some 300 Patriot missiles from partner countries because intelligence services estimate that Russia is holding 600 ballistic missiles in reserve and can produce up to 140 ballistic missiles per month.
The U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems can effectively defend against ballistic missiles, which fly fast and drop steeply, but they are in short supply due to the Iran war.
Ukraine urgently needs funding in order to contract future drone production, so there are no gaps in supply at the beginning of next year, Sybiha said.
Kyiv faces a projected budget deficit of roughly $27 billion this year, although the European Union has promised to help meet its financial requirements and strengthen its defense.
Russia is also facing economic and financial challenges due to high military spending and debt.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

3 Cape Bretoners were hit and killed by a train in Maine in 1970. Some want the case reopened
'Justice has not been served,' says Richard Novak, a brother of one of the deceased
Every morning, 78-year-old Richard Novak hears a passing train from his apartment in Bedford, N.S., and thinks of his late brother, Kenny.
Kenny, 15, was one of three Cape Breton youth who inexplicably ended up in Maine in July 1970 after deviating from a planned camping trip in Cape Breton Highlands National Park.
Kenny, David Burrows, 17, and Terry Burt, 20, were in sleeping bags on a rail track west of the border town of Houlton, Maine, when they were struck by a train early on the morning of July 10.
Novak, who has Parkinson's disease and is in failing health, has the same thought every morning as he lies in bed and hears the train.
"The first person I think of [is] Kenny, Terry and David, and what it would be like under that train and why would you choose the tracks?" said Novak.
The deaths were ruled accidental, with the Sydney-area youth believed to be asleep at the time of the collision.
Novak would like to see the case reopened, even though documentation from the time is sparse.
"What I'm trying to do is unite with the people from Maine and clear this up once and for all, so we can put it to rest and have some peace," he said.
At the time of the incident, Novak was living in Ontario.
"I've never felt so much pain in my life," he said of learning of the deaths.
Novak said Kenny was the youngest of six boys and one girl in the family. The 5-7, 145-pound teen with black hair collected comic books, loved music, skating and swimming, and had been studying Latin for three years.
Novak believes the group may have been going to a concert in the U.S.
It's a case with many unanswered questions, but here's what's known.
Timeline
On Friday, July 3, 1970, Kenny Novak and Burt were driven to the Highlands by Novak's mother, she told the Bangor Daily News, according to a July 19, 1970, article. She told the paper she believed Burrows joined them on July 5.
The three were last seen in Ingonish, N.S., on July 6, the newspaper reported, citing the RCMP.
It's believed they hitchhiked to the U.S. and entered illegally on Thursday, July 9, from Woodstock, N.B., which Houlton borders. There was no record of youths matching their description crossing officially that date, the Bangor paper reported in its July 11-12 edition.
The newspaper also reported that a border patrolman tried to stop three hitchhiking youth in Houlton, but they fled. The patrolman also tried to find the youths later using an unmarked vehicle, but was unsuccessful.
It was around 11:30 p.m. ET when 20-year-old college student Royden Hunt was at a dairy bar in Houlton, around a mile from the border. The business was closed and he was hanging around outside with some friends.
"Those three come along and were walking, and they stopped and talked to us and they asked us how they could get to [Interstate] 95," Hunt told CBC News.
Interstate 95 is a highway that runs from Maine to Florida.
How the trio ended up at the rail line
Hunt said he didn't usually pick up hitchhikers, but the trio seemed pleasant. And while the original plan was to drop them off a few kilometres away at the nearest spot on the interstate, Hunt let it slip that they were going to be travelling to his hometown of Island Falls, Maine, almost 50 kilometres from Houlton.
The trio asked if they could be taken there, but Hunt and his friend, Mike York, said that wouldn't make sense as there wouldn't be much traffic for hitchhiking options.
"Well, is there any place we can get on the railroad tracks?" asked one of the Cape Breton youth.
Hunt knew of a place called Smyrna Mills about halfway between Island Falls and Houlton that fit the bill.
"So that's what we did. We stopped, let them out … and it was only like 50 feet to the railroad tracks and they went to the railroad tracks and we left," said Hunt.
He believes they wanted to walk the tracks so they could stay out of sight.
Besides the circumstances, the timing stands out for Hunt because he had to drop off his friend York for a midnight shift at the gas station where he worked.
Hunt later learned that after they left the dairy bar, a border patrol agent showed up asking the people who remained outside whether they had seen the three youth. The people who were still there were friends of his and relayed that detail to him. (It's unclear if this was separate from the second effort made by the border patrol agent to find the youth, as referenced in the July 11-12 Bangor Daily News.)
Hunt and York, who is no longer alive, were the last people known to have spoken with the trio.
The day of the crash
The following day around 7 a.m., a 19-car train weighing about 725 tonnes was headed toward Houlton when it rounded a sharp turn. The engineer spotted what he thought was a rubber raft on the tracks, the July 11-12 edition of the Bangor Daily News reported.
"They're sleeping bags!" said the train's fireman, with the trio about 50 metres away.
The engineer tried to stop the train, but it was too late.
The trio did not move before being struck by the train, the engineer said.
Newspaper accounts report that Canadian cigarettes, canned goods, and maps of the Atlantic provinces, Maine, New England, Pennsylvania and New Jersey were among the possessions found on the trio.
The Cape Breton Post reported one of the sleeping bags had the name and address of one of the three youth, while other newspapers said the words "Sydney, N.S." were marked.
The Biddeford-Saco Journal reported a wallet found on one body contained a small sum of money but none of the individuals had identification. The article doesn't state how much money was found.
One of Hunt's memories of the trio is that one of them had a roll of cash, perhaps around $100 to $150 worth.
On the day of the crash, 18-year-old David Sjoberg of Houlton was working at a local funeral home doing odd jobs such as property maintenance, washing hearses and helping with visitations. It was his second year there as a summer job and he was off to college in the fall.
He recalls his boss telling him the bodies of the trio would be arriving.
"I remember they arrived in the morning because before I went to lunch that day, he said, 'When you come back, I'd like you to go down and help them out in the morgue,' sort of tending to what they needed to do with those bodies," said Sjoberg, who later became a pastor.
Besides the circumstances surrounding the deaths, the day stands out to Sjoberg because a cousin of his got married that night.
Autopsies
Autopsies by Aroostook County's medical examiner found the trio died from severe head and body injuries. Testing later conducted at a state lab found no alcohol or drugs in the bodies.
Sjoberg said he was not present in the morgue for the autopsies, but his boss had a request for him: Would he transport the bodies back to Cape Breton?
"As an 18-year-old kid, I think that sounded like a pretty exciting adventure," said Sjoberg. "Thousand-mile round trip, be gone two or three days, so I didn't hesitate to say yes."
By Sunday the 12th, according to newspaper accounts, the fathers of the three youth were in Houlton to confirm the identity of the bodies.
"[Frank] Novak, middle aged and with a crew cut, and Gordon Burt of Sydney and James Burrows of Sydney River agreed that their visit to the funeral home and personal belongings they were shown had convinced them their sons had been killed by the train," reporter Dean Rhodes wrote in the July 13 Bangor Daily News.
"I couldn't ask for nicer people," Frank Novak told the reporter. "Everybody made everything as nice as possible for us."
He didn't have an answer for why the trio ended up in Maine.
"We haven't got a clue," he said.
With the identities confirmed, Sjoberg started driving to Cape Breton on Sunday, overnighting at a motel along the way. He arrived in Cape Breton on Monday the 13th and brought the bodies to a funeral home. After a quick stop there, Sjoberg returned home.
He doesn't remember the incident being the talk of the town.
"I thought the story had died decades ago," said Sjoberg, who learned in recent years about a Facebook page dedicated to the case and concerns from family members about the investigation. There's also a petition calling for the case to be reopened.
One of Richard Novak's criticisms of the investigation is that it wasn't thorough enough. He believes the deaths involved foul play, with the bodies placed on the rail track to cover up for murder.
Sheriff department's investigation
Aroostook County Sheriff Darrell Crandall, who oversaw the investigation, died in 1996, but newspaper accounts from 1970 provide some insight into the investigation and his thinking.
The July 17, 1970, Cape Breton Post noted Crandall had not closed the investigation as he was still awaiting an autopsy from the state lab in Augusta, Maine.
Crandall, a former railroad brakeman, believed the incident was an unfortunate mishap with one fundamental question.
"Why did they lay down on the railway tracks?" he told the newspaper.
The sheriff said he had 70 men at his disposal in the surrounding area and "if there's anything we'll know about it."
Less than a week later, Crandall ruled the deaths did not involve foul play.
It had rained on the day of the crash, meaning the ground was damp, "which may have led them to decide on the rail bed as a dry sleeping area," according to the July 23, 1970, Cape Breton Post.
The Aroostook County Sheriff's Department did not respond to interview requests for this story.
In an email shared with CBC News, an Aroostook County official told Novak the department was "not in possession of … case reports, statements, forensic findings, evidence, case files, or any other records dating back to 1970."
Hunt said he's hunted in the area and you can hear the train from miles away.
"Where we let 'em out, that's in the middle of nowhere," he said. "I can't imagine that they run into anybody that would have brought any harm to 'em, a mile and a half up that track at 11:30, 12 o'clock at night. There'd be nobody out there. And to lay across that track, with their head on the track, and not hear that train coming … I don't know."
At the time, the rail line was lightly used, the Cape Breton Post reported, with an average of one train moving in each direction per day.
Hunt said he was interviewed twice by police officials, including once at a golf course.
Richard Novak said his late brother Lorne led the charge to get answers, but died last year. As a result, Novak has now been thrust into the role.
"Justice has not been served," he said. "They did not die accidentally."
