EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be why
- Published
Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car.
Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys.
It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car.
Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern.
So what could explain these reports of motion sickness?
Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles.
It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says.
"I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles.
But research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive.
Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point".
"There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says.
'Wonderful to drive... but my daughter gets unwell'
When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs.
Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it.
She only used to get motion sick on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute trip to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell.
On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before.
Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars.
Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says.
But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue, external, telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds.
What could cause it?
Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness.
Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles.
Humans have adapted to associate sound with movement in vehicles, experts explain. Because electric vehicles don't have the auditory cues and vibrations from the engine that we're used to, which indicate when the car is accelerating, this could trigger motion sickness, Di Giulio says.
Another reason is regenerative braking, the process whereby when drivers release the accelerator, the electric car starts to slow down and uses the energy to feed the battery. However, it is a process that needs to be done smoothly with the accelerator being released gently, or it can lead to harsh deceleration.
"It forces the person to perhaps feel like they're rocking back and forth for that brief moment when the speed of the car suddenly changes," says Hac.
This is something Carolyn Le, 24, from California, has noticed. She gets "horrendous" motion sickness when her friend drives her in his electric vehicle in busy cities, she says. The regenerative braking means it "constantly feels like the car is stopping all the time".
Electric vehicles can also accelerate and decelerate much more quickly than conventional combustion cars, which Di Giulio says can cause motion sickness.
Edmonds, of EVA England, says developments in electric vehicle design have made them better at moderating the acceleration so they don't gain speed as rapidly.
She adds that the association thinks motion sickness in an electric vehicle is caused by "other factors" like the motorist's driving style rather than the vehicle itself.
Some features of electric cars may feel unfamiliar to drivers at first, adds Mike Hawes, head of the Society of Motor Manufacturers.
He says EVs can offer a different driving experience. "However, drivers typically adjust quickly to these characteristics, and many models also allow regenerative braking to be tailored to individual preferences."
Some people are also just more prone to motion sickness, and genetics have the biggest influence on this, according to Hac, and experts say women and children are more susceptible.
Motion sickness typically peaks between the ages of eight and 10, after which it decreases through more exposure, says Prof John Golding, who has researched the subject at the University of Westminster, the Royal Navy and the RAF.
Hold your head still and open the window
As their popularity increases, avoiding electric vehicles can be a challenge - the number of new zero-emission cars registered in the UK rose by 40.5% in April to June 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, latest Department for Transport figures show. , external
At the end of June 2026, 5.8% of all licensed cars on UK roads were zero-emission vehicles, the data shows. The sale of new purely petrol or diesel cars is set to be banned from 2030.
Lucinda Harrison, 24, from London says she often books taxis that turn out to be electric vehicles, and has to endure the trip feeling nauseous, sweaty and clammy.
The thought of travelling in an EV fills her with dread, she says. Even just a five-minute lift from a colleague to a Tube station recently was enough to make her feel "horrific".
Academics say there are several steps passengers can take to reduce feelings of motion sickness.
- Look out of the front window and don't look at your phone or read a book
- Sit in the front passenger seat rather than in the back, if possible. If you do have to sit in the back, opt for the middle seat so you can still see out the front window
- Keep your head still by holding it against the headrest
- Recline your seat
- Regulate your breathing
- Open the window to let in fresh air
- Take travel sickness tablets if needed, though these can cause drowsiness
- Before a long journey, make sure you're hydrated, have slept well and have eaten non-greasy food
Experts also say we can become desensitised to motion sickness through prolonged exposure. The more journeys you take in electric vehicles, the less likely you are to become motion sick as your body adjusts, Golding says.
There are also things carmakers can do to alleviate motion sickness in electric vehicles, says Prof Cyriel Diels, professor of mobility design at the Royal College of Art. These include having software that smooths out rapid acceleration, adding sound systems and subtle seat vibrations to signal to passengers that the car is moving, and offering adaptive regenerative braking that reduces sudden deceleration.
Matt Adams from BEAMA, which represents UK manufacturers of electric vehicle charge points, says he's confident that "if future research identifies the reason for car sickness that vehicle manufacturers can respond and improve accordingly".
But for Lola, she just wants her boyfriend to trade in his car. She says that day can't come soon enough.

Jammu and Kashmir Bank is set to issue a recruitment notification for assistant and officer-level positions within the next few days, Managing Director and CEO Amitava Chatterjee said on Tuesday.
Speaking during the bank’s 88th Annual General Meeting (AGM) at the Sher-i-Kashmir International Convention Centre (SKICC) here, Chatterjee said the bank had finalised negotiations with the agency that would conduct the recruitment examinations for Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
“After 2021, the bank is going for recruitment of both assistants as well as officers. The agreement for conducting the examinations for Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh is being finalised, and the bank will come out with a notification in a few days,” Chatterjee said.
He said the recruitment would be carried out in accordance with the bank’s operational requirements and would also take into account the need for employees with proficiency in local languages.
“As far as the bank is concerned, we will do what we have done in the past. There is a requirement for people with local language proficiency, though the numbers will be limited,” he said.
Chatterjee said the bank’s presence across 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir had created a requirement for personnel familiar with local languages.
“The bank is present in 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir, and we need people with local language proficiency to serve customers there. So, the bank may decide in future to hire a few employees to support our existing staff strength,” he said.

After India won silver at the Asian Cup in September 2025, losing to China 4-1 in the final, the road ahead looked uncertain for the women’s team. Harendra Singh stepped down as head coach out of the blue, with the World Cup qualifiers fast approaching.
Hockey India, then, opted for the pragmatic choice of reinstating Sjoerd Marijne in January this year to lead the side out of the hole it found itself in. The Dutchman, who had inspired the women’s team to a rare fourth-place finish at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, had just two months to devise a plan to secure a World Cup berth with a new-look Indian team.
India secured qualification despite losing the final to England, then continued to build steam for important assignments in the year ahead.
The biggest boost came with a triumphant FIH Nations Cup campaign in New Zealand, which earned India a spot in the 2026-27 Pro League after its relegation in 2025.
But even after these performances, not many expected the side, ranked no. 9 in the world, to progress into the second round of the World Cup in the Netherlands and Belgium. Marijne had entrusted the youth, including 10 first-time World Cuppers, to come good despite tough first-round matches against China and England.
Marijne’s faith reaped rewards in the opening game, where India held China to a superb 2-2 draw that set the tone for the weeks to come. “In the past meetings, sometimes it did creep up in your mind that, ‘They have an Olympic silver, you wonder how good they will be,’” India forward Navneet Kaur admitted. “We have changed that mindset from then to now,” adding, “it doesn’t matter who is first or last, we need to play our game against every team.”
India’s disciplined defensive display across the World Cup helped it finish fifth, its best finish since the inaugural edition in 1972.
While the defensive solidity infused the group with renewed faith, the attack was found wanting after goalless displays against higher-ranked nations like Netherlands, England and Australia. A goal in the second-round game against the Aussies proved to be the difference between playing for fifth and sixth and reaching the semifinals.
READ | A wait ends, a new era begins - India’s women win hockey gold
Despite the disappointment of missing out on a last-four spot, players remained bullish about India’s chances of dethroning China and winning the gold medal at the Asian Games.
After the World Cup, Marijne heaped praise on the current group, saying the class of 2026 had better quality and balance than his Tokyo Olympics group.
“More of them speak English, I think the quality talent-wise is a little bit better than in 2021. We had more or less a lot of seniors but also experienced players. We didn’t have so much youth so that balance is now also very good. They really are pushing themselves and I think that is what I really like at the moment,” Marijne told Sportstar.
The team backed up that billing on the pitch in Japan, romping to the gold medal in style. India outscored all teams, raking up 69 goals – the most it has managed in 12 editions of the continental Games, while winning all seven outings.
While Navneet Kaur was India’s first-choice Penalty Corner (PC) taker at the World Cup, her junior Deepika has firmly dislodged her at the Asiad, with a staggering 19 of her 21 goals coming from short corners, compared with Navneet’s two.
The injection of youth in the form of Ishika, Rutuja Pisal, Baljeet Kaur, Sakshi Rana and Sunelita Toppo in the wings and midfield has provided much-needed work-rate and directness, both on and off the ball, allowing Navneet and Lalremsiami to thrive inside the 25-yard circle.
India dispatched the lower-ranked teams in the group stage with ease before facing its first big test in the semifinal against a stubborn South Korea. Despite its dominance on the ball, India found the breakthrough from a PC variation before doubling the lead.
It was not going to be an easy task against defending champion China, which India had failed to beat in its last five meetings. Just like in the previous two encounters between the sides, India took the lead, scoring the first goal China had conceded in the tournament. But on those occasions, India could not build on its advantage as China came back strongly, beating India in last year’s Asia Cup final before holding it to a 2-2 draw in the World Cup.
This time, though, was different. Even though China dominated the ball, India seemed to have learned from its experience, not allowing the world no. 4 side to have clear-cut chances inside the circle. China’s biggest chance to draw level came from the Penalty Stroke in the second quarter, but Savita Punia made a stunning save to keep India ahead.
While Marijne’s predecessor missed Savita’s services due to injury, the 36-year-old has yet again underscored her value in recent months while sharing goalkeeping duties with Bichu Devi. In the semifinals and finals, Bichu has started the matches, before Savita has come in to close out games in the second and fourth quarters.
China’s dominance continued in the third and fourth quarters, but India’s defence, led by Salima Tete, Sushila Chanu and Nikki Pradhan, continued to frustrate Alyson Annan’s side and hold on for a historic gold medal – India’s first in 42 years and a direct qualification for the LA Olympics in 2028.
Amidst the euphoria of having clinched the biggest achievements of their careers, the players promptly picked up Marijne and tossed him in the air in celebration to give him due credit for this turnaround.
After all, the result could kickstart a much-needed turnaround for the women’s game.

A delegation of the Kashmir Traders and Manufacturers Federation (KTMF), led by its president Mohammad Yaseen Khan, on Tuesday called on newly appointed Inspector General of Police, Kashmir Zone, Sujit Kumar Singh and discussed issues concerning the trade community across the Valley.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

India recorded 3,832 new leprosy cases among children in 2025-26, including 37 who had Grade-2 disability (G2D) at diagnosis — an indicator of delayed detection. The child caseload was 91.6% higher than the National Leprosy Eradication Programme's (NLEP) target of 2,000 cases for the year.
The figures, from the latest NLEP annual report for 2025-26, come even as India pursues the National Strategic Plan for Leprosy 2023-27, which seeks to interrupt transmission at the district level by 2027. Under the roadmap, a district is considered to have interrupted transmission after reporting zero new indigenous child cases for five consecutive years.
The NLEP's programme objectives include zero disability among new child cases and a national G2D rate of less than one case per million population. The roadmap projects 1,000 child cases and a G2D rate of 0.5 per million for 2026-27.
The appearance of children among newly detected cases matters beyond the absolute number. The World Health Organisation (WHO) considers new cases among children below 15 years an indicator of recent transmission, while G2D among newly detected patients indicates delayed diagnosis.
The WHO also says disabilities among newly detected child cases signal both delayed detection and ongoing transmission.
India recorded 63 children with G2D in 2019-20, followed by 35 in 2020-21, 41 in 2021-22, 55 in 2022-23 and 45 in 2023-24. The continued detection of children with G2D contrasts with the NLEP's objective of zero disability among new child cases.
The latest numbers therefore raise a fundamental epidemiological question: if India is working to interrupt transmission by 2027, why are children still developing leprosy, and why are some reaching diagnosis only after visible disability has appeared?
India detected 91,783 new leprosy cases in 2025-26, according to the Union Health Ministry. The prevalence rate was 0.56 per 10,000 population, and 1,945 patients had Grade-2 disability at diagnosis, accounting for 2.12% of all newly detected cases. The national G2D rate was 1.34 per million, above the NLEP's target of less than one case per million.
According to the WHO's latest global update, India reported the world's largest number of newly detected leprosy cases in 2025, with 91,783 cases, followed by Brazil with 22,901 and Indonesia with 16,292. Together, the three countries accounted for 78.3% of all new cases reported globally. The WHO notes that, although the update is for 2025, India reported data for April 2025 to March 2026.
India also reported the world's largest number of new child leprosy cases in the WHO's 2025 global update, with 3,832 cases.
The WHO figures and the NLEP figures refer to the same reporting period for India — April 2025 to March 2026 — although the WHO presents India's data in its 2025 global table. The WHO table records 3,832 child cases and 37 child cases with G2D for India.
Dr. Kabir Sardana, Professor and Head of Dermatology at ABVIMS-Dr. RML Hospital, Delhi, attributed the continuing burden partly to gaps in case detection.
"Data points to the fact that there is poor detection, which is why we are seeing more children with leprosy," he said.
The Health Ministry identifies high-endemic and hard-to-reach areas as priorities for intensified case detection. The NLEP emphasises active case detection, household contact surveys and focused campaigns, along with special plans for hard-to-reach areas. The programme also identifies stigma and discrimination as continuing concerns.
The WHO says prolonged, close contact with untreated cases allows transmission to continue, while the disease's long incubation period makes interruption difficult. New child cases are considered an indicator of recent transmission, although the presence of a child case cannot by itself establish when or where the infection occurred. The WHO notes that symptoms can appear years after infection.
Leprosy, or Hansen's disease, is a chronic bacterial infection caused mainly by Mycobacterium leprae. It primarily affects the skin and peripheral nerves. Transmission occurs mainly through prolonged, close contact with an untreated person. The disease is curable with multidrug therapy, a combination of antibiotics provided free through public-health programmes.
Children and household contacts are particularly important to surveillance because a new child case can indicate ongoing transmission within a community. However, the presence of a child case cannot by itself establish when or where the infection occurred. The average incubation period is about five years and can be considerably longer.
India's child caseload has fallen substantially from a decade ago, but the decline has not been linear. The country detected 11,365 children with leprosy in 2014-15, 11,389 in 2015-16 and 11,770 in 2016-17. The number fell to 10,287 in 2017-18, 9,227 in 2018-19 and 7,859 in 2019-20.
Child detections fell sharply during the COVID-19 period, reaching 3,753 in 2020-21, before rising to 4,107 in 2021-22. They fell again to 2,363 in 2022-23 and 2,335 in 2023-24, before rising to 3,832 in 2025-26. Changes in reported case numbers also reflect the intensity and reach of case detection, making it difficult to interpret the trend as a direct measure of transmission alone.
The Health Ministry has identified high-priority States and districts where the burden remains concentrated. Twenty-three districts in Chhattisgarh, 21 in Jharkhand, 18 each in Maharashtra and Odisha, and 10 in Madhya Pradesh had a prevalence rate above one case per 10,000 population, according to the Ministry.
These figures identify districts with prevalence above the elimination threshold; they should not be read as meaning that these are the only States or districts with continuing transmission.
For a disease that is curable, and for which early detection and treatment can prevent the progression to disability, the continued detection of children — including some already showing Grade-2 disability — highlights the tension between programme targets and what is still being detected in communities.

Scientists at the Institute of Advanced Virology (IAV) in Keralam are developing a dengue forecasting system that integrates epidemiological and weather data on a machine-learning platform to predict dengue incidence trends in advance.
The aim is to help public health managers plan resource allocation and preventive measures proactively, rather than responding only after outbreaks occur.
Climate factors are important early warning indicators for dengue because they directly influence the biology of the Aedes mosquito and the replication of the dengue virus.
Warm temperatures accelerate mosquito development, shorten the virus’s extrinsic incubation period—the time required for the virus to become transmissible inside the mosquito—and can increase transmission efficiency. Moderate to high humidity can prolong mosquito survival, while moderate rainfall creates breeding habitats. Torrential rain, however, can flush out mosquito breeding sites.
Favourable climate
Keralam, which remains warm and wet for much of the year, therefore has climatic conditions favourable to Aedes proliferation and dengue transmission. This has prompted considerable interest in developing forecasting models that combine meteorological and epidemiological data to enable disease surveillance to stay ahead of outbreaks.
“Our machine learning model integrates six years of epidemiological data (March 2020 to February 2026) with climatic variables, including rainfall, temperature and average humidity, to generate weekly dengue forecasts,” says Abhinand C.S., scientist in the Department of Virus Genomics, Bioinformatics and Statistics at IAV, who developed the model.
The Dengue Early Warning System (DEWS), the current version of the system, is accessible at https://dews.iav.res.in, and uses epidemiological data from the State Surveillance Unit (SSU) of the Directorate of Health Services and meteorological data from the India Meteorological Department.
The dengue case trends predicted by DEWS showed a positive correlation with actual case data from the Health department, Dr. Abhinand says. Further evaluation using the SSU data for March-July 2026 has indicated the model’s potential for early prediction of district-wise dengue trends.
The model incorporates daily epidemiological and climatic parameters, including temperature, rainfall and humidity, allowing a more granular representation of disease dynamics. Each district is treated as an independent unit, taking into account district-specific geographical and environmental characteristics, including waterbodies and drainage systems. This enables the model to be trained and optimised for individual districts.
For easier interpretation by public health managers, predicted disease burden is classified into four risk levels—very high, high, moderate and low, based on predefined prediction ranges. This provides a district-wise indication of the expected risk.
Prediction difficulties
Dengue is among the more difficult infectious diseases to predict because its transmission is multidimensional and can vary substantially between locations.
Beyond climate, factors such as urbanisation, human mobility, water-storage practices, population immunity to the four dengue virus serotypes and changes in vector biology can alter transmission dynamics. Models relying heavily on climatic variables may therefore struggle to capture sudden changes in these factors.
Under-reporting is another major challenge. A large proportion of dengue infections are asymptomatic or mild and may be mistaken for other viral fevers. Differences in testing and reporting practices can also create geographical biases. Thiruvananthapuram, for instance, has long been regarded as Keralam’s dengue hotspot, although public health experts have argued that its high reported burden also reflects stronger surveillance and testing.
The IAV acknowledges these limitations. Since DEWS is trained on historical data, sudden or substantial changes in climatic parameters could affect its accuracy. Variations in the reporting of confirmed dengue cases by the Health department could similarly influence observed disease patterns and the reliability of predictions, Dr. Abhinand says.
Yearly updation
“For the model to evolve from a research model to a routinely functioning public health forecasting system, DEWS will have to undergo yearly updation and further refinement, and perhaps be trained with more variables. DEWS is the first disease forecasting model of its kind to be developed for use by the State,” says IAV Director E. Sreekumar.
The platform could eventually be extended to other Aedes-borne diseases such as chikungunya and Zika, potentially strengthening Keralam’s disease surveillance capacity and enabling more timely, data-driven public health interventions.

Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
- Published
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.
The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.
"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."
Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
[The youth] just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created"
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.
"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.
More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.
Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.

  - Published28 April 2025
Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.
He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.
"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.
He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.
I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.
They promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths"
"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.
"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."
"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.
"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.
"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."
He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."
Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.
The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.
"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."
Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

When I started collecting physical media in 2009 at 13 years old, CDs still dominated the market. Big-box retail stores had music sections with rows and rows of sealed jewel cases, and it was normal to spend $25 on a deluxe album or a box set.
Less than a decade later, streaming had taken over. Vinyl records outsold CDs for the first time in 2022. The Compact Disc began to feel like an afterthought.
But now the CD is enjoying a surge in popularity thanks to cultural shifts like the rise in K-pop, the backlash against the streaming platforms’ policies, and Gen-Zers driving hand-me-down cars without Bluetooth connectivity. When I walked into a record store in July and found a deluxe CD for Madonna’s new album, Confessions II, on sale for $34, more expensive than some of the vinyl pressings, it finally felt like the format was officially back. (And yes, I bought it.)
According to 2026 data from the entertainment industry research firm Luminate, K-pop groups like BTS, Enhypen, and ATEEZ contributed to an overall 16 percent increase in CD sales so far this year, thanks to collectible editions that encouraged fans to buy multiple copies of the groups’ albums. This seems to be the major shift between the old way of buying music and the new normal: CDs are looked at more as merch—collectibles that support the artist—than as necessities to hear the songs. According to the same Luminate report, if K-pop were taken out of the data, disc sales would’ve still increased 6.7 percent.
Though the numbers show solid growth, CDs are nowhere near as hot as they used to be. The music industry sold 16.3 million discs in the first half of this year, a paltry number compared to the CD’s heyday around the turn of the millennium, when annual sales topped 900 million. Still, their collectible physicality has brought them back into fashion.
There really is no right or wrong way to collect CDs. If you keep a CD in its packaging, it will be protected for years to come. But here are some tips if you want to elevate your collecting experience and get more out of your collection, whether you’re new to the format or rescuing an old box of discs from the garage.
Get a CD Player
It might seem that owning a CD player is the obvious first step to collecting CDs. But according to Luminate’s report, only half of millennials and Gen-Zers that collect CDs have a player. Luckily, finding a good CD player is easier and more budget-friendly than buying a record player.
You might even have a CD player without knowing it; a Blu-ray player hooked up to a nice sound bar is a convenient set up to play CDs, since most Blu-ray and DVD players can handle audio discs. Even your Xbox can play them, though the disc drives on Sony PlayStation 4 and 5 consoles weirdly cannot play CDs.
If you need a CD player, the first thing to consider is what kind you want. A personal portable player lets you take your music anywhere. If your record player setup includes a stereo receiver, chances are it has a CD input that you can use to hook up a hi-fi player for at-home listening. This will give you the best audio from your discs. These component players can still be found at big-box retail stores or online music shops like Turntable Lab or RETROSPEKT that specialize in hi-fi systems.
Del Bravo Record Shop, one of the oldest record stores in Texas, has seen an increase in demand for personal CD players that it ships out of its San Antonio store. “They’ve been flying off the shelves,” says Jessica Campa, Del Bravo’s sales associate and social media manager. “We’ve also had about a 12.6 percent increase in CD sales so far this year.”
Bluetooth CD Players are the latest advancement; they let you connect wireless headphones or speakers. If you love the hunt, a thrift store or flea market can be a great place to find a CD player at a great price. Just be sure to test that it works before paying for it. Record stores sometimes keep a variety of used or new CD players as well, depending on their specialty.
The Record Store Is Still Your Friend
Independent record stores are the go-to place to get exclusive vinyl, and many of them still carry CDs. While online shops like Amazon seem like a convenient way to buy these small discs, record stores often receive promotional goodies like posters or stickers that they throw in for free along with your purchase. Oftentimes indie stores will get autographed albums during an artist’s release week to encourage shoppers to come into the store to buy the disc. These are often sold at the regular retail price and not up-charged.
Of course, record stores are great places to buy used discs, and most of the time, the discs are inspected by the staff and you can expect them to play properly and without skips. Stores sometimes even have listening stations so you can preview the used discs.
Track Your Collection
Knowing what music you already have is a great way to prevent accidentally acquiring doubles when you’re out shopping. Thankfully, you don’t need to rely on an Excel spreadsheet. Discogs, an online marketplace and music database for collectors, is well known among vinyl aficionados, but it’s just as helpful as a tool to keep track of your CDs. Not only does the free mobile app feature a barcode scanner that will show you the exact pressing of a CD, it will also show you the current market value of it, in case you come across a rare find in the wild or something that could be overpriced. You can also look up different versions of a CD to find that rare version, like the Japanese pressing with the extra tracks. Discogs will show you a list of the users who own that particular disc who’d be willing to sell it to you for a fair offer.
Inspect Thrifted and Stored CDs
Found that box of old CDs in the garage? Scored a 75-cent copy of Santana’s Abraxas at the thrift store? Be sure to not only check if the disc is actually in the case, but inspect the bottom of the disc—CDs are read by a laser that moves underneath the disc as it spins—for any scratches, discoloration, or spots, which could be a sign of disc rot.
Disc rot is exactly what it sounds like, the deterioration of the reflective layer where a CD’s music data is stored. Sometimes it’s caused by manufacturing defects, but usually it’s the result of improper storage. Over time, heat and humidity can turn these once seemingly indestructible pieces of media into unplayable garbage.
You can score some great finds when thrifting for CDs, but you never know the conditions the discs were stored in before they hit the discount shelf, so learn to spot the most common problems and be discerning. You may even want to bring a portable player with you when you shop so you can test your finds—with the seller’s consent, of course.
Invest in Proper Storage
Similar to a vinyl record, the best way to store a CD is vertically, in its original sleeve, jewel case, or digipack. Any solid shelf makes a good home, but used furniture stores or Goodwill shops will often also have dedicated CD shelving, made of wood or metal, specially designed to fit rows of jewel cases.
About those jewel cases: If they’re damaged or missing pieces, they don’t do as good a job protecting the CDs or artwork inside from spills or scratches. Go the extra step and invest in replacements for cracked jewel cases or damaged interior spindle trays.
If you listen on the move and like to take your discs in the car, a classic CD wallet or CD book is your best solution. You load your disks into the wallet’s plastic pouches and store the jewel case and the artwork somewhere safe, either on the shelf or in a box.
The demand for these nostalgic book-style cases has only increased over the years. “We stocked some recently,” says Steven Alejandro, who has been the general manager at Hogwild Records for over 30 years. “And then the supplier ran out, and now they don’t have any more to sell.”
If you’re lucky to find a case, or you’ve repurposed your parents’ old CD wallets, remember not to leave the case in a hot car, in the sun, or anywhere near a heat source for an extended time.
Keep Your CDs and CD Players Clean
The best way to maintain a physical media collection is to keep everything clean. Found your dream player at a garage sale? Chances are it hasn’t been properly maintained in 20 years. CD players do need to be cleaned every once in a while to ensure the laser lens is free of any debris or fingerprints that can impact playback and audio quality.
On the actual disc, fingerprints, dust, and anything else stuck to the bottom surface can cause audible skips during playback. It's best to use a microfiber cloth and, if necessary, a cleaning solution for extremely dirty CDs. Don’t wipe the disc in a circular motion. Always wipe the disc from the center outward, starting at the hole and pulling the cloth gently toward the outer edge of the disc.
Final Tip
Enjoy your CDs! Rip the contents to your hard drive if you need to, but they sound great when you just give them a spin. There’s a joy in collecting music, because while online streams may be temporary, the physical media we have will always be something we truly own and the actual definition of on-demand.

Indian kurash player Yash Kumar Chauhan has tested positive for multiple banned substances in a dope sample taken during competition on September 27 in the Asian Games and has been provisionally suspended with immediate effect, the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) announced on Saturday.
The 24-year-old Chauhan’s sample was found to contain at least three banned substances, including metabolites of steroid Metandienone.
Chauhan’s sample was tested by International Testing Agency (ITA), which takes samples and performs results management during the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on behalf of the OCA.
“The ITA, on behalf of the OCA , reports that a sample collected from kurash athlete Yash Kumar Chauhan (IND) has returned an Adverse Analytical Finding for non-specified prohibited substances Metandienone metabolites, GW1516 metabolites, Mephentermine and its metabolite,” the OCA said in a statement on Saturday.
“The athlete has been informed of the case and provisionally suspended with immediate effect until the resolution of the matter in line with the World Anti-Doping Code and the OCA Anti-Doping Rules. This means that the athlete is prevented from competing, training, coaching, or participating in any activity, during (this) Asian Games.”
Metandienone, an oral anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) derived from testosterone, is prohibited at all times (in- and out-of-competition) under the WADA Code and is a non-specified substance.

“Metandienone is a potent anabolic steroid which increases testosterone levels, causing muscle-mass growth, endurance and strength,” the OCA statement said.
GW1516 is also prohibited at all times (in- and out-of-competition) and is a non-specified substance. It is a drug that activates pathways involved in fat metabolism in the body and that improves endurance performance.
Mephentermine is prohibited under the WADA Code as a non-specified stimulant. It is prohibited in-competition and is a non-specified stimulant. It acts on the central nervous system and may increase alertness and reduce fatigue.
Chauhan has the right to challenge the imposition of the provisional suspension before the Court of Arbitration for Sport’s Anti-Doping Division. He also has the right to request the analysis of the B-sample.
The kurash competitions in the Asian Games was held between September 26 and 29.
Chauhan lost to Mirmamadov Shakarmamad of Tajikistan in a round of 16 bout in the 90kg category on September 27.
India won a lone bronze in kurash through Pincky Balhara in the women’s 78kg category.

Wolverine sits comfortably as my favorite Marvel hero right beside Spider-Man. I grew up with Hugh Jackman’s portrayal of Wolverine in the X-Men movies, along with Steve Blum and Cal Dodd’s masterful interpretation of the ol’ canucklehead across various Marvel media.
So, when Insomniac announced Marvel’s Wolverine back in September 2021 at the PlayStation Showcase, I was pumped. After countless hours swinging through the Marvel’s Spider-Man series with both Peter and Miles, I was eager to see their take on Logan, since he’s an incredibly complex character.
I expected Insomniac to take a similar approach to the 2009 X-Men Origins: Wolverine tie-in game with the combat. The story was messy, sure, but the combat was visceral, brutal, and perfectly showcased Wolverine’s violent power fantasy, which is exactly why I think it’s still an enjoyable game.
After spending 25 hours with it, I can confirm that Marvel’s Wolverine is a solid action game in my review. It’s nowhere near as bad as some of the criticism would have you believe, but it’s also far from the ultimate Wolverine game that many, including me, were hoping for. It has plenty going for it, but significant flaws keep it from reaching the heights of Insomniac’s Spider-Man series.
Wolverine’s Origin Gets More Complicated than It Needs to Be
Insomniac takes some big creative swings with the story in Marvel’s Wolverine, and not all of it lands. On the surface, Logan is dealing with amnesia, and he needs help to regain his memories and remember who he was before he became a weapon, while doing what he does best, a.k.a. tearing enemies to shreds.
You have your usual Marvel MacGuffin, the Helix Engine, a device capable of activating dormant mutants. Nathaniel Essex wants the engine to grow the mutant population and build a better future for his own kind.
Of course, in the middle of it all, there’s Bolivar Trask, an anti-mutant figurehead, who kidnaps mutants with the Reavers, deploys Sentinels, and delivers the usual “the world isn’t big enough for the both of us” brand of villainy.
That’s what the first act of Marvel’s Wolverine deals with. In the second act, you start to uncover Logan’s true origins, and it’s a far cry from Barry Windsor-Smith’s Weapon X comic, changing how Wolverine becomes the killing machine. The Helix Engine becomes priority number one for endgame villains like Lady Deathstrike and Essex.
However, the final act takes a nosedive, turning a solo Wolverine outing into an X-Men setup game. I’ll slice into spoilers now: Insomniac draws inspiration from comic writer Chris Claremont’s unused idea, bringing popular X-Men villain Apocalypse into the fray and making him the mastermind behind Logan’s adamantium-infused origin.
It’s incredibly bold, but doesn’t quite land for a Wolverine-focused game. The writing falls flat when the game introduces these larger-than-life elements. By the end, the story is revealed to be built on a centuries-long conflict between the Phoenix Force, Jean’s ultimate avatar, and Apocalypse’s Horseman of Death, which in this case is Wolverine.
It’s anything but grounded, but rich in spectacle, which, to me, doesn’t quite fit for an introductory Wolverine story. As the narrative grows ambitious, it loses much of the personal charm and intimacy that made the first act so compelling.
The balance between Logan’s personal stakes and the overarching X-Men story never quite comes together. But thanks to incredible performances from Liam McIntyre, Krizia Bajos, and Troy Baker, I remained hooked until the very end, even as I found myself conflicted by some of Insomniac’s narrative choices.
Had Insomniac taken a more grounded route like Larry Hama’s Wolverine stories in Madripoor, the story might have been better executed. I’m a sucker for character studies and less interested in a ‘jingling keys’ approach or endless fan service, so I was more invested in Logan’s personal journey before the bombastic spectacle took over.
However, I did appreciate that Insomniac didn’t play it safe with the story, even if its ambitious direction doesn’t always land.
Combat Is Where the Ol’ Canucklehead Gets Mean
What Insomniac misses with the story of Marvel’s Wolverine, they make up for in the combat. The combat system is ridiculously good, and very reminiscent of the X-Men Origins: Wolverine game. It’s brutal, fluid, responsive, and gives you multiple ways to slice through enemies.
The primary attacks with Square and Triangle start a combo, while parrying staggers enemies to perform a satisfying Barrage, which you can use to build your Rage Tier or restore health, depending on the skills you have unlocked.
The Skill Tree, while not as extensive, still works wonders in combat, giving you opportunities to implement many Special Techniques. “Overwhelm” and “Tornado Spin” were by far my favorite Special Techniques, offering a quick way to isolate enemies while controlling entire crowds with adamantium-coated swirls.
The most enjoyable part of Wolverine’s combat is building up to Rage Tier 3, which bathes the screen in greyscale and lets Logan go completely feral, ripping the hands and legs off Reavers and the Hand with continuous Critical Strikes.
Seeing chunks of Logan get blown off with Insomniac’s new blood technology was genuinely impressive, especially when it feeds directly into his Last Stand ability at Rage Tier 2, allowing him to recover from a fatal blow in exchange for his Rage Tier bars.
Adaptations and passive buffs kept combat fresh, as I built Logan to generate and maintain his Rage mode longer, unlocking AP by completing Nightmare Trials and finding Whisky Bottles in Marvel’s Wolverine.
Playing on “The Best There Is” difficulty is no joke, especially when multiple enemies or mini-bosses gang up on you. But it also pushes the combat beyond run-of-the-mill button mashing, forcing you to use every shiny trick in Wolverine’s adamantium arsenal.
Madripoor and Japan Are Gorgeous Wastes of Space
Every location in Marvel’s Wolverine is stunning, from Madripoor to Japan and Canada. The problem is that these beautiful hubs feel strangely hollow when there’s so little opportunity to explore them. You’re largely confined to dense streets and the occasional rooftop, following a one-note linear path through environments that feel like they were built to be explored more freely.
For the majority of my playthrough, I stopped to appreciate the world and capture clicks with Insomniac’s vastly updated Photo Mode, which only made me more frustrated that these locations weren’t explorable.
I’m not saying they should be as open as New York in the Marvel’s Spider-Man series. But given how Logan can jump, slide, and launch from one building to another, these hubs feel criminally wasted, with little to discover beyond Material Crates and Whisky Bottles.
This brings me to another problem with the Marvel’s Wolverine world design: Logan’s smooth traversal is extremely underutilized. You have Launch Points throughout Madripoor and Japan, yet you can’t use them because you have to stick to a one-note world design. Moreover, Logan can only climb certain surfaces with his claws, which makes the “exploration” all the more limited.
Sliding across rooftops, leaping from building to building via Launch Points, and using ziplines to traverse densely packed areas are some of Wolverine’s most enjoyable movement mechanics. But invisible walls and level boundaries will get in your way too often.
Just Follow the White Paint, Bub
The most controversial element of Marvel’s Wolverine is how far it takes handholding players with white cloth/paint. What makes it even more egregious is that it’s a linear game with only a handful of exploration opportunities, which makes the white markers stick out like a sore thumb. Meanwhile, the blue scent trail isn’t nearly as bad.
Sections with white paint/cloth markings where there’s nowhere to go but forward, especially during the traversal Nightmare Challenges, feel like Insomniac is afraid to let players off the hook. There’s a fine line between helpful guidance and excessive handholding, and Insomniac paints that line with white markings so you don’t lose track.
On the other hand, the blue scent trails or the Marvel’s Wolverine “fart gas trail” represent Logan’s feral senses, guiding him to characters during specific story sections or collectibles such as Whisky Bottles.
It’s still handholding, yes, but they aren’t as intrusive as the white paint/cloth markers, and only appear in a handful of sections. Thankfully, Insomniac reduced their opacity in a quick hotfix, and they now look the way they should have from launch.
Additionally, Marvel’s Wolverine is rated 18, so it’s targeted towards adults and mature audiences. Yet, the handholding made me feel like I wouldn’t know where to go without it. I’d have much preferred they remove the white markings and relegated Logan’s senses to R3 on the controller.
Despite everything, the blue scent trails didn’t bother me as much as the white cloth/paint, since it only appears when Logan’s picking up someone’s scent or a collectible is nearby. It’s a linear experience, yet the game feels the need to guide you every step of the way.
Liam McIntyre Carries Wolverine with a Standout Performance
Despite all the game’s faults, Liam McIntyre’s performance as Wolverine is nothing short of spectacular. Logan is an inherently complex character, balancing a deeply human vulnerability with the violence and rage that have defined him for decades, making him no easy character to portray.
McIntyre handles that duality remarkably well, delivering a nuanced performance that captures Logan’s humanity and his yearning for belonging without ever losing sight of the monster lurking beneath the surface.
Even though I’m not a fan of Logan and Jean as a couple (I’m more of a Logan and Mariko shipper), McIntyre and Bajos have incredible chemistry from the moment they meet, making their relationship worth rooting for.
Not much needs to be said about Troy Baker’s performance as Mister Sinister; he’s incredible as always. However, Brett Gipson’s portrayal of Sabretooth surprised me. He’s so compelling, even while tearing Logan apart, that I’m excited to see him return in a Wolverine sequel, if there is one, or even the X-Men game.
For all my qualms with the game, its performances remain a standout, with Liam McIntyre’s portrayal of Wolverine ranking alongside Yuri Lowenthal’s iconic performance as Peter Parker in Insomniac’s Spider-Man series.
Performance: An Adamantium-Smooth Frame Rate on My Base PS5
Marvel’s Wolverine is easily Insomniac’s best-looking and best-performing game yet, and it runs like a mutant on a mission. Across my 22-hour playthrough on the base PS5 (disc edition), the game held a steady 60fps in its default “Performance” mode, complete with ray-traced reflections throughout all four unique areas.
The game looks sharp, even on my 1080p TV, and I could see every pore on Logan’s face during close-up shots. Thanks to the PS5’s SSD, getting back into the bloody action took no longer than 2 seconds. Mission replays and Nightmare Challenges loaded as quickly as Wolverine unsheathes his claws, so the performance definitely doesn’t end up with the game’s woes.
However, I did run into one hilarious bug where Logan glitched out of the map while I opened Photo Mode to capture a shot of the Animated Suit. I’d hardly call it a performance issue. The blood and gore looked great on the base PS5, and I hope Insomniac brings the game’s detailed suit damage to Marvel’s Spider-Man 3.
Verdict: Bub, Even Your Healing Factor Can’t Fix This One
Marvel’s Wolverine isn’t a bad egg in Insomniac’s basket full of good eggs. It’s more of a cracked one. The developers still cooked a dish with it, but it fails to be as delicious as their previous web-filled offerings. The combat feels fluid and crunchy, Liam McIntyre and Krizia Bajos deliver phenomenal performances as Logan and Jean, the set pieces dazzle, and the game looks stunning on a base PS5.
However, the ambitious scale of the story, which is clearly a setup for the X-Men game, limited exploration opportunities within the gorgeous locations, and the egregious use of white paint and cloth, despite the mission design being linear, bog it down significantly. I had a good time with it, and I reckon most will, but maybe not at the premium $70 price point.
If you’re a fan of the character and want a brutal, visceral 15–20-hour standard action experience with excellent combat that feels surprisingly reminiscent of 2000s PC gaming, Marvel’s Wolverine will be right up your alley.
But if you’re looking for something that builds upon what Insomniac accomplished with Spider-Man, you might want to slice this one off your wishlist for now and wait for a sale. Wolverine has the adamantium skeleton of an incredible game; however, what we got is ultimately just “good”.

A court in Shopian on Tuesday sentenced a man to life imprisonment for the murder of a person in 2019, observing that the case did not fall within the “rarest of rare” category warranting the death penalty.
Principal Sessions Judge Shopian Mehmood Ahmed Chowdhary awarded life imprisonment and a fine of Rs 1 lakh to Bilal Ahmad Seh, who was convicted under Section 302 of the Ranbir Penal Code (RPC).
The court said the convict had been in custody since his arrest on April 21, 2019, and had spent nearly seven years in custody during the trial.
The case, registered as FIR No. 19/2019 at Police Station Zainapora, initially involved charges under Sections 302, 307, 147, 148, 506, 109, 341 and 34 of the RPC.
While deciding the quantum of sentence, the court considered the mitigating and aggravating circumstances and referred to the Supreme Court’s guidelines on awarding the death penalty.
The court noted that the case was based on four eyewitnesses as well as circumstantial evidence. It also took into account that the convict was a first-time offender, was a farmer by profession and had been supporting his family.
The court observed that there were no aggravating circumstances of such an exceptional nature as to warrant capital punishment.
“Life imprisonment is the appropriate punishment to be awarded to the convict for commission of murder of the deceased,” the court said.
The court also noted that other accused named in the case, including the convict’s brother and two sisters, had been acquitted, while proceedings against another accused had abated following his death. A juvenile accused in the case is facing separate proceedings before the Juvenile Justice Board, according to the case record.
Since the sentence is one of life imprisonment, the court directed that the case file and judgment be submitted to the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh for confirmation of the sentence as required under law.
The convict was directed to be sent to Special Jail Pulwama to undergo the sentence. The court also informed him of his right to appeal against the judgment and sentence before the High Court within 15 days.

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.
Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.
In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.
Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

City of Saskatoon cancels in-person count of unsheltered people over safety concerns
Concerns are 'related to protest activity,' city says
The City of Saskatoon says it won't fully conduct its in-person point-in-time count of people experiencing homelessness this year.
The count was supposed to happen Tuesday, with about 250 trained volunteers attempting to quantify the number of people in the city who don't have homes.
In a Friday news release, the city said the decision to cancel the in-person count was made due to "safety concerns related to potential protest activity which may affect the safety of volunteers, staff and community partners participating in the count."
The city said safety concerns have been heightened in recent weeks.
The fire department had warned that it planned to remove a west-side encampment occupied by more than 100 people, but the removal was paused after protests from those living there and the people who support them.
“If they want to say that, it’s like a kick in the head,” said David Fineday, an advocate who lives in the encampment.
“It’s giving these people a negative message … It’s not a protest, we’re not marching anywhere, we’re standing up here for our rights.”
Advocates filed an application for a court injunction to stop the fire department from removing part of the encampment, but that was rejected by a judge.
“The safety of volunteers, community partners, staff and people experiencing homelessness must come first,” Lesley Anderson, the city's director of planning and development, said in Friday's news release.
“We are grateful to everyone who was prepared to take part in this year’s Point-in-Time Count. Their continued commitment helps Saskatoon better understand homelessness and advocate for the coordinated supports our community needs.”
The release said the city will work with the fire department to estimate the number of people living in Saskatoon's various encampments and will also count the number of people staying in emergency shelters, transitional housing and other systems.
“Why are they studying us?” Fineday asked. “Maybe instead of doing a PiT count and spending a quarter of Saskatoon’s budget on the police, maybe they should spend that much on affordable housing.”
The primary limitation to the change of plan is that the 2026 count will not include information collected directly from unsheltered people.
The city's release said a more comprehensive version of the point-in-time count, including a full enumeration and survey, is already planned for 2027.
The 2025 count identified 1,931 homeless people in Saskatoon.

CJP’s Dipke warns of ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ at Mumbai protest, demands CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke demanded CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation at a Mumbai protest, alleging mass voter-roll deletions under the SIR process.
Targeting the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter-roll irregularities, Cockroach Janata Party founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday demanded Kumar’s resignation and warned of a “Jantar Mantar 2.0” agitation, followed by a demand for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s resignation if the CEC did not step down.
Addressing a gathering at Shivaji Park in Mumbai, Dipke said democracy is under threat as voter names have been removed from electoral rolls across India through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process initiated after the 2024 Lok Sabha elections.
“This represents roughly 13–14% of the total electorate, a figure large enough to sway election outcomes given that the vote-share gap between the NDA and opposition in 2024 was only about 2%. In Delhi, 40,000 votes were allegedly deleted from Arvind Kejriwal’s constituency, where Kejriwal lost by a narrow margin of 4,000–5,000 votes. In Tamil Nadu, 1 lakh votes were deleted, with DMK leader M.K. Stalin losing by just 10,000 votes. In West Bengal, 50,000 votes were deleted, and Mamata Banerjee’s party lost by 15,000 votes,” he said.
Deep Dive
However, HT’s analysis of SIR deletions by constituency has shown no correlation with the outcome, and some of the deletions have been caused by death and migration. But the exclusion of millions of voters from draft rolls — Delhi saw a 32.8% decline from the 14,510,299 names on the rolls in June 2026 — has resulted in public angst and anxiety.
Revelations by The Indian Express last month that two election commissioners disagreed with some of the decisions, and that the central database of electors wasn’t accessible to on-ground officers tasked with adding and deleting names, have caused a stir. The Election Commission has since clarified that all decisions have been unanimous, based on the majority, and also modified the SIR process to reduce the inconvenience to voters.

Actor Shabana Azmi, music director Dadlani and Mahatma Gandhi’s great-grandson Tushar Gandhi joined the protest in Mumbai, which saw a huge crowd and support from the youth.
Shiv Sena-UBT extended its support as the party’s local MLA Sawant joined the CJP team on the dais.
Dipke questioned why similar deletions did not appear to affect BJP strongholds, alleging selective targeting of opposition-led states.
He accused the BJP dispensation of orchestrating a strategy to divide voters along religious lines, stating that Hindu-Muslim politics will not work anymore and urging the younger generation and Gen-Z to think beyond religion.
Dipke also criticised the 2022–2024 wave of MLA and MP defections, alleging that 111 MLAs and 99 MPs switched parties in what he described as an “IPL-style auction” where legislators were bought and sold. He mocked the loyalty shift, saying, “It’s not love for Modi, but the legislators shifted because of the threat.”
Paying tribute to Mahatma Gandhi, Dipke launched a sharp attack on the BJP and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, saying Mahatma Gandhi, B R Ambedkar and Jawaharlal Nehru were the “soul, backbone and mind” of India and Modi cannot match their sacrifice, hard work and merit.
He said Gandhi had been persecuted less by the British than the people are being harassed by the BJP-led government. He also alleged that those subscribing to the ideology of Nathuram Godse were seeking to diminish Gandhi’s legacy. “Gandhi is the soul of India, Ambedkar the backbone and Nehru the mind,” Dipke said.
Referring to India’s first general elections, Dipke said Ambedkar and Nehru had helped give voting rights to people at a time when many were not even familiar with concepts such as fundamental rights, elections, the Lok Sabha and state assemblies. He said that this was in contrast to the present situation, alleging that people were being repeatedly made to stand in queues — during demonetisation, the Covid-19 pandemic and now for voter registration.
Eknath Shinde and Maharashtra politics
Dipke called the Shiv Sena headed by deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde a “shell company” of the BJP and alleged that regional forces are being systematically weakened. “In the 2024 elections, the BJP did not perform as strongly in Maharashtra, yet it still secured seats through the addition of 40 lakh votes. The central government should not repeat the July 20, 2026 mistake when Amit Shah’s lathi-charge on protesters at Jantar Mantar sparked nationwide outrage,” he said.
Lauding Mumbai police for peacefully handling the demonstrations, he slammed Delhi police over the treatment it gave to CJP supporters during the protest over NEET. He also dared chief minister Devendra Fadnavis — who had warned of police action on protesters — to arrest them. “You said we would be put behind the bars for three days. We are ready to even for three months,” he added.
