Nestle's dairy whitener collected from top Delhi hotel found to be 'unsafe', FSSAI bans sale
The sample was declared as “substandard” under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India banned the sale of Nestle's “Low Fat Dairy Whitener” after the sample of the product taken from a top Delhi hotel was declared to be “unsafe” and “substandard”. A notice was then issued to the food business operator (FBO), in this case Nestle, for non-compliance.
"A sample of Nestle "Low Fat Dairy Whitener" collected from M/s Bharat Hotels Ltd. (The Lalit), New Delhi, has been declared unsafe and substandard by Food Analyst reports under the FSS Act, 2006," the FSSAI said in a post on X.
“Directives have been issued to immediately prohibit the sale of this product,” the food safety regulator added. Responding to the FSSAI ban, Nestle maintained that the dairy whitener was “safe to consume”, adding that the product was in compliance for added phosphorus “as per prescribed limits”, ANI news agency reported.
Also Read | No FSSAI licence: Food unit shut down in Manimajra, challan issued
What did the FSSAI findings reveal?
According to the FSSAI, a sample of Nestle's “Low Fat Dairy Whitener” was drawn from the premises of The Lalit in Connaught Place in Delhi. The sample was sent for testing, following which the Food Analyst's laboratory report found the product to be “substandard” and “unsafe”, indicating non-compliance under the FSS Act, 2006.
A copy of the laboratory analysis report was provided to the food business operator (FBO) for reference and necessary action, FSSAI stated, adding that a notice was also issued to Nestle in connection with the matter.
FSSAI said that Nestle had been provided an opportunity to appeal against the Food Analyst's report under the FSS Act, 2006, within the prescribed time period. Nestle was further directed to immediately prohibit the sale of the dairy whitener, FSSAI stated.
Also Read | Delhi high court junks FSSAI order directing Red Bull to discontinue ‘energy drink’ tag
What was Nestle's response?
A spokesperson for Nestle India said the product was safe to consume and that it was compliant will all applicable regulatory requirements.
“Phosphorus is a nutrient that occurs naturally in milk and is therefore present in all milk-based products. FSSAI lab reports reflect total phosphorus against the additive limit, without accounting for the substantial natural phosphorus contribution from milk-based ingredients,” ANI cited the spokesperson as saying.
“Our product is in full compliance for added phosphorus as per prescribed limits under FSSR, including for as consumed basis. We have been in continuous engagement with the authorities as per due process established under law and have shared data across other same/similar milk-based products in the category to reflect presence of naturally occurring phosphorous,” Nestle added.
Nestle products under FSSAI scanner
This is not the first time Nestle has found itself in the crosshairs of the food safety regulator. Last month, Nestle India Ltd faced legal action after a sample of its baby food was found by the FSSAI to have violated quality standards. Apart from this, two other infant nutrition products of the firm were reportedly promoted in contravention of the rules for such products.
FSSAI said a sample of follow-up formula manufactured by the company was found to be substandard with respect to biotin content during laboratory analysis. “The sample was subsequently referred for re-analysis, and the referral laboratory also found the sample non-confirming with respect to the prescribed Biotin requirement under the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020,” the food safety regulator said.
Additionally, FSSAI said it had found issues with the promotion of two other baby food products– NAN Excella Pro Stage 1 and Lactogen Pro 1. Nestle had then said its products were “fully compliant with all the applicable regulations” and that it would continue to work closely with FSSAI.

I want this episode to be about the relationship between cricketers and their gurus. You know, they call them gurus, mentors, coaches or whatever. I have always been fascinated by the bond between a cricketer and the person who shaped him in his early years.
We all know the reverence Sachin Tendulkar has for Ramakant Achrekar, and what Achrekar did for him. Pravin Amre, too, came through the same system and treats him like a father figure. I have personally seen, up close, how cricketers continue to respect the coaches who were with them from childhood, from those formative days when they were still learning the game and, in many ways, learning life.
Tarak Sinha, known to his students as Ustad Ji, had so many such boys. I remember how Ashish Nehra took care of the playing field at the Sri Venkateshwara College. He would play at the Sonnet Club and cover the club’s expenses, too. I remember he came back from Zimbabwe in 2001 and gave his entire tour fee to Sonnet Cricket Club to develop the field at Venkateshwara College.
Nehra’s `Guru Dakshina’ is unforgettable. Sinha was known for being punctual on the ground. So one day, when he didn’t turn up, Nehra wondered why Ustadji wasn’t there. He was told that Ustadji was house-hunting because he had been served a notice by the landlord to vacate. Nehra felt very bad. Within a week, he gifted a house to Sinha. I remember the occasion because the house was close to mine. I went to the housewarming ceremony Nehra had organised. It was a very private affair.
Gurcharan sir, an exceptional man, has made life beautiful for an incredibly large number of people. He shaped the careers of international players such as Kirti Azad, Kartik Murali, Gursharan Singh, Maninder Singh, Ajay Jadeja, and Rahul Sanghvi. That is quite a roll-call. Some went on to have long careers in domestic cricket, but all of them carried something of Gurcharan sir with them. Among them, Ajay Jadeja was particularly close to him, and he remains so.
Gurcharan sir, honoured with the Padma Shri and the Dronacharya Award by the Government, devoted his life to cricket. He played for Patiala, Southern Punjab and Railways, and was very close to Lala Amarnath. After finishing his playing career in 1968, he did a coaching course at the National Institute of Sports (NIS) and was posted at the National Stadium in Delhi. He also worked at the Pace Academy that the BCCI had set up in Gwalior and served as the national coach for two years. He declined offers to travel as it would mean being away from the National Stadium for a certain period. That was one of the big sacrifices he made. He didn’t travel, and he missed family functions because he wanted to be there for the nets at the National Stadium.
Last week, Jadeja was in Delhi on a personal visit, and we went to meet Gurcharan sir at his academy. It was a wonderful experience simply watching the two of them together. We saw some wonderful things. Every evening, Gurcharan sir insists on coming to the academy from his home, which is about six to eight kilometres away. His son brings him to the academy every day to watch the nets and the little children play. Gurcharan sir is 92 now. He is in a wheelchair and is unable to speak, but he can still observe and comprehend what is happening around him. Jadeja, of course, was full of banter. If you sit with Jadeja, it is just banter. He can regale you with anecdotes for 24 hours, if you let him. But beneath all that banter is this extraordinary devotion to Gurcharan sir. Jadeja was not a regular cricketer to begin with. In fact, the story of how the two first met is quite amusing.
There was a match that Members of Parliament played at the National Stadium every year. They would also go to Gwalior to play when Madhavrao Scindia hosted them. On one such occasion, Jadeja’s father, Daulatsinhji Jadeja, a three-time Member of Parliament from Jamnagar, was also playing. They were travelling to Gwalior, and Jadeja tagged along.
That was when he first saw Gurcharan sir and noticed the respect he commanded from all those Members of Parliament. Jadeja was impressed by him too. His father then complained to Gurcharan sir, “This boy doesn’t go to school. He runs away. What do I do?” Gurcharan sir said, “Let me see what I can do. I’ll tackle it.” He then went up to Jadeja and told him, “Next time you run away from school, come to me. Jadeja says, “Sir was the first person who actually encouraged me to bunk school and come to him.” That was how the association began, at the National Stadium in New Delhi, very close to India Gate. It was an iconic place, and Gurcharan sir went on to give so many cricketers to the country.
I would say Jadeja was one of his favourites for many reasons. He was very gifted, very talented. You should have seen the happiness on Gurcharan sir’s face when Jadeja came to meet him after some time. At the same time, Jadeja was deeply pained to see his condition. He said, “Oh my God, I just can’t imagine Gurcharan sir not standing on the field. That was the sir I knew. He was always the first person to come to the National Stadium and the last to leave. And he spent an enormous amount of time with the ground staff. If he wasn’t with the players, he was with them.”
Gurcharan sir’s philosophy was simple: Cricket is played for cricketers. Yes, they are the stars, but, according to him, the real stars were the groundskeepers who prepared the fields and the pitches. Gurcharan sir understood their work because he worked alongside them.
I have also grown up as a journalist, going to the National Stadium, which was two kilometres from where I lived. In my early days, I would go there three or four times a week in the evening and watch the players practise. That is where I learnt cricket because Gurcharan sir was always there to explain things to me. And when I think about the relationship between a great player and his guru, I am reminded of another wonderful example: Kapil Dev and Desh Prem Azad.
Kapil never forgot the man who shaped him. He promoted and respected his coach, Desh Prem Azad, throughout his career. That, to me, is what makes these relationships so special. You may become a world-class cricketer, you may become a national hero, but somewhere in your memory there is still that first coach who saw something in you before the rest of the world did. That is what a guru can mean to a cricketer.
Jadeja recalled an incident from how he got to play in the Ranji Trophy. He was practising at the National Stadium and had played some junior cricket for Delhi when Kapil suddenly came onto the ground and requested Gurcharan sir to allow the youngster to travel with him. Jadeja, who had represented Delhi in junior cricket, had been selected to play Ranji Trophy for Haryana. Kapil had come to take him with the team that was leaving for Srinagar in a few days (in October 1988). Jadeja always felt this happened because he was getting the right cricket education from Gurcharan sir, who had such a reputation that Kapil needed very little convincing that this boy was ready to play in the Ranji Trophy after training with him.
What I loved most was the way his students cared for him. Jadeja and I were there for almost three hours, and he kept telling me that Gurcharan sir had not just taught him cricket. He had taught him life. “He taught us to be good human beings, how to be helpful, how to make the most of things and how to face challenges,” Jadeja recalled from one of his tours to England with Gurcharan sir. “He would make the boys do all the work. If we stayed in a Gurdwara, it was not simply to save money. It was to inculcate camaraderie among the players and to teach them that all times would not be luxurious. You had to make certain adjustments in life. You might be sleeping on cosy beds one day and on the floor the next. You might have to do the dishes or cook your own food too. We learnt all this because of Gurcharan sir,” Jadeja told me. And that was the other side of Gurcharan sir. He wasn’t just teaching cricket. He was preparing these boys for life.
Gurcharan sir was also known for helping them find jobs and ensuring they could look after their families. There is one incident, narrated by Gurcharan sir’s son Amrinder, which shows exactly what that meant. “We were practising at the National Stadium when dad saw Ajay Sharma standing there. He had come to meet a player. My dad asked him if he would like to take up a job. Sharma grabbed the chance. Dad sent him to Punjab Stores, a shop in Khan Market, to get an application typed. Ajay returned with the application, and Dad personally took it to a senior office in Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC). The next day Ajay got the appointment letter,” recalled Amrinder. Sharma retired from CWC as a Deputy General Manager.
See how this job was created. It was unbelievable. I must mention here that Sharma played for Sonnet Club, which had a bitter rivalry with the NIS team. When you look at cricket today, everything is so professional and, more importantly, so protected. You can’t imagine a coach doing all this now. I am sure they still do it, but nobody has the time because of the volume of cricket being played. For many cricketers now, of course, cricket is a full-time profession. It wasn’t back then. They had to take care of their families because cricket wasn’t getting them enough money.
Jadeja says he learnt all the intricacies of the game from him simply by listening. They would play league matches, and sir would be there, giving them first-hand advice on what to do. Those, Jadeja says, were priceless insights from a man who had seen cricket and life.
The coaches at Gurcharan sir’s Academy are not reputed names. They have all completed Level 2 with the BCCI, and he has given them jobs so they can dedicate themselves to training young people. And the talent was wonderful. There were two children, Yuvaan Shukla and Atharv Pande, both not even seven years old. Jadeja fell in love with their skills. One was bowling left-arm, tossing the ball, and the other was playing some remarkable shots. I am sure we are going to hear about these kids in the junior circuit.
As we drove back from the academy, Jadeja said something that, for me, summed up the whole relationship. “If I get a life again, if I have to be born again, I would love to have the same life, where I become a student of sir and learn the best things of cricket, the best things of life.”

India, which has recorded the maximum road deaths since such global data compilation started, registered 1.74 lakh such fatalities in 2023, and this was a little over 14% of the 12.2 lakh people who lost their lives in road crashes across the world.
NEW DELHI: ‘Road injuries’ was the eighth leading cause of deaths among males in India in 2023, and in the case of females, ‘falls’ was the eighth biggest cause of deaths, as per the latest WHO Global Health Estimates (GHE). Overall, road traffic injuries ranked the 10th leading cause of death for both males and females in India, while fatalities due to falls ranked 9th.India, which has recorded the maximum road deaths since such global data compilation started, registered 1.74 lakh such fatalities in 2023, and this was a little over 14% of the 12.2 lakh people who lost their lives in road crashes across the world. This has only increased in the past two years to reach 1.83 lakh in 2025. The figures underline the continuing scale of the road safety challenge in the country, where road crashes claim 500 lives daily.Falls in India claimed 25,150 lives, as per the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data, which was around 3% of the total 8.42 lakh lives lost in such incidents. Most of the deaths due to road crashes and falls are preventable. The data also highlights the significant burden of injuries that can result in loss of life and have wider social and economic consequences for families.
As per the WHO report, globally, road traffic injuries were the 8th biggest cause of death in low-income countries and the 10th biggest in middle-income countries. Globally, it was ranked 11th, indicating that the high number of such deaths not only has a huge burden on low- and middle-income countries but also a major concern for the global community, despite many developed nations having been successful in bringing down fatalities due to road crashes.
The differences in rankings across income groups also reflect the varying burden of road injuries across countries and regions.Road safety experts have maintained that low- and middle-income countries need to find solutions to this “avoidable disaster” taking into account the local conditions, including heterogeneous road users and poorly sensitised authorities about the concept of safety of all users. They said addressing the problem would require greater attention to the safety needs of different categories of road users and a stronger focus on preventing crashes and reducing their consequences.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday lauded the rhino conservation efforts in the country and said the Project Rhino has been initiated for financial and technical support to the range states for protection, habitat management, and understanding population dynamics of the endangered species.
On the occasion of World Rhino Day, Modi said the country celebrates the magnificent greater one-horned rhinoceros and lauds all those at the forefront of its protection.
“Assam now holds nearly 80 per cent of the world’s rhino population and Kaziranga’s efforts to end rhino poaching have been extensively appreciated,” he said in a post on ‘X’.
The prime minister said on one hand, rhinos have either returned or are well protected in parts of Bihar and West Bengal, on the other hand, success of reintroduction of rhinos in Dudhwa (Uttar Pradesh) is creating history.
“This shows the sustained commitment of our people towards animal protection and active wildlife management in the range states,” he said.
Taking species conservation in the country forward, Modi said he was happy to share that Project Rhino has been initiated for financial and technical support to the range states for protection, habitat management, genetic improvement and understanding population dynamics.
World Rhino Day is a day of awareness for all five rhino species and the work being done to save them. Since 2011, World Rhino Day has been celebrated internationally on September 22 by rhino experts and advocates around the world.
The day is especially important to raise awareness of the plight of rhinos because they are regularly poached for their horns which are sold illegally and used in traditional medicine — despite no scientific proof that these remedies work.

Tokyo consumer inflation was 2.7% in September, breaking 2% for the first time since December 2025, as the price of bento lunches jumped 28.1% year over year.
Consumer prices excluding fresh food — known as core inflation — also rose 2.7%, compared with a 2.4% median forecast published by Reuters. The figure was 1.8% in August.
The high reading could make a rate increase by the Bank of Japan more likely.
Some of the increase was the result of the ending of government support measures. Tokyo suspended the basic water fee for customers over the summer. The fee returned to utility bills in August or September, depending on the customer’s billing cycle.
Water utility prices increased 65.6% in September year on year.
The Tokyo consumer price index, which covers Tokyo’s 23 wards, is seen as a leading indicator for nationwide price trends. Japan’s nationwide CPI will be released in late October.
The BOJ has grown increasingly vigilant against inflation overshooting its 2% core inflation target.
BOJ Gov. Kazuo Ueda said last month that the bank’s job was to encourage prices upward in the past when Japan was struggling with deflation. But the policy focus now is to keep inflation anchored at 2%.
“In that sense, we believe that we have entered a new phase in policy management,” Ueda said.
Market expectations for a BOJ’s rate increase in December stood at 82% as of Friday morning unchanged from Thursday afternoon, according to data from Totan ICAP.
The yen was trading at ¥157.8 to the dollar on Friday afternoon, just slightly stronger than just before the CPI announcement in the morning.
The central bank is scheduled to hold a two-day policy meeting on Oct. 29 and 30.
Investors see little chance of back-to-back interest rate increases, with the market pricing in just a 17% probability of the central bank making a move at the meeting this month.
The BOJ raised its policy rate — the uncollateralized overnight call rate — in September to 1.25% from 1%.
Some analysts believe that the central bank will likely take some time to assess the effect of its latest rate increase.

Manipur govt assures action on ‘No NRC, No Census’ demand, seeks cooperation
JFD is a civil body continuing its movement to fulfil a five-point charter of demands, especially the updation of the NRC
The Manipur government on Saturday assured action on the updation of the National Register of Citizens (NRC), saying the government had acknowledged the memorandum submitted by the Campaign for Just and Fair Delimitation (JFD), and appealed to the organisation to put its September 30 deadline on hold.
JFD is a civil body continuing its movement to fulfil a five-point charter of demands, especially the updation of the NRC with 1951 as the cut-off year to safeguard Manipur’s indigenous population.
Manipur government spokesperson, Sapam Ranjan, made the remarks to the media at his residence in Konthoujam, Imphal West.
He said the government had acknowledged various memorandums submitted by the organisation and taken them seriously, adding that the government was making efforts to turn the demands into action.
One key demand among the five points in the JFD memorandum is “No NRC, No Census”, with the organisation demanding that the Manipur government urge the Central Government to update the NRC using 1951 as the cut-off year.

The government spokesperson said the government would like to continue its efforts to fulfil the demands in the public interest.

He urged the people of Manipur to cooperate with what the government has been doing for Manipur’s betterment and future.
“We are all in the same boat, and we will definitely take every matter with the utmost sincerity,” he said, appealing to the JFD to cooperate with the government and work together for Manipur’s progress.
JFD has been continuing its movement since March 11, 2026, and intensified it into active agitations, bandhs and lockdowns of government institutions starting August 10.

Car drives into large crowd of rugby fans, injuring multiple people in Sydney
Australian officials say a car drove into a large crowd standing on a road to cheer on the Newcastle Knights rugby team north of Sydney, injuring 10 people
NEWCASTLE, Australia -- A vehicle drove into a crowd standing on a road to cheer on the Newcastle Knights rugby team north of Sydney on Saturday, injuring 10 people, including several children, Australian officials said.
Two of the injured — a 5-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man -- were in critical condition, and the other eight were in stable condition at a hospital, according to New South Wales police. Those in stable condition included another 5-year-old girl and a 2-year-old girl.
Police said they arrested the 18-year-old man driving the vehicle and were investigating what happened. They said the crash was not believed to be related to terrorism.

Bruce Baird, a former federal Liberal MP and deputy leader of the party’s New South Wales branch, has died aged 84.
Baird, who also served as the NSW transport minister from 1988 to 1995, is the father of former state premier Mike Baird, the ABC journalist Julia Baird, and the marketing executive Steve Baird.
As a NSW minister, Baird was instrumental in lobbying for the 2000 Olympic Games to be based in Sydney. He then entered federal parliament as the member for Cook.
Baird retired before the 2007 election, when Scott Morrison won the seat and went on to become prime minister.
Morrison said Baird was “a giant, a mentor and a friend who celebrated and lived out his strong Christian faith, loved his family and served his country, his state and our community in the shire”.
“His achievements are significant, most notably the transforming effect he had on our home city of Sydney as the minister for Sydney’s successful Olympic bid. But there are many more.”
NSW Liberal leader, Kellie Sloane, said Baird was “driven by a strong sense of service, conviction, and compassion, earning the trust and respect of people regardless of their political affiliation”.
“Above all, Bruce was a devoted husband to his late wife Judy, and a proud father and grandfather.”
In a statement, a NSW Liberal spokesperson offered its “deepest condolences on behalf of all members to his family at this difficult time”.
Baird was a passionate supporter of refugees and advocated on their behalf throughout his career.
While a Liberal MP, he opposed the Howard government’s mandatory detention of asylum seekers. After leaving office, he became a member of Kevin Rudd’s refugee resettlement advisory council.
In 2010, Baird criticised the reopening of Curtin detention centre in Western Australia to house asylum seekers.
“Don’t confuse treating people badly when they arrive with effective border control mechanisms, they are two different things,” he told the ABC.
“If we rely on treating asylum seekers badly in this country then there is something about us that we need to have a hard look at. I don’t believe that is the Australian way.”
Baird was also a regular feature of Manly’s Bold and Beautiful ocean swimming club. A member of the squad also confirmed his death on Friday.
On Thursday, the club’s organiser, Peter Anthony, wrote to members describing Baird as a “wonderful friend to so many of us”.

Fintech soonicorn Niyo’s parent, Finnew Solutions Pvt Ltd, slashed its consolidated net loss by 58.1% to ₹32.6 Cr in the financial year 2025-26 (FY26) from ₹77.9 Cr in the year ago period. The startup attributed the reduced losses to operational efficiencies, primarily driven by AI-led gains across customer service, operations, marketing and product development. What also helped offset the losses was revenue from operations surging 80.1% to ₹158 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹87.8 Cr in FY25. Including other income of ₹16.2 Cr as well as other gains of ₹4.2 Cr, Niyo’s total income stood at ₹178.5 Cr in the fiscal year ended March 2026. Niyo’s EBITDA loss also narrowed 60% to ₹32 Cr in FY26 from ₹77 Cr in the year before. “We concluded the year with a robust balance sheet, and deeper partnership with our banking partners. This gives us the confidence and flexibility to continue investing in our technology and products. We expect to maintain our growth momentum and work towards becoming EBITDA positive soon,” said Niyo CFO Gourav Kumar. Founded in 2015 by Vinay Bagri and Virender Bisht, Niyo offers digital banking services for international travelers and students. Its offerings include international debit and credit cards, remittances, forex cash, flights, visa assistance, travel insurance, and international eSIMs. The startup’s primary product is a zero forex markup card, which allows users to load Indian Rupees and spend the money in over 180 countries. To enable this, it has forged partnerships with DCB Bank, SBM Bank and Visa. Niyo has raised close to $180 Mn to date and counts Accel, Lightrock, Multiples, Tencent, and Prime Venture Partners among its investors. Overall, Finnew Solutions' gross revenue from sale of services rose 52% to ₹187.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹123.4 Cr in the year ago period. Notably, deducting the ₹29.6 Cr consideration payable to customers from the gross revenue results in the operating revenue. A breakdown of the data revealed that gross revenue from network partner services nearly doubled YoY to ₹132.4 Cr in FY26. This business contributed 71% to the total gross top line in the fiscal under review. Meanwhile, technology-led financial services, the soonicorn’s second-largest segment, grew 6% to ₹46.9 Cr from ₹44.2 Cr in FY25. Services related to handling of foreign currency, travel currency cards and telegraphic (₹2.7 Cr), and other operating services (₹5.6 Cr) are other means where Niyo earned its revenue in FY26. Niyo said that it has been diversifying its revenue streams beyond its core travel offerings, with growing contributions from forex cash, remittances, flights, hotels, experiences, international eSIMs and insurance. The strengthening of the product portfolio, combined with improved customer onboarding and acquisition, has supported growth in both customers and revenue, said Kumar. “As we look ahead, our focus is not just on acquiring more customers, but on building deeper, longer-term relationships with our customers we already serve. With a strong cross-border customer base, we see a significant opportunity to bring more financial and travel products to them and create greater value over time,” added Niyo CFO. To further fuel its growth, Niyo also reiterated that it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire RemitX, the forex and cross-border payments business of listed financial services company Capital India Finance, for ₹11.4 Cr. Breaking Down Niyo’s FY26 Expenses The startup’s total expenditure rose 19.2% to ₹212.7 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹178.4 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Here is a closer look at where Niyo spent the most: Employee Benefit Expenses: Constituting 43.1% of the overall expenses, employee costs stood at ₹91.7 Cr in FY26, up 16.7% from ₹78.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Marketing And Branding: Marketing expenses rose 215.5% to ₹33.4 Cr in the year under review from ₹10.6 Cr in FY25. It constituted 15.7% of the overall costs. Network And Card Fees: Spending under this head rose 72.3% to ₹29.4 Cr, compared to ₹17 Cr.

The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) has modified the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) framework for Delhi-NCR, with changes affecting vehicles, construction activity and the implementation of pollution-control measures. The revised government framework, announced on September 29, 2026, divides GRAP into four stages based on Delhi's air quality. The measures under successive stages are cumulative. This means that a restriction under Stage I will continue under Stage II and so on. Restrictions on BS-III petrol and BS-IV diesel or below-standard light motor vehicles (LMVs) under GRAP Stage III have been extended to Sonipat apart from Gurugram, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Gautam Buddha Nagar. Now vehicles from three Haryana and two Uttar Pradesh districts will be under restrictions. So, here's what the new GRAP framework means for your vehicle if you are from these places. While restrictions under the old rules have been retained, certain new vehicle-related restrictions have been made added. Under the new framework, restrictions on certain inter-city and inter-state buses have been brought under GRAP Stage I, instead of Stage II. Buses from Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and adjoining states, including Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Jammu and Kashmir, will not be permitted to ply in Delhi-NCR unless they are EV, CNG or BS-VI diesel buses, according to the new changes. Another major change is the extension of CAQM's directions on construction and demolition activities to a wider set of areas, including urban, controlled and development areas, industrial areas and zones, and highway corridor zones in NCR states. The CAQM has also removed the earlier exemption for BS-IV and below goods vehicles carrying essential commodities under GRAP Stages III and IV. The revised government document classifies GRAP into four stages: | GRAP stage | Delhi AQI | Category | |---|---|---| | Stage I | 201–300 | Poor | | Stage II | 301–400 | Very Poor | | Stage III | 401–450 | Severe | | Stage IV | Above 450 | Severe+ | According to the framework announced by CAQM, measures under various stages of GRAP can be taken in advance if forecasts indicate that an AQI threshold is likely to be reached. If pollution unexpectedly crosses a threshold because of extreme meteorological or other episodic conditions, the corresponding measures can be imposed immediately. Whether a private car can ply in the region depends on the GRAP stage, fuel type, BS emission standard, vehicle category and location. There is no blanket ban on all private cars throughout Delhi-NCR under the framework. At Stage I, authorities will be ordered to strictly enforce PUC norms for the vehicles. Vehicles flouting the norms or those visibly polluting can be impounded and/or face penalty. During the Stage I framework restrictions on the entry of certain inter-city and inter-state buses into Delhi-NCR, although EV, CNG and BS-VI diesel buses are permitted. The revised framework does not prescribe a blanket ban on private cars under Stage II, instead, it calls for a higher parking fees to discourage private transport and encourages the use of public transport. At this stage, certain vehicles face restrictions. Under Stage III, NCR states and the Delhi government will have to impose strict restrictions on BS-III petrol and BS-IV diesel LMVs (four-wheelers) and lower-standard vehicles. The restriction covers Gurugram, Faridabad and Sonipat districts of Haryana, Ghaziabad and Gautam Buddha Nagar from Uttar Pradesh apart from Delhi. Noida, which falls within Gautam Buddha Nagar district, will also face restrictions in this stage. Stage IV further tightens the restrictions on goods vehicles but does not recommend for the introduction of blanket ban on all private cars. In this stage no heavy goods vehicle (HGV) other than LNG, CNG, electric and BS-VI diesel trucks can enter the national capital. Delhi-registered diesel BS-IV and below HGVs are also prohibited from plying in Delhi. After Stage III of GRAP comes into effect, BS-III petrol LMVs and BS-IV diesel LMVs face restrictions in Delhi and the specified high-vehicle-density NCR districts. Outside-Delhi registered diesel BS-IV and below light goods vehicles are also not permitted to enter Delhi under the Stage III provisions. Yes. The Stage III provision specifically allows persons with disabilities to ply BS-III petrol/BS-IV diesel LMVs where the vehicles have been specifically adapted for their personal use. For heavy goods vehicles under Stage IV, LNG, CNG, electric and BS-VI diesel trucks are exempted from the general restriction on entry into Delhi. Earlier exemption for BS-IV and below goods vehicles carrying essential commodities under Stages III and IV has also been removed. Not automatically, but the revised framework says that under Stage IV, state governments may consider additional emergency measures, including allowing vehicles to run on an odd-even basis according to registration numbers. So, the invocation of Stage IV itself does not mean an odd-even scheme automatically comes into force. Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.
All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, a slightly slimmer form factor, and an updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.
Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.
Accessories for Easier Reading
If you've ever had a long reading session that gives you hand cramps, these accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.
Cases and Covers
Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you're frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren't padded for serious drops, but they are some of the best Kindle cases I've found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs. Also, don't forget that the Kids' editions come with cases, so if you're buying one of those, you won't need a case.
About Those Older Kindles
Amazon doesn't release new Kindles often—the company usually takes a few years between models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor's stock starts to dwindle. It's not that we don't recommend these per se, but I only suggest these if you can find them on sale for the right price. And don't buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.
Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you're paying a fair amount less for the older device.
Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one. With this model, Amazon doubled the storage to 16 gigabytes and upgraded the display to 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution (up from 167 PPI). It's tough to find, and I usually don't see it for less than $75 these days.
Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It's waterproof too. We like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 gigabytes of storage. Don't recommend spending more than $100 if you can find them.
Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It's only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for under $200 on eBay.
Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it's only available secondhand means you'll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, don't spend more than $70 on this one.
Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn't spend more than $110 on this one.
FAQs
Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?
As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon's services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.
The following Kindle devices are impacted:
- Kindle 1st Generation
- Kindle 2nd Generation
- Kindle DX
- Kindle DX Graphite
- Kindle Keyboard (3rd Generation)
- Kindle 4
- Kindle Touch
- Kindle 5
- Kindle Paperwhite 1st Generation
What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?
Have an old Kindle lying around? Are you looking at a used one for sale? If you're trying to figure out what model it is, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.
Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It's best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you'll still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. These models include the Kindle 2nd Generation (International), Kindle DX International, Kindle DX Graphite, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4th Generation, and Kindle 5th Generation.
How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?
If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but there are millions of titles there, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.
If you already pay for a Prime account, you're eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. There are not as many options as with Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you'll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you'll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It's still something, and there are even a few magazines.
If you don't want another monthly subscription and don't want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can't read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:
- Get a library card for your local branch.
- Check your branch's website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.
- Download directly to your Kindle library. They'll automatically be removed when they're due back.
If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books can be loaned.
What Else Can a Kindle Do?
Kindles have helpful features you may want to take advantage of. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.
Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it's not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.
While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type—there's even a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu too.
When a Kindle is connected to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you've pressed. It will also read a book aloud, though it doesn't sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.
Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you've read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.
There's a web browser too if you're connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It's not the best, so I'd reserve it for emergency searches.
How Do You Update a Kindle?
When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when it's connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you're on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it's not on the latest software version, you'll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.
What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?
Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.
Is This a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?
The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, because Amazon often has steep discounts. Amazon has always had sales on some (if not all) of its Kindles on past Amazon Prime Day and similar events, like Amazon Big Deal Days.
You can also wait for other sale events if you're not ready to shop yet. Kindles are often on sale for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which will occur in late November. Other sales often happen from time to time, but these sale events have consistent Kindle deals, so they're a good time to wait for if you want a better price.
Are Kindles Good for Students?
Kindles are great for students, though the model they'll like best will vary on how they use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, get a Kindle Scribe model. These models also have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. You can get some textbooks on a Kindle too, and send library books to them. For students who love to read but don't want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will be best for them.

The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July

President Donald Trump appeared to share the personal phone number of a senator in his push to make daylight saving time permanent.
The president is putting pressure on Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make the move permanent. He urged people to call what appeared to be the personal cellphone number of Cotton, the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate where some Republicans are strongly opposed.
Proponents, including the White House, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.
Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it — and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill's enactment.
"For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it's very easy to do, it only takes one!" Trump wrote on social media, noting that passing the bill would give professional golfers more time on the greens. "So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all," Trump said.
Trump included a phone number with an Arkansas area code.
This is not the first time Trump has released personal information about a senator. While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Trump as "unfit for office" after Trump denigrated the military service of Sen. John McCain of Arizona. Trump then released Graham's personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones. Graham later became a close ally of Trump.
Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own. Saturday afternoon, though he is not the only Republican who opposes it.
"No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," he wrote. "Arkansans don't want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I'll always put Arkansas first."
A 2025 poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of U.S. adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to change clocks twice a year, while 47% are opposed and 40% are neutral.
Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill four years ago to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.
Trump’s Truth Social post in full:

See letter from Brian Rolapp, CEO of the PGA TOUR below. 65% PLUS want more sun in the afternoon, Daylight Saving Time (The way it is now!), but 100% don’t want to change their Clocks twice a year. The Conservatives have unveiled a proposed £700m childcare giveaway for high earners ahead of their annual conference, saying they would end the “cliff edge” where free entitlement ends at salaries above £100,000.
The plan, set out the day before the event begins in Birmingham, follows the earlier proposal by Kemi Badenoch’s party to abolish most stamp duty, another change to taxation that would disproportionately benefit wealthier people.
Under the current system, put in place under Rishi Sunak’s government, families with young children in England are eligible for 30 hours a week of free childcare, but this cuts off if one parent earns more than £100,000, irrespective of another parent’s salary.
Under the Conservative plans, this limit would be abolished, with all parents working 16 or more hours a week able to claim the childcare.
The party says it would cost aabout £700m a year, which it says would be paid for by cutting jobs at organisations such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.
In comments released to promote the idea, Badenoch said the current system was “absurd” and a disincentive to work more.
She said: “Conservatives believe that you shouldn’t be punished for working more, but this childcare cliff edge does exactly that.
“I’m a mum-of-three and I’ve had to make the same choices many families have had to make on work and childcare. Those choices are difficult already, government should not be making them harder.
“No one should be turning down a promotion or a pay rise because they literally cannot afford to earn more.
“It is often women who end up carrying more of the childcare responsibility so a system that makes it harder for them to progress in their careers is not helping families, it is not helping women and it is definitely not helping the economy.”
A Labour spokesperson said: “It tells you everything you need to know about the Tories that the first of their own tax policies they want to unpick is one helping higher earners. They clearly don’t want to admit that they set the thresholds in the first place.”
The idea of abolishing stamp duty on people’s primary residences in England and Northern Ireland was unveiled by Badenoch at last year’s conference, costing an estimated £9bn a year.
While some economists have argued that stamp duty can have a drag on the housing market and even the economy, as it disincentivises moving, scrapping it rather than reforming the tax would disproportionately benefit better-off people and those in London and south-east England.
The other main policy set out ahead of the conference was a plan to build 50,000 new prison spaces in England and Wales, a 50% expansion in capacity.
This would be paid for in part by slashing overseas aid to £1bn a year, a 90% cut on current plans. Under Keir Starmer, Labour said they would reduce aid from 0.5% of GDP to 0.3% by 2027, but even that lower proportion would still amount to £9bn a year.
When Reform UK announced plans to cut aid to £1bn a year, aid groups warned that this would not cover existing contributions to global bodies such as the UN and World Bank, shredding Britain’s international influence.

Mini-truck crashes into road divider in dry Bihar; locals loot liquor bottles as driver flees
Police said they were scrutinising CCTV footage and social media video clips to book people who had raided the vehicle and retrieve the liquor bottles from them
Dozens of local residents raided a mini-truck after the vehicle, loaded with alcohol, crashed into the road divider on Friday, setting off a scramble among locals who made off with liquor bottles.
Consumption, transportation, and sale of alcohol is banned across Bihar under its 2016 prohibition law.
Police said the incident involving an Assam registered took place near Kharhat Toll Plaza. The vehicle’s driver and the cleaner fled the spot. It is not clear how everyone got to know that the vehicle was carrying liquor.
But as news of the cargo spread, dozens of people rushed to the spot. According to a video clip that emerged on social media, many people including women and children picked individual bottles; some went for cartons.
“It was a usual accident at first site but as soon as the locals came to know about the liquor, they gathered in huge numbers and the looting of the liquor started,” a police officer said.
The video clip and photos of the public conducting their own raid caught attention of the district police headquarters, which rushed more police officers to the spot.
But by the time the police reached, there wasn’t much left to guard.
Sadar sub divisional police officer (SDPO) Sushil Kumar said the police had started scrutinising CCTV footage and social media video clips to identify those who picked up the bottles.
“All those involved in the loot will be arrested,” declared Kumar. He said the police was also searching for the vehicle’s driver who fled after the accident.
It is being speculated the vehicle was carrying the consignment from Assam or West Bengal or Assam and was headed to Bihar districts through Seemanchal.
Raniganj police said they had seized the vehicle and were trying to track the vehicle owner and the network.

The grandstands erupted with shock as engineers clutched their heads in the paddock. One driverless race car, produced by the company PoliMove, slammed into Unimore’s slowing vehicle in an event held by the Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League (A2RL).
At the famous racing track in Imola, Italy, Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari, both cars crashed in an area called Rivazza. This is the circuit’s final sequence, made up of corners that are notoriously difficult to navigate. Formula 1 champions have met a similar fate here. But this time, the impact posed no danger to the drivers because there weren’t any.
Launched in 2024, A2RL sought to introduce self-driving cars to the motorsport to test the boundaries of their current capabilities. And this year’s race at Imola revealed those edges, demonstrating of the gap between the computational abilities of autonomous vehicles and their capacity to respond when something goes wrong.
Only two of the five cars in the final completed the race. The UAE’s Kinetiz finished first, followed by Germany’s Constructor Racing. PoliMove clocked in at third place, though its battered entrant had to be replaced for the podium ceremony. Two-time winner TUM withdrew its car after it developed a brake problem during the formation lap.
Participating teams had just nine days of physical testing before the race, in conditions that included rain and hail. This also happened to be the league’s first international competition away from its usual testing ground at Abu Dhabi’s Yas Marina Circuit.
So why choose one of motorsport’s most unforgiving tracks?
“Because everybody can do ‘easy’, right?” says Nicola Palarchi, engineering director at Aspire, the company that founded A2RL. “We have to show we go where it matters.”
Palarchi made it abundantly clear that autonomous racing did not intend to compete with human racing, but rather stay its own motorsport. It could even support the latter.
Because autonomous racing is pitched as more than spectacle: It’s a laboratory with guardrails. Its proponents describe it as a way to test perception, prediction, and vehicle control at extreme speeds without endangering a human driver. These are all factors in the safety of driverless cars in the real world, and so measuring the limits at which these vehicles succeed—or perhaps more importantly fail—can inform future improvements in the technology.
The first hurdle is perception. The vehicle’s sensors identify its location and surroundings, informing planning software that then chooses a trajectory. Finally, the control system translates that decision into steering, acceleration, and braking. Racing makes each of these stages more challenging, since at high speeds, vehicles have less time to interpret incomplete information, predict another car’s movements and execute an evasive maneuver.
“The car will be blind for a certain point because the track drops off,” Alexander Winkler, A2RL’s head of sporting, had said before the final. If one vehicle stopped beyond that drop, he explained, the car behind could have less than a second to react.
That warning proved prescient.
Unimore said its car, Gianna, initiated a safety stop after losing all data from its lidar and radar sensors. GPS alone could not locate the car accurately enough to continue racing at speed. The team said future systems could use cameras and an inertial measurement unit to continue at a slower pace until precise localization returned. In other words, the car stopped because it lacked a reliable fallback.
PoliMove’s vehicle, Eva, detected Gianna ahead, according to the team, but could not avoid hitting it. Gianna had braked with a force of approximately 1 g with Eva just 1.5 seconds behind it.
PoliMove said its system identified the danger and began an evasive maneuver. But perception, decision-making, trajectory replanning, actuator response, and vehicle dynamics all introduce delays. Once Gianna braked that severely mid-corner, the team said, a collision was physically impossible to avoid.
Even F1 legends like Fernando Alonso and Carlos Sainz have crashed at this part of the track. However, the A2RL teams’ explanation exposes a problem that faster processors alone cannot solve: An autonomous vehicle may recognize a hazard and still be unable to respond before physics takes over.
TUM’s failure was less algorithmic but equally instructive. The team said its car, Hailey, retired after the rear-left brake became stuck at low-to-medium pressure during the formation lap. Even sophisticated autonomous software cannot compensate for mechanical faults.
Kinetiz’s car, Sparkz, took the lead all the way to a first-place podium finish with Constructor AI’s vehicle as the runner-up. But almost any result can be considered progress, when the failures produced useful edge cases: sensor loss, compromised localization, sudden braking, limited visibility, and interaction between autonomous systems making separate decisions.
Beyond crash data, Palarchi says these motorsport environments provide the opportunity to develop more resilient hardware. Temperatures in cockpits can get near 170 degrees F, and—while hopefully your robotaxi is not that hot—radars and lidars that can withstand high heat can be useful in our warming cities.
Chee Kiong Ong, deputy team principal at Kinetiz, also observes that predictive algorithms developed on the track could eventually help civilian vehicles respond to emergencies. “You could probably apply it to make the car stop itself in a safer manner or control it at the limits so that you can save lives,” he says.
One caveat is that unlike other lab testing, the companies aren’t required to share the precise data collected from their vehicles. The data from A2RL’s EAV 25, the racing car developed by the league based on modified Dallara SF23 cars, currently stays within the competition.
The next A2RL race returns to Yas Marina, where teams have spent years developing their software. Organizers are already considering making the competition harder by shortening testing periods, increasing the grid to eight cars, or restricting access to GPS.
Those changes could reveal whether the systems are becoming more adaptable. In the meantime, we’ll wait to see how this information transfers into real-life scenarios.

Mosquitoes suck. Literally, figuratively, and every other way. These bloodsuckers have been a worldwide menace since the beginning of recorded history. A popularly reposted infographic lists them as—by far—the world’s deadliest animal, thanks to the parade of nasty diseases they can transmit. West Nile, Zika, chikungunya, malaria, dengue—these are no longer illnesses confined to the global south. In recent years, all have been discovered in bugs in the United States.
Ridding your property of mosquitoes is a decidedly Quixotic effort. You can stem the tide for a while, but you can’t ever win the war. Once whatever abatement method you use has worn off, they swoop back in, thirstier than ever. Nevertheless, you have to do something. Left unattended, mosquitoes can quickly turn from a nuisance to an epidemic that makes your outdoor space completely unusable.
Outside of wide-scale community mosquito spraying programs, most personal and home-based mosquito abatement tools focus on repelling them rather than trying to outright kill them. Insecticides like DEET work by being rubbed onto the skin, while metofluthrin and allethrin work in vapor form, creating a cloud of repellent that works without you having to make physical contact with the chemicals. Trapping mosquitoes is another potential option, luring them into a chamber from which they can’t escape.
For years I’ve tried innumerable technologies and tactics to rid my property—and my very susceptible skin—from mosquitoes. Here’s what I’ve uncovered to date that works—and what doesn’t.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Featured Products
Best Personal Repellent Gear
This pint-sized repeller weighs a little more than a pound and recharges via a USB-C cable. Power it up and a heating element inside warms a vial of metofluthrin, releasing mosquito-repulsing vapor in your immediate vicinity, about 10 feet in every direction. It’s simple and extremely portable, making it easy to move from one area to another.
The system works. It warms up in just a few minutes and effectively keeps bugs at bay, provided you keep the repeller close by. Best of all, I was able to take it with me as I moved around the yard—but be warned, there’s some lag time for the vapor cloud to reform each time you relocate. A small chemical replacement cartridge lasts for about 36 hours; refills are $39 for a 2-pack.
Note that Thermacell markets myriad versions of this product, including a unit with a built-in light, one with a docking station for easier charging, one with longer battery life, and one that is ruggedized and can be worn around the neck on a lanyard. Any of the above will get the job done (and done well) in functionally the same way.
This butane-powered device offers a twist on the E-ZoneGuard line, containing no battery at all, which may be preferred in some exceptionally off-the-grid environments. Instead, a butane cartridge twists into the system. When activated (no flame needed), it heats up a replaceable chemical mat that slides into a groove on top of the device, this one using allethrin instead of metofluthrin. One downside: The vapor shield promised by the Fuel-Zoneguard stretches only about 7½ feet in each direction, more restrictive than the E-Zoneguard, and a butane canister will only get you about 12 hours of operation. Allethrin may also be less effective than metofluthrin against pests. That said, I experienced great results with this product and found the freedom from cables to be liberating. Refills run $19 for 24 hours of extra fuel and insecticide mats (sold together).
The Fuel-Zoneguard is also sold as part of a lantern or in a handheld form, designed for use on the go. (As with E-Zoneguard products, the underlying technology is identical.)
Best Large-Scale Repellent Gear
Take Thermacell’s E-Zoneguard system and make it yard-sized, and you’ve got LIV, a semi-permanent solution that uses the same repellent chemical (metofluthrin) but dramatically expands its coverage potential.
The system is built around a hub that plugs into wall power and connects to your home’s Wi-Fi. Up to 10 freestanding repellers connect to this hub via cables. You string them in a chain to surround your deck, your pool, or whatever else you want to protect from mosquitoes. Arranged in a rough circle, the resultant cloud of repellent serves as a large-scale barrier that can protect the whole family from being attacked. It’s all controlled via a mobile app (with Alexa support allegedly in the works), so you can fire the system up before you even head outside.
It’s one of the most effective systems I’ve tested, in large part because it pumps out so much repellent at precise locations. While nothing is perfect, LIV is about as close as it gets, protecting my entire swimming pool and deck at the touch of a button on its mobile app.
The only catch is that LIV is far from inexpensive, and Thermacell no longer sells it as a DIY solution; you’ll need a professional installer to complete the job. If saving your skin (and potentially your health) from mosquitoes is important to you, it could be worth it.
Tiki BiteFighter—from the company that makes the iconic torches—is an ingenious twist on the wider-scale repellent concept that takes advantage of wiring you may already have. The system works with string lights: Just remove a bulb from your lights and screw the Plug & Repel into the socket. When the lights are on, the device heats up a vial of metofluthrin that attaches to the bottom of the repellent unit, protecting the immediate vicinity from mosquitoes. (In theory, you can also use it with any overhead light socket.)
Naturally, the device comes with some caveats. The biggest is that it requires a (standard size) E26 socket to connect to; many string lights, including mine, use much smaller E12 candelabra bulbs, so compatibility can be a problem. Second, the range of BiteFighter’s vapor is considerably smaller than Thermacell’s: Tiki recommends plugging in a repeller every 12 feet. That can require a significant investment in hardware, mar your lighting aesthetic, and require lots of maintenance. (The system ships with a 12-hour metofluthrin pod; 48-hour replacement pods cost $10 each.)
Still, if you have the right environment, with compatible string lights surrounding or criss-crossing your outdoor space, the solution is much more affordable than a hard-wired system like LIV. If you only plan to use the system occasionally, the math is even more compelling.
Just OK: Mosquito Traps
These devices may look like old-school bug zappers, but they’re actually traps, designed to lure bugs in with a purple light, then sequester them in a chamber thanks to the tiny fan that sucks them in. Mosqitter's and Dynatrap’s devices work almost exactly the same way, boasting coverage that spans up to an acre, depending on the model you choose.
I tried both of these products—in Mosqitter’s case for months, letting it run all summer long—and found that while they were both effective at capturing insects, neither one attracted many mosquitoes. In both cases, I returned after a few weeks to find the trap chamber filled almost exclusively with moths. I don’t really love moths, either, but I don’t feel like I need to go out of my way to kill them.
I spoke to Mosqitter about my results and they suggested adding a packet of mosquito attractant to the device ($25, lasts a month), but this didn’t have any result on my mosquito catch rate. Again, mostly moths at the end of the testing period.
So, why am I saying these might be worth a try? As Mosqitter pointed out to me, there are countless species of mosquitoes—3200 globally, 174 in the US—and they don’t all behave the same. The ones around Austin may be resistant to the attractant and blasé about purple light, instead preferring to dine exclusively on human flesh. (This certainly tracks.) So while my results were lackluster, I’m willing to concede that users in other parts of the world, where the bugs are less hearty, may have better luck with it. If you don’t get good results, you can always return the gear for a refund.
If You Do Get Stung
Less effective
I’ve tried plenty of products that promise to kill or repel mosquitoes. These have not been effective—or, at least, not worth the money and effort involved.
This oddity arrives as a plastic bucket that you fill partway with water, mimicking a mosquito breeding site. A chemical-laced band hovers over this water, slowly contaminating it with a poison that kills adult mosquitoes and their eggs. The band must be replaced monthly. I tested this system for two months but found that the water evaporated much too quickly and, more importantly, the whole thing became an attractant for mammalian wildlife like racoons and opossums, which periodically tossed it around, maybe in the hopes of getting at the water. It’s a cheap option at $35, but not something I was keen to leave on my patio long-term.
The lowest of low-tech anti-mosquito solutions, Mosquito Dunks are small discs that you can drop into any amount of standing water, either natural (water feature like a fountain) or man-made (a bucket you intentionally fill with water as a trap). These contain a bacteria that’s toxic to mosquitoes but won’t hurt other wildlife, slowly releasing into the water as they dissolve over the course of a month. The only problem: They smell awful, and of course you need a reliable source of standing water for them to work at all. That’s fine if you have a handy pond that you don’t want to drain. Much less exciting in the average backyard.
$100/treatment and up
If you live in mosquito country, chances are your neighborhood is teeming with companies that promise to repel the bugs by spraying chemicals into the trees and foliage around your property, warding them off. I paid for a service to spray my property for years, and found that a very familiar routine developed: Immediately after each spray, my yard would be almost devoid of bugs, and my family would have two or three days of bite-free bliss. After that, the spray would wear off and the bugs would return, leaving us another 18 days or so until the next triweekly treatment. (Any amount of rain would also wash away all of the treatment chemicals even quicker.) Given the cost of over $2,000 per year, I’ve never been happier with a decision to cancel a service.
Mosquitoes just aren’t attracted to shiny lights the way other insects are. You’ll hear plenty of satisfying pops if you hang a bug zapper near your pool, but you won’t likely find many of the dead to be mosquitoes. Skip ’em.

An obesity drug from Boehringer Ingelheim and Zealand Pharma helped patients with diabetes shed as much as 13.1% of their weight, a disappointing result, Bloomberg News tells us. Boehringer has pitched the medicine as a way to help patients lose fat while preserving muscle, but without an edge, the drug becomes just one more contender in an increasingly crowded market dominated by Eli Lilly and Novo. Boehringer pushed back at the idea that the drug might only be a niche product, saying that upcoming studies in heart and liver health will more clearly show its potential.
The upcoming midterm elections are setting the stage for unusually significant changes to key Senate committees that play an important role in health care, STAT explains. Both the finance and health committees could undergo major changes, though for different reasons. Of course, if Democrats take control of the Senate, they would get to run the committees, though the GOP membership changes could still influence the panels’ directions. Specifically, five or more of the Senate Finance Committee’s 14 Republicans are set to leave. And the outlook for the Senate’s Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, or HELP, is even more difficult to predict with the departure of chairman Bill Cassidy.
Novartis signed a licensing deal worth about $7.8 billion with Chinese biotech company Abogen to advance RNA-based therapy, Reuters says. Novartis will gain exclusive rights to Abogen’s experimental drug, ABO2203, and options to license other therapies based on Abogen’s RNA technology. It will also have the option to license additional experimental medicines developed using Abogen’s RNA platform. The drug is designed to treat autoimmune diseases by targeting B cells, a type of immune cell that causes disease in conditions like lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.
