Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
- Published
The pilot who was stabbed on an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday has been identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar.
Capt Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia.
The captain, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken to a hospital in Tubak City, north-western Saudi Arabia, where he remains in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh.
Writing on X, Netanyahu said Capt Machchhar "saved the lives of 174 people" and prevented "a catastrophic mid-air disaster".
What do we know about Capt Machchhar?
Capt Machchhar joined Flydubai in 2022 - he was an experienced pilot by then, having worked at Indian airline SpiceJet since 2011.
He has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.
His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".
Last year, Capt Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.
Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work with his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]," he added.
Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family.
"Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.
He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely.
"In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.
At the time of the conversation, Capt Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had had to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues causing delays.
He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."
Indian social media has been awash with praise for Capt Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.
What happened on the Flydubai flight?
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.
The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.
Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.
At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.
But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.
He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-eastern Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.
The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Capt Machchhar.
Modi and Trump praise Capt Machchhar
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured.
"His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery.
Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger".
Speaking to reporters at the White House, US President Donald Trump said that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack.
"Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open."

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

Spotlight on new coaches as road to Afcon 2027 begins
- Published
Just eight months on from the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) - and with the world still waiting to find out the ultimate destination of the title - the road to the 2027 tournament begins in earnest.
The 48 sides still in contention will play two rounds of qualifying in this extended international window, which gets under way on Thursday.
Two more matches follow in November, with the groups reaching their denouement with the final two fixtures in March.
The top two in nine of the 12 groups will progress to the 24-team finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
Preparations for the tournament in East Africa may be lagging behind but, with the three hosts all guaranteed qualification, there is only one spot on offer in their respective groups. That means a second-placed finish may potentially not be enough.
Several managerial changes have occurred since the last Afcon in Morocco and this year's Fifa World Cup, while several star players have hung up their boots. Here's what to keep an eye on in the first two rounds of action.
- Senegal appeal date set after Afcon win overturned 
  - Published24 July
Big names in the dugout
Among several coaching changes, two in particular have caught the eye.
Herve Renard, the only man to win Afcon with two different nations, has returned to the Ivory Coast job some 11 years after leading the West Africans to the title.
The 57-year-old Frenchman starts his second stint with the Elephants at home against Ghana on Thursday in what is the standout match in the first round of fixtures.
In the opposing dugout, the experienced Carlos Queiroz is back at the helm after leading the Black Stars to the last 32 at the World Cup. However, Tottenham's Mohammed Kudus is among a number of players to withdraw from his squad.
Patrick Vieira is another high-profile arrival, as the 1998 World Cup champion with France takes charge of Senegal, the country of his birth.
The former Arsenal midfielder, 50, describes the role as "an absolute dream" yet he will begin with two away games against Mozambique and Ethiopia because Dakar is getting ready to host the 2026 Youth Olympics.
- Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 
  - Published23 July
Other new arrivals
Cape Verde were one of the great stories of the 2026 World Cup, pushing Argentina all the way in the last 32 before the debutants lost 3-2 after extra time.
Long-serving coach Bubista has since resigned from the Blue Sharks hotseat, with his former assistant Humberto Bettencourt stepping up.
He will begin his reign in Mali on Friday before hosting Rwanda on Tuesday.
Algeria, Tunisia and South Africa have also changed coaches since the World Cup.
The Tunisians have turned to former Esperance and Renaissance Berkane boss Moin Chaaban as they aim to move on from their disastrous World Cup campaign which saw Sabri Lamouchi dismissed after one game and Renard fail to orchestrate a revival.
Pitso Mosimane has been reappointed by South Africa some 14 years on from his last spell in charge - which saw Bafana Bafana miss out on the 2012 Afcon - and Brahim Hemdani has taken over Algeria after Vladmir Petkovic's departure.
Meanwhile, Afcon legend Claude Le Roy has returned at the age of 78 after signing on for a second stint with Congo-Brazzaville.
The Red Devils have not appeared at the finals since 2015, while Frenchman Le Roy is aiming to coach at a record-extending 10th edition of the finals.
Burkina Faso have turned to ex-Comoros boss Amir Abdou and, after a stint with Libya, 2021 Afcon-winning coach Aliou Cisse has his first competitive matches in charge of Angola.
The former Senegal boss starts with a tough away assignment in Egypt.
An era ends
Some big-name players have called time on their international careers since the World Cup, with several of them former Afcon winners.
Senegal are looking for a new number one after Edouard Mendy hung up his goalkeeping gloves.
The 34-year-old helped the Teranga Lions become champions at the 2021 and 2025 tournaments - even if the latter title is still disputed at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
Wing wizard Riyad Mahrez, who captained Algeria to the trophy in 2019, has quit international duty while Ivory Coast will have to cope without midfielders Seko Fofana and Jean-Michael Seri.
Ellyes Skhiri has also called time on his international career and will not be involved as Tunisia aim to reach a record-extending 18th consecutive Afcon.
Meanwhile, Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang has stepped back from Gabon duty, saying he felt "humiliated" by his treatment after their exit at the previous tournament.
The 37-year-old was excluded from the national team set-up after their group-stage exit. That sanction was later lifted, but Aubameyang ruled himself out of Sebastien Migne's Panthers squad despite his fine start to the season with Deportivo La Coruna.
Return of the Red Sea Camels
Elsewhere, Eritrea are back in the group stage of Afcon qualifiers - for the first time since the build-up to the 2008 edition - after seeing off Eswatini 4-1 on aggregate in the preliminary round in March.
Chad, Djibouti, Mauritius, Sao Tome and Principe and Seychelles are the other five nations already eliminated.
However, seven Ertirea players absconded after the away leg of their tie which was held in South Africa.
Occurrences of Eritrean sportsmen and women failing to return home to what is a one-party state and a highly militarised society has long been an issue, and was part of the reason for the East Africans withdrawing from qualifying for both the 2023 Afcon and 2026 World Cup.
Yet the Red Sea Camels, who have been drawn alongside Kenya, South Africa and Guinea in Group D, are now largely relying on talent drawn from the diaspora.
Just three home-based players have been named in the squad for their opening two fixtures, which see them take on the tournament co-hosts in Nairobi on Saturday before a 'home' game against Bafana Bafana in Cairo on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Somalia have reached the group stage of qualifying for the first ever time but face a very tricky draw alongside Ivory Coast, Ghana and The Gambia.
The Ocean Stars are ranked 53rd on the continent but, like Eritrea, can at least dream of reaching Afcon as the tournament returns to East Africa for the first time since 1976.

Toyama – Police searched the Toyama City Hall on Saturday over suspected violations of the statistics law related to allegations that its staff inflated the central Japanese city’s population figure in the 2025 census.
About 10 investigators in suits from the Toyama Prefectural Police arrived at the office around 10 a.m. with cardboard boxes in hand and headed to the building’s fifth floor, where the division in charge of census-related duties is located.
On Tuesday, the internal affairs ministry filed a criminal complaint against unidentified city staff for the alleged violations of the statistics law.
According to final figures released by the ministry Tuesday, the city had a population of 399,197, down from the preliminary figure of 402,133 released in May. The ministry said that Toyama’s population had been padded by at least 2,000, and that multiple city staff members were suspected of involvement.
Toyama Mayor Hirohisa Fujii denied at a news conference Friday that the inflation was motivated by a desire to keep the city’s population above 400,000.
“There were no instructions from senior officials” to inflate the figure, Fujii added. “I will take due responsibility at the appropriate time.”
The preliminary census population figure was used to calculate local allocation tax grants for fiscal 2026. According to a city estimate, Toyama may have received about ¥60 million more than it was entitled to as a result.
“We take the police search very seriously and will continue to fully cooperate with the investigation,” Fujii said in a statement.

How ‘Israel’s 9/11’ was averted after midair stabbing as co-pilot’s motive remains a mystery
Passengers on Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv have been celebrated as heroes for preventing disaster. Maira Butt looks at how it all unfolded

When the first reports about a diverted flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv came through on Wednesday, it appeared to have been caused by a tussle between two pilots.
Early claims even suggested one was Russian and the other Ukrainian.
But, in the age of social media, the true chaos aboard the FlyDubai Flight FZ1073 quickly came to light. Footage and images sent from the plane by blood-covered passengers showed them overpowering the co-pilot, who it later emerged was an Omani national.
The plane, a Boeing 737 MAX aircraft, was carrying over 170 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv when it plunged more than 17,000ft in two minutes as the fight broke out. An emergency alert was sent out and the plane changed course towards Jordan, eventually landing in Saudi Arabia.
Aviation experts told the BBC that the rapid descent led to damage pictured on the plane’s rudder adding that the incident could easily have led to the plane breaking up in mid-air.
Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was identified as the victim of the attack, while his arrested co-pilot was identified as Hamam al-Hammami on Saturday by sources cited in CNN.
The motive for the incident is still being determined but Netanyahu’s administration suggested early on that it was a suspected terror attack.
‘Blood everywhere’
A six-year-old on her way to the toilet accompanied by her mother, was the first to raise the alarm when the pair heard shouting coming from the cockpit, prompting cabin crew to rush to the scene. What they saw was a blood-spattered scene.
“There was blood all over the cockpit and very, very sharp fighting moves,” Nina Manes’ mother, Tali Manes told Israel’s Channel 12.
“I screamed, ‘He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!’ People looked at me and didn’t understand.”
Her husband Tzvika Manes said: “The shrieks of my daughters when the plane nose-dived [are still with me]. They said, ‘Dad we don’t want to die.’ [Their cries] were the triggers that caused me to run inside the cockpit.”
One passenger recorded the ordeal on his phone and later shared the footage to social media. With blood dripping down his face, he declared that the passengers had “subdued the terrorists”. “Whoever is hearing me, we need help,” he added.
On Saturday, UAE prosecutors said Cpt Machchhar had been attacked by a “crash axe”, a tool kept in the cockpit in case of emergencies, bypassing stringent security protocols.
Yaniv Hayun, a 50-year-old owner of a sewage plumbing company, was travelling with his wife and two daughters when the incident took place.
In his blood-spattered t-shirt, he was hailed as a hero by Netanyahu who personally thanked him for helping to subdue the attacker and to prevent the plane from crashing.
Along with Tzvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan, he broke into the cockpit to stop the attacker. By mimicking gestures he says he’d see on television, Hayun “grabbed the controls and started pulling back the handles”. He said he’d learned the techniques from watching Air Crash Investigation.
He said it took 20 to 25 minutes to fully subdue and bind the pilot and they used cords from headphones linked to the plane’s entertainment system.
Hayun was helped by a dentist, Dr Shota Musayev, who administered “life-saving medical treatment” to Cpt Machchhar, including treating him for severe wounds to his head and cuts to his fingers. He helped to successfully stop the bleeding and to stabilise his blood pressure before emergency surgery.
All five are expected to receive Israel’s Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, president Isaac Herzog said on Thursday.
Both pilots have been transferred to the UAE for further investigations and for medical treatment.
‘Suicidal and indoctrinated’
Netanyahu told Fox News that the attacker was “suicidal” and called out to the crew: “kill me, kill me!” after he was subdued.
“It’s clear he was suicidal, that’s not a question,” he added. The Israeli leader said that he had undergone a “Islamist radical indoctrination” and promised to reveal whether he had connections to Iran in the coming days.
The prime minister said those onboard managed to “prevent a 9/11 disaster, because that's what it looks like was happening”, claiming that the intent may have been to crash the plane.
A regional official familiar with the FlyDubai investigation told the Associated Press that investigators in Saudi Arabia were working with authorities from the UAE, US, Oman and Israel, and that “all possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into”.
“Nothing is ruled out for now”, the official said.
Al-Hammami was banned from flying last year over concerns that he had radical ideological views, according to Saudi state media.
Two Israeli security officials said that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, according to their initial assessments.
He was arrested by Saudi security forces after the plane landed in Tabuk, northwest Saudi Arabia, and was being questioned by investigators.
On Saturday, the UAE prosecutor general said that al-Hammami had attempted to carry out a “terrorist” attack, according to the country’s state news agency WAM.
Investigations are ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, he added.
Netanyahu said: “It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane … The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that’s a pretty good clue.”
Warnings and questions over security
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said on Wednesday that politicians had been warned in a national security briefing the night before that Israel’s enemies could attack in the run up to the country’s elections due to take place on 27 October.
A ban on pilots from states without formal relations to Israel was not enforced appropriately, according to a report cited by the Times of Israel.
Under the law, pilots from nations including Oman, which does not have formal ties with Israel, were banned from flying but airlines and security agencies did not enforce the rule.
Furthermore, Israel’s security agency, Shin Bet, had raised concerns about flights from the UAE for months before the incident.
Shin Bet director David Zini had reportedly clashed with Israeli airlines over restrictions on flights to the UAE, reasoning that security measures at Emirati airports were insufficient, according to Israel’s N12 News.
Israeli authorities were concerned with possible missile attacks or attacks at an airport, the outlet reported on Thursday. A scenario like Wednesday’s hijacking attempt was “not raised in any discussion”, they said.

Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar accuses BJP of targeting poor voters through Form 7
Shivakumar accused BJP and JD(S) leaders of using Form 7 applications to target poor voters. He said the government would protect voting rights while expanding doorstep services and welfare delivery.
Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar on Saturday alleged that attempts were being made to remove poor people from electoral rolls and claimed BJP leaders were trying to win elections through such a strategy.
He said his government would protect the voting rights of all citizens, including minorities, Dalits and backward classes, amid the controversy over bulk Form 7 applications seeking deletion of names from the voter list.
Shivakumar also used the occasion to outline a series of welfare and governance measures, including doorstep delivery of services through the Praja Seva Department, pension relief, distribution of residential sites to poor people, support for drought-hit farmers, and action on land-related grievances.
Addressing a Praja Seva Department programme at Piriyapatna in Mysuru district, Shivakumar said, "Some BJP workers, friends and leaders had submitted applications seeking deletion of people's voting rights, including those of poor people. We have also taken up the fight to ensure that no person's vote is deleted without proper documentation."
He said that BJP and JD(S) leaders were trying to win elections by depriving poor people of their voting rights and said such a move was against the Constitution. He added that the government had conveyed its concerns to the Election Commission.
The chief minister said the Praja Seva Department had been launched recently to take government services to people's doorsteps and resolve grievances without requiring them to visit government offices.
"The government must reach the doorstep of the people," he said, adding that ministers, MLAs and officials had been directed to visit every taluk twice a month, on the first and third Saturdays, and receive applications from people at the panchayat level.
According to Shivakumar, the department, launched on September 5, has already held programmes at about 620 locations and received applications from more than one lakh people.
He said most grievances were related to the Revenue, Rural Development and Urban Development departments.
He added that applications would be numbered and acknowledged, and officials would be monitored to ensure timely disposal.
A legal aid counter would also be opened to provide free help to people facing legal hurdles.
He said the decision to raise the annual income ceiling for pension eligibility from Rs 32,000 to Rs 1.20 lakh had benefited around 12 lakh people whose pensions had been stopped.
He also announced a plan to provide residential sites to five lakh poor people in the first phase, and directed Deputy Commissioners to identify government land and create new layouts wherever needed.
Referring to drought, Shivakumar said 217 taluks had been affected and that the government was planning a new programme called "Negilu Yogi" to assist farmers. Two taluks in each district would be selected for the scheme, he said.
He also launched Bharat Jodo Youth Associations to encourage people in the 16-35 age group to take part in sports, cultural activities, environmental work and other community efforts. Each panchayat would get Rs 10 lakh under the programme, he said.
Shivakumar said the government was reviewing reports of alleged misuse of its Gruha Lakshmi and Gruha Jyothi guarantee schemes. He described the proposed "Bhoomi Guarantee" as a sixth guarantee and said the government would focus on providing khatas and proper property documents, completing land subdivision or phodi, and addressing other land-related issues.
He added that around Rs 3,500 crore had been allocated under the employment guarantee programme and urged people to use the scheme to develop their land and create community assets.
"We have created a system where, if officials or MLAs are unable to meet you, officials will come to your doorstep, and MLAs will also come to you," he said.
He added that he would himself travel to different constituencies twice every month to receive grievance petitions and monitor their disposal.
"I have said from the very first day that I am not merely the chief minister; I am a people's servant," Shivakumar said, adding that people should not have to go around government offices or pay bribes to get their problems addressed.
He also directed officials to speed up disposal of applications filed under the Forest Rights Act and other land-rights provisions, while asking people not to resort to encroachment. "Nobody should evict you illegally. I will issue such directions," he said.
Speaking to reporters at another event on the Form 7 deletion applications, Shivakumar said the Election Commission had directed officials to verify each case before deleting any voter from the rolls. "The Chief Electoral Officer (V Anbukkumar) has sent a message to poll officials asking not to delete anything and to verify every single case. I am happy about that," he said.
He added that the EC had also asked officials to examine errors in the existing voter lists, particularly those affecting minorities, Dalits, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and economically vulnerable people.
Asked whether the state government would order a separate investigation into the alleged misuse of Form 7, he said, "Let us see what comes out of this". On the possibility of cases being filed against him for allegedly staging a sit-in on the steps of the CEO's office on Thursday, Shivakumar said he abides by the law.
"If I have committed any mistake under the law, let them file a case. Let us follow the law as the law says. Let us respect the law," he said. He added that he had not staged any demonstration and had only waited for a positive reply on his complaint to the CEO to initiate action against those who had misused Form 7.

A rumor spread in late September 2026 that CNN television host Anderson Cooper built a free hospital for homeless people. According to the claim, the journalist opened the Anderson Cooper Homestead Medical Center in New York, complete with 250 beds, 120 apartments and a range of additional services — all at zero cost to patients.
Snopes readers searched our website and emailed us about the claim, with one reader asking, "Did Anderson Cooper build a free hospital for homeless people in New York?"
Several Facebook users shared the rumor. The posts generally featured the same image allegedly showing Cooper cutting a ribbon in front of a building with a sign reading, "Anderson Cooper Medical Center."
(Jeannette Piña via Facebook)
According to the posts, Cooper said of the hospital, "This is the legacy I want to leave behind." The facility allegedly cost $142 million, with the Anderson Cooper Foundation raising all funds from anonymous donors over an 18-month period — complete with no public fanfare or announcements until opening.
In short, the rumor is false. No evidence suggests Cooper opened a free hospital for homeless people. The claim is nothing more than "AI slop," spam-type content generated using artificial intelligence tools that has, in recent years, deluged social media with untrue stories, as well as fake images and videos, usually featuring public figures.
CNN spokesperson Shimrit Sheetrit said via email that the rumor is false.
Researching the claim
Searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo uncovered no news media outlets reporting that Cooper opened a hospital. Even if a famous person secretly raised funds to open a hospital without publicity, news organizations would at some point publish articles about the facility's existence. Officials would eventually launch a website or use other online means to alert homeless people of the project and its offerings. No such information has been published or shared.
The story in the posts is inconsistent with the AI-generated images accompanying it. For example, the text in one post refers to the hospital as "Anderson Cooper Homestead Medical Center," while the image features a sign reading, "Anderson Cooper Medical Center." A different post (archived) contains other fake images of Cooper wearing completely different clothes at the supposed opening, with the different facility name, "The Anderson Cooper Center." The posts also say there was "no ribbon" and "no fanfare" at the supposed opening, despite the images containing both a ribbon and a crowd.
This claim possibly originated from a post on a Facebook page called The Silver Voice, which links to an external website hosting an advertisement-filled article. That website's domain name appears to be at least partially in Vietnamese, a language that often appears alongside "AI slop" website content, as Snopes has previously reported.
The heartwarming subject matter about Cooper's purported grand act of kindness resembles glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental." Creators of such content capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has also previously reported on this business strategy.)
AI-generated content and similar rumors
A scan of the Facebook posts' text with AI detection tool Pangram displays the results, "We believe that this entire text is AI," and, "100% of this text is AI." A scan of one of the post's images returns the same result.
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. With Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as some criticisms of the tool.
Reporters at fact-checking website Lead Stories previously reported on many other celebrities being named in similar "AI slop" stories about them opening free hospitals for homeless people.
Snopes also previously addressed a false claim that first lady Melania Trump and her son, Barron Trump, opened a hospital for homeless people, and a similar rumor about late-night host Stephen Colbert and his wife, Evelyn McGee-Colbert. The latter also features an AI-generated image that resembles the fake photo of Cooper.
For further reading, we previously reported about numerous fabricated stories that circulated online following the deadly Texas flash floods in July 2025, as well as how those false accounts show signs of originating in Southeast Asia.

Indian proposal for Ukraine truce ‘most comprehensive’, says Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha
Sybiha said similar proposals have been made by Turkey and Egypt, which proposed a truce in the Black Sea to restore grain exports from Ukraine.
Ukraine has received ceasefire proposals from four countries, including one from India that is the “most comprehensive”, Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha has said.
The other proposals were from Turkey, Egypt and the US, and Ukraine is ready for various options for a truce with Russia, Sybiha told reporters in Kyiv on Friday, according to a report by European Pravda.
Also read: Ukraine attacks major Russian refinery and oil pipeline hub with drones in Samara region
Ukraine is ready to consider different ceasefire formats, including along the front lines, but only if the truce covers attacks on energy and port infrastructure and the situation in the Black Sea, he said.
‘India’s proposal most comprehensive'
“We have four proposals. The most comprehensive is India’s proposal. We are ready for an energy and Black Sea truce, but only in this combination,” Sybiha said. “This [should be] a complete energy truce, a stop to attacks on all energy facilities, including port infrastructure.”
Sybiha said similar proposals have been made by Turkey and Egypt, which proposed a truce in the Black Sea to restore grain exports from Ukraine.
The fourth proposal by the US insists that Ukraine and Russia agree on an energy truce, he said. The US proposal was discussed during a meeting between President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump.
Also read: Russia-Ukraine tensions rising? Putin warns of using ‘all types of weapons’ if Kaliningrad attacked
“In general, we believe a truce could be one of the results of a meeting between President Zelensky and [Russian President Vladimir] Putin. We are ready for different formats of a truce, including an unconditional one along the line of contact,” Sybiha said.
Sybiha did not provide further details and it could not immediately be ascertained when India had made the proposal. There was no comment on the matter from Indian officials.
India's emphasis on ending the war
The Indian side has emphasised that it remains in touch with Russia and Ukraine and is ready to assist in ending the war, which New Delhi has repeatedly said has impacted food, fuel and fertiliser security, especially for the Global South.
While addressing the annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow on Thursday, Putin said Prime Minister Narendra Modi consistently raises the question of ending the conflict in Ukraine every time they meet. “He takes a keen interest in the matter and has excellent ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable…solutions. In this sense, [Modi] certainly maintains a neutral position while remaining committed to seeing the conflict end,” Putin said.
“We are also grateful to the Prime Minister for his ideas – I will not go into details now – and for his commitment to resolving this conflict, among others, peacefully and as quickly as possible,” he said.
Modi met Putin on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Kyrgyzstan in August and called for a shift from endless war to the end of war. The Ukraine conflict figured again in a meeting between Modi and Putin ahead of the Brics Summit in New Delhi last month. Modi last met Zelensky on the margins of the G7 Summit in France in June.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar travelled to Kyiv in early September, days after the meeting between Modi and Putin in Kyrgyzstan, and emphasised that the conflict cannot be resolved on the battlefield and that India stands ready to help in all efforts to end the war in Ukraine.

People who have a Medicare Advantage plan — and wind up needing care and prescriptions next year — are in for a rude awakening.
Medicare Advantage insurers are raising out-of-pocket costs for enrollees, drastically cutting money for dental work and other benefits, and eliminating plans that have broad networks of hospitals and doctors, according to federal data released this week and analyzed by STAT and several investment firms. That could result in more shock for older adults, like discovering their doctor is no longer accepted by their plan, if they don’t shop carefully during Medicare’s annual enrollment period for 2027 plans, which starts Oct. 15.
Big companies like UnitedHealth Group, Humana, and others are chasing higher profits by pruning benefits, after investors grew dissatisfied with margins that were smaller than the insurers had promised. The changes in plans even come even after the industry won a payment increase and delayed reforms from the Trump administration in April.

The Supreme Court faces another term jam-packed with controversy
The U.S. Supreme Court formally opens a new term on Monday, with big test cases on religion, bans on semi-automatic weapons, climate change, immigration and — waiting in the wings — election law cases.
It used to be that the first Monday in October marked the beginning of a new Supreme Court term. And that's still true, technically. But for all practical purposes, the formerly quiet summer months after the court finishes its opinions in all argued cases no longer exists.
Indeed, as Georgetown University law professor Stephen Vladeck observes, the number of emergency appeals has ballooned during the Trump administration, while at the same time, fully briefed and argued cases have dropped precipitously over the years.
"So now we have twice as many full court rulings on emergency applications as we have on the merits docket," Vladeck observes, adding, "That is a very new phenomenon."
The difference is that decisions on the emergency docket are rendered quickly, with little briefing, no oral arguments, and ultimately little or no explanation of the ruling. In contrast, a decision on the merits is typically worked on for months after full briefing and lengthy oral arguments.
Of late, the court seems to be making an effort to offer some limited explanations of its emergency docket rulings, but lower court judges, both liberal and conservative, complain that isn't enough to provide them with adequate guidance. And the Trump administration often takes what used to be the rare step of getting to the Supreme Court by leapfrogging over lower appellate courts that the administration views as hostile.
With that backdrop, here are the cases the court will be hearing in the coming weeks:
Climate change
The opening case, to be argued Monday, tests whether state and local governments can sue energy companies for allegedly deceiving the public about the damaging effects of fossil fuels.
"The theory is that the energy company defendants deceived the public for many years," says Deepak Gupta, who teaches at Harvard Law School and practices law in Washington, D.C. What the companies were telling the public for years, he says, is "the opposite of what the company's own scientists knew, and the local cost of that deception."
That said, however, most court observers see the case as an uphill battle for environmentalists.
Religion
Perhaps the biggest case of the term so far, in terms of ripple effects, involves religion, a subject on which the court's conservative super majority has dramatically changed its legal doctrine. Indeed for the better part of a century, the Supreme Court emphasized the First Amendment's separation of church and state, with the free exercise of religion playing an important — but secondary — role. Since President Trump's appointment of three new justices, however, things have changed.
"It's literally the opposite of what the law was not that long ago, and it's just a complete shift," observes Michigan State University law professor Frank Ravitch.
The court may, in fact, be on the verge of requiring taxpayers to fund religious schools that refuse to admit LGBTQ students and parents. Last term the justices deadlocked on the issue in a separate case after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself because of a conflict. The 4-4 tie vote automatically left in place an Oklahoma Supreme Court decision that barred overtly religious charter schools from from being funded by the taxpayers. But this year the issue is back in a case from Colorado. The case centers on a state law that provides universal preschool programs that are open to all students, regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation or gender identity.
St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colo., wants the state funding guaranteed in the state's universal pre-k law. But it doesn't want to admit LGBTQ students or students with gay or trans parents. The parish maintains such admissions would violate church's right to the free exercise of religion. The state counters that funding the church school would violate the state's anti-discrimination law.
The court's conservative majority has, in multiple cases, ruled in favor of religious exemptions from generally applicable laws. Until now, however, the court has never said that religious schools are entitled to full taxpayer funding. But given the current court's views, and with Justice Barrett participating in the Colorado case, taxpayers could well end up having to fund religious schools in Colorado and elsewhere.
Bans on semi-automatic weapons
In December the court will hear a case testing whether state and local governments violate the Second Amendment right to bear arms when they ban semi-automatic weapons, like the AR-15.
Former Solicitor General Don Verrilli Jr., articulates two different ways to look at the question.
On the one hand the AR-15 "can deliver upwards of 100 bullets per minute" without any enhancements, and 500 bullets per minute with various enhancements. On the other hand, he notes that millions of Americans own AR-15s, "and it would be quite disruptive to suggest all these Americans ... would be dispossessed of their weapons."
Lawyer Erin Murphy, who has litigated lots of cases on behalf of gun owners, says the "single most important question is who gets to decide what guns you have," and he argues it makes no sense to say, "You've got this right against the government, but the government decides which arms you can get."
Immigration
The Trump administration has repeatedly taken positions in immigration cases that no other administration has adopted. Most recently, the court announced it would hear arguments and decide a case testing whether the Department of Homeland Security may deport migrants to so-called "third countries," when their countries of origin refuse to accept them. Since Trump began his second term, his administration has deported thousands of people to third world countries where they have no connections, may not speak the language, have often been jailed and allegedly subject to torture. The court has twice blocked lower court decisions that prevented the third country policy, and now the justices have said they will hear arguments about the policy in December.
In a second immigration case, the issue is the Trump administration's policy of detaining undocumented immigrants without a bond hearing, regardless of how long they have been in the U.S.
Possible cases: The 10 commandments and much more
There are many more cases waiting in the wings that the justices may take up. Among them is a case that seeks to reverse a nearly half-century-old Supreme Court precedent; it bars public schools from posting the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms. Now, however, Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana and Alabama have passed laws that conflict with the Supreme Court's 1980 ruling, and the lower courts are split on the question. That split all but guarantees the the Supreme Court will revisit the question.
Another case that could to make it to the court this term tests whether states can regulate Kalshi, the $40 billion prediction market behemoth that has sports fans betting on everything from the next pitch to the point spread or at the other end of the spectrum, betting on the outcome of Supreme Court cases.
And then there are cases that the Trump administration has slow-walked for close to two years, after quickly losing in the lower courts. Prime examples are the administration's attempt to deny medical research grants to Harvard University, and other attempts to deny security clearances to law firms, as well as seeking money damages from law firms Trump views as hostile. Earlier this year the Justice Department told a federal court in Washington that it was dropping the law firm cases. But the next day it went back to court to reverse course.
"They don't want to take up cases that they're going to lose, but on the other hand, they have a boss who wants everything taken up there [to the Supreme Court]," says Stanford University law professor Pam Karlan.
Georgetown's professor Vladeck adds that in his view, "The real story of the upcoming term hasn't been written yet because what we're going to look back on as the biggest cases of the term … are not on the docket yet."
Elections
More immediately, the probability is that like it or not the justices will be drawn into the election. The Trump administration has sought to influence elections in numerous ways, and it's unclear what efforts the administration might take going forward.
Democrats have a battalion of lawyers lined up to deal with problems on the ground — whether it's moving polling places at the last minute or having federal agents stationed near polling places. But if there are serious voting problems, they will likely end up at the Supreme Court's door — on the emergency docket.

UP man poses as Lawrence-Godara gang member, threatens Haryana BJP leader; arrested
Zahid Hussain, a state executive committee member of the BJP, approached the Nuh City Police Station on September 28, alleging that he had received a threatening call the previous night.
Haryana Police has arrested a 19-year-old man in Nuh for allegedly threatening BJP leader Zahid Hussain by posing as a member of the Lawrence Bishnoi and Rohit Godara gang and demanding a ransom of Rs 5 crore. The accused, identified as Akash Yadav alias Anshu, is a resident of Etawah district in Uttar Pradesh.
Hussain, a state executive committee member of the BJP, approached the Nuh City Police Station on September 28, alleging that he had received a threatening call the previous night.
According to his complaint, the caller claimed to be associated with the Lawrence Bishnoi and Rohit Godara gang and demanded Rs 5 crore. The caller allegedly threatened to kill Hussain and members of his family if the ransom was not paid.
Police subsequently registered a case at Nuh City Police Station under relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and launched an investigation.
The probe involved technical analysis with assistance from the Cyber Cell to trace the mobile numbers allegedly used to make the threatening calls.
During the investigation, police found that the numbers used to contact Hussain were registered in the name of Akash Yadav alias Anshu. Acting on technical leads, a police team traced the accused and arrested him. A mobile phone was recovered from his possession at the time of arrest and seized for further examination.
Police then examined WhatsApp numbers linked to the device and analysed other digital activity as part of the probe. During questioning, the accused allegedly made significant revelations that are now being used to take the investigation forward.
The probe also led police to identify another individual whose possible involvement is currently being examined.
To facilitate further recovery, questioning and collection of digital evidence, Yadav was produced before a court and remanded in police custody for two days.
During the remand period, police recovered an additional mobile phone, which investigators said could be important evidence in the case. The device is being examined along with other digital materials to establish how the alleged threats were made and whether further individuals were involved.
After completion of the police remand, Yadav was produced before the court again and sent to jail.
Nuh Police said the investigation remains ongoing and efforts are continuing to establish the complete circumstances surrounding the ransom demand.
Investigators are examining whether Yadav allegedly acted alone or whether other individuals or an organised network were involved in the incident.
Police are also analysing the digital evidence recovered during the investigation and information obtained during interrogation to establish the role, if any, of the suspected associate and identify other persons connected with the case.
Further legal action will be taken on the basis of evidence emerging during the investigation, police said.
The probe will focus on establishing the chain of communication, identifying all those involved, if any, and determining the circumstances behind the alleged attempt to demand ransom from the BJP leader.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Expansive red flags raised by two Election Commissioners within the poll panel over the Special Intensive Revision of voters list triggered a massive political storm on Wednesday, with the Opposition accusing CEC Gyanesh Kumar of indulging in "one-man autocracy" and demanding his removal.
Officials said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had flagged multiple issues, including deletion of names, in various states during the voter roll cleanup but the poll body was unanimous in its decisions related to the pan-India Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voters' list.
The reactions poured in after a report in The Indian Express revealed that questions were raised on issues related to the SIR of electoral rolls within the three-member Election Commission (EC) itself, time and again by two of the three Election Commissioners.
The national rollout of the SIR has been under the supervision of all three Commissioners. But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months -- four times on a single day -- to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge, the report in the English daily said.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh shared the screenshot of the media report on X.
Ramesh said that on behalf of the party, his colleague Abhishek Singhvi will be speaking in detail to the media on the sensational revelations made in the leading national newspaper on the way "the CEC has destroyed the credibility and integrity of the Election Commission of India".
Congress general secretary in-charge organisation K C Venugopal said there is no doubt remaining that Kumar has no right to remain in office.
"How the hell can one man, acting on His Master's orders, strike off names at whim? How can he sideline fellow Constitutional officers to only take blatantly illegal steps that put our democracy in danger?" he said.
"The right to vote is an essential Constitutional power given to every citizen, the fundamental bedrock of our democracy. If it is to be taken away, due process must be followed with utmost probity," he said.
"Today, when we are staring at crores of genuine voters being excluded and a similar number of bogus voters being added to the rolls, it is clear that Gyanesh Kumar was the Chief Architect of the nationwide 'Vote Chori' exercise, with the the Modi top brass pulling the strings," he alleged.
"We demand Gyanesh Kumar's immediate removal and a Supreme Court-monitored impartial investigation to expose the rot that has destroyed the ECI's credibility," Venugopal said.
If Kumar remains in office, the people of India will come forward and make sure that our democracy is not destroyed by a mere bureaucrat, he added.
Congress' media and publicity department head Pawan Khera lashed out at Kumar, saying he is "planted" and being "protected" by the BJP to hollow out the Election Commission of India from within.
"It was already known that things were not exactly well within the ECI. But just how messy, dysfunctional and, frankly, disturbing things had become is laid bare by this brilliant expose by @IndianExpress," he said on X.
Kumar has to be the single most sold-out bureaucrat of the Modi era who has disenfranchised crores of Indians, and he must face the law, he alleged.
Congress MP Manish Tewari also reacted to the media report, saying that if the ostensible facts as reported are correct then it seems to suggest that there is an "invisible hand" running the Election Commission.
"If rules were not allegedly followed and decisions were taken that were not unanimous or by majority then all the decisions of @ECISVEEP are per -se arbitrary and capricious if not completely illegal," Tewari said on X.
"This is perhaps a fit case for serious considering an impeachment proceeding but more importantly the fundamental question is as to how will the credibility of @ECISVEEP be ever resurrected," he said.
Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal demanded Kumar's suspension and filing of an FIR to probe who is behind his actions.
Former chief election commissioner O P Rawat said changes to the statutory voter registration Form 6 are "absolutely wrong and illegal", while describing revelations of differences within the Election Commission as "very serious" and "unfortunate".
CPI(M) MP John Brittas said this is no longer an Election Commission, it is a "one-man autocracy" under CEC Kumar.
"Two Election Commissioners have formally objected 14 times in 10 months. They branded the addition of new voters and mass deletion 'unauthorised and illegal'. They recorded objections to secret deletions, restorations, and form 6 changes that harass young first-time voters - all while being kept in the dark," he said.
This is the open subversion of the EC and our democracy too, Brittas said.
"Parliament must immediately start the process for the removal of the CEC. We had in fact submitted a notice for removal on 24th April, 2026 as per the constitutional stipulations - solid grounds and around 70 members signing( 50 in the stipulated number)," he said.
The Constitution provides this power for precisely such moments of institutional capture and subversion, he said.
"The Supreme Court must annul the entire SIR process without delay. When two of the three Commissioners put on record that the exercise is illegal and destructive of the electoral roll's integrity, judicial silence becomes complicity," Brittas said.
What Kumar is doing is the death knell of a democratic nation, he said.
"Remove the CEC. Strike down the SIR. Or accept that free and fair elections in India are already being buried," the CPI(M) MP said.
Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut also cited the media report, and said "A-Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail! He will have to go! His masters will flee the country and run away!"
TMC Rajya Sabha leader Derek O'Brien said on X, "Five months ago, 60+ Rajya Sabha MPs (50 needed) wrote to Chairman RS moving Motion to remove CEC Gyanesh Kumar. After big news break today that two Election Commissioners objected to many of CEC's actions, it's time to bring out the RS Motion today. Impeach CEC to save democracy".

Milt Windler, one of the four leaders of Mission Control who in 1970 directed the round-the-clock efforts to bring the Apollo 13 astronauts back to Earth safely, has died at the age of 94.
Windler died on Thursday, surrounded by his loving family, according to a brief notice posted online.
Named a NASA flight director in 1968 after working on recovery operations during the Mercury and Gemini programs, Windler also led a shift of flight controllers for the Apollo 8 first circumlunar flight and Apollo 10 lunar landing dress rehearsal, as well as the second, third and fourth moon landings — Apollo 12, Apollo 14 and Apollo 15. He then served as a flight director for all three crewed missions to the United States’ first space station, Skylab.
“Apollo was such a rapid pace that I don’t think people had the chance to think about it very much. It has only become more clear to me later on that we were making history,” said Windler in a 2006 oral history interview for the University of North Texas. “You’d do a mission and then you’d immediately turn around and get ready for another mission.”
“It was not [a] time for reflection,” Windler said.
Maroon Flight
Each flight director chose a team name (at first colors). As the seventh person to be appointed to the position — and one of the first two to be selected from outside of the flight operations team — Windler became “Maroon Flight.”
On his first mission at the flight director’s console, Windler was assigned to the third shift, putting him at the head of the operations control room when it was time to send the first humans beyond Earth orbit. The trans-lunar injection, or TLI, burn placed Apollo 8 crew members Frank Borman, Bill Anders and Jim Lovell on a trajectory to advance the United States ahead of the Soviet Union by becoming the first nation to orbit people around the moon.
Realizing this, Windler, working with his wife, Betty, and other flight controllers’ spouses, secretly prepared a batch of small red and blue flannel banners, each with the numeral “1” in white at their center. He planned to distribute the flags to the members of his Maroon team to wave at TLI as a not-so-subtle message to their space race adversaries.
“However, it was decided that this display was inappropriate, especially since the mission was only half over,” wrote Windler in a 2020 letter accompanying one of the flags that had since been acquired by a collector. “Consequently, the flags were never displayed during the mission and American flags were used at the time of a successful landing on Earth.”
Later, Windler and all of his colleagues in Mission Control were provided with a dramatic reminder about why you do not celebrate until the crew has stepped onto their recovery ship. For Apollo 13, Windler was named lead flight director.
“What that meant was you did the ascent — the liftoff from Earth, I should say, the launch — and you did the lunar surface activity,” he told the UNT interviewer. “But then, of course, after we lifted off from the Earth, when we got more toward the moon, why, the whole mission changed.”
Flight director Milt Windler, Maroon Flight (at left) looks on as the director of flight crew operations Deke Slayton displays a makeshift “mail box” as devised to adapt square command module carbon dioxide scrubbers with the round receptacles in the lunar module on board the crippled Apollo 13 spacecraft in April 1970.
Credit:
NASA
Flight director Milt Windler, Maroon Flight (at left) looks on as the director of flight crew operations Deke Slayton displays a makeshift “mail box” as devised to adapt square command module carbon dioxide scrubbers with the round receptacles in the lunar module on board the crippled Apollo 13 spacecraft in April 1970.
Credit:
NASA
An explosion tore through the Apollo 13 service module, crippling the spacecraft and venting the crew’s oxygen supply into space.
Instead of overseeing the third time humans had walked on the moon, Windler — together with Gold Flight, Gerry Griffin — polled the flight controllers in the room to develop three options for when, where and how long to fire the lunar module’s engine to put the Apollo 13 spacecraft on a path back to Earth.
It would not be the last time Windler was involved in re-planning a mission already underway, but not because something had gone awry. As flight director during the Skylab missions, the challenge was working with emerging scientific events.
“We had to come up with a system that would allow us to plan in real time and accommodate the science people. If something interesting happened on the sun, which it did several times, then we needed to be able to schedule the ATM [Apollo Telescope Mount] work,” he said in 2006.
“We invented a way of flight planning in real time, or cycles,” said Windler, where one day the science people talked about what they wanted to do, and the ‘Science Czar’ got with them and said, ‘All right, then, we need these particular objectives for tomorrow.’”
After the Skylab missions ended, Windler went to work on the space shuttle and the development of the remote manipulator system or “Canadarm,” the winged orbiters’ robotic arm contributed to the program by Canada. He then retired from NASA and joined private industry to work on what would become the International Space Station, consulting on the operations aspect of the orbiting laboratory, and later, as modules were produced, on some of the verification procedures.
‘Pay more attention’
Born on Jan. 10, 1932 in Hampton, Virginia, Milton Windler graduated from Virginia Tech (Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University) in 1954 with a degree in aeronautical engineering. He joined the U.S. Air Force’s Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (ROTC) while still in school and then worked for the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA), NASA’s predecessor, before serving in the Air Force for four years.
Windler rejoined NACA at Langley Research Center in Virginia and was there for its transition to becoming a NASA facility. He relocated to Houston, Texas, just as the Manned Spacecraft Center (today, Johnson Space Center) was being established.
Milt Windler stands with fellow flight directors Glynn Lunney, Gene Kranz and Gerry Griffin for President Richard Nixon’s presentation of the Presidential Medal of Freedom to NASA’s Apollo 13 mission operations team on April 18, 1970.
Credit:
NASA
Milt Windler stands with fellow flight directors Glynn Lunney, Gene Kranz and Gerry Griffin for President Richard Nixon’s presentation of the Presidential Medal of Freedom to NASA’s Apollo 13 mission operations team on April 18, 1970.
Credit:
NASA
As a member of Mission Control during the Apollo 13 mission, Windler and his fellow flight directors and controllers were awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then-President Richard Nixon in 1970. Windler was also honored with NASA’s Exceptional Service Medal.
Milton and Betty (née Selby) Windler had three children and eight grandchildren. A memorial service will take place in the coming weeks at the family’s former church in Friendswood, Texas.
“If I did it again, I’d probably try to do something more about trying to pay more attention,” said Windler. “Apollo was — well, all of [the missions] were … bang-bang-bang. You couldn’t enjoy, really, in a way you couldn’t savor it, like maybe it would have been better to have done.”
Robert Pearlman is a space historian, journalist and the founder and editor of collectSPACE, a daily news publication and online community focused on where space exploration intersects with pop culture. He is also a contributing writer for Space.com and co-author of "Space Stations: The Art, Science, and Reality of Working in Space” published by Smithsonian Books in 2018. He is on the leadership board for For All Moonkind and is a member of the American Astronautical Society's history committee.

OpenAI says its review in response to the Medicare and Hugging Face agent attacks is costing the company more than US$500,000 per day, as it deploys AI to examine data that would take a human 66m years to read.
The company has warned the review is ongoing, and more organisations may be informed they’ve been targeted in the near future.
On Friday evening, OpenAI revealed agents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.
It is the sixth government website in Australia to be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announced OpenAI’s agents had hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.
The reason for the delay compared to the revelation of the Medicare attack is due to the sheer volume of data OpenAI needs to review.
In a blog post this week the company revealed the large amount of work involved in reviewing its agents’ activity.
OpenAI said it has to review 50 petabytes of data – roughly 50m gigabytes.
“We’re working back through the records month by month, looking for potential unintended activity beyond the cases we’ve already found,” the company said.
“To put that in perspective, if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute, reading nonstop without ever sleeping or taking a break.”
The company is searching records for where models accessed and changed websites, or took actions involving passwords, application programming interface (API) access or other sensitive credentials.
AI is being used to help sift through the records, and it was costing the company more than half a million US dollars per day to go through. OpenAI said it also plans to increase its computing power as the process is refined.
As of late last month, more than 100 organisations had been notified of having being targeted by OpenAI’s agents, but the company said notifying an organisation does not mean private information was accessed or that their system was compromised.
OpenAI said it expects to find more cases and notify more organisations about events that may have occurred months ago.
Organisations will be informed privately if they need to investigate and address potential security issues, and OpenAI has said it will publicly report findings about agent behaviour and identified weaknesses in safeguards for the broader AI sector.
“We err on the side of notification when our models’ activity exposes a potential security vulnerability, even in cases where it is unclear if the information accessed was intended to be public, so the organization can investigate and take appropriate action,” OpenAI said.
OpenAI discovered the latest NSW government website breach on Tuesday, and informed the state government and the Australian Signals Directorate after a 48-hour review.
The Medicare breach has prompted the Australian government to require departments and agencies to undertake a stocktake of legacy technology to reduce the number of ageing systems within government and reduce the cybersecurity risk they may present in the event of an AI agent attack.
Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will front a joint parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday.

On the eve of Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.
Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by volunteer youth group Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.
But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the Pharaohs’ origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.
Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.
The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.
Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.
“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.
“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”
Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.
One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.
Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.
“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.
“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.
This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.
Monica Hanna, an Egyptologist at the American University in Cairo, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.
“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”
Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.
They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.
“That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.
Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.
“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.
