Just before the state of Tennessee botched her execution and left her unconscious and on a ventilator, it offered Christa Pike a last meal.
She turned it down, asking instead that the money that was to be spent on her be used to buy pizza for homeless people in downtown Nashville, according to The New York Times.
Pike was to be executed on Wednesday at 10 a.m. By the end of the day, she would survive two lethal injection attempts, end up in the hospital, and force Tennessee to enact its second moratorium on executions in the last five years, according to the paper.
Pike, as of Oct. 3, was unconscious, intubated, and on a ventilator at a Nashville-area hospital following the failed execution.
The 50-year-old woman's execution had been a point of contention and concern for both her legal team and anti-death penalty advocates in the weeks before the incident.
She had been convicted and sentenced to death for torturing and murdering her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18 years old. Pike has admitted that she was without remorse when she was convicted, but has grown over the years to regret the life she took.
Her defense team argued during the trial that Pike was a victim of extreme trauma and sexual abuse, and that the weight of those factors on her actions was not considered during her trial and sentencing.
The family of the victim told the NYT that Pike deserves “swift justice.”
Pike received a short-lived stay of execution just 90 minutes before she was scheduled to die on Wednesday. A federal appeals court issued the stay, saying it needed more time to consider new arguments in her case.
Later, just after 5:45 p.m., the U.S. Supreme Court lifted the stay, clearing the path for the execution.
The Department of Corrections has insisted it followed its lethal injection procedures to the letter. Randy Spivey, Pike's attorney, claims otherwise.
He told the NYT that state protocol says the process should take 10 minutes, but it instead took an hour.
“I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt,” he said.
He told the paper that the legal team had warned the state that a lethal injection was a bad idea, noting that Pike has small veins and a blood disorder.
Spivey said Pike was even trying to help the executioner find viable injection spots.
“Over and over again she said, ‘Please try up on my shoulder higher, please try here, please try here,’” Spivey told the paper.
The state ultimately failed to execute Pike and instead left her unconscious and critically ill.
Despite the current moratorium on executions, there may be future attempts to kill Pike. Gubernatorial front-runner Sen. Marsha Blackburn said, if elected, she would try again to execute Pike, according to the NYT.
Whether the state can try again may be determined by the state of Pike’s mind when — or if — she recovers. The Supreme Court has previously ruled that a prisoner sentenced to die must have the cognitive abilities to possess a “rational understanding” of why they’re being executed.
Pike’s lawyers have asked Gov. Bill Lee to allow her to live out the rest of her life in prison. He has ordered an investigation to determine what went wrong during the execution.

I love Cancún's balmy, multi-blue-toned water, but I'm less fond of the crowds, nightlife, and traffic. These days, when I travel, I want as much peace and nature as possible, from calming ocean waves to the squeaky chatter of local birds.
I've been to Cancún countless times, but recently visited the nearby Isla Mujeres for the first time — and found it to be the quiet, tropical escape that I needed.
This island is just a 30-minute boat ride from Cancún, but it feels worlds away. It's also much smaller — the entire island of Isla Mujeres is 5 miles long, less than half of Cancún's Hotel Zone alone.
The island is ideal for those who, like me, want to avoid the crowds and loud music of Cancún and Tulum.
The island is just a quick ferry ride from Cancún
Isla Mujeres is an easy day trip from Cancún, but there are plenty of hotels — from luxury options to budget picks — for those who wish to stay longer.
On this trip, I picked an all-inclusive resort that provided a catamaran ride from Cancún, though there's also take a ferry for under $20 (one way).
The vacation began the moment I boarded the catamaran: I found a prime, comfortable spot next to the captain and enjoyed the scenic boat ride. The crew told us it's not rare to see dolphins along the way (although we sadly didn't).
One of the first things I did upon arriving was explore the island. It was fun to pass brightly colored homes painted in shades like banana yellow and aquamarine, and watch cute iguanas sunbathe.
I also stopped at popular Instagrammable spots and monuments, such as the Mayan goddess Ixchel statue at Punta Sur, toward the southern tip of the island.
Isla Mujeres is one of the best places in the world to swim with whale sharks
Every year, hundreds of whale sharks arrive on Isla Mujeres between summer and early fall for a bountiful plankton feast. I learned that this is widely considered one of the ethical places to swim with whale sharks because regulations are in place to protect the animals and their environment.
I was lucky enough to visit during the prime season to see these gigantic, gentle creatures on a boat tour. I also got an unexpected bonus: There were at least a dozen surprise manta rays swirling around.
Isla Mujeres is also a fantastic base for scuba diving. I didn't get a chance to dive on my trip, but next time I visit, I plan to explore the MUSA Underwater Museum, which has hundreds of life-sized underwater sculptures.
There are several white-sand beaches, but my favorite was the popular Playa Norte, located on the northern tip. I highly recommend stretching out on the sand and grabbing a treat from one of the roving ice cream vendors.
The food was incredible
Seafood is especially good here, and you'll find nearly every kind of Mexican food you'd expect on the mainland.
I tried tikin xic for the first time; locals told me that it was one of the island's most famous dishes. It's usually served whole, marinated Mayan-style with peppery achiote paste and spices. I couldn't get enough of the tender, smoky, and slightly spicy fish.
I didn't get to try these dishes while I was there, but I was told that cochinita pibil (marinated, slow-roasted pork) and marquesita (a fried, crepe-like wrap filled with cheese) were other local musts.
Isla Mujeres is a perfect place for Cancún and Tulum fans who want turquoise water without the crowds
I hate crowds and lines, and I loved feeling relaxed at every activity and restaurant. I found that I could also walk around town and feel comfortable and at ease, since the streets felt generally less populated with tourists.
For those who are interested, there was some nightlife, with live music and bars downtown — but in my experience, the party scene seemed to wrap up on the earlier side, around midnight.
This was a bonus for me, since I'm usually in bed by 9 p.m. and I don't drink alcohol. For a sober, early-bedtime girl like me, Isla Mujeres is the ideal alternative to Cancún.
I already can't wait to go back.

In September, a rumor spread online about an Australian man riding high after entering a cannabis plant in the tomato category of a local garden competition — and winning the first place prize.
For example, a Facebook page called The Local Situation posted the claim alongside an image purportedly showing the 83-year-old budding "tomato" gardener with his alleged gold medal cannabis plant (screenshotted). "Panellist Marjorie Budd said the panel was so taken by its lush foliage and rich aroma that nobody asked where the tomatoes were," the post adds.
The rumor spread elsewhere on Facebook (screenshotted).
Snopes readers searched our website to determine whether the story was rooted in truth or just blowing smoke.
In short, the claim is labeled as satire. The Local Situation Facebook page was the first to post the rumor. The account's content is dedicated to fake stories based in Australia.
"Real local issues with a satirical edge," the page's account description reads (archived).
The person behind The Local Situation said in an email to Snopes that the story was satire and had no connection to any real stories.
"I regularly do Cannabis related satirical posts to raise awareness for medical cannabis driving rights and cannabis legalisation in Australia," said the account owner.
Growing and consuming cannabis for recreational purposes is illegal in New South Wales and in most of Australia.
The image in The Local Situation's post was also generated using artificial intelligence, according to OpenAI's detector tool, which checks for an invisible AI watermark known as SynthID. (OpenAI is the company behind ChatGPT; its detection tool can only tell if the image was created using the company's own AI software.) The Local Situation also confirmed that the image was created using AI.
(OpenAI)
Other indicators the image is AI-generated include distorted faces in the background and unreadable text on name tags and labels.
Pangram, which is considered a leading AI text detection tool, determined that 100% of the text in the original post was also AI-generated. (Despite Pangram's comparative reliability, it is worth noting these tools are still fallible.)

Snopes has debunked similar fictional rumors, such as a claim that Canada faced a major donut shortage shortly after the country legalized recreational marijuana use.

Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as northern conflict escalates
- Published
Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict.
On Thursday, Ethiopia announced it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security.
Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic relations, saying Ethiopia's decision had left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action.
Meanwhile, a pro-government militia says it has seized the town of Milazat, which is just 20km (12 miles) south-east of Mekelle, the capital of Tigray, where the main anti-government group is based.
The BBC has not been able to verify this claim.
The diplomatic confrontation came hours after powerful explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, including near Ethiopia's military headquarters.
It follows a sharp deterioration in relations between the neighbours, with Ethiopia accusing Eritrea of supporting a new rebel alliance – an allegation Asmara has repeatedly denied.
Eritrea described the decision to expel its ambassador as "astounding".
"Eritrea has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia," its foreign ministry said, warning of "negative corollaries" from the decision.
The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian federal forces battle fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies across parts of the northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
Ethiopia has also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, giving him 48 hours to leave the country, according to state media. The government has not publicly given a reason for the decision.
Egypt responded by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period, according to the state-affiliated Al Qahera News.
Relations between Ethiopia and Egypt have been strained for years, largely over Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), a huge hydroelectric project on the Blue Nile.
Egypt, which relies heavily on the Nile for its water supplies, has long expressed concern about the dam's potential impact on its share of the river's water.

The cutting of ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea mark a dramatic reversal from 2018, when Abiy restored relations with Asmara after two decades of hostility, prompting joyous scenes as the border reopened and families separated for years were reunited.
The rapprochement helped earn the Ethiopian prime minister the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019.
The latest hostilities are the most serious since a peace agreement ended the devastating Tigray war in 2022. An African Union mediator previously estimated that about 600,000 people had died during that two-year conflict.
Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
A pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers had been involved on the front lines.
The BBC has not independently verified the allegation.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and the internet and phone lines have been cut, making it difficult to get reliable information from the region. It is not clear who was responsible for cutting communications.
In a rare response to the BBC before diplomatic relations were severed, Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel denied that it was involved in the fighting in Tigray, which borders his country.
He told BBC Tigrinya that Ethiopia's governing Prosperity Party was blaming neighbouring countries to divert attention from conflicts and other problems within Ethiopia.
The two countries were allies during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF.
But relations have deteriorated significantly since then, particularly over Ethiopia's push for direct access to the Red Sea.
Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993.
Abiy has repeatedly argued that access to the sea is essential to Ethiopia's long-term economic and security interests, while Eritrea has accused his government of harbouring ambitions over its ports.
Federal forces and their allies appear to have made gains in southern Tigray and are advancing towards Mekelle, the regional capital. In Alamata, a doctor told the BBC earlier this week that at least 52 civilians had been killed during three days of intense fighting.
The TPLF has also been fighting in neighbouring Afar, which lies along Ethiopia's crucial transport corridor to Djibouti and the sea. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to have fled their homes there.
Both the Ethiopian government and the TPLF accuse the other of starting the latest hostilities. Tigrayan authorities say their forces were responding to a federal offensive and drone strikes, while Addis Ababa says Tigrayan fighters launched attacks after taking control of federally administered airports in Tigray.
The African Union has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise restraint and resolve their differences through diplomatic channels, warning against actions that could further destabilise the region.
The UN has also warned that the deteriorating security situation is severely disrupting humanitarian work in northern Ethiopia. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said drone activity and air strikes were putting civilians, vital infrastructure and aid operations at risk, while insecurity and road closures were restricting humanitarian movements.
The UN has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

On the edge of Piazza Navona, one of the grandest squares in central Rome, Barry and Linda, visitors from Texas in the US, stepped out of a golf cart. They planned to cross the square on foot, perhaps stopping to admire Lorenzo Bernini’s 17th-century Fountain of the Four Rivers, before being picked up by their driver at the opposite end.
The couple had already done a walking tour on day one of their trip, and had been so exasperated by a stifling three-hour shuffle along a corridor towards the Sistine Chapel on day two that by the third day they wanted to give their tired feet a rest.
“When I first heard you could do golf cart tours in Rome, I thought to myself: that sounds a little weird,” said Barry. “But then we decided to try it out.” He said the most enjoyable thing about the experience was “feeling the breeze”.
Rome is a difficult city to navigate, noted Linda, especially its ancient narrow streets in the centre. “There are no sidewalks,” she said. “Our feet were hurting and we needed a break.”
For visitors, golf cart tours offer respite from the heat, crowds and cobbles. For residents, however, their proliferation in recent years has become another source of frustration in a city already wrestling with traffic and overtourism.
Taxi drivers are especially incensed, accusing golf cart operators of stealing their business, while one local newspaper said the city had been “taken hostage” by the vehicles.
Now Rome authorities are cracking down on the burgeoning trade. Police intensified checks this week after the news agency Adnkronos reported that 90% of the roughly 500 golf carts circulating in the city were operating without authorisation.
In recent days, police stopped 131 carts around Piazza Navona, the Pantheon, Circo Massimo and the Spanish Steps, issuing €38,000 of fines for offences ranging from unlicensed driving to illegal parking.
Rome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate an activity that “risks spiralling out of control”, Eugenio Patanè, a councillor for mobility, told the news agency Adnkronos.
Prices vary based on the type of tour and duration, but the cost per person can start at €100 and exceed €400 for a half-day trip. Barry and Linda paid €310 for their three-hour ride. “But it’s worth it,” said Barry.
Rome’s traffic problem is hardly new. Julius Caesar tried to tackle the issue more than 2,000 years ago by banning private vehicles and commercial carts from the city’s streets during the day. Today, pedestrians, cars, scooters, delivery vans and the occasional rogue horse-drawn carriage all jostle for space.
Tourists can also take tours in Fiat 500s, on Vespas with sidecars, and even in tuk-tuks. But the golf carts seem to have drawn a special kind of wrath.
“There are too many of them,” said Nora Fahmi, who works at Trevimage, an art photography shop behind the Pantheon. “We’ve had this shop for 13 years and have seen all sorts of things, but the golf cart situation is kind of wild.”
Nearby, two teenagers from Israel were taking a rest on a parked cart. “We just want a lift to the Colosseum but you have to book online,” said their mother, Miri. “Rome is too crowded and it’s difficult to walk.”
Elisa Isacco, who lives in the Monti area, spares no sympathy for the weary tourists. “What do they actually see or learn about Rome when they are on one of these things?” she said. “I find myself having to dodge them all the time – Rome is chaotic, it’s like a jungle.”
Amid the clampdown, several golf cart tour operators have banned staff from speaking to the press. But Leo Pavoncello, a driver for an operator in the Jewish Ghetto area, was happy to publicly defend the trade.
“Golf carts are silent and eco-friendly,” he said. “Rome is not an easy city to visit but these vehicles allow people with disabilities and families with children to see the sites in a comfortable way. On top of that, they provide jobs for young people.”
Pavoncello, who was subjected to the police checks and was found to be operating fully legitimately, argued that a few rotten apples were giving the business a bad name.
“I don’t understand why they are targeting us,” he said, although he suspects “taxi lobbies” are piling on the pressure. “But Rome is a touristic city that has always been full of traffic, and the golf carts are simply another mode of transport.”

Amid increasing competition in AI, Google has now unveiled its new, most powerful model Gemini 4 Argon. The model is targeting long-running workloads across software engineering, enterprise knowledge work and cybersecurity. Argon is initially being rolled out to a select group of “trusted cyber defenders” through Google's Fairwind programme, with wider access planned for developers, enterprises and consumers. Google said paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers will get access to Gemini 4 Argon first, although it is yet to announce a broader public release date. “It shows frontier performance in complex workflows, cyber defense and software engineering. Teams are using it extensively at Google, from coding to quantum computing, great feedback,” Google CEO Sundar Pichai said. Google said Gemini 4 Argon will launch at an introductory price of $2 per a million input tokens and $10 per a million output tokens. Cached input tokens will be priced at a 95% discount to the standard input-token rate. One of the biggest changes with Gemini 4 Argon is its 1 Mn-token output limit, up from the previous 64K-token limit. Google said the expanded capacity allows the model to sustain longer reasoning trajectories and work through complex, multi-step tasks in a single run. “Google engineers have been using Argon for their daily tasks, from everyday debugging to large-scale codebase migrations and algorithm designs. It sets a new state of the art on DeepSWE v1.1 (77.9%), which measures a model’s performance in real-world long-horizon software engineering tasks,” the tech giant said. Beyond coding, Google said Argon is designed for knowledge-intensive work across areas such as finance, legal research and drafting. As per Google Deepmind's tests, Argon performs strongly across a wide range of real-world tasks. In its testing, Argon scored highly in areas such as professional knowledge work, coding, scientific problem-solving and handling very large amounts of information. Its particularly strong long-context results suggest it can work with large volumes of information while still finding and using relevant details. The model also has multimodal capabilities for professional use cases. Google said Argon can analyse charts, understand long videos and work across multiple documents to support tasks that require visual and contextual understanding. Google Puts Cybersecurity At The Centre Of Argon Cybersecurity is a major focus of Gemini 4 Argon. The model is said to autonomously identify, validate and patch software vulnerabilities. The model is available without its usual cyber guardrails to the initial users and Google's internal teams. Cybersecurity company Wiz is already using Argon through its “Scan for Good” initiative, as per Google. In an early demonstration, Google said Argon identified a critical vulnerability exposing sensitive personal information in healthcare software used by hospitals globally. Google is taking a phased approach to the rollout because of the model's cybersecurity capabilities. The company said it is strengthening safeguards against misuse, including cyberattacks and CBRN-related threats, while also working on protections against indirect prompt injection attacks. The AI Race The developments come as Google, Anthropic and OpenAI are engaged in an intense competition to build and deploy models that offer superior performance while are more cost effective. Earlier in September, OpenAI launched its "most capable model yet", GPT-6 Astra, a more autonomous AI model. The model supports reasoning efforts ranging from low to maximum and comes with a 1.05 Mn-token context window and a maximum output of 1.28 Lakh tokens. Anthropic also recently launched Claude Opus 5.5, claiming that the model delivers performance comparable to its more powerful Claude Fable 5.1 on most tasks while costing 40% less to run than Claude Opus 5 on typical workloads. Claude Opus 5.5 is priced at $4 per Mn input tokens and $20 per Mn output tokens, with Anthropic also cutting cache-read costs by 60%. The company is positioning the model for agentic coding, computer use and knowledge work. On a different note, Google has also been expanding its AI push in India beyond model development. Earlier in September, the company selected four Indian startups (Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests and Climitra Carbon) for the inaugural Google DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet (APAC). The startups are part of a 16-member APAC cohort and will receive access to Google's AI stack, technical support and mentorship to develop AI-led solutions for environmental challenges.

Digger is poised to be one of the biggest box-office flops of the year
Tom Cruise-led Warner Bros. film is projected to rake in a disappointing opening weekend
Despite a major star's return to dramatic acting, a two-time best director winner at the Oscars and enough publicity to rival the moon landing, Digger looks set to become one of the biggest box-office disasters of the year.
According to Variety, the dark comedy from director Alejandro G. Iñárritu and starring Tom Cruise saw its costs balloon from an original budget of $125 million US to $160-180 million — putting a break-even return around $350 million US when including its marketing spend. (Warner Bros. pushed back on this, telling Variety their actual break-even point is around $300 million US).
It earned only $1.2 million US in previews. And according to the Hollywood Reporter, Warner predicts the film will only earn $12-15 million US domestically this weekend: a dismal opening for the studio in a year already littered with poor performers. Following their films The Bride!, Supergirl, The End of Oak Street and Practical Magic 2 all releasing to apparent losses, that string of failures will possibly be capped by one of Warner Bros.'s biggest flops of the decade.
A bizarre story about an oil tycoon tasked with saving the world from a catastrophe his drilling caused, Digger was always a risk. The R-rated black comedy opted to skip the festival circuit entirely — instead operating on the hopes that strong word of mouth and big-name buzz would convince audiences to get off the couch and head to theatres.
The strategy of avoiding early critical negativity and gunning straight for Cruise fans made a sort of sense: it represents the actor's first non-franchise film since 2017's Barry Seal biopic American Made.
And it is directed by Iñárritu: the auteur whose Birdman won best picture and director at the Oscars, while the following year's The Revenant snagged Leonardo DiCaprio his long-awaited best actor award along with another director win for Iñárritu. But as its earliest critical responses started to release last month, a wave of negative press threatened to sink those chances.
It has been called "the worst movie of Tom Cruise's career" by the Boston Globe, "a metafictional morass" from RogerEbert.com and "a lumbering white elephant of a movie that it almost makes you sorry for everyone involved" by the New York Times. In response to the negative reviews, the film's producers released an ad positioning Cruise's character cursing out critics.
But largely, even critics who loved the film — such as this writer — widely predicted that Digger would be too experimental and odd to ever hope to recoup its budget.
That puts Warner Bros. in a potentially difficult position; after a strong, awards-leading 2025 (including hits like Sinners, Weapons and One Battle After Another) their 2026 slate only offers modest success. Wuthering Heights, Lee Cronin's The Mummy and Evil Dead Burn did pull off positive numbers, though not a single Warner movie has earned above $100 million US domestically this year.
At the most extreme estimates, Digger's failure could put it into the arena with 2026's other big flops: Melania, which earned roughly $16 million US off a reported $40 million budget, and the Anthony Mackie-led Desert Warrior, which made less than $1 million US off its reported $150 million US budget, is still the biggest failure of the year.

Digger could still prove valuable for Warner Bros. Despite its dismal expected performance, there is still speculation on whether Cruise could be pushed to Academy Awards success in the end. And given Cruise films' strong brand recognition, it could prove to be popular on streaming.
But the failure comes as the last release before Warner Bros. is fully acquired by Paramount on Tuesday. Buried beneath every American city is a mysterious jumble of cables, pipes, and gas lines, entangled like a pair of wired headphones the moment you pull them out of your pocket. Every time a contractor sticks a shovel in the asphalt, they embark on a high-risk excavate-by-dots obstacle course, dodging color-coded clusters of spaghetti-like power lines, gas mains, sewers, and fiber-optic cables. A line of blue spray paint means water. Red means power. Yellow is gas. Orange is telecom.
Disney World solved a problem that could save America billions every year
Our cities are built atop a dangerous obstacle course of cables. The Magic Kingdom found a better way.
About 700,000 times a year — that’s once every 47 seconds — something goes wrong.
A backhoe slices into a cable and cuts off a 911 call center, or a woman comes home to find her dryer and hot water heater on fire after a contractor pierced her electrical line. Just last week, a contractor accidentally severed a single telecommunication cable that proved critical enough to ground flights at some of the nation’s largest airports on the eve of the UN General Assembly, ensnaring even world leaders like Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in delays.
The ground beneath our city streets has never been so crowded, driven by a furious race to lay fiber optic cables carrying the data that fills your social media feeds and transmits your ChatGPT queries. Nor have the systems we use to find out where it’s safe to dig — namely, a hotline and all that colorful spray paint — ever felt so catastrophically insufficient.
“If the locator mismarked the line, if the line wasn’t marked, if there was no map that even said the line was there,” said Sarah Magruder Lyle, president of the Common Ground Alliance, a trade association focused on underground damage prevention, “there are a variety of issues that could happen before the excavator even puts a shovel or a backhoe in the ground.”
According to Common Ground, such incidents cost the US about $83.2 billion per year, roughly as much as we invest in public transit annually nationwide. But the actual financial toll may be even higher, because every time a crew stumbles across a mislabeled power line or a gas pipe everyone else forgot about, it can delay construction for months on end. As Magruder Lyle put it, “if they get out there and they find something that they’re not supposed to, you have to go back and reengineer the whole project.”
Such surprises can also lead to tragedy. A 5-year-old named Alistair Lamb was killed in Missouri last spring after a contractor drilled into a gas line near his home, spewing fumes that leveled his house when his unsuspecting father flipped a light switch. And just this May, another unmarked gas line killed three people when contractors struck it, leading an apartment complex in Dallas to explode.
Yet the messy underbelly of our cities remains largely invisible, with accountability for issues foisted upon and at times evaded by a hodgepodge of finger-pointing private utility companies, agencies, and contractors. And that’s a shame because there is, in fact, a better way to bury the cables and pipelines that our modern lives depend on, and a multitude of better ways that we can find the ones we’ve already buried.
What Disney World gets right about the stuff we bury
To understand one utopian vision for how all this could work, look no further than the happiest place on Earth. That’s a moniker Disney World has earned, in my mind, not for its Mickey Mouse waffles (though my niece may disagree), but for its world-class utility corridors, also known as utilidors.
Directly beneath the Magic Kingdom is a sprawling network of tunnels. Initially designed to shepherd around Mickey and his friends, the system now also serves as one of the largest utility corridors ever created. Unlike the rest of America, where cables are typically dumped in ditches before being covered with dirt, the electrical lines that power Cinderella’s castle quite literally get the princess treatment.
Alongside water pipes, sewers, and animatronic control systems, these power lines lace the walls and ceilings of the utilidors, meaning they’re protected from weather and changes in the soil. They are also easy to monitor, catalog, and access if something needs fixing. While the cost of building a controlled system like this is much higher upfront than burying directly in the ground, the practice virtually eliminates the risk of accidentally rupturing a gas main or slicing a fiber optic cable during routine maintenance. Once they’re built, they can also drastically reduce costs in the long run because you no longer need to tear up a street every time a utility needs fixing.
“Obviously, it’s expensive,” said Debra Laefer, a professor of civil and urban engineering at New York University, “but in the long term, it would be hugely cheaper,” especially “in areas where we are digging all the time, there’s a direct business case for moving towards these utilidors.”
As fantastical as Disney World’s imagineered system may seem — and it was, to be clear, predicated on a not-easily-reproducible master plan — the idea of storing utility lines in easy-to-access tunnels is not just for amusement parks. It is possible even in places where most of those lines are currently lying in the dirt, as Prague proved back in the 1970s, when the city decided it was fed up with destroying its precious cobblestone streets every time a buried pipe or cable needed fixing. The city now boasts a sprawling utility tunnel network, occasionally patrolled, evidently, by a couple of robot dogs tasked with mapping out every cable.
Singapore has also spent years building out walkable utility corridors that operate much like the Magic Kingdom’s, transmitting water, data, and energy from the safety of well-organized underground tunnels. Some of Tokyo’s largest districts store their cables and gas lines in huge concrete utility ducts, and many Parisian water lines and fiber optics are kept across the city’s centuries-old sewer system, a catacombs of waste made easily navigable by blue-and-white street signs that correspond to the avenues above. Many university campuses across the US also boast their own sprawling utilidors.
In most cases, cities chose not to relocate utilities all at once, a feat that would probably be financially prohibitive and deeply disruptive. Rather, they took advantage of all the times they’ve needed to relocate utility lines anyway, a standard (and expensive) practice for big building projects like the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing or the Second Avenue Subway, a major transportation project in New York City that’s been consistently delayed by unmapped utility lines. A group of graduate students found that building such a tunnel in parts of NYC would likely cost at least twice as much as dropping a utility line in the ground, but could recoup the costs within 47 years.
“There are streets in New York City that have been excavated at least once a year, every year for the past 30 years,” Laefer said. If you just prioritize those streets, gathering the piping in a “big concrete box” underground, you could allow workers to complete most repairs without needing to disturb the streets or sidewalks above at all.
But building new utility tunnels would require that we first come to better understand the wires and piping already entangled under our cities, which if you recall, we have only a surprisingly flimsy picture of in most cities today. But if every surprise utility line is an opportunity to move it somewhere better, it is also an opportunity, at the very least, to map out where it is.
To that end, a few years ago, Laefer led a $1.2 million pilot funded by the National Science Foundation to create a test case for 3D-mapping New York City’s underground utilities, a project that’s since been adopted into a citywide initiative. The city says it plans to roll out the spruced up utilities locating system in 2028. The UK debuted a similar digital map of over 3 million kilometers of underground pipes and power, owned by hundreds of utilities and agencies a few years ago. The nation projects that it could help save over $500 million per year by minimizing delays and accidental damage. In places where Singapore has not yet stuffed its utilities into walkable tunnels, the city’s own mapping and utilities coordination has already saved it an estimated $230 million in avoided clashes since 2024. Not bad for an intervention that doesn’t even require any physical rebuilding.
So why hasn’t every American city copied London or Singapore?
Well, US cities tend to be plagued by even more private utilities and patchwork local and state norms and regulations than a nation like the United Kingdom. Getting them to pool together what they often consider proprietary underground data is challenging, and few local officials have opted to prioritize such efforts. But this may well change as more and more fiber optics go into the ground, more flights get canceled, more apartment complexes explode, more power lines flicker off, more sinkholes form, and more Americans come to be all too acquainted with the perils lurking just beneath our feet.
“I think at this point, it’s more about political will and money than any technical obstacle,” Laefer said. “Technically, we’re there. It’s just a matter of doing it.”

SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “Behemoth!” in theaters Dec. 4
Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” bowed at the New York Film Festival Friday, and Lincoln Center’s Tully Hall seemed a fitting place to showcase a film about a musician.
Written and directed by Gilroy, the film stars Pedro Pascal as a cellist who returns to Los Angeles after a life on the road. Music is in his DNA — his parents were musicians, as were his grandparents. Music serves as a storytelling device, with Alex’s performances, whether on stage or in films he worked on, triggering flashbacks that reveal why he left Hollywood and what brought him back.
Popular on Variety
Gilroy wanted distinct scores for each film Alex works on. Rather than rely on a single composer, Gilroy turned to nine composers: Michael Abels, Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Michael Giacchino, James Newton Howard, Henry Jackman, Nami Melumad, Brandon Roberts and Alan Silvestri, known as the Behemoth Collective, to deliver distinct cues for the fictional movies Alex works on. In doing so, each composer brought their unique voices to the film.
Speaking with Variety, Gilroy explains that he had been sitting with the idea for years. He recalled the first time he walked into the John Williams Scoring Stage, steeped in Hollywood history. “You get in there, and there’s the emotional power and the smell of that room. It’s such a place of work, and then this incredible magic thing happens and there’s no place for the music to go except into the microphones and into your ears. It can’t escape that room.”
He went on to say, “It’s a vivid emotional trigger and I just kept wondering every time I went there — why didn’t anybody make a movie about this? Every time I went, I was like, ‘God, there’s got to be a movie here somewhere.’ I couldn’t figure it out.”
Eventually, he did.
He wrote a script that is a love letter to movie music and the art of scoring, carefully curating a story that allowed him to seamlessly integrate the work of the Behemoth Collective into the film.
Gilroy didn’t want one composer. “I knew I had to have different voices, and once you’re going to open it up, you want to cast it like actors,” he explains. “I made backstories for all the shows, so all the shows have a story to them and I could tell all the composers what the plots of their show were.” With that he started going out to composers. “Henry Jackman was the first one who came on, and he was so enthusiastic from the beginning. He gave me the enthusiasm to keep going forward with it. I talked to some people that I knew. I knew I wanted Michael Giacchino for the cartoon cue. I knew that I’d bring Brandon back,” and so the collective eventually came together.
Variety spoke with all nine composers to break down their cues and the key instruments they used to bring the “Behemoth!” score together.
Michael Abels
Abels was tasked with composing the music for Alex’s solo cello practice sessions. In one scene, Alex practices in a room and the music transitions into a flashback of Alex as a six-year-old prodigy performing Bach’s Cello Prelude No. 1 on “The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson.” Abels explains, “The music morphs from a warm-up exercise into the actual Bach piece.”
Emily Bear
Bear wrote the love theme for “Season of Glass.” She says, “It’s inspired by the French and Italian film scores of the ’60s: a lot of lush strings, beautiful harmonics, a lot of jazz-inspired progressions, but in an orchestral setting.”
Gilroy provided a detailed backstory for the fictional film, describing a young widow, a wealthy East Coast summer setting and a boy preparing to go to war. Bear also wrote a waltz for a scene where the young widow teaches the boy to dance. Bear notes, “It’s this very intimate, slow, tentative waltz that has some contention building underneath, so we added a lot of counterpoint and weird chromatic stuff underneath.”
Lukas Frank
Frank composed the film’s original song, “Your God Is Dying,” as well as the “Serian Suite,” which is tied to Alex’s character. “The suite is the underscore that opens throughout. It comes in throughout,” Frank explains.
The prepared piano was a key element of the “Serian Suite.” “There’s someone drilling on a string to make this low droning sound,” Frank notes. “The whole movie opens with the sound of the pedal coming down off the piano, and then some simple strings come in.”
Michael Giacchino
Giacchino wrote music using a standard orchestra for the cartoon “Happy & Slappy,” which Alex’s father composed during his career.
“I had to write a cue that his father wrote for these cartoons back in the ’60s cartoon, similar to ’Tom and Jerry,’” Giacchino explains. The music is used in a scene where Alex watches his brother fight while the cartoon score plays, syncing humorously with the action.
Henry Jackman
Jackman created the music for “Spies Don’t Run,” another fictional film within the story. Jackman describes it as “slightly ‘Jason Bourne-ish’, with a Middle Eastern flavor.”
Jackman’s work involved multiple scoring sessions. But for “Spies Don’t Run,” he took to it seriously and ended up scoring a six-minute suite using “a combination of orchestra, a little bit of slightly abstracted vocals, with quite a lot of heavy percussion.”
Nami Melumad
Melumad contributed the cue for one of the films within the film, “Tolerance Hill.” She explains that Gilroy’s guidance helped shape her approach. “Tony described it as a period film within the story, but it also had to emotionally lead us through Alex, the main character, as he revisits his childhood home.”
Melumad turned to the harp, an instrument Alex’s mother played, to evoke warmth, nostalgia and sadness. “It’s very delicate,” she says.
James Newton Howard
Howard composed the emotional finale of the film. “It’s pure underscore — a solo piano expressing the sadness of what’s happening in the story,” he says. Howard created multiple variations, including a piano-and-cello duet and orchestral arrangements. “It’s where everything comes together,” he notes.
Brandon Roberts
Roberts was tasked with writing “Look Away Jones,” a piece intended to sound like music Alex’s father had written for a TV show. Roberts says Gilroy described it as a “full-on smoking jazz band theme song for this make-believe show about an ex-football star turned detective.”
To prepare, Roberts listened to a lot of Quincy Jones and other theme music from that era. “It was an issue of coming up with a theme that felt like it actually existed and could have been on network television at the time,” he explains.
Roberts collaborated with renowned flute player Katisse Buckingham, who played jazz flute and Tim Liu, who assembled a group of musicians. “They knocked it out of the park,” Roberts says.
Alan Silvestri
Silvestri composed the cue that plays during the scoring session for “Open World,” a big Hollywood blockbuster and is a decoy title for a fictional production called “Behemoth.” It then bleeds from the scoring session into a sequence in the film. Silvestri describes it as a “big caper moment.” He adds, “I approached it as if it were a high-stakes adventure.”
Silvestri used a large orchestra to create a score that played the heist completely straight, despite its humorous premise.

Ireland coach Hallgrimsson hopes squad bonds will be stronger after tough period
BACKA TOPOLA, Serbia, Oct 3 : Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has said his side will come out of the international window stronger after two fractious games against Israel that fans and politicians had called on his side to boycott.
The matches had been a focus of attention since the sides were drawn together in February, with Ireland one of Europe's most outspoken critics of Israel's war in Gaza. There have been numerous protests in Ireland asking for the team not to fulfil the fixtures with Israel.
Such was the opposition to the Irish team playing Israel that the Football Association of Ireland chose to hold the game behind closed doors in Backa Topola, a small Serbian town of around 12,000 people, rather than in Dublin.
Reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, who declined to be in the squad for the first game against Israel, will again be missing when the two sides meet in Serbia on Sunday, and captain Dara O’Shea will also miss out due to the birth of his child.
“Football-wise, what's to come most of all is to control our focus level and keep the focus on that one (Sunday’s game against Israel), don't lose it,” the Icelandic coach told a press conference on Saturday.
“There's been a lot of emotions from the people in Ireland about this, and obviously that affects the players as well. We want to do good, but it's always going to be a challenge when the environment is as noisy as it is.”
TWO PROTESTS
Thursday’s 2-2 draw with Austria in Dublin was briefly disrupted by two protests, but a superb goal from Troy Parrott against the Austrians and four points from their last two games have eased the pressure on the Irish team.
The FAI is continuing to investigate allegations that Irish players Adam Idah and James Abankwah were racially abused in Sunday’s 3-0 win over the Israelis in Hungary.
“It just goes to a process both in our departments and then to UEFA to look at,” Hallgrimsson said.
“It was something that was reported from both teams. I just hope that we can focus on football and that football will be the winner after this.”
The 59-year-old said the difficulties the team had faced would strengthen them.
“Surviving this camp, coming out of it together as one, would be a massive win for me, that is coming from my heart,” he said.
“I think all the challenges that this team has gone through, all the criticism, yeah, I think just surviving as a group after this game, that will be a big win for me and for this group, (and) for the (football) association.”
The news conference ended abruptly when an Israeli journalist asked about an allegation that an Irish player had called an Israeli player "a monkey" during Sunday's game, with Irish press officer Kieran Crowley strongly denying the allegation before quickly bringing it to a close.
Israel coach Ran Ben-Shimon refused to be drawn into off-field matters.
"This game is very important to us, (the) point(s) matter to come back to the group, and I'm focusing on how can I lead my team to have a good result tomorrow. This is my only focus, you can trust me on this," he told reporters.
Austria top Group B3 on seven points, with Kosovo second on four ahead of the Irish on goal difference, and Israel bottom with one point.

Two Iranians appear in UK court over alleged plot to target Jews
LONDON: Two Iranian nationals appeared in a London court on Saturday (Oct 3) charged with plotting acts of terrorism involving the use of a homemade bomb to attack the Jewish community in northern England at the behest of a figure believed to be based in Iran.
Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were arrested on Sep 20 at the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, when they are accused of carrying out "hostile" surveillance on potential Jewish targets in Manchester, prosecutors say.
These targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue, the scene of a deadly attack almost a year ago in which two Jewish worshippers were killed, prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court.
ALLEGED PLOT INVOLVED HOMEMADE DEVICE
"Both defendants are accused of preparing acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a homemade explosive device," Luckett said.
He said the men were accused of being in contact with a third party who is alleged to have directed and coordinated the attack planning and provided instructions on how to assemble a homemade device, which prosecutors allege would have been made from chlorine and brake fluid.
"It's assessed that this individual is also an Iranian national and most likely operating from within Iran," Luckett said.
The court was told both men had come to Britain from Europe in small boats. Salehi had arrived in 2020 and had been granted asylum, while Ahmadyan came in 2023 and his asylum claim was still outstanding, Luckett said.
The men did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey court on Oct 23.
The case comes a week after Britain said Iran was believed to be involved in a suspected plot to target the RAF Fairford air base which the US military has used to carry out raids against targets in Iran, leading to a dual British-Iranian national being arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
Police said on Saturday he had been released on police bail while the investigation continues. British counterterrorism police have said the Manchester allegations were not connected in any way to the Fairford investigation.
Iran has rejected accusations of involvement in a number of plots in Britain in recent years, and said allegations it was connected to the Fairford incident were baseless.
Britain has also seen a significant rise in antisemitism since the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023 that triggered the subsequent war in Gaza, including a series of attacks on Jewish sites in London earlier this year.
"It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime," Home Secretary (interior minister) Shabana Mahmood said in a statement.
"They target our Jewish communities and try to silence their critics overseas, often through proxies and criminal networks to hide their involvement."

Mumbai, October 3, 2026: Fugitive businessman Vijay Mallya still owes more than Rs 8,751 crore to a consortium of banks, the State Bank of India (SBI) has told the Bombay High Court, opposing his plea challenging the attachment of assets linked to the Kingfisher Airlines case.
SBI Details Outstanding Dues
In an affidavit filed before the High Court, SBI said that as of August 31, 2026, the total dues stood at Rs 8,751.86 crore, excluding legal and other expenses. The bank said recovery proceedings were continuing and that substantial amounts were yet to be recovered.
The affidavit was filed in a criminal application moved by Mallya challenging a December 2019 order of the Sessions Court concerning assets attached in connection with an Enforcement Directorate (ED) money-laundering case.
SBI said the consortium had temporarily recovered Rs 10,269.96 crore, against which a bond undertaking had been given by the banks. It also said Rs 544.58 crore had been recovered before the filing of the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) suit, while Rs 8,135.63 crore, excluding legal and other costs, remained to be recovered.
Shares Remain Attached
The bank further informed the court that 52,84,978 equity shares, which are part of the present proceedings, remained intact and had not been sold. SBI said the shares were among the assets covered by the ED’s money-laundering investigation and had been attached during the proceedings.
The affidavit said the consortium had approached the Sessions Court after the attachment of Mallya’s assets prevented the banks from recovering their dues. The court had subsequently allowed the banks’ application on December 31, 2019, permitting restoration of the assets for recovery in accordance with law.
SBI Seeks Dismissal Of Plea
“The decretal amount runs into crores of rupees,” SBI said, adding that necessary recovery action was still in progress. The bank termed Mallya’s criminal application “completely misconceived” and sought its dismissal.
The development comes against the backdrop of the ED’s stand that recovery of money by banks does not bring the criminal and money-laundering proceedings against Mallya to an end.

VAR did then award the visitors a penalty soon after. Rangers striker Bojan Miovski was judged to have stopped Bowie's rebound with his arm after Scott McKenna hit the post.
Questions had been asked about John McGinn's Scotland future but the Aston Villa skipper sent the 'keeper the wrong way to double their lead. It was his 27th goal for his country.
But with the visitors looking comfortable, it was a repeat of Hendry's red on Tuesday as McKenna was sent packing late on for his last-man challenge on Agon Elezi.
Scotland host Solvenia at Hampden Park on Tuesday night in the final Nations League match of this extended international break.

Police smash burglary ring that recruited illegal immigrants for 25 break-ins
The force says the syndicate targeted village houses and upscale homes during holidays when residents were away
Hong Kong police have busted a burglary syndicate that recruited illegal immigrants and is believed to be behind at least 25 break-ins across the city in recent weeks, with stolen cash and valuables exceeding HK$3.6 million (US$458,773).
Six people aged 31 to 45 – five mainlanders and a local resident – were arrested in a Friday operation following a review of surveillance footage, police said.
Three of the mainland suspects, all men, were illegal immigrants. Another two – a couple – are believed to be the masterminds, who entered Hong Kong on two-way permits, travel documents issued by Beijing authorities for visits to the city or Macau.
A local man arrested in the operation acted as the group’s driver.

Guests arriving at Disneyland Paris over the busy autumn period have been met with an unwelcome message: the parks are full. Both Disneyland Park and Disney Adventure World reached capacity on Saturday, 3 October, according to a report by Inside the Magic, with the resort’s official availability calendar showing no registration availability for guests holding undated admission. This means visitors who hoped to make a more spontaneous trip may find themselves unable to enter. The situation is particularly significant for people travelling to the resort without a dated ticket or confirmed reservation. Disneyland Paris does not publish a live figure for the number of visitors inside its parks, so there is no official public headcount for the day. However, capacity restrictions were in effect, and access for some categories of guests was no longer available. Inside the Magic also reported that both parks had been full during September, suggesting that the latest restriction is part of a wider period of heavy demand rather than an isolated occurrence. Disneyland Paris itself has been warning visitors that its parks are full on many dates because of high demand. According to the resort’s official guidance, guests with dated tickets can enter on the specified date, subject to the conditions attached to their admission. Those holding undated tickets, Annual Passes or Disneyland Passes must register their visit in advance, with admission dependent on availability. The resort also makes clear that tickets are not sold at the park entrances. That distinction is important because having a ticket does not necessarily mean that every visitor can simply arrive at the gates and enter. For certain ticket types, registration is required before the visit, and Disney says availability depends on park capacity. Disneyland Paris explains that its maximum capacity is based on the number of visitors the parks can accommodate while maintaining satisfactory conditions. The threshold can vary depending on factors including the attractions available and the parks’ operating hours. The latest capacity pressure comes as Disneyland Paris enters one of its busiest seasonal periods. The Disney Halloween Festival began on 26 September and is scheduled to continue through 1 November. The resort has introduced seasonal decorations, Disney Villains, special character appearances and the return of Mickey’s Halloween Celebration at Disneyland Park. Disney Fanatic previously reported that the parks reached capacity on the opening day of the Halloween Festival, with visitors encountering signs warning that the parks were full unless they had the required ticket and reservation. The resort is also operating with a significantly changed second park this year. The former Walt Disney Studios Park has been transformed into Disney Adventure World, with the new World of Frozen forming one of its major attractions. The combination of new experiences and seasonal entertainment has made advance planning increasingly important for visitors, particularly those travelling from outside the Paris region. For families who have already arranged hotels, trains and other parts of a holiday around a Disneyland Paris visit, discovering that park access is unavailable only after reaching the entrance can be especially disruptive. The resort’s advice is therefore straightforward: visitors should check availability before travelling and make sure they have the correct dated admission or registration required for their ticket. The recent capacity restrictions do not mean every ticket holder has been turned away. Disneyland Paris’ own rules distinguish between different forms of admission, and guests with valid dated tickets or qualifying hotel packages can have different entry conditions. For visitors planning an autumn trip, however, the message from the resort’s recent warnings is clear: checking park availability is now an essential part of the visit, rather than something to leave until arrival. Salah out of Egypt game because of artificial turf

Egypt have left Mohamed Salah out of their Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against South Sudan because the match will be played on artificial turf.
The former Liverpool forward, now with Turkish club Trabzonspor, has not travelled with the squad to the capital Juba for Tuesday's game.

"The Egypt national team's technical staff, led by Hossam Hassan, has decided to rest Mohamed Salah for the match against South Sudan scheduled for 29 September because of the playing surface," the Egyptian Football Association (EFA) said.
"It was agreed between the national team's technical staff and Mohamed Salah before the Angola match that he would not play against South Sudan, and the technical staff preferred this approach in order to protect the player," it added.
There is a perception of increased risk of injury on artificial surfaces despite technological improvements, though studies have shown, external there is no evidence of a greater risk of injury.
Salah left Liverpool at the end of last season after nine years during which he made 442 appearances and scored 257 goals, winning nine major trophies.
In six Turkish Super Lig games for Trabzonspor this season he has seven goals and two assists.

Imagine spending a decade trying to solve one of mathematics’ hardest problems. You finally make progress only to see an AI model produce a possible solution in a matter of days. This is what happened to Tristan Buckmaster, a 41-year-old Australian mathematician at New York University who has spent years studying the mathematics of how fluids move and behave. At the core of the issue are the Navier–Stokes equations, a set of mathematical equations developed in the 19th century to describe how fluids move. Engineers and scientists use them to model everything from airflow around aircraft to weather systems. But mathematicians still aren't sure whether these equations always hold, or could break down and produce an infinite or otherwise impossible result. Solving this is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems. According to OpenAI, it asked an unreleased AI model to work on the problem on September 1. Four days later, the model produced a possible proof. This is exactly where the controversy starts. Buckmaster and his collaborator Levent Alpöge had put drafts of their unpublished research into OpenAI’s coding tool, Codex. Buckmaster was concerned that OpenAI’s AI may have drawn on his unpublished work, but he had no way to prove that it had. While OpenAI denied that the mathematician's work influenced the system, it acknowledged that data from users’ interactions with its products may, depending on the settings, be used to improve its models. The entire episode is especially concerning for researchers, engineers and academicians, who routinely put unpublished papers, code, designs and ideas into AI tools. And if AI models are using the research work, how can researchers safely use AI without exposing work that is not yet public? Does India have rules to answer this question? Let's find out... In Indian Labs Draft AI Rulebook As AI seeps into all walks of life, all kinds of workplaces are utilising it, and research and academia are no exception. One of the significant examples is Google Deepmind’s AlphaFold, an AI system that predicts the 3D structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences with high accuracy. This also helped Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind win the 2024 Nobel Prize. This system has been utilised by over 3.3 Mn researchers worldwide to accelerate breakthroughs in biology, medicine, and disease research. In fact, research intelligence firm Wiley found that the overall usage of AI tools surged from 57% in 2024 to 84% in 2025, including specific use for research and publication tasks, which grew significantly to 62% from 45%. Indian academicians and researchers are also relying on AI at varying degrees. For instance, professor Arindama Singh, head of the department of mathematics at IIT Madras, uses AI for literature review and idea generation. However, he added that his approach to AI usage is cautionary, a practice he has been following even before the OpenAI-Buckmaster case blew up. “We do not give our complete solutions to AI for checking; we rather suggest an idea to check. We do not ask AI to check a new method in its entirety, or any patentable idea,” said Singh. Singh is not alone in drawing that line, and institutions are now trying to formalise what individual researchers have been doing by instinct. At IIIT Hyderabad, the caution extends to which models get used. The institute has no institutional AI subscription. It has compute of its own — smaller open-weight models running on campus servers, with individual projects maintaining their own GPU clusters. Those are what researchers are encouraged to use when the data is sensitive. The reasoning is jurisdictional as much as technical. According to Sandeep Kumar Shukla, professor and institution director, the problem with a frontier model is that the user controls nothing behind it. That thinking is now being written down. IIIT Hyderabad constituted a committee in May to frame an institutional AI policy, covering how much AI is permissible for students in homework and lab work, and for research scholars and faculty. Deemed university MAHE, Bengaluru Campus, is at a similar stage. Mangalampalli Surya Sudheer, assistant director of research told Inc42 it is developing institutional guidelines for the responsible and ethical use of AI, including the secure handling of unpublished research. As of now, researchers are expected to rely on broader principles of research integrity and confidentiality. Where Indian Law Leaves Researchers India's one serious attempt at a rulebook for AI training was not written with researchers in mind. For instance, in 2025, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade formed a committee to examine where generative AI meets copyright. Its working paper, released that December, proposed a hybrid licensing framework: AI developers would get an automatic right to train on any lawfully accessed copyrighted work, rights holders could not refuse, and creators would be paid a share of revenue instead. A second part on AI outputs is still expected. None of it is law yet. The framework treats the harm as financial. Creators lose money, so creators get paid. That works for a publisher or a musician. It works poorly for a scientist. "DPIIT’s proposed compulsory royalty model doesn't work here because money is not the only main harm for researchers," said Mishi Choudhary of SFLC.in, a legal services organisation that brings together lawyers, policy analysts, students, and technologists to protect freedom in the digital world. Lose priority on a result and you lose the credit, the citation, and sometimes the career step that follows. Choudhary's rule is a list of what should never go in: "unpublished manuscripts, proofs, source code, datasets, grant proposals, theses under embargo, patent sensitive material or confidential peer review material," unless the terms clearly prohibit training use. That last condition is where the legal exposure sits. "The real issue isn't whether you typed your idea into an AI tool, it is what the tool does with it," says Gunjan Paharia, managing partner at Zeus IP Advocates LLP. Her advice to researchers and founders comes down to five steps: Protect Your Idea First: File a provisional patent application before sharing a patentable idea with an AI tool. Read AI Tool’s Terms: Don’t rely only on what the product’s marketing says. Check whether your data can be used for training, whether humans can review it, and how long the company retains it. Where possible, use enterprise or API plans that explicitly prohibit training and data retention. Ask For Stronger Safeguards: If you are working with an AI provider, seek clear commitments on no training, no human review, data deletion timelines, breach notifications and applicable jurisdiction. Keep Sensitive Work Out Of AI Tools: Use AI for lower-risk tasks such as literature searches, translation, formatting and early drafts. Keep unpublished findings, core ideas, patent-sensitive material and confidential data offline. Keep A Clear Record Of Your Work: Maintain dated notebooks, version histories and other records that can establish when you developed an idea. Institutions should also have clear AI-use policies that researchers formally acknowledge. "Work that never should have gone outside your four walls cannot be fixed with careful process later," Paharia said. According to Shukla of IIIT Hyderabad, “There is no technological method for stopping them from looking at your uploaded information.” For researchers, the lesson from the Buckmaster episode is that AI comes with questions around confidentiality, ownership and credit. Indian institutions are beginning to address these concerns, but formal policies and legal protections are still evolving. Until clearer rules emerge, researchers are largely left to protect their own work by limiting what they share. At a time when AI is being touted as man's closest companion for everything, including research, the real question is: do we really understand the stakes here?

With the 1960 Indus Water Treaty in abeyance after the Pahalgam attack in 2025, Union Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal on Saturday (October 3, 2026) said the Centre was considering new hydropower projects, including Sawalkot, in J&K.
“Discussions are ongoing regarding Sawalkote. We certainly intend to take up work on that project in the near future. These projects would not only meet the local demand, but would also meet the power demands of other parts of the country,” said Mr. Agarwal.
The statement assumes significance in the backdrop of Pakistan’s objections raised on the construction of Sawalkote dam project in July last year and February this year with India and had sought consultation. India suspended the IWT after the Pahalgam attack, which left 26 civilians dead, in Kashmir in 2025 and started working on several power projects.
Built by the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC), the Sawalkot hydroelectric project was coming up at the cost of ₹5,129 crores on the Chenab River in the Udhampur, Reasi, and Ramban districts and will generate 800 megawatts of electricity.
“Major hydropower projects including Ratle, Pakal Dul, Kiru and Kwar are progressing well (in J&K). The Centre is also looking at other projects in the future,” said Mr. Agarwal.
Praising the Union Territory administration, Mr. Agarwal said the projects under the Chenab Valley Power Projects (Private) Limited were receiving full support of the local government. “We are making good progress. We are getting the full support of the UT administration. We will also think about other new projects,” said Mr. Agarwal.
On power deficit in J&K, Mr. Agarwal said around 14,500 MW of hydropower potential were identified in the UT and “the ongoing projects would help address the issue”.
On the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, Agarwal said around 50 lakh people across the country had joined the programme so far, while J&K had achieved its first milestone of 100 MW.
“J&K has achieved the first milestone of 100 megawatts. Once the momentum is there, the progress will definitely be fast,” he added.
Terming the rooftop solar programme in J&K “a good start”, Mr. Agarwal said, “We are now reaching the take-off stage. J&K has made a good start under PM Suryagar. Momentum has built and it will take off,” Agarwal said.
Earlier, Mr. Agarwal visited the Seva Setu Abhiyan Camp being organised under the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana in Srinagar, where he inspected stalls and help desks and interacted with vendors providing services related to the scheme.
The Seva Setu Abhiyan Camp is aimed at strengthening public outreach, facilitating citizen-centric service delivery and creating awareness among citizens about the benefits of rooftop solar under the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, said an official.

Senior Judicial Officer, Yash Paul Bourney was sworn in as the Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at a solemn ceremony held in the Chief Justice’s Court at the Srinagar Wing of the High Court on Tuesday.
Dr. Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, administered the oath of office to Justice Yash Paul Bourney.
The Warrant of Appointment was read out by M. K. Sharma, Registrar General, High Court of J&K and Ladakh, who also conducted the proceedings of the ceremony.
The ceremony was graced by Justice Rajnesh Oswal, Justice Mohd. Akram Chowdhary, Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal, Justice Rajesh Sekhri, Justice Mohd. Yousuf Wani and Justice Sanjay Parihar. Justice Sanjeev Kumar, Justice Sindhu Sharma, Justice Sanjay Dhar, Justice Rahul Bharti, Justice Moksha Khajuria Kazmi and Justice Shahzad Azeem joined the ceremony through virtual mode from Jammu wing of the High Court.
The family members, close relatives and friends of Justice Yash Paul Bourney were also present on the occasion, lending special significance to the ceremony.
Among other dignitaries present were Mir Syed Latif, Judicial Member (HOD) of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Srinagar Bench, Shaleen Kabra, Additional Chief Secretary, M.K. Sinha, ADGP CID, Achal Sethi, Commissioner Secretary Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs; Divisional Commissioner, Kashmir, IGP Kashmir, IGP Security, Senior Advocates; Executive Members of the Kashmir Advocates’ Association and the J&K High Court Bar Association, Jammu; Law Officers; Judicial Officers; and officers of the High Court Registry.
The Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India, issued the notification appointing Justice Yash Paul Bourney as the Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh on September 19, 2026.
Born on August 25, 1967, Justice Yash Paul Bourney hails from village Dadwara, Bhaddu, Billawar, District Kathua. During his distinguished judicial career, he has held several important judicial and administrative assignments. He served as Principal District & Sessions Judge at Leh, Baramulla, Udhampur and Jammu, besides serving as Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Srinagar and Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Jammu.
Justice Bourney also served in key institutional positions as Member Secretary, J&K Legal Services Authority; Registrar Vigilance, High Court of J&K and Ladakh; and Director, J&K Judicial Academy.
After serving as Principal District & Sessions Judge, Jammu, Justice Bourney was appointed on deputation as Member, J&K Special Tribunal, Jammu. He was serving in the said capacity immediately prior to his elevation as a Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan has said that work on the proposed Institute of Organ and Tissue Transplantation in Kozhikode will be completed in 30 months.
He was delivering a speech after opening the silver jubilee celebrations of the Kerala Heart Care Society here on Saturday (October 3). Mr. Satheesan said that ₹271 crore was being set aside for the institute coming up on a 20-acre plot in Chevayur. All the services related to organ transplantation would be brought under one roof to bring down the surgery cost to one-third. The facility would have 350 beds and 10 operation theatres. On the same premises, a dermatology hospital too had been proposed. A sum of ₹35 crore would be spent on the hospital, Mr. Satheesan said.
The institute would be elevated as a centre of excellence with a research programme attached to it. As many as 1,100 cornea transplants, 520 kidney, 50 heart, 40 lung, 120 bone marrow, 320 liver, 15 intestine, 15 pancreas, and 300 soft tissue transplant surgeries would be performed there in a year. Mr. Satheesan said that utilising the State’s climate and other advantages, Keralam would be transformed into a healthcare destination where foreigners and people from within the country could approach for treatment. Wellness centres, rehabilitation centres, and facilities providing medical treatment for stroke would be launched. An extensive campaign would soon be undertaken for prevention and early detection of diseases. K. Praveenkumar and K. Jayanth, MLAs, and K. Kunjali, president of the society, were present, among others.
The foundation stone for the proposed institute was laid by former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan in February this year. However, the work on the facility was reportedly moving at a slow pace after the change of government.

Pakistan summons Indian envoy to lodge 'strong protest' over alleged killing of 2 men near Punjab border
Pakistan's foreign ministry said it categorically ‘rejects any attempt to mischaracterize’ the two men killed along the border as “infiltrators".
Pakistan on Saturday said its foreign ministry summoned Indian Chargé d’Affaires to lodge protest over the alleged killing of two Pakistani men by Border Security Force (BSF) personnel in the Bedian Sector along the International Border on October 2, 2026.
BSF troops on Friday shot dead two suspected Pakistani intruders along the international border in Punjab's Tarn Taran district, officials said, news agency PTI reported.
Pakistan alleged that the BSF personnel ‘resorted to unprovoked lethal force against unarmed civilians.' “Such use of force was wholly unjustified and grossly disproportionate, resulting in the tragic loss of two precious lives. Pakistan categorically rejects any attempt to mischaracterize the deceased as ‘infiltrators’," Pakistan foreign ministry said in a statement.
Pakistan described the killings as a ‘violation of fundamental human rights, including the right to life’.
It further said the Indian side was called upon to conduct and ‘immediate, transparent and credible’ probe into the incident. It also sought disciplinary and legal action against those responsible.
“India was further urged to ensure respect for fundamental human rights and international law, strictly observe relevant bilateral arrangements and established border procedures, exercise maximum restraint in dealing with such situations, and take effective measures to prevent the recurrence of such incidents,” the statement issued by Pakistan's foreign ministry said.
‘Two men provoked Indian troops’
The firing incident reportedly took place at around noon on Friday along the border in Punjab where the two countries share a 553-km long border.
Tarn Taran Deputy Superintendent of Police (Bhikiwind) Atul Soni said three intruders were advancing towards the Indian side, but one later returned to Pakistan. The two others continued moving towards the Indian side despite warnings from BSF troops to turn back, Soni was quoted as saying.
According to a BSF sentry, the two men were also provoking the troops and saying they wanted to enter Indian territory, he was quoted as saying. The BSF subsequently opened fire, killing the two men, Soni said, adding that senior BSF officers visited the spot.
Pakistan says the three men were ‘unarmed’
Pakistani state media Radio Pakistan on Friday reported that two ‘unarmed civilians’ were killed by India's BSF personnel near the border in Kasur, a border city in Pakistan's Punjab province. The incident took place when three men of Ladhar village had come a few steps ahead of a border pillar, the report added, citing locals. Two of the three men were reportedly killed, while another one sustained injuries after the BSF opened fire. The deceased have been identified as Azmat Rasool and Mohsin Jutt.
Radio Pakistan further claimed that none of the three men had attempted to cross the border fence, while adding that the ‘incident constitutes a violation of the border agreement and the standard operating procedures governing the Pakistan-India international border’.

'So-called civilian govts at the mercy of Army': India fires back at Pakistan over J&K remark at UN
India said the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh were, are and will always remain "integral and inalienable" parts of India.
India on Saturday launched a sharp attack on Pakistan over its remarks on Jammu and Kashmir at the United Nations, telling the world organisation that the "so-called" civilian governments in Islamabad "serve at the mercy" of their Army and rarely complete their terms.
India exercised its Right of Reply in response to remarks by Pakistan at the UN General Assembly Third Committee meeting Friday, where the Pakistani delegate raised the issue of Jammu and Kashmir, news agency PTI reported.

"Categorically" rejecting the remarks, India said the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh were, are and will always remain "integral and inalienable" parts of India.
