Grand Theft Auto 6 brings several new mechanics to the franchise, including dual protagonists, a unique wanted system, an honor profile, changes to how cash is handled, and much more. With so many new features, GTA 6 has introduced new icons to help players keep track of them. So, here is a rundown of all GTA 6 UI and HUD icons to help you understand the meaning of every new symbol you encounter in the game.
Meaning of All GTA 6 Icons
GTA 6 releases on November 19, 2026, but we already got a detailed look at the gameplay with the Netflix Extended Look. Though it did not reveal every small or new mechanic Rockstar has baked into the game, it revealed a lot for us to go by.
Check out the complete list of symbols and icons you will see on the GTA 6 UI and HUD, along with their respective explanations.
| GTA 6 Icons | Description | 
|---|---|
| BUCKME | Shows cash stored inside the BUCKME bank account. Funds in the bank account are safe. | 
| Cash Wallet | Shows cash you have on you in person, and it can be up to $20,000. This money is at risk if you are on an active mission and can be lost if you get arrested or die in action. | 
| Health | GTA 6 health icon, paired with the health bar. | 
| Stamina | Affects your strength, and it’s paired with the stamina bar. Stamina is depleted when you sprint, cycle, or perform other physical GTA 6 activities. | 
| Oxygen | Oxygen tank capacity in GTA 6, paired with the oxygen bar. It only appears when you go underwater with a scuba tank. Decreases based on how long you stay submerged. | 
| Focus | This focus icon is paired with the focus bar in GTA 6. It offers heightened awareness and precision, giving you the ability to scan surroundings, find weak points, and slow down time to shoot enemies. | 
| Relationship Status | Represents the relationship status between Jason and Lucia. | 
| Good Deeds | Notifies when committing a good deed, like petting a dog. Affects your GTA 6 Criminal Profile positively. | 
| Neutral Deed | Criminal Profile is not yet updated or is in unknown status. Also, possibly notifies when committing a neutral act that doesn’t affect the Criminal Profile. | 
| Violent Deed | Notifies when committing a violent act or being evil, for the Violent Criminal Profile state. | 
| Psycho Deed | Notifies when acting like a Psycho, like punching a random person for no reason and adds negatively to the Criminal Profile. | 
| Wanted Star Level | GTA 6 Wanted System star. The more stars you have, the higher the wanted level. | 
| CCTV Profiling | The player’s criminal act has been seen or recorded by a surveillance camera. | 
| Weapon Profiling | The player’s GTA 6 weapon used in an act of crime has been identified. | 
| Couple Profiling | The police know that a couple is responsible for the crime. Read about the dual protagonists in GTA 6 and their Bonnie-and-Clyde dynamics here. | 
| Appearance Marker | The police know when either Jason or Lucia is responsible for the crime. | 
| Clothing Profiling | The player’s clothing worn during an act of crime has been identified. | 
| Vehicle Profiling | The player’s GTA 6 vehicle used during an act of crime has been identified. | 
These are most of the GTA 6 UI and HUD icons that have been revealed so far. All these icons were showcased in the GTA 6 Netflix Extended Look, and we will update this guide as more information comes out. Do you think we missed out on any icons? Let us know in the comments section below.

On 25 September 2026, several opposition parties, including the Congress, held protests across the country demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, while the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) had separately demanded his resignation and appealed to Gen Z to join its proposed agitation. In Delhi, police detained protesters, including Neha Bora, who had reached Jantar Mantar. The protests followed a report by The Indian Express that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had filed at least 14 written objections over the previous 10 months concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and other Election Commission decisions (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Gen-Z protesters taking to the streets of Delhi in September 2026, demanding the removal of EVMs and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Gen-Z protesters in Delhi in September 2026 demanding the removal of EVMs and the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
Fact: The viral video is not from the September 2026 protests. It shows a protest against EVMs held at Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, on 31 January 2024, organised by 22 organisations and addressed by Bharat Mukti Morcha president Waman Meshram. Gyanesh Kumar was appointed as an Election Commissioner only on 15 March 2024 and was not part of the Election Commission during the January 2024 protest. He later took charge as the 26th Chief Election Commissioner of India on 19 February 2025. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several social media posts (here, here, and here) (archived) from late January and early February 2024 featuring the same visuals. According to these posts, the visuals are from a protest against EVMs, led by Waman Meshram, with a large march to the Election Commission office scheduled for 31 January 2024 at Jantar Mantar, New Delhi.
Taking clues from these posts, we used relevant keywords and found (here, here, and here) that 22 organisations, including the Bharat Mukti Morcha, Rashtriya Kisan Morcha, and Bahujan Mukti Party, held a protest against Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) at Jantar Mantar on 31 January 2024. The protest was addressed by Waman Meshram, the national president of the Bharat Mukti Morcha.
We also found a Facebook post by Waman Meshram featuring pictures from the protest held at Jantar Mantar on 31 January 2024, showing a similar location as seen in the viral video.
We also found a video uploaded on Waman Meshram’s YouTube channel on the same day, featuring visuals from the same event and showing a similar crowd and location to those seen in the viral video.
PIB Fact Check also debunked the claim, stating that the video is old and dates back to January 2024.
It is important to note that Rajiv Kumar was the Chief Election Commissioner from 15 May 2022 to 18 February 2025. Gyanesh Kumar and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu joined the Election Commission as Election Commissioners on 15 March 2024. At the time of the 31 January 2024 protest, Gyanesh Kumar was not an Election Commissioner. He completed his tenure in government service on 31 January 2024 and was subsequently appointed as an Election Commissioner on 15 March 2024. Gyanesh Kumar later took charge as the 26th Chief Election Commissioner of India on 19 February 2025.
To sum up, a 2024 video of a protest against EVMs in Delhi is shared as a September 2026 protest demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.

Ganesh 'visarjan' over, Gyanesh Kumar 'visarjan' remains: Prakash Raj
"Ganesh visarjan is over in Karnataka, Andhra and entire India. Now, Gyanesh Kumar visarjan remains," he told reporters here.
Criticising the SIR process, actor and activist Prakash Raj on Saturday said the 'visarjan' (immersion) of Ganesha idols as part of Ganesh Chaturthi festivities is over and that the 'visarjan' of CEC Gyanesh Kumar remains.
Referring to media reports that 38 lakh appeals from voters (for inclusion) who were removed from the electoral rolls are pending before the tribunals in West Bengal and that it may take 10-12 years to decide them, he asked whether the huge number of applicants should wait that long.
"Ganesh visarjan is over in Karnataka, Andhra and entire India. Now, Gyanesh Kumar visarjan remains," he told reporters here.
Deep Dive
SIR was stated to be a cleaning-up process when it began, but it has been found to be a deleting process, not an inclusive one, he alleged.
Elections are not numbers but citizens of the country who are alive, he said.
He said he took a 10-day tour of different districts to meet people and he was told that their names were "deleted" just because they were not at home when a Booth Level Officer (BLO) visited.
Daily wage workers who have gone elsewhere for work have been removed from the electoral rolls, he alleged.
He also asked whether Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who conducts 'Mann ki Baat', had explained the SIR process in advance.
"Our demand is that SIR has to be stalled and scrapped," Raj said.
Meanwhile, Telangana BJP chief spokesperson N V Subhash slammed Raj for his "insulting" remarks against the Chief Election Commissioner who heads a Constitutional body.
"He (Prakash Raj) may be entitled to criticise the Election Commission, but comparing the CEC to an idol immersion crosses the line from political criticism to disrespect for a Constitutional institution. Democracy demands debate, not derision," Subhash said in a statement.
If Raj has objections to the SIR process, he can place the facts and evidence before the appropriate forum instead of resorting to "provocative street rhetoric," he said.
Meanwhile, a protest was organised here on Saturday by Telangana People's Front, Cockroach Janta Party and other organisations demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, scrapping SIR exercise and repeal CEC Act 2023.
The protesters displayed posters with messages such as "Gyanesh, It's Done Bro!", "Gyanesh Kumar Must Resign", "Save Democracy," among others.

The team behind the award-winning film NAZA, which details the Israeli military’s targeting policies in Gaza and its alleged acceptance of high numbers of civilian deaths, have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
The disclosure came in response to an Israel Defense Forces statement seeking to discredit the documentary.
In its response, which the IDF said was based on statements made by the film-makers and a review made by a representative who had attended a viewing, the Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on interviews with two dozen intelligence and other troops who had only a partial picture of the target approval process.
At the centre of the IDF’s rebuttal was its often repeated claim that its rules of engagement explicitly distinguish between militants and civilians and prohibit deliberately targeting civilians, while requiring commanders to take steps to minimise civilian harm, claims that have long been challenged over the years by critics.
While acknowledging that it used AI to help recommend potential targets in Gaza, the IDF also said final decisions made on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers.
The IDF also denied that it had approved, planned or carried out an attack anticipating 500 civilian casualties in pursuit of a single Hamas target.
The IDF statement follows previous efforts by Israeli politicians to dismiss NAZA – a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike – which have accompanied death threats against the film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and calls by the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for them to be stripped of their Israeli citizenship.
It also echoed previous complaints by some Israeli critics – including journalists – that the film’s military sources were anonymised, despite the fact that source protection in media investigations is commonplace and regarded by much of the media as an ethical requirement.
“The film NAZA presents a distorted, misleading, and unrealistic picture of the IDF’s target planning and strike processes. The film’s narrative is based on fundamental factual errors stemming from a skewed and manipulative portrayal,” the statement added.
Responding to the IDF statement, the Guardian, which produced the film, disclosed further details of how the team had verified the allegations which involved scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes.
A spokesperson said: “The IDF’s attempt to portray the 24 participants in NAZA as junior-ranking officers involved only in the early stages of the targeting process is false.
“They include officers and soldiers who were involved in multiple stages of the targeting process in Gaza, including intelligence, operations and the final authorisation process.
“The process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.
“Over the past three years we have together interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes.
“The Guardian stands fully behind the film, which builds on three years of detailed reporting by the Guardian and our partners. Several highly respected news organisations have subsequently confirmed the IDF’s use of AI-driven systems in the Gaza offensive and the loosening of safeguards to protect civilians, including the New York Times, Washington Post and Associated Press.”
While Netanyahu has claimed that Israeli military safeguards have led to one of the lowest civilian-combatant ratios in modern warfare, that has been challenged by the IDF’s own leaked casualty assessments, by the UN’s commission of inquiry in 2024 and research by NGOs including Action on Armed Violence.

The British invasion of the mid-1960s was a multi-pronged attack, an assault led above all by The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, and The Who. Their seismic impact on American and world culture has been well documented. But of the leaders of those three mega-bands, perhaps the most mysterious remains Pete Townshend, The Who’s songwriter and enigmatic eminence, thrashing chords and smashing guitars while Roger Daltry handled lead vocals.
His sheer brilliance and rock innovation is captured in the documentary Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes, which held its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival. It’s directed by Frank Marshall (The Bee Gees: How Can You Mend a Broken Heart) and Nigel Sinclair (producer, Billy Preston: That’s the Way God Planned It). Despite the enormity of The Who’s success – the rock operas Tommy and Quadrophenia, songs “Won’t Get Fooled Again,” “My Generation,” “Love Reign O’er Me” and so many others – somehow the band’s primary creative engine can remain obscured.
“A lot of people, when we say, ‘Oh, Pete wrote all the songs,’ they go, ‘What?’ They don’t understand because Pete’s also very quiet,” Marshall says in an interview at his home in Telluride. “He’s not the front man. Roger’s the front man… So, I do feel he’s underappreciated.”
Watch on Deadline
Key to understanding Townshend, as the film explores, is his background as an artist. He studied at Ealing Art College as a teenager and absorbed lessons from a teacher there, Roy Ascott, who propounded theories of technology and consciousness that would deeply influence Townshend. An exercise at Ealing in “auto-destruction,” where students smashed up pianos or other musical instruments, would lead to Townshend’s signature move with The Who, destroying his guitar at the end of performances.
“Actually, I have one of those smashed guitars, which I had a guitar builder lay out in an exposed frame like a skeleton,” Sinclair tells us. Smashing instruments “became a habit in shows. Obviously, in that club on Goldhawk Road, [Townshend] didn’t intend to do anything. His guitar went up into the ceiling and broke through cheap, old fashioned kind of stuff — with asbestos in those days. And it crumbled on Pete — the guitar and the neck was tipped over. So, he just threw it on the ground and smashed it. That was the first time. And the audience and Roger and the other [band members] are genuinely thinking, ‘What is he doing?’ And then [Keith] Moon, who only takes him about half a millisecond to tack, immediately started smashing his drum kit.”
More than mere theatrics, the frenetic smashing of instruments and The Who’s music itself, written by Townshend, channeled the sense of rage, frustration and angst felt by so many young British people in that post-war period of crumbled empire and dwindling opportunity.
“We see it in that first [Who] song, ‘Can’t Explain,’ when somebody said to him, ‘You’re expressing what we all feel and that connection,’” Marshall comments. “And he didn’t even know, but he was, as an artist, taking what was happening and channeling it into a song.”
Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes contains remarkable archive footage of the band in private moments and on stage, material unseen for decades. Archival producers Kate Griffiths and Catalina Curbishley were key to unearthing it.
“The Who had actually put all of their assets in frozen storage back in the ’80s. It’s in this house, in somebody’s back garden,” says producer Cassidy Hartmann. “Our team actually went in there and sorted through everything and found this material and we were able to transfer it. And once we saw it, of course we were astounded at what was there because it’s like the dream of every documentary filmmaker to find something like this that no one’s ever seen.”
“The treasure chest,” Marshall says.
Townshend was born in West London in May 1945, just days before Germany’s surrender, to musical parents – his father a professional saxophonist and his mother a singer. His parents’ marriage was a rocky one and as a small boy, Pete was sent to live with his maternal grandmother, a woman he would later describe as “clinically insane.” That devastating experience would unconsciously inform Tommy, the rock opera about a “deaf, dumb, and blind kid” who becomes a pinball wizard.
“A big part of our approach to the film was surrounding this idea of Pete as two people, as this divided person,” Hartmann observes. “And I think the trauma speaks to that. He says, ‘I divided then back when I was a kid and became this introverted, imaginative writer person.’ And then of course he also becomes this rock star on stage. And I think a big part of the tension in the film that we were interested in was that contradiction between those two sides of himself and his struggle to kind of reconcile those.”
Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes screens Saturday and Sunday at the Hamptons International Film Festival in New York. It also screens Sunday on the other side of the country – at the Mill Valley Film Festival in Northern California. “Behind Blue Eyes,” of course, is one of Townshend’s greatest compositions, a song at times plaintive and reflective, at other moments ferocious in its anger. That, and “Going Mobile,” “Baba O’Riley,” and “Won’t Get Fooled Again” were written for Lifehouse, a kind of futuristic rock opera Townshend created after Tommy. It was his single most ambitious project (which is saying something) but never came to fruition, for reasons explored in the film. Lifehouse remains the great white whale of Townshend’s career, and a narrative thread throughout the documentary.
“The engine for us was once we realized that he wants to feature this abandoned project, Lifehouse — which is quite hard to understand and of course collapsed for a number of reasons over the years — but it’s incredibly important to him,” Sinclair says. “It’s an itch that he never stops scratching… Frank said we needed to actually explore Pete as a person because what’s interesting about Lifehouse is it’s so important to him. That’s what drives [the film].”
Distribution plans for the documentary are pending. Given the track record of Marshall, Sinclair (Wilder, David Frost Vs.) and Hartmann (The Apollo, Lilith Fair: Building a Mystery), optimism on that front seems warranted. Marshall, a five-time Oscar nominee and six-time Primetime Emmy nominee is one of the top producers in motion picture history. At Telluride, the film became a hot ticket, generating interest from festival-goers including a certain Oscar-winning director, who had his own film in the festival, Ink.
“Danny Boyle was over there saying, ‘I’ve got to see the Townshend film,’” Sinclair reports. “So I spoke to him and said, ‘If you can’t see here, I’ll send you a link.’ So we’re feeling pretty good about getting it placed.”
Hartmann was born after the height of The Who’s success. “I learned a lot on this project. I developed a deep affection for Pete especially. And I did see an opportunity to introduce the band to a younger generation,” she notes. “I thought that there was an opportunity there for that to connect with a bigger audience than just The Who fan base. There was something relatable and universal in Pete’s story for anyone who’s a creative person trying to do something in the world.”

Blazing triple-digit heat bears down on Braves-Dodgers NLDS opener in Los Angeles
The Los Angeles Dodgers are hosting the Atlanta Braves in what is forecast to be the hottest postseason game at Dodger Stadium since 2017

The Los Angeles Dodgers are hosting the Atlanta Braves in what is forecast to be the hottest postseason game at Dodger Stadium since 2017.
Shade was at a premium on Saturday for Game 1 of the National League Division Series, which began at 1 p.m. local time. The game-time temperature of 100 degrees was forecast to reach 101 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius), about 20 degrees warmer than the average for early October.
The highest game-time temperature ever recorded at Dodger Stadium is 103 degrees (39 degrees Celsius) twice. The first time was Oct. 24, 2017, for Game 1 of the World Series against Houston. It was equaled on Sept. 8, 2024, for a regular-season game against Cleveland.
The Braves seemingly were unfazed by the blazing sun, cloudless skies and rising thermometer while taking pre-game batting practice. The two-time defending World Series champion Dodgers? They stayed inside.
“Remember, we're from Atlanta,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said before the game. “It's not that big of a factor.”
Braves center fielder Lane Thomas added, "I feel like this is a little cooler 98 than Atlanta.”
Some of their fans agreed.
“It's hot, but it's not bad,” said Helen Greene of Valdosta, Georgia, who was sitting in the sun nine rows behind the visiting dugout with her long hair arrayed under a Braves cap. “In Atlanta, my hair would have been up by now.”
Greene and her husband, Chad, were hydrating with water.
“I'll have beer later,” she said, smiling.
Tickets for Game 1 were still available early Saturday. The lowest get-in price ranged from $56 to $61, depending on the secondary marketplace.
Fans still gathered in the outfield pavilions in hopes of catching a stray ball off the Braves' bats pre-game. But other seating areas were mostly empty 90 minutes before first pitch.
Christopher Hernández of Long Beach and his girlfriend sat in the sun behind the Dodgers dugout with giveaway towels covering their heads.
“We play sports and we know how it feels to be in the heat and we know how to beat the heat, too,” he said, showing off a blue plastic bottle with a fan attached to spritz water. “It's not as bad as people think it is.”
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts planned to keep an eye on his pitchers and catcher Will Smith, who wears a mask and padding behind the plate.
“It’s the same conditions for both teams,” the manager said, “and you’ve got to just stay hydrated and manage it.”
Braves reliever Brent Suter graduated from Harvard in 2012, having majored in environmental science and public policy.
“In the back of my mind, I’m like 100 degrees in October in L.A., that’s definitely not normal,” he said before the game. “Obviously super El Niño is a big thing to do with that. It’s going to be a challenge for both sides to stay hydrated, especially the position players.”
Short heat spells in October are normal for Los Angeles, but the prolonged extreme heat warning — forecast to last at least a week — is keeping temperatures 10 to 15 degrees above normal. The average high in Los Angeles in early October is 81 degrees (27 degrees Celsius).
“Just making sure everyone is hydrated and staying loose and getting electrolytes in us,” Suter said.
Emergency medical teams were in their usual spots around the stadium, staying alert for anticipated cases of heatstroke, dehydration, excessive sweating caused by heat exposure, and the more typical drunkenness.
The Dodgers encouraged fans to wear hats and sunscreen. They were allowed to bring in non-alcoholic drinks of one liter or less in factory-sealed plastic bottles. Empty refillable water bottles were also allowed. Bottle filling stations and water fountains are scattered around the stadium.

BANIHAL, Sept 22: Two police personnel were found unconscious under suspicious circumstances inside a car at Ziarat Morh in Sana area of Batote tehsil of Ramban district on Tuesday evening, police sources said.
The two personnel were reportedly found in an unconscious state inside the vehicle and were shifted to District Hospital Ramban by local residents. However, both were declared brought dead by doctors at the hospital.
The deceased have been identified as Head Constable Farid Ahmed (No. 408/Rbn) resident of Bhatti Ramban and Selection Grade Constable (SgCt) Muhammad Yaqoob (No. 309/Rbn) resident Jatgali Ramban, both posted with District Police Lines (DPL), Ramban.
According to police sources, the incident came to light at around 8:30 pm when the two personnel were found inside a Fiat Vias car bearing registration number JK-19/5299 at Ziarat Morh.
Their bodies were kept at District Hospital Ramban for medico-legal formalities. SSP Ramban Arun Gupta and the Medical Superintendent were present at the hospital following the incident.
The exact circumstances and cause of their deaths were not immediately known. Police have initiated further proceedings to ascertain the circumstances leading to the incident.

‘Balanced and acceptable’: labour chief defends helper wage rise amid criticism
Chris Sun says the 2.35 per cent increase to HK$5,220 reflects Hong Kong’s stronger economy, but unions and employers’ groups remain unsatisfied
Hong Kong’s stronger economic performance over the past year is the reason for raising the monthly minimum wage for foreign domestic helpers, the labour minister has said amid disappointment from both unions and employers’ groups.
Defending the government’s decision to raise the monthly minimum wage by 2.35 per cent to HK$5,220 (US$665), Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said the government sought to keep the annual adjustment mechanism “balanced and acceptable”.

Stephen Harper warns Alberta separatism will bring 'no benefit'
Former prime minister says staying silent on upcoming referendum 'not an option'
Former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper cautioned against the prospect of Alberta separation in a column Friday, writing that even voting just to "send a message" would represent a fraught approach.
"No one will be surprised to learn that I am against separation. That would involve much risk and be extremely difficult to bring about," Harper wrote in the Calgary Herald.
"Besides, there is nothing resembling the credible leadership necessary to establish a new country."
On Oct. 19, voters will be asked whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada, or whether the government of Alberta should hold a second, binding referendum to separate from Canada.
- Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage
- Everything you need to know about the 10 questions in Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum
Earlier this year, as his official prime ministerial portrait was unveiled on Parliament Hill, Harper called for Liberals and Conservatives to come together amid reinvigorated separatist movements in Alberta and Quebec.
In September, Harper backed the federal government's decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States at the Canada Investment Summit, arguing that Canada needed to pursue "diminished reliance" on the United States in order to maintain its sovereignty.
Current Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has also said he supports a united Canada.
Speaking in Edmonton earlier this week, he blamed the Liberal government for what he said was its role in seeding discontent, but said separating from Canada wouldn't help resolve provincial grievances.
Harper dismisses voting to send message
While many Albertans may feel alienated from Ottawa, Harper wrote in his Friday column that pursuing independence would pose "significant risk."
"Whatever the results of the Alberta vote, it is incumbent upon Canada to move with immediacy and urgency to address the barriers, many self-imposed, to our long-term stability and prosperity," Harper wrote.
"It is on this objective that I believe the passion and legitimate frustration of Albertans should also remain focused."
Polling has consistently indicated that a majority of Albertans are in favour of remaining in Canada.
Separatist leaders have been trying to close the gap.
They've argued that voting to hold a future, binding referendum would provide Alberta leverage against Ottawa when it comes to resolving its grievances.
Keith Wilson, a leader of a pro-independence group, often argues on social media that voting for the separation option is an opportunity to send a message that the "status quo with Ottawa is unacceptable."
"For me, Oct. 19 is not simply a debate about staying or leaving; it is also about strategy. What position gives Alberta the strongest voice in determining its future?" Wilson wrote on Thursday.
"My case is that Option 2 creates leverage and strengthens Alberta’s hand at the negotiating table."
UCP MLA Jason Stephan argued the same this week after he confirmed to CBC News that he has voted via a mail-in ballot for Option 2: "I've always supported having a referendum on independence because I want Ottawa to be compelled to fix the things that are broken."
In his column, Harper disagreed with that argument, writing that "over two generations of Quebec politics were spent debating the goal of the separatists."
"Most voting for it will do so just to 'send a message,' in other words, to keep the threat alive in the hope of retaining the benevolent attention that the province has recently been receiving from Ottawa," Harper wrote. "I believe that approach is mistaken."
Cory Morgan, who heads the third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence, said the former prime minister's comments were unsurprising, given his reputation as a federalist.
But he added that recent developments, such as those tied to the West Coast oil pipeline, could be seen as the referendum already sending a message and getting results.
"It is getting attention from Ottawa for the first time in decades," he said.
Harper also contended that the federal government under his leadership helped stamp out separatist sentiment, including when it came to its approach to energy policy.
Poilievre also recently claimed that separatist sentiments were wiped out in Alberta and Quebec under Harper’s government — comments that received pushback from the Bloc Québécois.
A spokesperson for Harper declined to provide additional comment.

India is likely to have a much older population later this century, as the country’s age structure is beginning to shift and fertility has fallen “below replacement,” Moody’s Ratings said on Tuesday (September 29, 2026).
Moody’s said population growth has long been a tailwind for economic growth and creditworthiness, but falling fertility is now changing that picture.
Fewer workers will limit productive capacity, while fewer households and consumers will weaken demand. As a result, countries will have to rely more on productivity to sustain growth.
Moody’s said the global fertility rate had declined from 4.9 children per woman in 1950 to about 2.2 today, only slightly above the replacement rate of 2.1.
“What makes this episode particularly significant is that many of the world’s largest economies are ageing at the same time. In fact, more than 70% of the world’s population now lives in countries with fertility rates at or below replacement level,” Moody’s said in a report on global demographics.
It said fertility rates across much of Latin America were now comparable to those of Europe and Japan, while several East Asian countries had some of the lowest fertility rates ever recorded.
Japan has the most top-heavy population structure, with nearly 30% of its population over 65 and about 11% under 15.
South Korea is close behind, while China is moving rapidly in the same direction. Emerging markets, including Brazil, India, Thailand and Türkiye, are also progressing along the same path.
“Although India’s population remains relatively young, fertility has already fallen below replacement and the country’s age structure is beginning to shift, setting the stage for a much older population later this century,” Moody’s said.
Declining fertility ultimately reshapes age structures as well as population growth, it said. Countries experiencing the steepest fertility declines today will also age most rapidly in the coming decades.

University of Oregon receives 5 sexual assault reports in first week of classes amid Cornell ‘gang rape’ fallout
An alleged gang rape case at Cornell University from two years ago has sparked a national conversation on campus safety

The University of Oregon has received five sexual assault reports in the first week of classes — while an Ivy League school on the other side of the country deals with the fallout of an alleged gang rape that was not prosecuted for years.
A lawsuit filed last month by a former Cornell University student who goes by Jane Doe, alleging that she was drugged and gang-raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity at the New York school in October 2024, has sparked a national conversation on campus safety and the culture of silence surrounding sexual assault. The case has been reopened, and New York State Attorney General Letitia James has taken it over.
Now, the University of Oregon has alerted students to five new sexual assault cases that occurred on or near campus. The alert went out on Wednesday, two days after classes began.
Four of the reported sexual assaults involved students, and the fifth happened near a park next to university property. All of the cases occurred in the past week, the university said.
Authorities arrested someone in the fifth case, but it’s unclear whether anyone has been arrested in the other four.
While the five sexual assaults are not believed to be related, “several alleged perpetrators may have taken advantage of the fact that the victims were intoxicated at social events,” the University of Oregon said.
When reached for comment, the university said it could not confirm any other details at this time, citing multiple ongoing investigations.
The university told The Independent that it issued the alert, “because we are very concerned to see a pattern of assaults with similar characteristics and wanted to let our campus community know that these have occurred, that investigations are occurring at both the university and law enforcement levels, and most importantly, that our first concern is for survivors and that the university does not tolerate nonconsensual sexual activity in any form.”
Newly unsealed documents in Cornell University’s investigation into Jane Doe’s case have revealed how drugs played a role in the alleged gang rape.
One of Jane Doe’s roommates said she overheard the woman tell one of the men, “You had penetrative sex with me. I had so much ketamine, my eyes were crossed, and you still had sex with me,” according to documents obtained by CBS News New York.
In a summary of Jane Doe’s statement to university police that Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten released before he was removed from the case, the woman said she came to the frat house as a “5 out of 10” on a scale of drunkenness and that she became an “8 out of 10” throughout the hours-long ordeal.
She also said she took Ketamine multiple times.
“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me,” Jane Doe said during a May 2025 disciplinary hearing. “It just was a totally debilitating place to be in.”
Cornell University has defended its handling of Jane Doe’s case, which ended in expulsions and suspensions.
“Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” Cornell said in a Monday statement.
The school also welcomed the reopening of the case, which could result in criminal prosecution.

Rape Crisis also offers support. You can call them on 0808 802 9999 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, and 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland, or visit their website at www.rapecrisis.org.uk.

No one expected an American pope. Here's the inside story of how 'Bob' became Pope Leo
NPR's Daniel Burke and Scott Detrow covered the 2025 conclave that elected Pope Leo XIV. The following excerpt is adapted from their new biography of Pope Leo, American Pope, out Tuesday.
In the days immediately following Pope Francis' death, messages from friends poured into Cardinal Robert Prevost's phone.
Father Ramiro Castillo Castro, who had studied under Prevost in the 1990s, was among those who sent condolences. "Thank you, Ramiro," Prevost responded. "We have to pray a lot. Big hug."
"Polly and I send our love and prayers for you in these momentous days," wrote John Snider, a Lutheran pastor with whom Prevost had spent a summer in Minneapolis debating theology and learning how to minister to the sick and dying before they were both ordained.
Now, decades later, Snider was winding down his career, and Prevost was about to participate in a conclave to elect the next pope. "As I near retirement, 3 weeks, you are taking on such intense responsibility," he wrote. "God is with you!"
"Everything is in God's hands," responded Prevost, thanking the Sniders for their friendship through the years.
John Barry, Prevost's friend dating back to high school, was overcome by the news of Francis' death. "I know you were close to him and I'm sorry for your personal loss. The world has lost a great man. You also lost a friend," he wrote.
He offered his prayers and then turned to something that Prevost's friends around the world — in Illinois, in Peru, in Rome and elsewhere — were thinking.
"Okay, now Bob please don't get upset with me, but I believe what [their mutual friend] Jeanette first said — that you could possibly be the next pope. (Of course, you're too humble to entertain such thoughts.) I realize it's not a job a person would want, but in my heart I know you would make a great pope. You've obviously got the brains for the job. But your compassion, your kind heart, and your holiness are what really elevate you in my eyes. You're the best man I know. And this may or may not be a silly question, but if you do become pope, can I still email you?"
Amid the flurry of activity in Rome, Prevost found the time to quickly write back.
"I just leave everything in the Lord's hands," he responded. "Francis' passing is a true loss ... it will take time to process. ... Thank you for your prayers!"
"Since I really don't think there will be a need to change addresses," he added at the end, "you can still write. … Just tell your dad that you call me by the right name!" (This was a reference to a running joke between the two of them about how upset Barry's father was that his son called his high-ranking cardinal friend "Bob.")
For all his friends' intuition, Prevost was not one of the cardinals initially focused on as a "papabile," a papal contender (the phrase literally means "pope-able" in Italian).
There were many reasons for that. Most prominent: Prevost was American.
An American had never been pope, and the prevailing conventional wisdom was that one never would be elected. The country already had too much influence over world events, some argued.
The political situation in the United States may have made the prospect of an American pope seem even more unlikely. President Trump had returned to power and had spent the first months of 2025 asserting his "America First" agenda on the world through brute force. And just as cardinals arrived in Rome in the wake of Francis' death, Trump posted an AI-generated image on social media depicting himself as the next pope, offending the cardinals and Catholics around the world.
So no one expected an American pope, certainly not in that moment.
"We're talking about a country that has political, economic, military power in the world," Chicago's archbishop, Cardinal Blase Cupich, said in an interview with the Chicago Sun-Times, "and so I think it's a stretch to say that it's prudent to go ahead and have someone who is from that country. … I'm not going to handicap anybody in terms of their chances. But I think that'd be a stretch."
Prevost read the article.
"Cupich said they aren't going to elect an American," he told his friend Father John Merkelis after the interview. "I'm sleeping well at night."
Merkelis relayed Prevost's sentiment to their old friend and mentor Sister Thérèse DelGenio, who had worked with both of them as they learned to minister to addicts in Calumet City, Ill., in the late 1970s.
"Oops," DelGenio responded. "He forgot about the Holy Spirit."
"I had never met the man"
Over the course of the next week, cardinals from around the world descended on Rome to mourn Francis and begin the process of electing the next pope.
That included the most high-profile cardinal in the U.S., New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan. One of the few voting cardinals who had also participated in the 2013 conclave, Dolan reveled in his seniority, even as he batted aside questions about his electability.
"I've got a better chance at batting cleanup for the Yankees than I do being pope," he joked to a reporter at the airport.
Dolan was an ally of Trump's. He had prayed at both of the president's inaugurations and served as a member of the White House's Religious Liberty Commission. As the church's leading representative in the media capital of the world for more than a decade, he was far more visible than his colleagues. And, as a jovial extrovert, he prided himself on knowing many, if not most, of the cardinals in the conclave.
And yet, as he flew to Rome, Robert Prevost was not on his radar at all.
But when he landed, he was bombarded by other cardinals who immediately began asking about his fellow American. What was he like? What were his interests? His temperament? Dolan was taken aback.
"I said, 'Who?'
"I didn't even think of him as an American," Dolan explained. "I mean, the little bit I knew about him was good — I had heard good things about him. But I had never met the man."
When the questions kept coming, Dolan realized he had to change that fact — and fast. He saw Prevost at a gathering of cardinals. Unlike many others, he noticed, Prevost was not working the room or approaching others to greet them. It wasn't aloofness that drove that behavior, though. Dolan thought it might just be shyness. He approached Prevost with an outstretched hand. "Robert, my name is Tim Dolan. I don't think I met you before."
The movie Conclave drives up excitement for the real thing
Starting the day after Francis died, the cardinals began assembling daily in an auditorium off St. Peter's Square. Sitting in a steep lecture hall, wearing laminated name tags over their black cassocks and red sashes, they held General Congregation meetings that often stretched on for hours, during which they would discuss the state of the church, the priorities its next leader would have to face, and what sort of qualities they wanted to see in him.
"On some days, it was a little disorganized," Cardinal Joseph Tobin, of New Jersey, admitted. "They said it was kind of like listening to an argument in an Italian barbershop while watching an episode of The Sopranos." Whenever order was eventually restored, Tobin said, the sessions would gravitate to the same big questions: "What does the church need? What does the world need? What are we hoping for, what are we dreaming about?"
Outside the walls of Vatican City, Rome was abuzz with excitement. Thousands of reporters from all over the world had poured into the city to cover the conclave. Every morning, crowds of journalists and religious pilgrims would swarm as soon as they saw a man in a red skullcap and black cassock walk into St. Peter's Square. The reporters would ask questions about the latest intrigue, while the pilgrims would ask for prayers and blessings. Some cardinals would stop — more often for the prayer requests than the questions — but others would keep walking.
The 2024 movie Conclave, which had been nominated for Best Picture at the recent Academy Awards, also drove up interest in the proceedings. The sumptuously shot adaptation of Robert Harris' novel was a political thriller about the selection of a new pope as the church is at a moral and political crossroads. It depicted cardinals whipping vote counts and debating campaign strategies as they smoked cigarettes in stairwells and glided through the ornate halls of the Vatican.
Many of the real-life cardinals insisted they hadn't watched the film, but Prevost had. He had talked about it with his brothers. His high school friends had asked him about it, too. They'd all, Prevost included, jokingly tried to match up each movie character with his real-life inspiration. It was all in good fun, but Prevost insisted to them he wasn't a Conclave character. Harris had written the book in 2016, he pointed out, before Prevost had been made a cardinal.
"If it does happen, let it be OK"
As the meetings went on, more cardinals began to seriously consider Prevost.
He was a close ally of Francis and committed to many of Francis' top priorities: making decisions through the more communal approach known in the church as synodality, standing up for immigrants and speaking up on the environment. He had spent years as a missionary and was arguably as closely tied to South America and Peru as he was to the United States. "The least-American American" was a phrase that suddenly began to pop up in news articles, attributed to various cardinals.
Prevost was also becoming increasingly attractive to some of the cardinals who wanted stylistic changes from the Francis era. Dolan was among them. As much as he praised Francis' heart and pastoral energy, Dolan and others hoped for something different from their next leader. "Non-flashy. Reliable. Not impetuous, not unscripted," he explained. "Just sort of measured, circumspect. Calm. There's not going to be any bombshells. You know, you're not going to have to wake up in the morning and say, 'How are we going to answer the questions about this statement?'"
Dolan began doing more homework on the quiet American. At one point, he asked a colleague, one who had worked closely with Prevost, for insight.
"He runs a good meeting," came the reply.
"Well, that sure is Irish praise," Dolan thought. "Is that all you can say about it?" But then, the answer's meaning settled more deeply. "I thought, maybe he meant that he knows what he's doing," Dolan later recalled. "He's got an agenda, he's ordered, he's got certain goals in mind."
Dolan had been a public face of the American church for two decades. But sitting in the General Congregation meetings, he began to consider that the first American pontiff might be a radically different kind of figure. During one of the meetings' many coffee breaks, he brought an espresso to an older cardinal, one who was too old to vote
in the conclave. They sat there together in the auditorium sipping their drinks.
"So, who do you think?" Dolan asked.
The older cardinal looked down toward a group of their peers at the front of the room. He pointed at Prevost.
Toward the end of their 12 meetings, the cardinals continued to talk through the qualities they wanted from the next pope. They wanted someone to continue the fight against sexual abuse in the church. To fix the Vatican's disorganized finances. To continue Francis' push to reform the Vatican bureaucracy, the Curia. To work for peace throughout the world. They also wanted someone who, like Francis, prioritized the environment and the need to fully address climate change.
As he heard all this, Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto laughed. The 81-year-old Jesuit was too old to vote in the coming conclave, but he could suddenly see how it would play out. Abuse? Prevost had headed the Peruvian bishops' council to address it. Economic reform? He had played a leading role in working to address church finances in Peru, as well. Fixing the Curia? He'd been in Rome two years — enough time to learn the ropes, but not enough time to become an entrenched member himself. He kept going down the list of priorities.
"Check, check, check, check, check," Barreto said to himself. His friend Robert could become pope — if the cardinals could get over the fact he was an American.
Cardinal Joseph Tobin was coming around to the idea, too. He had known Bob, as he called him, for three decades. They had worked together in Rome, when Prevost ran the Augustinians and Tobin headed his order, the Redemptorists, and then again in Peru.
One night, Tobin, Prevost and several other cardinals gathered together to pray and share dinner. As the evening wrapped up, Tobin took his friend aside.
"I think you may be asked," he said. "So all I'm doing is praying for you."
Prevost didn't debate Tobin or try to dissuade him. He simply thanked him for his prayers. He knew he had no control over his destiny.
Forty years earlier, as a student in Rome, he had voiced a similar feeling in a letter to his friends John and Polly Snider as he waited for his next assignment. It might have been in Rome, he said, or the U.S. It might have been in Peru. He just didn't know. But he had trusted God at that moment, as he had at every other juncture in his life.
As the May 7 start to the conclave approached, he faced a similar crossroads. He had started, in recent years, to fantasize about retirement. Now there was a realistic possibility he'd head the church, and in the process become one of the most famous and influential people in the world. As daunting as that was, he was determined to, as always, give himself over to God's will.
"I took a deep breath," he later said. "I said, "Here we go, Lord. You're in charge. You lead the way.'"
In New Lenox, Ill., John Prevost was praying, too.
Like his brother, John had at first dismissed the idea of an American being elected to the papacy. But as he'd heard the reports and debates, doubts had begun to creep in.
After a Mass at St. Jude, the priest, Father John Merkelis, had approached him to say that his brother currently had the same odds that Jorge Bergoglio had faced going into the 2013 conclave. Merkelis took it as a sign. He joked to John that he had briefly considered pointing him out in the pews that night and telling the congregation they were joined by the brother of the future pope.
"Don't you dare," John Prevost quickly responded. He didn't want that kind of attention. He didn't want his brother to become pope, either. That would mean an end to his brother's visits home, an end to his life as he currently knew it.
He prayed that night for it not to happen. "Then I said, 'Well, if it does happen, let it be OK." Then, as his prayers continued, another shift. "Not my will," he said, "but, what's good for the church."
The day before the conclave began, Robert Prevost went to the Augustinian General Curia, as he often did, to pray and eat with about a dozen fellow Augustinians. He talked with Father Alejandro Moral Antón, the man who'd succeeded him as the order's prior general. They then prayed together to the Holy Spirit, asking it to accompany Prevost and the other 132 electors as they entered the Sistine Chapel the next day.
When the prayer was done, Moral Antón turned to Prevost and told him he was always welcome to return to the Augustinian community for meals, Mass and prayer, no matter what color he happened to be wearing.

Farage 'not being listened to' on safety threats, deputy says after terror plot charge
Nigel Farage's security concerns have been ignored, according to his deputy, Richard Tice
LONDON -- Anti-immigration Reform UK party leader Nigel Farage was ignored when he complained of threats to his safety, his deputy said Saturday after the man accused of killing former British politician Ann Widdecombe was charged with plotting a terror attack against Farage.
Richard Tice said Farage had discussed the risks to his security many times over the years and the charge amounts to a wake-up call.
“What’s particularly upsetting for those of us in and around him is sometimes he’s not being believed, not being listened to,” Tice told the BBC.
Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, including against Farage, the Crown Prosecution Service said Friday.
Authorities did not release additional information about the charge, but counterterrorism police in August said they had reopened a probe into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage's south London home.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood expressed sympathy for Farage and his family.
"I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning," Mahmood said on X. “Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all."
Mahmood said she would work to strengthen protections for politicians after Parliament returns from recess on Oct. 12.
Kerry was previously charged with murder in the July 8 beating death of Widdecombe, who was found dead in her house in an isolated southwest England village.
Widdecombe, 78, was a spokesperson for the Reform Party after a long career as a Conservative member of Parliament and government minister known for her blunt-spoken, socially conservative views opposing abortion and the expansion of LGBTQ+ rights.
She later found fame as a contestant on the reality television shows “Strictly Come Dancing” and “Celebrity Big Brother” and returned to politics.
Widdecombe's killing renewed concerns over the security for politicians, which had been tightened in the past decade after the murders of two prominent MPs. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.
Tice said the party had a series of high-level meetings with the government about security and that authorities had shifted their approach to treat threats more seriously.
Kerry is due to appear Wednesday in Westminster Magistrates' Court on the new charge.

Opponents of Anthropic's Dario Amodei are circulating a highly negative brief about him to the White House ahead of an important dinner with President Trump, per an Axios review of the document.
Why it matters: No company wants to be on Trump's bad side — and a Sunday night dinner between the president and Amodei could be what thaws relations after a year of tension.
Behind the scenes: The brief, which is not an internal White House document, casts Amodei as having "a long record of attacking Trump" and having "deep Democratic ties."
It notes the company's falling out earlier this year with the Pentagon as a "clear example of Dario showing he doesn't trust President Trump."
The brief is intended for Trump's eyes and is likely to get in front of him, according to a source familiar with the internal workings of the White House. Its origin is unclear.
It even reads in "Trump Talk," a name the president gives to his style of posting: "Dario claimed that AI would eliminate half of all entry-level white collar jobs as soon as this year. WRONG!"
Between the lines: The brief's creators are appealing to a president who prizes loyalty and puts a premium on praise.
Amodei's failure to communicate properly with the Trump administration has previously cost the company.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Yes, but: Trump has also been laser-focused on winning the AI race and Anthropic is one of the few companies on the frontier of the technology.
Anthropic is also valued at hundreds of billions of dollars and has plans to go public soon, making it even harder for the White House to ignore.
"The WH is trying to get everyone seated at the table," one source told Axios.
The bottom line: Anthropic and the White House both have something to gain from Sunday night's dinner, so long as Amodei's critics don't get there first.

How both parties have changed since 2024
The 2026 midterms will test Republican disillusionment with Trump — and Democrats’ new appetite for a fight.
Depending on your political appetite and your geographic location, you absolutely do not need me to remind you of the upcoming midterm elections. But for those of you unencumbered by an unhealthy attachment to political news, and unassaulted by the onslaught of ever-more-brazen political ads, consider this your official notice that the midterms are approaching. Fast.
In less than six weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices. The stakes are arguably unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical norms and limits.
So starting this evening, I’m partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s Midterms, Actually team for five weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the 2026 midterms. Together with outside experts, we’ll break down one issue each week and suggest further reading and races to watch in November.
Up first, and without further ado: the profound shift that both parties have experienced since the 2024 election. These are not your mother’s Democrats. Or Republicans.
Go a little deeper
To kick this series off, I asked Astead to imagine a hypothetical world in which he hadn’t followed politics since 2024. (An outlandish counterfactual: Astead is acutely plugged into politics.) But in this alternate universe, I asked, what would surprise him most about 2026?
Easy, he said. The GOP’s disillusionment with President Donald Trump, who remade the party in his image.
Let’s put some numbers on that phenomenon, to start. Trump’s approval rating has dipped to record lows, even among Republicans. According to an NBC poll conducted in mid-September, just four in 10 Republicans strongly approve of Trump’s performance, down 11 percentage points from the spring.
Republicans have soured on Trump over his handling of the economy and attacks on Iran, which violated his promise to keep America out of foreign wars. Trump’s delayed release of the Epstein files also fueled distrust in his base by exposing his own ties to the dreaded “elite insiders.”
In response, some Republican candidates have worked to distance themselves from Trump, even defying him in campaign ads. But it’s unclear whether that tactic will win over disillusioned or disengaged Republicans. If enough stay home, Astead said — especially with Democrats eager to vote — Democrats could flip the House and/or Senate and make Trump’s last years in office far more difficult.
And speaking of Democrats…they’re also undergoing a major transformation after their 2024 presidential defeat. That loss disproved their previous theory of Trump-era politics: namely, that Trump’s rise was an aberration that competence, decency, and normalcy would eventually overcome.
By contrast, today’s Democrats want a party that “fights,” Astead told me. “The open question is who they’re fighting: The oligarchy? Big Tech? The Billionaire/Epstein class? Trump’s Republican Party?”
Democrats face ideological questions, too. Since 2024, voters have lost trust in the establishment and in party leaders’ ability to pick the best candidates; left-wing candidates have thrived in that vacuum. It’s pretty wild, when you think about it, that a Muslim democratic socialist in New York ranks among America’s most popular Democrats.
For both parties, then, November 3 is a test of their respective visions for America. Not just between the parties — as in, Republicans vs. Democrats — but within them, as well. That, in turn, will help determine the rest of Trump’s presidency…and the 2028 presidential election.
But it’s only October 1. Let’s not get ahead of ourselves.
➨ Races to watch: Michigan’s Senate race, where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers; Florida’s 27th District, where Republican María Elvira Salazar publicly broke with Trump; and the Nebraska, Idaho, and South Dakota’s Senate races, where independent candidates will test both sides’ exhaustion with the two-party system.

The attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021, was not conducted mainly by extremists or fringe militia groups. It was, according to the data, the work of normal Americans.
That is the conclusion Robert A. Pape lays out in his new book, Our Own Worst Enemies: America in the Age of Violent Populism, citing data about those who were arrested and charged following the attack.
While Proud Boys and Oath Keepers gained most of the headlines, data collected by Pape as part of his work as founding director of the Chicago Project on Security and Threats (CPOST) found that the vast majority (90 percent) of those charged with crimes arising from the attack held no affiliation with militias or militant organizations.
Pape’s analysis found that 22 percent were business owners, and almost 30 percent held a college degree. Among the defendants were doctors, engineers, CEOs, and government employees. Nearly 40 percent held white-collar jobs, while just 8 percent of participants were unemployed.
The findings are key to understanding the warning that is central to Pape’s book: Americans do not understand that the threat of political violence is coming not from the fringes, but from the mainstream.
“As the 2026 midterms approach, US elections are entering a danger zone in which state power, protest, and political legitimacy increasingly collide,” Pape writes in the book. “For most Americans, political violence is still understood as episodic—shocking when it erupts but destined to fade. That assumption is reassuring. It is also increasingly dangerous.”
WIRED spoke to Pape about his book, his concerns about violence in the midterms, why it is so important to understand the attack on the Capitol, and what, if anything, gives him hope that democracy will win out.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
DAVID GILBERT: Your book is centered on the idea of violent populism. What is it, and why is it on the rise in 2026?
ROBERT A. PAPE: Violent populism is a dangerous political climate where substantial segments of the public increasingly accept physical force as a legitimate tool to gain, preserve, or defend political power. It is on the rise due to a profound cultural clash over the nature of American identity and citizenship, exacerbated by elite rhetoric that frames politics as an existential struggle between enemies. This structural dynamic transforms ordinary, mainstream citizens into active participants in political aggression.
You call the midterms “a stress test of whether American competition can remain bounded by nonviolence.” Are you concerned about the political violence around this election?
Yes, the level of concern for this election cycle is at an unprecedented high, surpassing anything seen since the deep social upheavals of the 1960s. With national anxieties amplified by a highly combustible domestic climate and global instability like the ongoing war with Iran, elections have increasingly become dangerous potential flashpoints. This dynamic represents a direct, critical test of whether our foundational institutions can still successfully enforce peaceful political transitions.
Heading into the midterms, a lot of people are focusing on possible action from extremist groups, such as militias. Is this the wrong thing to be worried about?
Focusing exclusively on fringe militias misdiagnoses the primary danger facing American democracy today. The real threat is that political radicalization has broken out of the fringes and fully migrated into the mainstream electorate. Our primary worry should be the tens of millions of ordinary Americans who now passively accept or actively endorse violence to achieve their political goals.
You write that Americans are misreading the warning signs of political violence, again. What are those warning signs?
The primary warning sign is the broad public normalization and passive acceptance of aggressive political acts as standard features of daily political life. This is signaled by an explosion of violent symbolism across the entire media spectrum and elite rhetoric that strips legitimacy away from opposing factions. When ordinary citizens begin to view political opposition as an existential, hostile force, the ground is fully prepared for real-world conflict.
You write in the book that the January 6th attack on the Capitol was a rubicon crossed between "routine political conflict and civil war." Why was it such an important turning point?
The January 6th attack shattered the all-important democratic norm that power changes hands through ballots rather than raw displays of physical coercion. It demonstrated that an electoral outcome could be violently challenged not by foreign adversaries, but by a massive crowd of American citizens targeting their own legislative body. This crossed line signaled that internal political disputes were no longer reliably bounded by a shared commitment to nonviolence.
The narrative around the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol is that it was driven by extremist groups on the fringes of American society. But that's not what the data shows, right?
CPOST data completely disproves the fringe narrative by showing the remarkable mainstream geography of those involved in the insurrection. The vast majority of the actors were not isolated radicals or card-carrying militia members, but “normal” political activists with stable homes, jobs, and 401(k)s. Only 1 in 10 were militia members. Nearly half were doctors, lawyers, CEOs, business owners, US State Department appointees—and some even attended the White House Christmas party the year before. Most represented a cross-section of middle-class America acting on a shared, mainstream belief that democratic institutions were no longer legitimate.
Why do you think the prevailing narrative around the January 6 attack on the Capitol has been so wrong for so many years?
The narrative has been wrong because public institutions and media outlets initially relied heavily on imperfect law enforcement databases that naturally isolated the most prominent, organized fringe actors. And they did not update their readers and viewers as the bulk of the data came in. This approach ignored the underlying, broader structural dynamics of public opinion and extensive survey research. By focusing strictly on the visible, oddball characters, analysts missed the massive wave of passive, mainstream support that actually fueled the event.
My reading of this book is that most people have a fundamental misunderstanding of political violence in America in 2026. Is that accurate?
That is completely accurate and is the central, urgent argument of the entire book. The greatest threat to the United States is not an out-of-control group of radical extremists, but the reality that millions of otherwise ordinary citizens now accept violence as a regular political tool. Once political violence is normalized by the mainstream, old institutional solutions cease to function effectively.
You compare the current embrace of violent populism by middle-class white America to the expansion of the second Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s. Do you think people will be shocked by that comparison?
Many readers will likely be shocked, because the modern imagination associates the Klan strictly with regional, low-income hate groups rather than a massive social movement. However, the historical data shows that the second KKK of the 1920s was a highly mainstream, middle-class organization driven by a cultural clash over American identity. Drawing this explicit parallel highlights how easily normal, institutionalized communities can slide into systemic intolerance when they feel their cultural dominance is threatened.
Do you think readers of the book will be surprised that defense of political violence is not solely the preserve of the right, but that people on the left also reinforce your thesis of violent populism?
Yes, readers who expect a one-sided partisan critique will be surprised to see that the call for political violence comes from both sides of the aisle. [Confessed health care CEO assassin Luigi] Mangione and the recent [accused] Trump assassin at the April White House Correspondents’ Dinner reflect political violence from the left, and they are far from alone. Original CPOST surveys reveal that violent style, aggressive symbolism, and the demonization of political opponents are heavily utilized by figures across the entire political spectrum. This multisided reality proves that violent populism is a systemic, societal failure rather than an isolated partisan phenomenon.
You say that it is not yet determined if the current transitional phase of American politics will “culminate in democratic renewal or deeper political breakdown.” Do you have a sense of when we might have an answer to this question?
We need to lean into the “good news” in my book: that 70 percent of Americans abhor political violence. This is the large, untapped resource that we need to lean into. My book is essentially for the 70 percent and a call to action for what they can do—beyond voting. The 70 percent are the heart of our democracy. Leaning into them is how we save our democracy and avoid a much deeper, systemic breakdown of American governance.
What, if anything, gives you hope that violent populism can be overcome?
Hope lies in the data that can give new active optimism to vast majorities of ordinary Americans on both the left and right that still share a fundamental desire for stability and governance. By recognizing that our enemies are not really each other, but the normalization of violence itself, we can deliberately choose strategies of restraint to rebuild our vital democratic norms—and find productive new solutions.

In Summary
- Xiaomi released a number of power banks in the Indian market recently.
- The most eye-catching of the new power banks is the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank, which is the successor to the Ultra Slim power bank launched last year.
- The UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is the slimmest power bank in its class – it is a mere 6 mm thin, and less than 100 grams in weight. It also comes with a super premium design, with a metal build and a fiberglass wireless charging area.
- It has a premium design and feel, but the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank comes with a stiff price tag of Rs 5,999, which many might find outrageous for a 5000 mAh power bank. But it could be perfect for many others!
Power banks and “beauty” are seldom used in the same sentence. They are notorious for being bulky, heavy, and brick-like. Even the ones that can be slapped on the back of your phone and attached magnetically often feel uncomfortable to use along with a smartphone. Unless one is using the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank.
Xiaomi pleasantly surprised us all with a super thin power bank last year, the Xiaomi Ultra Slim power bank, which was so slim and compact that many of us had mistaken it for a card holder. It, however, lacked wireless charging, so it could not be stuck onto the back of a phone. The UltraThin power bank fixes this shortcoming. It comes with a 5,000 mAh battery with up to 15W wireless charging support, and 22.5W charging support (up from 20W on the Ultra Slim). While these numbers are nothing to rave about, it is the design and build of the power bank that are showstoppers. But can its lightweight make up for its rather heavy price tag of Rs. 5,999? Let’s find out:
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Design and Appearance: A treat to hold and carry!
It is difficult to think that anything out of the ordinary can be done with the design of power banks, given just how simple and functional the devices are, but Xiaomi has managed to make the design of the UltraThin power bank its biggest USP. As the name suggests, the power bank is truly “ultra thin.” In fact, at 6mm, it is almost half as thin as the Ultra Slim power bank that impressed us last year, and is the thinnest power bank we have used to date.
The power bank is quite compact as well. It is 98.5 mm tall, 71.5 mm wide, and weighs just 98 grams, which means that it will not only easily fit on the back of any phone out there, but will add only about as much weight as a routine phone case. Even though the Xiaomi UltraThin powerbank is quite sleek, it still feels very sturdy. The body is made of an aluminum alloy shell, giving it that reassuring solid feel, and the wireless charging side comes with fiberglass.
The power bank is available in three different colors – Graphite black, Glacier Silver, and Radiant Orange. While we received the black color option, we think all three colors look very good – the bright orange is the exact shade of the iPhone 17 Pro series’ orange and will basically blend with your iPhone 17 Pro or Pro Max (Apple seems to have stepped away from the shade in its latest iPhones, though).
Our unit came with a matte finish, and the back has a small “Mi” logo in a glossy contrast. The thin sides curve softly around the edges, while the front (which is the part that connects wirelessly to your phone) has a huge circular mark to highlight wireless charging connectivity, along with some information. All the sides are bare except the base, which has a small power button, a USB Type-C port for charging, and four tiny LED lights highlighting the amount of charge in the power bank.
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic power bank is a treat to both hold and carry. It exudes premiumness, and its thin form factor makes it easy to carry around, regardless of whether you hold it in your hand, carry it in your trouser pocket, or in your bag. Or even on your phone. It was so thin and light that we actually used it as a bookmark from time to time.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Specs and Hardware: Decent, rather than exceptional
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is more about style and convenience than specs. It comes with decent enough specs, but nothing that will make people sit up in surprise. The power bank comes with a 5,000 mAh battery, which is a touch more than the UltraSlim, which had a 4900 mAh battery. Xiaomi has used an advanced silicon carbon battery instead of the usual lithium-ion one, which allows more mAhs to be packed in a much smaller form factor.
In terms of charging speed, the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank offers up to 15W wireless charging support and 22.5W wired charging support (up from 20W on the UltraSlim). That sounds brisk enough, but this 15W wireless charging speed is only delivered with the Xiaomi 17 series. For other smartphones that come with wireless charging support, you will get 7.5W charging speed, including the iPhones (MagSafe is supported, but the charging speed remains slow).
Xiaomi has added a number of safety features in the power bank as well. The brand says there are ten layers of safety protection on the device, including foreign object detection, overcurrent, short circuits, overvoltage, overcharging, overdischarging, and over-discharging, amongst other safety features.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Performance: Super convenient, but not super fast
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank’s spec sheet means that it cannot fully charge most modern smartphones from 0-100 percent – while it has a capacity of 5000 mAh, its rated capacity is lower (3000 mAh), as in most power banks. As a result, it was able to take our iPhone 17 (which comes with a 3692 mAh battery) from 20 percent to nearly full only once. And as its wireless charging speed for iPhones is fairly sluggish, it took comfortably over an hour. And it took even longer to charge our Pixel 10 Pro XL. That said, thanks to its slim size and light weight, you can just stick it to the back of your phone and forget it.
If you need relatively faster charging, you can connect your phone to the power bank with a Type-C cable and enjoy 22.5W wired charging speed, which is pretty much three times the 7.5W wireless charging speed with non-Xiaomi 17 series phones, and does get the phone charged much faster in comparison. However, if your phone comes with a relatively big battery (and many phones these days are comfortably above 5000 mAh), the power bank might only be able to get them up to 40 or 50 percent charged before needing charging assistance itself.
While you can use the power bank to charge two devices at once – wired and wirelessly – that compromises speed and its charging capacity a fair bit, as both get divided. The power bank also gets fairly warm while charging a phone wirelessly, which can make the temperature of the phone attached rise too. Our iPhone 17 often got very warm while charging.
The magnetic hold of the power bank is very strong. It latched on very easily to our iPhone and did not budge when we kept the pair of them in our pocket or bags, or even while using the phone. This is by far the most comfortable and convenient power bank to use with a phone – you hardly feel its weight.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Review Verdict: Pricey, premium and a convenience contender
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank comes with a very steep price tag of Rs 5999. You can get power banks with way more mAh, more ports, and much faster charging speeds at a lower price from Xiaomi itself. Other brands also have their version of slim power banks at far lower prices – Boat has the Magnacharge at Rs 1,599 and URBN the One Premium MagSafe at Rs 1,999. However, none of them brings the sleek form factor and the premium build that the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank offers, nor the long-term assurance that the brand offers. In fact, its only real competitor would perhaps be Samsung’s Galaxy Magnetic Wireless battery pack, which comes with a similar capacity and 15W wireless charging, but is bulkier and not exactly super affordable at about Rs 4,900.
If you are in the market for a power bank with more mAh in capacity and more Ws in charging speed, and what’s more, want both for a small price tag, the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is not for you. However, if you are someone who wants to invest in an ultra-portable, very premium power bank which can simply give your smartphone a power-packed nudge without adding too much bulk to your gadget life, or even to your device itself, the Xiaomi UltraThin Powerbank might be perfect for you. Yes, it is expensive, but it brings with it terrific design, ease of use, and convenience, which is likely to be coveted by many premium phone users, especially those who use iPhones and Pixels!
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank’s style is its substance. And it is substantially stylish. Yes, it does have a big price tag, but then, convenience can also be a powerful feature of a power bank.

- Impressively thin
