Indian spacetech startups TakeMe2Space, SatLeo Labs, and EON Space Labs sent AI computing and Earth observation technologies into orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 today. The Transporter-18 rideshare mission lifted off from California, carrying TakeMe2Space’s MOI-1A satellite with EON Space Labs’ MIRA imaging system onboard. SatLeo Labs’ TAPAS-1 thermal-imaging payload flew on Dhruva Space’s LEAP-2 satellite. Hyderabad-based TakeMe2Space’s MOI-1A is designed to process Earth observation data in orbit using AI, allowing customers to receive insights without downloading large volumes of raw imagery. Ahmedabad-based SatLeo’s TAPAS-1 is designed to capture land-surface temperature data, while Hyderabad-based EON’s MIRA captures imagery across multiple spectral bands. TakeMe2Space’s Bet On Computing In-Orbit MOI-1A is a 14-kg satellite with onboard computing capacity of 117 trillion operations per second (TOPS), 2 TB of storage, and a nine-band multispectral imager. Customers can deploy AI models directly on the satellite to analyse imagery in orbit, instead of downloading it to a ground station for processing. This can reduce the volume of data that needs to be downloaded by a factor of 1,000, TakeMe2Space founder and CEO Ronak Kumar Samantray told Inc42. The satellite identifies objects or patterns in imagery and sends back the results. He explained that a 2,000-km stretch of synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) imagery could generate around 300 GB of data. If an AI model is instead used to identify specific objects or patterns in orbit, the resulting output could shrink to only a few kilobytes. The startup’s first-generation satellites are designed around inference rather than AI model training. TakeMe2Space has signed up 23 customers for its in-orbit inference services. Around 80% are outside India, according to Samantray. These include international geospatial companies, while Indian educational institutions are using the infrastructure as an orbital research laboratory. The use cases currently span agriculture, defence, supply chain intelligence, mining and insurance. Building A Six-Satellite Constellation MOI-1A follows TakeMe2Space’s 2024 technology demonstrator, which validated onboard AI inference and data processing. The startup subsequently lost MOI-1 during the unsuccessful PSLV-C62 mission earlier this year. Samantray said the broad satellite architecture remains similar, but individual subsystems have undergone multiple development cycles since the earlier mission. The startup expects to make MOI-1A commercially available shortly after reaching orbit. It plans to launch its other Gen-1 satellite, MOI-1B, in November aboard ISRO’s SSLV. That satellite will carry a black-and-white imager primarily intended for object detection. TakeMe2Space then plans to launch larger spacecraft as it builds a six-satellite constellation. Its Gen-2 satellites will have roughly 10X the capacity of the Gen-1 spacecraft, according to Samantray, with around 100 TB of storage per satellite and significantly greater computing capacity. The startup also plans to introduce laser-based links between satellites, allowing them to exchange data without routing it through ground stations. For instance, one satellite could pass processed data to another with a better connection to a ground station for transmission to Earth. Two Gen-2 satellites, MOI-2 and MOI-3, are planned for launch in 2027, most likely aboard Indian launch vehicles. Samantray said the startup has not booked these launches yet because he expects Indian launch services to operate more regularly by then. The startup has secured a slot aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 mission in late 2028 for MOI-4 and MOI-5, which would complete the constellation, he added. Samantray expects each Gen-2 satellite to generate around $1 Mn in annual revenue. The startup is targeting about $6 Mn in annual recurring revenue from its in-orbit computing business by 2028. It is also designing Gen-3 satellites in the 1,500-kg class with around 25 kW of power, with a potential launch around 2029, he said. SatLeo, EON Expand Imaging Capabilities SatLeo Labs’ TAPAS-1, which the startup describes as India’s first dedicated commercial thermal payload, uses thermal infrared sensing to capture temperature information. Potential applications include urban heat mapping, crop-stress monitoring, disaster monitoring, and infrastructure surveillance. The payload flew aboard Dhruva Space’s LEAP-2 satellite, which also carries a star tracker from France’s Sodern. The mission will test TAPAS-1’s sensing, calibration, and processing capabilities in orbit. EON Space Labs’ MIRA, meanwhile, is a compact multispectral imaging system weighing 502 grams. Integrated with MOI-1A, it is designed to capture Earth observation imagery for applications spanning agriculture, mining, marine monitoring, supply chains, and insurance. Together, the missions bring specialised imaging and onboard data processing into focus as India’s spacetech startups work towards commercialising their technologies. IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka called the launch a “big day for India's private space sector”, saying it showed the “range and ambition” of India's private space ecosystem.

A four-person crew rocketed into orbit Thursday from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, heading for a six-month expedition on the International Space Station.
Riding a Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft, the four crew members departed from Space Launch Complex-40 at Cape Canaveral at 11:10 am EDT (15:10 UTC) Thursday. Nine minutes later, they were in orbit to begin closing in on the space station for docking Thursday evening.
The launch was delayed from mid-September to replace a balky valve in the Dragon spacecraft’s propulsion system, a task that involved cutting into a propellant line inside the ship to swap out a faulty component.
Jessica Watkins, a 38-year-old geologist turned astronaut, leads the four-person crew sent into orbit Thursday, becoming the first Black woman to command a spacecraft. Watkins is the only veteran astronaut on the mission—designated Crew-13—after spending 170 days in orbit on a long-duration spaceflight in 2022.
Pilot Luke Delaney, a Marine Corps veteran, was seated next to Watkins for the Dragon spacecraft’s ascent into orbit. Two international crew members rounded out the Crew-13 team: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, a former pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force, and Sergey Teteryatnikov, a Russian cosmonaut who served as a naval engineer before his selection to the Roscosmos Cosmonaut Corps in 2021.
Kutryk and his wife Heather are expecting their third child later this year. It’s rare, but astronauts have been off the planet for their child’s birth before. Most recently, NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, set to command the Artemis III mission next year, was flying aboard the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 2009 when his wife gave birth to their daughter, Abigail Mae, in Houston.
“Leaving these three (plus one on the way) is the hardest thing I’ve ever done. But that has always been the nature of exploration,” Kutryk wrote on X.
Watkins and her crewmates were on course to reach the International Space Station (ISS) about eight hours after launch, the fastest-ever launch-to-docking transit to the ISS by a US spacecraft.
NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, commander of the Crew-13 mission, arrives at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of launch.
Credit:
NASA/Kim Shiflett
NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, commander of the Crew-13 mission, arrives at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of launch.
Credit:
NASA/Kim Shiflett
“What an epic ride. What an epic ride it was,” Delaney radioed mission control soon after reaching orbit. “Today, we proudly continue the streak of humans living and working in orbit, building on the legacies of yesterday to pave the way for the future of space exploration.”
The ISS has been permanently staffed since 2000, with crews flying to and from the orbiting outpost on NASA’s Space Shuttles, Russian Soyuz spacecraft, and most recently, SpaceX’s Crew Dragon. NASA and its international partners plan to keep the space station operating through at least 2030. SpaceX’s plans to retire the Crew Dragon vehicle around 2030 have prompted NASA to work more closely with Boeing to bring its troubled Starliner crew capsule into service.
Honing their craft
Thursday’s flight was the 13th crew rotation mission launched by SpaceX under a multibillion-dollar contract with NASA, and SpaceX’s 21st human spaceflight overall, including test flights and fully commercial missions.
The company’s success with the Crew Dragon spacecraft restored the country’s ability to launch astronauts into orbit after a nine-year gap following the Space Shuttle retirement in 2011, ending NASA’s sole reliance on Russia for crew transportation. NASA’s other commercial crew provider, Boeing, has repeatedly stumbled on a series of test flights with its Starliner spacecraft.
SpaceX’s plans to retire Crew Dragon and the Falcon 9 rocket mean the fleets are now well beyond halfway through their operational life. SpaceX has nine more Crew Dragon flights in its backlog, including three additional crew missions to the ISS that NASA recently secured in a $946 million contract extension, bringing NASA’s total contract for 17 SpaceX crew missions to $5.92 billion.
That figure is a drop in the bucket next to SpaceX’s projected revenues from its ever-growing Starlink broadband service, the Starship/Super Heavy rocket, and orbital data centers. SpaceX, now a publicly traded company, is prioritizing its most lucrative lines of business, and flights to the ISS aren’t among them.
Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk poses for a photo with his wife, Heather, and children after walking out from the Neil Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of his launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
Credit:
Paul Hennesy/Anadolu via Getty Images
Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk poses for a photo with his wife, Heather, and children after walking out from the Neil Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of his launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
Credit:
Paul Hennesy/Anadolu via Getty Images
Bill Gerstenmaier, SpaceX’s vice president of build and flight reliability, declined to say in a prelaunch press conference Wednesday if there is a “hard cutoff” for when the company will no longer offer Crew Dragon flights to NASA. The recent contract extension may be the last.
“We were just awarded Crew flights 15, 16, and 17, so I think our real focus is to make sure we get the most out of those flights,” Gerstenmaier said. “So we’re working really super hard to make sure that our vehicles are ready, things are ready to go fly, and we’ll keep moving forward.”
Notably, SpaceX is winding down Crew Dragon and Falcon 9 at the top of their game. Gerstenmaier pointed to the valve replacement inside the Crew Dragon spacecraft for the Crew-13 mission as evidence of SpaceX’s commitment to fulfilling its contract with NASA.
NASA announced a postponement for the Crew-13 launch in late August to give ground teams time to resolve an oxidizer leak inside Dragon’s propulsion system detected during launch preparations at Cape Canaveral. SpaceX traced the leak to a valve. The spacecraft was already loaded with nitrogen tetroxide, or NTO, the volatile, toxic oxidizer used by Dragon’s control thrusters in combination with hydrazine fuel.
Teams devised an unprecedented bit of spaceship surgery to replace the valve without draining the propellant and disassembling the spacecraft, steps that would have triggered a much longer delay. The fix involved cutting into the propellant line, removing and replacing the valve, then welding the line together again. It was the first time SpaceX has performed such a repair with a fully assembled Dragon spacecraft loaded with propellant.
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft lifts off on the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.
Credit:
NASA/John Kraus
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft lifts off on the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.
Credit:
NASA/John Kraus
“By cutting it out, we physically went in and actually cut the valve out of the line,” Gerstenmaier said. “It was welded in place, and then we actually re-welded a new valve in place.”
Engineers are testing the bad valve to diagnose the cause of the leak, but NASA officials were pleased with the fix. No leaks were detected during final preparations for launch Thursday, and Dragon’s propulsion system appeared to be functioning well after arriving in orbit.
“We looked at the plans, all of the data coming out of that, the welds, the leak, everything looks great,” said Dana Weigel, NASA’s program manager for the International Space Station. [We’re] really happy with how that repair was done.”
SpaceX’s preference to cut out the valve in place, rather than take a longer stand-down, kept the Crew-13 mission on track to arrive at the space station in time to replace Crew-12, which will return to Earth in mid-October after eight months in orbit.
The Crew Dragon spacecraft was inside SpaceX’s fueling and hazardous processing facility, known as Area 59, at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, not at the company’s usual maintenance hangar a few miles away.
“I actually went down and looked at the vehicle itself, got in the clean room, and took a look to see where they actually had to cut the valve out,” Gerstenmaier said. “There was not a lot of room, but there was good access up on the platform. I think the unique aspect of this was the location where it was being done.
“We also did it with oxidizer onboard the vehicle, and the oxidizer tank was full, so we made sure that was all clear,” Gerstenmaier said. “We had to get special permission from the [Space Force’s Eastern] Range to do these activities, to do ‘hot work’ with NTO, with nitrogen tetroxide on the vehicle.”
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

World Contraception Day on September 26 offers an opportunity to look closely at a part of family planning that receives very little attention: contraception for men. The key question here is why the range of methods available to men and women remains so different.
Women today have options including oral pills, injectables, implants, intrauterine devices and permanent sterilisation, though access and affordability to safe and reliable contraception in our country continues to remain a major challenge. For men, the practical choices are still largely limited to condoms for reversible contraception and vasectomy for permanent contraception. Male and female reproduction are governed by the same broad hormonal axis, yet the biology, anatomy and mechanics of preventing conception create very different problems. Understanding those differences helps explain why a male equivalent of the pill has remained elusive.

Brazilians will vote in a highly polarized presidential race on Sunday. Here’s what to know
Millions of Brazilians are voting in an election featuring two main rivals: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Millions of Brazilians will vote Sunday in an election dominated by two rivals: incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro who Lula defeated four years ago.
Twelve candidates are on the presidential ballot, but only Lula and Bolsonaro are thought to have a real chance of becoming Brazil’s next head of state. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the top 2 will advance to a runoff on Oct. 25.
Lula, who at 80 is one of the world’s oldest heads of state, is running in his seventh presidential election. Bolsonaro, 45, is competing in his first and seeking to return his family name to power after his father governed Brazil from 2019 through 2022.
The two represent opposite sides of the political spectrum, with conflicting visions on issues ranging from how to tackle organized crime to the relationship Latin America's biggest country should have with the Trump administration.
Here’s what to know about Brazil’s election.
Brazil holds general elections every four years, and voting is mandatory. Those who fail to cast a ballot without justification face a small fine.
On Sunday, Brazilians will choose a president, state and federal representatives as well as governors and some senators. Elections for mayors and city councilors are also held every four years, but in different years.
Almost 160 million eligible voters will use electronic voting machines to punch in the digits corresponding to their candidates, preparing number-heavy lists.
Brazilian authorities adopted electronic voting machines in the 1990s to combat fraud. In earlier local elections, ballot boxes were stuffed or stolen, and paper ballots were routinely falsified, according to Brazil’s electoral authority. The country held no direct presidential elections between 1960 and 1989, a period that included military rule from 1964 to 1985.
Now, results are reported mere hours after polls close.
In the lead-up to the 2022 vote, Jair Bolsonaro repeatedly cast unfounded doubts on Brazil’s electronic voting system. No significant fraud has ever been detected.
Lula, who got his start as a union worker and has a missing pinky finger following an accident in a factory when he was 19, has at times inspired cult-like devotion. He spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were later annulled before winning a third nonconsecutive term in 2022.
Former U.S. President Barack Obama once called him “the world's most popular politician.” But during his current term, Lula's approval ratings fell as low as 24%, one of his lowest levels. Voters' concerns about crime and the cost of living could hurt him at the ballot box. He has promised to ensure Brazilians are the ones to benefit from the country's rare minerals and resources, protect the Amazon rainforest and continue his flagship welfare program Bolsa Familia.
With former President Jair Bolsonaro barred from running as he serves a 27-year-long sentence for a coup attempt, his eldest son has largely embraced his father's ultra-conservative agenda, while at times trying to strike a more moderate communication style to attract centrist voters.
His hardline security policies have been a pillar of his campaign, and polls show these proposals are popular among Brazilians. The senator has pledged to fight the country's criminal groups by building El Salvador-style megaprisons, following the Trump administration's lead by designating transnational gangs terrorist organizations and reducing the age to be tried as an adult to 16.
Deforestation in the Amazon rainforest, which plays a vital role in stopping climate change, hit a record high under former President Bolsonaro. His son has also denied human-caused climate change and only committed to stopping illegal deforestation.
Sen. Bolsonaro's admission of accepting millions of dollars from disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro to produce a film on his father's life has cast a shadow over his campaign. He is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in connection with the case.
Lula has repeatedly warned the U.S. not to meddle in Brazil's elections. The Trump administration did not respond to a request for comment on whether it is seeking to interfere in the vote.
Last year, Washington imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing — among other reasons — the trial of Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally. Earlier this year, the U.S. imposed a new round of tariffs, citing unfair trade practices despite running a U.S. surplus, and classified Brazil’s biggest drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organizations shortly after a visit to the White House from Sen. Bolsonaro. Lula opposed both moves.
A victory by Sen. Bolsonaro would add Brazil to a list of Latin American countries — including Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica and Peru — that have elected Trump-friendly governments in recent years.
Lula has made defending Brazilian sovereignty a major campaign issue. In the days before the election, his team launched a Portuguese version of the Bad Bunny song, “Lo que le pasó a Hawaii,” which invokes the U.S. colonization of Hawaii as a cautionary tale.

The setting for perhaps the country’s biggest exercise in public debate was quintessential rural India: fields of green paddy, a pond, a temple. On a normal day, as dusk falls in the village of Ajgara, in Uttar Pradesh, people gather beside the pond to chat about the price of crops, the weather, or the theft of a goat.
But for more than a month, metaphysics and ethical dilemmas replaced the usual topics. Is it permissible to use deceit to defeat an evil enemy? Is a lie justified to save a life? What is the nature of reality?
The debating tournament was the brainchild of Abhishek Pandey, district magistrate of Pratapgarh district in Uttar Pradesh. When he took up the post two years ago, he knew the area was rich in archaeological treasures connected to the ancient Indian epic, the Mahabharata.
Throughout the text, Yudhishthira, one of the central characters, debates the nature of human existence. In Ajgara he answers a string of philosophical questions to save the lives of his four brothers.
Pandey, 35, like most Indians, grew up on this story and was proud of the intellectual depth of the dialogues. When he attended Oxford University on a fellowship, he admired the debating society, which has a 200-year-long history. But India’s tradition of sophisticated public debate is much older, going back more than 3,000 years.
Pandey started to question why the tradition had not survived. “Indians have celebrated certain traditions for centuries,” Pandey says. “Why have we ceased to celebrate the legacy of debate and questioning?” Was it possible to revive this noble tradition, particularly when it was a vital component of a democracy?
He decided that the annual fair held in Ajgara in September would be a good time to stage the event. In the run-up to the fair, Pandey and his team arranged 1,500 debates across the district.
Age and education were no bar. The youngest participant was a 10-year-old schoolboy, the oldest an 80-year-old farmer. In debating for and against a motion, participants were judged on reasoning and moral clarity.
The overwhelming public response dumbfounded Pandey. Thousands of people participated in multiple rounds, and were whittled down to eight finalists – two women and six men.
While villagers milled around, enjoying the food, watching folk theatre, buying local crafts and taking a ride on a ferris wheel, a silence descended inside the debating tent.
The finale of the Great Ajgara Debate 2026 on 17 September lasted about six hours.
One topic was women’s rights. A finalist, Vivek Singh, argued that women might have equality on paper but society’s expectations of them impeded the exercise of these rights.
Another, Prajjwal Shukla, 24, argued that the real question was not what role society assigned to women but who had the authority to make those choices. Whether a woman chose a career, household responsibilities, or both, should be her choice and hers alone, he said.
“What amazed me the most was not the intellectual quality of the debates (which was great), but the atmosphere. Everyone listened respectfully, patiently, without interrupting. No one got personal. People sat for hours,” says Pandey.
Marx’s adage that history repeats itself, first as tragedy and then as farce, is a perfect description of how debate in India has descended from the sublime to the farcical.
In television studio debates everyone shouts at the same time. No one can finish a point. Personal abuse and gibes fly while the anchor whips them into ever greater frenzies.
Sadhana Dwivedi, one of the two women to progress into the last round of the Great Ajgara Debate, despises this new format.
“People need to learn to listen, to understand there may be value in another person’s point of view,” she says. “In a democracy, it is crucial for all opinions to be aired so that we can get to the truth.”
The turnout was a good demonstration of the thesis posited in economist Amartya Sen’s book The Argumentative Indian that India had a rich tradition of questioning authority and entertaining heterodoxy.
It is only in recent years that dissent has been suppressed, notably by the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party, which values conformity.
“It’s ironic, because the BJP wants to recreate a Hindu state but is not even acquainted with the traditions of ancient Hindu civilisation, such as that of debate and being open to different ideas,” says author and commentator Parsa Venkateshwar Rao Jnr.
At the end of the tournament, the eight finalists were garlanded and driven around in an open-top car to much cheering, feted as “intellectual heroes”. The winner was Shukla, who is preparing to sit exams to enter the civil service.
“I can’t believe I am the winner of a debate that took place at the exact same spot as in the Mahabharata all those centuries ago. I participated just because I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts,” he says.
Pandey is still processing the public enthusiasm. “My deputy asked me if we should get some police deployment because the turnout everywhere was so big, but I laughed and said no. That would be a sad affair.”
He hopes to spread the event across other Indian states and perhaps nationwide. “We have to inculcate a culture of debate. It’s the hallmark of a democracy.”
Meanwhile, he has planted his flag. The inscription on the stone slab he has installed at the site reads: “The Great Ajgara Debate. First Debate 3152 BC: Yudhishthira. Second Debate 2026: Prajjwal Shukla.”

The Kerala State Commission for Protection of Child Rights has directed the secretary of Karode grama panchayat in Thiruvananthapuram district to evict encroachers from a ‘puramboke’ land to ensure right of way for children. The commission was intervening in complaints over hurdles faced by the schoolchildren using the Kuzhinjanvila-Thazhevila road in the panchayat.
Acting on a complaint that a tiled roof building constructed after encroaching on puramboke land was preventing students from walking safely to school and coming in the way of smooth travel of school buses and other vehicles, the commission directed the Karode village officer, Karode grama panchayat secretary, and the Pozhiyoor station house officer to take action.
The panchayat secretary could seek the help of the station house officer (SHO) to evict the encroachers according to provisions of the Kerala Panchayat Raj Act. The Kerala State Electricity Board executive engineer (Neyyattinkara) was tasked with urgently shifting an electricity post that posed a hurdle to travel.
The commission’s full Bench comprising F. Wilson, B. Mohankumar, and K.K. Shaju also directed the vicar of St. Mary’s MSC church to relocate a church pillar situated at the starting point of the road. The petition was filed by A. Ajeesh, Kuzhinjanvila ward member of Karode grama panchayat.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it allegedly shows the Chief of the Army Staff, General Dhiraj Seth, dancing with Supreet Sapra, described as the wife of an Army major. The video features a purported CNN headline stating, “Indian Army Chief Dhiraj Seth Spotted Dancing with Army Major’s wife Supreet Sapra,” giving the impression that CNN published the video. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major.
Fact: The video has been digitally manipulated to make it appear as though Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth is dancing with Supreet Sapra. CNN has not published any report or headline matching the one shown in the viral video. The original video, shared in March 2026, features a different man and woman dancing at a gathering. Supreet Sapra has also clarified that she is not an Army major’s wife and that the woman shown in the viral video is AI-generated. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing has also confirmed that the video is digitally manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports carrying the viral footage on CNN’s official website or any report or headline matching the one circulating with the video.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed several inconsistencies. Though the man and woman appear to be dancing while holding glasses, the liquid inside them does not move or splash naturally as they dance. In one frame, the man’s ear and cheek area also appear smudged, while the faces of people in the background appear heavily blurred. The man’s face remains almost completely frozen with a wide smile throughout the video, further raising signs of AI manipulation.
We then ran the video through multiple AI detection tools, including DetectVideo AI and Meta AI’s verification platform. Both assessed the clip as likely AI-generated and detected AI signatures in the video.
The viral video contains an inset photograph showing a woman with a different man wearing a defence uniform. To learn more about the photograph, we conducted a reverse image search, which led us to an Instagram post (archived) by @sufimeranaam, dated 22 February 2026, featuring the same image. Newschecker contacted the account user regarding the viral video. She identified herself as Supreet Sapra and said, “I am Supreet Sapra, but I am not a major’s wife. My husband retired four years ago. The woman in the video is AI-generated, so apart from the name, everything is misinformation.”
Further investigation led us to an Instagram post (archived) by Rhythm Gupta, shared on 11 March 2026, with the caption, “Always dancing weirdly.” The video features a man and a woman dancing at a gathering. Their dance movements, the way they hold their glasses, and the song playing in the background are the same as those in the viral video. Although the background differs in colour and certain visual details, the overall setting and arrangement of elements are similar, and the movements of people around the dancing pair also closely resemble. This indicates that the viral video was likely manipulated using the earlier footage to make it appear as though the Army Staff chief was dancing with an Army major’s wife. Comparison of screengrabs from the viral clip and the Instagram video can be seen below.
The Indian Army’s fact-checking wing also clarified in an X post (archived) on 29 September 2026 that the viral video is digitally manipulated and fake.
To sum up, this viral video of Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major, is AI-manipulated.

How Gordon became one of England's main men
- Published
Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Declan Rice, Jordan Pickford and now Anthony Gordon.
All have become guaranteed starters and reliable stars for England, with the Barcelona winger the latest to look, according to captain Kane, like one of the Three Lions' "main men".
Gordon was one of England's standout players at the World Cup and earned a big-money move to European giants Barca in the summer, while his good form has continued into his country's Nations League campaign.
He scored the opening goal in England's 2-0 win against the Czech Republic on Tuesday night, after also netting in a 3-2 defeat by world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday.
In fact, the 25-year-old's England form has been building since the knockout stage of the World Cup began - his run of averaging a goal contribution every 69 minutes started with assisting both Kane's efforts in a 2-1 last-32 victory over DR Congo.
The former Newcastle player has scored three goals and provided three assists in his past six England matches, while he also won the penalty in England's dramatic last-16 victory over Mexico at Azteca Stadium.
And after a positive start in Spain, where he has already picked up five assists in La Liga, Gordon looks to be joining boss Thomas Tuchel's "undroppable" bracket.
Gordon belongs at top level - Kane
Tuchel likes to give his players clarity on their role and makes clear who they are up against in the squad and for a starting position.
When asked whether Gordon is getting to be one of the first names on the team-sheet, he said: "He's getting there. He's defending his shirt, he's defending his position - an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain.
"He was very decisive [against the Czech Republic] and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult but the technique and finishing was excellent.
"He scored against Spain so he has decisive actions and he's defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he's a very important player."
Gordon linked up well with his former Newcastle team-mate Lewis Hall on England's left and combined with right-back Trent Alexander-Arnold, who was making his first start for the Three Lions in nearly two years, for the opening goal.
Gordon said he had been "dying" to link up with Alexander-Arnold, who is also playing in Spain for Barcelona's rivals Real Madrid.
"It's a great compliment and it's great to play with him," Alexander-Arnold said of Gordon.
"I tried to get the ball, and try and see what the best play is and try and play forward and create something. And I was able to get the pass."
Captain and record goalscorer Kane is a guaranteed starter in England's biggest matches but the position to the left of Kane has been a problem area for the team, with no player able to make it their own.
Gordon looks to have secured that role and Kane said the winger is "showing that he belongs at the highest level, for Barcelona and England".
"His performances in the last couple of games have been some of his best that he has played in an England shirt," Kane said.
"I think he is just relishing putting the shirt on and being one of the main men in the team. He is an important player for us and he showed that during the World Cup."
It has not always been a straightforward route into the team for Gordon.
Marcus Rashford, Eberechi Eze, Phil Foden and Noni Madueke have all featured for England from the left in the past couple of years.
Gordon started to emerge as a clear option during Lee Carsley's time in interim charge, but said himself last October that he had only shown "50%" of what he can do for England.
Now that seems to be coming to fruition. Against the Czech Republic he attempted four shots, more than any England player and more than any of his team-mates against Spain too.
Gordon is ranked in at least the top four of England players for expected assists (0.9), expected goals (0.9), passes into the box (14), touches in the opposition box (29), chances created (eight), and shots on target (five), since the start of the World Cup knockout stage.
His importance is underlined by the fact he has contributed the same amount of goals and assists, six, as Bellingham since England faced DR Congo.
Battle with Rashford at England and Barca
There has been an interesting subplot with Gordon and Rashford competing for a left-wing space for England and effectively Barcelona.
Rashford was on loan at Barcelona last season but they opted to not make his move permanent, instead he returned to Manchester United while the Catalan club splashed out £69m to sign Gordon from Newcastle.
Gordon has the ability to take on his full-back on the inside or beat them for pace on the outside before putting in a cross.
"People raised eyebrows when Anthony Gordon went to Barcelona for the money that he did and Marcus Rashford came back to Manchester United," former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"He has become a key part of the England team. There were certain games in the World Cup where he was substituted and he shouldn't have been - I think others should have come off instead of him.
"Gordon [when he is] full of confidence running at pace like he does, he can go either way and he's causing full-backs all kind of problems."
Gordon says that since his move to Spain he has changed people's perception of him being a player who is only quick and presses well, even if they are two of his best attributes.
"I always felt in England, people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never actually respected the quality and IQ that I play with," Gordon told ITV.
"Only the players I play with ever seem to notice that. I think now I'm at Barcelona and I play a different style, those qualities are highlighted much more and people are actually starting to take notice that I'm not just quick.
"In England, it was never really respected because people just see me as really quick and really aggressive.
"In Spain, they really appreciate my IQ and quality because at Barca, if you're not technical, if you're not smart, you're going to stand out like a sore thumb."
Tuchel is starting to build a team he thinks can challenge and win the Euros in 2028.
But first he wants to win the Nations League, and if England are to do that, it is likely Gordon will have played a huge part.

South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
- Published
South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.
Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.
In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.
In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.
"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.
- Race policies or Israel - what's really driving Trump's fury with South Africa? 
  - Published23 February 2025
- Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims? 
  - Published2 June 2025
- Do Afrikaners want to take Trump up on his South African refugee offer? 
  - Published15 May 2025
An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.
The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.
Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.
Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".
Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.
The programme has its critics among Afrikaners in South Africa too.
"Why single out the white Afrikaner to say this group qualifies to flee to the US? This country suffers gender-based violence. Why not single out women?" Rudi Swanepoel, a pastor from Johannesburg told the BBC.
Swanepoel thinks it is not persecution but a "loss of privilege" that is causing some Afrikaners to feel aggrieved.
"To use the metaphor of a cake, 30, 40 years ago the white people of South Africa controlled the cake," he says. "Since democracy came, the obvious reality was we had to now start sharing that cake and those privileges."
Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.
But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

Two failed executions in Tennessee have left experts questioning the death penalty
Tennessee is facing criticism after the failed execution of Christa Pike
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article

Questions surrounding Tennessee’s administration of capital punishment have resurfaced following the botched execution of Christa Pike, marking the second time since 2022 that the state has suspended the death penalty despite accounting for only a small minority of executions across the United States.
Her legal team reported on Friday that the 50-year-old was left unconscious and hooked to a ventilator in a facility near Nashville. They stated that staff in the death chamber pricked her with needles at least seven times before administering two doses of lethal chemicals, leaving her hospitalised with severe burns and blisters on her arms.
The aborted procedure represents Tennessee's second flawed execution attempt within a four-month span. Figures compiled by the Death Penalty Information Center show that the state has conducted merely four of the more than 140 capital punishments carried out across the nation since 2022.
Following the failed attempt on Pike’s life, Republican Gov. Bill Lee called a halt to all executions statewide and commissioned an external inquiry to determine what went wrong, as demands for reform emerged from both opponents and proponents of capital punishment.
"Number one, I think we need to get better people that are doing these executions because I don’t know that they’re trained well enough to be doing this on difficult patients," stated Republican state Sen. Joey Hensley, a family physician who noted his suspicion that the intravenous line was improperly set.
In an emergency court submission filed on Friday, lawyers representing Pike explained that she suffered severe blistering across her arms days after the attempt, caused by the corrosive, bleach-like nature of the two pentobarbital doses administered to her body.
The legal team expressed their belief that faulty IV placement caused the pentobarbital to flow directly into her body tissue rather than entering her bloodstream properly.
"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body," they detailed in court documents.
The filing added that rather than "remedying this failure", correctional authorities simply prepared and delivered a secondary set of syringes filled with pentobarbital.
Tennessee has previously faced intense criticism over its execution procedures.
Earlier in the year, officials abandoned the planned execution of Tony Carruthers when medical staff managed to secure an IV in his right arm but failed to establish a secondary access point, despite trying locations on his other arm, hand, foot, and ultimately failing to secure a central line.
Lee instructed state authorities to wait at least a year before making any further attempt to execute Carruthers.
Four years prior, the governor initiated an independent review into capital punishment after halting Oscar Smith's execution at the last minute in April 2022 when drug testing errors came to light. Lee subsequently suspended all executions a week later, admitting the state had not ensured proper testing of its lethal drug supply.
Published in late December 2022, the commissioned review revealed that the state had consistently failed to follow its established capital punishment protocols since their revision in 2018.
During that period, Tennessee executed seven prisoners — two using lethal injections and five via the electric chair. The findings noted that in none of those instances, nor in the aborted Smith execution, had the pharmacy performed mandatory endotoxin tests, while the potency of midazolam went untested in one injection.
At that point, the state relied on a three-drug regimen comprising midazolam, vecuronium bromide, and potassium chloride, before later transitioning to single-dose pentobarbital injections.
Authored by former US Attorney Ed Stanton, the report also exposed that the state's unnamed primary executioner lacked formal healthcare qualifications, relying primarily on informal training while on the job.
In the wake of those findings, the Tennessee Department of Correction dismissed its chief legal counsel alongside another staff member.
Steve Ferrell, an attorney representing Pike, expressed doubt regarding any reform since those admissions, remarking that the review merely led to "a less detailed protocol and more secrecy."
According to Corinna Lain, a law professor at the University of Richmond who has authored a book on lethal injections, it is common for execution personnel to possess minimal medical training.
Lain explained that lethal injection gained widespread adoption because it appears less gruesome, concealing the inherent violence of state executions. However, she stressed that significant risks remain even when guidelines are followed—a point raised by numerous attorneys in lawsuits asserting the method violates constitutional protections.
Across the nation, Lain identified only roughly ten licensed medical physicians willing to assist authorities with executions. Practitioners she interviewed explained that participating directly contradicts their fundamental oath to care for human life.
Capital punishment remains heavily veiled in secrecy across many jurisdictions, where the identities of executioners, drug sourcing mechanisms, and sometimes even the events inside the execution chamber are kept strictly confidential from public view.
"Tennessee has botched executions so badly that two people this year have survived their own executions," Lain said. "That’s quite something."
Nevertheless, legal scholars including Jordan Steiker, co-director of the Capital Punishment Center at the University of Texas, anticipate that lethal injection will remain an option for states retaining the death penalty.
Steiker attributed this persistence largely to the judiciary's lenient stance toward state execution procedures, which has consistently granted authorities wide latitude to proceed with capital punishment.
"I think it gives states confidence that even if they take shortcuts, it’s unlikely that the courts will intervene in their ability to carry out executions," Steiker said.

Cats are finally getting the dog treatment. This smart cat collar features GPS location, activity, and sleep tracking, plus all-new heart and respiratory rate monitoring.
Advanced health monitoring with heart and respiratory rates. Weekly AI-powered health summaries. New visual health history timeline.
TIRED
Battery dies in about four days. Collar clasp and adjustments are tricky. Proprietary charger. Location data isn’t very granular. Needs a subscription to use.
As the pet tech industry expands rapidly, pet owners are more eager to adopt technology that tracks health metrics, similar to human wearable devices like smart rings, smartwatches, and fitness trackers.
I've been testing smart collars for the better part of the year, previously testing the Fi Mini and Tractive Smart Cat Tracker on my cat Basil, which monitored his location, movement, and sleep.
The Tractive Cat 6 Mini was released this spring, and I tested it on Basil for a month, comparing how this new-and-improved smart collar made specifically for cats with improved health features, like heart and respiratory rate, stacked up against other models.
This new model had surprisingly accurate health and activity stats that helped me understand Basil's routine and baseline a bit more than the previous models I've tested. I think these new health features would be especially helpful for people with aging cats or cats in poor health. (If you have an outdoor cat that roams, I'd go with the Fi Mini because it's more compact with a longer battery life.)
I valued the Cat 6 Mini's new AI-powered weekly reports and comparisons to similar cats to know if Basil is healthy. However, the collar itself died quickly, was a pain to charge, and GPS location accuracy could be hit-or-miss. Whether this smart cat collar is the right fit for you largely depends on your and your cat's needs.
Photograph: Molly Higgins
Feline Features
The Tractive Cat 6 Mini cat tracker is available in three colors: black, brown, and lavender. Unlike the previous Fi Mini and Tractive Smart Cat Tracker models I tested, which used an attachment that fits on the cat's existing collar, this device is the collar itself, and the entire thing needs to be taken off the cat to charge on its proprietary magnetic charger. (It takes about three hours to fully charge.) To set it up, all you need to do is download the Tractive app, choose a subscription plan, and set up your pet's profile.
For the 6 Mini model, there is one plan, but you can choose between one-, two-, and five-year contracts. One year is $10 per month, or $120 annually; two years is $7 per month, or $168 annually; and five years is $5 per month, or $300 every five years. The smart collar also has a two-year manufacturer's warranty. All plans include a 30-day money-back guarantee as well as family sharing, LTE cellular coverage, 365-day location history, and GPS data export.
The tracker weighs only 1.1 ounces and is suitable for cats weighing 6.6 to 17.6 pounds, to ensure the breakaway collar opens when it should. Basil is 17 pounds, and the Cat 6 Mini fits him well with room to spare. This smart collar fits necks between 7.5 and 9 inches, whereas the previous Tracker Mini model could fit virtually any neck size because it attached to your existing collar.
Tractive claims the collar's charge lasts up to seven days for indoor cats and that it needs to be charged nearly daily if your pet roams outside. When I tested the smart collar on my indoor-only cat Basil, the battery needed to be charged by the fourth day of use.
Because the device itself is the entire collar, I felt like I was taking Basil's collar off more often than I'd like in order to charge—I didn't like that he was collarless while it charged. My anxiety told me that in this brief moment of his nakedness, he would escape. Also, because charge time took several hours, there were a few times I forgot to put it back on him until the next day.
Another gripe I had was that it was very difficult for me to remove the collar and adjust its diameter. I'm physically disabled and have reduced grip strength and fine-motor function. The collar has a simple looped clasp, but the thick material was difficult to slide under the plastic buckle; it often fell too long or too short, and I couldn't take off the collar without pulling it to trigger the breakaway feature, which was stressful for Basil—especially since the collar needed to be charged every four days.
I would've preferred the clasp to open by easily squeezing the top and bottom to release. Again, this would probably not be as big of an issue if I were able-bodied, but it is a potential issue for other pet owners who may have reduced motor function.
Photograph: Molly Higgins
Once you've picked a coverage plan, you'll create your pet's profile, set your home's location so the device enters power-saving mode when at home, and set up a virtual fence so you'll be alerted if the pet leaves the safe area. Using the stats I provided, Tractive compared Basil to cats of similar age and weight to set a personalized daily activity goal and compared his health stats to those of similar cats.
Putting It to the Test
The Tractive app lets you track activity daily (by the hour) and over time, recording minutes to compare your cat's activity and sleep patterns. Each week, the app provides an AI summary of the previous week's activity and health stats. This pretty much always said Basil slept and relaxed a lot, but noted that he is more active than cats of similar age and breed. There's also average activity per day, which was around four hours for Basil, and average calories burned per day, which was helpful for knowing how much Basil should be eating.
Tractive estimates the cat’s daily calories burned by factoring in your pet's biometric info like weight, size, age, and spay/neuter status to create a baseline. The device contains a three-axis accelerometer that “continuously records the orientation and intensity of your cat’s physical movements,” while algorithms filter out minor movements like stretching to try to prevent false stat inflation. When the sensor detects physical acceleration, like running or playing, it logs these as the “active” minutes and converts them into daily activity time.
Screenshot courtesy of Molly Higgins
Sleep metrics break down the data by day and week and classify sleep into night sleep, day sleep, and “calm” time (when a cat is awake but not active). Each day's stats are compared to the average, which helped me track Basil's habits throughout the week. Similarly to how the device tracks activity, the built-in accelerometer motion sensor tracks when the cat is still and translates that into sleep and calm time, respectively, based on micro-movements.
You can opt out of Tractive using your cat's data for their anonymized global database and leaderboard comparison features. The device continuously syncs health metrics to the app via cellular networks, but you can request a full copy of what data has been gathered or request the permanent erasure of your data.
Screenshot courtesy of Molly Higgins
This model's new health metrics for cats include heart and respiratory rates. Basil's resting heart rate was consistently lower than that of cats of similar age and weight. On one day, it was 92 bpm, compared with the normal range of 105 to 168, according to the app. This was a bit alarming to me, and I plan to bring this data up the next time we visit the vet. The app also listed “potential reasons” for the low heart rate, including “fitness and conditioning” and “cold temperatures."
As with the heart rate, the app tracked respiratory rate over time by day and compared it with Basil's historical stats and those of similar cats. His daily average was 20 breaths per minute, which was within the normal range of 15 to 30. This number closely aligned with my personal tests using visual evidence and a timer on my phone.
Screenshot courtesy of Molly Higgins
Live and historical location services weren't as useful for Basil since he's indoor-only. Like the earlier Tractive model, the 6 Mini features a built-in SIM card, similar to what’s on your phone, which uses nearby mobile networks for location updates. You can set up to five virtual fences through the app, which will notify you when your pet enters or leaves these zones. However, similar to the previous model, the default virtual fence was too small around my apartment, so I had to expand it to cover my entire complex. This is concerning because if Basil escapes but stays near my building, I wouldn't receive an alert.
Since my cat is indoor-only, I ran some experiments to track location accuracy. I had my roommates take the collar with them when they left to run errands, and I timed how long it took to receive an alert that Basil had left the “safe zone." I also took the tracker with me along with my phone, and tracked how long it took to receive a notification via Bluetooth.
When I took the tracker outside the safe zone with my phone, I was alerted via a notification on my home screen that Basil had left the “safe zone” almost immediately after exiting it. It provides an approximate location rather than pinpointing the exact spot on the street where he'd be, but it is still more helpful than randomly searching in the event he did get out. If I were to engage it in lost mode, the battery usually dies within four hours, so there is also a bit of a time limit in the event he did escape.
The alerts when the tracker was away from my phone were less precise. I tested it three times—once I was notified within a minute, the next time took about eight minutes, and the last time it took about five and a half minutes to alert after exiting the allotted safe zone. I should note that I get very poor cell phone service near my home, which could affect tracking and notification timing. Tractive also falsely alerted me that Basil had left the “safe zone” about once a week (during one week of testing, it alerted me four times). Each time, he was sitting in my home with the smart collar still on. I noticed it tended to send me false notifications more often when the battery was low or while it was on the charging dock.

Up to five days in the power-saving zone (but during testing, it was closer to four max)

Overall, the Tractive Cat 6 Mini provides valuable health insights that I appreciate—I love that I can track averages and detect any changes in Basil's health or habits even earlier. I just wish the battery didn't die so damn fast and that the collar had a universal design that was more accessible.

'Cockroach' protesters demand India's election chief resign over voter list changes
Supporters of India's "Cockroach" youth movement are protesting in Mumbai, demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner over voter list revisions
NEW DELHI -- Hundreds of supporters of India's “Cockroach” youth movement held new protests in the country's financial hub of Mumbai on Friday to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner over the revision of voter lists.
The movement, which began as an online campaign and now calls itself the Cockroach Janata Party, organized street protests that forced India's education minister to resign in July. The Mumbai rally is meant to kick off a new period of demonstrations nationwide.
Separately, police prevented student and civil society groups from gathering Friday at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in New Delhi, to also demand the commissioner's resignation. Police detained dozens of protesters and some opposition leaders heading to the site, which had been barricaded off.
The protests add to mounting pressure on India’s Election Commission, which oversees polls across the country. Critics and opposition parties accuse it of altering voter registrations to give an advantage to the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Both the commission and the government deny any wrongdoing.
The Indian Express newspaper last month reported that two of the three election commissioners had formally objected to several decisions involving voter list revisions, registration procedures and the commission’s digital systems.
According to the report, the two commissioners questioned the legality of some of the decisions, but Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar disregarded their objections. Indian law requires the three-member Election Commission to make decisions by majority vote.
The commission disputed the report, saying it was based on “differing views and deliberations” among the commissioners rather than formal written objections.
India’s voter list revisions began last year in the eastern state of Bihar ahead of state elections, and have since expanded to most of the country’s states and federally administered territories.
Known as Special Intensive Revision, the revisions have drawn criticism over the documents required to establish voters’ eligibility. Critics say the requirements have been confusing and difficult for many voters to meet, potentially leaving millions off the registration lists and unable to vote.
Election Commission data shows voter lists in some regions could shrink by as much as 30%.
The commission says the objective is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries while ensuring eligible voters remain on the lists. Opposition parties and activists say it risks excluding legitimate voters. They also accuse the chief commissioner, Kumar, of political bias and allege the revisions benefit Modi’s party.
The Election Commission and Modi's party have rejected the allegations.
The youth movement, which emerged earlier this year out of anger over high unemployment among young people and leaked examination papers, has grown into a political force.
Led by Abhijeet Dipke, it rose to national prominence after organizing mass protests over examination paper leaks. The demonstrations culminated in the resignation of the education minister, a significant political setback for Modi’s government.
The movement has since sought to take up other issues beyond education, including government accountability and democratic institutions.

Temperamental traits and adverse experiences during childhood may together offer clues to vulnerability to major psychiatric disorders, a transdiagnostic study by researchers at NIMHANS has found.
The study, published recently in the Journal of Affective Disorders, examined 1,162 adults, including 532 people with psychiatric disorders, 457 unaffected first-degree relatives (FDRs) and 173 healthy controls. The participants were drawn from 393 multiplex families - families in which multiple members had been diagnosed with psychiatric disorders - involving schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD).
The researchers examined four broad dimensions of adult temperament - negative affectivity, extraversion/surgency, effortful control and orienting sensitivity - along with adverse childhood experiences (ACEs).
“Our findings suggest that temperament does not map onto psychiatric disorders in a simple, one-to-one manner. Rather, different combinations of temperamental characteristics are associated with different disorders, and some of these characteristics are also seen among unaffected family members,” said Srinivas Balachander, corresponding author and one of the lead researchers of the study.
Temperament shared within families
Using data from the erstwhile Accelerator programme for Discovery in Brain disorders using Stem cells (ADBS) project, (funded by the Department of Biotechnology and Pratiksha Trust), now known as the Rohini Nilekani Centre for Brain and Mind, at NIMHANS, the researchers found evidence of familial sharing across all four temperamental domains.
This was observed despite considerable variation in the psychiatric diagnoses within the same families. The finding is of interest because temperament is known to have a substantial heritable component, although the study did not directly establish that the temperamental characteristics observed were caused by specific genetic variants.
“In our study, considering the significant within-family heterogeneity in terms of different diagnoses, there was still a significant degree of shared temperament,” Dr. Balachander said.
Among affected participants, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder were associated with lower extraversion/surgency and orienting sensitivity. OCD was associated with higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity, along with lower effortful control and extraversion/surgency. Participants with AUD showed higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity and lower effortful control.
Some of these patterns were also observed among unaffected first-degree relatives. Relatives of people with schizophrenia showed lower extraversion/surgency, while relatives of people with OCD showed higher negative affectivity and lower effortful control.
“These findings are particularly interesting because some temperamental characteristics were evident even in individuals who did not have the disorder but belonged to families carrying a higher degree of familial risk,” Dr. Balachander said.
Childhood adversity and alcohol use disorder
The researchers also examined whether adverse childhood experiences altered the relationship between temperament and psychiatric disorders.
The clearest evidence for an interaction between temperament and childhood adversity emerged in alcohol use disorder. The overall ACE score was significantly associated with AUD, and interactions between childhood adversity and two temperamental domains - extraversion/surgency and effortful control - were also observed.
“Childhood adversity appears to add another layer to the relationship between temperament and psychiatric vulnerability. In our study, the evidence for this interaction was particularly apparent in alcohol use disorder, rather than uniformly across all four disorders,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers, however, cautioned against interpreting the findings as evidence that a particular temperament or childhood experience causes a psychiatric disorder.
The study was cross-sectional, meaning that the assessments were made at one point in time. The adult temperament measures were self-reported and could be influenced by current illness, treatment, illness duration or an individual’s perception of their own past Reports of childhood adversity may also be affected by recall and measurement biases.
Testing the findings
To examine whether the findings extended beyond the genetically enriched family sample, the researchers tested their statistical model using an independent community-based cohort from the Consortium for Vulnerability to Externalizing Disorders and Addiction (c-VEDA).
The analysis included 2,485 adults aged 18 to 23 years for whom the relevant temperament, ACE and psychiatric assessments were available.
The model showed an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.822 for alcohol use disorder, 0.742 for bipolar disorder and 0.752 for OCD. Its performance for schizophrenia was close to chance level, with an AUC of 0.526.
“The external validation gives us some indication that the associations identified in the family-based sample may extend to community populations for some disorders. However, the findings for schizophrenia did not replicate well, which is an important limitation and needs further investigation,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said the findings point to the need for prospective studies that follow unaffected family members over time. Such studies could help determine whether particular temperamental characteristics precede the onset of psychiatric illness or are partly consequences of illness and its treatment.
“Temperament and childhood adversity may eventually become useful components of broader risk assessment frameworks, but we need prospective longitudinal evidence before we can say that they have predictive or preventive value,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said that studying temperament alongside childhood adversity could eventually provide a more nuanced understanding of psychiatric vulnerability than considering family history alone. However, they stressed that the present findings do not establish that these measures can predict who will develop a psychiatric disorder.
The researchers said continued longitudinal follow-up of the cohort would be important to establish whether the observed temperamental patterns have value in identifying individuals at increased risk before the emergence of clinically significant symptoms.
