What does FDM stand for in 3D printing and how does it work?
FDM printers are incredibly common.
3D printers are all the rage, with professionals and hobbyists alike deploying the technology to print everything from razor parts to entire homes. Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is one of the most popular types of printing technologies and is ideal for those looking to break into the world of 3D creations. FDM printers build three-dimensional objects through layers of thermoplastic filaments that fuse together to form a cohesive object.
FDM prints often begin with a computer-aided design file, or CAD, that is translated into instructions your printer can understand. Next, the printer funnels spools of filament through a heated nozzle. The printer then layers this melted filament upon the build plate according to the CAD's designated pathways. Once that initial layer is complete, the printer will lay the next layer atop the model. The process continues in this way for hours or even days, depending on the printer used, the print settings, and the model size and complexity.
FDM printers are compatible with a variety of non-resin print materials. One of the most popular filaments is polylactic acid (PLA), an inexpensive biodegradable polymer plastic that has become a favorite of 3D printing fans for its ability to be printed at low temperatures, making it ideal for beginners. Another option is PETG, or polyethylene terephthalate glycol, a durable plastic often used in water bottles and praised for its glossy surface and print accuracy. If you are searching for a tough, sturdy material to use with your FDM printer, acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) is a great option. For higher-quality prints, you can opt for thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) or nylon filament. You can also use wood and metal filaments as well as high-density polyethylene (HDPE) and polyethylene co-trimethylene terephthalate (PETT). These possibilities make FDM printers fairly flexible, providing a range of color and material options. Some materials call for high temperatures that most beginner printers can't accommodate, and others require special nozzles or proper ventilation to eliminate fumes. So if you're hoping to print in a specific material, make sure your printer and space can handle it safely.
Pros and cons of FDM printers
FDM printers provide a quick turnaround, often taking anywhere from minutes to a few hours to finish a small print. The speed of the printing process makes them popular for prototyping, allowing engineers and other users to quickly and efficiently test and rework their designs. Moreover, the ability to use cheaper filaments helps make FDM prints fairly inexpensive. Add low equipment costs and minimal maintenance, and FDM printers are ideal for those looking for budget proof-of-concept or parts production.
But FDM printers have their limits. For one thing, FDM models are low resolution, meaning it is more difficult for them to produce the finer details of a print. Due to the relative thickness of each layer, FDM prints struggle to produce prints with small, intricate parts. As such, Apple probably won't use an FDM printer to make your next phone or watch — it opts for precise, industrial-grade printers that can print titanium. Warping is another common issue with FDM printers, as the filament often cools at different rates, causing uneven pressure to warp your designs. Because these printers lay down layers horizontally, FDM prints are also prone to breaking when facing acute pressure on the z-axis and shouldn't be relied on to make strong, sturdy pieces. A common FDM printing technique known as infilling, in which the model's interior prints with lower density to save time and filament, also makes them prone to breaking.
Good beginner FDM printers are affordable, reliable and somewhat low maintenance. However, if you want to create sturdy, precise structures, you may need to invest in a higher-end printer from a highly-regarded brand like Prusa Research, Bambu Lab or Ultimaker. For ultimate precision, consider stereolithography (SLA) and digital light processing (DLP) printers, which deploy light to cure layers of resin, creating models with fine details and smooth surfaces. Selective laser sintering, or SLS, deploys lasers to fuse nylon powders together and is ideal for creating sturdy, support-free structures. Multi Jet Fusion (MJF), direct metal laser sintering and selective laser melting are other worthy options, depending on your intended use case and materials.

‘We will not stop’: Students’ blunt message as school protests spread across France
More than 5,000 people have been arrested across the country this week as student demonstrations about overcrowded classrooms and school conditions turned violent. Jessie Williams reports

This week France has been rocked by nationwide student protests that turned violent, with thousands arrested, more than 100 schools damaged and dozens of teachers injured.
By midday on Friday, the ministry of national education announced that 564 schools have been affected. Dramatic pictures show fires in the streets, barricaded entrance gates and youths clashing with riot police. At least four hundred high schools, roughly one in 10, were closed due to the unrest.
The protests began last week over frustrations about school conditions with peaceful blockades of secondary schools around Paris.
They soon morphed into wider discontent with the government and spread across the country, after France's main union for secondary school students called for a nationwide blockade. University students and other supporters also joined the demonstrations.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told TF1 TV on Friday that police had arrested a total of around 5,000 people, most of them teenagers, since Monday.
Justice Minister Darmanin had earlier told RTL radio that parents of those damaging property should pay reparations.
So far 65 school staff have been injured, including 40 headteachers, and there has been significant damage to facilities, with classes now taking place remotely, French education minister Édouard Geffray told French media on Friday. More than 300 police officers have also been injured in the chaos.
Students claim there has also been police violence against the protestors, with officers in riot gear using batons and tear gas.
In Tours, a city in central France, a 16-year-old student was injured on Wednesday outside his secondary school after being hit in the eye with an LBD-40 – Lanceur de Balles de Défense or Defence Ball Launcher. The controversial riot gun used by French police has caused severe injuries at previous protests.
A 19-year-old university student in Tours and member of the student union Fédération Syndicale Étudiante, Martin, has been taking part in the demonstrations over the last few days. He told The Independent the injured boy was in a “critical state” and that he could be blind for the rest of his life.
“The police have shown an extreme brutality, hitting students and using excessive amounts of tear gas,” Martin (not his real name) said.
“Apparently high-schoolers are too young to be listened to but old enough to be repressed.
“The situation shows how the government is scared of the movement, they're struggling to contain the anger of the youth and the working class. Despite their best efforts to scare us we will not stop.”
Another student, aged 14, lost multiple teeth and suffered severe facial injuries in Val-d’Oise after being hit in the jaw by a tear gas grenade launcher. His mother told French newspaper Le Parisien that his mouth had been “torn apart”.
French authorities have opened multiple investigations to examine the accusations of police violence.
Amnesty International said the reports of secondary school students being assaulted are “extremely alarming”.
“Many are minors, children. They must be protected, not beaten with batons,” the human rights organisation posted on X on Thursday evening.
“Let's be clear: since the beginning of the blockades, there have also been acts of violence on the part of certain protesters. They are not acceptable. But even in these situations, including in the event of an arrest, the use of force must remain proportionate.”
The mayor of Tours, Emmanuel Denis, appealed for calm on Thursday and said the student movement’s demands are “legitimate”. He also said he was going to meet with their representatives on Friday.
Some parents also support the protests. Vincent Martin joined his daughter outside Helene Boucher high school, in Paris, saying students were ‘fundamentally right to demand ... better learning conditions”.
The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, the student union which orchestrated the blockades, said they want authorities to address the “shortage of teachers and staff, dilapidated high schools, overcrowded classrooms, and overloaded schedules.”
Martin said that one particular policy university students are protesting against is a new measure which will see the end of university fee waivers for non-European students.
“The end goal [of the government] is to the increase the fees for all students, because of the lack of budget for universities. The recent governments have been putting less and less money in public services such as schools and universities and hospitals while investing in the army and big companies,” he said.
Another university student in Tours, 21 year-old Vinnie, said that they are watching their universities “fall apart in real time” due to unrelenting budget cuts.
“What the government should do is very simple,” he said. “Unlock funding. Every year money is being pulled from every public service imaginable, every year everyone in public service is asked to do more with less.”
The education minister claimed on Friday that the student protest movement had been “hijacked” and that teachers had told him that “the people in front of me were not my students.”
A number of schools have been set on fire over the last few days, including the Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes in the west of the country, while staff at Victor Hugo high school in the southern city of Marseille were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.
French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin has said there is an “active and violent minority” taking part in the protests.
"We're not entirely sure that they are even high school students themselves," he told France's RTL radio.
"We have gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public order disturbance. When people target buses and set schools on fire, it is no longer simply a protest issue," he added.
Vinnie says that as with every protest movement there are some casseurs or vandals who try to cause destruction, which the students do not want.
“I have personally witnessed on the first day of the protests a small group of young men who were not students bring cardboard to the front of a blocked high school to light it up.”
“They don't all have the same motivation, some just want to destroy, some think it really is the only way to protest even when the protesters most involved disagree and some are actually opponents of the movements with goals of destabilising it,” he added.
Martin said that he has seen people who aren’t students join the movement “because what we're asking for is much larger than just about universities”.
“We're calling for a large movement uniting high-schoolers, students and workers, because we must stay strong together, especially against police violence and repression.”
He said that they have seen solidarity across all generations, notably from the former gilets jaunes protestors. He said he was looking forward to 17 October, when there is a large demonstration planned by the ‘yellow vest’ group.
Before that there is another big student protest planned for Tuesday 6 October. “In the mean time, we'll keep protesting in the university and beyond,” he added.
The demonstrations come at a tense time for the country as next year’s presidential election approaches.
The French prime minister and far-right politicians, like Marine Le Pen, presidential candidate for National Rally, have blamed the hard left for igniting the protests, particularly La France Insoumise (LFI) party.
LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who has attended some of the demonstrations, said he was in favour of non-violent protests, but argued that blaming the left would not solve the issues behind the demonstrations.

Portugal playmaker Bruno Fernandes said Cristiano Ronaldo remains the country’s greatest footballing icon despite walking out on the squad this week after finding out he would not start a match.
The 41-year-old superstar said on Wednesday he had left the team after coach Jorge Jesus said Ronaldo would not start against Denmark in the Nations League, a match Portugal won 4-2 without him.
Former Real Madrid and Manchester United attacker Ronaldo’s future with the national team, for whom he is the leading goalscorer and most capped player, is in doubt after his walk out.
“Regarding Cristiano, I had a conversation with him, and what I told him, and what I repeat here, is this — the most important thing is that, regardless of what happens, Cristiano Ronaldo will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team, of our football, and of the country, for what he has done not only in Portugal but throughout the world,” Fernandes told reporters on Saturday.
Manchester United midfielder Fernandes called for unity after a tumultuous few days in which Portugal fans’ opinions have been split over Ronaldo’s decision.
“He has a reserved place not only among the best of all time, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people, and the most important thing is that we stop dividing things,” said Fernandes.
“There are no divisions in the national team, it is one and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside...
“We are outside of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country does not divide itself, does not make choices, that it respects all sides, but, at the same time, Cris is and will be the biggest icon of our national team, he deserves everyone’s respect, regardless of who likes him more or (who likes him) less.”
Portugal beat Norway and Denmark away from home without Ronaldo starting and faces Norway again on Sunday.
Coach Jesus said Ronaldo was a “symbol of Portugal” and said there would be time to speak about him after Sunday’s game in Porto.
“I’m going to focus on the team, on the opponent which is Norway, one of the five best teams in Europe. That’s the problem right now,” said the 72-year-old coach.

Zimbabwe tycoon Wicknell Chivayo and wife killed in helicopter crash
- Published
Prominent Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife have been killed in a helicopter crash that left six people dead, his family have confirmed.
The helicopter came down in the Marondera rural area, about 70km (43 miles) east of the capital, Harare, on Wednesday evening. Police said all six people on board died.
Family spokesperson Herbert Chivayo confirmed the deaths of the businessman and his wife Lucy Muteke to state broadcaster ZBC, saying the family was devastated by the tragedy.
Chivayo was known for his lavish lifestyle, close ties to some African presidents and lucrative government contracts that had repeatedly attracted scrutiny.
He had denied allegations of wrongdoing linked to his business dealings.
Police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi said the aircraft crashed at about 17:00 local time (15:00 GMT) and had six occupants, but authorities did not immediately identify all those on board. Two of the six were pilots, according to government officials.
ZBC reported that the group was travelling from Gandami in Chikomba, where Chivayo and his wife were building a rural home, when the helicopter crashed at Kudenga Farm about 40 minutes after take-off.
"We are at a loss for words after the tragic news," the family spokesperson, told the ZBC.
The cause of the crash was not immediately known, and police said investigations were under way. Emergency services were sent to the scene on Wednesday evening.

Valeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.
“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.
A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”
Across the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi, or Southern, Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.
He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.
On Saturday morning, Russia targeted a second major bridge connecting Kyiv, damaging the road surface on the Northern Bridge and temporarily halting traffic.
Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.
For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plunge Ukraine into darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.
“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”
This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in an interview with the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.
“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.
Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.
The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.
Kyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.
At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.
Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.
“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.
Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.
“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.
“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.

From ‘red ocean’ to ‘blue ocean’: Why Singaporean firms are exploring Nanning to enter China’s market
Recent pyramid scheme arrests involving Singaporeans have put Nanning in the spotlight, but businesses told CNA they remain undeterred from entering the Chinese market - and that making inroads can take months or even years.
NANNING, Guangxi: Singaporean sales director Tracy Low, 46, came to Nanning in search of a partner to distribute her company’s coffee in China.
The company, Kim’s Duet, which sells Singapore-style coffee in single-serve sachets, began exploring the Chinese market earlier this year.
At the China-ASEAN Expo (CAEXPO) held in Nanning from Sep 17 to 21, Low met several potential distributors. 
“It could take between three to six months to filter these distributors before we engage them,” she said.
More than 50 exhibitors from Singapore took part in the five-day event - the highest number since 2023. Some were testing the market for the first time while others had spent years building contacts and turning discussions into business deals.
For many Singaporean companies looking to expand in China, Nanning offers a foothold in a less familiar market.
The capital of Guangxi has been in the spotlight after 52 Singaporeans were arrested over suspected involvement in pyramid-scheme activities, amid longstanding warnings over investment pitches that promised unusually high returns.
The Singapore Business Federation (SBF) said it was not aware of companies raising concerns about entering Nanning following the news.
Businesses had still been asking the usual questions about “market access, market opportunities, and how they can enter a market”, executive director for international business Soo Wei-Chieh told CNA.
Businesses described to CNA a slow process of breaking into China’s massive market - one that can involve spending months or even years finding the right partners, testing relationships and assessing whether opportunities can turn into real business.
A “BLUE OCEAN”
When most Singaporeans think of China, they often think first of major cities like Beijing and Shanghai, said Tan Teck Yong, chairman and CEO of Singapore education company KinderWorld International Group.
But Tan is looking further afield.
First-tier cities such as Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen are a “red ocean”, Tan said, referring to a business term for crowded and competitive markets.
The Guangxi region, by contrast, is a “blue ocean”, he said - a less saturated market with more room for growth.
KinderWorld first entered China in 2000 before expanding into Vietnam. For Tan, venturing into new markets is part of the company’s broader strategy.
“We are a Singapore company. Our motto is very clear: internationalise,” he said.
Since the COVID-19 pandemic, Tan has attended CAEXPO in Nanning three times, using the fair to build connections, meet officials and gain a better understanding of the local market.
Those visits became part of a longer process of exploring opportunities in Guangxi, he said.
Turning connections into concrete opportunities also takes time. Tan spent a year and a half in discussions before KinderWorld’s plans in Guangxi began to take shape. The group has since signed agreements with local education institutions.
And the Singapore government has been trying to get more companies to do just that.
“With our small domestic economy, many growth opportunities lie beyond Singapore’s shores,” Deputy Prime Minister and Trade and Industry Minister Gan Kim Yong said during a speech in March, as the government announced increased support for local firms venturing abroad.
Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong also visited Guangxi in May to better understand its role in ASEAN-China connectivity, with MFA describing the region as a “key gateway” linking China with Southeast Asia.
But for some businesses taking that step, unfamiliar markets can come with steep learning curves.
Wayne Eo, director of Singapore building materials company Sixth Harmony Global, knew little about Nanning before attending his first CAEXPO back in 2024.
He thought of it as an up-and-coming second-tier Chinese city but was surprised to discover modern high-rises and shopping malls.
People he met in restaurants and at street-food stalls were “all very earnest” and local food also took a bit of getting used to, he said.
“If you aren’t a bamboo fan ... you will be really shocked,” he joked, referring to the local fondness for bamboo shoots.
He has kept coming back since. Through CAEXPO, Sixth Harmony has expanded its contacts beyond Nanning and now supplies customers elsewhere in Guangxi and also in Guangdong.
“Nanning is the entry point for us,” Eo said.
BUSINESSES UNDETERRED BY PYRAMID SCHEME ARRESTS
Guangxi’s capital is also becoming better connected. Just this month, the Pinglu Canal opened, giving Nanning and other parts of inland southwestern China a shorter water route to the sea.
But its growing role as a link between China and Southeast Asia has also featured in pitches for a very different kind of opportunity.
Last December, Zhang Fan, a 40-year-old Singaporean working in cybersecurity, recalled being approached by a close university friend with an investment proposal.
He was told that Nanning was becoming a strategic geographical link and could even become “the next Shanghai” within a decade.
His friend had also offered to take him around the city to see its high-rises and development projects, presenting them as signs of the city’s potential.
The pitch came with eye-catching figures: an investment of as much as S$40,000 to S$50,000, he recalled - with the prospect of receiving more than S$1 million over two years.
But all that said little about whether the investment being promoted was legitimate.
Zhang ultimately turned down the proposal and said it “sounded too good to be true”.
News of the arrests over suspected pyramid scheme activities in Guangxi, however, has not deterred Singapore businesses looking for opportunities in the city.
“So far, no impact,” said KinderWorld International Group’s Tan. “Look, we are not here to look for money. We are here to bring our export, our education program into Guangxi and China.”
Singaporean sales director Low similarly said that the news had not made her particularly concerned or given her a negative impression of Nanning.
Her company was there because it knew little about the Chinese market and had simply wanted to find out whether there was a place for its coffee.
NO SHORTCUTS
For Eo of Sixth Harmony Global, China offers a vastly bigger potential market - but venturing into it has also meant learning to do business differently.
In Singapore, companies can easily reach customers relatively directly, he said. In China, different provinces may require different distributors, contacts and ways of working, he added.
Still, for a small Singapore company like his, even capturing a tiny fraction could matter, Eo said - but getting that slice still takes time.
For companies, it can mean spending more than half a year getting to know a potential partner before committing to more business.
So it often starts with small transactions - watching whether payments arrive on time and gauging whether both sides work well together, Eo said.
“We build some form of relationship, and have an understanding of each other. Then we trial a little bit of business here and there,” he added.
That approach broadly mirrors what lawyers recommend.
Liang Weitan, a partner in the China Practice at Singapore law firm WongPartnership, told CNA that genuine projects and investments should have identifiable partners, proper registrations and contracts - as well as clear funding structures and actual business operations.
“The absence of any of these should prompt further inquiry,” Liang said.
He also advises investors to check a Chinese company’s business licence and registration - along with other precautions like visiting its premises, examining contracts and importantly, establishing how a project would actually make money before transferring funds.
Samuel Chng, a research assistant professor at the Lee Kuan Yew Centre for Innovative Cities at the Singapore University of Technology and Design, urged Singaporeans to scrutinise investment opportunities carefully.
Even “promising market(s) can contain unsound ventures”, said Chng, who also heads the centre’s Urban Psychology Lab.
Taking time and “seeking independent assessments” can also help, he added.
“It would be prudent to pause and ask what evidence supports a particular business proposition, how it generates revenue, and whether its claims can be checked independently of those promoting it.”
KinderWorld International Group’s Tan advises smaller Singapore companies to keep their “eyes and ears open” while learning more about the market in China and finding reliable partners.
A good way to start would be through trade missions organised by groups such as SBF, Tan said - where companies can meet potential business and government contacts.
But SBF stressed that an introduction is not an endorsement. “What works for one may not always work,” said Soo.
For Eo, that caution is not a reason to shy away from an unfamiliar market.
There is always “the lure of very big markets”, he said, as well as the question of “how adventurous a business person can be”.
“It’s always about taking the first step,” Eo said.
“One (to) two years in, then we get a good hold on what’s happening.”

- The criminal profile in GTA 6 tracks how professionally or recklessly Jason and Lucia behave as criminals.
- The four different states of the GTA 6 criminal profile are Professional, Aggressive, Violent, and Psycho.
- Jason and Lucia have separate criminal profiles, and their individual behavior can affect parts of the story.
The Grand Theft Auto franchise has never encouraged players to behave humanely. In most GTA games, from GTA San Andreas to GTA 5, you might steal a car, rob a store, and accidentally flatten out half a sidewalk full of pedestrians. GTA 6, however, lets you put a little more thought behind the kind of criminal you want to become. There is a new criminal profile system in GTA 6, which has understandably drawn comparisons to RDR 2.
So, here is a detailed explanation of the GTA 6 Criminal Profile mechanic, including the honor ranks and how you must plan your heists before the Leonida cops ruin your evening.
What is the GTA 6 Criminal Profile?
The criminal profile in GTA 6 is a new system that keeps track of the way Jason and Lucia conduct themselves as criminals.
Note that there is a neat distinction between the criminal profile in GTA 6 and the honor system in Red Dead Redemption 2. While the latter is based on Arthur Morgan’s morality, Rockstar has taken a different approach this time around. The Criminal Profile in GTA 6 is based on how professional you are as a criminal.
Get this straight: you don’t become a saint by rescuing some kittens one afternoon, while spending the last night stealing a bank and shooting half the room. It’s GTA 6, and you will be expected to take on some dirty jobs.
The criminal profile is a metric that measures how clean your crime was. There is no good or evil in this metric. In simple terms, if you leave the crime scene without a trace, you’re an expert; but if you leave after a bloodbath, you’re a psychopath.
GTA 6 Criminal Profile States and Honor Ranks
Unlike the more familiar honor system, the Criminal Profile in Grand Theft Auto 6 works through four different states instead of a constantly visible bar. The four states in the criminal profile are as follows, and they are represented with different GTA 6 icons.
Professional
Professional is the most controlled state in the criminal profile. If you’re in this stage, you must be avoiding unnecessary escalation while completing the missions. Here, you don’t shoot everybody in the room; rather, you intimidate or restrain them using a weapon in GTA 6 and complete the job.
Rob Nelson described this kind of approach in terms of restraint and control. Here, the idea is to accomplish the job without creating casualties or chaos.
Aggressive
This is where the gloves start to come off. Here, you’re still capable of controlling situations, but you’re using force when it’s unnecessary. If you repeatedly choose physical force when a calmer approach was available, you push Jason or Lucia to this state.
The difference between a Professional and an Aggressive state is knowing the difference between violence being an option and treating it as the first thing on the menu.
Violent
The Violent state is where using excessive force doesn’t feel like an option anymore. It has become a part of your daily missions. So, if you’re routinely killing people who aren’t necessary targets and escalating the encounters to create more destruction, you will be moving away from the Aggressive state to being Violent.
Rockstar has already shown how GTA 6’s gore and dismemberment are significantly more brutal, so turning every robbery into a massacre can create harsh consequences.
Psycho
This is the extreme end of the known criminal profile states in GTA 6. You might reach this stage when you’re consistently creating excessive violence and chaotic behavior.
If your everyday heists and other missions include going far beyond what is necessary, you’re probably heading toward this stage. It can include anything like turning robberies into a massacre or ramming over people with your new car in GTA 6.
Can You Break the Criminal Profile in GTA 6?
This is one of the most intriguing parts of the criminal profile system in GTA 6. Yes, beyond the four known states, there appears to be a Shattered or Broken state that can be reached if you like to play the classic old-school GTA.
Once you reach this stage, it can apparently become irreversible for that playthrough. Rockstar says that your actions are supposed to have more weight, and some consequences cannot be reversed instantly with a handful of good deeds.
So, unlike San Andreas and GTA 5, you can’t just finish half of the GTA 6 map and then repair your reputation by greeting strangers for five minutes.
What Raises the Criminal Profile in GTA 6
One of the most important things is to understand that committing crimes won’t automatically make your criminal profile worse. The gameplay scenarios in the GTA 6 extended look are proof that the way you carry out your crimes is going to affect your criminal profile.
For example, you carry out a restrained approach that includes completing a robbery without killing people, avoiding collateral damage, and leaving once you’ve completed the objective. The money is secured, the escape route is clear, and there is minimal evidence of Jason and Lucia being at the crime scene. This is a completely Professional approach, and it won’t raise the criminal profile stage.
Whereas, if you decide to knock out the cashier who gave you a funny look and begin a war in the neighborhood, it will drag your profile to the Aggressive or even the Violent stages.
Does Criminal Profile Affect Jason and Lucia Differently?
Yes, another interesting detail about the GTA 6 criminal profile is that Jason and Lucia do not share a single criminal profile. Each character can develop their own state.
This means you might make Jason a highly disciplined professional while developing Lucia with a more violent reputation, or vice versa. This can be interesting, because Rockstar has already given the two separate identities. The approach might suit them more, with Jason being a trained army veteran and Lucia being a fighter.
Rob Nelson says that your actions may influence how the story unfolds depending on how you play. This makes the GTA 6 criminal profile more interesting than simply slapping an honor meter.
And that is all about the GTA 6 criminal profile. If you want to learn more about other major mechanics, the GTA 6 wanted system guide is there to help you out.
Is GTA 6’s criminal profile the same as Red Dead Redemption 2’s honor system?
No, the criminal profile in GTA 6 is inspired by some of the ideas behind the RDR 2 honor system, but it is not a morality meter. It focuses on the type of criminal you are and how efficiently you carry out the missions.
What are the GTA 6 criminal profile states?
The four known standard states in the GTA 6 criminal profile are Professional, Aggressive, Violent, and Psycho. There’s also a Shattered state that can permanently lock the profile for the whole game.
Do Jason and Lucia have different criminal profiles in GTA 6?
Yes, Jason and Lucia have separate criminal profiles. That means if you consider developing a character solely on an aggressive side, it can later affect how the main story unfolds.

Representing India at the United Nations high-level meeting on 'Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response' in New York, Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava reaffirmed the nation's commitment to strengthening global health security through international cooperation.
She stressed the need to translate lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic into sustained investment, institutional capacity and resilient health systems.
Addressing the meeting at the United Nations Headquarters on Friday, September 25, 2026, Ms. Srivastava outlined India's coordinated approach to pandemic prevention and response across government and society, which covers a wide range of potential health emergencies.
She spoke of the country's efforts to expand laboratory networks, emergency coordination, health workforce, stockpiles and clinical care capacity to ensure systems are equipped to respond effectively to health emergencies.
She noted that these efforts must be rooted in national health systems, development plans and domestic financing, with international assistance complementing national responsibility.
Drawing on India's experience during COVID-19, Srivastava called for digital public infrastructure to be recognised as a global public good.
She noted that digital solutions played an important role in surveillance, vaccination, risk communication, supply chains and continuity of health services during the pandemic.
Ms. Srivastava also underscored the importance of solidarity and fair access to essential health products. During the COVID-19 pandemic, India supplied 300 million vaccine doses to around 100 countries and two UN entities, while providing medical assistance to over 150 countries. She said this reflected India's commitment to the principle of ‘One Earth, One Health’ and to the Global South.
Referring to the WHO Pandemic Agreement adopted in May 2025, the Union health secretary described it as an important milestone and stressed that its credibility would depend on a fair Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing (PABS) system.
She emphasised that countries contributing pathogens and biological resources must receive timely access to vaccines, diagnostics, therapeutics, technologies and other benefits, while respecting national sovereignty.
Srivastava further stated that the political declaration should not prejudge ongoing negotiations on the PABS annex and should be implemented in accordance with national circumstances and capacities. On the 'One Health' approach, she called for its implementation, as appropriate, in accordance with domestic law, international law and national circumstances.
She also underlined the importance of member states' role in reviewing and consolidating pandemic prevention, preparedness and response tools, assessments and data, noting that such processes should be undertaken in consultation with member states given their policy implications.
Concluding her speech, Ms. Srivastava highlighted that preparedness is a shared responsibility and that equity must remain central to efforts to address future pandemics and outbreaks. "Global solidarity must be demonstrated through action," she said.
WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus pointed to the progress made in strengthening the global health security architecture since COVID-19, including the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations.
He stressed the urgency of concluding negotiations on the PABS system, noting that delays could affect the world's ability to respond to future pandemics.

The story so far: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has warned against the indiscriminate, repeated, or prolonged use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics, linking inappropriate use to avoidable renal complications and chronic kidney disease (CKD).
In its September 21 circular, it also reminded doctors, pharmacists, hospitals, and the public that these medicines are subject to prescription and other regulatory safeguards.
What does the latest directive mean?
The CDSCO circular is, in significant part, a reminder that existing rules already require medical supervision for these medicines and doesn’t amount to any new ban on painkillers or antibiotics.
Most NSAIDs are classified under Schedule H of the Drugs Rules, 1945. Most antibiotics are under Schedule H1. These medicines are therefore not meant to be sold at retail without a prescription from a Registered Medical Practitioner.
Schedule H1 medicines also carry a specific warning that they should be taken only on and according to medical advice.
The regulator has asked the public not to take NSAIDs or antibiotics indiscriminately, repeatedly or for prolonged periods without medical advice.
“Antibiotics should not be self-medicated or used for illnesses where they are not clinically indicated,” it said.
Also, doctors have been asked to prescribe them only when clinically justified, in the appropriate dose and for the appropriate duration, and to follow antimicrobial stewardship principles. Pharmacies, hospitals, and healthcare institutions have also been put on notice.
The kidney warning is particularly relevant to NSAIDs. These drugs can reduce blood flow to the kidneys and are associated with acute kidney injury, particularly among people who already have kidney disease, diabetes, or hypertension. Longer-term use has also been associated with CKD occurrence or progression.
Importantly, the warning does not mean that all painkillers or antibiotics are inherently unsafe. The concern is inappropriate selection, dose, duration, and unsupervised use.
How extensive is antibiotic misuse?
There is no single national figure that captures all inappropriate antibiotic use in India. Available studies, however, show that self-medication remains a significant problem.
A systematic review covering 66 Indian studies and nearly 30,000 participants estimated overall self-medication at 64.4%, although this included medicines generally and not antibiotics alone. Analgesics, antipyretics, antibiotics, and cough remedies were among the commonly self-medicated drug categories.
A community study from South-East Delhi found that 35% of 200 participants reported antibiotic self-medication. Fever, cold, and flu were common reasons, while pharmacies were the main source of antibiotics.
While these studies cannot be interpreted as a national prevalence estimate and represent different populations and locations, together they illustrate why prescription enforcement and antibiotic stewardship remain concerns.
What does antibiotic misuse do?
Antibiotics work against bacterial infections. They do not treat viral illnesses such as most common colds and influenza.
When antibiotics are used unnecessarily, incorrectly or for an inappropriate duration, bacteria can be exposed to the drug without being eliminated. Resistant organisms can then survive and multiply. This contributes to antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
The consequences extend beyond the individual who takes the antibiotic. Resistant organisms can spread to other people and through healthcare and environmental pathways.
WHO estimates that bacterial AMR was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021. In 2023, approximately one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections globally was resistant to antibiotics. WHO says misuse and overuse of antimicrobials are important drivers of the problem.
What does WHO say about antibiotic use?
WHO has increasingly moved towards antimicrobial stewardship — ensuring that antimicrobials are used only when necessary and that the right drug, dose and duration are selected.
Its AWaRe classification divides antibiotics into three groups: Access, Watch and Reserve. Access antibiotics are generally preferred for common infections because they have a narrower spectrum and lower resistance potential. Watch antibiotics have greater resistance potential and therefore require more careful use. Reserve antibiotics are intended for infections caused by multidrug-resistant organisms when other options are inadequate.
WHO’s analysis of 2022 antibiotic-use data found that only about one in three reporting countries/territories/areas met the target of having at least 70% of antibiotic consumption from the Access group. WHO has called for stewardship policies to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use and encourage Access antibiotics when they are clinically appropriate.
WHO’s 2025 global AMR surveillance report, based on more than 23 million laboratory-confirmed cases reported by countries, also underlines the continuing global burden of resistance and the need for better surveillance.
Which drugs are commonly misused, and who is most vulnerable?
NSAIDs are among the medicines of concern because they are widely used for headaches, fever, body pain, arthritis, dental pain, and other painful conditions.
Common NSAIDs include ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen, and similar anti-inflammatory painkillers. Their risks become more important with prolonged or high-dose use and in people with kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, dehydration or other risk factors.
Indian pharmacovigilance data, although based on reported adverse events rather than population prevalence, provide an important signal: in one analysis of NSAID-associated CKD reports, 82% of cases were among people aged 40–80 years, with diclofenac implicated in 43% of the reports.
For antibiotics, children are an important vulnerable group, largely because parents or caregivers may administer medicines based on previous prescriptions or advice from pharmacies and family members. The recent Indian meta-analysis found substantial antibiotic self-medication among children.
Older adults and people with chronic diseases also require particular caution because kidney function may already be reduced and multiple medicines may be involved.
What measures is the government bringing in?
India has been working on AMR for more than a decade. The National Programme on AMR Containment was launched in 2013, with surveillance, monitoring of antimicrobial consumption, infection prevention and control, and promotion of rational antimicrobial use among its objectives.
India launched its National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2.0 (NAP-AMR 2025–2029) in November 2025. It adopts a One Health approach, bringing human health together with animal, agricultural, and environmental sectors. It includes surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention and control, research and monitoring.
The government has also used the Drugs Rules to control antibiotic sales. Schedule H1 requires records of the supply of listed medicines, including details of the prescriber and patient, with records maintained for three years.
There is also a recent regulatory development in August 2026, when CDSCO issued a draft notification proposing four additional drugs for inclusion in Schedule H1.
Why have rules not worked so far?
The central difficulty is that regulation has existed for years, but implementation has been uneven.
India’s NAP-AMR documentation itself records earlier CDSCO awareness and enforcement drives concerning Schedule H and H1 medicines, including restrictions on selling antimicrobials without prescriptions. Yet studies continue to document antibiotic self-medication and access through pharmacies.
Similarly, antimicrobial stewardship programmes have been part of India’s AMR strategy since the first National Action Plan. The 2017–2021 plan called for stewardship programmes, treatment guidelines, multidisciplinary stewardship committees, and training.
The continuing problem, therefore, is less about the absence of rules and more about translating those rules into routine practice — ensuring that prescriptions are actually required at the point of sale, that doctors prescribe antibiotics appropriately, that patients do not demand or reuse medicines, and that hospitals monitor antibiotic consumption.

Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company’s new AI agent with code that the company open sourced. The company suggests projects like loading Muse on a color E Ink display to show reminders, adding it to an HDMI stick so you can display Muse on a big screen, or putting Muse on a small touchscreen device to make what looks kind of like a DIY Muse Charm.
Meta open sources code to let you make Muse AI gadgets
Meta now lets you connect Muse to your own hardware to put on your displays or a Raspberry Pi.
“Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says. “Program an off-the-shelf ESP32 board or set up a Raspberry Pi with our SDKs, then connect Muse to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench.” However, Meta cautions that you should “Proceed at your own risk!”
The company is also giving away a Muse Home Link gadget that it created. With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says. It manufactured 5,000 of the gadgets, according to Meta Superintelligence Labs’ Nat Friedman, and you can claim a waitlist spot for the Muse Home Link now ahead of shipping sometime this month.

SJM fans, we're going back to Prythian.
On October 27, Bloomsbury will finally publish Sarah J. Maas' sixth book in the "A Court of Thorns and Roses" series, "A Court of Splintered Harmony." The seventh book, "A Court of Forgotten Melody," will follow on January 12, 2027.
The October release marks Maas' first "ACOTAR" book since "A Court of Silver Flames," published in 2021.
However, a portion of the 2024 "Crescent City" book, "House of Flame and Shadow," took place in Prythian. Maas blended the worlds of "Crescent City," "ACOTAR," and "Throne of Glass," creating an interconnected literary universe. Plus, the book had lasting implications for "ACOTAR," so if you plan to keep reading the series, you should probably read all 16 of Maas' books.
With all that in mind, it can be hard to keep track of the details in the bestsellers' works. To prep for the release, here's a look back at everything you need to know before reading "A Court of Splintered Harmony."
Warning: major spoilers ahead for "ACOTAR" and "Crescent City."
Nesta and the Valkyrie take center stage in 'A Court of Silver Flames'
"A Court of Silver Flames" marks a turning point in the "ACOTAR" series, as Nesta Archeron becomes the protagonist, alongside General of the Night Court's armies and Inner Circle member Cassian.
Nesta is in a dark place after she was Made fae by the Cauldron, the King of Hybern killed her father, and she killed him in revenge during the war in "A Court of Wings and Ruin." High Lord and Lady Rhysand and Feyre instruct Cassian to train Nesta, Feyre's sister, in the ways of an Illyrian warrior to help her heal.
Nesta strikes a bargain with Cassian to train in exchange for a favor of her choosing, resulting in an eight-pointed star tattoo appearing on their spines. Once she commits to training, Nesta falls in love with it. She recruits priestesses from the library below the House of Wind to join her, including Gwyneth (Gwyn) Berdara. Emerie, an Illyrian, also joins them. Together, Nesta, Gwyn, and Emerie revive an ancient legion of all-female warriors called the Valkyrie (the two new books are part of "The Valkyrie Cycle," so the legion will likely play a significant role).
The new Valkyrie combine Valkyrie fighting techniques with those of the Illyrian soldiers, and their training heavily emphasizes working as a unit, as Nesta and her friends display when they compete and win the Illyrian ritual of the Blood Rite.
Cassian also supports Nesta as she explores the death powers she took from the Cauldron. She can use the magical Dread Trove, which includes a Harp, a Mask, and a Crown, because they were also Made. She accidentally creates a trove of her own, forging three weapons: a dagger, a short sword, and her personal sword, Ataraxia, which can kill immortals, like the death lord Lanthys.
Nesta ultimately uses the Dread Trove to stop time when Feyre nearly dies giving birth to her and Rhysand's son, Nyx (as does Rhys, as he and Feyre had bound their lives together). When she pauses time, Nesta gives the power she stole from the Cauldron back to save her sister. The Mother then blesses her, restoring a bit of her power.
Cassian and Nesta's mating bond locks into place in the final third of the book, and the novel ends with Nesta planning their wedding, which Rhysand is enthusiastically financing as a thank-you for saving his family.
Koschei was positioned as a looming threat
In "ACOSF," Cassian and Nesta work together to defeat Briallyn, a human queen cursed with old age when she used the Cauldron to become fae. Briallyn seeks the Dread Trove to reverse her curse, but Vassa, another human queen, tells Cassian that Koschei, a death god first mentioned in "ACOWAR," likely planted the idea in Briallyn's head in hopes of securing the trove for himself.
Koschei has been confined to a lake for a millennium after being tricked by an unnamed female fae warrior, as his brother, the Bone Carver, told Feyre and Cassian. Their sister, Stryga (the Weaver), was likewise confined to The Middle.
Koschei cursed Vassa to be trapped at his lake and turn into a firebird by day. Nesta's father made a deal with Koschei to temporarily free Vassa so she could fight in the war against Hybern with the forces he had raised, though Maas hasn't provided details about the terms of their bargain.
Koschei gives Briallyn the opportunity to take control of Cassian with the Crown from the Trove, but his plan fails when Cassian and Nesta kill her together. However, Koschei's attempts at freedom aren't done, as he was singled out as the villain in the description of "A Court of Splintered Harmony."
Maas set up new plots for side characters in 'ACOSF'
Although "Silver Flames" focused on Nesta and Cassian, Maas also advanced the arcs of other characters in the book.
- Elain Archeron: Elain lives at Feyre's home in the Night Court, and she has shown no sign of her seer abilities since the war. When the Inner Circle visits the Court of Nightmares, Cassian says she seems out of place there, thinking the black dress she wore "sucked the life from her."
- Lucien Vanserra: Lucien continued to travel the human lands as an emissary for the Night Court alongside his Band of Exiles, Jurian and Vassa. He longs to be with Elain, who has yet to accept their mating bond, and he remains unaware that Feyre realized he is the biological son of Helion, High Lord of the Day Court. His relationship with Tamlin is still fractured.
- Eris Vanserra: Lucien's eldest brother made a formal alliance with the Night Court, telling them secrets about his father to protect the future of the Autumn Court. He also fought Queen Briallyn with them after she kidnapped and controlled his soldiers. Eris continued to hint that there was more to his history with Mor than people believe, setting the stage for a revelation about their relationship down the line.
- Morrigan: At the end of "ACOWAR," Mor left for the fae court of Vallahan to get a peace treaty between fae and humans signed. They are resistant, and Mor was there for the majority of "ACOSF." Maas has been vague about how Mor spends her time in Vallahan.
- Gwyn: Gwyn, who has Autumn Court and nymph ancestry, and her twin sister were born after their mother participated in the Great Rite, creating the possibility that Gwyn's father is a High Lord or fae noble. Gwyn's sister died when Hybern soldiers attacked the temple where they were raised, and a soldier assaulted Gwyn while she protected children who were escaping. Azriel saved her, and Mor brought Gwyn to the library to recover. She is also writing a book about the new Valkyrie and has a beautiful singing voice.
- Emerie: Emerie was first introduced in "A Court of Frost and Starlight" and owns a clothing shop in the Illyrian camp Windhaven, which she took over after her abusive father's death. He clipped her wings, so she cannot fly. Emerie also comments on Mor's beauty when she sees her at the library, telling Nesta, "I always forget about how beautiful she is," with a blush, hinting at a potential attraction between them.
A 'Silver Flames' bonus chapter explores Azriel's love life
Maas has written three bonus chapters for "ACOTAR" over the years, which were released in specific editions of her books. Bloomsbury announced on September 24 that all three would be included in every edition of "A Court of Splintered Harmony," indicating the events of the bonus chapters are relevant to its plot.
In particular, readers might want to take a look at the bonus chapter that focuses on Azriel's experience on the Winter Solstice that occurs during "ACOSF."
After their friends have gone to bed, Elain and Azriel present each other with gifts, and they almost kiss after Azriel gives her a necklace, despite Lucien sleeping upstairs. Rhysand interrupts them, and he warns Azriel that Lucien could challenge him to a Blood Duel if he found out he kissed his mate, which could lead to political fallout with the Autumn Court and the Band of Exiles for the Night Court.
Azriel says he thinks Elain should be his mate, not Lucien's, because her sisters are mated to Rhysand and Cassian.
"The Cauldron chose three sisters. Tell me how it's possible that my two brothers are with two of those sisters, yet the third was given to another," he said.
After Rhysand orders him to stay away from Elain, Azriel goes to the training arena at the House of Wind, where Gwyn is practicing. His shadows react strangely to her. First, they do not warn him of her presence, and as the pair speak, they are drawn to her.
"Her breath curled in front of her mouth, and one of his shadows darted out to dance with it before twirling back to him," Azriel notes. "Like it heard some silent music."
Azriel also says his shadows "calmed" as he spent time with Gwyn, and as he left, he reflected that "he could have sworn a faint, beautiful singing followed him. Could have sworn his shadows sang in answer."
The musical language surrounding Gwyn and Azriel's interactions is interesting, given that "harmony" and "melody" appear in the titles of books six and seven. Gwyn also asks Azriel, the Shadowsinger, if he sings during the conversation, driving home the musical theme.
Later, when Azriel finds that Elain returned the necklace he gave her, he anonymously leaves it for Gwyn at the library.
Azriel and Nesta were central to the crossover in 'House of Flame and Shadow'
When "House of Flame and Shadow" opens, Bryce Quinlan is imprisoned in the Night Court after accidentally teleporting herself there at the end of "House of Sky and Breath." Azriel initially found her, and their weapons recognized each other: Azriel bears the dagger Truth-Teller, and Bryce has the Starsword, known as Gwydion in Prythian, twin blades that have been separated for centuries.
In "HOFAS," Bryce begrudgingly tells Rhysand, Amren, and Azriel about the Asteri, known as the Daglan in Prythian. Nesta arrives, and she senses Bryce's Horn tattoo, which was Made like she was.
Bryce escapes into the unexplored tunnels below the Night Court, using the glow from the star on her chest, which Nesta says matches the tattoo from her bargain with Cassian and a carving she saw at the prison. Nesta and Azriel follow her on the path the star is leading her, and they end up at the prison. Bryce steps on the star in the ground, and a vision of Silene, the ancient High Queen Theia's daughter, appears to reveal the Asteri's history on Prythian.
The Asteri's links to Pyrthian and Midgard are expansive, but here's what's relevant to "ACOTAR": The Horn on Bryce's back was originally part of the Dread Trove, and using it with the Harp can open portals to other worlds. Queen Theia wielded them to go to Midgard, hoping to seek more power than she had at her home, a mist-cloaked island that would be the Dusk Court. It was a trap masterminded by her general Pelius and the Asteri Rigelus.
When war breaks out in Midgard, Theia tries to send her daughters, Helena and Silene, back to Prythian, but Helena sacrifices herself to get Silene and the Harp home, keeping the Horn in Midgard. Silene turned her mother's abandoned court into the prison, filling it with monsters. She later married the High Lord of the Night Court and made their son's blood a key to the prison. The lore was lost to time, though the bloodline's ability to access the prison remained. Rhysand has accessed the prison with his blood throughout "ACOTAR," making him the heir to the Dusk Court.
Once the story ends, Bryce absorbs the power Silene left there and seems to unveil the court that had been hidden by the prison. Nesta kills an Asteri who was secretly trapped there, named Vesperus, beheading her with Ataraxia.
Bryce flees to Midgard with Gwydion and Truth-Teller, but eventually, she opens a portal to Prythian. She asks Nesta to borrow the Mask, temporarily trading her parents for it to show Nesta she will bring it and Truth-Teller back. Nesta agrees, and Bryce uses the Mask to help rid Midgard of the Asteri.
She returns the items after the war, and before they go back to Midgard, Bryce's mother, Ember, says Rhysand has been upset with Nesta for lending the Mask to Bryce.
Maas expands on that theme in a bonus chapter of the novel included in the Books-A-Million edition of "House of Flame and Shadow," told from Ember's perspective while she is in Prythian. Ember overhears Nesta fighting with Rhysand about her decision to give Bryce the Mask, during which she points out the Trove "answers" to and "obeys" her, not Rhysand. She also tells the High Lord she is not his subject, indicating she may not consider herself a member of the Night Court as the other Inner Circle members do. Nesta later tells Ember that Feyre stopped Rhysand from punishing her, but she also says everyone in the court is mad at her, with Cassian being the angriest of them all.
Bryce also leaves Nesta with Gwydion, encouraging her to explore her connection to it.
"I think that eight-pointed star was tattooed on you for a reason. Take that sword and go figure out why," she said.

New-age tech stocks remained under pressure this week, with 47 stocks declining as benchmark indices recorded their eighth consecutive weekly fall. Moneyview’s market debut this week took the number of new-age tech companies under Inc42’s coverage to 66. Despite the addition, their combined market capitalisation fell to $153.61 Bn from the $166.6 Bn commanded by 65 companies last week. Shares of Moneyview made their debut on Thursday (October 1) at ₹55.6 on the BSE, nearly 64% above the issue price of ₹34. The stock closed at ₹54.03, down 2.8% from the listing price but 58.9% above its issue price. Of the 65 stocks under Inc42’s coverage at the end of last week, 47 fell between 0.08% and 20.1% this week. Eighteen stocks gained between 0.17% and 22.55%. Turtlemint led the losers, falling 20.1% to ₹69.75, while PB Fintech declined 15.66% to ₹983 following IRDAI’s proposed changes to insurance commissions. ESDS was the second-biggest loser, falling 18.54% to ₹1,431.70 after announcing its Q1 FY27 results on September 24. However, it remained more than 91% above its listing price. Swiggy, Fractal, Menhood, and IndiaMART touched fresh lows during the week. Eternal, Lenskart, Ather Energy, Paytm, and Nykaa also declined this week. SME-listed Zappfresh led the gainers, rising 22.55% to ₹60.49 after hitting an all-time low of ₹47.10 on September 25. RentoMojo, Meesho, BlackBuck, and Go Digit also gained, while Aequs, Kissht, Nazara, SEDEMAC, and Zelio touched fresh highs. The stock markets were closed yesterday on account of Gandhi Jayanti. Beyond stock movements, the week saw GST notices, stake sales, and expansion plans across listed new-age tech companies. Here’s a closer look at the key developments. GST Notices Put Companies In Focus Kissht’s NBFC arm, Si Creva, received a GST show cause notice involving ₹44.06 Cr over alleged input tax credit discrepancies and tax shortfalls for FY23. This comprises ₹22.03 Cr in tax, ₹19.83 Cr in interest, and ₹2.2 Cr in penalties. The company said it would contest the notice. WeWork India received a ₹11.01 Cr show cause notice over alleged excess input tax credit utilisation arising from differences between its annual returns and audited books. Urban Company faced a ₹3.05 Cr demand over alleged incorrect input tax credit claims and tax shortfalls for FY23. ideaForge received a ₹109.17 Cr GST demand and penalty for allegedly paying 5% instead of 18% on drone sales between January 2022 and March 2024. It plans to appeal, citing a 2025 government clarification that drones attract 5% GST, and expects no immediate material financial or operational impact. Stake Sales And Purchases TPG, through NewQuest Asia Fund IV (Singapore), sold 40 Lakh Shadowfax shares at ₹284.03 apiece for ₹113.6 Cr, following its ₹202 Cr exit from FirstCry on September 25. SBI Mutual Fund bought 1.18 Cr Swiggy shares for an estimated ₹300.6 Cr, raising its holding from 4.7% to 5.12%.
