Inside India's forest villages, where a dangerous mix of crises led to 32 child deaths
- Published
Warning: This article contains details some readers may find distressing
At about 3am one morning in May, Bamita Markam began convulsing.
The three-year-old had spent days with a high fever and angry red sores on her body. Her mother, Koushila, had first taken her to a doctor, who prescribed an ointment.
Bamita seemed to recover, then became ill again. A faith healer, called to the house in Matla village, gave her syrups and tablets. Nothing worked. By dawn, Bamita was dead.
"She cried a lot," Koushila recalls. "She convulsed all night." The family tried to make her drink water. At one point she vomited blood. They buried her in a jungle after midday.
Bamita's death was one of at least 32 child deaths recorded since May in a cluster of remote villages in Balaghat district in India's Madhya Pradesh state, officials say. The victims ranged from babies just three or four months old to an 18-year-old, and most were Baiga, one of India's 75 "particularly vulnerable tribal groups", external.
Officials attribute the deaths to mainly measles and malaria, possibly aggravated by malnutrition and delays in treatment.
They believe eight to 10 deaths were associated with measles, roughly another 10 with malaria, with several children suffering more than one infection. The precise cause of every death is less certain.
"I have never seen an outbreak like this. My father was a two-term lawmaker, and I have served three terms, but neither of us has seen so many children die in such a short time," Sanjay Uikey, who has represented the area since 2013, told me.
But disease is only part of the story. In remote, forested parts of Balaghat, where Maoist insurgency once took root, reaching a health centre can be a challenge in itself.
In the monsoon, the terrain can make that journey harder. Paddy fields glow against red earth and low, forested hills. Narrow dirt tracks wind between fields and mud homes, often becoming slippery and impassable in heavy rain.
The countryside is lush, but the homes are sparse. Most Baiga houses have low mud walls, rough timber and bamboo, and tiled or thatched roofs patched with plastic against the rain.
Some homes are accessible only by these tracks. Doctors investigating the deaths have travelled through the mud in tractors. On a recent visit, we walked nearly 2km (1.2 miles) uphill to reach some of the more remote homes. The surrounding jungle was dotted with the graves of children who had died.
The nearest state hospital, a 100-bed facility in Birsa, is about 70km away. For families without vehicles, reaching it can mean muddy tracks, a makeshift bamboo stretcher or a motorcycle - and a day's lost wages.
When Bamita became seriously ill, the family did not get her to hospital. It was raining heavily. The tracks were muddy and slippery, and the family had no way of transporting her.
"If I was able to take her to hospital she might have lived," Koushila says.
Her other daughter, Ankita, keeps asking what happened to her sister. The six-year-old has been told what many children in these villages are told: "Mata aa gayi" - the goddess has arrived.
For some Baiga families, some illnesses - like chicken pox - are seen as the arrival of a disease goddess, who must be appeased rather than treated. Families perform a seven to nine-day ritual of bathing and offering cool water and neem leaves to the local disease goddess. Many believe that treating the patient before the ritual is completed could cause death.
For weeks, such beliefs shaped how families responded to sick children. Then the scale of the deaths began to emerge.
On 21 July, Parshuram Dhurwey, a local village council chief, heard that two children in the same household in Bondari village had died. The next morning, he heard of another death. He called local officials and went to the area.
They found a grim picture.
"Every other child was sick," Dhurwey says. "They had fever, they had rashes. Many were undernourished."
When government medical officer Nimish Gautam arrived, he found severely dehydrated children. The first case he saw was a teenage girl with several days of fever and rash, whose blood sugar appeared dangerously low. Her family refused to let the health team examine her properly.
"Police were brought in to persuade them to take her to a health centre. The family still refused," Gautam told me. "They said if we took her for treatment, she would die. So we kept her under observation, and she recovered."
In one village, Dhurwey says, officials forcibly entered homes and took five seriously ill children to hospital. All recovered.
By the time the outbreak became unmistakable to local authorities, children had already been dying for weeks. By September, Dhurwey says, 10 children aged about 18 months to 14 years had died across the four villages in his council - Adori, Kundekasa, Bondari and Usri.
The symptoms were frighteningly similar and frustratingly non-specific: fever, rashes, weakness, dehydration and, in some cases, seizures. Some children had scabies, fungal infections or bacterial skin infections alongside suspected measles and malaria. In a district where malaria is endemic, external, fever could mean several things at once.
Sagnibai of Bondari lost two children within 24 hours. Her daughter, Lamnin, 12, died on 26 June. Her one-year-old son, Sahil, died the following day. A local healer told the family it was Mata. They also had no money or vehicle to take the children to a doctor.
Her husband, Samaroo Dhurwey, remembers nights in which the children's bodies seemed to be "on fire". They could not digest food. They died at home.
Mahasingh Parte of Matla village lost two children - a six-year-old girl and a four-year-old boy - within two days of each other. The family followed a faith healer's instructions. "He said don't take them to hospital," Parte recalls.
Parte is a landless farm labourer who earns about 200 rupees ($2; £1.58) on a good day, he said. Work is scarce in the monsoon, and although a small primary health centre is just 5km away, he had never been there. Poverty and remoteness had stacked the odds against his children.
The question of what was making children sick became harder to answer as the deaths mounted.
An investigation by the ICMR-National Institute for Tribal Health Research (NIRTH) tested 10 samples collected from the affected villages on 7 August. Six tested positive for measles; four were negative.
Measles is highly contagious, causing high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash. Most children recover, but malnutrition can make measles far more dangerous, external, increasing the risk of pneumonia, severe diarrhoea and dehydration, and inflammation of the brain. The infection also weakens the immune system, leaving children vulnerable to other infections. Malaria can compound that risk.
But doctors cautioned that malaria did not necessarily follow measles, and not every fever and rash was measles. Instead, several infections and vulnerabilities collided.
"Sometimes there is no single factor behind the deaths," Gautam said. "There are malnourished children and there's zero health education and hygiene at home."
The Baiga villages are not entirely disconnected from modern India. Seasonal migration takes families to other states for chilli picking and other work. Children watch reels on smartphones, while many families have minimum single-bulb solar-powered electricity, bank accounts and, in some homes, piped water.
Yet malnutrition remains widespread, with children often poorly fed. A five-year-old who died recently of measles weighed around 5kg.
Gautam believes malnutrition is driven by early marriage and motherhood, with some girls becoming mothers at 16 or 17, when their bodies are still developing.
Closely spaced pregnancies, premature births and low birth weight can follow, while young mothers struggle to breastfeed and care for their children. Diet is another problem: many families rely heavily on rice and lentil soup, with too little protein and dietary variety. Studies on Baiga households have found widespread nutritional deficiencies, compounded by poor uptake, external of public services.
The gap between services on paper and on the ground was stark: the state response came weeks after deaths began, while health teams struggled to reach and persuade families.
Once the outbreak was recognised, health workers began door-to-door screening in affected villages. Mobile medical units carrying oxygen, nebulisers, suction equipment, malaria tests and medicines visited more than 20 affected villages.
One mobile doctor, Neeraj Sharma, says teams routinely saw more than 50 patients a day, about half of them children. They conducted 10 or more malaria tests daily, sometimes finding two positive cases a day.
More than 6,200 patients - mostly children - were eventually treated at home, according to Gautam. More than 630 were referred to district hospitals. About 600 returned home, while around 30 remain admitted.
Vaccination became an emergency response. Although official records suggested 90-95% coverage in some areas, health workers found children without records and families reluctant to vaccinate.
Authorities therefore offered the measles-rubella (MR) vaccine to all children under 15, regardless of recorded status. Of about 40,000 children identified in Birsa, roughly 27,000 had been vaccinated, Gautam said. Of the area's 180 villages, some 67 are predominantly Baiga and among the most vulnerable.
But vaccination is only one part of the protection children need. There are wider questions about whether basic nutrition and other health services are reaching those most at risk.
A 2024 audit by India's Comptroller and Auditor General found "serious irregularities", external in Madhya Pradesh's distribution of take-home rations meant to supplement the diets of children aged six months to three years, pregnant women and lactating mothers, including problems with beneficiary identification, production, transport and distribution.
The outbreak has now subsided. Officials say the last child death was more than two weeks before their late-September assessment, while teams continue visiting villages. In Kundekasa, a medical camp that once saw about 120 children a day was seeing fewer than 10.
Back in Matla, Bamita's mother speaks about the child who would ask for money for snacks, play with her sister and run inside whenever cars approached because vehicles frightened her.
"I had hope she'd study and make something of herself. I never regretted I didn't have a boy," Koushila says.
Then she looks at Ankita, the surviving sister.
"I want more kids," she says. "I feel alone. Ankita is alone. She keeps crying for her sister."

A viral video highlighting the poor condition of footpaths in Bengaluru’s Indiranagar appears to have prompted quick civic action, with Canadian vlogger Caleb Friesen saying some of the spots featured in his video have since been repaired. Friesen, who lives in Bengaluru and has previously posted about the city’s infrastructure challenges, recently shared a video documenting the condition of footpaths along 12th Main in Indiranagar. The video showed damaged pavements, piles of rubble and a large hole filled with rubbish. In a follow-up post, Friesen said some of the locations highlighted in the video had been fixed. In the video, Friesen walked along 12th Main and pointed out cracked and broken sections of the pavement. Describing the condition as “pathetic”, he questioned how such pedestrian infrastructure existed in a neighbourhood associated with Bengaluru’s technology and startup economy. “Bengaluru is a pretty important city here in India. It's one of the tech capitals of the country,” Friesen said in the video. He also pointed to Indiranagar’s position as a hub for startups and venture capital firms, arguing that the condition of its footpaths did not reflect the city’s reputation for technology and innovation. The video showed sections of broken pavement, scattered construction debris and a large hole containing rubbish. Friesen also questioned why the debris had been left unattended and suggested that the problem was not limited to the stretch he was filming. In the post accompanying the video, he said Indiranagar’s footpaths should be “walkable, safe, pedestrian-friendly” and a reflection of the innovation associated with Bengaluru. The clip triggered discussion on social media, with users sharing their experiences of Bengaluru’s pedestrian infrastructure and pointing to similar problems in other Indian cities. In his latest update, Friesen said some of the spots highlighted in his video had been repaired. “Great news! Some spots highlighted in this video were fixed today. Tomorrow more work will be done,” he wrote in the follow-up post. Friesen also said he was not in Bengaluru at the time and that another person would be at 12th Main along with area inspector Vijay Haridas, whom he credited with helping make the quick fixes happen. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) has previously responded to infrastructure issues highlighted in Friesen’s videos. In December 2025, a separate video by Friesen led to repairs on an Indiranagar footpath, according to The New Indian Express. The report said the civic body fixed the stretch after his video drew attention to damaged and obstructed footpaths. The latest episode highlights a recurring tension for Bengaluru: a city widely associated with technology, startups and venture capital continues to face basic urban infrastructure challenges. Friesen’s videos have repeatedly focused on the experience of navigating Bengaluru on foot, turning everyday problems such as broken pavements, obstructions and unsafe stretches into social-media conversations. A previous viral video by Friesen also helped draw attention to a long-abandoned walkway connecting Domlur and Indiranagar, which was subsequently restored after public pressure and efforts involving civic authorities and local residents. For the latest 12th Main video, however, the immediate update is that some of the locations featured by Friesen have been repaired, while he said more work was expected. Estonian aerial athlete Jaan Roose will attempt to cross a 160-metre long highline suspended 120 metres above central Seoul on Thursday.
Roose, a three-time slackline world champion, will step out on to a narrow polyester ribbon between the Koreana hotel and the Dong-A Media Center, near the capital city’s famous Gwanghwamun palace and square.
The 34-year-old has made a name for himself slacklining dramatic urban environments, such as his 185-metre high feat between Qatar’s Iconic Towers.
In 2024, he became the first person to slackline the strait of Messina between mainland Italy and Sicily, completing the 3.6km traverse despite a fall near the end, caught by his safety harness. Earlier this month, he covered 14.7km over 12 hours on a line above the Danube in Bratislava, Slovakia.
Large crowds in Seoul are expected to watch Roose walk the slackline – twice, at 1pm and 4pm local time – if the weather allows. The walk will be postponed if average wind speeds reach 10m/s or gusts hit 15m/s. Today’s forecast is sunny with light breezes.
Roose said a visit in 2022 to South Korea inspired his Gwanghwamun walk.
On that trip, Roose encountered jultagi, Korea’s traditional tightrope walking, which Unesco added to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2011.
Unlike tightrope walking elsewhere, jultagi is as much comedy as acrobatics. The walker sings, jokes and dances on the rope, trading banter with a clown on the ground as musicians play.

The Instagram accounts of three independent journalists — Bindu Gurjar, Lokbhadra Singh, and Monika Singh — were reportedly suspended earlier this month after they reported extensively on the deaths of tribal children in Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district, and raised questioned about the discrepancies in the government claims surrounding the death.
While Bindu and Monika’s accounts were initially restored after they appealed to Meta, last week, both the accounts were permanently disabled by Instagram. Lokbhadra’s account remained suspended throughout and he was compelled to open a backup account.
Another independent journalist, Saurabh Bhati, who runs a page on Instagram with Monika called The Unsalted, temporarily deactivated that page as well as his personal account as a precautionary measure, after observing the repeated suspensions faced by the other three journalists. The two accounts were later reactivated.
Speaking to Alt News, all three journalists narrated how they were subjected to surveillance, followed by plainclothes personnel, questioned about their movements and pressured through hotel authorities and local intermediaries, creating an intimidating environment that ultimately forced them to leave Balaghat.
Sudden Suspension, Eventual Deletion
Narrating her ordeal, Bindu said that her account was the first to be targeted — on September 5, a copyright strike was issued against her ground report from the Balaghat district hospital, even though it was entirely her original reporting. The following day, on September 6, she received alerts on her phone indicating attempts to log into her account from three different locations. Her account was eventually suspended around 2:30 pm. She initially tried to verify her identity using her Aadhaar card to regain access to her account but was unsuccessful. On September 7, the option to use the PAN card became available, and using this she managed to restore her account around 10:00 am.
However, 11 days after she regained access, Bindu’s account was permanently disabled by Instagram on September 18. She received a notification that she no longer had access to her account, and all her information had been permanently deleted. “You cannot request another review of this decision,” it stated. The account did not follow community standards on account integrity, the notice said. She has now opened a backup account.
A few hours later on September 6, Monika’s account was also suspended twice, but on each occasion, it was restored following an appeal.
However, the account was also permanently disabled with a similar notice on September 20.
Lokbhadra’s account, which had the highest number of followers among the three, was suspended multiple times. Speaking to Alt News, he said the first suspension came at 5:47 pm on September 6. The handle was restored within 30 minutes after an appeal was filed at 10:30 pm. His account was suspended again on September 7 and 8, and for a fourth time around 11 pm on September 9. He said that he did not appeal anymore as cyber experts advised that this could be the work of hackers who might launch another attack immediately upon an appeal. His account remains suspended as of September 23.
The reasons cited by Meta for suspending these journalists’ accounts were identical. It was stated that the account or the activity associated with it did not follow the platform’s “Community Standards on account integrity”. This includes creating an account that impersonates another person, using another person’s photos to deceive others, or generating content that purports to speak on behalf of another individual.

In a statement released on September 8, the Press Club of India condemned the suspension of these journalists’ accounts, demanding an impartial investigation and describing the move as an attempt to intimidate or silence them.
What Were These Scribes Reporting?
Reports of children dying from fever, rashes, or other symptoms began emerging from the tribal areas of Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district between June and July. Most of the deceased children belonged to the Baiga community, a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG). Additionally, some children were from Gond families residing in villages nestled deep within dense forests, located nearly 150 kilometres away from the district headquarters.
The government initially reported an official death toll of only eight children. However, by August, locals, tribal organisations and the opposition began claiming the figure was much higher, ranging from 24 to 30 child deaths. Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi raised the issue. Umang Singhar, the Leader of the Opposition in Madhya Pradesh, wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi citing 30 deaths and attributing them to a lack of water, nutrition, and timely medical treatment. The Madhya Pradesh high court sought a response of the state government to a public interest litigation that claimed that over 30 deaths had occurred and that approximately 400 children were admitted to a 50-bed hospital.
Towards the end of August, these four journalists arrived in Balaghat to report on the deaths of tribal children and uncover the reality. Visiting various villages and meeting affected families, they began investigating the death toll. Their reportage revealed discrepancies between the government’s figure and the rising numbers reported from various villages. The real figures, they reported, were much higher than eight.
Further, they highlighted the poor condition of the local hospital, where multiple children were being treated on a single bed. Subsequently, the reporters alleged that they were pressurised to meet officials and forced to leave their hotel — compelling them to leave Balaghat on the night of September 3.
The Ground Reality
Lokbhadra told Alt News that he arrived in Balaghat from Delhi on August 28. He mentioned that he had already learned through local and social media that while official figures cited only eight deaths, reports from the ground indicated 24 deaths. When he visited the district hospital the same day, the hospital staff informed him: “Over the past 12 days, more than 250 children exhibiting symptoms such as malaria or measles have been admitted.”
The next day, he reached the Bondari area of Birsa block, located about 120 kilometres from Balaghat. This was the area where the highest number of children had been affected. He discovered that the death toll, initially reported as 24, had actually risen to 30. There was no official record of these additional deaths at the time. He gathered separate data on these six children and began publishing on-ground video reports by visiting their families. The video embedded below is from Lokbhadra Singh’s backup account.
On September 1, he learned that the district magistrate (DM) was scheduled to visit the district hospital that evening. Consequently, he arrived at the hospital before the visit to observe the conditions there. “When I had reported on the hospital previously, I found four children sharing almost every bed. Some of them were suffering from malaria, while others exhibited symptoms of measles. As soon as news of the DM’s impending visit spread, cleaning operations began, bedsheets were changed, and new beds were set up.”
Upon the DM’s arrival, Lokbhadra asked him about the death toll discrepancy, to which the DM did not provide a clear answer at first. He further questioned the DM on the hospital’s poor condition. Shifting the blame to the child’s background, the DM answered: “Children from tribal backgrounds often have as many as four siblings, and their parents are also present, which makes it appear crowded.”
Journalists countered by asking how children could be kept in the same bed if one was suffering from malaria and the other from measles. The DM failed to provide a satisfactory answer to this as well. However, in the course of the exchange, the DM admitted on camera, for the first time, to the figure of 24 child deaths. “When further questions were asked, the DM became irritated, swatted the camera away with his hand, and walked off,” Lokbhadra said.
Videos of the incident went viral on social media within hours, and reports began circulating that the Balaghat DM appeared to be dodging questions from the media. These videos, posted on Lokbhadra’s account and others’, are now unavailable as his account no longer accessible.
‘Forced To Leave Balaghat’
“Around 2 am that same night, two individuals, one in police uniform and the other in plainclothes, arrived at my hotel room and asked the manager for documents verifying my identity, even though these had already been submitted at the time of check-in… I asked the manager if there was pressure from the police to keep me under surveillance, which the manager denied. However, when I stepped out of the hotel later that day, I spotted a vehicle bearing a police sticker and three or four plainclothes police personnel standing near the shops. As soon as I took out my camera, they were seen hiding behind posters,” Lokbhadra alleged.
“The same night after I questioned the DM, a local influencer visited my hotel, insisting that I meet the SP. I declined a private meeting at night and instead requested a formal press conference… The next day, while we were out reporting, another journalist staying at the same hotel informed us that some individuals had come to the hotel asking for our names and whereabouts,” he added.
A major district-wide shutdown protest was called by tribal organisations in Balaghat on September 3. On that very day, the hotel owner personally arrived and told the journalist that he had a family event, and the entire hotel needed to be evacuated to accommodate guests. No such information had been conveyed previously, Lokbhadra claimed.
After some discussion, it was decided that they would vacate their rooms in the evening after covering the protest. Throughout the demonstration, the same plainclothes individuals kept following them and recording videos, they alleged. He claimed that the journalists encountered the same police personnel all the way from their hotel during check out to the railway station as they were leaving Balaghat.
“Meanwhile, some local influencers from Balaghat started making videos against me, claiming that I lacked knowledge of media ethics and that my way of questioning the DM was inappropriate,” he alleged. He further claimed that he had received information from a local influencer that the SP had stated in a meeting that these four individuals from Delhi would be “taught a lesson”. Due to this “intimidating atmosphere”, they left Balaghat on the night of September 3rd.
‘Malnutrition, Staff Shortage & Lack of Medical Facilities’
Monika and Saurabh arrived in Balaghat on August 31, before which the former had been tracking the story from Delhi. “Initially, information was available only on the pages of local influencers and city journalists, there were no official records. The official death toll stood at eight, but after speaking with protesters and the families involved, it emerged that their children’s names were missing from the lists. On ground, we discovered that the figure had risen from 24 to 30,” Monika told Alt News.
“The children are suffering from malnutrition, even if no one openly admits it, because acknowledging deaths due to starvation would be seen as a major failure on the part of the administration. Children in these hilly tribal areas have weak immunity, and malaria strikes every year but rarely makes headlines, and while symptoms of measles are clearly visible on their bodies, officials avoid explicitly naming measles and speak only of malaria,” Monika said, adding that the district hospital admitted that the children are malnourished and suffering from both measles and malaria.
Monika also visited the primary health centre (PHC) in Songuda village, which she claimed lacked the facilities to treat even a single patient. “Patients were put directly into an ambulance and sent to the district hospital, around 90 kilometres away. In the long journey, many children, who are already in critical condition, would die on the way,” she alleged. “In some cases, families did not even take the children to the hospital because there is a greater reliance on faith healing in that area. Some children died on the way to the hospital, since doctors did not record the cause of death, their names do not appear on any list. Others were referred from the district hospital to a hospital in Gondia, Maharashtra. The change of state meant these children were excluded from the Madhya Pradesh list.”
She echoed Lokbhadra’s observations for the district hospital, where she claimed there was a severe shortage of beds, and three or four children suffering from conditions ranging from measles, malaria, and malnutrition to ordinary fever, would share a single bed. She visited the hospital both at daytime and at night, and highlighted the severe staff shortage. MP police personnel were performing nursing duties, such as administering medication, while actual nurses were few and far between, and doctors were largely absent, often taking considerable time to arrive when summoned for emergencies, she observed. “Children traveling nearly 100 kilometres for treatment often set out in the evening and did not reach the hospital until 2 or 3 am, leaving no one available at that hour to treat them,” she said.
Monika reiterated Lokbhadra’s claim that the district hospital was given a complete makeover before the DM’s visit on September 1. In the same ward where she had previously reported four children sharing a single bed, the DM found only one child per bed, and the entire area had been cleaned up, she said.
Monika also recounted the same situation faced by Lokbhadra — the constant police surveillance and pressure tactics which ultimately forced the independent journalists out of Balaghat. On September 2, she received a message from another journalist stating that some people had come to the hotel asking about her. On her way back on a bike, she noticed people in plainclothes tailing her almost everywhere.
Bindu Gurjar arrived in Balaghat on August 28. A protest was underway on the main road about a kilometer from the district hospital. Speaking to people there, she came to know that the government was acknowledging only eight deaths.
While preparing her report, she learned that the Baiga community was classified as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG), and under various government schemes, Baiga mothers received Rs 1,500 monthly to purchase nutritious food for their children. Yet the situation on the ground was dire, Bindu observed while reporting from the Balaghat district hospital.
She learned that separate wards had been designated for patients from tribal communities. Across those wards, there were over 100 patients, and almost every single bed was occupied by over two patients along with their entire families, she said, adding that the hospital lacked basic amenities such as sanitisers and masks.
‘Last Rites Done Before Parents Arrived’
A family at the hospital told Bindu that the parents of a child named Lavkush who had recently died did not live in Balaghat. They had gone to Bengaluru for work.
“By the time they were informed of the child’s illness, they were already on the way back. However, the child passed before they could arrive. In accordance with the traditions of the tribal belt, the last rites involved burying the child. This process was carried out without the parents’ consent. By the time the parents reached, the last rites had already been performed, sparking a dispute,” she told Alt News.
Bindu met Lavkush’s parents at the same hospital where their three other children were admitted and kept on the same bed. They were suffering from fever, symptoms resembling measles, and swollen eyes.
After speaking with the hospital staff, Bindu further learned that just one or two nurses were attending to over a hundred patients, and more than 250 patients had been admitted in the past 15 days. To address this shortage, personnel from the police lines were assisting at the hospital, an observation made by Monika earlier. The police, she said, worked four shifts per day, with ten people per shift helping to move patients around and support the staff.
In the course of her investigation, she also tracked the case of a girl named Kajal, who had died on August 29. Kajal had been referred to Gondia, where she passed away. Bindu’s team visited her village, Kisangarh, and witnessed her burial. Subsequently, Bindu and Lokbhadra launched an independent survey the same day. They recorded details, such as names, fathers’ names, village, the onset and nature of the illness, and prior medical consultations on printed forms.
On August 29, Madhya Pradesh chief minister Mohan Yadav visited Kisangarh village, where, according to Bindu, over eight children had died. He announced compensation of Rs 2 lakh for the families of the deceased children. However, it turned out that none of the eight children from that village, whose deaths had been reported, were on his list. As Yadav left without addressing the issue of accountability, Bindu said that locals there began raising slogans.
Bindu mentioned that she came under state surveillance after posting regular reports on the matter online. She recounted that on September 2, Dr. Nilay Jain, a surgeon at the hospital, had allegedly remarked, “Some people from Jamia Muslim University have arrived. I have spoken to the SP, and we will have to decide whether or not to allow them entry into the hospital.”
Meanwhile, a video had gone viral of Lokbhadra interviewing the sister of a deceased child, Rooplal, where she claimed that CM Yadav had dismissed her when she tried to talk to him about her brother’s death.

My brother was the first to lose his life…but his name has not appeared on any list, and no compensation has been given to us so far,” she told Lokbhadra.

Hardly a day goes by lately without news of AI agents autonomously hacking websites or AI tools being used by cybercriminals and scammers. But a recently patched vulnerability in the macOS version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT underscores the potential value to attackers of compromising AI software itself as these apps proliferate more and more.
The bug could have been exploited to essentially take over ChatGPT on a victim’s computer, giving an attacker access to all the chat logs and other data stored by the app, as well as interconnections like browser sessions. Discovered by researchers at the Objective-See Foundation, the vulnerability illustrates the deep system access and trust that AI platforms are afforded in order to work—and the target that this puts on their backs.
“Agents need a lot of access to do their job,” says Objective-See Foundation software analyst and longtime macOS researcher Patrick Wardle. “They are like the building manager who has access to the keys to all the rooms. So if they can be corrupted or subverted, that’s super problematic. It can mean that unprivileged code could then potentially have access to all the things.”
OpenAI publicly acknowledged the security flaw and fix in its system change log on September 25. “We continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster,” OpenAI spokesperson Shane Bauer told WIRED in a statement.
The ChatGPT macOS app includes multiple components that communicate with each other securely by checking for digital signatures. The idea is to confirm with these validity checks that both processes are OpenAI components and not outside, potentially malicious software making a request. And the system design goes so far as to require these signature checks at three layers of remove from the request, to ensure that malicious software isn’t somehow directing an OpenAI component to be a proxy and make a seemingly trusted request.
Objective-See Foundation researchers found, though, that there is a trusted component, a script interpreter, that would accept an untrusted script (or list of commands to run) and could then be manipulated to deliver this script into the main ChatGPT process. “They also check the parent and grandparent of that process, but the malicious script just spawns the script interpreter three times and then makes the request so it will satisfy the requirements,” Wardle says.
The vulnerability was “insanely trivial” to exploit, he adds, and his proof of concept only required about a dozen lines of code. In addition to accessing ChatGPT chat logs, the vulnerability could also be used to get ChatGPT to run commands for the attacker, such as accessing a browser or other sensitive applications, with the requests appearing as legitimate instructions issued by the OpenAI software.
Wardle will present analysis of a number of AI macOS application bugs at Objective by the Sea, an Apple-focused security conference in November.
He recently found a flaw, now patched, in the dictation feature of Meta’s new Muse AI assistant that could have been exploited by a local attacker to grab a mishandled authentication token and gain access to user data. And he says that he has already submitted a new vulnerability finding to OpenAI related to the integration between ChatGPT and the company’s new always-on Dots AI assistant. OpenAI is currently reviewing his report.
“AI companies are fixated on adding features right now,” Wardle says. “But as always, the more features, the broader the attack surface. So all of these companies need to be fully focused on security, and from what I can see, it still often seems like an afterthought.”

'He will never walk free': Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor
- Published
An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of his life" is winning hearts in India.
Trial court Judge Rajani Ranga's letter addresses the 10-year-old, who was sexually abused on 23rd July 2023 when she was seven, as "Dear child" and describes her as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".
The trial court gave the convict a life sentence, emphasising that he would remain in prison for "the remainder of his natural life" and also awarded the survivor a compensation of 1.05m rupees ($10,941; £8,274).
At the end of her order, Judge Ranga said she "must address the child victim - not in the formal language of a judgment but as a judge who has heard her voice, who has read her words, and who has been moved by her courage".
"When you said 'Jab tak uncle buddhe na ho jaaye, tab tak unhe jail mein hi rakha jaaye [Keep the 'uncle' in jail until he grows old], this court listened. And this court has answered your plea," she wrote to the child survivor.
"Today, this court has ordered that the man you called 'uncle' will never walk free again. He will live in a cage for the rest of his life. He will grow old in that cage. He will die in that cage. He will never be able to hurt you, or your little sister, or any other child, ever again," she added.
Calling her "the bravest little girl", the judge praised her "for coming to court, pointing out the man who hurt her and telling the truth".
"The man you called 'uncle' did a very bad thing to you. But you did not stay quiet. You told your mother. And because you had the courage to speak, he will never be able to hurt another child again.
"The court can promise you that he will never see the sun as a free man again."
Concluding her letter, the judge said the "court cannot give you back your childhood", but advised her to "now live your life. Go to school. Make friends. Laugh. Play. Dream. This court will always remember your courage".
Judge Ranga's letter is part of the order that was announced on 11 July, but as cases of child sexual assault are tried in special Pocso (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) courts, their judgments are never made public to protect the identities of the victims.
It came to light after it was reproduced recently in a Delhi high court order which rejected the convict's appeal for bail and suspension of sentence. The high court order named the convict, who is an adult, but gave no other details about him.
Describing Judge Ranga's letter as "a message of encouragement" to the child, the high court judges ordered the Delhi State Legal Authority to print out a copy and give it to the child along with the compensation money.
The emotional letter has moved many Indians who have shared it on social media, describing it as "a rarity" and "a ray of hope" and praising the judge.
Many have also expressed sorrow at the horrific nature of the crime where a child was sexually abused when she was just seven.
The judge's letter may be rare, but campaigners say the seven-year-old child's case is not a rarity - more than 69,000 Pocso cases were recorded in India in 2024 alone, according to government crime data, external.
And studies reveal that as in a majority of cases, abusers are known to the victims and are often trusted persons and care-givers, many cases are not even reported to the authorities.
Survivors say such abuse can scar them forever and affect their entire life.
In her order, Judge Ranga also addressed the issue of how such an assault can have a permanent impact on a child.
After "evaluating the nature of the crime, the depth of suffering, and the lifelong impact on the victim child", she said her order was "an attempt to heal and restore" the child.

Access to genomic testing and matched treatments remains profoundly unequal within and between countries, according to a new commission by The Lancet Oncology.
It has also identified substantial inequalities in cancer genetic testing research, reporting that only 2 per cent of biomarker-based cancer trials are conducted in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), compared to almost 81 per cent in high-income countries.
An international team of authors of the commission has warned of a "paradox of success" -- the rapid expansion of precision oncology has increased cost and complexity faster than the benefits it delivers at a population level.
Global spending on cancer medicines is estimated to have risen by around 75% over the last five years, reaching approximately USD 252 billion in 2024, and is projected to reach USD 441 billion by 2029, they have said.
The researchers analysed global data on clinical trials and genomic datasets, and conducted a survey of national cancer programmes.
The team estimated that seven to eight million (70-80 lakh) people with cancer worldwide need standard-of-care molecular testing every year.
However, the coverage remains far from universal, particularly in LMICs, it has said.
For example, an estimated 3.14 lakh women with ovarian cancer are eligible for BRCA -- the breast cancer gene -- testing annually, yet around half do not receive it, a gap driven largely by a low testing coverage in LMICs, the researchers have said.
To help health systems respond, the commission has proposed a framework for prioritising which molecular tests and matched therapies to implement, alongside a system-readiness assessment tool.
It has also set out a workforce-competency framework and principles for responsible data-sharing.
The commission has also put forth 10 core recommendations for an equitable, effective and responsible integration of precision oncology into cancer control and universal health coverage, and a phased implementation roadmap.

The Jammu and Kashmir Agriculture Production Department has received a proposal seeking transfer of more than 1,500 kanals of its land at Allowpora in Shopian to SKUAST-K for establishing a Centre of Excellence, with the proposal subsequently forwarded to the University for examination.
The issue was raised by MLA Shopian Shabir Ahmad Kullay through an Un-Starred Question in the Legislative Assembly, asking whether the government had received a proposal for utilisation/transfer of more than 1,100 kanals of land belonging to the Allowpora Seed Farm to SKUAST-K for establishment of a Centre of Excellence in Horticulture, including production of quality planting material, seed multiplication and seed development.
In its written reply, the Agriculture Production Department said it had received a D.O. communication from Kullay dated July 24, 2026, regarding the transfer of more than 1,500 kanals of Agriculture Department land at Allowpora to SKUAST-K for establishment of a Centre of Excellence for production of quality planting material.
“The proposal was received in the Agriculture Production Department and was forwarded to SKUAST-K for examination,” said the department.
According to the reply, SKUAST-K, in its communication dated August 19, 2026, proposed establishment of a Centre of Excellence for certified disease-free planting material, elite clonal rootstock multiplication and breeder/foundation seed production, besides diploma and short-term certificate courses, demonstration orchards, mother blocks, polyhouses and farmer-training facilities.
SKUAST-K has also proposed developing Allowpora as a regional scientific and skill hub for horticulture in South Kashmir, according to the reply.
However, in response to a separate question on whether a substantial portion of the farm was lying vacant or underutilised, the department said the 64.885-hectare farm was largely being utilised.
Of the total area, 58.90 hectares are presently being utilised for seed multiplication activities involving maize, oats, pulses, potato and floriculture seedlings, it said.
The department further said 20 hectares had been identified for establishment of a Saffron Corm Nursery, for which Rs 4.03 crore had been approved by the Government of India under PM-RKVY.
A Centre of Excellence for Precision Farming is also being established under the Capex Budget/SASCI scheme during the current financial year, with an allocation of Rs 4.96 crore, the reply said.
“In view of the above, it is not a fact that a substantial portion of the Seed Multiplication Farm, Allowpora is lying vacant or underutilized,” the department stated.
On whether the land would subsequently be transferred to SKUAST-K, the department said that since the land was already being utilised for various ongoing departmental activities, including seed multiplication, establishment of a Saffron Corm Nursery and a Centre of Excellence for Precision Farming, “transfer of the Allowpora Seed Farm land to SKUAST-K for the proposed purpose is not under consideration.”

The Best E-Readers That Aren’t a Kindle
Featured in this article
There are no fewer than 10 e-readers in my house at any given time, and I wouldn't have it any other way.
While nothing replaces the feel of a physical book, I usually reach for one of my e-readers as part of my nighttime routine. To me, these tablets are the easiest way to read because they grant immediate access to whatever is in my TBR pile at a given time. Whether it's a library book through the Libby app or a series I'm buying up because I can't wait any longer for a copy to be available, whatever I want to read, I can access it immediately on my e-reader.
It’s also convenient that e-readers (short for “ebook readers”) can store thousands of books at a time. These slim devices use E Ink screens to give text a paperlike appearance. They’re also designed to strain your eyes less than other digital devices, like your phone or computer screen.
And while many strongly associate Kindle with e-reader, you don't have to turn to Amazon for the best device. In fact, my all-around favorite isn't a Kindle at all, and there are plenty of other models to shop from that let you steer clear of the tech behemoth and its recent price increases. These are all my favorite e-readers that won't require you to support Amazon to enjoy the experience.
Updated October 2026: I've moved all Kindle recommendations (and details about the newly announced Kindles) out of our top picks to focus entirely on non-Amazon e-readers. There are also new sections for what I'm testing next and e-reader accessories compatible with my picks.

Honorable Mentions
Below, find a few more e-readers I like but don't necessarily love as much as my top picks.
Boox Go 7 ($270) and Boox Go Color 7 ($290): Boox is known for its wide range of e-paper tablets, including the Boox Go 6 (Gen II) I recommend above. If you're looking for something a little larger with a similar Android-based experience, the Go 7 and Go Color 7 are both solid choices. There are page-turner buttons, and it's a nice square shape that's easy to hold and use. If you, like me, don't use color features a ton, it's worth saving the extra money on the black-and-white model. Regardless, it's great that the price difference between the two models isn't steep.
Boox Palma 2 for $250: This is a fun, pocket-sized device, with fingerprint recognition, a faster CPU, and a newer version of Android than previous models. Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So loved using it with the Kindle app, but she wishes it cost less. Boox recently announced the Palma 3 is coming out (though it doesn't have a confirmed launch date) which explains why it's been unavailable for so long. The Palma 3 is next on my testing list, but if you want a similar device you can purchase now, the Boox Palma 2 Pro ($400) is available with a higher price tag, but color screen.
Nook GlowLight 4 Plus for $200: The 4 Plus is the only waterproof Nook in the lineup, and it has the biggest screen at 7.8 inches, along with 32 GB of storage. It also has physical page-turn buttons and a headphone jack for listening to audiobooks (you can also connect wireless earbuds via Bluetooth). Unfortunately, it was often slower than my Kindle and tended to freeze. While the large library has cheap and even free ebooks, it's not as good of a selection as Kindle Unlimited. The process of getting a book from the library on a Nook is also frustrating. You'll need to download either Adobe Digital Editions or Android File Transfer before physically connecting the device to your computer and then transferring the files.
Nook 9-inch Lenovo Tablet for $150: If you mainly read cookbooks or other color-intensive materials, and you want a dedicated reader, you might want to consider this affordable tablet from Nook and Lenovo, which has the Nook app built in. It's a tablet rather than an e-paper device like the rest of the gadgets in this guide, so you'll lose the E Ink screen and the distraction-free nature of an e-reader. You can at least turn off notifications while in certain apps, which I recommend doing for the Nook app. It uses Android 13 OS, and it's not built for heavy work, like video or photo editing.
Xteink X4 for $69 and X3 for $69: These are similar to the Xteink X4 Pro above when it comes to the app and basic capabilities, but you'll lose out on the touchscreen, home button, and front light. Instead, there are more buttons, providing a Tamagotchi-like experience as you tap them to go back and forth between menus and pages of your reading material. The X3 is super small, with just a 3.7-inch screen that fits on the back of my iPhone 16 Pro, and it has stronger magnets to put itself into place. But the standard X4 is more comfortable to read on than the X3 since it's larger (and won't require quite as many page turns, though it'll still need a lot) with a 4.3-inch screen, like the X4 Pro above.
What I’m Testing Next
There have been several new e-readers announced, mainly new models from Boox like the Palma 3 and Picco, that I'll be reading my latest books on this fall, which will include R.F. Kuang's Babel and the latest ACOTAR book, along with an alarmingly long list of suspended holds in my Libby app that I really need to work on. Here's what I'll be testing next:
Boox Palma 3 for $320: Boox's popular Palma devices are made to be mobile e-paper screens, and are a popular choice as a smaller e-reader. The new Palma 3 has been announced after months of the Palma 2 being out of stock, and it promises a 6.13-inch screen, dual-tone front light, a rear camera, dual microphones, and a customizable smart button. There's no timeline yet for its launch, but I'm hoping we see it available before the end of the year.
Boox Picco for $100: This miniature e-reader will have a tiny 3.97-inch screen and be Boox's smallest e-reader to date. The Boox Picco isn't the smallest e-reader ever—Xteink still holds that crown—but promises a different experience to Boox's other e-readers and e-paper devices by focusing on Boox's new Tiles app and productivity tools. Boox says it's the first of its Tiles ecosystem, so I'm keeping an eye out for more launches within that line. The Picco is currently available for preorder and is due to ship in October.
Boox Note Mini C for $550: When Boox announced the Palma 3, it also announced its new e-paper tablet, the Boox Note Air6 C, and a miniaturized version, the Boox Note Mini C. The Mini C has a smaller 8.52-inch screen that's more ideal for reading than the larger tablet, and I'm curious how it compares to both the Palma 3 and the Boox Go line.
The 2026 Kindles: Amazon has announced new versions of all three of its main e-readers, with a 2026 version of Kindle ($150), Kindle Paperwhite ($200), and Kindle Colorsoft ($290) coming out this fall, plus a Kids version ($180+) of each of these new models. There are now aluminum-backed versions of all three, though the Paperwhite and Colorsoft have it as part of the higher-end Signature Edition that comes with a few more features. I'll be testing and will add my top pick to this guide for reference, but this guide will focus more on non-Kindle e-readers going forward.
What If I Want a Kindle?
Maybe you've read this guide and decided a Kindle is best for you. That's fine! Kindle is my longest-used ecosystem and it's plenty convenient, especially if you already have ebooks purchased through Amazon. While I have an entire guide dedicated to shopping for a Kindle, here's a quick overview of my top picks (and other models you might spot).
Also, Kindle does have new versions of the base Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, Kindle Colorsoft, and its Kids versions of each model coming out. You might want to wait and see if you prefer the newest versions to these, and I'll be testing them soon to see how they compare to past Kindles and other e-readers. Kindle also raised the prices of most of its e-readers at the end of August, and the new models match that pricing.
Kindle Colorsoft Signature for $320 and Kindle Colorsoft ($290): The Kindle Colorsoft Signature is Amazon's first Kindle with a color screen. I do like the Colorsoft if you read books with illustrations or heavily annotate your e-books, but the Kobo devices I recommend can do the same thing for cheaper.
Kindle Scribe (3rd Gen, 2025) for $500 and Kindle Scribe Colorsoft for $630: The latest Kindle Scribe arrived in December 2025 with a color version. It also has a new exterior design that does away with the single thicker side and standardizes bezels and frames across all sizes, and a lot of AI features. The older Kindle Scribe (2nd Gen) is still my preferred option if you want a Kindle e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.
Kindle Scribe Without Front Light for $430: This is the third and final installment of Amazon's latest generation of Kindle Scribes. It's similar to the third-gen Kindle Scribe above, but it removes the front light and wireless charging. If you want a cheaper Kindle Scribe, I still prefer the second-generation model, though you'll lose out on AI reading features and the ability to connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive.
Great E-Reader Accessories
Looking to jazz up your new e-reader? Here are some of my favorite accessories to pair with my favorite non-Kindle e-readers. It's a tougher buy to find—since Kindles are so popular, most cases and accessories are made with those models in mind, but there are options out there for the rest of the e-reader world, too. Here's what I've tested and liked for my e-readers.
FAQs
How Do You Get Ebooks?
Ebooks can be cheap, but as with regular books, the cost can add up if you're a big reader. To keep costs low, take advantage of your library card and check out ebooks instantly from the comfort of your home. We have a detailed guide that explains How to Get Free Kindle Books With Your Library Card, but the short version is that most libraries distribute books via OverDrive. You can access these books a few ways: through Kindle or directly from OverDrive with a Kobo, or you can download the Libby app. These ebooks are automatically removed from your device and returned to the library when they're due.
Each e-reader's own book service varies in quality. My favorite is Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month, which includes millions of titles, including audiobooks and magazines. Amazon's Prime Reading also offers a handful of free books every month, which is good to know if you already have a Prime account. You can even lend books to friends and family for a short while (or have them share a book with you). For more details on each option, check out our guide to the Best Ebook Subscription Services here.
What File Formats Do E-Readers Support?
The most widely used format is EPUB, which works natively with all the e-readers in this guide except for Kindle—technically. You can still upload EPUB files to your Kindle, but you'll have to use the “Send to Kindle” feature (through Amazon, your email, or the Kindle app) to convert it to Amazon's proprietary format called AZW. (Newer Kindles support AZW3 and KFX, specifically). Other formats that will work with these e-readers include PDF, TXT, HTML, DOC, and DOCX.
Can I Install Apps on an E-Reader?
Kindle, Kobo, and Nook all use proprietary operating systems that don't allow you to install third-party apps. The Boox, on the other hand, runs Android (mainly Android 11 and newer). That means you can use it to download any apps available in the Google Play Store or side-load apps from your computer.
Do You Need an E-Reader? What About a Phone or Tablet?
You don't have to buy a separate device to read ebooks. Smartphones and tablets are perfect for this purpose. You can use Amazon's Kindle app to read ebooks (iOS, Android) and download OverDrive's Libby app (iOS, Android) for library-book access. However, the E Ink screens found in e-readers are just nicer to look at. I also like that these devices are one-trick ponies; there are no distracting notifications or social media feeds ripe for doomscrolling.
If you'd still rather have one smart device you can use for reading and other purposes, take a look at our Best Tablets and Best iPads guides for recommendations.
What About a Digital Notebook?
I've tried just about every digital notebook on the market; these devices are designed for handwritten notes on an E Ink screen. E-readers with that capability usually still prioritize reading, though there are plenty of models I like that can do both. The Kobo Libra Colour is my favorite option for annotating books, and it can double as a small digital notebook. If you want a larger option, check out my full guide to every digital notebook I've tested.
How Do I Test E-Readers?
The most important step I take when testing e-readers is to read on them! I spend hours reading books acquired in a variety of formats, including books I purchased directly from each brand's store, downloaded from local libraries via OverDrive/Libby, and PDFs acquired for free from God knows where.
In the process, I evaluate battery life, brightness, performance lag, screen responsiveness, and text sharpness. I check for extra tools, like whether the tablet in question accommodates accessories like a stylus. I also note features like waterproofing, annotation capability, and access to exclusive subscription services.

ASUS ProArt PZ14 Design and Build: Lightweight and practical, but the design is an acquired taste
ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a tablet-first Windows PC. The keyboard detaches completely from the tablet, and all components, including the processor, sit on the back of the display.
As a result, it carries all the weight. ASUS includes a magnetic case in the box that you can attach to the back of the tablet to use as a stand and to hold the ASUS Pen 3.0. I wouldn’t recommend attaching it without the case because, while you’re holding the tablet, the magnets are not strong, and it can easily fall off, which it did. But hopefully, thanks to the build, it survived accidental falls.
Thanks to the matte finish, the back of the tablet isn’t a fingerprint magnet either, but stains are visible if you look at it a certain way, and they wipe off easily with any standard cloth.
An ASUS design choice on the back can be a hit or a miss depending on your perception. Right off the bat, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 doesn’t look like a tablet. It felt like a very niche tablet designed for a specific purpose. It has a single rear camera. Thankfully, there is no bump, and it comes with a lot of stickers, which indicates it is more than just a tablet.
You get ProArt branding at the top in the center. Overall, the fit and finish are solid, but the looks can be hit or miss based on your perception. I wish it looked more like a tablet.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with dual speakers, with one on each side The power button is on the top in landscape and on the right in portrait, which is convenient for landscape use but less convenient in portrait.
And you can find the volume-down and volume-up keys on the right as well, making it easy to control with your right hand. The SD Express 7.0 card reader and two USB4 Type-C ports are on the left side.
The look changes entirely from the front. It comes with a 14-inch 3K OLED display with a 144Hz refresh rate and minimal bezels, similar to the iPad Pro, but wider overall. At the top, you get an 8MP IR front camera with no privacy shutter.
The tablet weighs just 790 grams, making it lightweight and easy to use, but the larger display is hard to hold for long periods when using it as a tablet. The tablet has rounded corners on the back, which make it easy to hold for long periods, and the textured finish on the front half provides better grip. The matte finish makes it less slippery.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 also has an IP52 rating. ASUS officially claims that it is tested to MIL-STD-810Hstandards . So you have the military standard, but don’t drop-test it like other laptops.
When I first held the ASUS ProArt PZ14, the back finish felt like plastic. However, ASUS claims the chassis uses an aluminum alloy. The sides feel very solid.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Display: A gorgeous 3K OLED made for creators
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 display is one of the best-looking, and if there is one reason to choose this tablet, it’s this display. Whether you are a business user, a graphic designer, or someone who wants to casually watch movies and play games, it delivers a great viewing experience.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with a 14-inch 3K OLED display. It comes with a 144Hz refresh rate for a smooth experience. The 14-inch display is a sweet spot. On your desk and used with the keyboard, it is a sweet spot and a perfect middle ground between the 13.6-inch and 15-inch laptops, but it feels very large in hand when you hold it and use it as a tablet.
The OLED display is one of the best I have seen on a tablet, matching premium, high-quality displays with 100% DCI-P3 color gamut and PANTONE validation. The blacks look deeper, and colors are represented very accurately, making it a good choice for designers and photographers who want to edit images accurately. The touch response is also fast, but Windows is the one to blame. It makes interactions less convenient, which I will cover more in the OS section.
The display also supports a stylus. ASUS includes the ASUS Pen 3.0 out of the box. Writing and drawing on the display feels faster and more fluid. But because of the glass finish, it feels slippery while taking notes. You can apply a matte-finish screen protector for a better typing and note-taking experience on this tablet. After the iPad Pro, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 provided the best note-taking experience, even better than the Apple Pencil in some cases.
ASUS, being extra generous, added the pencil-scribble sound while taking notes. Well, thank you, ASUS, for looking at those tiny details to enhance the user experience. But it sounds so artificial.
Next, this 16:10 aspect ratio is perfect for watching content. I watched three episodes of Better Call Saul (season 4) on Netflix, and the experience was better on the ASUS ProArt PZ14 than on my iPad Pro.
With 3K resolution and 243 pixels per inch, it is also one of the sharper displays. It looks sharp even when you zoom in on minor editing details.
However, if you often read web pages, blogs, or docs on this tablet, while it looks fine when using it in laptop mode, as soon as you pick it up and use it as a tablet, you are holding a massive tablet, and 16:10 feels very wide when you put it close to your eyes, which means you need to move your head to read the text. Also, portrait mode isn’t appealing either, with that 14-inch massive screen making it hard to read and scroll. With this large form factor, using it with a single hand is almost impossible. You can try if you want.
Overall, the display is one of the ASUS ProArt PZ14’s biggest strengths. Whether you’re watching content, editing, or designing, everything looks incredible on this massive screen.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Keyboard and Trackpad: Laptop-like typing, but better suited for a desk
ASUS also provides a keyboard out of the box. Unlike with the iPads, which you need to buy separately and are also expensive. Fortunately, the typing experience is as good as on thin-and-light laptops. However, if you’re used to mechanical keyboards or longer key travel, you might find it hard to type at first, but you can eventually get used to it.
Also, there are a few things that you need to know: the keyboard completely detaches from the tablet, which means it doesn’t have a hinge that holds the display and keyboard together. A small magnetic attachment on the bottom of the tablet connects to the keyboard.
You can just hover the tablet over the keyboard, and it attaches magnetically. However, the magnet isn’t as strong, so it can also detach easily. And since there is no strong hinge holding the keyboard and tablet together, you cannot place it on your lap and type on uneven surfaces, where the tablet takes the full weight and could tip back.
Fortunately, ASUS also included a full touchpad, and again, it’s almost like using the touchpad on a regular thin-and-light laptop. The speakers are very loud. They have rich sound. There is no headphone jack.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Specs and Performance: Snapdragon X2 Elite delivers plenty of power
Under the hood, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 runs on the Snapdragon X2 Elite X2E-88-100 processor. My variant has 32GB of LPDDR5X RAM and a 1TB M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD. That’s a large configuration by current standards.
Qualcomm is trying too hard to become a name for its PC processors after it conquered Android phones. The processor offers very solid performance. Tasks feel faster, and it compares with some of the best in the industry right now, including the Intel Core Ultra 7 series and Ryzen AI Max+, among others. In comparison, in Geekbench single- and multicore scores, Snapdragon X2 Elite has produced very good numbers.
You can see the benchmarks of the ASUS ProART PZ14 from third-party testers.
The tablet also offers a dedicated performance mode that provides extra power when needed. This results in smooth day-to-day performance; whether it’s opening apps, touch interactions, gaming, or uploading files, everything feels smoother on this tablet
The built-in SD Express 7.0 card reader delivers strong sequential read and write rates, including 730 MB/s sequential read speeds. So if you are a creator who copies videos and files to and from the tablet, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 won’t consume your time.
However, while the processor is solid in CPU performance, the GPU is still weaker on Snapdragon processors, and the same is true of the Snapdragon X2 Elite. It comes with an integrated Qualcomm Adreno GPU. That performs decently; however, it’s not as good as Radeon or Intel Arc GPUs.
Because of this, it might not excel at higher-end applications or even gaming. It can offer decent performance, but not top-tier.
While the GPU might not be the most powerful, the NPU performance is significantly better. The Snapdragon X2 Elite includes a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU rated up to 80 TOPS. This lets you offload a few AI tasks locally for better performance. For instance, if you are a creator, you can run AI models locally.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 also comes with a fan. Under load, the tablet tends to get a bit warmer, and the fan kicks in.
Overall performance is impressive for such a thin and light device. Daily use, such as browsing the web, watching movies and shows, and running a few high-end software applications, feels faster and handles every task without breaking a sweat.
Moreover, while compatibility with popular ARM apps on Windows has improved over the years since Qualcomm announced Snapdragon X Elite, some older programs and plug-ins still aren’t natively compatible with Windows on ARM, and some run via x86 emulation.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Battery Life: Easily lasts an entire workday
The battery life is incredible on this tablet, and Windows on ARM has already proved it. The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with a 75Wh four-cell lithium-ion battery. ASUS also offers a 68W USB-C charger in the box.
Even in performance and non-performance modes, battery life stays consistent. On average, I got around 12 to 14 hours of battery life with light to medium use and about 10-11 hours with heavy use, including gaming. With light use, just using the browser, I even got two days of battery life.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Windows 11 Experience: Full desktop software, but a poor tablet interface
Now let’s address the elephant in the room: Windows 11. I would say having Windows 11 is both the biggest strength and also the biggest weakness of this tablet. The ASUS ProArt PZ14 ships with Windows 11 or Windows 11 Pro out of the box, depending on the configuration. My unit comes with Windows 11 Home.
No matter which version you are on, Windows 11 isn’t optimized for the touch interface. In Windows 11 touch mode, it feels like a desktop and has very small buttons, menus, and toolbars.
If you primarily want to use the ASUS ProArt PZ14 as a tablet, and you’re used to iPad Pro-type interaction, you will definitely find it hard to use day-to-day. Fortunately, using the pen minimizes this. However, if you primarily use your hands, keep that in mind.
Also, this tablet has a core Windows problem. The biggest problem is the annoying Windows updates. They are still an issue even after Microsoft promised to reduce those interruptions. Unfortunately, I haven’t been able to set up the tablet from scratch because it’s a pre-owned unit, and someone else has already set it up for me, so I was saved from dealing with lengthy setup processes.
Another big limitation of Windows running on ARM is limited app support. While app support has improved significantly since I first reviewed the Snapdragon X Elite laptop, most popular applications are now natively available on Windows on ARM, but a few legacy applications still use Prism emulation, which affects performance and misses core features. However, if you mainly want to use it as a creator tablet, most creator apps are natively available on Windows, and a few games are also natively supported on Windows on ARM.
But the biggest advantage is that, since it runs on Windows, you can run full desktop-level software without any limitations. You can multitask with multiple windows. If you want better multitasking and portability at the same time, this is something you should get.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Ports and Connectivity: USB4 and SD Express are useful, but some ports are missing
Despite its tablet form factor, ASUS has included decent port support on the ASUS ProArt PZ14. It comes with two USB 4.0 Gen 3 Type-C ports that support up to 40 Gbps, which can be used to connect external SSDs, docks, and even an external monitor.
It also includes an SD Express 7.0 card reader, which is excellent for transferring video and photos from your cameras. There’s no HDMI port, which I miss, but you can easily work around it with external peripherals. The camera quality is also good, much better than the webcam quality on other ASUS laptops I have tested. The rear camera is also decent in good lighting, which you can use to scan documents quickly. The tablet also supports Wi-Fi 7 or Bluetooth 6.0.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Verdict: A powerful Windows tablet for creators on the go
So, that is everything that you need to know about ASUS ProArt PZ14. With its excellent display, tablet-first design, portability, battery life, and solid performance, it is a great pick for anyone who wants a powerful tablet on the go.
The 3K OLED display also makes it a great option for entertainment whenever you want to watch content or even play games. Overall, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a great option for a creator-first experience and for anyone who values portability and wants an all-in-one tablet that can replace a conventional laptop and a tablet at home. However, the tablet costs Rs 2,69,990 for 32GB LPDDR5X RAM. It is expensive.

27-yr-old doctor found dead in Hyderabad service apartment, cops suspect foul play as partner missing for two days
The deceased, a paediatrician who recently completed her postgraduate medical training in Warangal 150km from Hyderabad.
A 27-year-old doctor was found dead under suspicious circumstances in a service apartment in Hyderabad’s Hafeezpet area on Friday afternoon, three days after she checked in with a male friend, police said.
The deceased, a paediatrician who recently completed her postgraduate medical training in Warangal 150km away, was found on a bed in an advanced state of decomposition, Miyapur Circle Inspector N Jayaram told HT.
Cops suspect foul play
Police said they suspect foul play and are treating the case as a potential homicide.
Jayaram said the doctor reached Hyderabad from Warangal and checked into the private service apartment at Aditya Nagar three days ago.

Police discovered the body after the woman’s parents, alarmed that she was not answering her phone, requested the police to check on their daughter.
“Based on the complaint given by the parents, we traced the location and reached the service apartment. On checking the premises, we found the decomposed body of the woman on the bed under suspicious circumstances,” Jayaram said.
Male friend missing for two days
Preliminary inquiries indicated that her male friend hadn’t been seen in the area for the last two days. “We are making efforts to trace him and ascertain the circumstances that led to the doctor’s death,” the inspector said.

Her parents told the police that she had been in a relationship with the man since her undergraduate days in Mahabubnagar. The relationship continued when she joined the post-graduation course in Warangal.
“Investigations revealed that the doctor and her boyfriend had a dispute over a gold chain she had given to him. Three days ago, he had called her to Hyderabad to discuss the same and both checked into the service apartment, where the incident took place,” Jayaram said.
“We have sent the body of the doctor to Gandhi Hospital for a post-mortem examination. We shall be able to know the exact cause of the death after the autopsy. Investigation is on,” the inspector said.

Illinois catering business ordered to shut down after high school football team got sick before homecoming
The unlicensed caterer served a taco bar with fajita chicken, seasoned taco beef, cheese, flour taco shells, cheesy pepper beans, cilantro corn rice and pico de gallo or salsa

Illinois health officials shut down an unlicensed, home-based caterer after a high school football team dinner sickened at least 45 people and forced the school to postpone its homecoming game.
The Rock Island High School football team’s Sept. 24 dinner was held around 5:30 p.m. in the school cafeteria, where about 75 players, coaches and parents were served a taco bar catered by Sunshine and Spice. The Moline-based home operation is about 10 minutes from Rock Island, local health officials confirmed to KWQC.
The menu included fajita chicken, seasoned taco beef, cheese, flour taco shells, cheesy pepper beans, cilantro corn rice and pico de gallo or salsa.
By about 11 p.m., 23 players, five coaches and three parents were experiencing vomiting and diarrhea, football team trainer Kyle Hoffmann reported to Rock Island City Health Inspector Andy Swartz the following afternoon, the news outlet reports.
At least 45 people total eventually reported illness. None required hospitalization, though one player saw a doctor. Most recovered within 24 hours.
The high school postponed its homecoming game until all affected players had been symptom-free for at least 24 hours, as advised by the Rock Island County Health Department and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, per KWQC.
During the investigation, Swartz met with Sunshine and Spice owner Joshua Harris and found that the home-based catering operation was not licensed or food-safety certified. Swartz ordered the business to stop operating immediately and gave Harris information on how to obtain the required licenses, according to the news outlet.
Harris told Swartz that the meal’s ingredients were purchased from Walmart in Moline, Spotted Apron in Geneseo and farmers markets in Davenport and Coal Valley.
Harris said in a statement to KWQC that Sunshine and Spice was sorry for what happened and denied intentionally providing unsafe food.
“First, Sunshine and Spice wants to sincerely apologize and send even more prayers to anyone affected by last week's Rock Island Football Team Meal. We provided a taco bar-style potluck before the team was dismissed to prepare for their Homecoming Game,” Harris said.
He further explained how he prepared the food.
“All of the food purchased from Walmart on Wednesday Night was fully cooked (beef, chicken, rice). We put all of the leftovers in plastic bags provided by the team parents for anyone to take home. We have cooked for numerous parents of the team/school in the past and have no reason EVER to provide a sub-standard meal or purposely attempt any tampering shenanigans.”
Harris continued, “We are saddened by this whole situation. We have been working side by side with the Rock Island County Health Department and Rock Island City/County Law Enforcement Agencies to be a part of their continuing investigations. Again, we want to extend our deepest apologies and continued prayers to those affected.”
Health officials said the investigation remains ongoing and that leftover food from the dinner was seized for testing.
Swartz worked with county health officials and the Illinois Department of Public Health to survey people who became sick. According to the results, obtained by KWQC, the most commonly consumed items were cilantro corn rice, fajita chicken, cheese and flour taco shells:
- 92 percent consumed cilantro corn rice
- 88 percent consumed fajita chicken
- 88 percent consumed cheese
- 88 percent consumed flour taco shells
- 83 percent consumed seasoned taco beef
- 58 percent consumed cheesy pepper beans
- 58 percent consumed pico/salsa
Rock Island lost their Friday game to East Moline United Football, making their 2026 record 0-7.
