This is one of the cheapest ways to add Dolby Atmos to your TV
Immersive sound doesn’t have to break the bank.
If you're a cinephile or sports fanatic, watching a movie or live game at home always feels lackluster compared to experiencing it in a theater or stadium, partly because of your TV's subpar built-in speakers. Although it's hard to replicate the true feeling of either, Dolby Atmos does a solid job of adding more immersion to your at-home watch party, and it doesn't have to cost you an arm and a leg.
While LG, Sony, Hisense and several other brands manufacture TVs with integrated speaker arrays that support Dolby Atmos, they may not fit everyone's budget or appease audiophiles. So, unless you're just a passive streamer who doesn't care about sound and simply likes to have something playing in the background, it's always a good idea to invest in some solid speakers. In most cases, a soundbar will do the trick.
Instead of spending thousands on a multi-speaker setup, choosing a wallet-friendly soundbar lets you get a taste of Dolby Atmos for a fraction of the price.
Why are some TV speakers so disappointing?
Nowadays, with thin designs being the industry standard, most TV speakers are forced to remain compact and either downward- or rear-facing, meaning your wall, media stand or floor (if the TV is mounted) absorbs the sound before it ever reaches your ears. Knowing modern TVs are barely thicker than a smartphone, manufacturers simply lack the physical space required for the premium drivers or resonance cabinets needed to produce truly dynamic audio.
This typical design is a major bottleneck, stripping away the height channels and depth essential for genuine spatial audio. This leaves you with flat acoustics, muddy dialogue and underwhelming bass. This is especially noticeable if you like streaming music on your TV, as it dampens vocal clarity and can even make your favorite song sound flat-out wrong.
On the other hand, even some top-of-the-line TVs with internal Dolby Atmos support struggle to project sound forward into your room, causing dimensional audio cues to scatter in the wrong directions. Without specialized upward- or side-firing drivers, many of those sound effects will get lost.
Immerse yourself with a soundbar
Depending on the brand, an Atmos-compatible soundbar will typically cost much less than a full home theater setup, but it will come with some major trade-offs.
For instance, many budget models rely on virtualized Dolby Atmos rather than genuine up-firing speakers, meaning they depend on special sound-coding to mimic overhead speakers. While the level of immersion is virtually incomparable to actual upward-firing drivers, it still offers a clear upgrade over most internal TV speakers.
Compatible options that rely on virtual processing, including soundbars from Amazon, TCL or even more dependable names like LG, don't have the required height channels to fully take advantage of Dolby Atmos, but some of these will run you under $200. Before buying any of these affordable soundbars, make sure your TV supports Dolby Atmos passthrough. In case it doesn't, an affordable 4K streaming device like the Roku Express 4K+ or Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K will do the job without breaking the bank.

Ai+ Smartphone has launched the Nova 2 Power 5G, the latest addition to its Nova 2 series, combining a dual-tone design with a 7,000mAh battery and 5G connectivity.
A statement issued here said that the smartphone made its debut at a fashion show in New Delhi, where it was showcased alongside contemporary athleisure designs by Just Billi by Rashmi Chhabra. The company said the launch was aimed at positioning the device at the intersection of technology, fashion and personal expression.
The Nova 2 Power features a 6.75-inch HD+ punch-hole IPS display with a 120Hz refresh rate and is powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 7100 processor. It comes with 6GB+128GB and 8GB+128GB memory configurations, with storage expandable through microSD.
For photography, the device features a 48MP AI primary camera, an 8MP ultra-wide camera and a 13MP front camera. The smartphone packs a 7,000mAh battery with 33W fast charging. It also carries an IP65 rating and supports dual 5G SIM, Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.4.
The Nova 2 Power is available in Blue Gold Fusion and Blue Fusion colour variants, with additional colours listed by the company including Ocean Green, Deep Purple and Midnight Black.
Madhav Sheth, CEO of NxtQuantum Shift Technologies, said the smartphone was designed to combine expressive design with performance and endurance.
The Nova 2 Power 5G will be available on Flipkart from September 24, with prices starting at Rs 15,999, including bank offers.

Drone maker ideaForge Technology has received a GST demand and penalty order totalling ₹109.2 Cr over alleged tax underpayment on drone sales. The order comprises a tax demand of ₹54.6 Cr and an equal penalty. In an exchange filing, ideaForge said it received the order from the Additional Commissioner of CGST and Central Excise, Belapur, yesterday. It covers the period between January 2022 and March 2024. The tax authority alleged that ideaForge incorrectly paid GST at 5%, resulting in a shortfall of 13 percentage points. ideaForge said it had submitted its response to the show cause-cum-demand notice. It also pointed out that the government clarified in 2025 that the GST rate applicable to drones is 5%. The company said it would appeal the order after consulting its tax advisers and expects a favourable outcome. It does not anticipate any immediate material impact on its financials, operations, or other activities while the matter remains unresolved. The tax dispute comes after ideaForge reported a net loss of ₹2.3 Cr in Q1 FY27, compared with a net profit of ₹61 Cr in Q4 FY26. However, the loss narrowed over 90% from ₹23.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Its operating revenue rose to ₹68.6 Cr from ₹12.8 Cr during the same period, although it declined 51% sequentially from ₹141 Cr. ideaForge started FY27 with an order book of more than ₹300 Cr and added to its growth pipeline during the June quarter. The company raised ₹500 Cr through a QIP in July, with domestic and international institutional investors participating in the issue. It also received a government LoI for financial assistance of up to ₹151 Cr under the RDI Scheme to develop YETI, its middle-mile logistics platform. Shares of ideaForge ended yesterday’s trading session 0.13% higher at ₹734.30 apiece on the BSE. With the GST notice, ideaForge has joined other new-age tech companies facing tax demands. In June, Zomato and Blinkit parent Eternal received a ₹9.63 Cr GST demand from Andhra Pradesh authorities over alleged short payment of output tax, with interest and penalty also applicable. The same month, coworking company Awfis received a GST show cause notice involving about ₹7.1 Cr over alleged discrepancies in its FY23 filings.

Former India opener Virender Sehwag’s son Aryavir has been appointed captain of Delhi men’s Under-19 squad for the Vinoo Mankad Trophy, the Delhi & District Cricket Association announced on Saturday.
The 16-member team was selected during a meeting of the Junior Men’s Selection Committee. The competition will be held in Visakhapatnam from October 8.
Aryavir’s first India Under-19 assignment was against Australia last month. He scored 28 in the first game, was run out for 47 in the second and got another start in the third before falling for 34.
The 18-year-old got a brief taste of senior-level cricket earlier this year, playing two matches for West Delhi Lions in the Delhi Premier League and scoring 24 runs.

Badnawar (Madhya Pradesh): A speeding trailer struck a motorcycle from behind at the Pitgara village intersection on the Lebad-Nayagaon four-lane highway at 7 am on Saturday, killing a couple and their 13-year-old daughter on the spot and critically injuring their younger daughter. The trailer driver fled.
The intersection is a short distance from Badi Chaupati. The motorcycle got lodged in the trailer and was dragged about 50 metres before detaching. The impact badly mangled the bodies.
The deceased were identified as Rahul Singh Bhati (35), his wife Pooja (30) and daughter Suman (14). Younger daughter Shivani (12) was given first aid at the Civil Hospital and referred to Ratlam in critical condition.
The family was heading to Dhamana village to sow garlic, hoping for a good harvest. The couple also has a son named Dilkhush, who was at home
Angered villagers from the victims' village and nearby areas blocked the highway. SDM Priyanka Mimrot, SDOP Arvind Singh Tomar, SHO Amit Singh Kushwaha and tehsildar Suresh Nagar arrived with police and tried to persuade the crowd, but it refused to relent.
The protesters demanded speed breakers at the intersection and adequate compensation for the families.
The blockade lasted until 10 am, with the bodies remaining at the scene and vehicle queues stretching over seven kilometres on both sides.
Villagers collected about Rs 50,000 for the last rites and handed it to the family and officials assured them appropriate action would be taken. The bodies were then sent to the Civil Hospital for post-mortem.
Meanwhile, reports said the trailer had been intercepted at the Bilpank toll plaza, after which the blockade was lifted. Traffic took considerable time to normalise.

'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.
And with the World Championships in Beijing next year and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Korir believes there is another chapter to write.
"I know I'm a champion in life, because conquering fistula alone is being a champion.
"Now I'm looking forward to be a champion in sport."

The transport ministry ordered Tokai Kisen on Friday to suspend some of its vessels following multiple law violations, including operating vessels under the influence of alcohol.
This is the first time a ship suspension order has been issued under the marine transportation law.
Between January and June this year, the ministry conducted an extraordinary inspection of the company and found 13 cases of violations of the law. In August, the ministry imposed administrative penalties, including an order to dismiss officials in charge of safety and ship operation management.
According to the ministry, on New Year’s Day this year, crew members of two large passenger ships, including their captains, drank alcohol on board and went on duty without taking an alcohol test.
Within the company, drinking on New Year’s Day has become a custom believed to have started at least 30 years ago.
The ministry also deemed the company’s internal inspection system ineffective. In April, a jet ship crew member falsified an alcohol test result.
On Friday, Tokai Kisen was ordered to suspend one large passenger ship and two jet ships for 20 days from Oct. 9.
At a news conference on the day, transport minister Tatsunori Ibayashi urged the company to “squarely face its responsibility and work to prevent a recurrence, with a determination to renew its corporate culture.”

South Australia's 2026 harvest begins as timely rain delivers for the state
In short:
Farmers on South Australia's west coast have delivered the first load of grain for the season.
Primary Industries and Regions SA estimates 11,591,000 tonnes of grain will be harvested in South Australia in 2026/27.
Recent storm rain has delivered a boost for regions not yet harvesting.
The harvesters have started rolling in South Australia for one of the most eagerly anticipated crops in years.
Jesse Chandler was the first to front up to the silos at Thevenard with a load of Commodus barley on September 24.
He farms with his brother Harlee, father Milton and mother Tracey at Charra, halfway between Penong and Ceduna on South Australia's west coast.
Milton Chandler said it was the earliest they had ever harvested.
"I think it was 14 or 15 [2014 or 2015] we reaped the Friday before the AFL grand final and delivered on the Monday and this year we reaped on the Thursday so we're a day in front," Mr Chandler said.
"Earliest wheat we put in was on the 8th of April and I was nervous about that, but we've got quite a bit of heavy country and when it gets wet we've just got to go."
Mr Chandler has estimated they would harvest about 4 tonnes to the hectare with their barley.
"Normally even in our good years we'll have a period during the growing season when the crop will have a bit of a moisture check but this year it's almost been textbook."
"I've been farming here since 1980, and this is the best it's ever looked. It's great, and it's fantastic that it's statewide so it's a real positive for everyone.”
Crop estimate increased
Primary Industries and Regions SA's (PIRSA) crop and pasture report has revised up the state's crop yield forecast again.
The September report found all regions of South Australia had average to above-average winter rainfall with August being the fourth wettest on record.
Disease pressure has increased under the wet conditions with rusts, powdery mildew, net blotch, black leg and sclerotinia reported across several regions.
Overall PIRSA now believes the area sown this year was 4,234,000 hectares and estimates 11,591,000 tonnes will be harvested.
Growers have said they will need every tonne to make up for low grain prices and high input costs.
"We did buy a little bit of diesel through seeding at $3.27; that hurt a little bit, that was a bit of a wake-up call," Mr Chandler said.
"Even though the [grain] prices aren't great hopefully we can [compensate] that with some big yields.
"Logistically it's going to be difficult to deal with it [the size of the crop], but what a great problem."
The September 24 delivery was not the earliest crop that has been harvested in South Australia.
Records show grain has been received as early as September 19 in the past.
Bunge director of industrial management Gavin Cavanagh said the bulk grain handler had been planning for harvest to be two to three weeks earlier than normal.
"We are expecting that we will receive more than we normally would in October given the good start the farmers had and the early plant on the back of those good opening rains,"
Mr Cavanagh said.
Bunge does a big recruitment drive each year for harvest, putting on an extra 1,500 jobs each year, including overseas workers.
Mr Cavanagh said the changes to visa requirements had not affected its ability to fill roles.
"It hasn't impacted us directly; the majority of travellers we recruit are already in the country.
"From our point of view, we're confident that we've got the right amount of people in the right locations to support our farmers in their delivery pattern."
Perfect timing for storms
With warm, dry weather in SA in recent weeks, the recent storms that delivered about 15 to 40 millimetres of rain across the state were very welcome.
Loxton grain grower Robin Schaefer said he thought he was going to get only a couple of millimetres but ended up tipping 17mm out of the gauge on Friday, October 2.
"It was a lovely surprise," Mr Schaefer said.
"Some of our very early barley is pretty close to going now so that won't benefit, but the majority, I'd say at least two thirds or more of our crop would still benefit".
With so much moisture early in the season the plants have put on a lot of vegetable matter.
"The lentils up here, the biomass is amazing, hopefully that will translate into grain but there's certainly lots of pods on them"
"It does vary a little bit from farm to farm with a number of drought years in a row and the price of fertiliser people couldn't put as much as they would have liked in a year like this to take advantage of it but we're thankful for what we've got.
"It's just wonderful compared to a drought and I think there will be some very tidy yields around right through the Mallee."

Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned
- Published
Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say.
The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region.
A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes.
"It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic.
He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT).
Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion.
He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters.
There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage.
The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment.
Meanwhile, Ethiopia's foreign ministry has said it is closing its embassy in neighbouring Eritrea and expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats "for involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security".
Earlier, in a BBC interview, Eritrea's government denied that it was backing the new rebel alliance.
- Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? 
  - Published5 days ago
- WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? 
  - Published3 days ago
Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
They both accuse each other of violating a 2022 peace deal that ended a brutal two-year civil war, which according to an Africa Union mediator is estimated to have cost 600,000 lives.
Last month, seven armed movements, including the TPLF and an Amhara militia known as Fano, formed an alliance with the stated aim of removing the government in Addis Ababa.
There is disagreement over which side started the latest fighting.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.
It is difficult to verify what is happening on the ground and access to the internet and the main telecoms service provider in Tigray have also been cut.
Within Tigray, the national army and a pro-government militia appear to be advancing towards the region's main city of Mekelle.
In the southern Tigrayan town of Alamata, a medic told the BBC on Wednesday that 52 civilians had died in three days of heavy fighting.
The TPLF is also reported to be fighting in neighbouring Afar region, a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.
A humanitarian source has estimated that tens of thousands have fled their homes in Afar, according to the AFP news agency.
Fighting around Lalibela in the Amhara region, a Unesco world heritage site where foreign tourists have been stranded for more than a week, has involved the national army and Fano fighters, now allied to the TPLF.
The government has accused neighbouring Eritrea of backing these groups.
One pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers were involved on the front lines.
But in a rare response to the BBC from Eritrea's government, Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel dismissed the allegations.
He accused Ethiopia's ruling Prosperity Party (PP) of seeking external scapegoats for the country's mounting challenges.
"The PP regime has made it a habit to apportion blame to its neighbours in order to deflect attention from the myriad internal conflicts that it is fomenting in various parts of the country," he told BBC Tigrinya.
Eritrea was a key ally of Ethiopia during the Tigray war, fighting against the TPLF.
But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports.
Ethiopia lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993.
Abiy has even hinted at taking the port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - by force as he sees direct access to the sea as important for Ethiopia's long-term future and economic prosperity.
As concerns over security mount in Ethiopia, the country's National Intelligence and Security Service (Niss) announced on Wednesday that it was imposing an indefinite ban on drone flights in Addis Ababa and surrounding areas.
The agency said it would not issue permits for drone operations and warned that legal action would be taken against anyone flying drones in restricted areas.
Niss said the measure was necessary to protect national leaders, critical infrastructure and major public events.

Football Leaks whistleblower Rui Pinto is set to lose his witness protection status in Portugal, his legal team said on Friday, days after an independent commission found Manchester City guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules.
Pinto, whose disclosures helped trigger scrutiny of Manchester City’s finances, entered Portugal’s witness protection programme in 2020 after agreeing to cooperate with authorities and provide files obtained through the Football Leaks operation.
“In a few days, without being heard beforehand, as required by law, he would lose the protected, confidential residence assigned to him and be forced to find new housing urgently, with no guarantee that police protection will continue,” Pinto’s legal team said in a statement posted on his X account.

“His situation is now critical. The threats against him are not merely theoretical; he was assaulted in Lisbon last April.”
Launched in 2015, Football Leaks published millions of confidential documents from the football industry, including transfer agreements, contracts and other deals involving clubs, players and agents.
Football Leaks’ data seen by Reuters showed how some of the richest and most prominent figures in soccer avoided tax by channelling earnings offshore.
Pinto was arrested in Hungary in 2019 before being extradited to Portugal, where he later cooperated with authorities and was placed under witness protection.
His lawyers said the programme would end on October 10 and argued the decision leaves him at heightened risk, noting legal proceedings stemming from the leaks remained ongoing, including the recent Manchester City case.
“If abruptly deprived of his protected housing and plunged into a state of extreme precariousness, Rui Pinto would be more vulnerable now than at any time since 2020,” the statement said.

A purported Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping (here & here) claims that the Rajasthan High Court has given a judgment that provides for six months of imprisonment and a ₹50,000 fine for any candidate who fails to secure at least 100 votes in the Sarpanch elections. Let us verify the authenticity of the claim made in this post.
Claim: A Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping claims the Rajasthan High Court has ordered a six-month jail term and a ₹50,000 fine for Sarpanch candidates securing under 100 votes.
Fact: The viral newspaper clipping is an AI-generated fake image. The Rajasthan High Court has given no such judgment, Dainik Jagran published no such report, and Indian electoral laws contain no provision imposing jail time or fines for low vote counts. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, an initial search confirmed that the Rajasthan High Court has not issued any such judgment regarding low vote counts in Panchayat elections. Additionally, we found no news reports published by Dainik Jagran corroborating this matter. Moreover, no such law, Court order, or judicial mandate exists under the Election Commission of India or Indian electoral statutes (such as the Representation of the People Act, 1951) penalising candidates with imprisonment or fines purely for receiving a low vote count. Under current election rules, the only major consequence for a poor electoral performance is the forfeiture of the security deposit, which applies if an unelected candidate fails to secure more than one-sixth of the valid votes polled.
Further, we ran the viral newspaper clipping through the OpenAI content detection tool, which confirmed that the clipping is an AI-generated image created using OpenAI tools. Earlier, we debunked a similarly fabricated clipping that falsely claimed a woman gave birth to puppies in the United States.
To sum it up, the viral newspaper clipping is a fabricated AI-generated image, and there is no legal provision or court order mandating jail time or fines for securing low votes in a Sarpanch election.

A magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Victoria in the early hours of Saturday morning, shaking Melbourne and waking people across the whole region.
Geoscience Australia said it detected an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8 at 2.01am near Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with the tremors felt across the city’s eastern suburbs.
Geoscience Australia said it had received thousands of reports from people who said they had felt the earthquake.
Posting on Facebook, Brian Morley in Narre Warren said “felt it and woke me up”, while Theresa Stevens said: “Shook our house in Garfield.”
Other posts indicated the quake had been felt in Preston, Heidelberg Heights, Venus Bay and many other parts of Melbourne.
The quake was estimated to have struck at about 10km below the Earth’s surface.
Victoria’s State Emergency Service said the earthquake was a “timely reminder” to remember the drill to follow during an earthquake and that was drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy piece of furniture and protect your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.
The Bureau of Meteorology said there was no tsunami threat from the quake.

Tamil Nadu is recording around 200 cases of dengue a day. Fresh cases are being reported in places including Chennai and its neighbouring districts and cities such as Coimbatore and Madurai.
Officials of the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine said the caseload remained steady and was not at outbreak proportions. A. Somasundaram, Director of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said cases had not risen exponentially, with the numbers remaining broadly steady. “We are seeing nearly 200 cases a day. The numbers are not doubling or tripling, which usually happens in an outbreak. Right now, there is a static trend in the number of dengue cases, and we are expecting the cases to decline soon,” he said.
Cases are being reported across cities including the Chennai belt (Tiruvallur and Kancheepuram), Coimbatore, and Madurai. This could partly be due to a “natural bias” with these areas having more hospitals and testing facilities, Dr. Somasundaram said.
“We have specifically instructed staff to increase the number of tests for dengue for better surveillance and patient management. This is so we don’t miss a case, and when samples are tested, we can identify pockets of cases or clusters, which are likely to bring about an outbreak,” he said. There are over 4,500 government and private laboratories in the State, he added.
Surveillance measures to identify Aedes mosquito breeding pools are continuing, but the number of pools detected has started to decline as a result of source reduction measures. The mosquito density is slowly coming down, the official said. About 25,000 Domestic Breeding Checkers (DBC) have been engaged across the State, with 20 persons covering one block.
Dr. Somasundaram said while preventive measures had been intensified, they had been holding daily monitoring meetings with District Health Officers via video conferencing. “We are analysing the case trend, whether increase or decrease or static, and number of laboratory tests conducted. We are also monitoring fever triaging, patient management, and discharge policy. Patients are being categorised as having mild, moderate, or severe symptoms and treated appropriately. Right now, the severity of infections is less. Fogging operations and source reduction measures, along with work taken up by DBCs, are being supervised. We are also looking at creating awareness among the public,” he said.
With October and November being crucial months, he said, there could be intermittent or heavy rain and people should ensure that their household environment is clean. “Avoid storing water unnecessarily. If you have too, keep containers closed properly,” he added.

The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.
The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.
Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.
When Ars Technica talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project, but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that Nvidia still actively manufactures the Shield and sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.
Nvidia isn’t a victim here, though. As a key player in AI hyper scaling, the company is more responsible than most for the sky-high cost of components. It has also become one of the most valuable firms in the world thanks to its market-leading AI accelerators and GPUs. As a consequence, we’re seeing new products launch at higher prices than their predecessors, and many end up getting more expensive during their lifetimes. Game consoles have been particularly affected, with Nintendo, Microsoft, and Sony all bumping the prices of their current-gen hardware. The PS5 Pro, for example, has gone from $699.99 at launch in 2024 to $899.99 today.
Stock of the Shield TV Pro has been slim for the last few months, probably because it became too expensive to manufacture new units with component prices rising so quickly. At $300, it will make sense for Nvidia to churn out more devices. However, this higher price will cause an already niche set-top box to be even less appealing to people who just want to stream Netflix.
Unless you need the Shield’s extensive codec support or Plex server capability, it makes more sense to get a cheaper streamer. The Shield is still out of stock on Nvidia’s store, but it’s available at the new price from Best Buy.

Q: I get headaches whenever I use my phone or computer for a long time. Are screens damaging my brain?
A: Screens are not known to damage the brain simply through use, but prolonged use can cause eye strain, dry eyes, blurred vision, neck and shoulder tension and headaches. Poor posture, glare and inadequate breaks can worsen symptoms. Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look about 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Adjust brightness, reduce glare and blink regularly. Frequent or severe headaches, especially without screen use, need medical evaluation.
Q: Is every headache a migraine?
A: No. Headaches can result from stress, tension, dehydration, poor sleep, eye strain, infections, sinus problems, stomach problems or migraine. Migraine may cause throbbing pain, nausea and sensitivity to light or sound, though symptoms vary. A new, unusually severe or rapidly worsening headache, especially with weakness, confusion, fainting, seizures, vision changes, fever or difficulty speaking, needs urgent medical attention.
Q: I have a headache, so I take a painkiller immediately. Is that okay?
A: Occasional appropriate use may be fine for some people, but frequent painkiller use can cause medication-overuse headaches and, depending on the medicine, stomach, kidney or liver problems. If you regularly need painkillers for headaches, find the cause rather than repeatedly treating the symptom.
Q: Do I really need a flu shot if I usually get only a mild flu?
A: Influenza can be mild but can also cause serious illness, especially in high-risk people. Flu vaccination reduces the risk of influenza and its complications, though it does not prevent every cold or respiratory virus. Because influenza viruses change, seasonal vaccination is recommended for many people according to individual risk. Ask your doctor if it is appropriate for you, particularly if you have chronic diseases, are pregnant or belong to another recommended group.
Q: Can the flu shot give me influenza?
A: No. Injectable flu vaccines do not contain live influenza virus capable of causing influenza. Soreness, tiredness or a mild fever can occur briefly after vaccination and usually reflect an immune response. You can also catch another respiratory virus around the same time. Remember that protection takes time to develop.
Q: My eyes burn after looking at my phone for hours. Do I need “screen glasses”?
A: Not necessarily. Digital eye strain can cause burning, dryness, temporary blurred vision and headaches because we blink less while concentrating. Take regular breaks, blink consciously, reduce glare and keep the screen at a comfortable distance. Prescription glasses may help if you have an underlying vision problem. Blue-light glasses are not a magic solution. Persistent pain or significant vision changes need an eye examination.
Q: Does using a phone in the dark permanently damage eyesight?
A: Ordinary phone use in a dark room has not been shown to permanently damage eyesight, although the bright screen against a dark background can cause strain, dryness or headaches. Keep some ambient light on and adjust screen brightness. Persistent blurred or double vision, eye pain or headaches should not simply be blamed on the phone.
Q: I use my phone until I fall asleep. Does it really affect sleep?
A: It does. Screen use keeps the brain engaged, while light from screens can affect the body’s sleep-wake rhythm. Messages, videos and social media can be particularly stimulating. Keep the phone away from the bed, choose quieter activities before sleep and maintain a regular bedtime. Persistent sleep problems need further evaluation.
Q: Can sitting in front of a screen all day cause neck and back pain?
A: Yes. Prolonged sitting and poor posture can cause neck, shoulder and back pain, while looking down at a phone can add neck strain. Change position regularly, keep the screen at a comfortable height, support your back and move around during the day. Exercise and strengthening can help. Persistent pain, numbness, weakness or pain spreading into an arm or leg should be assessed.
Q: I feel dizzy and get a headache after spending hours on my phone. Is it because of radiation?
A: There is no good evidence that ordinary mobile-phone use causes headaches or dizziness through the radiation emitted by phones. However, prolonged use can indirectly contribute through eye strain, poor posture, dehydration, lack of sleep and inactivity. Look at the whole pattern and take regular breaks. If headaches or dizziness keep returning, particularly without screen use, consult your doctor.
Q: Are “sugar-free” foods healthy?
A: No. “Sugar-free” does not mean nutritious. Sugar-free biscuits, chocolates and snacks may still be high in calories, refined flour, saturated fat or salt. Some contain sugar alcohols or other sweeteners that can cause gas, bloating or diarrhoea when consumed in excess. They may also keep our preference for very sweet foods alive. Sugar-free is a label, not a health certificate. Always check the complete nutrition label.
Q: Are zero-sugar drinks harmless?
A: Not necessarily. They can be a better choice than sugary drinks if you are trying to reduce sugar and calories, but they are not automatically healthy. Some sweeteners can cause gas, bloating, abdominal cramps or diarrhoea, particularly in people with sensitive digestion or IBS. If a particular drink repeatedly causes bowel discomfort, stop it and see whether symptoms improve. Zero sugar does not mean zero consequences.
Public Advisory: Not every health problem needs a tablet—and not every health myth deserves to be believed. From WhatsApp remedies and “natural” cures to advice from friends and relatives, health information can easily become distorted. Before starting, stopping or changing a treatment, ask the doctor—not the WhatsApp group.
NOTE: These responses are for general awareness and do not replace professional medical advice. Older adults often have multiple illnesses and medicines, so individual medical advice should be taken from a qualified healthcare professional.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): From crime reporting and forensic examination to prosecution, court proceedings and final justice, a five-day exhibition inaugurated by Union Home Minister Amit Shah at BHEL Dussehra Maidan on Saturday seeks to explain how India’s new criminal justice codes will work in practice.
Spread across 14 zones, the exhibition uses live models, digital technology, videos, charts and demonstrations to explain key provisions of the new codes and create awareness among citizens about changes in the criminal justice system.
ONE ZONE AT A TIME: Fourteen zones trace the journey from crime reporting to investigation, trial and justice
Zone 1 introduces visitors to the new criminal justice codes - the BNS, BNSS and BSA, 2023 - and explains their key provisions and practical applications.
Zone 2 focuses on emergency services and the control room under the concept of ‘One Nation, One Emergency Number’, Dial-112.
Zone 3 showcases crime-scene investigation and forensic examination through a realistic 3D crime-scene model.
Zone 4 focuses on police stations, while Zone 5 focuses on medical services and evidence. Zone 6 demonstrates the importance of forensic science laboratories in the justice process.
Zone 7 focuses on prosecution, covering its role from preparation of the charge-sheet. Zone 8 presents the district court system.
Zone 9 is dedicated to prison reforms and the e-Prisons system. Zone 10 presents the dignified setting of the High Court, including a model of the main courtroom of the Madhya Pradesh High Court, Jabalpur.
Zone 11 highlights achievements in the fight against Naxalism, presenting the state’s efforts and police achievements through photographs and digital displays.
Zone 12 focuses on cyber security and awareness. It provides information on the ‘Safe Click Campaign’.
Zone 13 showcases the state’s achievements in implementing the new criminal justice codes.
Zone 14 showcases social initiatives such as Operation Muskaan, Women Help Desks and ‘Say No to Drugs’, along with a live quiz.

An explosive and newly partially unsealed court filing alleges that the US Department of Homeland Security built up dossiers on ICE observers—including their photos, license plate numbers, and other information—and stored them in a system called the Investigative Case Management database, which was built by Palantir.
Palantir did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for DHS calls the case “meritless” and says that “the underlying lawsuit is based on the lie that there is a database of ‘domestic terrorists’ run by DHS.”
Plaintiffs allege in the filing, which is heavily based on documents produced by the government and depositions of DHS agents, that agents had a practice of intimidating protesters and observers. They did this, the filing says, by doing drive-bys of the observers’ homes and, in the case of at least one observer, requiring that she be referred to secondary inspection any time she tries to cross the border until at least January 2027.
"The government is treating people who exercise their First Amendment rights and seek to hold it accountable as criminal suspects, and that's what we're asking the court to stop,” says JoAnna Suriani, an attorney at Protect Democracy who is representing ICE observers in the case.
The filing focuses on agents’ conduct during “Operation Catch of the Day,” an immigration enforcement surge in Maine this past January. It is part of a proposed class action brought in federal court in Maine by four observers: Elinor Hilton, Colleen Fagan, Polyxenia Pantos, and Carlyn Williams. It was filed under seal in September, and a redacted version was made public Friday.
In particular, it describes how one DHS agent, referred to as “Agent J.C.” in the filing, used the Investigative Case Management (ICM) database, which the government describes as the case management system the ICE component Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) uses to document its investigations, to flag observers.
According to the filings, J.C. created ICM records on at least six observers; the government puts the number of people at eight. He labeled two people he filmed at a Home Depot parking lot with “Threat to Law Enforcement, Professional Protestor,” according to the filing, and sent photos of them and others to a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer so he could run a facial recognition search on them using an app called Mobile Query.
On January 20, Pantos briefly watched and photographed an arrest in Portland, Maine, standing a few car lengths away beside their spouse's car. Hours later, per the filing, J.C. ran the car's plate and pulled a report on the owner—Williams—from Accurint, a LexisNexis database for law enforcement, which listed her address, phone numbers, and cohabitants. J.C. then allegedly circulated her photo to his team, asking, “Was this the protestor.” Another agent, per the filing, replied that it didn’t match the woman he had dealt with at the scene; J.C. then told colleagues he was "adding them in ICM now."
According to the legal filing, that afternoon, J.C. called Williams on her cell phone, identifying himself only as "the Department of Homeland Security." According to Williams, he told her she "should encourage" her spouse, Pantos, "not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist." J.C. testified in a deposition that he warned Williams she would be arrested if she “continue[d] to do this.” Government attorneys asserted in a court filing that he denied referencing a “domestic terrorism watchlist.”
According to documents produced by the government, Williams’ ICM record says that she was the registered owner of a vehicle used to “interrupt ICE arrests” and that her driver’s license photo matched a video of "aggressive woman [who] interject[ed] herself into an arrest." According to a 2016 DHS privacy assessment, ICM automatically shares the subject records agents create with CBP’s TECS system, where they act as "lookout records" for screening travelers at the border.
ICM is the system used by HSI agents to create and track case files. ICE awarded Palantir the contract to build ICM in 2014, and the system is built on the company’s Gotham software, which ICE says was customized specifically for operational needs. In 2022, ICE awarded Palantir a new five-year ICM support contract initially valued at up to about $96 million. In 2025, the agency added nearly $30 million to that contract to develop a new platform called “ImmigrationOS.”
Todd Lyons, the former acting director of ICE, wrote in an April letter to Rep. Maxwell Frost, the Florida Democrat, that ICE “does not maintain any kind of database of U.S. citizens protesting ICE activities.” He also said DHS isn’t keeping a “separate, standalone database” of people it hasn’t arrested or detained.
The government’s motion to dismiss argues that these were isolated incidents and that DHS policy prohibits this conduct. It says J.C. made records on people he believed were “potential threats to law enforcement” and “did not attempt to nominate any individuals to the terrorist watchlist.”
Attorneys for the observers say that DHS’s efforts have had a chilling effect on their First Amendment rights. According to the motion, Pantos stopped all ICE observation work after J.C.’s phone call to Williams, who briefly continued to observe ICE activity and then stopped all together too.
The observers are asking the court to order that Williams’ records be archived, to bar DHS from using the information it collected about the plaintiffs against them, and to prohibit agents in Maine from threatening observers with watchlists or following them to their homes.

Al Qaeda figures and more: Two posts surfaced on Omani co-pilot's profile after flydubai incident, says report
The posts featured cockpit footage and images of figures associated with al Qaeda. The second post featured an AI image depicting Islam’s three holiest sites.
Amid uncertainty over the identity and motive of the attacker involved in the flydubai flight incident, a report claimed that two posts were made on the Omani pilot's LinkedIn profile hours after the alleged crash attempt.
The profile belonged to Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, CNN reported, citing sources.
Both posts were published within a short span on the same day, around nine hours after the incident. According to the CNN report, it remains unclear who published them or whether they had been scheduled in advance. However, the LinkedIn profile has since been deleted.
Deep Dive
The posts featured cockpit footage, references to Israeli airlines and images of figures associated with al Qaeda. The second post, meanwhile, featured an AI-generated image depicting Islam’s three holiest sites.
First post featured cockpit footage, al Qaeda figures
The first LinkedIn post contained a series of clips filmed inside the cockpit of a Boeing 737 Max aircraft, the CNN report said. Notably, the aircraft that was diverted to Saudi Arabia during Wednesday’s incident was a flydubai 737 Max 8.
One of the clips, which the US news outlet said it geolocated to Dubai International Airport, showed the person filming zooming in on an aircraft belonging to Israeli airline El Al.
The cockpit screen visible in the video displayed flight number OMA624 and the date October 11, 2023. The flight number corresponds to a route that typically operates between Dubai and Muscat, while the date falls within the period when al-Hammami worked for Oman Air.
The video also showed more aircraft belonging to El Al, as well as one operated by another Israeli airline, Arkia.
The video however ended with photographs of Ayman al-Zawahiri, who led al Qaeda after the death of Osama Bin Laden, and Humam Khalil Abu-Mulal al-Balawi, who was responsible for a 2009 suicide bombing that killed nine people, including seven American CIA officers and contractors. Al-Balawi was loyal to al Qaeda, the CNN report added.
Second post showed Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem
The second LinkedIn post reportedly featured an AI-generated image depicting Islam’s three holiest sites in Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem, connected by a continuous glowing trail.
A poem recited in the background spoke of rejecting humiliation, not fearing death and defending one’s dignity, CNN report added.
What the LinkedIn profile said
The profile said al-Hammami had worked at Oman Air for seven years before leaving in February 2025. It then listed him as joining Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and leaving in January 2026.
The page did not mention Flydubai. However, one source confirmed to CNN that the profile belonged to the pilot involved in Wednesday’s incident.
The same two videos were allegedly posted around the same time on an Instagram account carrying the same name and photographs. That account has since been deleted as well.

The story so far
The groundwater resources of Kerala have been under severe stress due to changes in rainfall pattern following climate change, high population density as well the fact that approximately 62% of the population relies on groundwater from an estimated 6.5 million open wells for their domestic needs. The State’s fragmented wastewater management system and the unscientific construction of septic tanks and pit latrines at homes close to shallow and open wells have resulted in persistent faecal contamination of ground water in the State, which has been documented by several studies.
A 2024 study in the Journal of Environmental Management reported that 7.4% of the State’s population could be making do with poor quality of groundwater and estimated that 0.59 million people in 252 local self government bodies in the State could be continuously exposing themselves to health risks from consuming ground water from wells which may not be chlorinated regularly.
And the latest report on E.coli contamination comes from Pala, where a water quality assessment conducted in flood-affected areas along the Meenachil river detected E. coli bacteria in 67% of the samples, raising concerns over the safety of drinking water sources in and around Pala.
Researchers attributed the spike in bacterial contamination to the recent floods, which may have allowed contaminated surface water to enter water sources.
How is contamination taking place?
It is a dangerous combination of high population density, unplanned urbanisation with hundreds of septic tanks and wells sitting close to each other in small plots and the State’s natural hydrogeological features that allow surface pollutants to reach the water table quickly. In recent years, unpredictable and heavy rainfall has been adding to the State’s woes, as oversaturation of the soil and the overflow of drainage systems can quickly allow pollution and microbial contamination to infiltrate ground water.
Environmental scientists explain that groundwater is drawn mostly from shallow, unconfined aquifers, which are recharged directly by rainfall and surface infiltration. In most areas the local water table might be sitting just below the level of the river bed and it naturally leaks water downwards to recharge the underlying unconfined aquifers. If rivers are polluted, then all groundwater resources in the surrounding area would also be carrying the same pollutant.
What is the extent of groundwater contamination in Keralam?
A community-level GIS study of 449 households in an urban area of Thiruvananthapuram in 2018 had reported that most of the wells were in an intermediate-high contamination risk state, with more than 77% of wells having a septic tank within 7.5 m radius. Coliform contamination was prevalent in 73% of wells, and the groundwater was predominantly acidic with a mean of 5.4, rendering it unfit for drinking.
This picture could be true for the rest of the State also. Because of the State’s unique geography and highly dispersed, continuous rural-urban settlement pattern, just about 5-6% of major urban zones are connected to a centralised pipe-based sewerage network system. The State’s sanitation strategy relies heavily on onsite sanitation systems, with individual household septic tanks and soak pits for sewage disposal.
Unscientific construction of these household sanitation systems has rendered much of the groundwater resources unsafe for human consumption, unless properly treated.
What are the health impacts?
Safe drinking water is one of the crucial social determinants of health. It is thus unfortunate that a State which has made enviable strides in developing its public health sector has paid little attention to ensuring that people have access to safe drinking water. While people in urban areas have to a large extent, access to treated water supply, in many rural areas of the State serviced by local small water supply schemes, water distribution lines often run close to sewerage lines and even small breaks in the pipelines can lead to the contamination of drinking water
Recurrent outbreaks of water-borne diseases like Hepatitis A, Shigellosis and norovirus outbreaks have been the bane of the State in recent years, especially in the northern districts of the State, indicating the scale and impact of groundwater contamination. Hepatitis A in particular has been taking a heavy toll on the State since the last three years, with significant mortality and in many instances, leaving people with severe morbidities
Epidemiological studies conducted by the ICMR and Health department into amoebic meningoencephalitis, which has emerged as a significant public health problem in Keralam in recent times, has traced the infection to the use of non-chlorinated well water which has high concentration of E.coli, in which free-living amoeba thrive
What is the sewerage infrastructure status?
To modernise sewerage infrastructure, the State is executing projects under the AMRUT 2.0 Mission, a Central initiative aimed at ensuring universal access to safe water and reliable sewerage connections across urban areas. The CAG’s 2025 report stated that at the closure of the AMRUT Mission (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation), Kerala’s overall achievement was just 11.25% and only 0.13% households got sewerage connections.
Keralam’s geography, population density, lack of vast tracts of uninhabited land means that many proposed treatment plants end up being close to residential areas, which triggered huge public protests. Such protests led to the cancellation of multiple approved septage treatment plant projects in many parts of the State. There are also reports about the State’s financial crunch affecting project payments leading to delays in implementation

Here’s a fun history lesson for you. Don’t worry, we’ll make it quick! In 1966, nearly 51,000 people died on US highways. The overwhelming evidence suggested that many lives could have been saved with modern seat belts, which by then had been around for several years. The automotive industry responded by rallying together, and, in a triumph of self-regulation, voluntarily put the safety feature in every new vehicle that rolled off the line.
Kidding! Of course they didn’t do that. In the fall of 1966, Congress established the Department of Transportation and then passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act as well as the Highway Safety Act, giving the federal government sweeping new authority to set safety standards. By 1968, seat belts were required in every new car. Despite a massive increase in highway traffic in the last 60 years, far fewer fatalities happen on the road today.
I was thinking about this while watching various AI CEOs huddle around US president Donald Trump on Tuesday, congratulating themselves and each other on having signed an AI safety accord. My colleague Maddy Varner wrote about the specific stipulations here, but the short version is that it’s largely up to the AI labs to keep themselves in check.
Or, as Trump put it even more succinctly in the Oval Office on Wednesday: “They’re gonna police, and they’re gonna police each other, and they’re gonna self-police, they’re gonna police themselves. It’s going to work out very well.”
So this is the current state of AI safety regulation. On one side are the AI executives, employees, and tech luminaries, who are all saying that there need to be clear, thoughtful, tactical rules introduced to avoid potential disaster. (Bill Gates, for instance, has been on a media blitz playing Cassandra about an AI apocalypse.) On the other side is Trump’s magical thinking that if you say something enough times, it must be true.
That’s not to say any of this is simple or easy. The question of how to properly “pace the frontier,” as some of those same executives like to say, remains open. Even if all of the major AI labs were to agree to a slowdown, there’s no good way to keep them to their word, and China would likely continue on its own path regardless. The US economy is increasingly propped up on the AI industry, which itself has become an ouroboros of financing deals and circular investments; any meaningful crackdown risks major instability that reaches well beyond Silicon Valley.
The automotive industry is also admittedly an imperfect analogy for all kinds of reasons. There’s no seat belt equivalent for AI, no straightforward solution that can demonstrably reduce risk overnight. (It also took decades for the majority of states to pass laws mandating that people actually wear them.) The potential harms are less certain and less quantifiable. AI doomers will tell you the technology could result in human extinction in a decade; skeptics argue that’s sci-fi marketing malarkey.
We’ve talked about various AI risk scenarios before, but no one can say for certain what’s going to happen next. If you’re looking for data points to calculate your own personal p(doom), I’d point to a recent CNN report about how the US military supposedly nearly boarded a Chinese ship in part because a false AI-generated report said it was carrying nuclear materials. What, if anything, does the AI accord accomplish to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future? Unclear.
The correct answer to all this uncertainty surely isn’t “I guess we’ll find out.” But that’s exactly what self-regulation encourages. To its credit, OpenAI has delayed and even canceled the release of its most advanced models over security concerns. But not before they went on various, extensive hacking sprees, new details about which are still trickling out at a steady pace.
In an interview with TIME published on Thursday, Trump suggested that the Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation were sufficient “guardrails” for the artificial intelligence industry. Are they? It’s far from clear if AI companies can even be held legally responsible when their models go rogue. And it’s not like AI agents themselves are being served subpoenas.
The truth is, no one knows how to solve for AI safety right now. It’s going to take massive amounts of coordination, resources, and regulatory authority to develop the right framework and enforce it, which is exactly the kind of thing governments are designed to provide. Instead of even attempting to work through any of that, the Trump administration is getting out of the way and telling everyone to step on the gas. Don’t bother buckling up.

Tony Gilroy blasted the “tragic” nature of the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger at the world premiere of his new film, “Behemoth!” Produced on a $36 million budget, “Behemoth!” is representative of the mid-budget, adult-oriented drama that once sustained Hollywood’s theatrical business — and allowed filmmakers like Gilroy to make a name for themselves in the industry. He fears the impending merger (which David Ellison just announced would place both of the historic movie studios under a company named Skydance) threatens to dismantle the very “healthy and beautiful business” he has worked in for over three decades.
	“People say the movie business is in trouble,” Gilroy told Variety Friday night at Alice Tully Hall. “You go around, you stand anywhere you want, what do people talk about? Did you see this? Did you see that? What episode are you on? The business is solid, and to destroy the architecture that made it so in the name of venture capital, it’s tragic.”
Starring Pedro Pascal as a gifted cellist re-immersing himself in the world of Hollywood film scoring, “Behemoth!” marks Gilroy’s first major project since completing his work on the Emmy-winning series “Andor.” It was also selected as the centerpiece of the 64th New York Film Festival, following James Gray’s star-studded opening-night film “Paper Tiger” and preceding Ava DuVernay’s closing-night documentary “14th.” While introducing his new film, Gilroy praised the festival’s lineup as a bright spot amid an increasingly turbulent Hollywood landscape.
Popular on Variety
	“Thank you for making [the festival] so elegant and glamorous, and for surrounding us with so many amazing films,” Gilroy told the crowd. “The way this is curated this year, this is a freakin’ lineup! Holy sh*t. And everybody knows it. When so many things go to shit in Hollywood, this is like a thank you. Thank you for letting us bring our soufflé to your groovy party.”
Gilroy also thanked Matt Greenfield and his partners at Searchlight Pictures, the indie studio owned by the Walt Disney Company, which also produced “Andor.”
“This is not an easy movie to greenlight, and it’s not an easy movie to sell,” he concluded. “But here we are. We’re here. We got here calmly, gracefully, no drama, and our joie de vivre intact.”
Skydance has tentatively set Tuesday, Oct. 6, to close the merger, which will consolidate Hollywood’s traditional Big Five studios (Disney, Universal, Sony, Warner Bros. and Paramount) under just four corporate owners. While Ellison has maintained that Paramount and Warner Bros. will retain their separate studio identities under Skydance, industry figures — including “Behemoth!” producer Sanne Wohlenberg — fear the consolidation will make the “possibilities for a filmmaker alarmingly limited.”
“God, it’s certainly turbulent and uncertain times, isn’t it? It never seems to get any easier,” Wohlenberg said. “I do think you have to take a deep breath and keep believing that things will be circular and come back. When you look at history, there have been many, many bad times. UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford released on bail
- Published
A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.
The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished.
A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend.
Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.
The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said.
Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.
The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.
They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.
RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.
In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
Late on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a TV show that it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved in events over the weekend.
Without providing evidence or giving further details, he told Fox News network's "Hannity" programme: "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."
Speaking earlier at the Oval Office, US President Donald Trump said he would not have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released.
"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

Srinagar has an estimated 64,416 stray dogs, according to a scientific survey conducted by the Srinagar Municipal Corporation (SMC) in 2023, the Government stated today. America's $28B hemp THC industry is under threat from a looming ban
Sen. Mitch McConnell closed a loophole in the hemp law he championed

Inside a commercial kitchen near Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns pours a blue-green substance into gridded moulds to create a flagship product for his business: high-strength THC gummies containing the main psychoactive component found in marijuana.
He could soon be forced to close the operation. The United States’ multibillion-dollar market for intoxicating hemp items — spanning THC-infused seltzers stocked by Target stores to smokable cannabis flower — faces potential shutdown after Congress voted to plug a federal loophole that permitted the trade to expand.
Industry lobbyists and several lawmakers are working to rescue the sector. A short-term federal spending bill signed by President Donald Trump last month pushed back the implementation date of the "hemp THC ban" from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11, granting Congress additional time to consider regulating the products rather than an outright prohibition.
“It’s such a weird spot to be in,” said Hohns. “You worked 100 hours a week for the past four years, and, yeah, you made some money. But now you might have nothing to show for it.”
Marijuana and hemp are the same plant — cannabis. Marijuana is cultivated for high levels of THC in its flowers. Low-THC hemp has historically been grown for its sturdy fibers, food or wellness products. “Rope, not dope” was long the motto of farmers who supported legalizing hemp.
To give farmers a new cash crop, Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell successfully pushed the legalization of industrial hemp in the 2018 farm bill.
But the way that law defined hemp — as having less than 0.3% of a specific type of THC, called delta-9, by weight — opened a huge loophole. Beverages or snacks could meet that threshold and still contain more than enough THC to get people high.
Vape oil, gummy candies, chips, sodas and other unregulated, untested products laden with hemp-derived THC spread around the country, including in gas stations or convenience stores, where they were available even to teens. Some businesses started selling marijuana under the theory that raw marijuana’s THC is in a form called THC-A, which only turns into impairing delta-9 when heated or burned.
The products evaded state prohibitions on recreational weed or undercut heavily taxed and regulated cannabis where it is legal.
Dozens of states responded by regulating or banning impairing hemp products.
McConnell finally closed the loophole late last year by inserting a hemp THC ban into a measure that ended the longest government shutdown in history.
The ban, which limits the amount of THC in hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container, wouldn’t take effect for a year.
The ban “threatens to reduce retail revenues by $28.3 billion, displacing 225,000 jobs and reducing state sales tax potential by $2.1 billion,” according to a report last month from Whitney Economics, which studies the market.
The industry hopes to save itself by restricting impairing products to people 21 and older, limiting how much THC can be in a package, and banning imported cannabis compounds.
The owners of Kentucky’s Cornbread Hemp, Eric Zipperle and Jim Higdon, are prepared to cap their products at, say, 5 milligrams if that’s what it takes to win support from lawmakers. But the 0.4 milligram limit would destroy their business, they said.
“If it goes through in December, this place is toast — it’s gone,” Zipperle said.
They have 105 employees, sell hemp beverages in 18 states and expect to bring in $65 million this year.
The 0.4-milligram cap is so low that it would ban even some non-impairing CBD products, such as topical lotions, said Jonathan Miller, general counsel of the industry group U.S. Hemp Roundtable.
Hohns, who runs Deutermann Farms in Clayton, North Carolina, entered the hemp industry after losing his job as a personal trainer during the COVID-19 pandemic. North Carolina has not legalized either medical or recreational marijuana, but many of the edibles Hohns makes are more potent than what's available in states that have.
“When I started seeing THC edibles being sold … I was like, I got 18 months to two years to make money in this industry,” Hohns said. “No way is the government just going to sit here and let us do this when this was supposed to be for fiber, plastics, building materials, rope.”
That was more than four years ago. Hohns kept his capital investments minimal, fearing a shutdown. He has considered making other products, such as creatine gummies, if he has to get out of the hemp THC business.
Things have been more stressful for others. Drinkin' Buds, a cannabis beverage company in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, has mothballed production. Co-founder Matt Swanson took himself off the payroll on Thursday.
“There’s just so much uncertainty,” Swanson said. “I'm actively looking for employment.”
Among those who have come to the defense of the hemp industry are alcohol retailers, including Total Wine & More. Sales of cannabis seltzers have helped offset falling alcohol sales.
Opponents include people who say the products are dangerous.
“I have sympathy for people losing their jobs, but I also have sympathy for the many, many more people whose lives are affected by this,” said Kevin Sabet, CEO of Smart Approaches to Marijuana.
The regulated legal marijuana industry, which sees hemp THC as unfair competition, also supports the ban. Cory Harris, a lobbyist for state-legal cannabis operators, suggested that dire predictions about its effect on the intoxicating hemp industry are overstated.
While the ban would end interstate sales of products like THC seltzers and gummies, some could find a home in legal in-state markets, he said. It's possible THC drinks could be sold at stores in the states where they were produced. States like North Carolina could adopt legal hemp programs.
“If you go from having virtually no rules to suddenly having an awful lot of rules, that’s a buzzkill,” Harris said. “Welcome to our world. But if you establish your whole business within a legally questionable loophole, that’s just sort of the risk you take.”

How big is Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak?
News of a fifth measles death in Pennsylvania underscores a longstanding issue about the disease. The full scope of the outbreak — in the state and in the country — isn’t known or even knowable.
Only confirmed cases are reported. As of Wednesday that total was 943 in Pennsylvania, about a quarter of the 2026 national total. About 20% of infected people end up needing hospital care and some other portion will see a doctor. But some will never come to the attention of public health.
That’s especially true in a place like Pennsylvania, where a number of counties have large numbers of Amish people. (It was true, too, in last year’s outbreak in Mennonite colonies in Texas.) People in these communities don’t interact much with the wider world. Measles vaccination rates are low, families are large, and people may not seek care unless the illness becomes severe.
At some point, researchers will come up with modeling estimates that may give us a better idea of how big this outbreak actually is. But for now, we’re just seeing a portion of the iceberg. “It is much worse than is being claimed,” says Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “I think we don’t know how bad.” — Helen Branswell

People with disabilities are struggling to find caregivers — and when they do, they’re more likely to experience problems with the quality of their care.
The grim findings come from a survey of 524 disability care providers published Wednesday by ANCOR, an advocacy group for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.

The World Health Organization said on Friday, September 25, 2026 that the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to two additional health zones, bringing the total number affected to 63 across seven provinces.
The newly affected zones are Bulu in Sud Ubangi province and Dungu in Haut-Uele province, which borders South Sudan.
As of September 23, Congo had reported 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths, according to the WHO.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said conflict and population displacement were making it more difficult for health workers to reach affected communities and trace people who may have been exposed to the virus.
"It's very difficult to see Ebola in isolation because even our response in Ebola is affected by the conflict because there is displacement and there is access problem to some areas," Tedros said. He said restricted access could leave contacts untraced, while displacement and crowding increased transmission risks.
Tedros said cases were declining overall and that contact tracing, safe burials and community engagement had improved, although transmission remained uneven across affected areas.
The lack of approved vaccines and treatments for the Bundibugyo strain was also complicating the response and could make people reluctant to seek care at treatment centers, Tedros said, adding the WHO was working to accelerate clinical trials of vaccines and treatments.
Turning to the risk of future global health emergencies, Tedros said countries needed to strengthen pandemic preparedness. “Ebola will not be a pandemic, but there could be a respiratory pathogen that can become a pandemic," he said. "Before that hits, we need to prepare."
The World Health Assembly adopted the Pandemic Agreement in May 2025 to strengthen global prevention, preparedness and response to future pandemics.
"We continue to see significant mis- and disinformation about the WHO Pandemic Agreement, with false claims. It's a power grab that cedes sovereignty to WHO," Tedros said. "This is completely untrue."
