The delay in inducting new fighter jets is hurting the Indian Air Force, and the country needs to produce up to 40 aircraft a year to plug capability gaps and build long-term combat strength, IAF chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh said on Saturday.
He said the IAF is counting on the timely induction of the LCA Mk-1A, new multi-role fighter aircraft (MRFA) and additional Sukhoi-30MKIs to shore up its fighter fleet and keep the number of its combat squadrons from falling below 30, while underscoring the need to deploy fifth-generation aircraft too.
“There is some extra delay this time, and there is no doubt that it is going to hurt us,” Singh said at his annual media briefing ahead of the 94th IAF Day on October 8. “We need to induct two fighter squadrons every year. That means anything between 36 and 40 aircraft should be produced and inducted into the IAF for us to stop going down from the current 30 fighter squadrons and start improving towards the target of 42. Actually, we need even more than that.”

Singh said the IAF could finalise the MRFA contract by the end of the financial year. It refers to the proposed purchase of 114 Rafale fighter jets from France to sharpen the IAF’s combat edge at a cost of roughly ₹3.25 lakh crore.
“Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) is talking about producing 20 LCA Mk-1As every year. If the MRFA deal goes through, we will get about 12 aircraft per year from that contract. That makes the number around 32. We also have a contract for 12 Su-30 aircraft. Let’s say if six come in one year and six come in another year, so we will be in the region of 35-40 aircraft per year. Under the MRFA model being considered, the Rafales will be made in India by French plane maker Dassault Aviation and a local partner. France is expected to supply 20 Rafale jets in fly-away condition while the remaining will be made in India under the government-to-government deal.
The LCA Mk-1A is finally nearing induction after missing several deadlines. Both the IAF and HAL are confident that induction will start by year-end. It will replace the IAF’s workhorse MiG-21s, which retired last year after more than six decades of service. The IAF has placed two orders for 180 Mk-1A fighter jets worth a combined ₹1.1 lakh crore. The first contract for 83 aircraft was signed in February 2021, followed by a second one for 97 fighters in September 2025. The deliveries, likely to begin in December, are under the first contract.
The first Mk-1A aircraft, ordered in 2021, was due for delivery in March 2024. That deadline was missed due to a combination of factors, including US firm GE Aerospace’s inability to supply the F404-IN20 engines on time and delays in securing key certifications.

Venus is shrouded in a veil of mystery. The yellowish “lower haze” at the bottom of its atmosphere was discovered by the Venera and Pioneer Venus probes in the 1970s. These spacecraft were some of the first to successfully send images of the planet back to Earth, but the haze they saw went unexplained for decades. Now the mystery Venus was keeping has been unveiled.
What nobody knew then was that the haze is an accumulation of particles from meteorites. “Shooting stars” that burn up in the atmosphere leave behind cosmic dust particles, and after sulfuric acid interacts with these particles, it leaves behind a haze. Planetary scientist Hiroki Karyu and his research team at Tohoku University in Sendai City, Japan, finally figured out how the haze formed using a microphysical model. This type of model involves microphysics—the micro-scale processes that create clouds and precipitation on Earth and other bodies.
“The continuous influx of cosmic dust is sufficient to sustain this lower haze layer with the particle size distribution observed by the entry probes,” Karyu said in a study published in Nature Astronomy. “These haze particles of cosmic origin act as efficient condensation nuclei, promoting cloud formation in the main cloud deck even far from their initial source.”
Hazed and confused
Previous speculation suggested the haze formed from volcanic ash. Venus is known as the most volcanically active planet in our Solar System, with signs of volcanism first observed by the Magellan spacecraft in the early 1990s. Recent studies discovered the planet is more volcanically active than previously thought, but the researchers found that ash belched out by Venusian volcanoes is not the source of haze particles.
Surface dust was also ruled out. Karyu found that even if there were much larger influxes of volcanic or surface dust on Venus, the particles would still not be able to interact with the atmosphere’s sulfur in the right way to form the haze.

Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges. While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. About 60 of the 73 new-age tech companies are currently profitable. In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively. It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42's purview are about a decade old. From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra's IPO materialised within four years of its operations. Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal. Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem. The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups. The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of PhonePe, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts. Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Overall, the Delhi NCR region is home to 25 listed new-age tech companies, ahead of Bengaluru's sixteen and Mumbai's thirteen. While fifteen companies, including Eternal, Delhivery, and Lenskart, call Gurugram their home, Awfis, EaseMyTrip, MapmyIndia and E2E Networks are from Delhi. Noida on the other hand is home to six listed new-age tech companies, including Paytm and IndiQube. Delhi NCR contributes $112.2 Bn in the cumulative $178 Bn market cap of new-age tech companies. Dubai Crown Prince and UAE Deputy Prime Minister Hamdan bin Mohammed has praised Indian flydubai pilot Captain Smit Machchhar for his courage, saying he had demonstrated the “highest degrees of courage, responsibility, and care for human life.”
Hamdan shared a photograph from his visit to Smit Machchhar, who is receiving treatment in hospital, and said the UAE leadership extends its “appreciation and praise” to the pilot.
In a post on X, Hamdan said Smit Machchhar had become part of the UAE’s national story and praised his contribution in protecting lives.
Quick answers to key questions
On September 30, during flydubai Flight FZ1073, Captain Smit Machchhar was seriously injured by his co-pilot in an alleged attack that resulted in a rapid descent of the aircraft before emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Captain Machchhar is being praised for his remarkable courage and quick thinking during the cockpit attack, which allowed crew members and passengers to intervene and avert a potential disaster.
Despite sustaining serious injuries, Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door, enabling crew and passengers to subdue the co-pilot and ultimately make an emergency landing.
Captain Machchhar has received praise from various public figures, including Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Bollywood stars like Shah Rukh Khan and Salman Khan, acknowledging his bravery.
As of the latest updates, Captain Machchhar is under medical care and is recovering well, with the Indian Embassy confirming they are in contact with his family and supporting his recovery.
“We are proud that he is part of our team… part of the story of our nation” Hamdan wrote, adding that Machchhar was also part of the UAE’s “human experience”.
He concluded the message by describing the UAE as a “a nation of compassion… a nation of peace… and a nation of life.”
Smit Machchhar was seriously injured during an alleged attack inside the cockpit of a flydubai flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
Despite his injuries, the pilot was able to respond during the confrontation, while crew members and passengers intervened. The aircraft subsequently made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Machchhar remains under medical care as authorities investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The Indian Embassy in the UAE said Machchhar remains under medical care and is recovering well.
“Indian braveheart Capt. Smit remains under excellent medical care & is recovering well,” the embassy said on X, adding that it remains in contact with his family and local authorities.
Machchhar was initially treated in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, before being transferred to Abu Dhabi for further treatment.
The incident took place on September 30 aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, a Boeing 737 MAX 8 carrying 170 passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv.. The aircraft was forced to make an emergency landing in Tabuk after a violent confrontation inside the cockpit.
According to UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, the co-pilot attacked Machchhar with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft. The UAE has described the incident as an attempted “terrorist act”. Investigators are continuing to establish the circumstances and motive.
Despite his injuries, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door. Passengers and crew then intervened and subdued the co-pilot, while two off-duty pilots helped operate the aircraft before it landed safely in Tabuk. The plane reportedly lost more than 16,000 feet during the incident.
The co-pilot has been identified by multiple reports as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national. He had previously been grounded in Oman amid concerns over alleged extremist views.
Investigations involving UAE and Saudi authorities are continuing, with authorities examining the circumstances and possible motive behind the cockpit attack.

Ethernet cables can do more than just improve home internet
They can also transmit power, video and audio.
Ethernet cables are probably one of the least exciting tech accessories you own. But you may not realize they can do more than just connect devices to your router. They can also carry video, audio and power. However, just because they can do that doesn't necessarily mean they're the best option.
Long-distance video
HDMI usually connects two devices that are relatively close together, but some people's setups need video to travel over longer distances. This is one area where the same cables you use for Ethernet (category cables) could find a second use.
Ethernet cables won't do that on their own. For this setup, you'll need to buy HDMI extenders to pair with your Cat5e, Cat6 or similar cables. Those adapters put a transmitter at one end and a receiver at the other, while using the cable as the connection between them. That lets you send video much farther than you typically could with an HDMI cable.
Despite the familiar cable, this isn't actually Ethernet networking. (AV over IP, on the other hand, does use your local network to transmit audio and video.) Here, the category cable is simply carrying the signal between two extenders. It could be handy if you already have an unused cable in your walls or you need to reach something distant, like a projector.
Still, it isn't necessarily the best solution even for those cases. Active optical HDMI can also handle long distances, and some cables support formats like 4K at 120Hz that many extenders don't. Think of category cables as a potentially useful option for some niche setups, rather than a go-to solution.
Replace audio cables
These same category cables can also carry multiple channels of analog audio. With the right adapters, a single cable can carry several channels. For example, a studio could use it to connect microphones in one room to recording gear in another without pulling a bunch of individual cables through a wall.
For most setups, standard XLR cables are easier and pretty cheap. But if the wiring is already there, category cable can be a clever way to replace several cable runs with one. Some setups also need shielded cable, especially if the microphones get power through the connection.
PoE
Speaking of power, Power over Ethernet (PoE) is where category cables can find a second life that's more than just a clever gear hack. PoE lets one Ethernet cable carry both data and power. It's especially handy for security cameras, Wi-Fi access points and other devices that aren't near an outlet.
For example, a camera on your porch could use one Ethernet cable for both power and its network connection. Or you could run it to a Wi-Fi access point on your ceiling. The cable just needs to lead back to an accessory that provides PoE, like a compatible switch or injector.
Unlike the other uses, PoE isn't just an oddball option, it's a truly useful standard. However, you still need to make sure your equipment supports it and provides enough power for the device.

West Indies coach Daren Sammy, on the eve of the third and final ODI against India, said that a win against the world’s top-ranked side would give his team the much-needed confidence at a time when the players brace for pay cuts back home.
On Saturday, Shai Hope made his coach’s wish come true, leading from the front with an inspirational unbeaten 162 (143b, 17x4, 3x6) to guide his side to a five-wicket win and salvage pride by avoiding a whitewash at the Maharaja Yadavindra Singh International Cricket Stadium.
Chasing 352, Hope, opening the batting, scored his second century on the bounce as the Caribbean outfit hunted down the target with 10 balls to spare.
IND vs WI, 3rd ODI - As it happened
Hope set the tone in the PowerPlay with exquisitely timed shots through covers, down the ground, and off the pads. The skipper, along with Amir Jangoo (67, 56b, 5x4, 1x6), the other centurion from the second ODI in Guwahati, stitched together a 109-run stand for the second wicket off just 99 deliveries. The Indian bowlers looked flat and struggled to create chances in dewy conditions. However, against the run of play, Jangoo was run out when his partner sent him back. Keemo Paul chipped in, scoring a quickfire 44 (35b, 5x4). Once Paul departed, Hope dug deep despite battling fatigue. With the asking rate climbing above 11, Hope swatted Kuldeep for a six and a four in the 46th over. He followed it up with a brace of boundaries off Gurnoor Brar and Anshul Kamboj and, in the process, brought up his 150 as well.
Earlier, India posted 351 for seven, riding on K.L. Rahul’s well-paced unbeaten 129 (87b, 10x4, 6x6).
Electing to bat, the Men in Blue were rocked early in the third over when Jayden Seales struck twice. He had Gill caught down the leg-side and cleaned up Virat Kohli with an in-dipper that uprooted the middle-stump.
Rohit Sharma (92, 85b, 10x4, 3x6) and Ruturaj Gaikwad (57, 69b, 1x4, 4x6) steadied the innings with a 137-run stand. The former started cautiously against a disciplined opening burst from Seales and Matthew Forde before shifting gears.
After Rohit’s departure, Rahul took charge. The latter hit boundaries through conventional strokes, the best being the straight drive off Seales. During his knock, Rahul surpassed 10,000 international runs. At the back end of the innings, he showcased his repertoire and brought up his ninth ODI ton in style, pulling Seales over fine-leg for a maximum.
However, on this day, Hope did spring eternal for West Indies.

North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, a day after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.
Japan’s coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.
Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.
South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.
Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches across the Korean peninsula.
The missile test might be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.

At first glance, the patterns running across a bolt of Oshima tsumugi could be mistaken for a print. But on closer inspection, they are part of the silk’s construction: threads meticulously dyed before weaving, then painstakingly aligned on a loom.
“It’s almost mathematical,” says Mark McNulty, former sales and marketing specialist at kimono boutique Ginza Motoji. “It has to line up perfectly. “You don’t just weave, weave, weave. You have to completely adjust.”
Originally made by artisans on Amami Oshima, an island roughly halfway between Okinawa and southern Kyushu, Oshima tsumugi is one of Japan’s rarest and most elaborate textile traditions. It involves around 60 individual processes performed by highly skilled specialists, and a single, five-square-meter tanmono (standard bolt of kimono fabric) can take up to a year to complete.

In September 2026, a rumor (archived) circulated online that water levels in Wyoming's Yellowstone Lake dropped 11 feet between Sept. 26 and 27.
For example, a Facebook user wrote on Sept. 29:
YELLOWSTONE NATIONAL PARK - Scientists are investigating after portions of Yellowstone Lake reportedly dropped nearly 11 feet overnight when an unknown underground channel opened beneath the lake bed.
Rangers first noticed the change Sunday morning after several docks were found sitting completely above the waterline. Geologists believe shifting rock beneath the lake may have opened a previously sealed underground passage, allowing millions of gallons of water to drain into Yellowstone's extensive subterranean geological system.
The rumor also spread on X and Threads (archived, archived).
The rumor originated from the Facebook page Casper Planet, which described its content as satire. The page's About section read, "Snews that doesn't matter directly to your Snews feed. Did we say this is satire? Well it is, names/locations are made up."
In addition to Casper Planet's own declaration of the satirical nature of its content, we found no reporting from reputable sources on Google, Yahoo or DuckDuckGo (archived, archived, archived) that supported the Facebook page's claim about Yellowstone or cited the "geologist Dr. Aaron Keller" who featured in Casper Planet's post.
The image that Casper Planet used to illustrate the satirical story was fake. The highly regarded Pangram artificial intelligence detection tool found the image to be "fully AI." Open AI's Verify scanner found that someone had generated the image using Open AI's tools.
Though Casper Planet did note on its page that its content was satire, it did not say so on the actual post. Shares of Casper Planet's posts on X and Threads contained no indications (aside from the nature of the content) that the story was satire.
The United States Geological Survey's water level readings from the Yellowstone River at its inlet into Lake Yellowstone did not show an 11-foot drop in water levels between Sept. 26 and 27. The USGS found that water levels between 9 a.m. on Sept. 26 and 9 a.m. on Sept. 27 varied by inches, not feet.
Snopes has previously investigated other satire claims shared by Casper Planet, including whether an ancient city appeared under Wyoming's Horse Peak Mountain or whether Wyoming wolves mauled a Colorado man who tried to join their pack.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

BUNIA, Congo — Congo’s Ebola outbreak has killed more than 4,000 people, authorities said, as they struggle to contain what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
The latest figures released by the Health Ministry on Thursday showed that 4,018 people have died among 8,300 cases recorded since the outbreak was declared in eastern Congo on May 15.
Some health workers, meanwhile, gathered at the epicenter in Ituri Province to demand payment for wages owed them. The protesters, who included surveillance team members, waved placards saying, “No money, no data!” and “No payment for months.”
Some of the workers haven’t been paid for August and September, said Biongi Beiza, one of the protesters in Bunia, Ituri’s capital. “There is no explanation from the administration,” he said.
Congolese authorities did not immediately address the issue. Front-line workers have gone on strike several times since the outbreak began, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
A senior U.N. official said an Ebola-hit displacement camp housing a transit center for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week as they were looking for weapons in Kigonze, on the outskirts of Bunia, forcing 19,000 people in the camp to flee.
Creating such transit and treatment centers has been a struggle, requiring money and staff, all of which are in short supply, said Julien Harneis, the U.N. senior Ebola coordinator. “When we lose a center, that means we lose capacity, we lose investment, and we have to start again. And above all, it means that people do not get access to the care that they really need,” Harneis said.
Infected aid worker evacuated to the Netherlands
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived in the Netherlands late Thursday on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
“The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country,” MSF said.
At least 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
Mobile labs are helping detect cases quickly
One way local authorities have tried to contain the outbreak is through mobile laboratories. In Butembo, an Associated Press journalist watched a medical team operating one such lab near an Ebola treatment center on Thursday.
Test results that used to take 72 hours can now be obtained in six hours with the mobile labs, said Lota Kalubi, a doctor at the treatment center.
The labs have also made it easier to get to locations usually difficult to reach, said Michel Ngimba with the National Institute of Biomedical Research in Butembo. “So we can go, if today we have an emergency, for example, in Katwa, we can start up the vehicle, and we can move the lab to Katwa,” said Ngimba.
Insecurity and community resistance are hampering containment efforts
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm about the virus’ rapid spread into new health zones, stretching limited resources. The current outbreak is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people, WHO has said.
The number of newly confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hot spots, Africa CDC said on Thursday. While the spread of the disease has slowed in some areas, it has accelerated in others.
Confirmed cases fell from around 850 cases and 470 deaths a week in mid-July to an average of 490 cases and 230 deaths in September.
A Congolese politician was beaten to death earlier this week in one of the emerging hot spots after defending government measures to deal with the outbreak, highlighting tensions and mistrust in communities.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach that involved working with local leaders to educate people about the virus, but those efforts face resistance from residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons including how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks and chronic corruption.
— Dieudonne Dirole and Ope Adetayo
Adetayo reported from Lagos, Nigeria. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi in Butembo, Congo, Chinedu Asadu in Abuja, Nigeria, and Mike Corder in the Netherlands contributed.

India's Asian Games 2026 campaign ended on a winning note as the Harmanpreet Singh-led men's hockey team thrashed Malaysia 5-1 in the final on Saturday. How to know it's time to replace your Apple Pencil's tip
You won't need a sharpener for your Apple Pencil, but that doesn't mean your tips will last forever.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
The Apple Pencil is a nifty little gadget that lets you draw and doodle on all manner of Apple tablets. Now that the iPhone Duo is allowing for Apple Pencils to be used with an iPhone model, the gizmo's popularity is sure to see a spike. However, just because it's a tool that interfaces on digital screens doesn't mean it can't wear out like a normal pencil. When you're using Apple's signature stylus, there are a few signs you need to track to stay on top of wear and tear.
There's quite the line of Apple Pencils on the market, from the Pro to the USB-C (not to mention the older first and second generations of the Pencil). Despite this variety of models, the detachable tip of an Apple Pencil is a commonality across these many styli. In that spirit, there are a number of common signs that signify whether your pencil is nearing the end of its rope.
Signs you need to replace your Apple Pencil tip
While using an Apple Pencil won't burn up any graphite, the tip of the pencil will still wear into a more jagged shape over time, as opposed to a fresh tip's even roundness. As a pencil wears down, usage will produce more friction, and the tip will be more rough to the touch. Eventually, an Apple Pencil's tip will wear down enough to expose the metal underneath — at which point you definitely need a replacement.
If you're not keeping a close eye on your pencil, this will probably manifest first through that increased friction, but your tip will also lose connectivity over time, which you'll certainly pick up on as it happens. As these issues pile up, you'll want to switch to a new tip sooner or later — and hopefully before you accidentally scratch up your screen. In general, you'll want to replace your tips every two years, though avid users may need a replacement in less than a year.
The market for Apple Pencil tips
Despite the gaps in features and price points between different Apple Pencils, all of these models have pretty similar levels of hardiness, both with battery and durability. The tips of the Apple Pencil are the major factor in this equation; fortunately, they can be easily replaced.
Apple sells pencil tips in packs of four for $19, which are compatible with all makes of Apple Pencil. It's pretty simple to buy these every so often to keep your Pencil in shape, but the replaceable nature of Apple Pencil tips leaves third-party options wide open. Brands like PenTips and Delidigi offer alternatives that emphasize aspects like drawing feel and writing feel respectively; the PenTips Lite offers great precision for drawing (of a quality good enough for artists at Disney) while Delidigi's Fine Point not only lasts long, but grants precision with a ballpoint feel.

Sliding student scores spark fresh calls to revisit how we're teaching math
Vast research on how kids learn not always translating into classrooms, professor says
Earlier this week, Kendra Corbett stood at a blackboard breaking down an addition question for her Grade 3s, laying out step by step how to determine the answer and occasionally testing out suggestions her students called out.
A little later, she split her class into groups. Some youngsters played math games while others worked on an assignment using base ten blocks — manipulating the small plastic cubes, bars and squares (denoting units of one, 10 and 100, respectively). Corbett settled in with a handful of kids for a focused lesson on ordering numbers from least to greatest. All the activities allowed for practice learning three-digit numbers.
"We assume kids come in knowing what numbers actually mean. If they can count to 10, that doesn't necessarily mean they understand what 10 represents," said Corbett, a teacher in Upper Grand District School Board in Orangeville, Ont., some 60 kilometres northwest of Toronto.
"If they don't have the foundation of knowing what numbers actually mean and understanding of magnitude, then they're really going to struggle later on."
Knowledge and understanding of math rests on building blocks that students usually start developing in primary school. But with recent international and provincial assessments warning about sluggish and waning math skills among Canadian students — a slide that pre-dates the pandemic — some experts say we should revisit how we teach math and pay numeracy the same attention literacy has received in recent years.
What worries Canadian mathematician John Mighton are the changes happening over time, specifically the growth in students who are slipping to lower levels — where some can only handle basic math or are considered below functional numeracy — and the wider impact of that trend.
"That's a real threat to our country, to our economy, even to our political system. How can you think your way through problems that involve risk or probabilities or science if you can't do the simplest math?" said Mighton.
"It's a tragedy that we think math is not as important as it as and that we're not doing something about it."
Back in 2002, Mighton founded JUMP Math, an education charity that's grown to work with students and teachers in K-8 schools across Canada and abroad.
Teaching novices a new concept takes a different approach than teaching those already fluent in a topic, he says, yet much math instruction of the past 20 years has treated kids like experts before they're ready.
"From day one, you're given a lot of rich problems … highly contextualized, lots of complexity, lots of language. People don't feel they're really giving kids math unless they're doing that kind of problem," Mighton said.
"We mistake the end where we want to get kids to — we want them to be great chess players, great problem solvers — with the means to get them there," he said.
"Guide kids more, scaffold more, give more practice, build foundational knowledge, so the kids can become experts …When you do that, kids become much better problem-solvers."
Building a solid foundation and then strong reasoning and problem-solving skills are especially important amid the rise of artificial intelligence, he says.
"It's a dangerous idea that kids are just going to be able to deal with all the challenges that are coming from AI … if they don't have any domain-specific knowledge, particularly in mathematics.
"You're going to be so easily fooled and misled and you'll make disastrous decisions if you don't understand the math."
Not a return to rote learning
As with the recent shift toward more explicit, structured and phonics-led literacy teaching, there's a growing call for more systematic, teacher-led, direct instruction in math.
That doesn't mean rote learning, Mighton says, but does mean relying on evidence-based practices. He encourages teachers to use screenings, for instance, and regular low-stakes assessments to help them to make adjustments that propel students' progression.
There's a wealth of research about how children learn — on their attention spans, their ability to absorb information, barriers to that, and more — yet that research doesn't always translate into classrooms nor into the training that aspiring and working teachers receive, says neuroscientist Daniel Ansari, a professor of psychology and education at Western University in London, Ont.
He also advocates breaking up math learning into multiple, simplified steps, because it helps developing minds more readily pick up information.
"Sometimes teaching can assume that children start out as experts and they are required immediately to focus on their understanding, explaining their answers. And these sorts of things can overwhelm their cognitive systems and thereby prevent information making its way into long-term memory," he said.
Ansari says educators can absolutely strike a "balance between explicit instruction and letting children discover things working by themselves," but adds teachers must keep in mind what's developmentally appropriate and what learners are ready for.
Take timed practice — a.k.a. those "mad minute" sheets with rows of addition, subtraction, multiplication or division questions to be answered as quickly as possible — as an example.
Introduced too early, it overwhelms cognitive capacity, Ansari says. But once students have some time to learn and a bit of practice, "mad minutes serve as a way of increasing and deepening their fluency — and then it can also become something really fun."

- Alberta educators call mandatory screening tests time-consuming, ineffective, survey says
Rather than touting a "back to basics" mentality, Ansari instead suggests we consider "how can we improve things further, pick some things that we maybe discarded too early? Keep some things we're doing right now, but reassess some others."
Back in Orangeville, Upper Grand K-12 math lead Ashley Kozak has overseen a multi-pronged plan to improve early math learning. It includes central math facilitators, creating new teaching resources, employing an early math screener and, for the schools with the greatest need, sending in support teachers to deliver focused tutoring.
Updated math training for Grade 1 and Grade 3 teachers and principals has also boosted educator confidence, Kozak says, adding the board saw improvement in its latest EQAO results.
While she loves seeing kids' "a-ha" moments when visiting math classes, she says it's even better seeing students confidently approach the next questions.
"It's more than memorization. It's about problem-solving. It's about making those connections," she said. "Seeing that ... makes me feel like 'OK, we got this. We can do it.'"

The Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) expressed concern over the sharp disparity between the prices charged to retailers and consumers for essential medicines, particularly cancer drugs, observing that steep mark-ups placed an enormous burden on taxpayers and amounted to “carnage”.
A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta questioned the Centre on why the 16% retailer margin provided for under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013 should not be applied uniformly to essential medicines to curb steep mark-ups over the price to retailer (PTR).
“Why not keep the 16% margin on MRP, which is prescribed in the DPCO, on everything? ... Ultimately, the loser is the taxpayer. This is carnage, as simple as that,” the Bench remarked.
The observations came while the top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha, seeking its intervention to regulate the prices of drugs, medical equipment, and generic medicines, and make them more affordable.
Justice Mehta pointed, in particular, to the nearly ten-fold mark-up on an essential cancer drug, which was supplied to retailers for around ₹3,000 but sold to consumers for ₹27,000. He questioned who ultimately benefited from the nearly ₹24,000 difference. “You tell us why this difference... Where does this chunk of money go? Ten times...” Justice Mehta remarked.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, acknowledged the concern and said the government would have to find a way forward while “balancing equities”. He, however, said it was private hospitals, rather than pharmaceutical companies, that benefited from the steep mark-ups. “The pharma company is not the gainer. The gainer is the private hospital,” the Solicitor General submitted.
The Bench also flagged the practice of private hospitals insisting that patients purchase medicines from their in-house pharmacies, leaving them with little choice to procure the same drugs at lower prices elsewhere.
It also pointed to the impact of such inflated prices on public finances, observing that when treatment is covered under government-funded health schemes such as Ayushman Bharat, the cost is ultimately borne by taxpayers.
“Suppose the patient is taking treatment through government services... The government doesn’t pay, the taxpayer pays. This affects a larger section of society,” the Bench remarked.
Mr. Mehta sought time to place before the court details of the existing mechanisms governing drug pricing and assured the Bench that he would make his submissions on the next date of hearing. The Bench accordingly posted the matter for further hearing on October 12, 2026.
The petitions have sought directions to make drug formulations more affordable by curbing alleged overpricing of essential medicines by pharmaceutical companies and retailers. They have also sought stricter enforcement of price controls under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013 to prevent violations of the prescribed pricing mechanism and disproportionate profit margins across the drug supply chain.
Earlier, the top court had described the wide difference between the price to retailers and the MRP of medicines as “dacoity”, while drawing attention to the financial distress faced by patients struggling to meet treatment costs.
“The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what is it? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment,” the Bench had remarked.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tori Dunlap, founder of Her First $100K and author of "Financial Feminist." It has been edited for length and clarity.
My parents were very good at teaching me about money, not just by what they said, but by what they did. They were middle-class — by no means rich — but they made very smart financial decisions and equipped me with a lot of financial skills.
By college, I was the friend whom other friends came to ask about money. I set myself a very public goal of saving my first $100,000 when I was 25 — which I achieved. By 27, I was a millionaire, and now, at 32, I'm a multimillionaire.
Yet I don't look or act the way many believe a multimillionaire should. Here's what I refuse to spend on — and what's become even more important to me as I build wealth.
I don't spend on signifiers of wealth
I'm often told online that I don't look like a multimillionaire should. My hair, for example. If I'm going to be on television, I'll get it blown out. But when I'm creating content for my community, it's often pulled back.
I get my hair done about every three months, which is more than most people. Yet I'm not going to spend the money — or, more importantly to me these days, the time — to have it done constantly. It's just not a priority for me when I have a company to run.
I drive a 12-year-old Toyota
I still drive the same Toyota RAV4 that I went into debt to purchase when I was 22. It's a cute car, it's dependable, and it does everything I need it to.
Maybe I'll change my mind and get a flashier car in the future. It's fine for people to change their minds about what's important to them. But I'm not going to buy a luxury car just to show my wealth.
I rented until last year
Until last year, I rented an apartment even though I was a multimillionaire. I could afford to buy, but I didn't have the time to search for a house.
Then, my landlord decided to sell. That happened to me twice in a row, and made me realize I was willing to invest the time to find a house I love. As I've built wealth, time has become the currency that matters most to me.
I don't think there are silly purchases — just ones we don't think about
I'll never be the financial expert telling you that spending on lattes is stupid. I'm not saying that spending on hair, cars, or homes is silly either.
What's stupid, to me, is spending on things that don't matter to you. If you're buying a certain bag, vehicle, or home just to keep up with the Joneses and look wealthy, you're not being intentional.
In my book, "Financial Feminist," I say that we don't need to stop spending money. But we do need to stop spending on things that we don't care about.
I indulge, but not always publicly
I spend pretty unabashedly on travel. To me, it's one of the most important things.
I'm also proud of the house I bought last year. It's newly renovated and has a beautiful view. Yet, I don't share it online because my privacy is more important to me than showcasing my home. I've been very intentional about keeping some things private, including my partner and house.
My markers of success aren't material
The vision we've been sold of financial success is sexy: it's designed bags, sleek blowouts, and marble columns. I'm out here showing a different version of success.
For me, success means having enough financial security that I never have to be in a situation that doesn't respect me. I want to be able to donate to causes I believe in, and always pick up the check for friends and family without worrying about it.
Women in my community have been able to leave abusive relationships or toxic workplaces because of their financial independence. They can improve their communities and families. For them — and me — those markers of success matter so, so much more than any material markers of wealth.

Farmer asks Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar for scheme to help unmarried men find brides
At a Praja Seva event in Piriyapatna, a farmer urged DK Shivakumar to introduce a scheme to help unmarried men, especially farmers, find brides. The plea highlighted growing distress among rural bachelors, though the chief minister laughed off the request.
A farmer on Saturday urged Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar to introduce a scheme to help unmarried men, especially farmers, find brides. The farmer said, "There are so many men aged between 35 and 40 who are still unmarried. Poor fellows are dying by suicide. They have become frustrated with life. They need women to marry." He made the appeal after telling the chief minister, "Sir, please. Poor people are dying by suicide. Please, something has to be done."
He said the issue had become a major problem across the state and asked Shivakumar to come up with a scheme to address it. "They have spent so much money. "If daughters are not given to the farmers who grow crops and provide food for everyone, what can be done," he asked, adding that the issue was not just his personal problem but one faced by people across Karnataka. Hearing the plea, the chief minister laughed it off.

How the system failed us: Former foster youth tell their stories
Tyrome Laundersville was 9 years old and he didn't understand what was happening the day his mother and father put him in the family car at their home in Iowa and drove him to foster care.
He was excited, at first. He remembers thinking: "'Oh we're going somewhere fun.'"
Their destination was a psychiatric residential treatment center.
Most children in foster care live with families, with relatives or with other foster parents. But about 10% of disabled kids in foster care live in group homes and institutions, compared to just 4% of those without disabilities.
An NPR investigation found children with disabilities, including physical and behavioral health disabilities, are the largest group that goes into foster care — and they have the worst outcomes.
We obtained federal data on more than 500,000 children and youth in foster care in 2025. We calculated that disabled children stay in foster care 50% longer than kids without disabilities.
They're less likely to return to their parents or to be adopted.
To get past the numbers and better understand the issues of children with disabilities in foster care, NPR interviewed former foster youth about their experiences — like Laundersville.
When Laundersville was 9, his occasional screaming, aggression and property destruction were things his parents just couldn't figure out.
The hope was that he'd get treated at that facility and come home.
What happened was that he kept getting moved from place to place.
"Being a child who's nonstop moved around in a facility in that situation from 9 years old until I was 18, it's really hard," Laundersville told a group of child advocates and researchers in a speech in 2024. "I missed my parents. I'm not going to deny that. And even when I was mad or hurt, I still wanted them there. I still forgave them. I wanted them to fight for me. And I needed that connection. And when it wasn't there, it just left me feeling abandoned."
Laundersville would get lots of labels from doctors: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder. ADHD. Bipolar Disorder. Oppositional Defiance Disorder.
Going to locked-down residential treatment centers — some where he needed permission just to use the bathroom — only made his problematic behaviors worse, he said.
He'd have meltdowns at one facility and then get sent to another that was bigger, more restrictive and more punitive.
"I had a hard time with aggression, both verbally and physically," he said. "I wasn't just being bad. I was hurt. I was angry. And I didn't know how to properly express myself after the many years of just not being heard. I just wanted someone to understand me and not judge me for my behaviors and actions that I've always had my whole life."
One person who understands is Marissa Pike, of Massachusetts.
"When I was frustrated, I would scream and yell and that was my way to express that I was angry and I was mad," she said. "And so I just was kind of labeled as problematic. I was labeled as confrontational. I was labeled as aggressive and defiant."
Pike was 12 when she went into foster care. Because of her behavior, she says she got moved to 30 placements in less than 10 years.
Some were psychiatric centers and hospitals. She was medicated with anti-psychotic drugs.
But Pike was misdiagnosed.
It would take a few years before she was diagnosed with autism. It was at the core of all the behaviors that kept getting her in trouble.
"I would be overwhelmed doing something and I would refuse to go where the staff would want me to go," she says.
Simple activities or routines at a treatment center could overstimulate Pike and set off a cycle of meltdowns and punishments.
"As a kid, it would be like, 'Oh, we're going to go outside and play dodgeball. And then we're going to go in and we're going to go right to dinner and wash your hands' and stuff like that," she recalls of the regimented life at treatment facilities. "And for me it was like, 'OK, I just did dodgeball. And now I'm like, I need time to decompress' because dodgeball is vicious with kids."
But she says she "didn't have the skills" at the time to say she needed a few moments to relax. Now, as an adult — she's 28 — she can look back and understand she was "just overstimulated and probably needed some noise-canceling headphones and 15 minutes, then I would have been fine.
"But I didn't know that then," she says.
Nor did staff at the institution.
When she refused to come inside, staffers grabbed her, which only made her more upset. When she got angry, staff restrained her, with one, two or three staffers holding her down. That only upset her more.
There were times when she was held down for long periods of time — an hour or more, she says — which triggered rules that she needed to go to the hospital, because prolonged restraint can cause injuries and be dangerous.
Eventually, episodes like this got her sent to the next institution.
Restraint and other punishments are used to control children when they have explosive outbursts, but recent brain science shows those techniques can harm children. They create stress that put a child's body on alert and trigger additional explosive outbursts that the child can't control.
The foster care community, with long ties to institutional care, has been slow to change.
At school, JoJo Kimble got accommodations for her autism.
But in foster care in South Carolina, that autism diagnosis got erased.
She was 15. Suddenly, she got labeled as having bipolar disorder instead.
"It's easier to treat," she says. "You can't treat autism with medication. You can treat depression, the symptoms of depression … with medication and all types of therapy."
Kimble said with the new label she was sent to a series of institutions, including therapeutic group homes and psychiatric hospitals.
Now, at 23, she's out of foster care and back into the separately funded and operated system of public services that treat people with developmental disabilities like autism.
As a result: She lives on her own now. She's in college and studying to become a nurse. She's helping a professor research the impact of childhood cancer on families.
Rasheeda McCrae, who is legally blind, says when she went into foster care at 14, her case manager put a priority on getting a roof over her head but didn't pay much attention to her disabilities.
McCrae has low vision, the result of being physically abused when she was a baby, and behavioral health issues.
She moved in with a Baltimore foster mother in a dark house with several flights of steps that were difficult to maneuver.
Her caseworker, says McCrae, now 35, took her to the home with McCrae's two trash bags of her clothes.
"She didn't even go upstairs," McCrae recalls. "She just came in, dropped my bags, dropped me, did the paperwork and left."
The foster mother was kind but didn't know how to include her blind foster daughter. The other children in the house watched TV together and rode bikes.
"But for me," McCrae says, "I just stayed in my room because I felt uncomfortable and different from everybody else."
After two years with the foster family, she moved to live with an aunt.
Adriene Caldwell, who was 12 when she went into foster care in Texas, says her foster mother was cruel. The woman and her children lived in the nice part of the house and the foster girls — three to five at a time — ate dinner separately in the basement.
"We were second class," says Caldwell, who writes about her experience in a memoir published this year, Unbroken: Life Outside the Lines. "We had to sit on the floor. We were considered dirty. We were not allowed on the furniture."
Caldwell says she went into foster care diagnosed with mild depression and obsessive compulsive disorder. But the foster mother's treatment and cutting remarks increased her depression, and, at one point, Caldwell tried to end her life.
Caldwell, now 46, says the process for reimbursing foster parents gave them little incentive to help children succeed.
"The higher the emotional needs, the higher the payment," she says of what her foster mother was paid.
Other former foster youth with disabilities spoke of positive experiences — especially those who lived in family foster homes.
In Iowa, Samanthya Marlatt was placed with foster parents who were both blind.
"Having a foster parent with a disability was, like, really cool for me to see," she says.
Marlatt has a different disability: cerebral palsy, for which she wore leg braces. It's hard for her to walk long distances.
She watched how her foster parents advocated for themselves to get accommodations that helped them work and live. They got the city to install beeping signals at the crosswalks near their home. They used guide dogs.
From that blind couple, Marlatt says she learned how to advocate for herself.
She and her husband have tickets to a play coming to Ames and she knew to ask for seats where there was a handrail to make it easier to reach.
"It was cool because I saw that, in real time, all of the things they were able to do," says Marlatt. "And then I was able to remember I could do those things, too."
Learning to advocate for herself was contrary, she says, to the lesson she and most kids in foster care learn.
"And this is a big thing in foster care," she says. "I didn't want to ruffle any feathers because I was always afraid of being moved out of where I was and being put in group care. And I really didn't want to be in group care. So if I didn't make a fuss, then I would be fine."
Later, Marlatt became a foster parent herself.
Now she's raising her own daughters. She's in school, completing a master's degree to become a clinical mental health counselor.
Other former foster youth spoke of adults who made a difference: The staffer at the residential center who listened, or a doctor who made the right diagnosis, or a caseworker who kept someone in a family home.
But often, that key adult was someone totally outside the foster care system.
Like for Marissa Pike, the woman with autism from Massachusetts.
"I was 14 or 15," she remembers. "I was walking back from something one day and I met this random lady and I started talking to her."
That "random lady" and Pike became friends. She was the one who spotted Pike's Autism Spectrum Disorder.
The woman called Pike's caseworker and said, "My boss has a son with Asperger's," a term used then for a form of autism. "Marissa presents a lot like him."
Pike says getting the proper diagnosis changed her life.
Now Pike's a foster parent. She was named Foster Parent of the Year in Lynn, Massachusetts, last year. She's adopted two of those kids she once fostered.
At night, she rides ambulances as an emergency medical technician. She's in school, too, getting her master's degree in social work.
Tyrome Laundersville – who missed his parents in Iowa – is another example of someone who got key help from an adult outside the foster care system.
He became homeless when, at 18, he left foster care.
The mother of two friends at his high school invited him to live with them.
"She treated me like a human being. She had a big heart," he says.
That woman was very poor then, he says. She had trouble heating her run-down farmhouse in the winter.
"She made me the person I am today," he says. "She taught me how to cook, how to ride the bus, how to use a checkbook, how to apply for a job — things that he says he wasn't taught when he was in foster care, living in residential treatment centers.
She helped him finally figure out how to regulate his behaviors, which were still a problem when he aged out of foster care.
"I had behaviors. I had everything that I had in placement — the aggression, the property destruction," he explains.
"But she lived on a farm. And she told me: 'If you're going to break my s***, go out to the barn. So I would go out to the barn and punch hay bales and do all of that. And, honestly, she gave me a space to where I could let out my anger and figure out myself and how to control myself while also still supporting me and being that loving person."
Today, Laundersville lives on his own. He's in college, too.
He wants a job where he can change policy for helping foster youth.
That's something these disabled former foster youth share in common: They want to use their lived experience to make foster care a better experience for the children and youth who go there now.

- The claim that an all-female team led the botched execution of the Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike on Sept. 30, 2026, is still under investigation.
- Pike was taken to a hospital after she appeared to survive receiving two doses of the sedative pentobarbital.
- While Pike's lawyer later appeared to confirm that Pike's reported request for an all-female team to administer her lethal injection had been fulfilled, local media reported that a male doctor had administered Pike's injections or overseen the attempted execution.
- Because of the lack of confirmation from official sources to settle those conflicting claims, we could not determine whether the team that attempted to carry out Pike's execution was all female. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We contacted the local media outlets that reported the presence of a male doctor at Pike's execution and await replies to our queries.
In early October 2026, after the Tennessee Department of Correction failed to execute death row inmate Christa Pike on Sept. 30, 2026, a claim circulated online that Pike's execution team had been all female.
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death in 1996 for the killing of her Jobs Corp training program classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. She also was convicted of attempted first-degree murder in 2001 after attacking another inmate.
The department halted Pike's execution in the evening of Sept. 30 after she appeared to survive receiving two doses of the sedative pentobarbital. Pike was taken to a hospital and her lawyers said on Oct. 1 that she was in critical condition, The Associated Press reported.
Some social media users appeared to suggest that there was a connection between the failed execution and the alleged all-female lethal injection team. One X user wrote (archived), "I'm just going to say it, I think that the all-female execution team botched this on purpose."
I'm just going to say it, I think that the all-female execution team botched this on purpose.
— Cassandra MacDonald (@CassandraRules) October 1, 2026
The claim also circulated elsewhere on X (archived). Snopes readers searched our site for more information about the rumor.
At the time of this writing, conflicting claims circulated about whether an all-female team had carried out Pike's botched execution.
Speaking at a news conference after the execution attempt, Pike's lawyer Randy Spivey appeared to confirm that her execution team had all been women by saying that the team he saw at the execution was "consistent" with a reported request Pike made for an all-female team.
However, local media in Tennessee reported that Dr. Mark Fowler, a man who also was involved in the botched execution of Tony Carruthers in Tennessee in May 2026, administered the lethal injections or "oversaw" Pike's attempted execution.
When reached by Snopes via phone on Oct. 2, Fowler would not comment on whether he was involved in Pike's attempted execution. The Tennessee Department of Correction also declined to comment on whether Pike had an all-female execution team.
Given the lack of confirmation from official sources to settle conflicting claims, we leave this claim unrated.
The Tennessee Department of Correction had not confirmed at the time of this writing exactly what led to the failure to execute Pike. Therefore, it was impossible to say whether an all-female team affected the outcome of the execution.
Snopes contacted reporters for WSMV and WVLT, the two local news stations that reported Fowler's apparent involvement in Pike's attempted execution, to ask how they knew Fowler was present. We also contacted lawyers for Pike for the latest update on her health and case. We await replies to our queries.
The New York Post reported in September 2026 that Pike had requested an all-female execution team "citing past sexual abuse." Pike reportedly also said that if her request was not possible she would prefer to be executed by hanging.
Snopes contacted lawyers for Pike to access a copy of this reported request and await a reply. Spivey appeared to acknowledge the existence of the request when he responded to a question about it during a news conference (archived) after the failed execution (at 33:41):
MODERATOR: We have a question from Heather Derell. Was she granted the all-female execution staff she requested?
SPIVEY: I want to be careful with that because I understand the rules around identifying that, and I will say that I think what TDOC has said is that they would make every effort to comply with that, and what I saw was consistent with that.
At a news conference on Oct. 1, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said (at 0:54, archived) he had called for a "thorough and comprehensive and third-party review and investigation into the protocol" at the execution attempt. Lee also said that the state's last planned execution of the year would not take place while that investigation was ongoing.
Pike appealed to Lee for clemency and to have her death sentence converted to life in prison without the possibility of parole on Sept. 14. Lee rejected that appeal on Sept. 28.

Delhi NCR-based NBFC Seeds Fincap raised more than ₹100 Cr ($10.4 Mn) in a Series B funding round led by the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, with participation from existing backers Z47 and Lok Capital, alongside Norinchukin Capital and Alteria Capital. The company will use the fresh capital to scale its branch network, enhance risk-management systems, and expand into new markets. “This capital will enable us to deepen our presence, strengthen our technology and people, and expand our ability to serve more entrepreneurs and underserved communities,” said cofounder Subhash Chandra Acharya, who serves as its MD and CEO. Founded in 2021 by Acharya, Avishek Sarkar and Sumeet Dhall, Seeds Fincap provides credit products ranging from ₹50,000-1 Lakh to underserved individuals and micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises. The startup utilises a proprietary, cash-flow-driven assessment approach to underwriting, supported by technology and field operations. It claims to have been profitable in both FY25 and FY26 with total disbursements of approximately ₹620 Cr in FY26. According to the company, it has ₹722 Cr in assets under management (AUM) and is now targeting ₹1,000 Cr in AUM by March 2027. Furthermore, the startup claims to have 164 branches with over 70,000 active members, as of August 2026. Lending tech startups are expected to account for more than half of India’s fintech market, which is projected to grow to generate over $250 Bn in revenue by 2030, driven by rising credit adoption. Furthermore, some of the more mature players in the space are finally hitting the public markets too. In recent days, SEBI cleared the proposed IPO of Social Worth Technologies, the parent company of lending tech startup Fibe (formerly EarlySalary), while digital lending unicorn Moneyview completed its stock market debut. Earlier in the year, Kissht and Aye Finance also listed publicly.

The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.
The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.
Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.
When we talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project, but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that the Shield is still being actively manufactured and that the company sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.

Kartal wins again as Zverev sets up Djokovic tie
- Published
Great Britain's Sonay Kartal maintained her winning return to the WTA Tour with an impressive straight-set victory over home hope Wang Xinyu at the China Open.
Kartal, 24, produced a dominant display to see off the Chinese 31st seed Wang 6-3 6-2 in only her second tour match after six months out with a back injury.
She was expected to face newly crowned world number one Elena Rybakina in the last 32, but the top seed from Kazakhstan fell to a shock three-set defeat by Armenian world number 118 Alina Charaeva.
Elsewhere, men's top seed Alexander Zverev cruised past China's Juncheng Shang 6-0 6-3 to book a quarter-final against Novak Djokovic.

  - Published2 days ago
- 'Just a number' - Rybakina's rise to world number one 
  - Published9 September
- Sabalenka 'trying hard to be easier on myself'

Kartal made the quarter-finals in Beijing in 2025 but had slipped down to 129 in the world after missing the majority of this season, including the past three Grand Slam tournaments.
She retired injured from a last-16 clash against Rybakina at Indian Wells in March and did not return to competitive action until last month's Billie Jean King Cup Finals.
Yet after earning a comfortable win over Spain's Andrea Lazaro Garcia on her return to tour duty at the China Open, Kartal followed that up with a clinical performance in beating Wang.
She produced 12 winners and made just 11 unforced errors, compared to her opponent's 24, converting five of her 14 break points with some impressive groundstrokes.
"I am super happy to play here and I think that shows in my tennis," Kartal said in her on-court interview, as she recalled her run to last year's quarter-final.
"I've had a long time out but I am happy to make a return to this event - I am looking to equal or hopefully do better this year."
To do that, Kartal would have been preparing herself to face Rybakina, but the US Open champion was well below her best in a disappointing 6-3 4-6 3-6 defeat by unseeded Charaeva, who had never before faced a top 20 player on the WTA Tour.
Meanwhile, Kartal's British team-mate Harriet Dart produced an encouraging display in a three-set defeat by American 10th seed Iva Jovic.
The 30-year-old British qualifier looked capable of causing an upset after claiming three breaks of serve in the opening set to charge into an early lead before eventually losing out 2-6 6-3 6-3 to the rising 18-year-old.
Zverev into last eight as Sinner puts off comeback
Zverev maintained his fine form in a season that has seen the German win his first two Grand Slam titles - the French Open and US Open - to set up a tantalising clash with Djokovic on Sunday.
Djokovic, 39, has won the China Open six times and has never lost a match at the event in Beijing, but Zverev knows that he will rise to number one in the world for the first time in his career should he win the China Open and Shanghai Masters, which starts on Wednesday (7 October).
The 29-year-old German's chances were boosted on Saturday when current world number one Jannik Sinner announced his decision to withdraw from the Shanghai Masters.
Italian Sinner is recovering from a knee injury and has not played since beating Zverev in the final of Wimbledon in July.
Sinner took the number one spot in April from Spain's Carlos Alcaraz, who returned from four months out with a wrist injury at the US Open in September.
World number three Alcaraz made it through to the quarter-finals of the Japan Open in Tokyo in Saturday, saving four set points in the opener against Italian Matteo Arnaldi before powering back to win 7-6 (8-6) 6-1.
Alcaraz will next play Canadian Denis Shapovalov following his 7-5 3-6 6-4 victory over Chile's Alejandro Tabilo.

British police arrested five men Sunday on suspicion of terrorism near a U.K. air base used for U.S. operations in Iran, as President Trump said the suspects had been under investigation.
The latest: "Working with Britain, it was an amazing job," Trump told reporters Sunday morning. "We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great and we got them."
The big picture: Officials declared a major incident and set up roadblocks overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England.
The incident, which British investigators did not immediately link to Tehran, comes one day after Trump said he'd rejected the latest Iranian proposal to end the war — though he told Axios's Barak Ravid on Sunday that he expects fresh talks this week.
State of play: Police received a call around 12.45 a.m. Sunday local time relating to "three suspicious vehicles" that appeared to be traveling towards the air base used by the U.S. 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron, per a Metropolitan Police statement.
Armed officers responded in the area of Whelford, a village some 33 miles from the city of Oxford. There they arrested the men "on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act" and they were further arrested "on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act," according to the statement.
Zoom in: U.K. counter-terrorism official Vicki Evans said officers established a 400-meter cordon (roughly a quarter-mile) around vehicles in the area while the British Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit conducted examinations.
"As a precaution, around 85 households have been evacuated whilst these examinations take place," she said in a statement.
A nearby leisure centre was opened for people evacuated from the area.
Context: RAF Fairford is the U.S. Air Force's preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe and supports a variety of missions and exercises throughout the year, according to the Air Force.
Flashback: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned in July that any base used for attacks on Iranian territory would be considered a "legitimate target" in a statement that specifically referenced U.S. B-1 bombers flying from RAF Fairford.
What they're saying: The 501st Combat Support Wing told Axios that no U.S. Air Force personnel were involved in the incident.
"The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," the statement said. "We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities."
Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

The Trump administration published a final rule aimed at lowering Medicare prices for drugs administered in doctor offices, but it applies to only four companies and saves 96% less than initial proposal, STAT notes. The Global Benchmark for Efficient Drug Pricing, or GLOBE, is one of two mandatory pilot programs that are part of President Trump’s plan to get drugmakers to lower prices in Medicare to levels charged in other rich countries, a policy generally referred to as most-favored nation pricing. The other pilot, called GUARD, is still in the proposed stage.
An investigational combination therapy from Eli Lilly led to significant weight loss in a mid-stage study, but high rates of people stopping the treatment may raise questions about its tolerability, STAT writes. Lilly tested different combinations of its blockbuster GLP-1 drug Zepbound with eloralintide, a candidate that targets the amylin hormone, in people with obesity and type 2 diabetes. After 48 weeks, participants who stayed on the treatment at the highest dose of the combination therapy lost 23.3% of their weight. That is more than the weight loss seen with those taking only Zepbound and those taking only the highest dose of eloralintide — 14.8% and 11.1%, respectively.
