The US has arrested another suspect accused of smuggling high-end computer servers containing export-controlled Nvidia chips into China.
In a press release on Thursday, the Department of Justice accused 38-year-old Greg Lui of using false paperwork to mask shipments of servers worth more than $300 million that he allegedly knew were ultimately destined for China.
As the CEO of Earthmade Computer, Lui allegedly conspired with freight-forwarding firms in South Asian countries like Malaysia and Singapore to illegally divert chip shipments into China, including Nvidia’s A100 GPUs and H100 GPUs, the FBI’s indictment alleged. These are not Nvidia’s most advanced chips. However, the chips can process large amounts of data and train large language models, which the US fears could pose national security risks if China suddenly gets access to enough chips to drastically advance its AI or strengthen its military.
Emails and bank records exposed the smuggling scheme, the DOJ alleged, which started in October 2023 and continued until August 2026.
One key piece of evidence is a 2024 email discussing an order for 70 servers with export-restricted GPUs that were fraudulently claimed as destined for Malaysia. After “Lui submitted a purchase order to a US manufacturer for 27 of these servers for approximately $7,614,000,” the DOJ alleged that a co-conspirator told a Malaysian government official that all 27 were shipped to China.
A similar shipment of 92 export-controlled servers was allegedly routed through Singapore to Malaysia, then Hong Kong. Finally, the chips went to a Chinese firm based in Hangzhou, the FBI alleged, which The Wall Street Journal last year described as China’s AI hub.
Yet another flagged 2024 shipment shows how far Lui allegedly went to fool US officials.
When shipping 100 Malaysian-bound servers—each containing Nvidia H100 GPUs worth over $22 million—Lui allegedly submitted fraudulent documentation from a fake buyer identifying its CEO as “Jackie Lui.” Three years prior, Lui “purchased the identifying documents of an individual whose identity is known to the grand jury and used this identity to conduct business transactions in furtherance of the export evasion scheme,” the FBI alleged.
In 2024, Lui’s firm allegedly received more than $176 million from the scheme. Payment records from Lui’s accounts with Bank of America and JP Morgan provided further evidence of how he allegedly operated the smuggling business.
Arguing the evidence backs the charges, the DOJ wants to seize all funds gained through the scheme. Arrested on three counts, Lui is accused of conspiring to violate the Export Control Reform Act and the Export Administration Regulations, as well as federal smuggling and money laundering laws. He faces up to 20 years in prison if found guilty of either the conspiracy or money laundering counts, and the smuggling charge carries a maximum penalty of up to 10 years.
Nvidia denied seeing red flags
Lui’s arrest comes after an Nvidia senior manager based in Taiwan was linked to a similar smuggling scheme allegedly run by ex-Supermicro staff in that country.
At that time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urged Supermicro to fix its compliance problem while claiming there was no evidence of smuggling. Since then, as more arrests have followed, Nvidia has pivoted from denying smuggling to downplaying the role smuggled chips and servers play in China’s AI industry, which is now largely powered by Huawei chips. On Thursday, a spokesperson told Bloomberg that “less than one half of one percent to Nvidia products” have allegedly been diverted to China.
“Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has,” Nvidia’s spokesperson said.
Experts suggest that the black market is “hard to measure,” though, and likely much bigger than has been reported.
Increasingly, Nvidia faces questions about its own “blind spots” when it comes to compliance with export controls, according to a lengthy Bloomberg investigation “based on conversations with dozens of people across five countries.”
Officials around the world suspect that hundreds of thousands of AI chips are being exchanged in a sprawling shadow trade likely powering small data centers and potentially even “a handful of hyperscalers” in China. These chips could fill a hardware gap that China doesn’t expect to address on its own until 2030, one “top executive” told Bloomberg.
Rushing to cut off the supply, US officials want Nvidia to voluntarily tighten its protocols and flag more suspicious shipments. That way, the chips don’t end up going to leading Chinese firms that Donald Trump has accused of stealing US technology to quickly expand Chinese AI capabilities, like DeepSeek.
“Government officials and industry experts are increasingly pointing to gaps in Nvidia’s due diligence, questioning how the company failed to catch red flags,” Bloomberg reported. Officials suggested the most scrutinized shipments ought to be facilities in Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore.
Nvidia screens buyers and has blocked shipments when end buyers are unknown, but it’s not detecting seemingly obvious fraudulent shipments that some US officials think could easily be flagged.
For example, Nvidia and Supermicro visited a Taiwanese facility that bought high-end chips that were quickly passed on to a Chinese firm. Eventually, Taiwan’s Coast Guard “noticed discrepancies in shipping manifests,” Bloomberg reported, and seized the bulk of export-controlled servers. However, the FBI alleged that Nvidia could’ve stopped the shipments before they started since the facility “was clearly insufficient to house all the ordered servers.” Instead of exercising “basic scrutiny,” both chipmakers authorized the deal anyway, Bloomberg reported. Even more alarming, in another case, Nvidia didn’t notice that a small data center in Thailand diverting chips was relying on fake leases to purchase bulk orders. Nvidia won’t comment on whether that site was ever visited, Bloomberg noted.
Nvidia disagrees that it could’ve thwarted shipments officials have flagged. A spokesperson told Bloomberg that “a startup’s growth plan in a friendly nation is an opportunity for America, not a ‘red flag’ to be feared.” Most likely, Nvidia won’t turn down orders that don’t seem to fit existing facilities, since “Nvidia-powered servers are financeable asset that help startups secure capital and infrastructure, including data center space,” the spokesperson said.
Most glaringly, Nvidia continues to work with at least one entity that the US has recently flagged as potentially evading export curbs. Nvidia told Bloomberg it wouldn’t comment on whether it has conducted the urgent checks the US government requested to ensure Megaspeed wasn’t diverting tens of thousands of excess AI chips into China. The company will keep working with Megaspeed until it’s ordered to stop, the spokesperson said.
“When the law is clear, American companies honor US laws as they are, not as America’s critics wish they were,” Nvidia’s spokesperson said.
Rather than scrutinize its customers’ orders in countries neighboring China, Nvidia chose instead to make “an internal whitelist of Asian firms pre-approved for AI chip purchases,” sources told Bloomberg.
Nvidia wants more chips in China
Overall, Bloomberg’s report suggested that unless the US specifically bans sales or requires actions, Nvidia will continue doing business that ensures its AI chips dominate the market and power the world’s leading AI models.
Stricter rules are unlikely to follow, despite some calls in Congress to pass laws cutting off China from more chips. Industry opposition already watered down one anti-smuggling bill, Bloomberg noted, and Huang recently snubbed a congressional invitation to testify on the problem.
Additionally, Huang’s growing influence over Trump has spurred the president to similarly relax more export controls. So far, the Trump administration has been happy to let Nvidia police itself while moving slowly to block suspicious shipments, sources told Bloomberg.
Critics worry that Trump’s most recent attempt to rebrand “artificial intelligence” (AI) to “super intelligence” (SI) will only confuse the public even more about AI risks, while serving primarily to make Trump feel like the US has already achieved a milestone in AI that is, in reality, quite far off.
With US firms like OpenAI seemingly losing control of their frontier models, Trump’s understanding of AI risks also continues to draw scrutiny.
But Trump wants to be trusted as the sole authority on AI, no questions asked. At a recent United Nations assembly, Trump claimed his rebrand is simply because the president thinks the word “artiﬁcial” makes the technology sound “fake,” the South China Morning Post reported. He’s used security scandals to argue that frontier AI now goes beyond “merely imitating or automating aspects of human intelligence” and that supposedly makes “super intelligence” a “better reﬂection” of American AI firms; “growing capabilities and potential,” SCMP reported.
Trump officials have already adopted SI as a preferred term. In the DOJ’s press release, Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg declared that “SI is the defining technology of the era.” Even though AI leaders know the term is technically inaccurate, CEOs like Huang and Elon Musk have also committed to using SI.
Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, told SCMP that Trump’s just trying to project American dominance while ignoring risks. By overhyping today’s AI, the president hopes his rebrand will tie his legacy to the moment AI exceeded human capabilities.
Chan joined California governor Gavin Newsom in warning that the rebrand risks heightening “some people’s perception of risk and fear” amid frontier AI firms claiming that the technology could soon pose existential risks.
Newsom outright rejected Trump’s rebrand—describing it as an “impotent and craven failure to address well-documented emerging security and safety risks.”
And “respectfully,” so does China’s foreign ministry, SCMP reported. Both governments have immense influence over AI regulations and will continue using AI, not SI.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

Google took the wraps off its much-talked-about Googlebook notebook recently, with Googlebooks from five leading brands: HP, Asus. Acer, Lenovo and Dell. What exactly is so special about them, and should you be interested in one? Here are eleven things that we think you need to know about the new Googlebook that might help you make up your mind about them, even as the first batch of Googlebooks gets set to arrive in early October:
Table of Contents
Built on Android, designed to work in sync with your (Android) phone
“If you use an Android phone, your laptop shouldn’t treat it like a stranger,” says Google, so it is hardly surprising that one of the USPs of the Googlebook is the fact that it works seamlessly with your phone, provided it is an Android phone. Googlebooks are built on what Google calls a “share Android foundation,” so you can log in to them with your Android username and password, and access apps and files on your phone on the Googlebook, and do much more, effortlessly. We have no news on compatibility with iPhones at the time of writing.
Comes with a touchscreen
While touchscreens were broadly optional with Chromebooks, as of now, all Googlebooks come with a touchscreen display of up to 2.8K resolution. The touch interface is an integral part of the Googlebook experience. As of now, there is no talk of Googlebook tablets, but given the touch UI, we expect to see them at some stage.
Premium innards (Top-of-the-line chips, lots of RAM)
Unlike Android and ChromeOS, which were both optimized to run even on relatively modest specs, the Googlebook is clearly a high-end beast. All Googlebooks have to come with Intel Core Ultra Series 3 or Snapdragon X Elite with dedicated NPUs capable of over 45 TOPS. They also come with a minimum of 16 GB RAM. The Googlebook at this point seems clearly to be designed for high-end work.
…and outards too
It is not just their hardware; the Googlebook itself also has to be made of premium materials, such as carbon fiber, magnesium and aluminum. Trackpads also have to be made of glass, and the keyboards have to be backlit.
A bar that glows!
They might be sleekly designed and made of premium materials, but perhaps the most striking feature of the Googlebooks is the thin glowing bar on their lids. This Glow Bar lights up in different shades when one starts up the Googlebook, shows battery level, and also “supports other playful patterns” on different occasions, such as when one is using Gemini.
Keyboards that are slightly different
While the keyboards on Googlebooks are broadly similar to those seen on Windows notebooks, there are some subtle differences. Keyboards on the Googlebook come with two special keys – a special key labeled G to invoke Gemini. The capslock key on a Googlebook also acts as a Quick Insert key. Pressing it gives you access to a number of features such as clipboard history, instant translation, emojis, and local search tools. There is also a dedicated shortcut key for Rambler, Google’s voice dictation app that’s making waves these days. Don’t get fooled by those classic keys – there’s a lot under the surface of a Googlebook keyboard!
Runs on Googlebook OS
The operating system of the Googlebooks is – well – Googlebook OS. It is a blend of Android and ChromeOS, and was codenamed Aluminum. It is built on Android and has the same security architecture as ChromeOS. Yes, not many prizes for innovative nomenclature, but then this is the tech world which has operating systems called One and Nothing, so who are we to judge?
Gemini is literally a cursor wriggle away
Every Googlebook comes packed with AI and AI tools, and a super special way of summoning Gemini, Google’s AI assistant. You do not need to hit a button; just wriggle the cursor, and Gemini will pop up! Google calls it the Magic Pointer, and it certainly adds a new dimension to accessing AI on notebooks.
All of Android’s apps and a “desktop Chrome” experience
At the time of writing and based on what has been made public, the Googlebook’s main source of apps is the Google Play Store for Android. What’s more. Android apps and games run natively rather than in a special environment (as on Chromebooks), delivering smooth performance. You also get a proper “desktop” Chrome experience, so all extensions will work, and there is also support for Office 365. What’s more, Android apps and games on a connected Android phone will also work smoothly on a Googlebook. Many of the apps are optimized to run on the large screen and come with support for keyboard and mouse. We do not know if APK files can be installed or if apps can be “sideloaded” onto Googlebooks at this time, though.
PC games can be played…but on the cloud!
But what about PC games? After all, the Googlebooks do boast some seriously powerful hardware, including high-resolution displays, flagship chips, and stacks of RAM. Well, at the time of writing, PC games cannot be directly installed on the, but one can stream PC games via GeForce NOW. We hope that changes in the coming days, given Google’s specs and price tags.
10 years software support
Impressed by the seven years of software support on the Pixel phones? Well, the Googlebooks come with a massive ten years of software support. And given that the hardware inside is top-notch and the frame is made of premium materials, there is every chance that these notebooks will stand the test of time.
And one more thing: They are going to be premium devices as of now!
The current set of Googlebooks unveiled by Google starts at USD 899, with some even starting at prices in excess of USD 1000. Given the current hardware and material requirements laid down for them and the trend of rising component prices, it is likely that Googlebooks will remain premium devices for a while. Of course, we would love it if they became more affordable. Premium tech is wonderful, but affordable tech is love.

Latvians vote for a new parliament as fears of Russian hybrid attacks loom
Latvians are electing a new parliament as pro-Ukraine Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs seeks a full term
RIGA, Latvia -- Latvians are electing a new parliament on Saturday as pro-Ukraine Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs seeks a full term. The vote comes as the small republic on NATO's eastern flank contends with growing concern about potential Russian aggression.
A political crisis in May over the handling of stray drones suspected to be from Ukraine brought down the governing coalition that had been under strain due to multiple other issues. The parliament, or Saeima, then approved a four-party coalition led by Kulbergs of the centrist United List party, previously in opposition.
Latvia, like its Baltic neighbors Lithuania and Estonia, strongly supports Ukraine in its fight against Moscow’s invasion. It borders both Russia and Moscow-allied Belarus.
Kulbergs, 47, is now seeking his own mandate from voters.
“I hope we get a good result. This would give us an opportunity to make changes, put Latvia on the right track for defense and economy,” he said outside a polling station in Riga after casting his ballot.
“A strong economy can only bring strong defense, so that is the mission for the next four years if I’m given the right to lead the country," he added. "Our party is ready to make changes."
A multiparty coalition will almost certainly be needed to govern in a splintered political landscape. Parties must take at least 5% of the vote to win parliamentary seats.
"What I want to see is just democracy in action, just people actually going to vote and voicing their opinions on who they want to govern the country for the next term," said Jānis Artis Briedis, who voted in Riga.
Nearly 1.56 million people in the nation of more than 1.8 million are entitled to choose the 100 members of the single-chamber Saeima for a four-year term.
“It’s obviously a very decisive election, and I expect that we’ll vote for parties that will be making nationally correct decisions for the defense and the economy, so I think the coalition will be maybe not ideal, but it will be still OK and we’ll be moving in the right direction,” Reinholds Pirags said after voting.
Concern about potential Russian hybrid attacks — a term used for non-conventional hostile acts such as sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and an array of other methods — has been mounting across parts of Europe in recent months; Latvia, among other nations on NATO’s eastern edge, is particularly exposed.
NATO has reinforced its protection of Latvian airspace for the election period, with Germany sending four Eurofighter jets to Latvia for about a week.
The Latvian State Security Service said last week that it hadn't yet detected any significant or systematic efforts by Russia or others to influence the election in favor of any party or candidate, the LETA news agency reported.
Polls are expected to close at 1700 GMT.

Indian police detain several people in Gen Z-led protests against voter roll changes
NEW DELHI: Indian police detained several people in the capital New Delhi on Saturday (Oct 3), disrupting a second day of protests backed by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party and other opposition groups against changes to voter rolls.
The protesters say the changes benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing party and are demanding the resignation of India's election chief.
The demonstrations mark the latest in a series of youth-led protests that have emerged this year, putting pressure on Modi unprecedented in his 12 years in power.
About 100 demonstrators removed security barricades on Saturday and chanted "vote thief, leave the post" and "Gyanesh Kumar, step down" before police forcibly detained some of them.
Independent Member of Parliament Kapil Sibal, left-wing All India Students' Association President Neha Bora and political activists Prashant Bhushan and Yogendra Yadav were among the protesters, according to a Reuters witness.
The police declined comment on the number and identity of those detained.
"First they removed people from the voters list and now they are not letting us raise our voice against this. This is not acceptable," Bora told Reuters.
The chief of the Election Commission, Kumar, has not commented on the protests and the demands to step down.
On Friday, police stopped a group of protesters from gathering, bundling them into buses. Several nearby metro stations remained shut amid tight security.
Though police released many of those detained on Friday, they charged several of them with allegedly violating orders banning mass gatherings in Delhi, according to a police source.
Critics say a nationwide voter-verification exercise launched last year has led to millions of eligible voters being removed from electoral rolls.
The commission, long regarded as one of the country's most trusted institutions, says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible voters.
On Friday the commission directed officials to register newly eligible voters and those omitted from electoral rolls.

Trump’s “Most EXCLUSIVE DINNER IN THE WORLD”
The latest way Trump is using crypto to profit off of the presidency.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is once again selling access to the highest bidder(s).
What’s happening? On Thursday, the Washington Sun’s Jeff Stein reported that Trump will reprise his 2025 “crypto dinner” later this year, hosting some of the top investors in the $TRUMP memecoin at his Virginia golf club.
The top 185 holders of $TRUMP will receive an invite to the event, which the website describes as the “Most EXCLUSIVE DINNER IN THE WORLD.” The top 29 $TRUMP holders will also be eligible for a “special VIP reception.”
What is $TRUMP? As my colleague Adam Clark Estes explained last year, memecoins like $TRUMP are “all but make-believe.” The coin is a crypto token, or “a type of digital asset that’s built on a cryptocurrency’s blockchain, but it is not a full featured cryptocurrency, like bitcoin.”
In other words, buying it doesn’t get you very much — the value of the coin has collapsed since early last year when Trump took office — but it will get you a chance to have dinner with the president.
What’s the context? This will be the third major event Trump has hosted for buyers of $TRUMP, following a May 2025 dinner at his Virginia club and a “crypto and business conference” earlier this year at Mar-a-Lago, where Trump gave a keynote speech.
But it’s just one of the many, many ways that Trump and his family have found to enrich themselves through crypto: There’s also another memecoin, $MELANIA, and his lucrative crypto firm, World Liberty Financial, which received a $500 million investment from a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family last year.
Strictly speaking, as Stein points out, Trump himself does not own the company minting $TRUMP, though he still profits handsomely, to the tune of $636 million last year, from transaction fees and other revenue. And he’s made even more off World Liberty Financial, which he and his sons do own, along with others: $799 million in 2025 alone, according to financial disclosure forms filed earlier this year.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Opinion: A Hawk is not the same as a Hawkeye
Opinion: A Hawk is not the same as a Hawkeye
Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri may not have been exactly hawk-eyed at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing this week when he asked former special counsel Jack Smith if he had gone to an Atlanta Hawks basketball game in February 2024. Schmitt implied that Smith met up in Atlanta with the district attorney who was investigating election fraud charges against then-former President Trump.
Smith said, "I definitely did not go to a Hawks game, I am sure of that," and Sen. Schmitt replied, "I think you've already perjured yourself." Then he called him a "villain" and more names I'd rather not repeat at breakfast time on a Saturday morning.
Further questioning from Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota established that Smith had been to a basketball game that night, but not in Atlanta. He was in College Park, Md., to watch the University of Maryland Terps take on Caitlin Clark and the University of Iowa.
The Iowa Hawkeyes. Not the Atlanta Hawks.
Sen. Klobuchar, a Democrat, suggested to Sen. Schmitt, a Republican, "That might be the confusion over the names of the team, but perhaps you should have looked at it more carefully. … I think people should have their facts straight before they accuse people … ."
The names of sports teams can be confounding. If I invite you to a Panthers game would you expect to meet me for a kickoff in North Carolina or a puck drop in Florida?
But was Sen. Schmitt's misstatement an innocent gaffe to be laughed off, like then-Vice President Dan Quayle inadvertently giving the wrong spelling for "potato" to a New Jersey sixth grader, or was it a public effort to discredit Smith with information that would not be hard to fact check?
"We had information, of course, about him being at a basketball game," Schmitt told KTVI-TV in St. Louis the next day. "My job is to ask the questions, and his job is to answer the questions. …
"But I guess the one thing that Jack Smith and I can agree on is that we're a fan of college sports and college basketball." This is as close as the senator came to saying he'd made a mistake.
For the record: the Iowa Hawkeyes won that night, 93 to 85. Caitlin Clark scored 38 points. And I'll bet everyone who watched remembers exactly where they were that night.

Emiway Bantai is making his Bollywood soundtrack debut with ‘Choozay’, a song from the upcoming comedy film Udta Teer. Composed by Sachin-Jigar and penned by Amitabh Bhattacharya and Emiway Bantai, the track is sung by Emiway and Jigar Saraiya. The song brings Emiway’s rap style into the film’s music and marks a new phase in his musical journey.
Emiway Bantai makes his bollywood soundtrack debut with ‘Choozay’ from Udta Teer; song out now
Featuring Ayushmann Khurrana, Sara Ali Khan and the ensemble cast of Udta Teer, ‘Choozay’ combines rap and melody. Emiway’s vocals and flow form a central part of the track, while Jigar Saraiya lends his voice to the song. The accompanying video features Ayushmann, Emiway and Jigar and reflects the playful tone of the track.
Ayushmann Khurrana said, “‘‘Choozay’ has an infectious energy that hits you almost instantly. It’s one of those songs that brings together so many exciting creative forces, Emiway’s raw and distinctive rap style, Sachin–Jigar’s incredible musicality and Amitabh Bhattacharya’s brilliant writing. Everyone has brought something unique to the track, and that’s what makes it so much fun. I’m really excited for people to experience the song and the world we’ve created around it. I genuinely feel ‘Choozay’ is going to be one of those tracks that finds its way onto every playlist and stays there.”
Music composers Sachin-Jigar said, “Some sounds just have an energy that you keep wanting to return to, and this is one of them for us. We’ve always enjoyed creating music in this space, and our work with Amitabh Bhattacharya has resulted in some memorable collaborations over the years. ‘Choozay’ gave us the chance to revisit that world while bringing something fresh to it. Emiway coming on board was a fantastic fit, his rap style, attitude and unmistakable flow bring a whole new dimension to the composition. The combination has made the track incredibly exciting, and we’re genuinely looking forward to seeing how audiences react to it.”
Emiway Bantai said, “ I’ve been offered several Bollywood projects before, but none felt like the right fit. Finally, with Udta Teer, it clicked for me, it felt fun and exciting to begin with. Stepping into Bollywood with ‘Choozay’ is a really special moment for me. I’ve come a long way with independent music, and being able to bring my sound into the world of cinema feels like a new chapter. Working with Sachin–Jigar, Amitabh sir, and Ayushmann Khurrana has been an incredible experience because everyone brought their own energy and perspective to the song. I’ve always wanted to explore new spaces without losing what makes my music mine, and ‘Choozay’ feels like the perfect beginning to that journey.”
Udta Teer is presented by Dharma Productions and Sikhya Entertainment and produced by Karan Johar, Adar Poonawalla, Apoorva Mehta, Guneet Monga and Achin Jain. The film stars Ayushmann Khurrana and Sara Ali Khan, alongside Raghubir Yadav, Brijendra Kala, Gulshan Grover, Suhail Nayyar, Rahul Bose, Mukul Dev, Ram Kapoor and Supriya Pilgaonkar. It is written and directed by Akash Kaushik.

Here is a story that on the face of it seems so wildly unlikely it can only be true. Indeed, the very concept of a romantic documentary sounds almost oxymoronic, an indication of how much nonfiction films have become synonymous with grim histories full of suffering and injustice. Let’s hope this sweet work, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel (who’s made his share of hardcore, suffering-intensive docs including Oscar-winning short The White Helmets) launches a new trend in nonfiction film-making for stuff that makes you happy-cry.
The basic meet-cute happened in 1975, when PK (played by Chirag Lobo in the film’s extensive re-enactments) met Lotta (Mina Dale) in Delhi. He was a poor street artist, a Dalit, the lowest possible caste, once called Untouchables. The real PK Mahanandia appears on screen to explain how he had left his rural village for Delhi in order to get away from all that caste hierarchy. When he met Lotta he pretty much knew he’d met the woman of his dreams because he’d been carrying a horoscope his father had commissioned for him when he was a baby that prophesised he’d fall in love with a woman whose family owned a jungle. Lotta, a backpacker from Sweden, hailed from a clan back home that owned a forest, so that was good enough for PK to believe he’d met his fate. After a chaste holiday romance bloomed between these two crazy kids, she went back to Sweden and he decided to bicycle the 6,000 miles all the way there from India to prove his love.
As we hear the now elderly young lovers describe what they were thinking at the time, we watch Lobo and Dale act out the journey, with poor PK getting into a few scrapes that set him back a few steps as he plods his way westward. Some of the most touching interludes are the interactions he has with strangers along the way that seem incredibly naturalistic and semi-improvised. Cynics might quibble that one can’t help wondering what darker parts of the story have been left out, and note that the actors chosen to play the lovers are a few notches more conventionally beautiful than the actual people – but every love story has its soft focus, flaw-concealing fudges so we’ll let it slide here.

OpenAI safety employee quits, says 'time for trial and error is over'
Oct 3 : A former OpenAI safety employee who recently resigned criticized the company's approach to AI safety, arguing that a fast-paced culture focused on rapid development increases the risk of failures.
Writing in "I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken," published by the Atlantic on Saturday, David Robinson said AI companies, including OpenAI, were not being "nearly careful enough" and should place greater emphasis on safety expertise and research before developing more capable systems.
• "The time for trial and error is over," Robinson wrote, arguing that advanced AI systems require safeguards more akin to those used in industries such as nuclear power and aviation.
• Robinson said OpenAI relies heavily on what it calls "iterative deployment," releasing systems and strengthening safeguards when problems emerge.
• The comments add to a debate within the AI industry over whether companies are moving too quickly to develop increasingly powerful systems. OpenAI and rival Anthropic have faced scrutiny after incidents in which safety controls failed, or experimental systems behaved unexpectedly.
• Robinson, who said he spent 3-1/2 years at OpenAI, helped draft the company's preparedness framework and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches, wrote: "As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed."
• "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement.
• Robinson also warned that AI capabilities were advancing faster than researchers' understanding of alignment, a field focused on ensuring AI systems act in accordance with human goals and values.

China launches anti-dumping probe into chemical compound p-nitrotoluene from the EU
China has launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals, from the European Union, as trade tensions between the two sides grow
BEIJING -- China on Saturday launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals, from the European Union, as trade tensions between the two sides grow.
Trade tensions between the EU and China have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports. EU measures are aimed at slowing down the inflow of electric vehicles and fast fashion from China, among other products.
The Chinese Commerce Ministry said in a statement the probe was initiated after a complaint from China’s domestic industry.
Preliminary evidence showed that prices of p-nitrotoluene from the EU dropped by nearly 60% cumulatively between 2022 and 2025, it said.
EU trade officials are set to travel to Beijing on Oct. 8 and 9 for high-level trade talks intended to smooth out some of the tensions.

UAE says co-pilot on FlyDubai plane that nearly crashed attacked captain with cockpit's crash axe
The co-pilot has been identified as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami
The co-pilot suspected of stabbing the captain of an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight before passengers and others stopped the attack is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami, three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and Western diplomat, said on Saturday.
The United Arab Emirates said the co-pilot attacked the captain with the cockpit's crash axe and tried to take control of the plane in a "terrorist attack."
All three people who identified the co-pilot spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. The Gulf diplomat said investigations are underway to establish whether he acted as a "lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups."
The co-pilot, who officials said nearly crashed the sharply plummeting flight with 182 people aboard, was barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a separate person familiar with the matter said.
The co-pilot was then hired by the UAE-based airline FlyDubai, the person said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired. Oman's barring of him was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
An official says the co-pilot was born in the UAE
How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators. Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don't maintain diplomatic relations with it. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.
There was no immediate comment from FlyDubai, the UAE government or Oman Air. Oman's government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident.
The co-pilot was born in the UAE and his mother is Syrian, according to another regional official with knowledge of the investigation.
The official confirmed that the co-pilot worked with Oman's national airline but was removed from flying because of concerns that he showed signs of extremist views. He was later moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, the official said.
Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot's motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigation.
UAE senior diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash on Friday called the attack a "dangerous terrorist act" in a post on X. The incident is a test for the UAE government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
A social media account was deleted the day of the flight
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot's background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radicalization," but provided no evidence.
The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarmingly unusual sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilize the plane. It made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Investigators have not publicly identified the object used to stab the captain or said whether it was carried onto the plane or came from inside the aircraft.
Both the captain and co-pilot were later taken to the UAE as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.

Singapore launches matchmaking service for government workers
- Published
Singapore has rolled out a matchmaking service for its government workers, an initiative that comes as the country wrestles with a record-low fertility rate.
FirstDate, which launched this week for those aged 21 to 35, boasts "a different approach to dating", where it uses a Nobel-winning algorithm to match participants to one date at a time. "Swipe fatigue ends here," its website reads.
Participants sign in using the national digital identity system and answer a survey about their interests, habits and values.
FirstDate's launch drew mixed responses among Singaporeans, with some describing it as "dystopian" and others saying they would be keen to give it a shot.
On its website, FirstDate highlights the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage algorithm which powers the programme.
The mathematical framework pairs two equally sized groups of people based on their preferences.
The late mathematician Lloyd Shapley was awarded the 2012 Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences for discovering the algorithm, which has been used in public school admissions, medical residency matching, and dating apps, among other things.
"At the end of the day, I think the experience of meeting someone through an application doesn't change much across the [different types of] applications," Elizabeth, a 29-year-old who works in Singapore's defence ministry and is keen on trying FirstDate out told the BBC.
"But it is nice to know that the likelihood of being scammed is much lower. We're all public servants looking for a partner, right?"
But some social media users say the initiative, which is currently in its pilot phase, discriminates against those not working in government.
Others criticised the age limit. "They are only doing this to raise the total fertility rate. They don't actually [care] about whether we find a partner otherwise.
"Since there are higher risks involved in having kids at 35 and older, the government just writes [the older singles] off," wrote another Reddit user.
It is not clear if the pilot programme will be available to the wider public in future. The BBC has reached out to GovTech, the statutory board behind the pilot, for comment.
The pilot launch comes as Singapore's birth rate has slumped to historic lows. For the first time in the past 60 years, fewer than 30,000 babies were born in 2025.
The number of deaths meanwhile have been rising steadily in the greying nation, hitting about 26,500 in 2025.
In August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a series of new measures to better support families and to encourage couples to have children, including almost S$70,000 ($54,000; £41,000) in financial support for every child by the time they turn 17.
FirstDate is not the first time the citystate is trying to play Cupid to its citizens.
In 1984, it set up the Social Development Unit (SDU) tasked with organising social events to encourage graduate singles to mingle.
Its exclusive target audience of university graduates was criticised as being elitist, but authorities justified the approach saying non-graduates did not seem to have difficulty finding partners. The SDU was eventually phased out.
The next year, the government set up another agency to promote marriages among non-graduates.
The idea of a government-run dating service is not unique to Singapore. In September 2024, Tokyo's metropolitan government launched an AI-powered dating app in an effort to combat the country's declining birth rate.
The app, which is open to single residents in the city, resulted in 265 couples getting married, according to government data released in July this year.
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia in Singapore

Police in Indiana have made an arrest in a decades-old cold case involving the deaths of a young boy and his stepmother.
Michael Jerome James, 35, has been indicted by a grand jury for allegedly murdering both Chynna Dickus and her stepson, Blake Dickus, according to the Franklin Police Department.
On July 24, 2006, Sean Dickus returned to his home and found the bodies of his 10-year-old son, Blake, and his wife, 26-year-old Chynna, according to Fox 59.
Over the 20 years that the case went unsolved — billboards and posters were put up offering $25,000 rewards for information that led to an arrest.
Then, last month, the billboards began offering more. Beginning in September, the reward for information leading to an arrest rose to $100,000. It seems that did the trick.
Now, police believe they have a suspect.
“For 20 years, Blake and Chynna’s families have carried the weight of an unimaginable loss waiting for this day,” a statement from the FPD said. “On behalf of the Franklin Police Department, I want them to know that we have never forgotten their loved ones, and we have never stopped seeking justice. Today’s development is an important moment, not only for our department, but most importantly for the families and Blake and Chynna whose lives were taken from them.”
FPD Police Chief Kirby Cochran said that investigators used forensic science and persistence to bring the case against James.
Grand jury members reviewed the evidence for three weeks before delivering the indictment.
Johnson County Prosecutor Lance D. Hamner said on Friday that the cold case motivated him to become a prosecutor.
“This tragic crime occurred during my first tenure as Johnson County Prosecutor in 2006, and the tragedy has remained with me ever since,” Hamner said. “In fact, a primary driving force behind my decision to leave the bench as judge and run for prosecutor once again was to seek justice in this case. This was something I could not talk about at the time.”
He said during the presser that his office cannot share further details about the evidence leading to James' arrest or the grand jury's deliberations at this time.

No PUC, no petrol: Haryana NCR pumps told to verify certificates before refuelling from October 1
This comes after a directive issued by Haryana transport department on October 30.
Petrol pumps in Haryana national capital region (NCR) districts will be required to verify pollution under control (PUC) certificates before refuelling of vehicles from October 1. Vehicles without a valid PUC certificate will be denied fuel under the Centre’s air pollution control measures.
A directive issued by Haryana transport department on October 30 said that as per the Commission for Air Quality Management’s (CAQM) direction number 101, the no PUC, no fuel rule will come into effect in NCR with effect from October 1.
As per the directions, petrol, diesel and CNG stations will be required to ensure that vehicles have a valid PUC before they are refuelled.
Also Read | Noida petrol pumps face chaos over ‘No PUC, no petrol’ rule
The directions issued by Commissioner and Secretary, Transport, Atul Kumar to the state co-ordinator of Indian Oil Corporation Limited, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum said that petrol stations will use Automated Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) cameras to match vehicle registration numbers with the online PUC database. “However, till ANPR systems are fully installed and becomes operational across all NCR districts, petrol pump operators have been instructed to ensure that their staff should manually verify the PUC of vehicles before refuelling,’’ the order said.
State officials said the government was in the process of installing ANPR cameras in NCR petrol pumps. With ANPR technology, vehicle registration numbers can be captured at fuel stations and used to facilitate verification of PUC status, they said.
The transport department order said that if a vehicle owner is unable to produce a valid PUC certificate, then the petrol pump must refuse fuel and record the vehicle’s registration number for official purpose.
The order said that driving or operating a vehicle without a valid PUC can attract a fine of up to ₹10,000 under the Motor Vehicle Rules. Vehicles found without a valid certificate are to be directed to the nearest authorised PUC testing centre so that they can obtain the required certification before refuelling, it said.

The Transport department has also instructed petrol pump operators to put up prominent bilingual signs in English and Hindi at fuel dispensing points in this regard.
The instructions, the order said, are aimed at ensuring that motorists are clearly informed about the requirement before attempting to refuel.
“The petrol pumps have been directed to implement the measures immediately and submit an action taken report within three days. Any laxity in implementing the directions could lead to strict punitive action,’’ the order said.

On the streets of Barcelona, fiery red and gold Chinese dragons (presumably with very sweaty people inside the costumes) danced among delighted crowds, while Chinese acrobats elicited gasps of amazement as they rolled, tossed and threw spherical lanterns in the air, keeping - as if by magic - the candle inside them upright at all times.
Shanghai made history this week: the first Asian metropolis to be invited as the city of honour to Barcelona's famously rambunctious cultural festival, La Merce. Vast street processions here are overwhelmingly aimed at celebrating centuries-old Catalan traditions. So it was quite something to witness velvet-clad Catalan pipers, sashaying down Barcelona's main boulevards, their medieval tunes intermingling with lilting music that accompanied flocks of brightly dressed Chinese performers.
Shanghai Vice Mayor Lu Shan flew to Barcelona to speak at La Merce's opening ceremony. Chinese and Catalan cultural traditions differ in form, he remarked, but they share "a common spirit".
Spain and China are experiencing a period of mutual appreciation. But that sense of bonhomie is far from shared across the EU.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited China's President Xi Jinping four times in as many years. He's urged the EU as a whole to improve relations with China since Donald Trump's re-election two years ago.
Sanchez's move has sparked resentment and disapproval among a number of Spain's European partners who view Beijing as a strategic rival and possible geopolitical threat to the EU. Privately, they ask if Madrid's welcoming stance - opening up its market to Chinese businesses - is enabling China to become the (economic) enemy within the bloc too.
Pedro Sanchez is not the only EU leader going off piste. Global volatility means other EU countries feel squeezed and exposed and unsure they can rely on America under President Trump. His policy on trade and defence is seen as unpredictable and, at times, aggressive. And so EU member states are selecting strategic partners that they believe suit their national needs, even if that alienates or irritates fellow member states.
So do these new-found alliances risk a permanent splintering of unity in the EU or even Nato?
Spain accused of self-interest
Germany and France - the EU's biggest powers - have just united around a more aggressive approach towards China. They want to give Brussels the muscle to shut subsidised Chinese competitors out of the EU market to address ballooning trade imbalances with Beijing that the European Commission claims have reached a whopping €1bn (£850m) a day.
Other EU countries fret about China's tight relationship with Russia. Beijing has denied helping Moscow's war effort in Ukraine but defence experts point to technological and economic support from China, which they say has enabled Russia to sustain its military assault.
That's why, as Spain enthusiastically courts Beijing, it stands accused of looking after its own, rather than wider European interests.
"It's a bit chicken and egg. Did Spain distance itself from European allies, or did they distance themselves from us?" asks Victor Cortizo, a lawyer and academic specialising in Sino-Spanish relations.
"I think it's more us. It's Spain. But legitimately so. Realpolitik is a thing. If I get closer to China because that attracts Chinese investment and bolsters my economy, then that is strategically more appealing than supporting allies who are also only looking out for themselves."
Cortizo and I were surrounded by towers of crates as we spoke, at the end of the longest freight rail link in the world. It runs over 13,000km (8,000 miles) between Yiwu in eastern China and Madrid, largely bringing car parts and electrical goods to Spain and transporting delicacies like Spanish ham and red wine back to China. The link is a symbol of the burgeoning relations between the two countries.
"Our prime minister has made the decision to pursue national gain over EU relations," Cortizo told me. "Chinese investment in Spain has doubled over the last year alone."
Rising Chinese investment
According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.
Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".
"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.
The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around €1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.
Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.
According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.
China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.
That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.
And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.
"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.
But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.
There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
However, Miguel Otero, China specialist at Madrid's ElCano Royal Institute, accuses Spain's European allies of being condescending and hypocritical.
"France, Italy, Germany, they all have their own strategic relationship with China," he tells me. "Spain isn't going much further. It's been catching up with them." In fact, he says, now that Europe can no longer rely fully on the US, Spain's priority is to diversify. It wants to do business not just with China but also Canada, Brazil, India and Africa. Spain is not China-obsessed, he says.
But there's also the question of security.
On his latest trip to Beijing in April, Prime Minister Sanchez met the founder of Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Ming Yang, which had just had its plans to open the UK's largest wind turbine manufacturing plant in the Highlands blocked on national security grounds.
This followed uproar in the EU after Spain's Ministry of the Interior awarded Chinese tech giant Huawei a €12.3m contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data last year.
MEPs from several political groups in the European Parliament said Spain's contract could endanger the EU as a whole.
"When you introduce a high-risk vendor... we do not just risk a localised data breach, we risk poisoning the well of European intelligence sharing," said Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Pirate Party MEP, part of the Greens group back in February.
Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez, a member of Spain's centre-right opposition party, said the decision puts "the entirety of the EU at risk".
Spain's defence ministry continues to deny there is any risk, but former US Ambassador to Nato Julianne Smith, the co-founder of geostrategic advisory firm Clarion Strategies, warns the episode could really erode European cohesion.
"As EU countries seek ways to hedge against what some see as an unpredictable and unreliable America, they have to be careful not to rush towards alternatives that stand to weaken the EU's collective hand," she tells me.
"Some of those growing relationships, such as Canada's rapidly expanding relationship with the EU, could produce real dividends," she added. "But others, such as Spain's decision to deepen its relationship with China, could further derail the EU's ability to speak with one voice and create added security vulnerabilities for both Spain and wider Europe."
More emerging alliances
Spain is far from alone amongst EU countries in striking up controversial alliances.
Finland has a massive 1,300km-long land border with Russia. This has left it feeling exposed since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Finland already has the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership per capita in the EU. It has the largest reserve military force in both the EU and Nato. It has built cavities under bridges that can be packed with explosives, should Russian armoured vehicles enter its territory. This is a country that believes military preparedness is an existential necessity.
In 2022, it decided there was safety in numbers. Helsinki ditched its traditional strategic neutrality and rushed to join Nato.
Now though, there are fears that Washington might not respect the alliance's mutual defence clause in case of an attack on a member country.
No longer confident the US would come to the rescue if needed, Finland has turned to Israel to purchase advanced defence equipment, including the David's Sling air-defence system and Spike anti-tank missiles.
Finland renewed its contract with Israel at the height of the recent Gaza war despite its government having publicly expressed considerable reservations about Israeli activity in the occupied Palestinian territories and at a time when many other EU countries also feel deep unease about Israel's policies and activities in Gaza and the West Bank.
"There is a sense in Finland that we can't always afford [to have] a moral superiority. Survival comes at a price," says Minna Alander, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defence and Security Programme at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA).
"Finns and political opposition parties do question whether Israel is a country whose defence industry they want to support [because of its actions in Gaza and the West Bank] but the Finnish government has kept out of the debate, saying the deal with Israel fulfils Finland's needs," she tells me.
In the end, Alander says her fellow Finns have "a less sentimental mentality".
Greece's shift
Greece also feels threatened by a far bigger, immediate neighbour. It perceives Turkey as a "constant and significant danger to its national security and sovereignty", Nick Malkoutzis, co-founder of political analysis website MacroPolis, tells me.
In the past, the US mediated disputes between the two countries. Both are members of Nato. But under Donald Trump, Nato insiders say the US is increasingly perceived as missing in action politically and diplomatically, with Washington's focus very much elsewhere.
In late August, Greece and Israel signed one of the largest defence export deals in both countries' histories. The "Achilles Shield" agreement provides Athens with Israeli technology aimed at protecting Greece against a range of threats, including drones, aircraft and missiles.
There is a history of public sympathy with the Palestinian cause in Greece and many people have been sceptical about ever closer relations with Israel. But Malkoutsis says the public and political reaction to the "mega-deal" with Israel has been "more muted than might have been expected".
He says this is because there is a bottom line - a common understanding of the fundamental need for Greece to strengthen its security in relation to Turkey that takes priority over everything else.
With Israel a close ally of Washington, Greece hopes that "buying Israeli" will also help maintain decent relations with the US, even in these turbulent times.
But it's a delicate dance because Greece and Finland both very much want to be seen as "good Europeans", feeding into the European collective, according to Malkoutsis.
He says EU countries "scrambling in all directions" complicate everyone getting on the same page and speaking with one voice on defence and security which is the opposite of what Brussels and Nato say they want.
That said, European countries banding together in smaller groups to pursue common interests is nothing new. The E3 "gang", composed of the UK, Germany and France, was originally formed in 2003 to co-ordinate diplomatic negotiations with Iran in the hope of a nuclear deal. It's now a more ad hoc communication channel for Europe's three largest military and economic powers.
Nordic and Arctic nations have their own formats for working together to promote regional defence, while the "Visegrad Four" made up of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia was for many years a well-known pressure group in EU circles.
However, Nato and the EU are convinced that the continent is under intense pressure, unprecedented since the end of the World War Two. Their leaders say it is time to form a united front. An aggressive Russia growls threateningly at the door, bolstered by Beijing, while the United States, Europe's former best friend abroad, seems, at best, distracted by other priorities.
Splintering, fracturing and rampant "mini-lateralism" will only be applauded by Europe's adversaries, they believe. China and Russia are watching closely.

Germany's political center fights for relevance after far-right and far-left gains
Following far-right and far-left gains, Germany's center struggles for relevance
BERLIN — Berlin's markets brim with the rich pickings of harvest. Picking up her weekly shopping, pensioner Ute Istock quips that the choice of apple varieties is as broad as that of candidates on the ballot sheets in last month's city election — adding that this is not necessarily a good thing.
"Voting has become tricky," Istock admits. "It's no longer clear how a party will end up governing effectively because there are too many parties and forming viable majorities is becoming impossible."
Germany's political center is fighting for relevance after recent electoral gains for the far-right and the far-left.
Istock reveals she voted for the far-left Die Linke party for the first time because she feels the centrist parties are out of touch.
"Voters no longer feel represented by the political center," she says. "This is why we're voting in such a confrontational way."
This confrontational voting sits uncomfortably with Istock and other German voters because increasing political fragmentation, unstable coalitions and a dire economy echo a past that led to the rise of fascism almost a century ago.
It also sits uncomfortably with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) were trounced in the Berlin elections and suffered their worst-ever result in a state election held the same day.
"Trust in state institutions is declining," Merz said minutes after exit polls were announced. "And radical parties on both the left and the right are exploiting this."
Merz's conservatives govern together with the center-left Social Democrats in a coalition of what used to be two big-tent parties with significantly different political positions. They now rely on each other for increasingly slim majorities, and governing together is making the parties appear less distinguishable.
A prominent Social Democrat, Matthias Mirsch, recently complained in parliament how reductive political discourse has become.
He was speaking after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a landslide victory in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt.
"It's damn difficult to govern in these times," Mirsch said, "where things quickly boil down to yes or no, black or white, and the middle ground doesn't count."
Berlin-based communications adviser Maximilian Flügge blames this narrowing of debate and a shrinking political center on the medium conveying the messages.
"Algorithms are simply not made for the political center. Algorithms are trained to promote outrage," he explains. "The political center relies on nuance and compromise — neither of which goes viral on social media."
Despite his party's recent electoral defeats, Merz remains defiant amid speculation that he might be replaced. He insists he'll push on with the tax and welfare reforms he says are needed to jumpstart Germany's economy.
After some soul — and strategy — searching, Merz has admitted that citing statistics alone won't sell it: "We must try — I myself included — to reach people on an emotional level," he told journalists in a recent press conference.
Flügge says Merz's centrist government is too negative in messaging about its reform agenda — in stark contrast to the far-right AfD, which promises voters that "everything is possible!"
But part of that vision includes so-called "remigration" — a policy that advocates deporting people on a massive scale, including immigrants with German citizenship.
And while Merz may struggle to explain his own party's vision, he doesn't hold back when describing the far-right's policies.
"The word 'remigration' is nothing more than a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin color," Merz recently told lawmakers in the Bundestag.
His assertion prompted applause. But it also prompted jeers from the sizable AfD opposition.
Their leader, Alice Weidel, now claims that it is the AfD that is Germany's new big tent party.

Of the remaining 60% that physically crossed Hormuz, most was moved using shuttle tankers, Emmanuel Belostrino, head of global crude and geopolitical market data at Kpler, said in his analysis.
Disruptions to energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz notwithstanding, crude shipments from the West Asian Gulf region, excluding Iran, have returned to pre-war levels as countries cut dependence on oil tankers to navigate through the choked strait. According to maritime intelligence and research firm Kpler, at least 16.5 million barrels per day (mbd) of crude left the region between Sept 1 and 28, matching the prewar average. During the peak of the West Asia war in March, the average was 10.5 mbd.
While 83% of the region’s crude crossed Hormuz before the war, 40% was exported in Sept through pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the UAE without crossing the key chokepoint.Of the remaining 60% that physically crossed Hormuz, most was moved using shuttle tankers, Emmanuel Belostrino, head of global crude and geopolitical market data at Kpler, said in his analysis.Belostrino said more than 70% of the crude that crossed the Strait of Hormuz in Aug changed tankers offshore in the Gulf of Oman.
Crude via other routes made up the difference
Confirmed crude crossings were still more than a quarter below the pre-war level, but volumes moving through alternative routes had more than doubled and made up almost exactly the difference. Saudi pushed more crude through the east-west pipeline to Yanbu, with loadings rising from 0.8 mbd before the war to 4.3 mbd in June. UAE sent crude through the Abu Dhabi crude oil pipeline to Fujairah, where loadings rose from 1.1 mbd to 2.7 mbd.
325 million barrels released from oil reserves: IEA
The International Energy Agency said member countries had released 325 million barrels of oil and oil products from strategic reserves, out of 400 million barrels pledged in March.

The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival.
The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”.
The CAGT, which is also known as the China General Technology Research Institute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency.
China’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work.
This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned businesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers.
Last year, MI5 issued another China-related security alert, warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence.
Wednesday’s alert said academic institutions or researchers should be aware of the 2023 National Security Act, which makes it an offence to engage in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence agency. The warning is likely to send a chill through the UK’s cash-strapped higher education institutions, which have for years turned to China for funding and collaboration opportunities.
The UK is one of the leading countries to partner with China’s higher education sector. In May, China’s education ministry announced 219 new transnational education partnerships, with more than a fifth of the approvals being with British universities. That puts the UK at the top of the list of partner countries, ahead of Russia, France and Italy.
Chinese students are also the largest group of non-EU international students in the UK, generating about £600m a year for the higher education sector.
There has been growing concern in the UK that partnerships with China pose a risk to national security. The 2023 Intelligence and Security Committee report on China said UK academic institutions “provide a rich feeding ground for China to achieve both political influence and economic advantage” and flagged the risk of China “directing or stealing UK academic research”.
In this case, MI5 said that more than 100 academics linked to the UK had contributed to projects funded by the MSS via the front company. The areas of interest were AI, cybersecurity and steganography, the embedding of hidden data in pictures online.
Sam Goodman, the senior policy director at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said UK academics were “between a rock and a hard place” when trying to navigate areas of advanced interest that could be of interest to Chinese intelligence. “There is a lack of a coherent steer from government on something like AI. It isn’t particularly clear on AI at this juncture what levels of collaboration we can have with the Chinese,” Goodman said.
Analysts say the UK should do more to highlight which areas are of potentially dual-use interest to Chinese intelligence and provide more guidance to universities and academics.
“It’s all very well issuing these warnings,” says Charles Parton, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. “Actually far more important, surely, is a consideration of which technologies can be cooperated with China, and which can’t.” He said naming specific Chinese companies as a risk would not help UK researchers to do due diligence on every potential partnership. “The Chinese are not stupid. If they want to hide the origin of someone, they’ll do it,” Parton said.
Meia Nouwens, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said more clarity was needed on the UK side to help guide researchers working in sensitive fields.
Nouwens said: “A problem has been that in the past there hasn’t been a great deal of discussion of what areas of research constitute a national security risk. Without understanding the limits are of what the UK seeks to protect, it is impossible to have a conversation about managing risk.”
The MI5 alert specifically accused the CAGT of being a front for China’s intelligence. But any research institution in China is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. “Research institutes that are conducting research on areas of strategic interest for China such as technology will have oversight from the party-state,” Nouwens notes.
That does not mean any collaboration with Chinese educational institutions is inherently dangerous, but it does mean UK academics working in sensitive fields will feel increasingly uneasy about working with a country that has financially underpinned the UK’s higher education sector for decades.

Hawaii's iconic 550-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch collapses
- Published
Hawaii's famous Hōlei Sea Arch, a 90-foot-tall (27.4m) lava rock structure that formed about 550 years ago, has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean.
The collapse's exact time is not known. The arch was still projecting into the water from the coast of Volcanoes National Park on 23 September, but was gone by 27 September, the National Park Service (NPS) said.
"The coastline flanking the sea arch has shown signs of instability for years," NPS, which warned in 2021 that the arch would eventually crumble, said in a statement.
Located at the end of Chain of Craters Road on the island of Hawaii, also called "the big island", the formation was a popular - and heavily photographed - tourist destination.
The arch is believed to have fallen when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo last weekend.
The park service said earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcano eruption and summit collapse had damaged the cliffs near the arch.
Its ultimate collapse marks "the latest transformation of the park's remote and rugged coastline".
In January 2020, new cracks and instability in the cliffs led the park to close the original arch viewing area, and a few months later, a new viewing area opened at a safer distance, NPS said.
Waves from a tropical storm later that year broke off a chunk of rock from the bottom of the arch.
"This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span," the park service said in 2021. "The sea arch will eventually crumble into the sea. However, others will replace it as the cliff slowly migrates inland."
Thousands of people have liked and commented on the NPS social media post about the arch's collapse, including sharing their memories of visiting the arch and posting photos of it.
"Nothing and no one is here forever," one Facebook user commented. "Millions of years from now the sun will die. Appreciate the good, the beauty, now."

) India is among the top countries with 90% of the world's chewing tobacco-related health burden, and South Asia is the "epicentre" of chewing tobacco, according to new research published in The Lancet Global Health journal.
Researchers estimated that chewing tobacco contributed to 251,000 deaths globally in 2023 -- there were 241 million chewing tobacco users globally, with use peaking among individuals 60 to 64 years old, they said.
The analysis, part of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (GBD 2023) and covering 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023, distinguishes the burden of chewing tobacco from that of other forms of smokeless tobacco, the team said.
"Chewing tobacco is not a uniform public health problem, and our findings show that a relatively small number of countries bear an overwhelming share of its health burden," lead author Gabriela Gil, research scientist at Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), University of Washington, US, said.
"Understanding how patterns of use differ within these populations is critical to designing more effective prevention and tobacco control strategies," Gil said.
The researchers said despite decades of progress in tobacco control, the global prevalence of chewing tobacco use has remained relatively unchanged. Stroke and lip and oral cavity cancer were found to comprise much of the health loss attributable to chewing tobacco use globally.
South Asia had the highest concentration of chewing tobacco use, with 14.6% of people aged 15 years and above chewing tobacco products in 2023.
The region accounted for 2,10,000 chewing tobacco-related deaths -- about 84% of the global total, the study estimated.
However, more than 90% of chewing tobacco-related deaths and disability burden among men was found to occur in 10 countries, including India, Bangladesh, China, Pakistan and the US.
Among women, more than 90% of the burden was concentrated in countries, including India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Indonesia, Myanmar and China.
The researchers said the figures reflect total deaths and disability, meaning countries with larger populations may account for a greater share of the burden even if their rates are not the highest.
Patterns of chewing tobacco use also varied substantially by age and sex.
"These findings show why chewing tobacco control cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach," senior author Emmanuela Gakidou, professor in the department of health metrics sciences at IHME, said.
"Prevention and cessation strategies need to reflect how patterns of use differ by country, age, and sex, as well as the cultural and social factors that shape tobacco use in each setting," Gakidou said. PTI KRS
