Republic of Ireland news conference ends abruptly amid accusations
- Published
For more than 11 minutes of Saturday's pre-match news conference, Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions centred on Sunday's Nations League Group B3 'home' game against Israel in Serbia.
The Icelander revealed that Dara O'Shea - captain in place of the injured Nathan Collins - was not with the squad, as his wife was due to give birth. He may arrive back in Backa Topola prior to Sunday's 19:45 BST kick-off.
Hallgrimsson also gave his thoughts on the strain of this four-game international window and reflected on Thursday's 2-2 draw against Austria.
As the first section of the media conference, which is allowed to be broadcast live, was ending, the mood soured.
One reporter tried to quiz Hallgrimsson on his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday when a co-pilot attacked a pilot on a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane.
The Republic of Ireland manager was also asked by another journalist about alleged racism by Irish players during last Sunday's 3-0 win over Israel in Hungary and refused to give up the microphone.
Promptly, the news conference was brought to a close by Football Association of Ireland (FAI) head of communications Kieran Crowley after calling those allegations "completely untrue".
The allegations of racism by an Irish player comes after it was confirmed the FAI is investigating reports of racist abuse directed towards Republic of Ireland striker Adam Idah by Israel fans in Debrecen.
Minutes before the news conference was brought to an abrupt halt, Hallgrimsson insisted he would not be drawn on either matter and would not "get involved in that as others will process that".
"It is a game with a lot of emotions attached," Hallgrimsson said.
"I haven't read anything and it's not something I want to get involved with. It goes to a process, both in our department and with Uefa.
"Something was reported by both teams so I just hope we can focus on football and football will be the winner after this.
"I have not gone into details looking at this as I have enough to think about."
- Second Israel game won't be a friendly - Hallgrimsson 
  - Published4 hours ago
The Republic of Ireland boss revealed the team have taken to a group prayer before leaving the dressing room before recent games "just to cool our heads before we go on to the pitch" and said that has been led by midfielder Conor Coventry whom he joked is now known within the squad as "Brother Coventry".
It has been a challenging international window for the Republic of Ireland with the Israel double-header dominating discourse in Irish football.
Since the teams were drawn together in February, a 'Stop The Game' campaign was launched by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine to boycott the fixtures in protest of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war.
'Togetherness is stronger than individuals' - Hallgrimsson
Before last week's 'home' game for Israel in Hungary, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the fixtures, saying "it would be wrong to participate" while a vote by players to play the games passed by a "significant majority", according to FAI chief executive David Courell.
There were protests during the game against Austria in Dublin on Thursday, with tennis balls thrown on to the pitch and a protester briefly interrupting the game when he ran on to the turf, waving a Palestine flag.
Hallgrimmson said under the circumstances, it will be a "a big win for this group and the association if we go through undamaged".
"The most pleasing thing for me is to see the togetherness and how they stand up for each other. Whatever they have done, they have done it with respect to the situation, to each other and after this, this bond of brothers will be stronger than ever. All the obstacles this group will face in the future will be lesser than it is.
"When we look back, this camp will be a moment we grew the most and stepped up as leaders, supported each other and stuck together. The power of togetherness is stronger than individuals."

The 31 Best STEM Toys for the Techie Kids in Your Life
Featured in this article
Anyone who has ever watched a toddler methodically take apart a Tupperware drawer knows that many children are natural-born engineers. Your job as a parent is to nurture their creativity … and clean up the mess afterward. I've tested tons of STEM toys with my kids over the years, some with help from other parents on the WIRED Reviews team and some with help from my wife, who is a teacher and can road-test them in the classroom.
Wrap up a few of these STEM toys (also called STEAM toys; we love you too, arts!) for your future scientist to assemble, squish, or dismantle. Hopefully, they'll thank you for the early encouragement when they're older. Be sure to check out our assortment of other buying guides, including the Best Subscription Boxes for Kids, Best Speakers for Kids, and How to Build the Lego Collection of Your Dreams.
Updated October 2026: I've added Gravity Maze, an Engine-Building Kit, and Rush Hour Deluxe.
- Creative Kit Plus Plus Mini Interlocking Building Blocks Set There’s something super-satisfying about these tactile building blocks. They come in a range of appealing colors and have a slightly squishy form that makes them delightful to build with and pull apart. Because the pieces are all the same, children don’t have to spend ages searching for a specific block as they do with Lego. They can pick by color or just experiment, and it’s as easy to create bracelets and headbands as it is to construct robots and bridges. These building blocks were very popular in the classroom with 7- and 8-year-olds. Some kids had fun just playing without something specific in mind, while others planned scenes and put their engineering skills to use to realize them. There are also some instruction booklets with suggestions. For kids aged 5 years and up.
- Sound Stage Qubs Qubitunes We’re in love with this screen-free play stage and speaker for kids. The cute wooden design includes a slot to insert a cartridge and a circular sound stage divided into four sections where you can pop characters on top to change the audio it plays. This basic functionality allows for a clever variety of add-on packs, from stories about quirky characters in the Groblies ($20) to a cooking game called Bernard’s Kitchen ($20) with different ingredients. My favorite is the Little Maestro set ($20) featuring players in an orchestra covering Mozart, Vivaldi, Beethoven, and Bach. The stereo speakers are quite good, it has a headphone port, and the Qubitunes can be recharged via USB-C for up to six hours of play. My wife has this in the reward area of her classroom, and it’s the most popular option with 7- and 8-year-olds. For kids aged 3 years and up.
- Wind-Up Flashlight Ambessa DIY Kinetic Flashlight Kids can build this wind-up flashlight themselves and learn all about electronic components and kinetic energy in the process. The thoughtful design includes 10 separate parts, and there are 16 steps to follow to assemble it. No batteries are required, and the kit is designed to be easy to disassemble and use again, making it perfect for a classroom setting. Our testers were delighted that simply winding the completed flashlight brought it to life (three minutes of winding provides 30 minutes of light). For every kit purchased, the maker, Ambessa, donates one to a refugee child out of school. For kids aged 8 years and up.
- Knight School Particula GoChess Mini I have been struggling for a few years to get my now 7- and 9-year-old interested in chess, and the GoChess Mini works wonderfully. This lightweight, portable board is beautiful to use—the pieces have a nice matte finish and are pleasingly weighty. Once you charge the Bluetooth-enabled board and connect it to the app, you can either play against remote players, against yourself, or get AI-enabled assistance to help guide your moves. You can scale the amount of assistance, whether it’s a little or a lot, and different-colored lights show you the advisability of different moves as you pick up each piece. One evening of charging results in weeks of playtime; my kids will play for hours and discuss each move as they go. It’s great.—Adrienne So Particula also offers a Harry Potter-themed GoChess Mini Board ($350) which appears in my best smart chess boards guide. For kids aged 6 years and up.
- Marble-Powered Computer Upper Story Turing Tumble Turing Tumble is a wonderful way to teach kids coding fundamentals. It combines the simple pleasure of marble runs with a beautifully illustrated sci-fi comic book packed with challenging puzzles. The board resembles a pachinko game, and you have to slot in different pieces to divert the blue and red balls and get the required pattern at the bottom. My 9-year-old spent hours working through the puzzles, reconfiguring this marble-powered computer. As the challenges grew tougher, the whole family joined in to find solutions. Well-designed, satisfying, and rewarding, this is a good pick for most kids. For kids aged 8 years and up.
- Coding Ball Sphero Bolt The Sphero Edu app is packed with computer science lessons and activities for different age groups. Bolt has an 8 x 8 LED board on top, various sensors inside (compass, light sensor, gyroscope, accelerometer), and supports infrared communication. My wife is a teacher and uses this in the classroom to teach basic coding skills, giving students challenges like navigating a maze. She says many kids grasp the concepts much faster than they might with a book or screen, because they can see the Bolt moving in physical space. For kids aged 9 years and up.
- Marble Puzzle ThinkFun Gravity Maze Kids love marble runs, and ThinkFun combines the joy of dropping marbles with a clever logic puzzle design in Gravity Maze. There are 60 challenge cards ranging in difficulty, and you must figure out how to place the available pieces to build a 3D maze that guides the marble to your target tower. For kids aged 8 years and up.
- Endless Building Fun Valtech Magna-Tiles The return on investment with Magna-Tiles staggers me. It's been years, and at 6 and 8 years old, my children can still occupy themselves with these for hours. Translucent Magna-Tiles click together to form both two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects. Younger kids can make a house with a backyard and fences, or ice cream cones. With an older kid, the sky is the limit—or, rather, your credit card is, since there are wheelbarrows full of expansion sets you can buy. My daughter can currently build a full village in an afternoon for her stuffed animals. If these are too pricey, there are alternatives that work just as well, like Picasso Tiles, which are $23 for 60 pieces. —Adrienne So For kids aged 3 years and up.
- Robo Fun Robotical Marty the Robot V2 Combining coding with robotics can be a great way of engaging kids, and Marty the Robot V2 is an irresistibly charming biped with nine servo motors inside that enable him to walk, kick, wave, sidestep, and even waggle his eyebrows. There’s a customized microcontroller inside, various sensors, Bluetooth connectivity, and a speaker, so there’s plenty of potential for kids to code various routines and an extensive knowledge base with lessons and tutorials. Robotical has designed Marty for kids of all ages, so at the basic level, you can use color cards (green to move forward, for example) to control him. Older kids can use Scratch, a simplified coding program with drag-and-drop blocks on a connected Android or iOS device, and when they’re ready to advance, they can move on to Python. Marty is cute and fun but very expensive, though it’s mainly geared toward use in schools, and there are lots of good resources for educators. For kids aged 5 years and up.
- Construction Capers Geomag Classic Magnetic Building Set My entire household found this magnetic construction set irresistible, and there has been a new 3D structure on the coffee table every morning. The kit comprises glow-in-the-dark magnetic rods (crafted from recycled plastic), steel spheres, and plastic bases in different shapes. You also get storage boxes to put everything away in. There’s a guide in the box with a few suggested structures, but creating your own is a big part of the appeal. There are sets of various sizes. For kids aged 3 years and up.
- Early Engineering National Geographic 4-Cylinder Engine Building Kit You can build a four-cylinder engine with this 175-piece kit. It’s fun to assemble, but there are lots of fiddly pieces (tiny screws and springs), so younger kids may need supervision. Once built, simply insert three AA batteries (not included), push the button, and it comes to life, with moving pistons, valves, gears, and light-up LEDs to help kids understand how engines work. The instruction booklet also includes a brief potted history. For kids aged 10 years and up.
- A Twist on a Classic Particula GoCube No one needs a Bluetooth-enabled Rubik's Cube, but once you get your hands on a GoCube you probably won't be able to put it down. Smart sensors inside the beautiful, glowing cube connect to a companion app on your phone and sense where each block is positioned. You can learn algorithms and strategies that will help you get your solve-time down. And if you give everyone you know a GoCube, you can also stage live competitions with friends and family! —Adrienne So For kids aged 8 years and up.
- Sand Castles Kinetic Sand My kids love this moldable sand and have happily spent countless hours over the years making tabletop structures. It behaves like wet sand and never dries out, so you can shape it with your hands or use tools and molds to make castles. It comes in many colors and clumps together easily but doesn’t stick to your hands or surfaces. While it’s generally easy to clean up, it’s a good idea to confine play to a tray or table and supervise your kids, or you may end up picking tiny bits of pink sand out of your carpet. For kids aged 3 years and up.
- Remote-Controlled Robot Wonder Workshop Dash This super-cute robot looks like it rolled straight out of a Pixar movie. With a big, expressive eye atop three balls, it zips around with real personality, which helps it successfully combine play and learning in a way that all educational STEM toys aim for but many fall short of. Dash has lived with us for several years now and of all the coding robots I've tried, it remains my favorite. It’s a durable toy that works on a simple level like a remote-controlled car, but it also ties in with various apps to play games, solve puzzles, and create programs. Lego connectors for Dash’s head add to the creative possibilities. Wonder Workshop also offers some optional accessories. For kids aged 6 years and up.

Congress legislator from Bandipora constituency, Nizamuddin Bhat, Tuesday alleged that Jammu and Kashmir’s dual power structure has spawned a “devil’s authority”, creating administrative paralysis.
Talking to Greater Kashmir outside the Assembly complex, MLA Bandipora said the civil secretariat stands divided with no hierarchy and no link between authority and subordination.
“There is one elite class which is controlled by the Lok Bhavan and another class of officers which is controlled by the popular government. Naturally, there are two types of decisions,” he said.
“This is the first problem, and the second problem is the lack of power with the elected government,” he added.
MLA Nizamuddin Bhat said the Lieutenant Governor earlier held absolute authority before the formation of the popular government.
“He made the law. He broke the law. He could do whatever he wanted to do because there was one single authority. This is the nature of democracy. Now they (elected government) is in power but with limited authority,” he said.
He said authority now stands divided at administrative, political, constitutional and legal levels.
“You have divided the law as well because there is one constitution which is in J&K. We are being attributed to the Reorganisation Act. When there are two laws, there is no need to go to the second law,” he said.
About the Wular Lake, MLA Nizamuddin Bhat said the lake was the largest clean water body in the world once, hosting a larger community. “But when human fiddling, population boom and negligence at the administrative or environmental level came, our natural assets suffered,” he said.
He rejected the popular notion that the lake was fed by the Jhelum, Kishan Ganga or their tributaries, calling them merely flowing streams. “Wular’s source is not in Jhelum, not in Kishan Ganga, not his tributaries. Jehlum passes through the middle. When Jehlum has a level, it comes to the level of Wular. When Jehlum weakens, the ground is visible below. So that is not the source,” he said.
The actual source, he said, was a natural, gushing, oozing spring in the Watlab area that cleaned the lake and maintained its water level as well.
MLA Nizamuddin Bhat said the Wular project was conceived at Rs 360 crore, with Rs 307 crore allocated in 2011 and Rs 120 crore released, leading to the formation of the Wular Development Authority (WDA).
“Then that Wular Development Authority was also divided. So there too, devil authority was formed again. To save this lake, Rs 360 crore was not enough money to make an authority, create human resources, infrastructure, then add inhabitants of the lake. That cannot be done in Rs 360 crore,” he said.
Asked about the Manasbal and Wular development authorities, both linked to tourism and equipped with monetary and human resources, MLA Bandipora Nizamuddin Bhat said the core question remains unanswered.
“Why has Wular lost its size and the level of the water? Why has that declined?” he asked.
He said the government has not adopted the scientific approach it should have and has failed to stop human fiddling.
“Sand mafia is either growing on Jhelum or is growing on Walur. Look at the banks of Wular; they are so deep. The sound of fish is also gone. The sound of sandals is also gone. The water is also unclean, ugly,” he said.
MLA Bhat said he raised the issue at various forums.

The 52nd episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu examines the growing use of artificial intelligence in healthcare, including its potential applications in drug and vaccine development, medical imaging and clinical decision-making.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, speaks to Abdul Gaffur, infectious diseases expert, Apollo Hospitals, Chennai, about the opportunities and limitations of AI in healthcare and the questions its growing use raises for patients and healthcare professionals.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being explored across healthcare and medical research. The episode discusses how AI could help researchers identify potential drug candidates, analyse large volumes of information and accelerate some stages of medical research.
The conversation also looks at the possible use of AI in vaccine development and other areas of biomedical research. While these applications could support research, the discussion examines the need to consider the limitations of AI-generated outputs and the importance of scientific and clinical validation.
A key focus of the episode is the use of AI for health-related information. AI systems can produce answers that appear confident and authoritative but may contain incorrect information. The episode discusses why patients should be cautious about relying on AI-generated responses for medical advice and why such information needs to be assessed against reliable medical sources and professional advice.
The discussion also examines the use of AI in clinical care. AI-powered clinical intelligence could potentially bring together information from radiology, laboratory investigations, pharmacy records and medical records to support doctors in screening and triaging patients.
The episode looks at how such systems could assist healthcare professionals without replacing clinical assessment. It also considers the importance of understanding the limitations of AI when it is used in decisions that can affect patient care.
Data is another aspect of the discussion, particularly as healthcare AI systems may involve large amounts of medical information. The episode considers questions around the use of health data and the need for appropriate safeguards as AI becomes more integrated into healthcare.
The conversation also touches on the potential misuse of AI in biology and why advances in artificial intelligence need to be considered alongside questions of safety and responsible use.
The discussion focuses on both the potential applications of AI in healthcare and the limitations that need to be considered as these technologies are increasingly used in research, clinical settings and the communication of health information.

Ten captive-bred Great Indian Bustards to be released in Jaisalmer on Oct 3-4
Ten captive-bred Great Indian Bustards are set for release at Ramdevra and Sudasari in Jaisalmer on October 3-4 under the GIB conservation programme.
Ten captive-bred Great Indian Bustards (GIBs) are set to be released into their natural habitat in Rajasthan’s Jaisalmer on October 3 and 4 as part of an effort to rebuild the critically endangered species’ wild population, officials said.
Union environment, forest and climate change minister Bhupender Yadav is scheduled to witness the release of the state birds.
As per the proposed schedule, the birds will be released at Ramdevra on October 3 and Sudasari in the Desert National Park on October 4. Senior officials and wildlife experts from India and abroad are also expected to attend the programme.
Prior to their release into the wild, the birds have undergone extensive rewilding training in a specially designed tunnel at the conservation breeding facility, where they were trained to adapt to conditions similar to their natural environment while being kept away from human interference.
The initiative is being carried out under the supervision of the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) and aims to gradually restore captive-bred GIBs to their natural habitat.
Initially, the birds were proposed to be released in Gujarat’s Kutch region. However, following consultations with experts, the plan was changed to the Thar Desert, the species’ natural habitat. Ramdevra and Sudasari were subsequently identified as suitable sites for the first phase of the release.
Final call on how many GIBs will take flight
Ten birds at the conservation breeding centres are currently healthy and considered ready for release. However, the exact number that will be released directly into open habitat will be decided after a final technical assessment by WII scientists.
The birds will be scientifically monitored after release to track their movements, behaviour, habitat use, adaptation and survival in the wild. The monitoring will help conservationists assess how captive-bred birds respond after being returned to their natural environment.
From captive breeding to the Thar Desert
The Integrated Great Indian Bustard Conservation Project was launched in 2016, followed by a large-scale conservation breeding programme in Rajasthan in 2019.
An interim facility was first established at Sam in Jaisalmer before a modern conservation breeding centre was developed at Ramdevra.
The first captive-bred GIB chick at the centre was born in March 2023. The birds subsequently underwent rewilding training in 2025 to prepare them for eventual release into the wild.
Divisional Forest Officer (DFO) of the Desert National Park Chandrapal Chauhan said the release would mark an important milestone in the conservation programme.
“This is one of the most important and joyful moments of the entire project. The birds have been kept away from human interference and trained to adapt to a wild environment inside the specially designed tunnel. Strict protocols have been established under the supervision of WII experts. Releasing the Great Indian Bustards at Ramdevra and Sudasari is a major milestone in their conservation,” he said.
Release plan follows Supreme Court guidelines
The initiative is being undertaken in accordance with the priority area and guidelines laid down by the Supreme Court, covering 14,013 sq km.
Wildlife experts and conservationists said the return of captive-bred GIBs to open habitat could mark an important phase in efforts to rebuild the population of the critically endangered species. They also said the conservation of the GIB is closely linked to protecting the grassland ecosystem and the wider biodiversity of the Thar Desert.

Why am I suddenly buying up every 3D Blu-ray I can find after 3D became one of the biggest tech flops of all time?
3D movies are finally worth watching
It took decades, but the technology is finally ready.
3D movies are finally worth watching
It took decades, but the technology is finally ready.
The technology’s finally ready for 3D movies to shine, more than 15 years since James Cameron’s Avatar wowed me on the big screen and went on to become the highest-grossing film worldwide. Video glasses are giving me the experience I’ve always desired.
I’ve always loved 3D movies, but viewing them was awkward. Walking into a movie theater with a pair of polarized glasses, I would only get half the resolution and roughly half the brightness, since those glasses had to split one reflected image between my two eyes. Almost every 3D technology cuts something you care about in half, whether it’s resolution (see also: Nintendo 3DS) or the refresh rate and flicker you get with active shutter glasses.
But what if you had a full screen for each eye? That’s what video glasses can provide.
Last year, I began testing a pair of Xreal One Pro glasses, which primarily give you a gigantic flat screen, like a private theater, for whatever you plug in. But that screen doesn’t technically need to stay flat. If you press and hold the right button, Xreal can give you independent left and right views for side-by-side (SBS 3D) content. With proper content, you get a full 1080p view for each eye.
There are SBS 3D toggles in popular video player apps for VR headsets like the Meta Quest and Steam Frame, too — and the Apple Vision Pro and upcoming Meta VR Glasses let you natively stream 3D films.
They’re breathtaking.
The water in Moana, a glass-covered clock in Zootopia 2, the helmets in Gravity, suiting up in giant robots in Pacific Rim, lightcycles in Tron: Legacy, comic book panels coming to life in Into the Spider-Verse — there’s just so much more depth to see.
When the ocean parts to let Moana through, it no longer feels like looking at a flat wall of water. It’s a living chunk of ocean with life swimming inside. The Lego Movie went from “wow those are some realistic-looking CG Lego bricks on a flat screen” to “I just got teleported into an entire Lego diorama.” In Avatar, the holographic displays in the ops room are mind-blowing. Even the flat rectangular monitors have 3D layers within.
Cockpits and helmets and Tron: Legacy lightcycles and Mad Max: Fury Road’s convoy of battling vehicles — anything with transparent glass is a treat. There’s distinct detail on the faces inside the glass, the structures outside, beads of water or scratches on the glass itself, even reflections of the outside world, depending on the film.
Billie Eilish’s new concert film, shot by James Cameron with 16 twin cameras including four remote-controlled AGITO camera rigs, looked incredible in the Meta VR Glasses during a brief demo. He got up close and personal with the concert, like few VR concert recordings do. In a demo with the Google / Xreal Aura, I watched a tiny bit of the interactive nature documentary Galapagos: The Last Eden and was entranced by the gorgeous baby seals, the grains of sand in their shiny fur, the fuzzy depth of the hair on their skin.
Regardless of the hardware, it almost feels like I can reach out and touch a character’s face in 3D, feel their emotions and wrinkles and scars more vividly, once they have depth.
Or, in the case of Werner Herzog’s cult-classic 3D documentary Cave of Forgotten Dreams, I could appreciate how the world’s oldest surviving art isn’t flat — the 32,000-year-old cave paintings took form thanks to their three-dimensional canvas. “A bulging rock is now a bulging neck of a bison that attacks you,” Herzog explained to us earlier this year.
When I fired up Gravity for what I thought would be a brief test, late at night in bed, I wound up watching the entire film. It all feels a bit like when I bought my first decent set of headphones — I never knew what I was missing, but now I want to revisit all my favorites to experience them more deeply.
Not all 3D content is equal. Few live-action movies were truly filmed with twin cameras in recent years. In fake or poorly converted 3D movies, you’ll often see a “billboard” effect where it looks like there are flat layers of people or objects in the background instead of true depth.
But the biggest catch is that 3D movies aren’t easy to just buy and play. Even though 3D films are still coming to theaters, you can’t necessarily stream them or buy a high-quality copy. 4K Blu-ray doesn’t support 3D at all. 3D Blu-rays were the last discs to offer 3D, and as FlatPanelsHD pointed out last year, that means most physical 3D movies are stuck in the past at 1080p, 24fps, without HDR.
Even 3D Blu-rays aren’t necessarily easy to find: I had to nab a copy of Cave of Forgotten Dreams off eBay, and paid a pretty penny to ship a rare-ish copy of Into the Spider-Verse from Thailand.
Here’s the good news: The leading headset makers are starting to convince Hollywood it’s time to stream their 3D collections instead.
In 2024, the Apple Vision Pro launched with by far the best 3D movie experience yet, now with 4K, HDR, spatial audio, some (Avatar) films at 48fps, HEVC encoding, free 3D upgrades for many films you’d already purchased in 2D, and exclusive access to the largest catalog of 3D films in existence on Disney Plus. (Modern Disney animated films are natively rendered in digital 3D, and most Disney-owned Marvel films got a 3D conversion to jazz up their theatrical appeal.)
Soon, you’ll no longer need a $3,500 Apple headset to watch those films or convert them from old discs — you’ll be able to stream them with a $350 Meta Quest 3S or $600 Quest 3, as well as the new $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, Meta director of entertainment Sarah Malkin confirms to The Verge.
Meta’s headset will offer 3D movies to subscribers in the Disney Plus, HBO, Paramount Plus, and Peacock apps, she says, with some of that starting later this fall.
And by the time the Meta VR Glasses launch in spring, there will be “hundreds of 3D films available” to rent or buy though Meta’s TV app, as well as some free 3D content. They shouldn’t cost more than traditional movies, either, she says: “Our 3D movies will also be in line with typical pricing for 2D Ultra High Definition (UHD) films.”
(In case you’re wondering, she also says the Meta VR Glasses’ three-hour battery life quote should cover a full 3D movie “watched in Theater mode if starting with the device fully charged.”)
In the meanwhile, I’m experiencing 3D the hacky way: by ripping discs. Every time I walk into a thrift store, I hunt for a 3D Blu-ray or two. I pop them into an old external USB Blu-ray reader, then let MakeMKV spend half an hour per movie to produce a 30-to-40GB multi-view (MVC) file. I pop that into BD3D2MK3D for another 50 minutes per movie to spit out a high-quality 3840 x 1080 “Full-SBS” file that’s half the size of the MVC.
I drop that onto an SD card, pop it into the Steam Deck, plug in the Xreal glasses, fire up VLC Media Player, then flip the glasses into 3D mode. It’s a lot of friction, but for me, the payoff is worth it.
Even though I’m mostly watching old movies, it feels like a taste of the future. But you know what they say: Everything old is eventually new again.

Yemeni army claims 1,540 Houthi casualties as fighting intensifies in Taiz
The Yemeni government has claimed that 1,540 Houthi fighters were killed or wounded during the past 24 hours as the battles raging in the southwestern governorate of Taiz intensified.
The Yemeni army said it carried out 474 operations against Houthi positions, reinforcements, command centres and military capabilities across several fronts, with most of the reported casualties concentrated in Taiz.
Military spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said that the raids included warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and rocket launchers.
The latest claims come as Taiz heats up as one of the main battlegrounds in Yemen's renewed conflict.
Government forces have reported repeated clashes across the province in recent weeks, including around Bani Bakari, Maqbanah, al-Aqroud and the northern and eastern approaches to Taiz city.

ixigo backed e-intercity bus operator Fresh Bus reported a 2.4X jump in its FY26 operating revenue to ₹63.5 Cr from ₹26.3 Cr as it expanded its electric fleet and route network. The startup’s top line grew on the back of a rapid expansion of its bus fleet and routes, founder and CEO Sudhakar Reddy Chirra told Inc42. The expansion also led to the startup’s bottom line for the fiscal swelling 33% to ₹43.6 Cr from ₹32.8 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal. The startup’s bottom line was weighed down by a sharp increase in expenditure over the fiscal. Its total expenses rose 81.4% YoY to ₹107.2 Cr from ₹59.1 Cr in the year-ago period. The jump in expenses in FY26 was primarily linked to the expansion of the fleet, according to Chirra. Lease costs rise with the number of buses, while maintenance, captain salaries, tolls and distribution expenses increase as operations scale, he said. Fresh Bus’ Growth Plans The startup is now targeting a revenue of ₹180 Cr in revenue in FY27, while reducing its loss to around ₹25 Cr-₹30 Cr, Chirra said. Chirra claims that the startup became contribution-margin positive in March 2026, with a current contribution margin of 15%-17%, according to Chirra. He expects Fresh Bus to turn profitable around April-June 2027. The startup is looking to improve its bottom line by reducing up to 30% of its costs by doubling down on larger bus fleets. This will benefit increasing fare rates as well customer stickiness, the founder believes. Founded in 2019, Fresh Bus operates electric buses on intercity routes. It leases buses from fleet providers including Vertelo and Drivn and offers users a digital platform to search for and book tickets. The startup claims to have completed 25 Lakh journeys for 9 Lakh passengers. At the end of the fiscal year, Fresh Bus operated 100 e-buses across 10 routes, primarily in South India. It intends to double this number to 200 by the end of FY27 and broaden its route options to 16. Beyond FY27, Fresh Bus plans to reach 500 buses by March 2028, initially focusing on southern India before expanding westward and then into the north. It expects to reach 1,000 buses across the three regions by March 2029. The startup currently operates at 85-90% occupancy, with around 1.6-1.7 Lakh seats offered each month, Chirra said. Established routes such as Bengaluru-Tirupati, Bengaluru-Chennai and Hyderabad-Vijayawada have repeat ratios of more than 55%. Moving forth, the startup is planning to deepen its presence in southern India, with routes including Chennai-Madurai, Chennai-Tanjavur, Chennai-Trichy, Bengaluru-Trichy, Bengaluru-Madurai and Bengaluru-Tanjavur planned by March. In August, Fresh Bus and ChargeZone expanded their partnership to support 400 additional electric buses, taking the fleet supported by ChargeZone's charging network to 500 buses. ChargeZone will add 30 MW of charging capacity to the 10 MW already dedicated to Fresh Bus. The expanded network is expected to connect 20 cities and 17 additional towns across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana over the next 15 months Fresh Bus had last raised ₹87.5 Cr in Series A funding in August 2024, with participation from Maniv Mobility, Shell Ventures, Alteria Capital and Riverwalk Holdings. The company had said the capital would be used to add 150 electric buses and expand its route network. In August 2026, ixigo agreed to sell a 17.39% stake in Fresh Bus to Twelve Stone LLP for ₹36.6 Cr. Moreover, it recognised a ₹11.22 Cr share of loss from Fresh Bus in FY26.

Prosecutor says 2 Iranian men scouted a UK synagogue for a chlorine bomb plot
Two Iranian men have been accused of plotting to bomb a Manchester synagogue
LONDON -- Two Iranian men conducted surveillance of a Manchester synagogue that was the site of a deadly attack a year ago as part of a plot to bomb it this year, a prosecutor said Saturday.
Salam Ahmadyan, 36, and Rahman Salehi, 34, researched attacking the Heaton Park Congregation Synagogue in Manchester in northwest England and the Jewish Museum in nearby Cheetham Hill, the court was told.
Ahmadyan and Salehi were arrested last month and charged Friday with engaging in conduct in preparation for terrorist acts.
Neither entered a plea during an appearance in Westminster Magistrates’ Court, where Judge Nina Tempia ordered them held until an Oct. 23 appearance at the Central Criminal Court in London.
Prosecutor Mark Luckett said the duo were directed by a third person believed to be in Iran who coordinated plans and provided instructions on making a homemade chlorine bomb.
The defendants were observed carrying out "a hostile reconnaissance within Manchester’s Jewish community," Luckett said.
The Heaton Park synagogue was the site of an attack on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish calendar, on Oct. 2, 2025, when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, crashed his car into the gates and then began a knife attack while wearing a fake suicide belt.
Congregation members Melvin Cravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 53, died in the attack and three other men were seriously wounded. Al-Shamie, who allegedly pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group, was killed by police.
Ahmadyan and Salehi entered the U.K. without authorization in the past six years after crossing the English Channel by boat, the court was told. Salehi was granted asylum and Ahmadyan has a pending asylum claim.
Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat. She also said it was unconnected to a suspected terror plot at U.S.-runRAF Fairford air base, which some officials have said was linked to Tehran.
“I’m aware that the news of this alleged plot coming during the High Holy Day period has caused a great deal of concern," Evans said. “It also coincides with the anniversary of the devastating terrorist attack last year at Heaton Park synagogue and comes in a wider context of increasing antisemitic incidents across the U.K., so we are very aware that this will likely increase what were already heightened concerns amongst the Jewish community."

The Kindle will turn 20 in 2027. Amazon says it plans to celebrate the milestone throughout the year, but to kick things off, it's starting with an entirely refreshed Kindle lineup.
On Thursday, the company introduced a handful of new Kindle models: a new 6-inch base Kindle, a 7-inch Kindle Paperwhite, and a 7-inch Kindle Colorsoft. You can buy Signature Editions of the latter two and Kids versions of the entire range, which include artist-designed kids cases, a year of Amazon's worry-free guarantee for damage, and a year of Kids+, the company's subscription service that offers unlimited access to ad-free, child-appropriate books.
The highlight is Amazon's use of aluminum for the Kindle's construction rather than traditional plastic. The starting tier is plastic, but you can upgrade to an all-aluminum model (Amazon uses 80 percent recycled aluminum) if you prefer that Kindle model and you just want something more robust.
It can get a little confusing with all the different SKUs, so here's a quick rundown:
Lighter and Premium
The base Kindle, the aluminum version, and the Kids Kindle are on sale starting today. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft are available for preorder on a rolling basis and will launch at the end of October.
The base Kindle's screen offers 30 percent faster page turns than its predecessor, Amazon says. The build is a whole millimeter thinner at 6.8 mm, and Amazon cut the weight by around 18 grams to 140 grams. The Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft are both similarly lighter (204 grams) and thinner (6.8 mm), retain the waterproof design, and feature adjustable warm reading lights. The screen refreshes 30 percent faster than the base Kindle, and the screen has a higher pixel density that makes text appear sharper.
Upgrading to the Signature Edition for both nets you the aluminum build, an ambient light sensor that adjusts brightness automatically, an accelerometer that lets you turn the screen to landscape orientation and have the pages adjust accordingly. The upgrade also adds the ability to use a double-tap gesture to turn pages.
Uniquely, the Signature Editions feature pogo pins that let you charge via Amazon's new $60 dock, which props the device up as it charges. There's also a new Page-Turn Cover ($80)—a case with physical page-turn buttons that magnetically attaches to the back of the devices and pairs via the pogo pins, which Amazon says offers page-turn buttons to the vocal minority that still loves them (around 5 percent of Kindle users) without adding unnecessary bulk to the device.
Don't worry, you don't need the case, the Signature Edition, or even a new Kindle if you just want page-turn buttons. Amazon is debuting its own Kindle Click, a $35 page-turn accessory that pairs over Bluetooth for the non-Signature (and older) Kindle models.
Kindle Ablaze
The Kindle business is booming. Amazon's Kevin Keith, vice president of product, says Kindles have seen double-digit growth over the last three years, with 2025 being the highest sales year in more than a decade. He says 60 to 65 percent of people buying new devices have never had a Kindle before, with Gen Z, millennials, and even Gen Alpha driving the lion's share. This past January saw the highest single-month Kindle reading volume in history.
At the same time, Kindles are more expensive than ever. “Memory pricing is a little bit crazy,” Keith says, referring to the memory shortage behind the general price bump on all electronics. Amazon upped prices of existing Kindles earlier this year; the new devices match those prices.
Part of the redesign aims to lower overall manufacturing costs and standardize the hardware. Take the refreshed display on the base Kindle—Keith says many of the improvements trickle down from the development of the Kindle Scribe. For the first time, the base Kindle has a display that sits flush with the body, just like its pricier counterparts. (It previously had a raised plastic bezel around the screen.) That whole front panel is also available in a new color: Ube (purple).
While Amazon has made Kindles with colorful fronts (like the matcha green Kindle from 2024), it hasn't done this with flush displays. That's because simply coloring the front would make the Ube color, for example, scatter around the screen as the frontlight reflects it, casting a purple hue on the display. To counter this, Keith says Amazon developed a new “edge-to-edge” color technology that prints two different colors under the cover lens: the Ube color backed by a layer of black. The black absorbs the light, which solves the problem. Amazon says it perfected this tech in the Scribe and ported it down here.
Color is important. Keith says alternative colors typically make up just 15 to 20 percent of sales—the rest being classic options like black or white—but the matcha green model captured a surprising 55 percent. Amazon also chose that color because, at the time, it noticed a general increase in the popularity of matcha in drinks and sweets (it also noted that folks on #BookTok are reading in coffee shops). Hence the new ube color, which is based on the popular purple yam of the same name.
“We've been tracking food trends, and two years ago, ube just exploded—ube was growing 200 percent year over year,” says Chris Green, Amazon's vice president of design. “We expect it to do far better than the matcha.”
For the aluminum housing, instead of milling the device's frame from a block of aluminum and using a lot of water in the process, Amazon stamps a flat sheet, which then goes into a forge that presses down to create the backplate and sides. The process supposedly takes seconds compared to the hours it can take to machine a single aluminum device frame (like an iPhone or MacBook) saving material and energy. It helps lower the Kindle's carbon footprint, which is now equivalent to 11 hardcover books.
Green says these improvements bring down the device's density. The density of the average human body is around 1 gram per cubic centimeter; an iPhone is around 2.2 grams per cubic centimeter. The new Kindles are around 1.2 grams. Lowering that number can help make the hardware “disappear” during prolonged use.
“I truly want people to never think about the Kindle,” Green says. “I just want them to think about the magical world that the author has created inside of this device.”
For Green, who has designed nearly all of Amazon's hardware in his 19-year tenure at the company (and yes, he says he's embarrassed by the Fire Phone), chasing that 1.2-grams-per-cubic-centimeter target is all about getting the gadget out of the way so the Kindle can mimic the analog calm of physical print.
“More people are reading on paper, more people are reading on Kindles,” Green says. “Is it a backlash to AI? Probably. People are trying to find things more authentic—we're in a crisis of authenticity.” Surveys have shown that overall leisure reading is down across the US, but the people who are reading are buying more than ever.
As for the 20th anniversary of the Kindle in 2027, Keith says the company may roll out a significant refresh to the Kindle's user interface, though he didn't share more. Expect special anniversary editions of some Kindles. When I asked whether we could expect the return of the Kindle Oasis—an asymmetrical e-reader with physical page-turn buttons—Green chuckles.
“The first Oasis was one of my passion projects,” he says. “I loved that. I really, really loved that product. But I was a vocal minority on that—most of the people wanted slabs.”
So, probably not.

Vaccination plays an important role in preventing infectious diseases and reducing the risk of serious illness and complications. While childhood immunisation is a key part of disease prevention, vaccination needs can continue into adulthood depending on age, health conditions, occupation, travel and other factors.
The Hindu is hosting a free webinar, “Vaccines: Armour Against Infectious Diseases,” on Sunday from 11.30 a.m. to 12.30 p.m.
The discussion will look at the importance of timely childhood vaccination, completing the recommended schedule and what parents should do when doses are missed. It will also address vaccination when a child is unwell, vaccines recommended in specific situations, and common concerns about vaccine safety and side-effects.
The session will also examine adult vaccination and how immunisation needs may change with age and health conditions. It will cover vaccination for older adults and people living with chronic illnesses, catch-up vaccination for those who are unsure of or do not have records of previous doses, vaccines recommended for international travel, and vaccination during pregnancy.
The discussion will also address how people can review their vaccination requirements and stay up to date with recommended vaccines.
Speakers at the webinar include Janani Sankar, Medical Director, Kanchi Kamakoti CHILDS Trust Hospital, Chennai, who will discuss childhood vaccination and the practical concerns parents face around immunisation, and Dilip Mathai, senior consultant in Infectious Diseases, Naruvi Hospitals, and Professor of Medicine and Adult Infectious Diseases, who will focus on adult vaccination and immunisation across the life course.
The session will be moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, The Hindu.

“In what world,” New York Gov. Kathy Hochul asked on Friday, “would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang raped while she was intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?”
The Cornell case, explained
A timeline of how a student went ignored at Cornell.
Hochul was speaking about the case of a former Cornell student who said she was raped by several members of the university’s Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. At the time, the district attorney filed no criminal charges.
The case has rocked the nation and forced a renewed reckoning over how sexual assault is dealt with in higher education. While the district attorney has defended his handling of the case, many politicians and legal experts are now examining whether certain details of the alleged victim’s account were neglected, and prosecutors have reopened the case.
Amy Wang is a staff reporter at the Washington Post who’s been covering the story over the past week. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about what allegedly happened on the night in question, what happened afterward, and what we still don’t know.
Since the two spoke, New York state Attorney General Letitia James has also been assigned to oversee the case and said it is now “an active criminal investigation.” As new information comes to light, further legal action could be taken.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation between King and Wang, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
In October of 2024, a young woman went to a fraternity house near Cornell University’s campus. Who is this young woman, and why did she go to the frat house that night?
The young woman is only identified in documents as Jane Doe, so we don’t know her name. She was, at the time, 20 years old. She was a sophomore at Cornell. And around 11 pm on the night of October 19, 2024, this Jane Doe goes to a bar on campus, and then, after that, goes to the Chi Phi fraternity house to hang out with a friend.
She said that she was already pretty intoxicated at that point, and she’d had maybe 10 drinks in about three hours. Her friend at the fraternity house hands her a beer. After that is where she alleges that another member of the fraternity pressured her into taking drugs, specifically ketamine and marijuana, and drinking more alcohol. She alleges that two members of the fraternity assaulted her, and that one of them later sent a Snapchat message out to active Chi Phi members. The message is pretty graphic, but essentially invites them to join in, and several did.
In about three weeks, this young woman was going to go to the Cornell campus police and report what happened that night. But in the interim, what was going on? What was happening?
We now know, based on reporting by the New York Times and CBS News, this young woman was a member of a campus sorority, so she went to a member of her sorority and was trying to make sense of what happened. She was still processing it in real time. She wasn’t using, according to their reporting, the word “rape” or “assault.” And she was also seeing rumors circulating around campus about what had taken place at the fraternity house and was growing concerned about how they portrayed her.
She, in the interim, also received a text message from one of the seven men at the fraternity essentially apologizing for how things went down the other night. She is not yet accusing them of assault, but is chatting, even seeks to reassure him in that first message.
On October 22, she then makes an appointment at the campus health clinic because she had what she thought was a UTI and wanted to be tested because she told the doctor that she had gone through a traumatic experience.
According to the New York Times reporting, you could see her thinking about what happened kind of evolve over those few weeks. She at some point says that this is starting to ruin her life, and she’s sleeping and crying and she’s feeling ashamed. She’s just really grappling with what had taken place, trying to make sense of it. By November 3 is when, according to these investigative documents that were obtained by the Times, she kind of comes to this conclusion that what happened at the party at Chi Phi was assault.
She texts one of the seven fraternity members and says, “This was not consensual. I was given more ketamine than I can remember,” and that she was uncomfortable. A few days later, November 7th, 2024, according to these documents, she goes to the ER and asks for a rape kit. And the following day is when she goes to Cornell University Police.
When she goes to the police, how does she characterize what happened to the police? What does she tell them?
What she tells the police is that she believes she was assaulted, and she tells the police that it had started out as something that was consensual. And then at the end she says, “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped.” She tells police she was extremely uncomfortable and that she kept taking ketamine in part because she thought she might black out and pass out. She had thought of at least two of the men as her friends. After the events of that night, she is then confronted with rumors that were spreading across campus, sort of depicting her as loose and blaming her essentially.
What happens after Jane Doe talks to the police? What do they do?
When she talks to Cornell University Police, they summarize what she said in a six-page statement that she then signs. And that is the statement that is submitted to the Tompkins County district attorney.
And the district attorney would be the person who would bring charges or decide not to bring charges. What does he decide?
Yes, so the district attorney decides not to bring charges in 2024 based on, he has said, the sworn statement that she signs to police.
The DA says no charges for the seven men. Were they disciplined in any way?
We don’t know exactly how each of the men were disciplined. Cornell has said that they faced a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions and suspensions. One of the details that had gone particularly viral about this is that the disciplinary measures included for some of the students to write essays. Cornell has not denied that, but it has specifically denied that the students only had to write essays as a disciplinary measure. The university has cited privacy laws and said it really can’t release any more specifics about how individual students were punished or not punished.
What did Jane Doe do after first talking to the police and then learning the DA wasn’t going to press charges?
After she goes to police, we know she remains on campus and she has to continue seeing some of these men. And she also participates in the school’s Title IX investigation, which takes place over several months and concludes at some point in 2025.
I want to ask you about the DA. He is out in public defending his decision to not press charges in 2024. How is he defending himself?
The DA is a big part of the story. This is the Tompkins County District Attorney. His name is Matthew Van Houten. And he has said that in 2024, based on the written statement from Jane Doe, they did not have what they needed to press criminal charges.
It’s important to note that we, as in the public, we’ve not actually seen a copy of Jane Doe’s sworn statement. The DA issued a press release in which he summarizes that statement. And in that summary, he describes her characterization of this as voluntary and conscious and consensual. That is at odds with some of the investigative documents that we’ve seen reported since then, including that transcript of Jane Doe’s interview with Cornell Police in which she very confidently says that she believes she was raped and even says that she was physically hit during that night.
The DA said that he did not see, before the lawsuit, the screenshot of the Snapchat message where the frat members are talking pretty crudely about the situation, and he also says he didn’t see the transcript of the interview between Jane Doe and police.
We now know the names of the seven men who were there that night. Have they said anything?
The seven men themselves have not publicly said anything, and the lawyers for three of those seven men have publicly denied the allegations. One of them says that his client went into the room, but immediately left and didn’t participate in the assault.
This is a story that is developing very quickly, and it seems like new information is coming out just about every day. What do we know about what happens next?
So there’s at least two things going on here. There is the reopened criminal investigation.
Separately, there’s the civil lawsuit that Jane Doe filed last month, and that is not dependent in any way on how the criminal investigation goes, but that will also proceed against the university, the seven fraternity members, and the fraternity itself.

Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle a mounting housing crisis after government measures were struck down by the opposition.
Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid, and other housing issues, were rejected in parliament on Friday.
Authorities said 70,000 people were protesting. Organisers put the figure at 500,000.
“It’s a shame,” Nando de Anguulo, 26, who joined the protest in Madrid, told Reuters. “It only proves that it is us the people who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, Spanish media reported on Friday, and would be watching the strength of Saturday’s protests before making a decision.
The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta.
Protests on Saturday were peaceful in 50 Spanish cities. In the south-eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and teargas to break up the protests.
About 30 people managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building in the city, before they were ousted by police.
One protester in Madrid, Marcos Sainz, a librarian aged 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000) but that a one-bedroom flat often now cost 1,000 euros – or half the median monthly salary in the capital.
He told AFP he would protest rental spikes “until someone dares to regulate it all as (otherwise) we’ll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid”.
Javier, 31, a solar panel installer, said: “We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.” He added: “I spend half of my salary on a tiny room”.
“What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, an energy that is showing that eight days of people power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government,” Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants’ Union organising the protest, said in a statement.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” she said.
On Friday, Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
Despite the anger of the protesters outside parliament, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.
The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.
News of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.
The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report.

Putin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad
- Published
Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad to have come under direct attack.
The Russian president insisted that Moscow was "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders that it was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030.
Throughout this week, Russia has accused Nato of preparing to blockade its territory, which borders Lithuania and Poland, warning that it would even be prepared to use nuclear weapons if the West tried to cut off Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia.
Nato has sought to calm the situation, stressing that it was a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to stop its "nuclear threats".
Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months.
Last week alone, Poland said a Russian helicopter had strayed into its territory adjacent to Kaliningrad and Lithuania said its population felt "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes.
In a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin told his audience that he believed that international conflicts were highly likely to continue, but would get better as "Western hegemony" weakened.
Although the Russian leader himself began the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, he again blamed the West for provoking the invasion, arguing that Moscow had simply been forced to defend itself and take up arms.
He also insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea.
"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," he said.
Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war.
Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since the war in Ukraine started in 2022. Other civilian infrastructure is also regularly hit, with a key bridge in Kyiv attacked by drones on Thursday.
Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said.
He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea that he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear.
"We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that."
He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled.
Western officials have long feared that, rather than invading Kaliningrad, Russia would use the relatively small distance between the exclave and ally Belarus - known as the Suwalki Gap - were it to attempt to seize Lithuanian territory by force.
Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC last week that his country had made evacuation plans in case Russia invaded and thousands of Nato troops are stationed there.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and that the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful".
Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said that unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used.
He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly be fired at the end.
He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence.
"The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said.

Forget summer camp. Some high school students are spending their summers studying soil, raising animals and learning agriculture – experiences their families hope will help them stand out in college admissions

Some American parents are paying thousands of dollars to send their kids to farm school – where they hope the phone-free experience of mucking out pigs, harvesting crops and chopping wood will give them an edge in the hyper-competitive world of college admissions.
At Vermont’s Mountain School of Milton Academy, 10th-, 11th- and 12th-grade students spend a semester living and learning on a 418-acre campus, with most students in their junior year. The program combines traditional academics with farm work and campus chores, and includes a strict break from technology. Tuition is nearly $40,000, according to the school’s website.
The cost covers room and board, activities, field trips and community programming. Students continue academic classes, including AP Calculus, while spending about eight hours a week on farm work and chores such as harvesting crops, caring for livestock, washing dishes and cleaning classrooms.
About 50 students attend each semester, according to U.S. News & World Report, and about 30 percent receive financial aid, the school’s director told The Wall Street Journal. The hands-on work is designed to teach students the practical tasks involved in maintaining a community. Some arrive with little or no farming experience and have to learn basics such as planting seeds and identifying plant roots, while others learn proper harvesting techniques and ways to avoid back injuries.
The semester also includes a four-day wilderness trip, giving students time in nature without the digital devices they typically use at home and school. A few students told the WSJ in September that they saw the unusual experience as worthwhile, rather than resenting the chores or tech restrictions.
“It’s fun,” student Max Sherman said about washing dishes, while Cassie Scott got excited about being outdoors and told the outlet: “This is the closest I’ve been to nature in a while. I’m literally hugging a tree.”
Meanwhile, student Estela Whitney, responsible for feeding food scraps to piglets and making sure they had water, recalled a lesson she learned once after arriving hours late and finding the animals hungry.
“I’m going to be a lot more careful to not make that mistake again,” Whitney said.
Some students and their parents hope these schools will give them an edge in the fiercely competitive college-admissions process.
At Olney Friends School in Barnesville, Ohio, students use the school’s 350-acre organic farm as an extension of the classroom, according to its website. They apply biology, chemistry, math and environmental science to real farm work, from testing soil and planting crops to caring for animals and managing resources.
The hands-on work also helps students develop practical skills such as responsibility, teamwork, problem-solving and resilience. Farm chores offer a break from screens while teaching students about sustainability and where their food comes from. Much of the farm’s produce eventually makes its way into school meals.
“This type of authentic education is what universities are increasingly looking for in college applicants,” the Olney website states.
Meanwhile, Stephen Turban, co-founder and director of Lumiere Education, sees value in agriculture-focused summer programs for high school students. The program pairs students with Ph.D. mentors to conduct research and write original academic papers.
In a November 2025 article, Turban, who studied statistics at Harvard, worked at McKinsey and pursued a PhD at Harvard Business School, highlighted 15 agriculture summer programs for high school students. The programs, offered by colleges and universities across the US, cover topics including agricultural research, animal science, sustainable farming, food systems, environmental science, food technology and agricultural business.
“Taking part in an agriculture program can also strengthen your college applications. It shows early initiative in exploring an important and evolving field, along with skills in research, data collection, and problem-solving,” Turban wrote. “Colleges value students who can connect academic study with real-world application, and agricultural programs show that you’ve already started doing that.”
But admissions consultant Adam Nguyen questioned whether attending these schools actually gives students an edge in the college-admissions process.
“Admissions officers don't reward expensive randomness. That will backfire, for sure,” he told the WSJ.
Farm schools also offer students a rare break from their phones. Many require the surrender of devices upon arrival, with internet access limited and technology largely reserved for schoolwork.
At the Vermont school, faculty member Bruce Brough said students once worried most about encountering bears during the solo trip. Now, he said, they are more concerned about being alone with their thoughts.
Myers added that the “solo” experience encourages students to consider: “Who am I when I don't have a screen?”

Dolly Parton’s nephew has said he needs more time to get a lawyer in place to defend himself against a temporary restraining order granted to her estate against him.
A serious rift in the country music legend's circle opened and spilled into public view weeks after her August 25 death
Bryan Seaver filed a motion Friday in a Tennessee court asking that a hearing on the order now set for October 9 be delayed by about 10 days.
She's Alive, the entity founded to manage and protect her estate, accused Seaver in a court petition of threatening to commit violence and destroy Parton’s legacy and business empire.
It is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell.
The petition names Seaver, who was handpicked by the star to announce her death from cancer, and his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services.
Seaver's new motion says “the defendants lack any legal knowledge or skills to proceed in this matter without retained counsel or what, if any, challenges can or should be raised.” It says the delay is necessary because the lawyer he wants to represent him cannot meet with him until Monday, and says he won't object to the restraining order being extended until a new hearing date.
Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles, the judge overseeing the case, has not yet replied to Seaver's motion. In granting the restraining order, she said the court took into account the repeated threats cited in the complaint, as well as the alleged demands for payment and Seaver’s “claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate.”
In the petition and other court documents filed by She’s Alive, Seaver is accused of sending increasingly threatening messages starting just before Parton's death. She’s Alive terminated Seaver and SAPS in the week before the petition, saying his “terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable.”
Seaver has not responded to email and phone messages from The Associated Press seeking comment.
Parton was a widely beloved country music giant, philanthropist and cultural icon who wrote hundreds of songs, including classics like “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You,” that earned a total of more than 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams.

On Friday, Amazon committed to donating more than $1 billion over the next five years to communities neighboring data centers.
In a press release, Amazon Web Services’ CEO Matt Garman said that communities would decide how to prioritize funds across “education, job training, energy affordability, water, and energy preservation, and local priorities.”
Laying out other community commitments, Amazon also promised to ensure data centers wouldn’t increase power bills or wipe out local water supplies. Regarding the latter, Amazon promised to be “water positive” by 2030, while claiming that 75 percent of projects have already met this goal.
Rolling out these commitments, Amazon seemed bent on convincing Americans that the swelling data center backlash is based on lies. Echoing Donald Trump’s claims that foreign disinformation campaigns are fueling widespread protests, Garman urged that calls for data moratoriums must end or else American frontier AI might fall behind China’s.
According to Garman, US rivals are trying to “trick us into slowing down,” and Amazon’s commitments are meant to reassure Americans that everything’s okay and that we should instead plow ahead, as Trump endlessly advocates.
However, advocates at Stand.Earth—a global nonprofit that’s been fighting for environmental protections in communities hosting data centers—told Ars that Amazon is the one being “misleading” by spreading “corporate propaganda.” Seemingly in crisis mode as billions of dollars in data center projects have been blocked nationwide, Amazon’s promised donations represent “a flailing attempt at damage control for the harm its data center build-out has already caused,” Stand.Earth said.
Most problematic, Stand.Earth suggested, is Amazon’s plan to back a power plant that experts expect will become the largest source of US climate pollution. Glaringly, Amazon’s data center commitments don’t mention the power plant and scarcely address pollution, apart from promising to exclusively rely on back-up generators that use the lowest possible emissions.

Capcom’s Pragmata might be all about the horrors of AI, but in practice the studio doesn’t seem so down on the tech. During the Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026 programmer Satoshi Ishida gave a presentation with the mouthful of a title: “The Outlook and Future of the REX Project, Further Evolving the RE Engine for the Next Generation.” During the talk he laid out the challenges facing studios producing games at the scale of Resident Evil, which can make even simple tasks extremely time consuming. The solution Ishida said is “successfully integrating AI technology into development workflows.”
Capcom is preparing for a ‘future where we create games together with AI’
During a presentation on the future of RE Engine, Capcom laid out its plans to embrace AI in ‘development workflows.’
Capcom has said previously that it will not use AI-generated assets in its games, and instead would focus on using the tech to make development more efficient. Ishida’s comments seem to lineup, though definitely seem to leave the door open to more extensive use. He laid out a plan to turn RE Engine slowly, and incrementally, into an “AI-generation game engine” building towards a “a future where we create games together with AI,” according to IGN’s translation.

National Conference leader and MLA Uri Dr Sajad Shafi Tuesday said the government must hand over the defunct Salamabad Trade Facilitation Centre to local stakeholders for promotion of tourism.
Talking to Greater Kashmir outside the Legislative Assembly, Dr Sajad Shafi said the infrastructure at Salamabad has been lying unused since LoC trade was suspended several years ago.
“I requested the Chief Minister to hand over the tourism (facility) to us so that we can utilise it. Our local people can benefit from it,” he said.
The MLA said the trade centre was a source of livelihood for many local families before its closure.
“When the Salamabad Trade Facilitation Centre was there, many people got employment. Now they are unemployed. When the tourism facilitation centre will be back, unemployment among the youth will be reduced,” Dr Shafi said.
He said a road being built from Gulmarg by the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) will touch Uri, opening new tourism circuits in the region.
“We are building a road from Gulmarg which will touch Uri. Tourists will come to Gulmarg. Beyond that, there are beautiful places — they will see our Pandu Temple, Chhatti Padshahi, Baba Rangi Imam, Baba Kazi Nag, Baba Fareed,” he added.
“People are tired of seeing Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Yusmarg, Sonmarg. They must come and explore Uri,” he added.
MLA Dr Sajad Shafi said Uri has two hydroelectric projects, one built by Sweden, which remained functional even during the 2005 earthquake as they are fully underground.
“From a security point of view, it is a border area. Operation Sindoor took place. There were many conflicts. Nothing happened to those powerhouses. That is also something to look at. I want Uri to be brought to the tourism map in a new way,” he said.
MLA Uri further said that the rare Markhor species is found only at the Limber Wildlife Centre in Lashipura. “I want to give a huge boost to tourism,” he said.
