Effects of preventive treatment for tuberculosis could start to wane after just one year of completing the antibiotics course in high-burden settings, while the protection lasts for at least eight and 13 years in medium and low-burden countries, a study has found.
Findings published in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine show that tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) offered a strong protection during the first 12-24 months across settings with all levels of TB burden.
Consisting of antibiotic medicines that can prevent inactive TB infections from developing into active disease, TPT is considered an important public health tool for protecting individuals and countries from the deadly infectious disease.
Preventive treatment can include medications, such as isoniazid and rifapentine -- typically prescribed for four months -- and is critical for the World Health Organization's goal to end the global TB epidemic by 2035.
TPT has been shown to be highly effective, but how long this protection lasts -- and whether its duration varies by region or community risk level -- remains unclear, researchers at the US' Boston University and the University of California, Berkeley, said.
They estimated TB risk among people with TB infections in 24 countries and found that TPT offered strong initial protection, but long-term protection varied depending on the burden of TB disease in each area.
"Of 4,66,523 participants from 47 studies, we included 84,128 individuals from 44 cohort studies across 24 countries. TPT was highly protective within the first year but declined over the course of follow-up in all settings, with greater effects observed in low-burden and medium-burden settings," the authors wrote.
The results showed that high-burden countries should consider combining TPT with other interventions to achieve the long-term benefits these medications are capable of providing, they said.
Lead author Lauren Linde, an epidemiology doctoral student at Boston University's school of public health, said, "In this study, our results corroborated something that was already well-established -- TPT is highly effective at preventing TB progression among close contacts and people who have been infected with TB."
"However, our finding that the initial effect of TPT declined so rapidly in very high-burden settings strengthens the case for not placing too much emphasis on TPT in isolation from other interventions that address ongoing community transmission," Linde said.

Police have charged an 18-year-old man with offences including dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm after he allegedly crashed into a crowd in Newcastle today.
Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe was arrested at the scene after the car ploughed into Newcastle Knights supporters, injuring 10.
What's next?
He will appear in Newcastle Bail Court tomorrow.
The alleged driver of the car which ploughed into a crowd of Newcastle Knights supporters has been charged.
Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, has been charged with three instances of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, three instances of negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm and three instances of cause bodily harm by misconduct, according to court documents viewed by the ABC.
Samarasinghe will appear in Newcastle Bail Court tomorrow.
He was arrested at the scene after a car, police allege he was driving, crashed into a crowd at a roundabout on Newcastle Link Road, at Wallsend in Newcastle's west at about 9.30am on October 3.
The crash injured ten people who were taken to John Hunter Hospital, including a 5-year-old girl the ABC understands is still in a critical condition.
A 67-year-old man was also injured and is in a serious but stable condition.
Crowds shouted at Samarasinghe as he was bundled into a police car and driven away from the scene.
Two other people were removed from the car by authorities after the "crowd turned on them".

One imam in Houston has been videoed with some of his supporters calling for Muslim business owners to stop selling haram products, like pork, alcohol and lottery tickets, that are prohibited under Islamic religious law.
As far as Snopes could tell, the request was coming from one individual imam and is not a coordinated or widespread movement. The imam's messaging is directed toward Muslim business owners, not all business owners, and is framed as a request rather than an order. No such wider order has been issued.
Under the First Amendment, all American have the right to freedom of speech and freedom of religion.
In September 2026, a claim spread online that Muslims in Texas are ordering local businesses to stop selling products Islam considers "haram" (forbidden), such as pork, alcohol and lottery tickets, within 30 days.
Multiple Facebook users posted similar captions saying Muslims have "taken to the streets in Houston" and other Texas cities, going "store to store" issuing "threats" of protests or more "if there's a continued noncompliance" (archived, archived).
Snopes readers searched our site and contacted us looking for more information regarding the rumor.
In short, the claim is exaggerated.
Footage does show one Houston imam, Qasim ibn Ali Khan, protesting with signs and asking Muslim convenience store owners to stop selling products deemed haram. One video posted on Khan's TikTok account in May 2025 (screenshotted), that features no signs of being generated using artificial intelligence, shows him telling employees at two Houston convenience stores that he planned to demonstrate if the staff did not remove haram products within 30 days. He did not specify where he planned to hold such demonstrations, only saying they would take place "around the city." Therefore, there is an element of truth to the claim.
Khan posted a follow-up video in July 2025 (screenshotted) showing him and his supporters protesting outside one of the convenience stores that features in the May 2025 clip.
It was not possible to determine whether the stores removed their haram products.
Similarly, it was not possible to find evidence of an "order" being issued — Khan specifically says in first the recording that he has no power to enforce his request — nor evidence of a coordinated, widespread movement to get businesses to stop selling haram products. Furthermore, Khan's rhetoric in the video shows he was making a request of specifically Muslim-owned businesses.
As such, we rate the claim mostly false.
Snopes attempted to contact Khan for comment, but got no response. We will update this article if we hear back.
Forbidden products across religions
Each of the world's religions, and the denominations within them, have different interpretations of religious law.
Using dietary restrictions as an example, Christian denominations rarely impose restrictions on what people can eat, though some practice abstinence from drinking alcohol. Hinduism promotes, but does not mandate, vegetarianism; Jainism requires vegetarianism, among other restrictions; observant Jews must follow kosher; and Islamic dietary law requires Muslims to not drink alcohol or consume pork.
As stated above, the grouping of forbidden practices in Islam is called "haram." In contrast, approved practices are called "halal," which is why some food products have a halal mark.
Texas Republicans, Islam and the First Amendment
Ahead of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, Republicans in Texas have made the idea that Muslims wish to implement Shariah law (Islamic religious law) in the United States a talking point in their campaigns.
(It should be noted: the phrase Shariah law can be interpreted in various ways to mean different things. In this case, Republicans appear to mean fundamentalist Shariah law, the strictest form, which applies Shariah principles to all matters of justice).
On Sept. 6, 2026, Amy Mekelburg — who is known for posting anti-Muslim videos online and who founded an organization the Southern Poverty Law Center considers an anti-Muslim hate group — posted one of Khan's TikTok videos to X. The footage shows Khan speaking outside a purportedly Muslim-owned convenience store. It's likely this is the origin of the claim that Muslims were ordering a ban on haram products.
In the clip, Khan says he asked the store to stop selling products deemed haram and that Muslim merchants should have "a higher standard," but he also states that he and his followers have no authority to force anyone to stop selling haram products:
We can't stop them, of course, this is the United States of America, and people have the freedom to sell what they want, as long as they're supported by the United States government.
Khan is correct — the First Amendment guarantees both freedom of speech and freedom of religion. As Texas Gov. Greg Abbott reportedly said during a September bill signing, according to the Texas Council for American-Islamic Relations, "Texas law and Texas courts govern those businesses and those neighborhoods. No ranting imam can change that."
In the video, Khan also says his request is being made specifically to Muslim business owners, not all businesses, as suggested in the social media posts spreading the claim in question:
Of course, you have the right to sell what you want, but as a Muslim, you should have higher principles, higher code of ethics that are supported by the Quran and the Sunnah [teachings] of Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
Despite thorough searches, it was not possible to find evidence of a widespread campaign making similar requests to businesses, Muslim-owned or otherwise.

The Maebashi Tobi Traditional Culture Preservation Society performed "kiyari" (traditional work chant) at the opening event of the inaugural Maebashi Biennale.
| ZORIA PETKOSKA
Maebashi, Gunma Pref. – The Maebashi Biennale’s choice of opener is unorthodox to say the least.
Standing on a two-tiered structure built inside the atrium of Arts Maebashi is a group of carpenters dressed in haori coats and straw sandals, singing a kiyari (traditional workers’ chant) while rhythmically lifting a massive pillar.
The demonstration is presented by the Maebashi Tobi Traditional Culture Preservation Society and Dot Architects, with “tobi” referring to craftspeople in the construction industry who work in high places.

Byndoor MLA Gururaj Shetty Gantihole on Saturday said the Praja Seva Andolana is a programme that concerns the people, and the public should make use of it. People’s representatives and officials should work effectively to deliver government services and facilities to the common people in a timely manner, he said.
Mr. Gantihole was speaking at the Murgolihaklu Nandikeshwara Sabha Bhavan in Bijur village of Byndoor taluk, presiding over the Praja Seva Andolan of Bijur Gram Panchayat in Byndoor Hobli. He said officials should listen seriously to the problems of the public in the meetings and work towards providing effective and permanent solutions to them.
People’s representatives and officials should go where the people are. The grievances submitted in the meetings should be followed up continuously. This is a people-oriented programme bringing together officials, people’s representatives and the public to redress public grievances on the spot.
Udupi Deputy Commissioner T.K. Swaroopa said said the government has launched the Praja Seva Andolana with the aim of creating a feeling among the people that the government is always ready to serve them by going to their doorsteps and providing solutions to their grievances within the time limit.
A total of 54 applications related to various departments were submitted at the meeting.
Additional Deputy Commissioner Abid Gadyal, Zilla Panchayat Deputy Secretary S.S. Kadrolli and others were present.

The Jammu and Kashmir government has approved the diversion of 51.501 hectares of forest land for 33 projects in Uri over the 2024-25 to 2026-27 financial years, with 20.9352 hectares allocated for the Srinagar-Baramulla-Uri Road, the Legislative Assembly was informed Tuesday.
The figures were disclosed by the Minister for Forest, Ecology and Environment Department, Javed Ahmad Rana in response to an unstarred question by Uri National Conference MLA Sajjad Shafi, who sought details of forest and agricultural land affected by government and private construction in the constituency.
The Ministry said the projects were cleared under the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Abhiniyam and related rules.
These projects include work by the Jal Shakti Department, the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) and the Uri-II Stage-II hydroelectric project.
The government said the diversions were in the public interest and subject to “statutory environmental safeguards, conditions and compensatory measures” to minimise and mitigate their impact.
“Under the applicable provisions, user agencies must provide equivalent non-forest or State forest land for compensatory afforestation,” it said.
If such land is unavailable, the government said afforestation is carried out over twice the diverted area on degraded forest land.
Approved plans provide for 1,000 plants per hectare and 10 years of maintenance.
Depending on the project, agencies must also fund slope stabilisation, muck disposal, wildlife mitigation, Catchment Area Treatment and biodiversity management measures.
The Ministry said compensatory, mitigation and strip plantations have been undertaken near developmental and hydropower projects in Uri through CAPEX and CAMPA schemes, wherever feasible.
The response also lists the Uri-I Stage-II hydropower project and several water-supply schemes in Boniyar and Uri among the projects involving forest-land diversion.
Plantation and compensatory afforestation sites have been identified under approved plans, and the respective user agencies or companies are required to bear the costs, the Ministry said.

A layoff after more than three decades at Hewlett-Packard pushed May Lee into a career she had never planned. At 60, she is working seasonally in Antarctica, where her days now begin at 6.30 AM and can end with a visit to a nightclub despite the sun still being visible outside. Lee worked at HP for more than 30 years before she was laid off in February 2025. After struggling to find another job in the technology sector, she decided to explore a long-standing interest in Antarctica. She had previously visited the continent twice as a tourist but had never considered working there. She eventually secured a seasonal position with Amentum as a supply technician at McMurdo Station, one of the major US research stations in Antarctica. Her experience was documented in an as-told-to account published by Business Insider. The transition from Silicon Valley to McMurdo was particularly striking for Lee because of the strict routine. Most workers follow what the station calls “town hours”, working from 7.30 AM to 5.30 PM, Monday to Saturday. Lee describes herself as a night owl and said she had become accustomed to the flexibility of Silicon Valley workplaces. At McMurdo, however, there is little room for that flexibility. She generally wakes at 6.30 AM, gets ready by 7 AM and walks to work for a 7.30 AM start. If she wants extra sleep, she sometimes skips breakfast. There is no conventional commute either, as people generally walk between locations around the station. Her work is considerably more physical than her previous office-based career. Lee managed Warehouse 120, which handles IT and communications supplies. At the beginning of each shift, she checked priorities with her senior, the station's term for a manager. Workers then came to the warehouse for supplies, while she tracked inventory and investigated discrepancies. She also received incoming cargo, operated a forklift and entered deliveries into the station's database, checking quantities against cargo records. During the early part of the season, C-17 aircraft transported supplies from Christchurch. As temperatures increased and the ice became less stable, smaller aircraft were used instead. Food is another part of life governed by the Antarctic supply chain. Lunch begins at 11.30 AM in the station cafeteria, which has pizza, burgers and a buffet. Fresh produce is more readily available while C-17 flights are operating. Workers call these supplies “freshies”, with some reportedly storing bananas in personal refrigerators to make them last longer. As the season progresses and conditions change, some supplies become more restricted. Eggs, for instance, are plentiful earlier in the season but can be limited later. Lee nevertheless described the food as varied and good. After work, life at McMurdo takes on a different rhythm. Workers are discouraged from staying beyond their scheduled hours, and Lee usually finishes her time card at 5.30 PM before heading to dinner. Limited internet access also means residents spend less time online and more time together. Lee volunteers at the library and hosts an 80s-themed programme, “Ms. Purple!!'s 80's on the 8”, on Ice Radio. The station also has activities including crafts, line dancing, science talks and the New Year's Icestock festival. There are even nightclubs, particularly popular on Saturday nights. During the Antarctic summer, daylight can continue around the clock, creating the unusual experience of leaving a nightclub at 2am while it still looks like daytime. Sundays provide a break from the regular six-day schedule. Lee said she can sleep until noon and sometimes barely makes it to Sunday brunch. She also uses the day for hiking, running, preparing for the week, working on her radio programme and attending science talks. The experience has changed what Lee expects from her working life. After spending decades in the technology industry, she plans to return to McMurdo this year, this time as a broadcast engineer. “I can't wait to go back this year working in a new role as a broadcast engineer,” Lee said. From a reduced foodgrain production target for the ongoing crop year and a deficient monsoon in nearly half of India’s districts to falling stock valuations, Tamil Nadu’s growing share of factory output, and another medal-winning run by Indian chess teams, here is this week’s news in numbers.
Food shock
The Indian government has set a foodgrain production target of 373.93 million tonnes (mt) for the 2026-27 crop year, about 0.7% below the record output estimated for 2025-26. The lower target comes amid deficient monsoon rainfall during the kharif season and the threat of El Niño. Foodgrain production had increased 7.7% in 2025-26 and 5.3% in 2024-25.
The lower target largely reflects subdued expectations for rice and maize production. Announcing the target, agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said crops had been damaged across about 611,000 hectares in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan and Gujarat because of heavy rains, floods or droughts.
Deficient rains
India’s southwest monsoon season ended at 87% of its long-period average (LPA), making it the fourth-weakest since 2001 and the 13th-weakest since 1901, according to the data released by the India Meteorological Department (IMD). The June-September monsoon began with rainfall 35.4% below normal in June, followed by a 1% surplus in July, a 16.3% shortfall in August and a 7.6% shortfall in September.
India last recorded a below-normal monsoon in 2023, when rainfall was 95% of the LPA. The deficit was spread across the country, with 43% of India’s 734 districts recording deficient rainfall. Among major agricultural states, Bihar, Punjab and Karnataka each recorded deficient rainfall in four of five districts.
Silver linings
The Indian stock market continued to weaken, with the benchmark BSE Sensex losing 2% in the first three trading days of the week. The index is now down 16% from its all-time high. The correction has, however, pushed a larger share of stocks into lower valuation bands, as measured by their price-to-earnings (PE) multiples, according to a Mint analysis of 3,756 BSE-listed companies based on ACE Equity data.
The share of stocks trading at a PE multiple above 40 fell from 36% in September 2024 to 26%, while the share in the 10-25 PE band rose from 18% to 26%. While lower PE multiples can signal attractive valuations, they can also point to weaker earnings growth.
News in numbers
1%: The increase in the minimum support price of wheat for the upcoming rabi marketing season. The highest increases were for safflower, at 10.3%, and rapeseed and mustard, at 6.7%.
103,000: Houses sold across nine major Indian cities in the July-September quarter, down 6% from a year earlier, according to PropEquity data.
16: Indian men who joined the boards of S&P 500 companies this year, according to ISS-Corporate and data provider Equilar. Only white men and women secured a higher number of board seats.
$6 trillion: Annual global revenue the artificial intelligence (AI) market will need to generate by 2031 to justify the capital being deployed to build AI infrastructure, according to Bain & Company.
₹645 crore: What ITC paid to raise its stake in Sproutlife Foods, which owns nutrition and healthy foods brand Yoga Bar, from 47.5% to 100%. ITC first invested in Sproutlife in May 2023.
State of manufacturing
The number of registered factories in operation in India increased 2.6% year-on-year in 2024-25, while employment in them rose 7.3% to 16.6 million, according to the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) 2024-25, released by the statistics ministry.
Tamil Nadu accounted for the largest share of manufacturing employment at 15%, followed by Maharashtra at 13.1%, Gujarat at 13%, Uttar Pradesh at 8.7% and Haryana at 6.4%. Gross value added (GVA) by factories increased 9.6%. Among the five states with the largest GVA, four saw their share of national factory GVA decline. Tamil Nadu was the exception: its share rose from 10.3% in 2023-24 to 10.9% in 2024-25.
Medals on board
India’s men’s and women’s chess teams finished among the medals at the recently concluded Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, but could not defend their titles. The men finished second and the women third, with Uzbekistan A winning the men’s competition and China the women’s.
India also won the title of best overall side and individual medals for six of its 10 players, including a gold for Savitha Shri. It was the sixth consecutive time that the Indian men finished in the Olympiad’s top 10, while the women extended their top-10 run to five editions.

As the Paramount-Warner Bros merger goes through, Bill Maher has a message for his new Skydance bosses.
On Friday’s episode of Real Time, the comedian pleaded with the Ellisons not to listen to their pal Trump’s criticism of him now that they own his show’s longtime home HBO.
“The merger went through. Paramount now owns Warner Discovery, which owns HBO, which owns my ass,” he said during his opening monologue. “Whoever owns me now, don’t believe what Trump is tweeting about me. Did you see what he said about me this weekend? He said my ratings are so low, ‘it’s just sad.'”
Maher continued, “You know what, Mr. President? Your insults don’t bother me. Make up whatever shit you want about me, just don’t mention I went to Cornell.”
Watch on Deadline
On Wednesday, a federal judge cleared the way for the $110 billion deal to close, approving the settlement between Paramount and a group of state AGs that filed an antitrust lawsuit to block the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition.
CEO David Ellison revealed on Friday that the combined company will now be known as Skydance, under which Paramount and Warner Bros. will supposedly remain individual entities.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

NEW DELHI: Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Saturday said that amid uncertainty, “now a standing condition” of the global economy, national security requires structural autonomy in strategic inputs, as strategic resource security sits at the centre of macroeconomic policy.Besides, she argued for private investment to lead the cycle, including in research and innovation and skilling to prepare people for a changing world of work, while asserting that global financial architecture should reflect where growth was coming from.“We need to keep building resilience as we go along; it’s not a one-time exercise. Watch: Luxury prison in Indonesia demolished after public outcry
A prison compound in Indonesia has been demolished after public outcry following the discovery of luxury apartments on its grounds.
Investigators reported finding luxury facilities in Cibinong Prison in Bogor, near Jakarta, allegedly used by favoured inmates during a surprise inspection on 23 September.
The units contained amenities including air conditioners, big-screen televisions, refrigerators, sofas and dining areas. Investigators also reported finding a gym, a golf simulator under construction and luxury vehicles in the complex.
Officials said the residences appeared to house inmates, although prison officials claim they were for staff.
The incident has drawn widespread public attention and renewed scrutiny of Indonesia's prisons, which have long faced allegations that wealthy or well-connected inmates can obtain preferential treatment through bribery.

This year, members of Seattle Mountain Rescue have been setting off into the wilds of the US Pacific Northwest wearing an unusual piece of kit.
They’ve been hiking into the wilderness with powered assistive devices attached to their hips and legs. Designed to increase lower-body strength when climbing or carrying heavy loads, these pieces of equipment are being tested to see if they can boost rescuers’ speed and endurance when it matters most—during searches for stranded people.
Devices like these are called human exoskeletons. They attach to parts of the body to create an external—or “exo”—mechanical structure. This powered frame enhances the wearer’s physical capabilities.
In physically demanding fields, workers are increasingly using these devices during strenuous tasks. IKEA has used SuitX exoskeletons for several years now. These assist warehouse workers with handling heavy materials. Ford, Boeing, and Mazda Toyota have also all adopted the tech on some of their assembly lines.
In Finland, a recent project called ExoPELA assessed whether exoskeletons could reduce muscle load and strain in rescue and firefighting work. It found noticeable benefits for users in certain real-world tasks.
And in early 2026, the Ukrainian military revealed its soldiers had been using Hypershell exoskeletons on the front lines to help with carrying artillery shells. According to test results, soldiers wearing the devices “become less fatigued, work faster, and maintain combat effectiveness for longer,” Colonel Vitalii Serdiuk told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper in March.
Multiple consumer and clinical devices, designed for everyday assistance, rehabilitation and exercise, are also now available. Some estimates have valued the total sector at around $500 million (£370 million) currently, and predict it could double or triple in size by the mid-2030s.
Exoskeleton technology has progressed significantly over the past decade. This has largely been thanks to robotic motors, sensors, and control systems becoming more affordable and accessible. However, the concept of augmenting human performance with exoskeleton-like devices dates back much earlier.

Injured Assefa narrowly misses world record in Berlin
- Published
An injured Tigst Assefa hobbled over the line at the Berlin Marathon on Sunday after looking set to smash the women's world record.
The Ethiopian still won with the third-fastest time in history in two hours 11 minutes four seconds.
But the 29-year-old, a silver medallist at the Paris Olympics two years ago, had been cruising to a new record before fading in the final stages.
Kenyan athlete Ruth Chepngetich's time of 2:09:56, set at the 2024 Chicago Marathon, remains the world record time, though that result is overshadowed by the three-year doping ban she received in 2025.
Assefa, the 2026 London Marathon winner, started rapidly and led the field by a minute at the 15km mark. She was ahead of the record pace at 35km and is a renowned fast finisher - but began to suffer clear discomfort and her pace slowed.
However she still broke the Berlin course record of 2:11:53 that she set in 2023 - which was also her previous personal best.
In addition, she improved on her time of 2:15:41 at the London Marathon earlier this year.
"We have to bow our heads to this performance. She was on a world record course for most of the race but then something happened to her tendon," said race director Mark Milde.
"To finish like this, I've never seen something like this. The pain is hard to imagine.
"With a heavy heart, we saw her set a course record, but it could have been a lot more."
The top five finishers were all from Ethiopia, with Bedatu Hirpa second and Dera Dida third.
Guye Adola - another Ethiopian - won the men's race with a time of 2:02:50.

Amazon has made a series of new public commitments to communities where it’s building data centers, including making an official announcement that it no longer uses nondisclosure agreements in its arrangements with county officials.
In a blog post published Friday, CEO Matt Garman detailed the steps the company says it’s already taking around data centers. In addition to stopping the use of NDAs, Garman says $1 billion will be invested over the next five years in communities that house the company’s data centers. The money will go toward free community college programs, workforce training, and energy efficiency upgrades for schools, homes, and community buildings.
In the post, Garman acknowledged how the fierce backlash against data centers across the country is hampering the AI buildout.
“Right now there are over 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the country,” he wrote. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to [the AI] race, and the consequences would last generations. As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”
Nondisclosure agreements have become a key point of contention amid the massive data center buildout. Typically, local officials who sign NDAs with data centers looking to develop projects in their area are unable to share information with the public, including the energy and water use of certain projects. Many NDAs bar officials from revealing even basic information—like the tech companies involved in building out the data center. In July, the New York Times reported on how secret agreements at all levels of government were crucial in building out plans for Hyperion, its massive data center in Louisiana.
There has been a rush of recent local legislation attempting to address the secretive paperwork. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, and Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer have all cracked down on data center NDAs in recent executive orders. Multiple states, including New York, New Jersey, Indiana, and Ohio, have considered recent legislation banning the practice.
At the federal level, a bipartisan group of lawmakers recently introduced the No Secrets for Data Centers Act in the House. Earlier this week, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD), one of the bill’s sponsors sent letters to Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle demanding information on their use of data center NDAs; Amazon told the Wall Street Journal that it was no longer using NDAs. (Google, Meta, and Oracle did not return the Journal’s request for comment.)
Amazon has been at the center of some high-profile controversies around NDAs. In Tucson, Arizona, Amazon was revealed last year to be the tenant of a controversial data center thanks to a public records request from a local outlet; an NDA had been in place barring county officials from sharing the identity of the end tenant. (Amazon has since exited that project.) In South Bend, Indiana, where the company has invested more than $13 billion into a massive data center campus, some elected officials have claimed that local government employees have been unable to answer questions about the project due to signing NDAs with the company.
Thanks to the opaque nature of data center financing and construction, end tenants like Amazon are often not the companies directly interfacing with government officials. As the Houston Chronicle reported last month, a top official in Wharton County, Texas, signed an NDA not with Amazon, but with contractor VisionFirst Advisors, which prevented him from sharing details about the Amazon project.
Amazon did not respond to WIRED’s queries about whether the promises around NDAs also extend to its contractors.
Much of the new blog from Garman is also dedicated to dispelling what he calls “misinformation and outright lies” around data centers and their water use, energy use, the use of diesel generators, and impacts on communities. “This build out is so important geopolitically that there are widespread reports of various countries intentionally seeding misinformation in the U.S. about data centers to trick us into slowing down,” he wrote.
As WIRED has reported, the idea that China is intentionally seeding widespread dissent and misinformation around data centers is a consistent message coming from the White House and tech leaders. Experts, however, say that this narrative is widely overblown, and that there is little evidence of Chinese misinformation driving the data center backlash.

This week, SpaceX celebrated the first orbital launch of its new Starship rocket. I’m not sure many people, at least those outside of SpaceX, expected it to take 14 flights of Starship before it technically reached low-Earth orbit, but Monday morning’s launch finally added that to SpaceX’s list of accomplishments with its new super-heavy rocket. Starship had gone 99 percent of the way to orbit before, only held back by safety concerns around the possibility of stranding the huge rocket in space.
What was most notable for SpaceX with this Starship flight was that it unlocked a massive growth potential for Starlink, with the first 26 of the network’s new-generation Starlink V3 satellites successfully deployed Monday.

Rocket Lab scores its biggest launch contract yet. Rocket Lab has signed what it calls its largest Electron launch service agreement to date, a 20-mission agreement with Synspective, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports. Synspective is a Japanese company with a growing fleet of radar Earth-imaging satellites. It is one of Rocket Lab’s most loyal customers, with the company’s light-class Electron rocket having launched 13 of Synspective’s StriX radar sats since 2020. The most recent Rocket Lab launch for Synspective occurred last Friday, September 25.
Dedicated launch … Rocket Lab’s Electron launch vehicle is sized for dedicated launches of payloads like Synspective’s StriX satellites. The latest agreement extends Synspective’s total bookings with Rocket Lab to 47 launches, including the 13 already flown. “Signing 20 launches in a single deal is a massive vote of confidence not just in Electron but in the launch cadence, mission reliability, and orbital precision that Rocket Lab consistently delivers,” Rocket Lab’s founder and CEO, Peter Beck, said in a statement.
Portuguese company acquires what’s left of Orbex. A Portuguese space technology business has snapped up the assets of Orbex, the Scottish rocket maker that collapsed earlier this year, the Scotsman reports. The buyer, Omnidea, plans to establish its UK operations at Orbex’s former manufacturing facility in Scotland, having agreed to a deal to acquire the assets and intellectual property (IP) of the defunct rocket developer. An initial team of ex-Orbex employees will join the business, with Omnidea planning to recruit further as the operation develops.
No Prime resurrection … Omnidea, once a partner of Orbex, says it plans to use its new Scotland base as a center for “structures development and fabrication” and as a “hub for flight and ground system electronics.” Omnidea is a supplier of propulsion, fluid control, avionics, and thermal management components in the European space industry, but the company is also exploring other markets. It looks like Orbex’s Prime rocket, which never ventured near a launch pad, is still dead.

Crew-13 launches toward ISS. A four-person crew rocketed into orbit Thursday from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, heading for a six-month expedition on the International Space Station, Ars reports. Riding a Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft, the four crew members departed from Space Launch Complex-40 at Cape Canaveral at 11:10 am EDT. Nine minutes later, they were in orbit to begin closing in on the space station for docking Thursday evening.
Some notes … This mission is nothing particularly new for SpaceX (it’s the company’s 21st human spaceflight launch). But it is noteworthy for a few reasons. The commander, Jessica Watkins, became the first Black woman to lead a mission into space. Her crewmate, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, went to space while he and his wife are expecting their third child later this year.
It’s rare, but astronauts have been off the planet for their child’s birth before. Most recently, NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, set to command the Artemis III mission next year, was flying aboard the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 2009 when his wife gave birth to their daughter in Houston. This launch was delayed several weeks to fix a leaky valve on Dragon’s propulsion system, work that involved cutting out the suspect valve and welding in a new one, an unusual but apparently successful repair method.
Canadian company pursues medium-lift rocket. More countries are becoming interested in developing their own access to space, including those that have historically paid US companies to launch their satellites. Canada is no different, and the Trump administration’s seeming obsession with lobbing threats and tariffs across the northern border has only crystallized Canadian interest in sovereign access to space.
This spring, the Canadian government announced the first awards to three companies—NordSpace, Reaction Dynamics, and Canada Rocket Company—to support work on rockets with “light lift” capability. Now, one of these rocket developers, Canada Rocket Company, says it is skipping over the small launch segment and going straight to a more ambitious medium-lift rocket, Ars reports.
R-2 V2? … Canada Rocket Company is following the lead of several US launch providers in going for a bigger rocket. “The advice we got from having spoken with about 150 engineers, from the director of Starship engineering all the way down to some entry-level folks, is that you’re not going to be able to de-risk a rocket development program by building a smaller rocket,” said Hugh Kolias, chief executive of the Canada Rocket Company, in an interview with Ars.
The company’s R-2 rocket somewhat resembles SpaceX’s Falcon 9 in renderings, with nine engines and landing legs that signal a future path toward reuse of the first stage. It could carry up to 12.5 metric tons to low-Earth orbit. If all goes well, Kolias said, the company could be ready to launch by 2032.
SpaceX rideshare launch deploys 130 payloads. An artificial intelligence prototype from Google, a methane-tracker, pharmaceutical manufacturing labs, and more hitched a ride onboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, on Thursday afternoon, Spaceflight Now reports. The rideshare mission, known as Transporter-18, carried 130 payloads into a polar Sun-synchronous orbit. It was SpaceX’s second launch of the day, following the successful flight of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission from Florida a few hours earlier.
Bread and butter … Much of the growing ecosystem of commercial satellite startups sees SpaceX’s rideshare launches as key enablers to their businesses, offering relatively inexpensive access to space on a predictable schedule. These kinds of launches, at least on Falcon 9, will likely go away in a couple of years as SpaceX transitions to the much larger Starship rocket. But for now, a bevy of satellite companies continue relying on Falcon 9 launches. The customers on Transporter-18 ranged from tech powerhouses like Google to scrappy startups like Starfish Space, alongside top remote sensing companies such as Planet Labs and ICEYE.
Starship reaches new heights in low-Earth orbit. SpaceX’s Starship rocket thundered into the sky over South Texas early Monday. It was the 14th test flight of the world’s most powerful launch vehicle. This time, however, the rocket’s massive upper stage squeezed out some extra oomph from its Raptor engines and accelerated to orbital velocity, Ars reports.
On all of Starship’s previous flights, SpaceX intentionally dialed back the full capability of the rocket to fly a suborbital trajectory, slow enough for Earth’s gravity to pull the vehicle back into the atmosphere before it could complete a full lap around the planet. After several successful suborbital flights in a row, SpaceX officials decided this launch should go all the way to low-Earth orbit. And it did.
Debuting Starlink V3 … What’s more, SpaceX packed 26 of the company’s newest generation of Starlink broadband satellites into the rocket’s cargo bay. One by one, the flat-packed satellites—too large to fit inside SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 rocket—were released from Starship’s payload deployer using a system of pulleys and cables to eject the satellites overboard like a Pez dispenser spits out candy. SpaceX cut a planned 10-hour test flight to three hours after one of the ship’s Raptor engines failed during ascent, but the vehicle was still able to make a pinpoint splashdown at one of its backup return sites north of Hawaii.
NASA will pay to human-rate ULA’s Vulcan rocket. NASA announced on Monday that it will exercise options to purchase two additional flights on Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft, as well as financially support the company in its efforts to return the crewed vehicle to flight and find a new rocket after the Atlas V vehicle retires, Ars reports. NASA is making the moves to preserve a path for its astronauts to low-Earth orbit as SpaceX nears retirement of its Falcon 9 rocket and Crew Dragon spacecraft. When that happens, Boeing’s troubled Starliner spacecraft will likely be the only commercial means of launching US crews to orbit.
A post-Atlas future … During a news conference on Monday, Dana Weigel, manager of NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, said the space agency would pay $359 million to Boeing to help the company complete a rebuild of the reaction control system thrusters that have overheated in flight. It would also certify United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket for human missions. NASA also said it would exercise options to order two additional crewed missions on Starliner, bringing its total spaceflights on the vehicle to six. Any future Starliner flights beyond that would require a new rocket, like ULA’s Vulcan, as the Atlas V rocket is no longer in production.
SpaceX completes three launches in 13 hours. SpaceX pulled off two Falcon 9 rocket launches and a Falcon Heavy mission in less than 13 hours Thursday, marking one of the busiest days ever for the company’s launch teams. The action began, as noted previously in the Rocket Report, with a Falcon 9 launch from Cape Canaveral, Florida, carrying the next four-person crew to the International Space Station. A few hours later, another Falcon 9 lifted off from California on a rideshare mission. The launch of SpaceX’s triple-body Falcon Heavy rocket with a classified National Reconnaissance Office payload from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, rounded out the triple-header Thursday night.
And four landings … This was the first time a Falcon Heavy rocket has launched a payload for the NRO, the US government’s spy satellite agency. Little is publicly known about the payload except that it launched into a highly inclined orbit, flying northeast from Florida’s Space Coast. To add an extra flourish to the launch triple-header, SpaceX returned both Falcon 9 boosters to their launch sites in Florida and California and landed both side boosters from Falcon Heavy back at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. That makes three launches and four landings (plus a Dragon docking at the ISS) in one day.
Blue Origin foresees growing launch cadence. As Blue Origin continues to recover from a New Glenn pad explosion in May, the company is seeking permission to significantly increase the vehicle’s launch rate, Space News reports. This is a big surprise, but a draft environmental assessment released this week puts some numbers to Blue Origin’s plans. The company is seeking permission from the FAA to increase the rate of New Glenn launches from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station’s Launch Complex 36 from 12 to 50 per year.
Reuse built in … The proposal would include 50 launches of the rocket and 50 landings of the rocket’s first stage on a drone ship in the Atlantic Ocean. It would also allow up to 100 static-fire tests, one for each stage of the rocket for each launch. The proposal also covers recovery of the rocket’s payload fairing, which Blue Origin has not attempted on any of the three launches of New Glenn to date.

Canada scores a dairy win on U.S. soil as farmers grumble about Trump's trade war
Both sides in trade dispute have been 'needless, pointless and childish,' says one retiree
On the most elite stage in the world of competitive dairy, a Canadian teenager and her "favourite cow" scored two major wins while on U.S. soil.
Never heard of competitive dairy? Let me assure you, it's a really big deal. One win — let alone two — at the World Dairy Expo in Madison, Wisc., can be life changing for farmers and their cows.
It can boost the value of an animal by tens of thousands of dollars. Future offspring can become more valuable too. And of course, there's an element of national pride, especially when Canada and the U.S. are locked in a trade war.
Alyson Doiron, a 16-year-old high school student from Cap-Sante, Que., glows as she poses for photos with her aforementioned favourite cow — Arolene Dempsey Ella, who goes by "Ella" for short, was the five-year-old cow awarded the top prize at the International Junior Holstein Show.
"She's an easy cow to work with. We love her so much," Doiron told CBC News.
Doiron cheered and cried as she was given the prestigious honour on Ella's behalf, at the Expo on Sunday. Even though this is a global gathering, the actual competitions are between animals from Canadian and American farms, due to health and safety regulations.
"This means a lot to me," she said with a nod to her home province. "It just proves that in Quebec, the [cow] show is really really strong," she said.
Sore point for some Americans
In the arena where the cows are judged, Canadian, American and Mexican flags hang in the rafters. It is a reminder, as constant as the smell of manure, that cross-border competition and co-operation are valued in this space.
"I think it's important for us to be here," said Brian Carscadden, the executive senior manager and part owner of Blondin Sires, a Quebec-based dairy company that has milk production and artificial insemination operations.
"If you think of the Westminster Dog Show, it's not unlike that. If you can win that, you've got a dog that's worth some money. It's the same here with your cow."
Carscadden and his team drove more than 1,500 kilometres from St. Placide to Madison, with 25 cows in trailers in tow. He says his business has not been affected by the trade war yet, and that it does not come up often in conversations at the Expo.
"There's jokes here and there," from his American friends, he said, along with "the odd snide remark … that makes things interesting."
"I always advise my Canadian colleagues that it's not our country, it's not our politics, don't talk about it."
Americans at the Expo are far more direct.
The trade war is a sore point for some, including voters who are connecting dots between U.S. President Donald Trump's broad economic agenda and increases in the cost of living.
"There is no lowering of grocery prices, no lowering of gas prices. I mean obviously it's all going higher and it makes me struggle," said Paula Lawver.
She's a single mom from a farming community in Indiana, and is at the Expo with a group of students from her son's high school. She describes herself as a conservative voter with conservative values, but does not consider herself a Republican.
She calls the dispute with Canada "nonsense," and says it will influence her vote in the midterm elections this November. Lawver says she will not support candidates in favour of tariffs and trade wars.
Seth Muck, a farmer from New York state, says he too may reconsider how he votes in the midterms.
He says in the past he's voted "hard, hard Republican, hard conservative." But after feeling the impact of Trump's global trade agenda, he's considering backing candidates with a "bit more moderate-type agenda."
Muck says his cash crops and farm inputs have been affected the most, noting that the price of fertilizer is double what he paid last year. Though he still holds out hope that economic conditions could improve.
"Perhaps it's going to take a bit … like ripping off a Band-Aid," he said.
Even among those willing to be more patient with Trump and his economic vision, CBC News did not find any Americans at this Expo supportive of the heated rhetoric that has upended the Canada-U.S. relationship.
"I think it's needless, pointless and childish. Both sides," said Gary Craugh, a retired farmer from Wisconsin.
Another retired farmer from Wisconsin, John Galgowski, says he's baffled by it all.
"I throw up my hands and go, 'Why are we doing this?'"
Galgowski does not support the Trump administration, and says the way the country has been run since Trump returned to office has only reaffirmed his position.
"It's just bad times," he said.
The way these voters described their experience is very different from how the Trump administration is framing the moment.

About 120 kilometres from the Expo, in Milwaukee, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer hosted a gathering of G20 trade ministers, where he unapologetically advocated for the "America first" trade agenda, arguing that the strategy is working.

Trump administration reverses stance on integration of people with disabilities
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
For nearly 50 years, the federal government has said people with disabilities should live, work and learn in the most integrated setting possible rather than be segregated in institutions like nursing homes.
The Trump administration just took its most concrete step yet to reverse that position.
Last week, a federal judge agreed to strip out mentions of "integration" from federal regulations tied to Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, a landmark civil rights law that prohibits disability discrimination. The judge did so after the Justice Department declined to defend its own rules in a lawsuit brought by several states challenging the legality of those rules.
Part of what is so striking about Texas v. Kennedy is that the federal government was originally the defendant in that lawsuit, brought by states fighting what's known as the integration mandate. Then, it switched sides and agreed with the states that the requirement should be undone.
Bruce Darling, president and CEO of the Center for Disability Rights, says when he heard about the ruling, it felt "like a knife in your chest. Because what we're hearing, what people are hearing, is that the federal government has made a determination that [disabled people] don't have a right to live in freedom, that they can be locked up against their will."
The court's decision removes regulations from Section 504 that explicitly required federally funded programs to provide services in the "most integrated setting."
"That lack of clarity will impact people's rights. It will likely impact what states do and how they behave," says Jennifer Mathis, a disability rights lawyer who helps lead the Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law.
Mathis says it's important to note that the court's decision did not undo integration protections tied to the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) or those established by decades of case law, including the landmark Supreme Court decision known as Olmstead.
"My concern is that right now, where we're at is disabled people have a right to integration on paper. It is in the law, but whether it gets practically enforced is a serious question," Darling says. His organization is putting its energy behind a proposed law that would cement protections around integration, while others are working with states to strengthen their disability laws.
The Justice Department did not respond to multiple requests from NPR asking why it is changing course after decades of legal and bipartisan support for community-based services.
After 50 years, the government changes its position
In 1973, Congress passed the first civil rights law for people with disabilities: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. But it took advocates years of fighting — until 1977 — to get actual regulations that would make that law enforceable.
The Department of Health and Human Services, under President Joe Biden, updated the regulations in 2024 so it would be clearer to states what they had to do to uphold the law. "They thought it was important to do that so those rights would be as clear as possible," Mathis says.
In recent months, the federal government, under President Donald Trump, began to publicly change its position: First, in June, the Justice Department issued an opinion saying it no longer interpreted disability law to "require states to treat mentally disabled patients in the most integrated setting appropriate to their needs." The memo even noted its position is "out of step with the common understanding" of the Olmstead decision.
Then in July, the Justice Department announced it would stop relying on its own longstanding guidance explaining how it enforces the integration mandate.
These actions led up to the federal government switching sides in Texas v. Kennedy. Finally, last week, a federal judge agreed to throw out the integration mandate rules under Section 504, including language that was first introduced nearly 50 years ago.
Mathis says this kind of about-face is highly unusual. "It is pretty significant and pretty unprecedented to see the federal government asking a court to vacate its own rules."
That could leave more of the work of defining and enforcing the right to community living to people with disabilities, private litigators, advocacy organizations and the courts.
All this, says Mathis, comes at a time when states are already under immense pressure from the federal government to cut Medicaid spending, which pays for disabled people to get many of the services they need. "States are looking for things to cut," she says. Mathis worries that because the government has changed its stance on integration, states would be freer to cut spending on programs for community-based living.
How enforcement is already changing
One of the clearest examples of the effects of the federal government's changing position involves children with complex medical needs in Florida.
Back in 2013, the Justice Department sued the state of Florida, arguing that it failed to provide adequate services to children who needed in-home care. As a result, some of their families were forced to put their children in nursing facilities. Other children were at risk of the same.
The federal government won its case in 2023, and the state of Florida was required to provide these families the services they needed to keep their children at home. But in August, the government told the federal court to throw out its victory and allow Florida to have the case heard again in district court, citing the Justice Department's new opinion on the issue.
Mathis calls the reversal shocking. "To do that in a case that involves ripping children away from families, taking them out of the homes where they have families that want to take care of them, and to force those children to grow up in an institution, really is just unthinkable to me and is incredibly heartless."
The Florida case suggests that coming battles for community integration may increasingly play out not through federal enforcement, but case by case, in the courts.
What disability advocates are doing now
The disability rights community is rallying around a number of actions to try to combat the federal government's latest actions.
"There's nothing that is more cherished and hard-won than the right to live, work and participate and be included in your community," says Alison Barkoff, who worked on disability rights enforcement during the Obama administration and is now a health law and policy professor at George Washington University. She says the disability community is hard at work trying to protect those rights.
Thanks to recent advocacy efforts, Barkoff says some members of Congress have reaffirmed their commitment to the rights of people with disabilities to get services they need in their community. Just this week, a group of bipartisan lawmakers introduced a resolution asserting the federal government's longstanding interpretation of Olmstead. In July, 100 members of Congress signed a letter asking the Justice Department to rescind its June opinion.
There is also movement at the state level: Delaware already passed a law incorporating the regulations in Section 504 that were stripped from federal law. Barkoff says other states are moving in a similar direction: "I've probably gotten calls in the last week from at least a dozen state leaders across the country about how to codify the integration mandate … in state law. I see a lot of momentum," she says.
Bruce Darling of the Center for Disability Rights helped draft the Latonya Reeves Freedom Act, a bipartisan bill that would codify integration for disabled people into federal law. He says his organization has been working to convince lawmakers to sign onto it.
Although the bill has some bipartisan support, it has failed in the past and would have a difficult road ahead, facing an executive branch now challenging integration. But Darling says he's hopeful that members of Congress are now more aware of the challenges facing his community.
"I think that the issue has really come to a head now and folks can see that Olmstead is seriously at risk, that we need to do something," says Darling. "I don't know, I'm optimistic."

Quick Answer
Turn rough screen recordings into polished demos with tools that auto-zoom on clicks, follow and smooth the cursor, add clean framing, and highlight key actions. Options include Screen Studio, FocuSee, Screen Awesome, and ScreenCursor.
When you record a two-minute walkthrough of your app, for instance, a setting buried five menus deep, or a spreadsheet trick you are proud of, there is something that can leave you frustrated. You press play, and the cursor is dancing all around without highlighting what you actually wanted to show. Either the text is too small to read on a phone or the whole thing looks like security-camera footage of your desktop. The old-school way is to use a video editor, add zooms by hand, pan the camera to follow your cursor, and nudge keyframes for an hour. Thankfully, there is a newer batch of screen recorders that automatically do that part for you.
In this guide, we have covered four of them. They not only differ in price, platform, and functionality, but each one also has one detail that surprised me.
|  | Screen Studio | FocuSee | Screen Awesome | ScreenCursor | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Works on | Mac only | Windows and Mac | Chrome (also Edge, Brave and similar) | Chrome (Mac, Windows, Linux) | 
| Price | $9/mo billed yearly, or $29/mo | Free trial, paid plans | Free | $49 one-time (early pricing) | 
| Best for | Maximum polish on a Mac | All-in-one AI extras | Privacy and zero cost | Pay-once simplicity | 
Table of Contents
Why do raw screen recordings look so rough?
When you use any standard screen recorder, like the one built into your OS, it captures pixels and nothing else. It has no idea what mattered. It doesn’t know if you clicked a tiny button that you want the viewers to look at. The result? You get a full-screen recording of everything, including your cursor wandering here and there. Viewers watch these videos on laptops and phones, and since the important part is not zoomed in or clearly shown, they will miss it. A better screen recording would be one where:
- Zoom is on the action so people can actually read what you click.
- A camera that follows your cursor instead of leaving viewers guessing.
- A cursor that glides rather than jitters.
- A clean frame, such as a gradient background and rounded corners.
With all of the above, your screen recording not only looks professional but also provides clear instructions for viewers.
Screen recorders with auto cursor follow and zoom
Here are some of the best screen recorders that you can use for automatic cursor follow and zoom.
Screen Studio: The one the others get compared to
If you are on Mac, then Screen Studio is one of the best options for screen recording with automatic cursor follow and zoom. When you’re recording using Screen Studio, it looks at what you did, like where you clicked, and zooms in on the moments that matter. Every zoom is balanced and animated automatically; you don’t have to worry about handling them. The best part is that you can choose between two styles: Classic zoom is the one you usually see in polished product videos. Then there is Loupe zoom, which is a magnifier-style alternative. If you want to zoom somewhere the app did not automatically add one, you can drop it onto the timeline and point it where you like. Notably, the cursor gets the same treatment. Shaky movement is smoothed out into a steady glide, and clicks get a soft ripple. Fast movements pick up motion blur so they look filmed rather than captured. You also have the option to change the cursor’s size and style later. Some of the notable features of Screen Studio are:
- Edit by transcript: Delete a sentence from the transcript, and it disappears from the video. Filler words and long pauses can be cleared in one pass.
- One recording, many shapes: Record once, then switch the aspect ratio between wide (16:9), square (1:1), and vertical (9:16). Zooms can be re-aimed, layouts rearranged, and captions moved to stay readable. You can also choose the “Reel mode” that shows where Instagram’s or TikTok’s interface would cover your video, so you’re in the grey area where your inputs get hidden.
- Hide the private stuff: If the recording shows an API key or email address, you can mask it after the recording is complete, and the mask blends into the interface around it.
- iPhone and iPad framing: Plug your iPhone or iPad into a USB cable, pick the device, and record. Screen Studio wraps the footage in a matching device frame.
FocuSee: The Windows-friendly all-rounder
FocuSee comes from the house of iMobie and is a screen recording tool that works on both Windows and Mac. This already makes it the practical choice for many people working on either OS. FocuSee’s auto zoom follows your clicks and even your typing. This tool adds a spotlight to highlight areas worth noticing, making it much easier for anyone following your instructions. You can also choose a “3D Motion” mode that adds tilt and perspective that follows your cursor, for a more cinematic look. The cursor can fade out when you are not actively using it or don’t need it and reappears when you do. Similar to other screen recording tools, you can swap the cursor style and click animations. There are a bunch of features that deserve to be highlighted.
- A built-in teleprompter: You can show your script on screen while recording with the option to adjust the font size, speed, and position. If you tend to forget the script midway, this alone might sell you.
- An annotation suite: You can add text, shapes, arrows, callouts, spotlights, and blur effects. Moreover, you can stack several layers to walk viewers through a tricky step, or blur out something sensitive.
- An AI avatar: This one is for those who are camera-shy or do not want their face in the video. FocuSee can create a digital presenter, or in simple words, an AI avatar. It is a niche feature, but a handy one for company tutorials.
- Smart cleanup: You can remove filler words and silence with just one click, and also enhance voice and reduce noise with just a button.
- Background fixes for your webcam: It can blur or replace a messy room behind you after recording without needing a green screen.
- Add Subtitles: FocuSee supports speech recognition in over 50 languages, with accuracy above 98%. You can add your own subtitles and make it easier for the follower to go through the steps.
Screen Awesome: Free, and it can’t upload your recordings
Screen Awesome is a different kind of tool. It’s actually a free Chrome extension built by a developer named Nitinbhai Viras. On one hand, most apps say “we respect your privacy” and simply ask you to take their word; Screen Awesome does things a bit differently. Screen Awesome points you at Chrome’s own permission screen and requests no access to any website. It is not allowed to contact any server. That means it cannot upload your recordings, even if it wanted to. The best part is that you can verify this yourself in about 30 seconds. Head over to chrome://extensions, find Screen Awesome, click Details, and look at the Site access line. According to the developer, it reads none. On the extension’s settings page, there is a button that jumps you straight there. On top of this security, you get this tool for absolutely free. Here are some features that set Screen Awesome apart:
- Auto-zoom to clicks: While recording a browser tab, Screen Awesome notes where you click. A virtual camera follows each click and pans between them. You have the option to preview it, turn it off, or export the file. This works for tab recording.
- Serious annotation tools: Arrows, pen, highlighter, shapes, text, speech bubbles, step counters, emoji stamps, and a blur that destroys the pixels rather than just smudging them. You can edit all of these marks.
- Product-shot framing: You can place a recording on a backdrop with rounded corners, a soft shadow, and an optional browser window around it, and also change its aspect ratio to 16:9, etc.
- Formats: You can export your recording in MP4, WebM, or an animated GIF.
- Webcam and voice: Screen Awesome lets you mix in your microphone and the tab’s audio, and even add a movable webcam bubble while recording if you want to show your face.
ScreenCursor: Pay once, and record in Chrome
ScreenCursor is another screen recording tool that works as a Chrome extension. However, its approach is the opposite of Screen Awesome’s. Notably, it does one thing and tries to do it well, which is turning clicks into camera moves with as little fuss as possible. When you hit the record button, ScreenCursor waits three seconds before it starts. That gap is deliberate, and it exists because Chrome shows its own “sharing your screen” bar while recording, and unfortunately it cannot be switched off. With this delay, you get the time to collapse the bar before the screen recording starts. Every click, drag, and keystroke gets zoomed in. Each zoom happens a beat before the action; this way, viewers are already looking at the right spot, then the camera holds steady and follows your cursor. ScreenCursor gives you the option to manually retime a zoom, push its depth in or out, switch the motion between snappy and gentle, or delete the zoom you don’t want. Here are some of the highlights of ScreenCursor:
- Zoom focus point: Right-click any zoom, drag a box over the part you want people to see, and the zoom shows exactly that. You can use this on recordings of desktop apps, since ScreenCursor can record your whole screen.
- Customization: You also get wallpapers, gradients, or use your own image as a backdrop. There is a browser frame that carries the real page title. Editing is also possible, as you can split the clip, delete boring stretches, and speed up slow ones.
- Price and limits: It costs $49 once, which is labeled “early pricing,” with $79 shown as the regular price. After one-time payment, you will continue to receive updates and can work on up to three of your own computers.

Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave lands on TIME100 Next list
- Published
Shoko Kawata, Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave, has been named one of the 100 most influential rising stars by TIME Magazine.
The recognition comes weeks after the 36-year-old gave birth to her first child on 15 September.
Earlier this year, Kawata, who is mayor of Yawata City in Kyoto prefecture, was plunged into a national debate about whether elected officials should take time off for childbirth.
Her decision to take maternity leave drew a mix of support and backlash across Japan, a country that is struggling to lift birth rates.
Some on social media said having a baby is tough and Kawata is doing her best. Japanese society has failed to design systems with pregnancy in mind, one claimed. Another said Kawata is setting a wonderful example by putting her family first and making it easier for other women to enter politics.
But critics argued that stepping away from public duties is "irresponsible", and that if Kawata wanted to get pregnant "she should have done so before taking office". One said top officials wanting to take extended leave "should resign".
Others insisted salaries should be cut during maternity leave.
In a sit-down interview with the BBC before giving birth, Kawata brushed off the criticisms, proudly declaring she enjoys her job and believes now is the time for her to have a child and start a family.
"If we were to criticise politicians taking maternity leave, it means we are effectively excluding all women in their 20s through 40s - women who are capable of becoming pregnant - from public office," she said.
While Japan provides maternity leave for city workers, there is currently no legal framework for local elected officials. So Kawata worked with her office to create a plan. She transferred her authority to her deputy mayor Shigeto Nose for 16 weeks, while working remotely when she could.
On 15 September, Mayor Kawata announced she gave birth to a baby girl. She posted a photo on X, external, thanking those who had supported her, and doubled down on her goal to advocate for social issues nationwide.
"As I face the countless challenges that lie ahead and learn what it truly means to be a parent, I want to reflect those experiences in real time into the policies I pursue," she wrote.
"I want to confront the many challenges facing parents and children today from that same perspective, as someone living through them myself, and think about how we can find a way forward together."

Fact Check
While it is unclear that whether the police are claiming that the entire video of the event is AI-generated, or the portion where the cops are seen watching and recording the performance, Alt News found that one of the dancers present in the viral clip posted several videos of the event on her Instagram page, @queen__juhi_002__.

These videos all show police personnel in the vicinity of the dancers, watching the performance and some filming it. However, at the time of writing this article, her Instagram page was taken down. Below is a screen recording of a video posted by the dancer herself, where the performers are seen wearing the same attire as in the video posted by Rai.
A closer look shows that police personnel are visible on the stage as well below the stage. Below are the highlighted portions of the phone recordings that clearly show the dancers. One of the keyframes also shows an audience member on a video call.
The setting and backdrop of the videos posted by the dancer and the one posted by Rai also match. Below are two screenshots comparing a keyframe from the video posted by Rai and keyframes posted by the dancer.
A video posted by another Instagram user, @aman_bhu_2427, showed a different angle of the same dancers in the same performance. We found another video on Facebook where the structure of the stage can be clearly seen and a red temple can be seen behind it.
To sum up, the above videos posted by the dancers themselves and the attendees prove three things:
- The incident did take place during the Baba Lat Bhairav baarat procession. Several social media users posted videos of the same programme captured from different angles.
- The uniformed police personnel were standing on the stage as well as below the stage watching the dancers as the performance went on.

Thus, the Kashi DCP’s claim that the video is AI-generated does not hold up.

For years, Snopes has covered strange and unique stories about popular cultural figures. John Wayne, the famed actor who appeared in more than 100 movies from Hollywood's silent film era to Westerns and war movies, has been a frequent subject of rumors that focused less on his work on the big screen and more on his words and actions as a public figure — including his endorsement of white supremacy in a 1971 interview.
That's not to say every rumor that's circulated about Wayne is true. Below is a complete collection of our fact checks about Wayne.
